One of the most complex and most detailed 4X games of all time.
A true successor to Master of Orion
..................
With the exception of a few flaws like :
1) Lack of espionage
2) Simple pop-up for invasions without much fancy graphics
3) Some mild stuttering and a few minor bugs
...................
The rest of the game is as swell as it can get:
1) Superb tech tree (detailed and streamlined from GCII + unique techs for all races)
2) Wonderful grid placement for improvements
3) Galaxy wide resources + planetary resources
4) Improved tactics for battles over GCII
5) Beautiful cinematics
6) INSANE map sizes (though seriously a game may take a year to conclude at max size)
7) Impressive customization of spaceships + new carrier types
8) Improved AI + Diplomacy options
9) Transformation of "galactic wonders" into "buildings needing resources" (much better in my opinion, since buildings won't be "snatched" by enemies)
10) Hex tile system is an improvement over square ones
11) Ideologies as new addition
12) Insane number of building types thanks to each civ having their own unique buildings
13) 100+ opponents - that's CRAZY
14) Dedicated company which does its best to improve it with patches etc. Stardock doesn't fail.
15) Extremely customizable custom civs
16) New galaxy "terrain"
17) LOTS AND LOTS of random events + alignment events (I rarely see pics being reused!)
18) Quite stable (on an i5-3570K, 8GB, 1TB WD Black, R9 270X = no crashes so far in 10+ hours of play so far at Excessive map size + 8 major civs + 150-200 turns into the game)
19) Very atmospheric thanks to all the cinematics + events + survey events + beautiful diplo screens
20) Promises from company for future additions and features
21) 95% of its features are an improvement from Galciv 2: TA. 5% being lack of espionage and lack of graphics for invasions.
......................
Overall, I recommend this.
FINAL VERDICT:
90/100
(Would have given 4 more points if espionage + invasion graphics are added in)

I shouldn't have finished this game because I hated it. My brother who I co-oped the whole thing with hated it as well. We were actually sort of excited to play it too after working through the entirety of The Clone Wars show in November/December. I didn't think Lego games had changed too much over the years, but this game changed my stance on that. There were just so many awkward moments of level design that left my brother and me bewildered as to what the devs actually wanted us to do to progress forward. They also did this half♥♥♥♥♥RTS level experiment that is simultaneously dumbed down for the age-group of the target demographic and bit too complicated and irritating for that same age group. As an adult it's hard not to wonder what the hell they were thinking when they put those levels together. They also decided to dump them all into one of the level arcs too, leading to some bizarre pacing where we were stuck playing a bunch of them back to back (boy were tempted to co-op the delete button there). The game makes almost no effort to make good use of the source material- they skipped over a lot of episodes that had good potential and opted for some of the weakest ones. I do recommend checking out the show on Netflix though. It is the proper 2:35 presentation and has a lot of story arcs that are the some of the best Star Wars stories out there.
Verdict: Hard pass.

I can not currently recommend this game for the full $50 price. Maybe later when the price drops or some patches come out to fix some things.
There is just some real irritating flaws in the game that when combined with the other problems drop the game down the the blah level. Most could be fixed easily. Two and five probably will never change which is what will keep this game not much above the blah level.
1. Capitals on a planet, The AI places them at random wherever it wants. Considering capitals give bonuses to surrounding buildings it makes a big difference on where it was placed. It seems to me that if I find an unsettled planet I should be able to choose the location of the capital. So because the AI chose a dumb spot for a capital you lose those bonuses because they go to waste. The best example would be if hexes were about the size of Australia and you were to colonize a planet with land masses like Earth, why would you place your capital in Australia and forfeit all bonuses?
2. No retreat option for combat. Similar games (Master of Orion and Endless Space) at least gave you the option to retreat during combat, meaning you could take some damage and/or losses but at least have a chance to run away. So later in game if the enemy is bigger and faster then you do not stand a chance of getting away. At that point you might as well concede the game. Simply because a fleet can attack as many times as it has movement points.
3. You can draw production in a shipyard from multiple planets over long distances to build colony ships, but somehow people just can not make that same trip. Yet these same people are going to climb into that ship you just built and travel ten times that same distance. So now you have to waste multiple turns just putting people into your colony ship.
4. Technology specialization. What was the point in this feature? The specialization technologies can traded and you can find the specialized in anomalies. Which if you receive a tech you have no made a choice, you lose that choice. So if you wanted to specialize in a certain bonus, but a friendly AI gives you a different specialization tech, then maybe next game, unless you get lucky and find another AI to trade for it. The fact that you lose your choice of specialization is extremely lame. Never mind how it can get exploited in multiplayer.
5. Battles are either "quick result" or "watch battle" meaning you have zero control on that battle. All of the battle tactics are based on what job tags you gave the ships in your fleet. Which means no singling out a target to kill first. The battles for the most part are not worth watching anyways because either option is going to give you the same outcome.
6. Construction ships and using the station option to call for one. Someone had a great idea to be able to have a space station go "Hey I need a construction drone to build another module" and you click that button. Then a construction drone will be built and sent to that station. Sounds cool right? Real cool up to the point that this feature will clear any orders an existing drone currently has. So if you manually sent a drone to build a new station, it wont reach it. So that means you have to wait to use this feature until your manual drone is done. This feature will clear orders a drone already has, but will not clear guard or sentry, so makign them in advance and planning on using this feature does not work.
7. Excess research and production is lost. When the game calculates the end of a turn if it finishes building or researching something any points over that mark are NOT carried to the next project, the points are just gone. This just seems to make the game drag on and it also makes specialized manufacturing planets nearly pointless because so much can go to waste.
8. Ship designer spamming designs. Whenever you get new technologies the ship designer will spit out new ships designs, which later in the game leads to having way too many designs to sort through. Stardock solved this in previous versions and other games by adding a feature able to turn off the auto-designer. Considering that feature exists in multiple other Stardock games the feature should exist here.
9. Cultural expansion is ridiculous. It expands faster than you can explore early on. If you never explored it then how is your culture affecting it? About equal to the Roman Empire holding cultural sway over North America before they even knew it existed. The only way to catch up later is you disposable scouts with stacks of engines, lifesupport, and scanners which is about mid game. Since I have only played insane maps, then smaller maps probably run a higher chance of culture flipping.
10. Rush production is really flawed. If you rush a production in queue then no other production points are gained from that planet or shipyard for that turn. On top of that rushing production is a set amount, even if you have the production item almost complete.
11. The pirates are pointless. Four hundred turns in on a insane map size and I am discovering the same low tech pirates that were encounted in the first dozen turns. This makes them nothing but a nuisance, one that apparently the AI ignores. Not even sure if they attack the AI or not because the pirates will not attack anything stronger than them. So basically then end up as nothing but clutter to make your end turn processing longer.
These are the just the basic things I can think of that should have been ironed out during the beta.
Now for the technical aspects.
1. The sound for cut scene movies. Apparently someone forgot to include cut scene movie volume with the sound options in the game. So it just comes out as a bunch of mumbling.
2. End of turn processing on large map. This is really what kills the gaming mood. I made it up to around 400 turns on an insane map before it was just too ridiculous to play. The time to process became about 2-3 minutes a turn, which really sucks if the only thing you do on your turn is spend a few seconds to click next turn.
The other issue is every time the end turn process it kicks in all the fans in my computer into overdrive just to keep up with the processing. Meanwhile you can not touch much with getting the "not responding error" from Windows. Which by the way if you are seeing that blue circle between turns, it aint a Stardock logo thing, that is Windows saying "hey this program aint responding." Which leads me to wonder if running the game is really good for the computer.
3. Ship designer, great feature (seriously.) One tip though, you might want to save your game before using it. Otherwise you could be sent back to your last autosave it decides to crash.
4.  I received the achievement for the completing the first part of the campaign game simply by clicking to start it. Sounds petty and nitpicking, but think about it for a moment. That is really sloppy coding and testing. Where else in making the game were they sloppy? I think the first patch today fixed this along with a dozen other achievements, which basically proved my point.
5. After about 200 turns the text on the UI starts disappearing. Which is really annoying with diplomacy options.
I was one of those customers burned years ago by Stardock with Elemental: War of Magic. This release reeks of the same issues. The whole "release it and patch it later" attitude. About the same effect as buying an early access game when they are on the .8x builds.
So in short, if you are on the fence on buying this, let me knock you off it. Wait and watch, in the mean time take a browse through the forums. Sure in six months of patch it might be a decent game, but news flash I doubt it will still be $50 price tag on it.
If you are mainly thinking about the game mainly because of the ship editor then do yourself a favor and go find a free 3d animation program like Blender and learn something in the process.

Great game, a little hard to get into during the beta stages. After a few updates I could start to see this was going to be a very good 4X game. As GalCiv II being one of my favorite games, I can say without a doubt, this is a worthy successor to the previous game.
Now this game does have some flaws, some black screening can occur (after a short little bit the game does come back.) that can be a little annoying, and the AI can be very not smart at times. Such as electing the most war mongering race to lead the United Planets. Also having no espionage is disappointing. The diplomacy is not very in depth, the same with Galciv II, not including many components. One thing that really pisses me off though is- Why do the other races automatically hate you if you have a different ideology! I guess I could see if a Benevolent race hates a Malevolent race but why do Pragmatic races hate Benevolent/Malevolent races, there supposed to be neutral right?
Most of those things are minor, not affecting the game too much (except for the damn ideology's) in any way, and most of the good features triumph over the bad ones.
Ship customization, is the best of any game I have ever played. They nailed it, 10/10. Vastly improving from GalCiv II and overshadowing any other 4x games that have ship customization. One thing that has always bugged me is if in a space 4x game, doesn't have customizable ships, games like Endless Space are very very simple in the ways of customization, only having a few presets on ships and only able to add or remove components of the ship (still a great game). Back to GalCiv III, another thing the game is good at is, Race Making. It's great, you can make lore about your race, your leader. You're even able to import pictures for your race, making you able to make anything you want. Ship combat is fine, nothing too special, but nothing to get angry about.
TL;DR- Good game all in all, some issues that could be worked out, but solid game overall.

Part of the fun for me was finding the optimal setup between traps. However in Unchained you barely have time to search the map, before the game auto starts. You can't pause either. - Forced autostart before game starts (no time to strategize).
- No pause botton.
- No retry botton (you have to exit application and relaunch, ROFL).
- No headshot mechanic (meaning all you do now is hold down mouse1).
- No sprint on shift
- Small resolution launcher window
- Maps too complex (too many orc paths)
Likes:
- New heroes
- New skills
- New gamemode
- New mobs
It feels like most of my dislikes could be fixed rather easily, but i'm not holding my breath.

I hope you have a GTX 980 and an i7-4770k, otherwise - you aren't enjoying this game on ultra graphics.
But, if you're willing to turn the graphics down a tad. The Witcher 2 improves upon the original in almost every conceivable way. Immensely better graphics, way better combat system, way friendlier user interface both for mouse/keyboard and controller, better animations, and a more engaging story. As old as it is, the game still looks extremely impressive. There are a great deal of natural landscapes and vista scenes that just make for great eye candy, for example. The castle siege at the beginning is quite a sight, too.
Unfortunately, like the first game, that beauty is somewhat skin deep. Just like so many areas in The Witcher were cordoned off with invisible walls and fences or unopenable doors, so too are areas in the sequel. The game makes a point of showing you that you can use your medallion to find alchemy/other ingredients, but the perceived ability to run around the map and find things fades pretty quickly when you realize all of the lootable objects are blatantly obvious and  never in the middle of nowhere. As much as I'd like to call it open world, it isnt, not any more than the first game.
Most important of all the improvements in Witcher 2 is the combat system. Good lord, the combat system is so, so much better than the original unengaging, frustrating, and primitive click-timing based system that so many games like Tera and Neverwinter capitalized on. It's an MMO game style and it has no place in a single player game, so thankfully it was changed. W2 combat plays much more like an action RPG where left and right click or the equivalent gamepad controls determine strong or regular attacks. The timing of your button presses still affects your combos and the animations, and you still get the combo bonuses from the first game but they are a little less goals this time around, and more like rewards.
I do have negative things to say. People worship this game and Witcher 1, this game especially, for being so much different. Having played it now, I can conclusively say they are wrong. The game does have DLC. It does have QTE's - extremely stupid ones for that matter. It has plenty of cutscenes, a bad save system that scares you in to manually saving whenever possible, and it does one of those awesome things like God of War 2 and 3 both did where you start out   - in the tutorial - having skills, then dumps you with a crappy Geralt who has to relearn everything he learned in the first game, as if the first time he lost his memory wasn't enough. They don't even try to cover it up with a story excuse. How about just being super powerful for a moment, then facing equal or tougher enemies immediately once all game mechanics are introduced? Nah? Also, you have to meditate to use potions, and the entire quick menu section is conviluted, but at least you don't need a campfire this time around.
Overall though, Witcher 2 is a very good RPG - beautiful, fun combat, entertaining story (That  bears a lot of similarity to Game of Thrones at times. Kingslayer, Vallettes always pay their debts, king with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ children blah blah, etc.)  Definitely buy this game if you liked the first one or were interested. It's worth the price it's at.

Take my recommendation this way: if you like good stories, this game is for you. But if you appreciate good game mechanics, you're in for a disappointment. As we all know, games are meant to be played. And playing should be fun, right? For me. this wasn't the case with Witcher 2.
Here are some huge issues with the gameplay:
1. Controls and menus are crap. Movement feels weird and you can't step down or run over obstacle that's higher than 30 cm. Paths are your friends.
Also simple things like changing spells/items is tedious as hell. For example, here's how you change spells when playing with gamepad:
1. Hold LT.
2. Tap stick once to left.
3. Tap up or down repeatedly until you find the correct spell.
4. Tap A to select the spell.
So fluent! Some improvement over how the weapon wheel works in other games where you hold one button, point stick to the general direction of the desired weapon and release button. You could use the next spell button, but in that case you have to run through all the five spells if you accidentaly scroll over the spell you were looking for since there's no previous spell command.
Oh, and you better learn those spell names fast since there's no tooltips in the weapon wheel where you could check what the spell actually does. Scrolling through multiple menus are required for this simple task.
3. Inability to drink potions during fights. Didn't you know that after that long cutscene, you'd end up in a tough fight? Too bad, enjoy dying many many times before you decide to load up previous save, hurry through the dialogue so you don't waste your potion effects during cutscenes (yea, time runs normally during cutscenes) and try again.
4. Crafting system is pointless. You'll collect hundreds of items, yet they're used for nothing. During the entire game, I crafted maybe 5 pieces of usable armor, four of them during the last 1-2 hours of the game.
Maybe I'll add more later if I can edit this review...

Geralt of Rivia is back, and in a improved way. The Witcher 2 follows the mature themes that were established in the first Witcher but with several improvements that enhances the experience for the player.
The gameplay has changed significantly since the first one. Rather than the "Pick your swordstyle and click" style, we have the typical hack n' slash combat. While satisfying at first, it leaves out any real combo system that can make the combat more meaningful. The biggest problem with combat was how enemies can simply repel your attacks with a shield which leaves Geralt stunned for a whole second, making him vulnerable to attacks. I found this system extremely frustrating especially in boss battles.
The RPG elements themselves are a bit tweaked from the first one. The Witcher 2 has simplified the character building process, and while it's not bad per se, I had hoped for something a bit more complex. Some skills will be chosen almost always over others simply because of their huge advantage. The potion making remains the same from the first game, which is great since it already was a very well made system. I did, however, have a problem with the inventory system. Rather than improving on the first Witcher's inventory system (which wasn't half bad), they instead dumbed it down. The player is no longer able to pick up an item of their choosing from a chest. Instead, just clicking on a chest will automatically move all items to your character, an annoying feature when you're just after the gold and not the 99th piece of cloth.
Graphically, the game is beautiful. It is arguably one of the best looking RPG's even by today's standards. Everything from the looks of the characters to the detailed world, Witcher 2 is nothing short of eye candy. With better graphics comes higher hardware requirements, so be ready to run this on a beefy computer to truly experience the Witcher 2 in its full glory.
Along the gorgeous graphics comes a fantastic soundtrack that captures the life of the residents in the Witcher world. The music managed to add atmosphere in the game and relay a sense of danger when approaching enemies. Just be ready to hear the combat music a few times, you will die... a lot.
The environment and story is what really makes the game tick. While not necessarily being an oscar winning story, it does provide an entertaining and mature theme, and there are times where you will have to make choices... very tough choices. The reason for this is that there are no true good or bad choices. Everything is in the grey, and you must weigh the different choices against each other. This provides the game with excellent replayability since choices will heavily affect each playthrough. My only complaint here is that the game is roughly 20 hours or so shorter than the first Witcher. But then again, this game does have higher replay value than the first one. In fact, depending on what you do in the game, you may experience a completely different playthrough than your friends. Still, 40 hours of gameplay for just one playthrough is not bad at all. Remember also that you can import your save from Witcher 1 into Witcher 2. Characters that you befriended in the first game will send you letters, give you free items, and so on.
Overall, while the Witcher 2 isn't the perfect game, it still is one of the better RPG's out there. It provides a mature story with choices, excellent characters, and amazing environments with graphics that complement them. Whether you played the first one or not, I believe every RPG fan should play the Witcher 2.

If you liked (or think you would like) games like Journey, or if you love underwater environments in games & can't fill your cravings with only the likes of Subnautica, buy this game. If you are a stress-filled person who needs something they can sit down to play & appreciate the beauty of with minimul other brainpower required, buy this game.
If you are none of these things, wait until the game goes on sale, then buy it anyway.
If you're afraid of deep water (Thalassopobia/Bathophobia/etc) you may want to hold off, but who knows? Maybe this is just the experience you need to start easing that fear.
:
The power of solid art direction shines strong in this game, showing us yet again that even with a minimal number of polygons, a 3D game can still be beautiful. The underwater environment in
is full of light, life, & color, with undersea flora & fauna all around as you explore the ocean floor &, later, the flooded remains of a sunken city. Bright splashes of darting pink fish & orange st& out against blue water, green vegetation, & grey stone as you explore, catching your eyes & keeping you looking around at all times, soaking it all in.
4/5
:
In addition to all of the sounds of undersea life, splashes, & rumbles of water that you'd expect,
also boasts a beautifully composed symphonic soundtrack. While unobtrusive for the most part, it comes out in full force to reinforce moments of wonder or haunting loneliness, always perfectly in step with what's happening on screen & enhancing the mood. The soundtrack alone may not be the only thing you remember this game for, but it's definitely a critical component to the experience that ties it all together.
4/5
:
You step into the shoes- well, flippers- of an unnamed diver on a quest to do-- something. While there is nothing in the way of objectives, the game continuously pushes you forward in a linear fashion nonetheless. There are no branching paths, you can't backtrack very far (if at all) outside of your current area, & the "puzzles" (if you can even call them that) are incredibly simplistic, generally just involving you exploring a few feet to find a switch to hit to open the next doorway. It's basically a walking simulator- like Journey- except underwater.
~3/5
:
There is no way to lose this game. The only "Enemy" shows up halfway into the game & is only able to slow you momentarily, if you're dumb enough to swim right into it. Outside of that, your greatest challenge will probably be just in wrestling with the camera.
1/5
:
Probably the worst aspect of the game, which is... kind of a major problem. While a controller is the recommended input method, I actually felt that Keyboard+Mouse was more accurate & responsive in the end.
You have standard up/down/left/right control over your diver, a button to accelerate (or dive if you're above water) & another button to perform a small boost/dash move that replenishes shortly after each use. You may find yourself mashing this button continuously, as I did, but how fast you're able to go + where, however, is largely up to the game's whims; it will regularly turn you around if you're heading somewhere it doesn't want you to go, or slow you down if you're too close to an edge (perhaps so you can't jump or otherwise force yourself out, I suppose), or make you swerve unexpectedly due to reasons unknown to all but the Heavens themselves.
Your primary button-press method of interacting with the world can be used the rest of the time to make small sonar-like ping noises. If you happen to have one of the game's small companion robots with you at the time, they'll ping along happily- perhaps trying to catch some of the magic in Journey, pinging along with your travel partner- but outside of the clearly-marked interaction points in the world, it ultimately serves no purpose at all. More confusing, then, is the fact you can charge this sonar ping up for a moment before firing, which... changes nothing.
By means of another button, you are able to hang on to & hitch a ride on most sea life that is as large/larger than yourself. These fish can be faster than moving under your own steam, but some can be nigh impossible to control, and most can't be brought between areas.
Finally, the last button that does anything allows you to do a small roll underwater, which can kill some speed & serves
other than to give you an achievement if you happen to press it while riding an animal.
The camera itself is fairly wonky, & doesn't really like doing what you tell it to- it's often more reliable to realign it by moving your character entirely instead of trying to move it directly with the appropriate control. It cares more about whatever the game wants you to notice at any given moment than it does about what you actually want it to do. Sudden transitions between having the control taken from & returned to you can lead to some frustrations due to things such as accidentally turning your character around in the process.
2/5
:
There are actually a number of reasons to play through the story at least twice, from simple ambiance & the joy of swimming freely, to accomplishing the token achievements gained from various goals such as hunting down collectibles or riding on certain animals as they jump out of the water. Aforementioned collectibles in particular actually do add a good deal of new depth to the game- collect all 3 in each of the 8 chapters, & you unlock a powered-up form that allows you to swim fast & dash continuously, a mode previously only available in the endgame. This powered-up mode can be quite fun in areas where you were previously limited, allowing you to jet around & dive from the water like a dolphin on methamphetamines with a rocket booster attached.
Even if speed's not your thing, once you unlock any number of "meditation" spots throughout the game, you can return to them at any time via the menu & enjoy watching the simulated wildlife in that areae to your heart's content. Your replays can be anything from exciting to soothing, depending on what you're looking to get out of the game, & it largely delivers.
3/5
If you like sea life, exploration, going fast, going slow, relaxing, going with the flow, etc... this game may be for you.

It's solid. Entertaining in short bursts. Played it for quite a bit and probably will play some more. I am a bit disappointed with it though.
You see, it describes itself as a roguelike rhythm game. There isn't much rhythm in there. Now, the problem might be, that I am a classicaly trained musician and the way I see rhythm is probably a bit different. My issues might not be revelant to other players.
How I would describe this game is a roguelike with simple mechanics but with a quite clever gimmick. Turns happen on their own in regular intervals, not when you move (as in classic rogue-likes). Enemies move in certain patterns (some move every turn, other every other turn etc.) The tricky part is to quickly evaluate your enemies and make right decisions in a short time given. To help you move in the right time turns are sincronized with music. That is really all there is to it. Also, the game is very forgiving when it comes to moving on time.
Occasionally, things get a bit more interesting. There are traps, which accelerate/slow down turns (and music.) There is one boss fight, where rhythm is irregular (one beat is skipped.) There is one miniboss, which disables the music until you kill it (never found it to be an issue... everyone can just tap a perfectly even rhythm, right?)
There are some choices in the design, which I am still not sure whenever I like or not. From the opening menu to the closing credits, Giant Squid's ABZU transports you into a living and breathing underwater world. You'll dive into an ocean full of breathtaking visuals with wonderful mysteries hidden in it's depths. It only took a little under two hours to play through ABZU, the whole time I was absolutely lost in it's colorful world and loved every minute of it. Most of us have gotten emotional playing video games in the past; for me the hospital scene in Last of Us comes to mind, but it took many hours to get invested enough to really get choked up. You'll experience wonder and sadness one minute, then pure joy and exhilaration the next. The fact that ABZU successfully pulled on my heart strings given the little time spent with it is impressive. That being said, I couldn't help but feel like Giant Squid could have giving us a bit more insight into the rich world they created. I believe a longer playtime would have allowed us to get invested in the connections made throughout the game.
The main purpose is to explore and advance by solving some basic puzzles which break barriers allowing you to progress. In the process you will be unravelling the ocean's remarkable secrets, discovering it's distant past, and ultimately shape it's future. The game give you a clear path to follow while still giving you enough room to explore the areas. As soon as I was able to freely swim around I found the fluid movement exhilarating. I genuinely loved exploring because it was fun not because I felt obligated to advance to the next area.
People throw around words when reviewing games; life-altering, revolutionary, etc, which often invoke a feeling of pressure to enjoy the game and see what everyone else is seeing. At times this can ruin your experience with an otherwise great game so I'll avoid that approach. I will say that the visuals and the score are both equally breathtaking and memorable, a crowning achievement that cement Giant Squid’s ABZU at the top of Best of 2016 lists. I thought I’d seen the best this generation had to offer but after playing ABZU I realize I was obviously wrong.

It's easy to recommend this game. Dust: An Elysian Tail has taut gameplay, gorgeous locations, fluid animation, great voice acting, and an overall immersive but not too overbearing experience (~15 hours if you're aiming for 117%).
Unfortunately, the game's (rather obviously) flawed as well, most of which feel like if a few more weeks were spent on it, they could be fixed and make the game near perfect. To avoid nitpicking I'm just going to highlight the most glaring.
First off the story, while well put together, is cliche (although not entirely predictable, thankfully) and a little hard to really grab your attention. Same with the characters really, they're great and well voiced but they don't quite grab you (and what's with the shading or the character designs in places? It really contrasts to the amount of detail put into the gorgeous backdrops). This is a real shame considering how the main villain is actually relatively likable. Some ideas that look like they could be important plot points are dropped entirely (ex: the technology you find late game).
Next is the fact that after you unlock the main map and talk with the villagers in the first town you begin opening up various other locations, many of which optional, which really opens up the game and makes it feel less linear than it is. By Chapter 3, there aren't any other side areas to unlock or explore and levels become increasingly linear up to the end (and it becomes painful as it drags in the middle).
Finally, bosses are really easy. Every single one will go down to slash, Fidget, and heal combos. You're more likely to die to mooks than the bosses, even if they do hit hard.
That said, this is still an amazing game. Despite the dragging middle, every segment of the game is well thought out and enjoyable to play, broken up well with short segments of conversation that don't go on for too long. The final boss especially is awesome (though I wasn't as excited for the ending and the section before the final boss is a little confusing and frankly cheesy). While save locations are frequent, the game doesn't hand hold you and allows you to live and die and discover its large number of secrets by yourself.
I recommend playing on Tough as you'll rarely die in Normal. If you're used to hack and slash games and are confident in your platforming, try Hardcore. Also, make sure you have a controller. The precision this game needs practically demands it.

Great game, a little hard to get into during the beta stages. After a few updates I could start to see this was going to be a very good 4X game. As GalCiv II being one of my favorite games, I can say without a doubt, this is a worthy successor to the previous game.
Now this game does have some flaws, some black screening can occur (after a short little bit the game does come back.) that can be a little annoying, and the AI can be very not smart at times. Such as electing the most war mongering race to lead the United Planets. Also having no espionage is disappointing. The diplomacy is not very in depth, the same with Galciv II, not including many components. One thing that really pisses me off though is- Why do the other races automatically hate you if you have a different ideology! I guess I could see if a Benevolent race hates a Malevolent race but why do Pragmatic races hate Benevolent/Malevolent races, there supposed to be neutral right?
Most of those things are minor, not affecting the game too much (except for the damn ideology's) in any way, and most of the good features triumph over the bad ones.
Ship customization, is the best of any game I have ever played. They nailed it, 10/10. Vastly improving from GalCiv II and overshadowing any other 4x games that have ship customization. One thing that has always bugged me is if in a space 4x game, doesn't have customizable ships, games like Endless Space are very very simple in the ways of customization, only having a few presets on ships and only able to add or remove components of the ship (still a great game). Back to GalCiv III, another thing the game is good at is, Race Making. It's great, you can make lore about your race, your leader. You're even able to import pictures for your race, making you able to make anything you want. Ship combat is fine, nothing too special, but nothing to get angry about.
TL;DR- Good game all in all, some issues that could be worked out, but solid game overall.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is a light rogue like game that owes a lot of its design philosophy to Spelunky. It does away with the depth of most roguelikes and instead concentrates on serving up a bite size piece of dungeon crawling in a challenging cute form, with many of the game design elements from Spelunky directly converted into its top down view point.
So far, so similar.
But CotND has a gimmick up its sleeve. The soundtrack. Everything in the game moves to the beat of the soundtrack, animations, movement, attacks - even your own input has to move to the beat of the soundtrack, like some mad version of Dance Dance Revolution where each step lets you explore further into the dungeon.
Move out of step with the beat and you will be punished - losing bonus and also potentially missing your chance to move or attack. Learn to step with the beat, learn how the monsters move with the beat, and suddenly you will be popping along to this fiendishly addictive game.
If the idea of playing a roguelike to the sound of a beat sounds weird - it kind of is. And I'll admit I wasn't entirely sure if this would turn out to be a flop or a cool idea. But once you play it, it just makes sense, and adds a very unique aspect to the game - that of timing. Where you have to move to the beat - staying still just isn't an option, and yet a move will push you into the path of a deadly foe, or out of striking range of a target. A new dimension of just how to "wait" or move in such a way as to hit an enemy becomes part of the game.
The soundtrack itself that supports the main gimmick of the game is absolutely top notch, and there are a few great touches to the game - such as the singing shopkeepers - that just make this game work really very well indeed.
An all round excellent experiment in combining the winning formula of Spelunky with a top down roguelike all to the beat of a soundtrack. Don't be put off because this game is kind of... left field. It manages to weld everything together beautifully, and is definitely a game where you will just want One More Try, because This Time, I've Got It.

I really held off on this game because of the horrendous reviews, but once I played it I was confused on why the reviews were so bad.  It seems the bad reviews focused on 2 things, 1) all the glitches/bugs and 2) the repetetive gameplay.  In relation to #1 I must say this game has ran trouble free, bug and glitch free and had not crashed a single time, I'd say it's one of the more stable PC games I've played.  Now from what I understand there were indeed a ton of issues when this was released so I'm sure the reviews are deserved.  But I'm not sure why many new and recent reviews still downgrade it for this.  I have a 4th gen i5 with a gtx 970 and can run at 4k at about 30fps, but I choose to run at 1440 and that gets me 50fps, which occasionally dips down to mid to high 40s at the worst, but overall it's very smooth and playable.
As for the repetitive gameplay, I kind of get that complaint but it's really not much worse than other similar games like saints row or GTA, although where those latter 2 games shine is their incredible stories.  The story was very very strong until about 1/4 through the game, then it devolved into taking over districts and here is where it does get a bit repetitive.  But really each mission is enjoyable on its own and unique in that you create your own situations.  What I do see as repetitive is they use the same exact levels/structures for different missions, so you very often get that feeling of deja vu as you traverse a warehouse or other structure, and I mean exact.
Gameplay is mixed but overall positive.  Combat is enjoyable, melee is a bit shallow with really just one melee button and an occasional counter you use, but it really doesn't come up often.  Shooting is accurate, but has a noticable stutter to it which doesn't seem to be associated with the framerate, so aiming can be hit or miss, although I can mitigate this somewhat adjusting the DPI of my mouse.  My only gripe is the horrible AI has made me lazy.  Hiding around a corner and whistling you can literally clear out an ENTIRE level of thugs this way, including the boss.  Seriously, I've done this and piled up 30+ bodies in the same spot.  You don't even have to whistle, the AI has this weird tendency to make the thugs always walk right towards you when you are hiding, even if they suspect nothing.  So just hide around a corner and melee/knife them as they come towards you.  Also typical of other games if you are in combat but hide somewhere, eventually the guards will forget, which I've never understood with dead bodies lying around and a killer on the loose.  One positive is driving, it's spot on.  I've long hated GTAV for it's♥♥♥♥♥♥poor driving mechanics, but in M3 the driving is very easy and even powerful cars which break loose a lot are easily controlled.  It may not be quite realistic, but what is realistic about a game like this?  I'd rather avoid the frustration of trying to drive a "realistic" vehicle in a video game and just have fun.
So overall a nice game, I'd say a solid 3 out of 5 stars and no more.  Some repetitive gameplay but both the story and the unique nature of how you handle  missions softens the repetition and makes them enjoyable.  Story is so-so but still brings you in and in touch with the protaganist.  Combat and driving are fun but a bit on the simple side.  AI is poor, and that will make you a lazy player if you let it.  My opinion don't pay full price for it, I got it on the summer sale when it was like $17 and well worth it at that price.  $30 maybe.  $60 hell no.

About as close to perfect as a console port can get. Perfect art direction, perfect sound design, and the best swimming animations I've ever seen. Abzû tells a wordless story and, like a good magician, carefully crafts its campaign to give players the illusion of total freedom, which is important for a linear and narrative-driven game. Much of what players will take away from the game depends on what they themselves put into it, as both the story and characters are ambiguous enough to embody the player's own ideals.
The gameplay itself is immensely satisfying and, despite the stern warning to use a controller, works just fine with mouse & keyboard. With either input method the learning curve is steep but forgiving, and all of the fast sequences where precision is implied will gently nudge the player onto the correct course. If you can achieve even the basics of control, the game will do its best to make sure you can still enjoy it.
For those looking for negatives, menus cannot really be operated with the mouse and it can be difficult for explorers and achievement hunters to keep track of how many items they've found in a given stage. The very last scene of the game asks you to "Press Start to exit," (where it should say "Esc" if you're playing with a keyboard), but beyond that the game itself worked flawlessly.
Highly recommended. 9/10.

I've just come from my second deep dive into the world of ABZÛ, and I feel so relaxed and calm right now. This is a visual experience with few parallels, a dreamlike and abstract voyage into the heart of the ocean. The lighting, color palette, soundscape, and environments are simply stunning. The character's fluid movements, and those of the marine wildlife that surround her, feel natural and effortless. It's easy to lose track of time simply swimming around the beautiful ocean floor, ruined temples, and coral reefs you encounter along the way. It's equally fun to swim alongside other marine life, burst out of the water with them, or simply watch them swim around. At times, the swarms of fish become so impressive in size and number that you may forget you're playing a game. All in all, if you ever wanted to know what it was like to zoom around with a school of fish, this is your game.
ABZÛ is a fairly linear experience, and can be completed in around 2-3 hours, though there are a few collectibles and cleverly hidden secrets which may take a bit longer to find. Thankfully, once completed you're able to return to specific chapters if you missed anything, or also "meditate" which lets you simply tune in to the animals around you. There are a few game elements that could be considered puzzles, and others that could be considered hazards, but if you're looking for a challenge, look elsewhere. This is more of a relaxing experience, though it is quite a bit more exciting than many "walking simulators" out there. ABZÛ has a wonderful rhythm that presents a perfect blend of mystery, awe, exploration, excitement, discovery, and just a hint of danger, all in the right proportions. Through some sort of sorcery, the music is always timed perfectly to complement whatever is going on, and when the fish and other animals move alongside you, it feels nothing short of magical.

For a game that takes up 400MB and feature Xbox Live Indie-like graphics on the Unreal Engine, This is an amazing satirical game that puts you in a position of a starving indie game developer in what seems to be New York city. If I had to pair it up with another game with the same kind of Satire, I'd have to say DLC Quest fits this one.
It's Free-To-Play (and Not Pay To Win), and definitely worth a try if you're waiting on that new Call of Battlefield Star Citizens to finish patching up. :)

This a heartwarming / heartbreaking story about a travelling con-man who goes by many names, and Efi, a dragon who can see and eat lies. The premise really is quite unique and the story fully makes use of it. There are also subtle symbolisms if you take the time to notice them. All 3 games in LiEat are about an hour long each, and each involve solving some kind of mystery. They mostly play like an adventure game with multiple endings where the two play detective and hunt for clues and pick out lies.
The translation is pretty spot-on, but some subtleties are always lost. For example, the con-man calls Efi 'runt', which might be a tad rougher than the more endearing 'chibi' in the original. Other than the illustrations by Ike which either have striking perspectives or are absolutely adorable, Miwashiba did everything else himself - writing, music etc. and it's great!
The conclusion is quite awesome in tying up all the loose ends. Such is its finality, that Miwashiba said in the afterword in the novelized prequel that there cannot be a fourth game, otherwise everyone's characterizations would break. However, for the 3 games we did get, give it a shot and you won't be disappointed.

Probably one of the most aesthetically pleasing games I've played in a long time. Journey, another game made by the same people, was just as good as this one. So if you think you might like ABZU, you'll love Journey.
The game itself is just unique; that's the best word I can use to describe it. ABZU immerses you into a world underwater, beautiful with stunning colors and graphics. The game has a flow to it that allows the player to be completely involved in the game but also understand it simply, There's no direct explanation throughout the story, however one isn't really necessary, and would probably disrupt the flow. It's sort of fitting that a game focused on underwater exploration "flows," isn't it?
I got a good 5 hours of gameplay until I finished it. Of course, the game is so charming that there's a likelihood I will replay it several times over, so that doesn't matter to me. To those that do want a game that has hours upon hours of gameplay, this probably isn't the game for you. Even so, it's inexpensive for such a gorgeous experience, so I definitely recommend giving this a go; after all, there's nothing quite like a game made by Giant Squid.

I got this game as part of the Humble Bundle, usually the games in these bundles can suck a few hours away and are entertaining.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is an exception.
What can I say about this game? It caught me by massive suprise and I couldn't have been happier that it did. The most notable thing is the art style of the game, all of it is handdrawn apart from a few CGI objects within the game. Dust himself looks amazing and his movements are very fluid. This moves onto my next point, the combat.
The combat is very simple, here's some enemies, swing your sword get items and pickups and whatever. But Dust plays with the system a little bit, you CAN just blitz through some segments with simple and powerful combos, but the key to getting stronger in Dust is not the amount of enemies you kill, it's the combos you can climb to, and this requires you to vary up your combos with slightly weaker attacks and other game mechanics that I won't spoil for you. Overall the combat is very satisfying and although a little easy at first it becomes a challenge after a certain point. Arguably most important is leveling up as a mechanic, it feels really good to level up Dust and you can customise him to your will depending on your play style. The platforming within the game is simple at first but gets suprisingly complex and there are a number of sidequests which actually have story and length to them, and aren't simple "go here and kill this" or fetch quests.
Next is the story, it is a very simple premise. Main character has amnesia and wants to find out who he is, but Dust depicts his journey so well and his development is noticeable especially in late game. You get embroiled with the law of the world in Dust and this affects your perspective of the story in a positive way. It's not all serious though, the game is aware that it's in a postmodern era of gaming so it has up to date humour, fourth wall breakage and odd quests which are memorable and strange, yet funny.
The performances of the main cast are brilliant, especially Dust's companion Fidget. No big budget voice actor in this game just good old fashion talent. Although some of the supporting casts performances are on par with the main cast, some are questionable but it doesn't put a downer on the experience.
Dust: An Elysian Tail is an example of a very accessible Indie game and is worth the investment with multiple difficulty levels and collecting all the treasures and equipment in the game, I've only just started doing both of these and I've clocked well over 24 hours, I highly recommend this hidden gem of a game.

Yes, yes, yes yes! I loved this game!
Like many others have said, combat is indeed boring - it's a very specific style, so unless you're a huge fan of it there isn't much you can do to like it better -, and considering you get to combat quite a lot in a game like this, I was expecting to NOT recommend it, but... everything else was so fiiiiine I didn't even get bored for having to smash the same button over and over. Seriously, look at the screenshots here in the Store. The background is so damn fine you can just keep looking at it forever if you get tired of looking at the monsters getting cut.
Combat excluded, this game is flawless.
Artwork is GORGEOUS, the way the back and fore grounds blend is beautiful, soundtrack is actually very thought of (for a game of slashing monsters), voice acting is pretty good, writing (dialogs, papers/letters you pick up, story) is amazingly well done (did I mention this was mostly made by a single dude?) and other game mechanics make it up for the combat.
There's one point where you get to the snow and it was SO magical. The snow in the ground will "react" in several ways depending if you jumped, if you just walked, if a monster walked, if you moved to attack... This is just one of the little details that made me like this game so much.
Also, there's this "extra", which makes you go around freeing your "friends", and at the map you free them, the game changes to copy that friend's game. Like, when you're freeing The Kid from Bastion, you have an empty map that is filled with ground when you walk around, just like in Bastion. Or when you're freeing the little guy from FEZ, your screen gets cut in like 9 pieces all out of place, so you don't know where you'll end up if you walk off the screen. These were great!
Save scumming and cheesable AI are usually marks of bad design, but for some reason both of those come together in Hotline Miami to make a fun game.

Despite this, the game is entrancing and is worth a shot by anyone who enjoys the roguelike and rhythm genres.

As a fan of the GalCiv franchise since version 1 it's refreshing to see some of the changes in this new iteration, though it seems to be mostly a glossy coat of paint over a game that hasn't essentially changed much. That being said the interface had been clunky at best in past versions and this is a pretty outstanding advancement - crisp videos, sharp layout, intuitive interfaces (sometimes a little TOO intuitive to where you don't realize you can interact with something). Some aspects of the game have been streamlined to make gameplay faster and smoother, which also means some aspects of the game us micro-managers used to love are now gone. The new tech tree is interesting but I got stuck in a sub-tree and couldn't figure out how to get out without reloading the game. The AI has definitely improved in this iteration which is refreshing - in previous versions the AI was overpowered in many ways and downright stupid in others. The ship-building seems a little more clunky to use than in prior versions while at the same time looks a lot nicer - not a great trade-off but I imagine the interface will get some improvements in future patches. Overall still a great game and worth the buy! Great job Stardock bringing the game up to date with technology and design once again.

There isn't anything bad that can be said about The Binding of Isaac. It's probably one of the best Roguelikes I have ever played and I do not regret buying it. The story seems pretty simple at first, but as you play, you discover that the meaning behind Isaac's story transcends the initial assumption that it's all about trying to escape his mother's wrath. It's MUCH deeper.
As for the gameplay, there isn't much to say. The controls are simple enough. The buttons aren't complicated and it's easy to adapt to. Plus, the floor of the first room of the first level even tells you what the controls are. Very newbie friendly. Though that's probably as newbie friendly as this game gets. The Binding of Isaac is definitely not kind towards its players, both greenhorns and veterans alike. The enemies in the game can at times be quite overwhelming, but that's based on your luck.
After all, this game is VERY luck based. The dungeon layout, enemy patterns, bosses, items, treasures and everything else is completely random. Some rooms will have nothing in them. Others will have locked treasure chests with no keys anywhere else on the floor. Others will have small numbers of flies flying around. Others will be full of monsters shooting you from all angles. Even mini-bosses can come at you out of nowhere.
However, there is one thing that will keep you coming back for more, despite the heavy beatings you're going to take on a regular basis. The fact that every playthrough gives you the chance to unlock more bosses, items and levels will make you want to keep going until you fight the final boss... no... not that final boss. No. Not that final boss either. The REAL final boss. That's right. This game technically has six final bosses. You'll know when you get to the real one. It'll be kinda obvious when you get to them.
Oh and the Wrath of the Lamb DLC adds in a load of items, enemies and bosses to aid you in your adventures. I would definitely recommend getting the DLC if you're going to buy the base game. The two go hand in hand and it doesn't feel right to have one without the other, especially since the items you unlock with the DLC can be used in conjunction with the rest. Most items in the game can be combined to create incredible attacks. Ones that can decimate bosses in a couple of hits. Don't believe me? Better buy the game and find out then.

I really like this game. Despite it's problems, I see this as a game that had a lot of potential but just fell short of being at pretty good, but was just enough to be ok. Although I defintely acknowledge the criticims and have a complaints of my own.
+ Well written story, voice acting, writing
+ Amazingly 60s soundtrack. Do-wops, R&B, and of course, classic Rock N Roll
+ Nice textures and pretty vistas
BUT...
- Janky lighting, ugly orange tint, and some visual bugs. (Alot of the bugs got patched out, but they're certainly still there).
- I hear framerate tends to be bad at times. I haven't experienced it personally. (I upgraded to a 1070 sometime before the release of the game. I wouldn't call the framerate stable, but I haven't had too much drop off.)
+ Gunplay is solid and when AI isn't being stupid, feels pretty fun.
- As mentioned, the AI can be pretty dumb sometimes. Also stealth is pretty basic and with a silenced weapon, becomes too easy.
- Missions tend to get repetitive and only vary in location.
- Those. Freaking. Phones boxes. (You have to collect 3 dohickies for 1 "transistor" to use on 1 phonebox. yay...)
-The Underboss system is disappointing. The city is split into 9 districts with the Bayou being no man's land. With 3 Underbosses, it's pretty obvious what you're going to do if you don't like only one particular underboss.
- These two small gripes are my own. The prolouge is cut up in a strange manner and the only way to switch between lethal and non lethal takedowns are through the option menu. Why not just map it to pressing/holding the takedown button?
? Lastly, I'm not sure how much this would get on someone's nerves, but I might as well explain it. The game used to be locked at 30 FPS, so the base game cutscenes are rendered at 30 fps, even though the game can go higher now. The dlcs (if you choose to play them) don't have this issue.
This game is rough around the edges and deserves at least a meh, but if you can see past the mediocrity delivered by a fairly new studio (and the fact that this game is only a Mafia game in name and it has Vito in it) there's some fun to be had and I would get it at a discounted price.

Buy this game. It's super cheap, but that isn't why you should buy it. You should buy it because this game is a masterpiece. It's short, only about three or four hours, but it's to the point. The story - an episodic tale of the adventures of a young dragon girl who can eat lies, and her "papa," a con man whose job is to lie - is excellently told and quite poignant. The turn based RPG gameplay is simple and fun; I never felt as though a battle dragged on for too long, and I had fun too! The music is effective and beautiful; the piano/organ is always a good conveyor of subtle melancholy, which this game has a strong undercurrent of, and while this game does indeed deal with heavy themes, it indeed knows how to lighten the mood at the drop of a dime, much credit to the music. The character designs are very cute; it has that chibi look to it, but also has a dark tone to it. It's very adorable but, there is something about how they went about presenting it that gives you a bit of pause, especially given the characters themselves. They are very well written, and their stories are very interesting to discover, and very sad too. How they use the main gimmick of consuming lies instead being consumed by them to solve the mysteries within each episode  is very clever. Overall, this is at essence a thing of beauty. I may never play this again after I write this, or I may make a point of playing it weekly just remind to myself that good things do exist, but either way I am wholly satisfied with this purchase.

After winning a YouTube giveaway for an early access code, I was very excited to get my hands on ABZU, a beautiful looking game that I have been waiting on for some time now. My experience with ABZU did not disappoint, and was enough to lure me from consoles to PC.
ABZU is a unique game with some of the most fantastic music I have ever heard. With a unique visual style, this underwater adventure is extremely immersive, and just a few moments into the opening sequences, you are already submerged in mystery and curiosity. The environment is continually changing around you, and your interactions with it and its inhabitants further develop this immersiveness.
The controls are simple and fluid. Even with a keyboard and mouse, doing underwater flips, riding on sea turtles, and changing directions felt extremely satisfying. All the animations are smooth and flow really well, adding to the experience of deep sea swimming.
The story is very interesting, and while silent, keeps me wondering what will happen next. You discover each sequence on your own, and this game appeals to both players who like to get the story done in one go, and players who like to take their time and admire every little detail packed into the beautiful game world.
If you are looking for a simple, relaxing game to play, ABZU is a must play title.

I'll start off my review with a simple sentence: I enjoy Paladins.
That being said, it definitely has it's flaws.
The thing I like about it is that it's F2P...mostly. You can use real currency to unlock things, but you can also use an in game currency to buy characters if you play long and hard enough. And there are even ways to earn real currency in game.
Speaking of which, the characters. There are a lot of them. It's unfortunate that you have to unlock them, but hey, not everybody is valve and can have stuff be f2p and run a game entirely on cosmetics. It's either that or charge 60 dollars for the game, like Blizzard.
With that being said, this game is not just an OW or TF2 clone. Sure, there are similarities between the two, but there are always similarities between games of the same genre. Look at LoL, Dota 2, HotS, and now Smite. Look at pretty much any RTS game out there. You can sit there and pick out everything that is similar, or exactly the same, but you can also sit there and pick out the differences as well.
Speaking of differences, one of the biggest differences between TF2 and OW is also one of the games biggest flaws; the lack of an option to change characters mid game. Sometimes team compositions can suck, and you're left with 3 damage dealers, a flank, and an ill suited support. But once you make your champion selection, after the time counts down, you're locked in. This leads me to my next criticism.
The community. Most people are stubborn and won't switch their character over to a needed character, even with the situation demands it. So if you're on a support char, and you tell a damage picker to switch to front line before the game starts, you'll most likely be told to switch yourself, even though your position is more necessary than theirs is. I know communities can be bad in any game, but since this is a game that is heavily team focused, having a stubborn community isn't helpful.
The characters might be very varied, but at the same time, they're not perfect. There are some that are clearly underpowered, and some that are clearly overpowered. However, rather than balance the characters, Hi-Rez's focus seems to be on making new characters, which only helps the power creep build, as the new characters will either be stronger, or weaker, than the current meta leaders. And if a character isn't a meta leader, it's probably not going to get played anyway.
But overall, the game is fun. There's really no penalty to loss (Ranked is currently a joke right now, but it's beta), and the matches normally don't take too long. It's a good f2p counter to OW, for anyone that likes more characters than tf2, rather than weapon customization and hats.

Quite a fun little casual time management game.
You play a nurse at hospital who is going to work through her training by spending a bit of time in each of the hosptal departments. There are 10 levels per department and each level adds new twists and new things to manage. Gameplay is typical time mangement stuff:  Patients will enter the department and be seated in the waiting area and a little icon will appear above their head showing what sort of treatment they need. A little timer will begin to count down and if it runs out they will lose a heart, lose all their hearts and they will leave in a huff. Basically the quicker you get each person to where they want to go the better and you will need to pay attention to whose timer is the lowest so that you treat them first so as not to lose any hearts. Complete all of a patient's treatments and they will go to the counter and you will score points for every remaining heart.
Each level has a certain amount of points you have to score to earn the level bonus of one to three stars. Each star you get also earns you a little bit of money which you can use to upgrade things in the department you are working, for example more comforatable chairs in the waiting room so that patients lose hearts slower. Each level also has a special bonus challenge that requires you to meat some special requirement, such as never running out of medication or getting so many patients to the counter with full hearts.
The game also has a story that links things together with tragic patient stories, inter hospital romances and other drama. It's can be a bit melodramatic but it's still kind of fun and engaging and helps give you an extra incentive to push on through the levels.
The graphics area about what you would expect from this kind of title and if you have ever played a Gamehouse game before, you will instantly recognise their style. It's all pretty good and helps bring the aformentioned story to life as each character is distinct and emots well. The music is also quite catchy and the main theme is very hummable and it also has some more tense pieces to match the more dramatic beats of the story.
All in all if you like casual time management style games, this is one of the better ones out there. Gamehouse tend to produce good quality stuff in this genre so if you have played other titles from them, this is more of the same. Emily from the Delicious series even makes a cameo in some of the levels.
A solid well rounded time casual time management game with a likeable story and cast.

BLUF: Surprisingly fun game that's playable and enjoyable in single player despite being tarnished by a clunky interface, poor camera controls/angles, and few small bugs, but completely unplayable in multiplayer due to game breaking bug and lack of multiplayer saving.
When I first checked this game out and watched gameplay videos, I thought it looked boring. But when it went on sale recently, I figured I'd give it a shot since it was cheap enough that it wouldn't be a big deal if I didn't like it, and if it did turn out to be good then I would have got it at a great price. After playing it a bit I ended up really enjoying it, so much I bought another copy so my friend and I could play together. Then I played it some more, and then the two of us played it a couple times. We both have had a lot of fun with it.
So why the downvote? First of all, the interface is a bit clunky, as are the camera controls and views. And there are some small bugs here and there. But despite these things, I would still give it a big thumbs up. And frankly, if you only want to play single player, I would also recommend it. But it is a BIG no-go for multiplayer. This is for two reasons. The first is that, despite many people asking for it for over 2 years, there is no multiplayer save feature. And it's going to take at least a couple hours to complete a map, and probably quite a bit longer. So if you can't finish it that amount of time, or it takes longer than expected and you run out of time, you're out of luck. All that time will be wasted, and you'll have to restart from scratch later. Still, even with this issue, I would very tentatively recommend the game, as long as you know what you're getting yourself into.
But then there's the second issue, which is game-breaking and completely kills any fun you may have been having. The second time my friend and I played together, after an hour or so and a lot of progress, I randomly got disconnected from teh server. My connection was fine, mind you, and our voice chat session didn't falter. Apparently they just have crappy servers. I reconnected to the game only to find all the trucks were relocked for me. I was working on getting things back when, after a few minutes, I got disconnected yet again. So  I reconnected and went back to work on getting the trucks unlocked, only to have it disconnect me AGAIN after another few minutes. At this point I'd had enough, and wasn't going to keep wasting my time. Even if it stopped doing it every few minutes, for all I knew, I could spend another hour working on things only to disconnect and be thrown right back to square one. And doing a quick search revealed that several other people have reported the same or similar issues (some had it even worse with the garages and cloaking being reset). Supposedly, bugs very similar to this have been fixed in the past, yet somehow these problems still remain. In any event, if I can't trust that I won't lose hours of progress from a simple random disconnect that can happen at any time, not to mention repeatedly, then I'm not going to waste my time. And since the game is dead, these issues aren't going to be fixed (especially since they were ignored when development was still ongoing). It's a real shame, as my friend and I both really enjoy the game, but this makes it unplayable.

Though perhaps not as impressive as it once was, Final Fantasy VII is still a fun, engaging, and timeless RPG. I first played it when I was 10 years old, and it changed my understanding of video game narrative. For the first time, I saw the potential of this medium to tell powerful and moving stories on the same level as film or literature. For that reason alone, I can't help but recommend this game. That said, it has not aged well visually, and the flawed (though still largely competent) translation is now more obvious than ever. In spite of that, it remains impactful and moving, thanks in no small part to Nobuo Uematsu's incredible score, which ranks among the best ever seen in a game.
As far as this PC port is concerned, it's alright. The game controls fine with the keyboard, and former faults, namely the use of low quality MIDI for the soundtrack, have all been addressed. On the whole, it's more or less indistinguishable from the PS1 version, for better or worse. It would be nice to have some extra bells and whistles, but unfortunately the best we get are some token achievements. Square's DRM is inexcusable, but at least it doesn't run through an additional resource hog of a client like Ubisoft's Uplay. Even so, I can respect those who let that be a deal breaker.
All in all, it's a great game, one of my favorites for sure. It's not the best version, but it's not bad by any stretch.

As always - I've recorded my gameplay so you can see what's involved:

This game did deserve a lot of it's bad rep during release, mostly because the game was a buggy mess. They're almost entirely gone now, but it still has it's flaws. What little glitches I have seen, they are often few and far between. You do get the occasional face rigging glitch, where Lincoln's lips seem to flap with enough force to generate lift. Sometimes your cars float away, and that's okay.
I think the story was enjoyable enough, it was an interesting take on a locale that is hard to visit (mostly because being black in the 60's is hard to depict without♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥someone off)
A lot of people say that it's nothing like Mafia 2, and they are correct. Mafia 2 is like the first two Godfather movies, and Mafia 3 is like an off the walls, unlicensed, blaxploitation movie where you're the angriest brotha in town and you gotta lay down the law and blow up some whities. If you come in expecting Mafia 2, you may be let down. I enjoyed both games equally, but they can be hard to compare at times.
The game had a lot of moments that were kind of predictable, such as the typical Vietnam era song blaring while you were hunting down a plump honky in the Bayou, armed only with your knife.
The gameplay can be a little repetitive at times, but the gunplay, combat, and driving all made up for it (at least, in my opinion.) I do raise an eyebrow during the turf claiming sequences, in which you clear out 2 areas, and to fully take over the district, you often head back to a locale where you have literally just killed every living thing. I didn't mind it too much, but I would imagine a bunch of goombas trying to fight Lincoln Clay wouldn't want to go back to a hideout he just completely decimated.
The game, visually, is gorgeous. Sometimes it doesn't run as well as it should, but they genuinely did a good job at recreating New Orleans in an original, visually appealing way. People tend to complain that open world games are overdone, but I feel that New Bordeaux is a welcoming breath of fresh air to the genre. It sure does rain a lot though.
The vehicle handling is enjoyable I think people tend to forget that cars from the 60's aren't exactly super cars. They all handle, brake, and steer poorly. The game appears to capture that really nicely.
On the downside, I do not enjoy the police notoriety system. It feels like lazy AI, but maybe the racial disparity at the time explains a lot of left out features.
Hit a person's car and a cop sees? You're dead. Run over a mailbox? I guess you're getting shot on sight.
The same rule applies to hailing a cab. I can't tell if it's because they just chose to leave it out, or whether or not your melanin levels cause cabbies to ignore you completely.
Anyways, this game is pretty darn good. I enjoyed it, a lot. My expectations weren't the highest going in, and I was pleasantly suprised. The game doesn't deserve to be mindlessly♥♥♥♥♥♥on for it's day one failures. If you can get the Digital Deluxe edition on sale, you'll totally get your money's worth.

A few weeks ago I was introduced to the Heart's Medicine sequel through a Youtuber's play through.  It reminded me of the Diner Dash games (and the likes) I enjoyed as a teenager in middle/high school.  Intrigued, I saw that the first game was on sale as part of the Summer Sale.  It was a quick buy and what a great buy it was!
The story is great and despite the dark turn some aspects take, there's a pleasant light-hearted feel you take away throughout.  Some might find it overly positive despite some subject matter, but to me personally, it never felt cheesy or over the top.  The characters are great, the dialogue is great and it gives the game a great flow.  The gameplay is great; addictive, fun and there's a decent amount of replayability, especially with regard to getting all those achievements.
My qualms with the game are small, but they involve control on the mac.  Since I wasn't using a controller, the mousepad had some buggy moments.  I am resigned to the fact I'll never get some achievements because pulling out glass shards with a mac mousepad doesn't work.
Verdict:  A game I wholeheartedly recommend and have no shame admitting to playing over 30 hours on :)

I like what the designer, Sirlin, has to to say about making a fighting game about choices and not reflexes and rote practice, but this is a poor execution on those design goals. After three hours of playing I still have no understanding of how my choices impact winning or lossing over the course of a game, even if I was able to win more than lose vs the ai. If anything, it felt harder to understand than most fighting games, at least at the start, and I have a lot of experience playing card games! Worse, winning or losing any particular hand just feels random due to the rock-paper-scissors nature of the contest. When choices feel meaningless in the moment to moment, it makes the gameplay too dull to make the effort of learning the underlying systems feel worth it.

I liked Delicious Emily: Message in a Bottle well enough to buy the gamehouse bundle. I was looking forward to more of the DE addictive gameplay and ludicrous storylines. This game disappointed me.
Instead of the insane sitcom plot of Delicious Emily, we get a semi-sane hospital-drama plot. A plus or a minus depending on how much you like helping your boyfriend / hospital director ditch his opioid habit via cutesy casual gameplay. Find all the pill bottles in time for a bonus!
More importantly - the gameplay is heavily loaded with minigames. Run the patient through the x-ray machine in under 5 seconds for a minor bonus! Set all the dislocated bones in 3 seconds, or the patient starts losing hearts!
So, if the Delicious Emily gameplay had a minor emphasis on reflexes, and a heavy emphasis on planning things out so that you take the optimal route and serve as many customers at once before they start losing patience, Heart's Medicine is the opposite of that. Most of the time, the optimal strategy is to serve each patient as quickly as possible when they come in, and pray you don't mess up the minigames. Do that, and the "serve several patients in a row" bonuses are mostly irrelevant (except for checkouts).
Since my reflexes aren't exactly great, I found the gameplay to be pure torture.
(Edit - you can pass each level and go on with the plot regardless of how well or poorly you've done. Getting three stars + bonus challenge + captured guinea pig [yes, really] per level is just a matter of earning trophies, which I usually don't care about. But... there's really no point in making any sort of effort to play the game if you're not going to ace every level, since that's the only challenge you'll find)
