DeviantART and FurAffinity got together to produce the single most unsatisfying metroidvania ever made, and like both those communities the quality of this game largely depends on which part you happen to be looking at at the time. This goes for everything from the art assets to the music to the animation and writing (but never the plot, the plot is consistently terrible).
A good first example is your main character(s), Dust and Fidget. They're fairly well drawn (most of the time), and while they aren't the most original characters (brooding amnesiac warrior, blue, and comedic animal sidekick, orange) you actually enjoy moving them around the screen! Their animations are fluid, and Fidget's body shifts to fly against things like a strong wind or to keep up with you when you're moving fast. You can tell that a lot of work was put into them, which is why I have to wonder why so much work was put into making them as hard to see as possible. You'll be fighting in pitch-dark caverns, or raging blizzards, or with the camera zoomed all the way out, the random weather effects have a preference for torrential downpours every fifteen seconds, and with all this on top of the tons of enemies and various weapon and attack effects (theirs and yours) it's a wonder the game runs half as well as it does with as much as there is on screen. The level shown in the fourth screenshot on the store page is probably the worst offender, because in addition to the ugliest enemies in the game it introduced scads of allies
everything is either exploding or on fire,
some of the enemies are
.
There are more problems than not being able to see the good animations, and those include being able to see the bad. You can't tell from the still image, but the deer in the first screenshot on the store page move like something from Scribblenauts or South Park; they don't seem to move their knees and you can see where the legs on the rig meet the body and it's such a jarring transition from the seamless little bunnies from just a screen earlier. Likewise, the town guards in Vaguely Asiatic Villiage are a jerky collection of bodyparts brought into unlife by Flash and commanded to randomly bend over and pick up invisible objects, the end result a bit like a marionette being controlled by a butterfingered puppeteer. By far, though, the worst offenders are the soldiers and spaceships of the volcano level. Just look at the fourth screenshot on the store page, and look how jarring that CG-rendered spaceship looks compared to the hand-drawn enemies and environments from every other screenshot. Now imagine that in motion! It's something straight out of A Valley Without Wind, and I can't understand what would lead them to add such a thing. There's no lead up to CG-rendered space ships, there are no indicators that CG-rendered space ships will be making an appearance, and there's nothing you can do about it.
The phrase "there's nothing you can do about it" actually segues into my biggest complaint, the empty feeling this game's plot leaves you with. Despite the bright colors, lush backgrounds, and (occasionally) cute furry characters, Elysia or Falana or whatever Not-Asia is called is a dark, depressing world. Everything you do is met with failure as part of the game's theme of "even when you do everything right, you can't fight fate". And while I can understand the creator was in a bad place when he made this game, it creates a sort of dissonance in the tone of the game when you have genuinely laugh-out-loud banter alongside a furry analogue for the holocaust. When I remember the scenes with Dust and Fidget poking fun at each other or breaking the fourth wall, or even taking some beautifully-aimed jabs at other indie games, it hurts, because they took characters we actually cared about, the
characters we cared about, ran them through the grimmest, darkest plot they could find, and still expected us to care, even when the plot didn't make any sense, even when the plot never made any sense. By the end of the game, when you're met with another failure in a string of horrible failures, you're not even relieved it's over because you still have so many darn questions! Why were any of the events in the game occuring? Why did anyone, at any point in time, think that any of your actions mattered? Why did anyone tell you they mattered? They didn't, and the game drives it on home every other step of the way that they didn't, except for side quests which somehow matter within the confines of the sidequest, and are coincidentally where all the game's good dialogue, and its heart, lie.
It's pretty interesting, has its quirks and could use some more polish, but overall it's nice.

If you like rock, paper, scissors, A LOT, maybe this is the game for you?  It's been said that this is like a fighting game and mimics the mind games of high level fighting games.  To me, this doesn't feel anything like fighting or playing fighting games (which I'm quite good at).  It's modeled after rock-paper-scissors with a few traditional card game tropes like pairs and straights.  I found entire experience rather frustrating.  Blows tend to miss more often than not.  You spend turns waiting for cards to play, then get blocked or doged when you finally have something exciting.  It feels like you're losing even when you're winning because the satisfaction of actually pulling off that combo was ruined by the sour taste in your mouth from losing the last few consecutive encounters.  If you're looking for a game that actually feels rewarding, that accurately mimics fighting games, check out Battlecon Devastation (sadly, not on Steam yet), the mechanics of the game and the strategies of the decks much more accurately model fighting games in my opinion.

Lego Star Wars III - The Clone Wars follows the TV series: Star Wars - The Clone Wars. How well it does, I don't know, as I haven't regularly watched the show. It did, however, let me play through the very few parts of the show I remembered, so I'll have to leave how well it followed the show to the assumption that it does a decent job.
As for the level design, there are plenty of good levels in this game, but are sadly overshadowed by the abundance of strategic open battlefield levels. You have to destroy enemy bases and build your own. It's fun and makes for a great side activity to be included (as it did in the game's Republic Assault missions) but it's also put in place of some of the actual story missions which just seems a bit lazy to me.
The controls feel like the other Lego Star Wars games (I used a gamepad controller) but with what I would consider a major improvement. They removed the short combos from the previous games and replaced it with the ability to fight indefinitely. One thing I do miss, however, is the ability to use stronger lightsaber attacks by timing your next move instead of button mashing.
Overall, I love this game but wouldn't give it a perfect score.

So it has finally reached 1.0...
Having been a founder from early on, I have a good perspective on how things evolved and changed up until release. I held firm to the belief that GalCiv3 was not ready for release prior to 1.0. Now that most of the really big issues have been dealt with, I no longer hold to that belief.
Yet while the game is certainly in a playable state for a release candidate, GalCiv has a long way to go still. Nearly all the features in the game still need refinement and further development, and some of those features that need a lot of improvement I'll note below:-
Invasion Mechanics: Are non-existent, and not much has changed from GalCiv2. You invade a planet. You get a screen. You click. It's over. You find out if you won or lost. That's pretty much it. It's a very boring mechanic, lets be honest. Yes - the devs have stated that some planned concept content was cut cause it didn't make release, and they want to work on this for later on. But I'm reviewing a game in its current release state, I'm not about to review a game for what might or mightn't happen later on down the road.
Battle Viewer: Essentially a copy/paste job from GalCiv2 battleviewer with a few tweaks, but not much different here. Could be spruced up? Yes.
Multiplayer Missing Features: Sadly the multiplayer side of GalCiv is a mixed bag. They 'snuck' some features out that were in early access and now you can no longer play multiplayer on maps above huge and you can't use custom races. The official statement concerning this is that there were new instability problems with those features and they had to be removed to be worked on. I just hope Stardock stay true to their word and fix whatever issue they're having. It still rubs me up the wrong way that they removed them without comment first in the update, and only expressed their reasons for it when pressed on it.
There are other elements of the game that need a lot of refinement, most of which falls down to balance. Stardock have had a good track record in early access fixing lots of crucial issues. I hope that track record continues.
So is it good? Is it just a copy paste of GalCiv2?
It's certainly good, and while some elements are most definitely copy pasted from the 2nd game, generally GalCiv 3 is a different experience. Not vastly different however.
The map now has hex's instead of squares. Ships now have combat categories so when you design a ship, you can choose if it will be support/escort/capital, etc. These play a role in combat and are essentially a way for you to construct formations of ships. A nice tweak to the combat. Ships also have new stats like tactical speed that will aid them in combat, allowing for ship design strategies to be more involved. Ship designing in GalCiv2 was mostly a paper/rock/scissors affair, and while there is still an element of that in the game, it has a less of an impact in combat.
There are now trade resources (their may have been similar ones in GalCiv2 if I recall) and strategic resources which is one of my favorite new features, although I wish the AI would use them a tad more intelligently, if they use them at all.
The graphics have obviously received a makeover, and the game is optimized enough that they don't have much of an impact on performance.
If there is one thing I remember most about GalCiv 2 is the AI, and how good it was. It had its flaws, like any AI, but it was very impressive for its time, and I would consider it the best strategy AI in any game by far.
Sadly, the same can't be said for GalCiv 3. The AI has a long, long way to go before it even evolves into what the AI was in GalCiv 2, and I hope that this is an area that receives special attention. Regardless, as it stands, the AI is miles ahead of the AI in Civ 5, so, that's a good thing, right?
Despite the differences and tweaks made, GalCiv 3 still feels very... GalCiv. That is what the developers intended, to make a game without losing that GalCiv appeal. Sadly, I think they went a tad too far.
The first and second game were released during a time when carnivorous space apes (Drengin) and evil squirrels (snarti) were fine. Cheesyness in all its glory was good. Toilet humor and lame jokes were told a-plenty in both games, and it got away with it cause they were great games for its time.
So while GalCiv3 evolved, sadly the humor and 'feel' of it didn't evolve. There was plenty of opportunity to increase immersion and to allow the game to mature, to 'level' up, cause we no longer live in those cheesy times when lame jokes could be told for a cheap laugh. You either shape up, be serious and tell the story you want, or you tell it while a minor race informs you how they set their own atmosphere on fire while letting out a fart...
GalCiv3 actually has a rather 'grown-up' campaign. Yes it still features the space apes, but it is an improvement over the last, and considering I very briefly played the last one and got fed-up with it, I'm hoping this one can keep me interested, as I usually just dive into a sandbox game.
It's just a shame that other elements, other races, do not seem to maintain any sort of consistency. I believe they missed a good opportunity to level up their style, unfortunately, they stuck to their guns a bit too much.
And lets mention races. There is 1 new race. The Iridium Corporation. That is it. 1 whole new race. This is perhaps the biggest disappointment for me, personally. Just 1 new race is just poor play Stardock, it really is. Some might think they shot the idea down due to the campaign, as in how else would they fit the new races into their story? Simple: You don't. You have new races for those delving into the sandbox, and you kept out any mention of them from the story. There you go. Granted, we get lots of new minor races, which is a plus. And of course you can make your own custom race, but the custom editor is no excuse for Stardock to get lazy! And sure, new races might arrive in the form of dlc/expansions, but for only just 1 new race for a brand new sequal, tut tut... bad form I say.
Despite its flaws and despite the game still needing lots more work on it, I still recommend GalCiv3 as it has surpassed GalCiv2 in some areas, and will hopefully continue to evolve with future content.

A frustrating but overall nice turn-based/real-time strategy/RPG hybrid game.
The gameplay is very similar to Icewind Dale. You get to control a party of survivors in real-time, however you can pause the game at any moment to choose what should be that character's next action.
The action is very intense as you can often become overcrowded with dozens of zombies in just a mere few seconds. The feeling of the weapons, from baseball bats, pistols, to even grenades is perfect. Letting a zombie to slowly walk right up to your character's face to finally blow his/her brains out with a well timed shot is deliciously rewarding. The game world, characters and zombies are all well designed, but the voice acting is atrocious. The game is well presented, the graphics are good, but the camera system can be extremely frustrating to control at times. Getting used to the poor camera system and controls can be a hard task.
The game uses a checkpoint system to save your progress during missions, but they're quite rare and some checkpoints are optional. These are often placed in an alternate route and protected by a bunch of zombies. While the checkpoint system builds up tension and greatly increases the challenge, it only leads to frustration because you can easily loose an hour of gameplay if the game crashes (and it does often in some missions).
I would recommend to buy a 4-pack when on sale (or even better, get it in a 1 dollar bundle) to play with your friends because playing solo can be VERY tiring as you'd have to micro-manage everything.

I'll start off my review with a simple sentence: I enjoy Paladins.
That being said, it definitely has it's flaws.
The thing I like about it is that it's F2P...mostly. You can use real currency to unlock things, but you can also use an in game currency to buy characters if you play long and hard enough. And there are even ways to earn real currency in game.
Speaking of which, the characters. There are a lot of them. It's unfortunate that you have to unlock them, but hey, not everybody is valve and can have stuff be f2p and run a game entirely on cosmetics. It's either that or charge 60 dollars for the game, like Blizzard.
With that being said, this game is not just an OW or TF2 clone. Sure, there are similarities between the two, but there are always similarities between games of the same genre. Look at LoL, Dota 2, HotS, and now Smite. Look at pretty much any RTS game out there. You can sit there and pick out everything that is similar, or exactly the same, but you can also sit there and pick out the differences as well.
Speaking of differences, one of the biggest differences between TF2 and OW is also one of the games biggest flaws; the lack of an option to change characters mid game. Sometimes team compositions can suck, and you're left with 3 damage dealers, a flank, and an ill suited support. But once you make your champion selection, after the time counts down, you're locked in. This leads me to my next criticism.
The community. Most people are stubborn and won't switch their character over to a needed character, even with the situation demands it. So if you're on a support char, and you tell a damage picker to switch to front line before the game starts, you'll most likely be told to switch yourself, even though your position is more necessary than theirs is. I know communities can be bad in any game, but since this is a game that is heavily team focused, having a stubborn community isn't helpful.
The characters might be very varied, but at the same time, they're not perfect. There are some that are clearly underpowered, and some that are clearly overpowered. However, rather than balance the characters, Hi-Rez's focus seems to be on making new characters, which only helps the power creep build, as the new characters will either be stronger, or weaker, than the current meta leaders. And if a character isn't a meta leader, it's probably not going to get played anyway.
But overall, the game is fun. There's really no penalty to loss (Ranked is currently a joke right now, but it's beta), and the matches normally don't take too long. It's a good f2p counter to OW, for anyone that likes more characters than tf2, rather than weapon customization and hats.

Yes, this game is really only around 2 hours, depends on your playstyle.
However, that is an incredibly fulfilling 2 hours, spent peacefully roaming the undersea world, unraveling its mysteries, and discovering yourself. Within those two hours I laughed, I cried, and I felt personally affected by a video game on a scale not since I beat Pokemon Gold for the first time.
This is the newest game from Matt Nava, the art director behind FLOW and Journey, so you can expect a similar-themed game with breathtaking visuals, and a linear adventure set within huge undersea environments. In ABZU, you play as a cyborg diver that explores the deep ocean and comes across its abundance of life, and the mysteries its past holds.
ABZU is very peaceful, but there are a few scary moments, especially if you are somebody who suffers from thalassophobia (intense fear of the sea.) The sheer amount of colour and depth to this game is beyond anything i've yet to experience and sets the bar for visceral storytelling. There are no words in this game-- the story is told through your travels and a few cutscenes.
Austin Wintory's soundtrack is just as appealing as the graphics, soothing and atmospheric, mirroring the vibe of ABZU categorically. I will purchase this if it comes up for sale.
Gameplay wise, ABZU is what modern gamers would refer to as a "walking simulator" style game, or in this case, a "diving simulator." You control a nameless, mute cyborg diver who explores a vast ocean teeming with life, and equally full of mysteries. The controls are very smooth and feel natural. I am not a diver in real life, but the movements of the protagonist look pretty convincing. Along the way, you befriend a great white shark, and come across some underwater drones that help clear obstacles.
The world of ABZU is too much for one game, much less for two hours of gameplay. There is massive amounts of lore that begs to be established. ABZU is strikingly similar to Journey. The two share various parallels and this is often the subject of mass criticism, many even labeling ABZU as "Journey, underwater." This is not the case here, but the two share a lot in common. In the style of Journey, there are many abandoned, ancient structures with very similar architecture. This stands out to me as being the most common ancestor between the two games.
At any rate, I do appreciate this game very much for what it is, but I do have my fair share of gripes.
PROS:
-Breathtaking graphics
-Minimalistic gameplay/ease of use
-Incredible story
-Oozing substance and atmosphere
-Soundtrack is great
CONS:
-Way too short...
-Lacking the passive and seamless online function of its inspiration
-Lots of lore, zero explanations (maybe i'm not reading into it right)
-Puzzles were too easy
Final verdict: 9/10
For us PC gamers who vie for a Journey clone, this is the closest we will get. It harkens back to the early 2000s adventure games like Jak and Daxter, and Shadow of the Colossus, where a small player is cast upon an ever-changing huge world.

To start off, I played a demo of this before I bought it, so my play time is actually a little more than Steam shows.
Sudokube is a new and challenging twist on the classic Sudoku. Spin a 4x4x4 cube to arrange 16 alphanumeric characters (standard hex values) across the faces of the cube without repeats across rows, columns, or faces.

The game is rather simplistic but offers a decent difficulty for those interested in this side scrolling adventure.
You have only one weapon, an assortment of accessories to boost your stats, a flying magical squirrel as a sidekick, and a combo counter.  While not overly difficult, Dust presents a multitude of enemies that swarm the character which can disrupt combos and land damaging hits.   Learning how to combo is a must in this game when enemies will simply launch themselves at you.  A dodging system is included as well as a parry system.  Both are effective in this beat em up.
The story is pretty plain.  Nothing much to say about it.
One complaint I have are the game crashes I experienced.  While few and far between, I have noticed that my game crashes when I do not go to certain locations in a proper order.  An example was near the beginning of the game when I had to fetch a young boy from a group of enemies.  Upon gaining the quest and going to leave the village to the left side, my game crashed.  While I thought it was an error of my own computer, I tried again and the game crashed again and again.  I took a different route and I was able to continue unhampered.  This happened again during my efforts collecting 4 items from 4 Houses.  I went in the direction of the 4th House, not the 3rd, and the game ended itself unexpectedly.
The game is good for mashing out combos and finishing in a short period of time, but nothing makes me wish to play it again.  6/10

Wow, this was a game. It's got a fantastic premise and great implementation, complete with a short but sweet story that matches the theme perfectly. Its literally everything I want from an indie game, except for one thing.
This game is ♥♥♥♥ING INFURIATING. Harder than Dark Souls. Harder than any rage quit game. It doesn't have "Artificial Difficulty," where you die, learn how to not die, then move on. No, it's just ordinary difficulty. By the time you're on zone 4, you can expect to be fighting 4 or 5 enemies at once, enemies with complex attack patterns that can teleport your character and reverse your controls, and if you f*** up once, you're so deep in murder beasts that you may as well restart. This game has a threefold difficulty, and each one multiplies the others. If ONE of them was changed, this game would be great fun, but as is, I spent 8 hours playing the last zone and I only managed to make my way to the final boss once. Here's what hurts.
A: All upgrades are temporary. There is a SMALL pool of "Permenant" Upgrades that you can purchase that persist through death, but for the most part, all of the upgrades you can buy are you unlocking items that you -might- find in the dungeon. Every time you die, all your equipment, bonus health, and gold, get removed.
B: The Zones are LONG. One zone consists of three levels and a boss. In order to gain a checkpoint, you ned to beat all three levels AND the boss without dying even once. Once you die, its back to square one.
C: The game is both complicated and fast. This isn't a problem in zones 1 and 2, where the enemies are simple, but once you get to zones 3 and 4, EVERYTHING is a threat that can kill you, and it stacks enemies together whenever possible. Not only that, but each level in a zone has a faster beat than the one before it, with zone 4 lvl 3 at a manic two beats per second. Two turns every second. At that speed, there's no time for reaction, you have to plan out the entire battle ahead of time, which is hard considering that you can't always predict enemy movements. One mistake, and your plan is garbage, just like your body. Now, don't get me wrong, this manic, difficult, fast paced gameplay is exciting and a serious blood rush and I enjoy it... when I have enough equipment to stand a chance. The problem comes in when you spawn in with one dagger and a bomb and you have to fight through a few mobs before you can get enough gold to buy things from the shopkeeper.
All in all, the game, as it stands, requires inhuman reflexes, an ability to memorize and predict at least 5 enemy movements at once, at least 4 turns in advance, and the manual dexterity and rhythm skill to pull everything off.
That said, I did say there were a few things that could be changed to make me SEVERELY reccomend this game, because it's GREAT fun. This game is so much fun, which makes it dissapointing when it tarnishes that fun by crucifying you for even the smallest mistake. So, here are my suggestions for ways to make this game less punishing.
Idea One: Have a better checkpoint system. In addition to a checkpoint at the beginning of every zone, make it so that you have the option to start at the last zone you completed. Beat zones 1 and 2? Good, start at 2 when you die at three. Beat 2 and 3? Start at three. That way you wouldn't lose ALL of your progress.
Idea Two: Have Permanant upgrades that actually help. Give the option to purchase a basic Iron weapon that will spawn in with you, because that dagger is pitiful. Maybe have an upgrade to start with gold so you can buy things from the shop. Galactic Civilizations is a classic, and I purchased this game almost immediately while it was in early access. Unfortunately this game has missed the mark, Stardock just didn't do enough with the franchise to give it 'new life', and while some things they did were exceptional (the customization of everything, see below), it has too many negatives to warrent a recommendation, especially for the price of $50, this is not a $50 title.
What GalCiv3 did right:
- Ship customization is FANTASTIC, they hit the ball out of the park with this one.
- Custom race creation and balance is really interesting and in-depth, great stuff.
- Custom game setup options are plentiful, letting you tune the game to the experience you want.
Areas GalCiv3 falls short:
- The Combat animations are bare bones at best, and while this would be bearable (the particle effects are good, as are the ship models which are completely customizable as mentioned above), the camera controls/modes for viewing are beyond poor, the ship pathfinding for movement is really poor (battles just proceed in exactly the same paths again and again) and the space skyboxes are AWFUL. This really lets it down.
- As just mentioned the space skyboxes are not very pleasant
- The Campaign is not really worth bothering with. It sadly feels like a last minute stitched together skirmish game that unfortunately really doesn't show much love and care.
- The User Interface isn't fantastic by any means. While it's not terrible, there are many unnecessary/overly complicated tabs and windows that just don't need to be there. A Perfect example is the comparison between the Research page in this game compared to the Research page in another Stardock (published) title "Sins of a Solar Empire", SoaSE does a much better job than this game in terms of UI in areas like that. GalCiv just feels clunky.
- No where near enough new content or innovation to make this a worthy successor to GalCiv2. I could have forgiven it if it was an almost PERFECT execution (I adore Homeworld: Remastered, while it does have a few faults, that game is a stunning remake), this game just has so many flaws I just don't get excited when playing it.
TL;DR: Customization options are fantastic, but the game just doesnt feel polished. Clunky UI, clunky battle camera, unpleasant skyboxes, campaign is eeeeh and overall just not a worthy sequel to GalCiv 2.

ORIGINAL REVIEW:
I'm a little disappointed, to be honest, that there don't seem to be many reviews that are completely honest about the state of the this game. I love Stardock and the GalCiv franchise, so this negative review is being written out of love, not spite. It isn't a bad game, but it certainly isn't yet what I'd term "ready for launch."
I'll start with what I've noticed in the first couple hours of playing, so that anyone else who's thinking about shelling out $50 for the game has at least some idea of what's what.
1. Battlecam is a mess. In the normal mode, ships eventually fly out of view of the camera during battles and you can't see what's going on. If you switch to free mode, the controls are so sensitive that the slightest touch will send the camera flying off into the far distance or way too close, making it impossible to see anything. It's very difficult to get the camera into just the right frame.
2. Tutorial is not very thorough. I've played GalCiv I and II quite extensively, and there are a number of new features in this game which are not adequately explained in the tutorial, i.e. intricacies of adjacencies, behavior of ships in battle based on various stats, and more.
3. No espionage. I heard this will be included later as DLC, but why are they going to be charging for something that was a feature in previous games?
4. Units don't gain experience in battle anymore.
5. AI frequently says inane things to you during the game. I had a computer that was "close" to me in diplomacy who nonetheless kept threatening me for no reason.
6. Soundtrack is not seamless, with very noticeable pauses between switching tracks.
7. From what I can tell, you can't concentrate production values on individual planets anymore to focus on military, research, or social production, nor can you adjust taxation level to help with morale. If I'm wrong about this, then that just goes to show that things are not well-explained in the game.
8. No more asteroid mining to help with production.
9. It seems like there's also no more political parties, meaning you can't be ousted from government. I'm not really sure what morale does, in this case. Either way, it makes the game less interesting.
And a number of graphical stutters. I'm sure I'll find more issues as I continue to play--and I do intend to continue to play, and will update my review once I've had more time with it. I have a lot of love for this series, and I want it to succeed. I know from playing the previous games that Stardock will pour a lot of effort into making this the best game they can. However, I cannot honestly say that this game feels ready or polished and, in fact, it rather feels like a rehash of old territory, but with features taken away.
I really hope they make significant progress. I want this to be the best GalCiv yet. It just isn't so far.

This is a worthy sequel to one of the most engrossing and original RPGs to come out in years.
Best features:
- Visually stunning. A blend of technical wizardry and gorgeous design - if your PC can handle max settings and ubersampling then you're in for a treat!
- Sophisticated storytelling. This game does not patronise the player - the sheer depth available within the backstory and surroundings puts most contemporary RPGs to shame.
- Decisions. The huge and meaningful choices you are faced with contribute to some very immersive storytelling.
- Quality franchise. The world in Sapkowski's books makes most fantasy games look pitifully childish by comparison.
- Soundtrack. Way above average for a game.
Worst features:
- Savegames. Once savegames stack up (which they will) the main menu will load very slowly and eventually trying to load a game will crash to desktop. Easily fixed by archiving your saves elsewhere, but not good enough.
- Pacing. Major plot triggers are sometimes sudden and unexpected, so the game whisks you along too fast. Ideally the quest designers would have found a better way to blend narrative with exploration. It sucks to sit through a long story sequence only to reload because you decide you weren't ready yet.
- Decisions. I like puzzle games in general, and I must say that puzzle platformers have really come of age lately with many good and original concepts. In that regard, About Love, Hate & the other ones, is a brilliant example of its genre.
You control two different characters, Love and Hate, both having unique traits making them need to work together to solve the puzzle of each level. Movement is done by clicking the mouse on the screen that - in effect - works as a grid of possible positions - so not the usual stepless movement most abundant in platformers, but it works really well, and as you click a new position for your character to take, their movement towards it is beautifully animated and paced just right.
Backgrounds and cut scenes add to the aesthetic appeal of the game. Surprisingly, even at level 30, the repetitive spoken words of the characters still hasn't got on my nerves. I think it would have done had not the gameplay been appealing and enjoyable.
So far, puzzles are not extremely challenging, but they are fun, making for a nice, relaxing casual puzzle game.
In short, for anyone who likes puzzle games in general, and puzzle platformers in particular, I'd highly recommend this one.

This review will not be kind, and I will be covering nothing but its flaws. If you're looking for someone to sing The Witcher 2's praises, there is nothing for you here. Just downvote me and move on.
After spending 31 hours playing this game, I am finding it extremely hard to understand why this game and the developers (CDPR) are seen as some sort of hallowed, sanctified version of perfection and PC development done right. CDPR (and this game specifically) are brought up as a shining beacon almost every time there is a discussion about other devs making stupid decisions (whether it's QTEs in Tomb Raider, or devs not optimizing for the PC platform, etc), and I honestly could not tell you why.
I really tried to like this game. I REALLY did. I played the vanilla version, and when I found the combat to be impossibly clunky and frustrating, I downloaded the Full Combat Rebalance mod, which definitely fixed the combat but unfortunately didn't fix any of the rest of the clunky, frustrating base game.
-The texture work is distractingly disjointed (with awesome high-res textures right next to disgustingly cheap ones). Overall the game looks good, but why put hours and hours into an awesomely-done texture, and then stick it next to an asset ripped from Mario Kart 64?
-The dialog is well-acted but was recorded at seemingly random volumes. Two characters talking calmly when all of a sudden one of them is talking REALLY REALLY LOUDLY, BUT STILL IN A NORMAL VOICE. It is beyond weird, and ridiculously lazy/shoddy.
-The story is political intrigue by everyone towards everyone, secretly involving everyone. It gets UNBELIEVABLY tiresome, and you stop being surprised by it halfway through. Twists stop being interesting when that's all there is.
-Dialog-based intimidation and charm are always successful (at least for me) so there's really no reason for them to even be there.
-EVERYTHING is pre-scripted. fist-fights are QTEs, story battles that are supposed to be time-based will continue until you kill X number of enemies, and even WALKING THROUGH A DOOR is a scripted event. No loading screen, just stand in front of door and press X, Geralt centers himself against the door, opens it and goes through, and closes it behind him. Repeat for EVERY character! If you have a group of 5 guys, each individual one centers themselves, opens, walks through, and closes. Unimportant, sure, but it is SO HIDEOUSLY STUPID, and would be SO easy to fix.
-Story fights that need to be repeated over and over and overandoverandoverandover.
-Speaking of fights: Combat ends up being a slash or two and a sign or two, followed by 27 rolls around the arena while your signs recharge and the enemies un-bunch. Repeat for 40 minutes.
-You cannot walk freely. You can't jump, and can only climb in pre-ordained places. You can only jump down in pre-ordained places. The whole thing is SUPER stuffy, and this game does NOT deserve to be called "open-world" at all.
Ugh, there are so many more things that I could not stand about this game, but I'm done spending time on this "review" so I'll stop.
If you've made it this far, it's worth saying that the game is not TERRIBLE. If you can put up with its problems, you might enjoy it. I, however, had been lead to think that it was a fantastic world-changing game, and when it turned out to be merely a good game marred by frustratingly stupid design decisions, I was beyond annoyed. Combat was a let-down, the plot was a let-down, movement in the world was a let-down, etc.
I have been a PC gamer all my life. My Dad bought me the full version of Doom when I was 8. I cracked Dark Forces to work without the CD when I was 10. I've played Strife, Ultima Underworld, Wing Commander, Earthsiege & Mechwarrior, Jedi Knight, all the Descents (including both Freespaces), etc.
I have ALWAYS loved the PC, but this latest brand of blind fanboyism just because some dev shows 12% more attention to the platform? I want none of it. Either a game is good because it's good, or it's bad because it's bad. THERE ARE NO OTHER QUALIFYING FACTORS. I wanted to love this game, but I couldn't even like it. 31 wasted hours. Fool me twice, CDPR.

Just finished this on my first playthrough. The Witcher 2, just like its predecessor, proves that Bioware and Bethesda are not the only games in town when it comes to CRPGs with Western plot sensibilities. This game picks up where the first game finishes, including letting you have some of your equipment from the previous game. The best equipment from the first game is very very weak compared to what you'll soon be wielding in W2, however. The story is very engaging, with options to branch off at different points. The quests available are actually quite different in Chapters 2 and 3, depending on which major path you choose at the end of Chapter 1, so this may be worth a second playthrough. The graphics and gameplay are quite good, my only criticism being that it was hard to get close enough to traps and loot to actually manipulate them without getting hurt (in the case of traps). Other than that, the game was a great example of interactive story telling. I highly recommend it, though you should definitely play the first game beforehand, if you haven't already.
One thing to note: this is a "mature" game. The themes, language, and visuals are not kid-friendly. If you are a parent, you should plan on playing this after the kids go to bed. There is nudity and lots of profanity, as well as frequent discussions about prostitution and illigitimacy, among other things. Maybe not a problem for you, but you should be warned up front. This is not family-friendly fare.

Pros:
- With this game, not only do you get somewhat of a challenge (depending on how quickly you can figure out puzzles), but also an incredible art style and adorable little characters.
- Cute concept – Hate, as shown on the right in the picture above, can force the other ones away by interacting with them, and Love, on the left, can bring them toward him. Love and Hate have to work together most levels to reach the button, which then advances you to the next level.
- I was stumped on a few levels and had to take a break before being able to solve them.
- 4 total scenes for this game – cave, castle, machine, and ice mountain – that provide a good contrast to the same basic structure.
Cons:
- A bit short – not enough levels/range of difficulty for me.
- I’d say this is only an easy to medium ranged puzzle game. If you play it straight through like I tried to do, it may get more difficult. My brain decides to poop out on me every once in a while.

A friend of mine told me about this game about a year ago, when it first came out.
We tried it in school and after a few rounds others also showed interest. So they tried it too and just couldn't stop playing.
That's where the addiction started to grow.
It soon became a habit that, as soon as whether I came into the classroom and sat down or until I took my notebook out of my schoolbag, I got asked: "Duck Game?"
You could already tell, that nearly every break was used for playing Duck Game.
But after a few months the premade maps got repetitive and we found out, that we could build our own.
Well ... damn.
So everyone, who was playing along, wanted to build his/her own map. :')
Then another few months later we encountered the opportunity to make our own custom duck hats.
... oh my gosh :P
Everyone wanted to have/make their own hat(s). :'')
It was a hard time for me as I soon had no time in the breaks (and also in some lessons!) to use my notebook for own purposes, like research, checking my mails or just social networks and surfing.
So I started to resist the requests what didn't work that well at the beginning, but I managed to put an end to the addiction of Duck Game in May/June 2016. Not an easy task to accomplish.
So that's my story about Duck Game.
Duck Game is a local/online multiplayer arena platformer for up to four players, featuring deathmatch, team deathmatch and single-player challenges, a map-editor and a variety of hats to be activated/discovered and mods to be purchased by in-game credits.
And this game was created by one man, Landon Podbielski.
There's a wide range of weapons in the game which are spread on the maps and you have to pick them up. But no map features every weapon (except you build your own map where you place every type) so you also have to be able to use any weapon in any situation. All projectiles from firearms and every single swing from a melee weapon are a one-hit-kill. The different types of weapons only differ from the range, the speed and the spread of the bullet(s)/edges. It features very fast paced movement, you're able to swim, glide, slide and pretend to be dead (ragdoll mode). And you can quack!
This game runs on 1080p at smooth 60fps and features a lovely retro-arcade pixel shading.
And all the assets, sprites, whatsoever are created by hand by Landon Podbielski, the one-man developer team behind Duck Game.
As already mentioned there are two ways to customize your Duck Game experience:
The mapeditor simply lets you build your own maps with all objects, weapons and decorations available.
You can also upload your maps to the Steam workshop.
And of course the possibility to create your very own hat. Therefore you'll need a software which allows you to draw pixels and export to PNG file like Photoshop or
and the template from this site
If you have friends and want to challenge them but all the other games get old, get yourself a copy of Duck Game.
You can fight in deathmatch, teamdeathmatch or unfair (a team of three against one). Also there are no rules except the last survivor in a round gets +1 point, but you could also play where one with the least amount of points is the winner ;)
And if you don't have friends ... well the single-player challenges are cool?
No seriously, this is a multiplayer experience.
Overall a solid 85/100
Cheers :)

I can't remember what made me decide to check out Dust: An Elysian Tail in the first place, but I'm glad I did. It's just the sort of 2D, side-scrolling platformer that I enjoy, and I can't believe this game was more or less made by a single person.
There are so many things I could praise in this game. The in-game graphics are colorful, hand-drawn, and really a joy to look at; the controls and combos are fluid and easy to get the hang of; the story and characters are much more interesting than I would have expected, and the writing it pretty damn good, if a little cliche in places. It's obvious that a lot of love went into creating this game and building this unique fantasy world. Moreover, it's just the right length for a game of this type, but still has plenty of side-quests to keep you busy if you want to keep playing.
All that said, there are one or two things that keep me from giving it a perfect score. For starters, my installed codecs interfered with the game in a way that wasn't immediately noticeable. None of the video cutscenes were playing for me (which also affects certain background elements, like the animated campfire at the map screen), and this didn't become obvious to me until the last third of the game, at which point the subtitles started playing for a video that hadn't appeared. After turning off the DirectVobSub codec (not even sure why that, of all things, was causing the problem) the videos began playing without issue, and I realized that I'd missed a few bits of animation that, while not crucial to the enjoyment of the game, really add to the overall feel of the game. To me, it seems strange that these codecs could affect the game in this way, but I've been out of PC gaming for a long time, so maybe it's not as unusual as I think it is. Still, it's a shame there was nothing to tip me off about it until towards the end of the game.
Other than that, some people might be turned off by the animated cutscenes themselves. They do look like something from Newgrounds, and to be fair, they probably were created in flash. However, while they could be better, they're not too bad all things considered.
One thing I see a lot of people say is that they won't play this game because of the "furries". I've never understood this mindset, personally. I understand that there are some (or a lot, even) of people in the furry community whose internet-drama or strange tastes give the community as a whole a bad reputation, but this game has absolutely nothing to do with that. I'm not going to avoid things with anthropomorphic characters just because of a community, otherwise I'd be avoiding things like Sonic the Hedgehog, Kung Fu Panda, Bugs Bunny, and who knows what else. That's just silly.
When I started playing this game, I put it on easy. I hadn't really played games of any sort for a good while, and I thought I'd better start out slow. However, by the time I reached the first real chapter of the game, I was so hooked that I knew I had to restart on the normal setting, since I'm the type of person who won't play through an entire game twice.
...Normally, that is. I'm already tempted to play through again on a higher difficulty setting!
This game has depth and rewards the player that dedicates some time to discover it is FAR more than "Rock, Paper, Scissors" in a card game.

This is not a problem I had with Dust. This beautifully illustrated game flows brilliantly, has a gorgeous soundtrack, and did I mention how nice it looks? The combat flows as well as the exploration and my only gripe with the game is that it seemed a bit too easy playing through on normal; I didn't even have any trouble dispatching any of the bosses and I can count the times I died throuout the entire game on one hand. However this is only a small issue and easily fixed by playing on a higher difficulty and so is nothing to grumble about. Even if there were no option to make combat harder, there are plenty of puzzles too play with also which strike the crucial balance between being challenging and frustrating, making me thing but only besting me when I had played into the early hours of the morning which is a risk this game carries.

If you're a fan of mindgames, this game is for you. Fighting games, when you perfect your execution, become 100% about predicting what the opponent will do, and deciding what the optimal response is to that.
The game is somewhere between rock-paper-scissors, poker, and a fighting game. Every character plays uniquely, and controls game flow in their own way. The rock-paper-scissors mechanic is the most evident on a passing glance, which might give the game a shallow appearance, but the addition of varying damage on your rock and paper options, and varying abilities on each character means that every individual iteration of RPS has a grander significance in the match as a whole. It may well be worth losing three matches to win one very important one later.
If you want to learn basic fighting game strategy, this game will teach you. If you already know it but want to compete with friends who may not have the same level of execution skill as you, this game will do that.
Yomi has the rock-paper-scissors of movement vs attack vs throw, it has mixups, it has meter building, it has supers, and it has much more. The game emulates a fighting game as perfectly as you can in a turn-based format. I think anyone who has a competitive spirit will find enjoyment in it.
The only flaw I would find with this game is it is difficult to grasp the rules in the early stages in a digital format. The physical game made that simpler. I don't know if this is a concern possible to fix in this format, but your first couple games might be rough. Pushing past that is definitely worth it, though.

Yomi is a video game adaptation of a card game that's an adaptation of a fighting video game. Say what? In Yomi, each character is represented by an unique deck that consists of Attacks, Throws, Dodges, Blocks, and Jokers. What makes each character unique are the variable numbers of each cards, character abilities, life, etc. The game plays like a rock-paper-scissor game where things like attacks beats throws, throws beat dodges and blocks, etc. But the game is so much more than that. Depending on which card you use, winning gives you different benefits. Winning with an attack leaves your opponent open to combos (playing straights or special cards to link cards), or winnign with a dodge lets you counter-attack with a single attack. I own the physical card game and this PC version is very faithful to the original source. I highly recommend it to people who love card games or always wanted to play a fighting game but are not too great with inputs, memorizing moves, and other stuff.

It is becoming common to see PC ports of console and handheld games. It is not surprising seeing to see mobile games joining in as well. However, there is a vast distinction between how they are treated initially. While console and handheld ports are only called out if the port was obviously not well done, mobile ports are almost instantly called out as being the worst. This can be the case, but not always. There are some great mobile games that made their way onto Steam, and Blue Giraffe’s games are one of them.
Heart’s Medicine - Time to Heal, being the second installment in the series, brings us straight to a tense situation as you open up to a rushing ambulance. Joe at the wheel trying to drive in the rain while Allison tries to stitch up Daniel as Jenny tries to help. As Allison progresses in treating Daniel’s injuries enough so he can survive the trip to the hospital, the ambulance quickly loses control and plummets off a cliff. You are than left on a cliffhanger as it goes three months earlier to this scene.
This opening easily sets up the type on tone you should expect and a literal cliffhanger that teases you to find out more. Before you do, be ready to learn what has happened that made it escalate, and it does not disappoint. We learn that Allison, whom the series follows, is starting as an intern in Surgery department. But the head of Surgery will not take more than one intern and the other intern happened to be there before you. Sadly, Allison has to wait longer to be in the Surgery department by starting at the bottom of the internship. Luckily this hospital does contain friends, so those who are teaching you already know you and bond even more. And well, all the drama would not be in your forefront as it builds up.
With the first game not available on Steam, it does not seem like you need to play it to get what is happening in this one. As far as I could tell, the first game may of had why Allison decided to get into the internship and establishing the relationships between the characters.
This is where the gameplay starts to help drive the story. The best comparison someone can make is to Diner Dash, as they both focus on your speed. As patients walk in, you need to see where they need to go, correctly assign them, and wait till they tell you what they need. Allison brings in her part as she needs to pick up items you queue up and walk to the patient to administer it. The items come in three categories: some are infinite no matter what, others you need to restock, and ones you need to combine items. As bonuses are included to how quick you are (quick assign, quick treatment, and treatment chain), this can easily throw you off. Especially first getting them and if it takes a while for Allison to pick them up, it can cause some quick treatments to be sacrificed. These treatments can also cause either a touch input, like sliding down a slider, or a minigame to be activated depending on the color of the quick treatment timer. Not to mention the treatments that do not need any input from you cost different amounts of time. There is a lot of learning you do without knowing so you can gauge Allison’s actions to get every quick treatment.
Not to mention there are challenges in each level. One is to just find a guinea pig named Oliver whenever you hear the queue. The other is displayed on the top right of the screen. It can be story based or just something random that I can only imagine Allison doing as either a dare or to make her day interesting. A lot are time based, such as having to clean something up or to use an item within seven seconds of grabbing it, while others are numbers based, like get 15 hearts in this minigame. You do not need to do these challenges, as the story will still turn out the same, but they will give points that may put you over the three star mark. Once the treatment is done, they will be in line to get checked out where you can get a max of five people waiting to get a combo.
I absolutely love the minigames. It gives another level of interactivity as you learn how to do it and try and find out how to do a shortcut. With only 10 shifts per department, not including the extras, you do learn fast as they spread out giving them to you. As you move departments, these minigames change to reflect what that department does. So the Pharmacy will have you find the correct medicine box while the Emergency Room will have you stitch up a wound. And man the sound design in these minigames makes it better.
The point system is not for nothing as well, as with each star, maximum of three, you get 300 coins to spend on upgrades for the department. You do need to know that you will not get enough to buy everything before you leave. It is easy to spend it on upgrades immediately, but replaying it will make you more stingy. Trust me, you need to upgrade the last department.
What stops someone from just sitting there the whole level? It so happens that they thought about this. It is hard to not get a single point. Even if you forgot that a patient wanted something or need to be checked out constantly, you will get points. Try and sit it out, and just get Oliver and maybe the challenge, it will know and make you retry it.
Want more challenges? You’re in luck as there are specific challenge levels spread around! Most are just a harder challenge to do while some brings in Emily, from another series named Delicious Emily, so you can serve food in the hospital canteen. This lets you gain diamonds so you can bring in items to decorate an area of the renovated hospital and so you can get an achievement. Doing everything initially took me 11 hours to do, with the main gameplay taking around 7-9 hours, so the challenges can bring more replayability.
What will happen in the next installment in the Heart’s Medicine story? How is Allison doing after her internship? What drama is going to follow? Answers reside in the next installment, Hospital Heat, which is out now.
+ Good storytelling, certainly went into the hospital drama well
+ Solid gameplay that easily takes in casuals
+ Great audio and music used
+ Pleasing art style
- Can be too repetitive
Heart’s Medicine - Time to Heal is a great casual game. The story providing the drama it promised while also bringing in those heartbreaking moments that always hit you even if you seen it before. The visuals certainly catches the eye as well, and became an easy way to pinpoint other games the same team has made. I certainly would not of found Heart’s Medicine on the app store and I’m glad it made its way to the Steam store.

Being a fan of rougelike as well as music based games, I had high hopes going into Crypt of the Necrodancer, and boy did it deliver.
Soundtrack - 8.5/10:
Not the sort of thing you might listen to outside of the game, but ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant within it.
Progression/Balance - 9/10:
This game is hard.  And every time you die, it's 100% your fault.  Each situation has it's own solution and way out, you just better keep up with the beat.
Replayability - 8/10:
There is a lot of enemy variety, but unfortunately you are going to find the discolored mobs with double health. This is a game where you'll notice the sacrifice and craftsmanship put into it as you play.  I read the man responsible for Dust's "post mortem" blog where he talks about his motives for developing the game and the experience of doing it, and in reading this, Dust went from amazing to inspirational in my eyes.  I'm even a little envious.
It's stylish. You'll meet lovable characters with things to say. Beautiful set pieces; you'll gawk at the hand drawn locales.  The music is epic and beautiful.
If the creator of Dust isn't involved in the video game industry after this pet project of his, a crime has been committed.  An art crime.  And a crime against the concept of rewarding merit.  This guy has more dedication for the art of making video games with substance than all of EA summed together.  Hyperbole, maybe, but this really at least *felt* like the first game with soul I've played in a little while.
That said, I believe you should purchase this game and enjoy it.  You'll even find tons of hidden references to other video games, mostly indie, and even a major nod to the NES's Castlevania 2.
If I had to strain and find a nitpick, I could comment on the combat which is somehow both fresh and may feel limited...  The gameplay is tight, well-controlled and the fighting element of Dust will be whatever you make of it (there's four or five advanced moves to study).
Practice.  Explore the combat.  And I mean it.  You'll need to practice a little in order to keep the combat fresh and feel like you're playing the game in style.  You can just hack and slash through (and shortchange yourself) or try to rack up combos for experience.  Even dodging / countering is somewhat integral while fighting as Dust and they add to the experience, but these elements could largely be ignored by players unwilling to invest a little effort into the game.
Learn the combat system and play with style and the game is fun - but as it progresses, the game may lose appeal if you've been sticking to the same basic moves and trudging through.

In short this game is the first game to use 64bit (a technology over a decade old yet due to consoles was never used in gaming before now). As seen with this AI this step into 64bit has made this game exponentially better, as it is the best 4x AI I have ever played against. This AI is multi-dimensional in terms of play styles and personalities of each of the Races and the it has this impressive ability to pick up new factions. For example you create a race via custom race editor that you can play which is really cool. However it gets grander when with a few settings the AI can actually play your previous race creations as Major factions. I repeat Major faction not minor so this they way you can customize your entire gameplay experience even if you do not like the default vanilla races, or expand it and have 16 races instead of the original 8 lol.
This idea also applies to the Ship designer in regards to simplicity and adaptability it is very easy to pick up and learn the basics and as you play with it you quickly discover it has incredibly powerful advanced options from size, 3 axis offsetting parts, all the way to even adding animations to individual parts or sections. This allows you to be incredibly creative further more these ships can be saved and exported to other games later on as this feature can be quite a time-sink making you fall in love with your creations. Therefore the import and Export tool is incredibly satisfying to see thought was put into taking a old feature and keeping it great if not make it greater.

This is a worthy sequel to one of the most engrossing and original RPGs to come out in years.
Best features:
- Visually stunning. A blend of technical wizardry and gorgeous design - if your PC can handle max settings and ubersampling then you're in for a treat!
- Sophisticated storytelling. This game does not patronise the player - the sheer depth available within the backstory and surroundings puts most contemporary RPGs to shame.
- Decisions. The huge and meaningful choices you are faced with contribute to some very immersive storytelling.
- Quality franchise. The world in Sapkowski's books makes most fantasy games look pitifully childish by comparison.
- Soundtrack. Way above average for a game.
Worst features:
- Savegames. Once savegames stack up (which they will) the main menu will load very slowly and eventually trying to load a game will crash to desktop. Easily fixed by archiving your saves elsewhere, but not good enough.
- Pacing. Major plot triggers are sometimes sudden and unexpected, so the game whisks you along too fast. Ideally the quest designers would have found a better way to blend narrative with exploration. It sucks to sit through a long story sequence only to reload because you decide you weren't ready yet.
- Decisions. This may seem odd, as I already listed this as one of the best things about the game, but the developers get a bit too excited at times and some of the big decision points in the story feel very artificial. Binary choices appear which are at odds with the plot, presumably just because the game hasn't thrown one at you in a while.
Hopefully I've made these minor drawbacks sound like what they are; minor. I was extremely impressed with The Witcher 2. It's a seriously high-quality effort from a studio that has the guts to do things a bit differently.
If you're even remotely interested in RPGs and fantasy, my advice is to play it.

This review will not be kind, and I will be covering nothing but its flaws. If you're looking for someone to sing The Witcher 2's praises, there is nothing for you here. Just downvote me and move on.
After spending 31 hours playing this game, I am finding it extremely hard to understand why this game and the developers (CDPR) are seen as some sort of hallowed, sanctified version of perfection and PC development done right. CDPR (and this game specifically) are brought up as a shining beacon almost every time there is a discussion about other devs making stupid decisions (whether it's QTEs in Tomb Raider, or devs not optimizing for the PC platform, etc), and I honestly could not tell you why.
I really tried to like this game. I REALLY did. I played the vanilla version, and when I found the combat to be impossibly clunky and frustrating, I downloaded the Full Combat Rebalance mod, which definitely fixed the combat but unfortunately didn't fix any of the rest of the clunky, frustrating base game.
-The texture work is distractingly disjointed (with awesome high-res textures right next to disgustingly cheap ones). Overall the game looks good, but why put hours and hours into an awesomely-done texture, and then stick it next to an asset ripped from Mario Kart 64?
-The dialog is well-acted but was recorded at seemingly random volumes. Two characters talking calmly when all of a sudden one of them is talking REALLY REALLY LOUDLY, BUT STILL IN A NORMAL VOICE. It is beyond weird, and ridiculously lazy/shoddy.
-The story is political intrigue by everyone towards everyone, secretly involving everyone. It gets UNBELIEVABLY tiresome, and you stop being surprised by it halfway through. Twists stop being interesting when that's all there is.
-Dialog-based intimidation and charm are always successful (at least for me) so there's really no reason for them to even be there.
-EVERYTHING is pre-scripted. fist-fights are QTEs, story battles that are supposed to be time-based will continue until you kill X number of enemies, and even WALKING THROUGH A DOOR is a scripted event. No loading screen, just stand in front of door and press X, Geralt centers himself against the door, opens it and goes through, and closes it behind him. Repeat for EVERY character! If you have a group of 5 guys, each individual one centers themselves, opens, walks through, and closes. Unimportant, sure, but it is SO HIDEOUSLY STUPID, and would be SO easy to fix.
-Story fights that need to be repeated over and over and overandoverandoverandover.
-Speaking of fights: Combat ends up being a slash or two and a sign or two, followed by 27 rolls around the arena while your signs recharge and the enemies un-bunch. Repeat for 40 minutes.
-You cannot walk freely. You can't jump, and can only climb in pre-ordained places. You can only jump down in pre-ordained places. The whole thing is SUPER stuffy, and this game does NOT deserve to be called "open-world" at all.
Ugh, there are so many more things that I could not stand about this game, but I'm done spending time on this "review" so I'll stop.
If you've made it this far, it's worth saying that the game is not TERRIBLE. If you can put up with its problems, you might enjoy it. I, however, had been lead to think that it was a fantastic world-changing game, and when it turned out to be merely a good game marred by frustratingly stupid design decisions, I was beyond annoyed. Combat was a let-down, the plot was a let-down, movement in the world was a let-down, etc.
I have been a PC gamer all my life. My Dad bought me the full version of Doom when I was 8. I cracked Dark Forces to work without the CD when I was 10. I've played Strife, Ultima Underworld, Wing Commander, Earthsiege & Mechwarrior, Jedi Knight, all the Descents (including both Freespaces), etc.
I have ALWAYS loved the PC, but this latest brand of blind fanboyism just because some dev shows 12% more attention to the platform? I want none of it. Either a game is good because it's good, or it's bad because it's bad. THERE ARE NO OTHER QUALIFYING FACTORS. I wanted to love this game, but I couldn't even like it. 31 wasted hours. Fool me twice, CDPR.

Just finished this on my first playthrough. The Witcher 2, just like its predecessor, proves that Bioware and Bethesda are not the only games in town when it comes to CRPGs with Western plot sensibilities. This game picks up where the first game finishes, including letting you have some of your equipment from the previous game. The best equipment from the first game is very very weak compared to what you'll soon be wielding in W2, however. The story is very engaging, with options to branch off at different points. The quests available are actually quite different in Chapters 2 and 3, depending on which major path you choose at the end of Chapter 1, so this may be worth a second playthrough. The graphics and gameplay are quite good, my only criticism being that it was hard to get close enough to traps and loot to actually manipulate them without getting hurt (in the case of traps). Other than that, the game was a great example of interactive story telling. I highly recommend it, though you should definitely play the first game beforehand, if you haven't already.
One thing to note: this is a "mature" game. The themes, language, and visuals are not kid-friendly. If you are a parent, you should plan on playing this after the kids go to bed. There is nudity and lots of profanity, as well as frequent discussions about prostitution and illigitimacy, among other things. Maybe not a problem for you, but you should be warned up front. This is not family-friendly fare.

I can't even remember for long I have been playing Yomi. I distinctly remember playing the Print and Play physical version in college... that must have been 4 years now at the very least. Needless to say, the game holds up well to repeated play and the Steam implementation leaves nothing to be desired (maaaaybe automated tournaments?).
What
like mindless Rock-Paper-Scissors at first turns out to be a complex interplay of resource management, evaluation, risk-management and reading of the opponent both in terms of making educated guesses about their hands and getting into their heads to guess their chosen combat option.
The character cast is large (10 +10 in the expansion), diverse and very well balanced. The community is active, welcoming and regularly organizes leagues and tournaments at
.
Maybe most importantly, this is NOT a collectible card game. 10 characters have to be unlocked by purchasing the expansion but every character is represented by a single, fixed deck. What may be a downside for those who like customization, this is great for competitive players who are looking for an even playing field. In-game purchases exist but are restricted to cosmetics, stat-tracking and (also grindable) overpowered fun-versions of the characters that can only be used in custom games.
Highly recommended for fans of card and fighting games alike.
Note that you can try the game for free at

I havent finished the game yet but from what I've finished; I've really enjoyed the game so far.
While the game itself is short, each part of the story is split into 3 chapters / games.
For everyone who likes story-driven RPG games, I'd suggest this to you!
However, the game is very weak on the fighting system. You don't need to grind as much as you might expect from the usual JRPGs. Which is fine, but it still needs a bit of extra work in my opinion. There is no variety of monsters aside of the bosses, I wish there were more disgungished differences between the lie monsters but theres barely any in-battle. (Outside of battle they have different looks yes, but in-battle, there isn't much difference. They all have the same attack moves so there's nothing special to it?)
Aside of that: visuals. The visuals in this game are good! As a fan of anime art-style, I felt the art style used here really fit the characters. The pixel art as well is very lovely and I do fancy it quite a bunch. At start the weird filter of the game's first chapter bothered me, but as I proceeded the story; I began to understand it was part of the atmosphere each chapter gives you.
The music is fantastic, very soothing and very nice to listen to. It's very fitting to the atmosphere the visuals & story is trying to give you.
The characters are fantastic as well, there is literally no other complaint other than I wish I knew more about them! Theo does his job great playing the "mysterious" character, and Elfie is way too adorable! Honestly in every JRPG I tend to hate one specific character because of traits that I don't like, but I don't really think theres any character to hate here. All of the characters you get introduced to are reasonable and have well thought-out backgrounds. Some remain more mysterious than the other, which is fine as it leaves things better to interpretation to how they may be like outside of our protagonist's views! Each story is left with an "open-ending" to what happens next to these characters aside of the protagonists and I like that.
Honestly, my only complaint about this game is: I wish it was longer! I wish the plots were longer as well, or that one chapter had more to it than the main plot and the tiny errands you do! Because the plots are so short, the maps are short as well. There is barely anything to explore. However if you're bored, inbetween you might come to find some interesting things. (I stole money from the snake lady just by checking out one of her bookshelves haha!)

This is a game where you'll notice the sacrifice and craftsmanship put into it as you play.  I read the man responsible for Dust's "post mortem" blog where he talks about his motives for developing the game and the experience of doing it, and in reading this, Dust went from amazing to inspirational in my eyes.  I'm even a little envious.
It's stylish. You'll meet lovable characters with things to say. Beautiful set pieces; you'll gawk at the hand drawn locales.  The music is epic and beautiful.
If the creator of Dust isn't involved in the video game industry after this pet project of his, a crime has been committed.  An art crime.  And a crime against the concept of rewarding merit.  This guy has more dedication for the art of making video games with substance than all of EA summed together.  Hyperbole, maybe, but this really at least *felt* like the first game with soul I've played in a little while.
That said, I believe you should purchase this game and enjoy it.  You'll even find tons of hidden references to other video games, mostly indie, and even a major nod to the NES's Castlevania 2.
If I had to strain and find a nitpick, I could comment on the combat which is somehow both fresh and may feel limited...  The gameplay is tight, well-controlled and the fighting element of Dust will be whatever you make of it (there's four or five advanced moves to study).
Practice.  Explore the combat.  And I mean it.  You'll need to practice a little in order to keep the combat fresh and feel like you're playing the game in style.  You can just hack and slash through (and shortchange yourself) or try to rack up combos for experience.  Even dodging / countering is somewhat integral while fighting as Dust and they add to the experience, but these elements could largely be ignored by players unwilling to invest a little effort into the game.
Learn the combat system and play with style and the game is fun - but as it progresses, the game may lose appeal if you've been sticking to the same basic moves and trudging through.

Being a fan of rougelike as well as music based games, I had high hopes going into Crypt of the Necrodancer, and boy did it deliver.
Soundtrack - 8.5/10:
Not the sort of thing you might listen to outside of the game, but ♥♥♥♥ing brilliant within it.
Progression/Balance - 9/10:
This game is hard.  And every time you die, it's 100% your fault.  Each situation has it's own solution and way out, you just better keep up with the beat.
Replayability - 8/10:
There is a lot of enemy variety, but unfortunately you are going to find the discolored mobs with double health.  Some of the creeps can get a little repetitive, but they're not meant to be a huge deal.  The bosses and tougher mobs are fresh every time, and each room requires a different fast-paced approach.
Overall, this is a great rougelike, a great rythym game, and a decent rpg.  Would definitely recommend while it's on sale, but full $15 is up to you.

After the disappointment of LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga I was not expecting to like this game; I thought it would be like the first game except without the familiar story. When I started playing however it was apparent that there have been significant improvements. There was a colourful and varied range of characters that seemed to have more personality to them; the tedious challenge mode and super story modes had gone; there was a nice level hub with plenty of things to unlock; the levels were enjoyable. So all in all it was going well and it didn't matter that I knew nothing about the plot of the clone wars. Then came the ground battle levels. These kind of RTS type levels are quite frankly terrible, the units you build do nothing significant, the two sides just keep ineffectually sending wave after wave of troops at each other. The only reason to build up your base is to get the more powerful vehicles needed to destroy the gold and silver buildings then once you have those you can ignore all your units and go and destroy the enemy base on your own. Then there is the sheer quantity of these levels outside the main story line there are about 15 of these that you have to compete twice, once for each side. It is like they removed the tedious parts of the first game then felt they had to fill the void with something doubly tedious. Once you have the super speeder red brick you can churn your way through these a little more easily. So overall I'm giving it a thumbs up because it is enjoyable and a little better than LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga but it does not measure up to most of the other LEGO games.

Heart's Medicine - Time To Heal is the 2nd game in the series.  It is a Time Management game themed in a Soap Opera style hospital.  You move patients to different areas and perform mini games to help them heal.  Once the activities are done, you need to check them out and earn hearts.  Finish each level with the most amount of hearts for Stars, with a different challenge to earn gems.
If you have played Diner Dash, or Delicious, then you have an idea around the basic game play.   The Minigames are a great touch to the casual time management game.
What shines in this game is the story.  This game really tries to cover some tear jerking subjects, and the story has you wanting to complete the next level so you can see what else is going on.
Overall, the gameplay itself is nothing to brag about, but the story is what is going to get you to sound like a crazy person when you tell you friends how much you love this game.
You don't need to play the first game to enjoy this.  The first game (at the time of writing) is not available on Steam, but is available on the developer's website to play.

Final Fantasy VII is the greatest role playing game achievement of my generation.
