may have a rather cumbersome title, but its gameplay is far from that. In fact, it's a very good puzzle game - it may have the looks of a platformer, but just like
, to which it shows some resemblances, its not. The developers are the four guys of  Black Pants Studio, a German indie development studio who have given us the amazing
/ in 2012. With this second game, released late 2014, they have really established themselves as a studio to watch.
Controlling two small cubes, representing the two characters love and hate, the player can alter his surroundigs to a certain extent by influencing the position or behaviour of "the other ones". This in order to get to the "red button", which has to be pushed to move on to the next level. An amazingly simple and original concept, almost executed to perfection. Almost, since the difficulty of the 80 levels rather varies a lot: the first ones are, as they should be, very simple, but the more difficult ones are not only found towards the end, but also quite early on. This may discourage players looking for a very relaxing session, but its only a very minor quibble. Some may even find it an advantage. Otherwise, this game offers the perfect amount of casual gameplay, to be taken in as short snippets as one wants since most levels can be completed in a couple of minutes or less.
The visual style is spot-on too, with four different worlds offering the necessary contrasts yet staying within the same basic concept. A few cutscenes offer some cute, silent storytelling, where the two minimalistic figures even manage to convey some emotions. Great!
Overall score: 8,5/10

Galactic Civilizations 3 is the latest in a series of space 4X games by Stardock. With this game really what you see is what you get- it really is a highly evolved space based version of civilisation. If you like Civilisation chances are you will love this. That being said there are both positive and negative aspects to this title which sets it apart from its brother. During this review I plan to outline those elements to help you make up your mind on this product. Full Disclosure, I have been a very long term fan of Stardock and their business practises- I backed the game at the $100 “all dlc included” level and in doing so you could say I have a vested interest in seeing this game succeed. That said, I still feel like I should be able to help you make up your mind.
I have been following Galciv3 since it was first announced and released into early access. One of the first things someone may ask is; how much has changed since this game entered early access? Well the game has seen an entire UI, graphical and gameplay overhaul since the initial alpha stages. Generally the patches came out once ever few months and overhauled the entire game each time. I expect this to be a similar pace to what we will see when development of DLC , Expansions and Patches begins. Stardock is very transparent with their community and often lets users see content long before release during dev streams. To get a good idea of just how much has changed, try watching one of their oldest streams before watching one of their newer ones... it is night and day.
Things are changing sure, but how is the gameplay? Well, upon starting a new game players’ have the option of customising everything similar to Civilisation. They may tweak the universe to be as hostile or peaceful as they want, crowded or sparse. Players can even design their own civilisation by choosing traits, style and AI personality. Upon starting players are given a scout ship (exploration), a colony ship (settler) and a survey ship (dedicated goodie hut finder). From here the player strives towards one of multiple goals. All the usual suspects are there in the form of Conquest, Time, Research and Diplomacy- but the game also offers alternative victory options such as influence and ascension. The maps can be any size from small 5 min blastoffs to full multi day megamatches. However if you plan on playing on the highest map size (insane) you will really need a beefy PC. Often the slightly smaller sizes of Gigantic, Immese or Excessive are much more “playable”, but they have made recent strives which have allowed me to play Insane til victory comfortably.
So just how IS performance anyway? The first thing you need to know about GalCiv3 is that it REQUIRES a 64bit OS to play- if you do not have one you really should be barking up another tree. The game seems to use a large chunk of ram and I can imagine Ram speed being a much higher requirement then in most games. Unlike Civilisation games, GalCiv3 boasts pretty impressive multi-core management. Each AI player runs on a single core/thread until all your cores are doing something. After that deal out starts again. Turn speeds will eventually become an issue, but the release version seems much better than it was even a few days ago.
The game is not flawless in its current state. There are bugs and the occasional tooltip error but Stardock says that they plan on supporting GalCiv3 for many years. Currently the plan is to release a series of DLC and Expansion packs slowly over the next few years along with free and sizable patches. How well they actually go with this is yet to be determined but they were generally pretty good with that during the past two GalCiv games. My biggest issue with the game at this time is more the perceived loss of character in the random events. The pictures for these events are not yet as diverse and interesting as they seemed in previous games and I often found myself selecting choices based on stats and ideological desires instead of picking what I would actually do. Another thing which personally irks me is the lack of “Wonders”. Generally there are only a small number of ‘one per galaxy’ buildings which are placed at late places in the tech tree. While in a game of Civilisation the question is “is it worth aiming for this wonder which everyone else could be aiming for”, in Galciv3 it is more like ‘oh, I must be the first person to get this tech. better build the wonder. No need to rush though, likely they have specialised in a different tech tree.’
In a first for the series Multiplayer is also included- though it is normally always best to play with someone you actually know as games could last a long time. Unfortunately the “Play by Email” option which was once common for games such as this is not possible. Multiplayer has not tarnished the familiar features though, nor has it taken centre stage. The signature Ship Designer feature is still very much in play, as is a scripted story based campaign. You can still watch your space battles in a pretty impressive (but hands off) way and you still have a (disappointingly simple) invasion screen. There are no Planet Busters currently (eg Terror Star) but they are planned for a later Expansion pack (much like in previous titles). Overall the gameplay is fluid and polished- playing the game feels much better than playing GalCiv2 did.
Overall I would easily recommend this game, especially if you like the promise of future DLC and Expansion packs. Pros:
+ Fluid mechanics and smooth gameplay
+ Diverse selection of traps, trap parts, gear, guardians, and consumables to mix and match in play
+ Variety of playable characters and maps
+ Variety of enemy minions to kill
+ Daily rewards for logging in and completing quests
+ Orcs Must Die! humor
+ Constant updates
+ Free-2-play (optional microtransactions if that's your thing)
Cons:
- Loot system is a gamble (you will most likely use the starter traps most of the time until you reach a higher difficulty level)
- Some traps are extremely situational or practically useless compared to others
- PvP matchmaking (PvP can be frustrating if solo queing)
- Some minor bugs
Play this game if you:
* Enjoyed playing Orcs Must Die! 1 and 2
* Do not mind grinding for better traps, gear, etc.
* Have a couple friends to play with (or are planning to join a guild)
* Want a challenge, especially solo PvE
* Relish in the demise and death of orcs

The Witcher 2 is one of those rare games in which you do not predict what is going to happen, one of those amazing games that, if you make the wrong decision, you will face the consequences. The thing that makes this so good is that not everything is clear, it is not black and white/paragon and renegade actions.
Of my current hours (37.7), I have played within the span of 3 days. It is an addictive and excrutiatingly hard game(on dark difficulty, which I decided to start on) and while the learning curve is quite steep for begginers, it's well worth it.
Alas there are a few cons to every masterpiece, for example, very little carry over from the first Witcher game (coming from a Mass Effect background) and was quite dissapointing that there were very few references to Alvin or any of the major decisions you made (eg. The scoia'tael beating on your♥♥♥♥♥even if you helped them in the first). Also, I finished the game without any need for the alchemy skill tree, and a lot of tasks such as building the Oathbreakers outfit is long and tedious.
The lack of big bossfights were a little dissapointing and for me personally, the bosses were too easy (except that damn squid).
However, the game makes up for it with breathtaking graphics (especially seeing as it is around 4 years old) and quite fluid combat, along with amazing storytelling elements and interesting plot lines. Although the lore can be boring for some and confusing for others at times as the game attempts to keep you in the dark on various matters.
All in all, fantastic game.

Hunger Dungeon, or more commonly known as Cannibal's basement, is a role-playing video game developed and published by Square in 1990 for the Family Computer as the third installment in the Physical Feeling in a Certain Location series, the sequel to Thirst Office, and the last main series game for the console. It is the first Physical Feeling in a Certain Location game to feature the job-change system. The story revolves around four orphaned youths drawn to a crystal of light. The crystal grants them some of its power, and instructs them to go forth and restore balance to the world. Not knowing what to make of the crystal's pronouncements, but nonetheless recognizing the importance of its words, the four inform their adoptive families of their mission and set out to explore and bring back balance to the world.
The game was originally released in Japan on April 27, 1990. It had not been released outside Japan until a remake was developed by Matrix Software for the Nintendo DS on August 24, 2006. At that time, it was the only Physical Feeling in a Certain Location game not previously released in North America or Europe. There had been earlier plans to remake the game for Bandai's WonderSwan Color handheld, as had been done with the first, second, and fourth installments of the series, but the game faced several delays and was eventually canceled after the premature cancellation of the platform. The Nintendo DS version of the game was positively received, selling over one million copies in Japan.
It was also released for the many other systems: the Japanese Virtual Console version (Famicom version) on July 21, 2009 (Wii) and January 8, 2014 (Wii U), an iOS port of the Nintendo DS remake on March 24, 2011, an Android version on March 12, 2012, a PlayStation Portable version on late September 2012 (Downloadable only version outside Japan via PlayStation Network) and Microsoft Windows via Steam in 2014.

There are a lot of things that I have problems with when it comes to games. One of the biggest ones is 'overstaying your welcome'. See, I don't handle horrendously long games that well. Well... that might not be true. It's probably better to say that developers don't often make a long game a good one. I think this is driven by an industry standard in which long games = better games? Or perhaps you can charge more for a longer game, people might like to pay for a certain number of hours of playtime. But quite frankly, I think that's a horrible justification for long games. That's essentially saying that you made a game long to make the game long. It's like padding on a woman, sure, it might make them seem more appealing. But at the end of the day you're both disappointed. Ironically for the reason behind this game! Lying.
The game's title is a very clever combination of the words 'lie' and 'eat'. You will at some point in the game eat lies. Simple enough, right? Right. You play... well I don't want to spoil the plot for this one so let's just call them Dude and Efi. Efi is the dragon, she can eat lies. Dude is an information broker, but he seems to play detective. That's where the lie-eating dragon comes in. You, the player, deduce what the lies are, and then eat them. You arrive at the scene. Something has gone down. You talk to everyone, gather clues, and then when you're ready to do your deduction game, you're given a few 'lies'. Of the lies, there will be truths hidden. What this means is that you'll have to use your notes and what the lies are saying to deduce which are actual lies and which are truths. You don't want to eat the truth (apparently it tastes bad).
Combat is turn-based like every JRPG and their mum. But that's not so bad because the combat doesn't make up the bulk of the game. Combat is a fine method of progressing through a game, but it cannot carry a game. That's where the rest of the game's elements come together. LiEat has a magnificent aesthetic. It reminds me of Pokemon Gold and Silver era. It's also kind of amusing when you realize how the art links together, but that's probably just my gaming quirk. For instance, there's a room with a giant eye in it. Really, it's just two layers. A hole, and a background with an iris looking drawing on it. As you move through the room, the iris background moves with you, making it appear as though the eye is following you for creepy effect! Is that impressive? Not really. But it's my blog and I'm going to squee over it because I think it's awesome. The art style just really comes together. It has this Victorian feel to it... if I'm using that adjective properly.
The music is fabulous! The music really sells the theme. It's classy, it's silly, it's spoopy, it's whatever the tone needs it to be. And it's amazing how I never noticed the transitions until I noticed the transitions. That's not the way I meant to word that. What's a better way to say this? I never noticed the transitions until it was apparent that the mood in the story had changed to fit it? Maybe the best way to say this is that I never noticed transitions. The music always fit the tone and you, the listener, could not distinguish when the tone changed because it's just done that well.
The story is generally rather basic. You could likely tell how things were going to play out well in advance. And perhaps that's the game's intention. Each game (LiEat 1, LiEat 2, LiEat 3) started with some kind of storybook sequence. A myth, a dream, something like that. And you could tell how the dream applied when you started playing the game and talked to all of the characters to get a feel for the scenario that you were about to play. The dialogue is well-written, each of the characters are as interesting as they need to be for their involvement in the plot.
Of the three games, I think the second one was the one best made. The first one felt like the stretching of legs, to see if this game concept would work. The characters are so adorable how could this game concept not work? The deduction game in the first one is rather simple. I got the bad ending first because curious =(
The second game was where the writers really seemed to hit their stride. The setup was great, the characters were rather flaunty, and the deduction game (while still simple) felt more involved. It felt like more work had gone into it somehow. I don't know if that's true, but it's how I felt. And Efi just seemed to be on her game for funsies the most in this one.
I don't think the third game had a deduction game, and this might be why I rate it second. I tend to favor the third game more because it ties together the threads of the first two games, but it didn't have a deduction game and the method to getting the good vs bad ending seems a bit too simple, which I'll spoil because it's that bad. To get the good ending you need to be a certain level before fighting the final boss. That's it. That's not what I want for my story endings! I want some choice that I made earlier in the game to be more significant! But the story itself reveals so much about the characters in the game. And I was more invested in the characters in these games anyway. So I rate three below two for gameplay, but three above two for story.
The thing that wraps this up in a nice little bow is that it's wrapped in a nice little bow. The game is as long as it needs to be. This is the way I like my games. Show up, get in, get out. It didn't drag itself out for the sake of runtime. It didn't drag itself out enough to make me lose interest in the characters. It had three short stories that it wanted to tell. It told these three short stories in a timely manner. And for that I applaud it. It's self-contained, a lesson that I think more developers should take to heart.
At the end of the day, I highly recommend this game. At the time of writing it's $2.39 on Steam. That's like $0.80 per short story. It's worth it, I promise you.

I love this game. It made me smile immediately on starting, and blew my mind pretty much throughout its duration. Sure, it's not long, which for some people is a dealbreaker but I don't mind short games and think it was worth every penny.
If I want more, I will play it again. It saves chapters when you complete the game, and I'm not sure if those remain if you start a new game but I feel that I will be able to dive back in whenever I want without too much issue. Even just the tutorial level would be enjoyable to swim around when I'm bored and have some time to kill.
Anyway. Abzu is a beautiful, serene, delightful game. And sometimes tense, surprising, and even a little scary! What's not to love about a game where you can ride around on a dolphin?! And leap out of the water. I can't count the number of times I dove deeper just to swim as fast as I could to take a flying leap out of the water.
I highly recommend Abzu for anyone who isn't put off by games that aren't action-oriented. I was never bored, and found myself saying "Wow" and embarrassing amount of times, especially later in the game.
As far as gameplay, it is fairly simplistic but it's still enjoyable and the exploration aspect is interesting. There were a few times in deep water I was hesitant to really explore for those collectables and the animal spawning thingies, because let's face it--even in a game the ocean is intimidating. There were a few times, without my robot buddies, where I felt very suddenly alone. Murky waters and the absolutely massive scale of certain areas in the game really makes you feel small and scared. There is one point in the game, I am sure you will know it when it happens, that was just a moment of vague terror as I saw an area opening up before me. One of the few truly worrying moments of the game, after a somewhat disconcerting revelation. Followed by another revelation of the sort that, in retrospect, wasn't surprising but that surprised me anyway.
For the few moments you feel small, and alone, there are many more moments in which you still feel small but in sheer awe. Again, I mention the scale. There are structures and creatures in this game that are just... huge. And swimming up to them is one of the most amazing things. There are moments of the game that aren't even spoilers but that I still don't want to spoil for people because not knowing what's coming and then having it happen left me blown away quite a few times. Probably still would have had I known in advance, but still.
The controls are smooth, in my experience, and somehow surprisingly intuitive once you get a handle on them. They can still be tricky or difficult at times but I never felt like they didn't make sense or didn't respond, more that they responded in a way I sometimes forgot to expect. Although sometimes I did feel like the triple-A press didn't work as it was meant to (gradually increasing speed with each press until your fins light up) but considering this game JUST came out, a few bugs are too be expected.
Speaking of bugs, there are a few graphical glitches, though they lessened when I lowered the fish quality, and was most frequent in huge areas with many or large animals. It was more a problem before the first update. I am sure they will iron that kind of thing out.
It should be noted: story-wise, this is not a blatant plot. It's a wordless game (which doesn't necessarily preclude story) and it shows you the story more through pieces of world-building and occasional events than anything else. There will be no concrete answer. You will have to piece together the things you see. I am okay with that, I think it suits the game very well, and while I am extremely curious about the world of the game, I feel that the concrete answers of some other types of games might take away from the wonder of Abzu. (I wouldn't mind a little book with more info though ;P )
Long-story short, while not for those who prefer action and concrete plotlines, Abzu is nothing short of magical and it has immediately become one of my favorite games. I look forward to replaying it many times to bask in its beauty and swim with the creatures of the deep. (And to have epiphanies when I realize what was and was not foreshadowing)

Fun, fast paced, and super-tense competitive card game where you don't have to collect stuff, build decks, or unlock stuff -- just pick a character and fight!
This game captures the feeling of playing a 2D fighting game very well. Every combat-reveal is super tense and exciting, and you get a real feeling like you are playing against your opponent. Matches are full of drama and twists and turns.
Logistically, it is easy to find a match (I have never waited more than a couple of minutes) at all hours of the night, which is important for a game like this, because the single player is dull and just for practice really. Multiplayer is where it's at. While you wait to be ready to jump in, there are a few short tutorials and reference cards to get you up to speed with how the game works and what each character is capable of.
As a final word of praise, there is real depth and replay value here, with 10 characters to learn in the base set, and 10 more in the expansion. Not just how to play as them, but how to fight against them, as well. Every character is unique and balanced in their own way.
The interface could use some improvement, and I would like some additional features. Hopefully development is ongoing; I've seen indications that it is. Because this game is too great to just leave alone!

Currently the game in the Steam store is just to buy the base characters (10 total), with the other 10 being an expansion you purchase in-game. There are intentionally broken EX characters you can use to goof around with friends, but you can't take them into ranked games.  There's been some confusion as to what you're actually getting so I'm setting the record straight.  Ignore all the people who says it's pay-to-win, there's 0 things you can buy that improve your chances of winning.
Yomi is what happens when you take a deck of playing cards and throw it in a blender with the fighting game genre.  There are combos and combo-breakers, blocking and throws, special moves, super moves with a type of "meter" system, heck there are even knockdowns and mix-ups!  It all translates really well to card format.
The main gameplay is basically rock-paper-scissors on steroids.  Imagine if there were situations where paper could beat scissors but they had to have fulfilled a special condition first, while rock gave triple the points of the others.  It gets crazy and complicated, yet still manages to be nicely balanced, as you can always overcome a disadvantages situation if you know what your opponent is about to do.  The trick is making it as difficult as possible for your opponent to know what YOU'RE planning.  There's 20 characters with different abilities based on actual fighting game concepts, even including a "ranged" character in the mix!
The graphics are pretty basic (this is a card-game after all) but they get the job done.  The art for the special moves is nice at least.  The music is intense and sets the mood, though in the abstract I do kind-of giggle thinking about epic music playing in the middle of a methodical card game.
Despite all the complexity of the system, it's fairly good at helping new players get into the swing of things.  There's a good tutorial and the fighting game metaphor helps players of that genre get into the mindset to deal with the things the game can throw at you.  Basing the character decks on a traditional 52 card system (plus 2 jokers) provides a nice foundation for keeping track of your options, and it has real gameplay implications too.
Overall, Yomi is a really fun, intense, strategic card game that is a great translation of the fighting game genre.

Steam is full of many indie greats. Brilliant, inventively crafted games that spring out of nowhere, and create gameplay formulas so well refined they earn themselves a place within the halls of all the greatest classic.
Whether its the addictive simplicity of One Finger Death Punch, the relaxing, almost zen like experience of playingE uro Truck simulator, or the stylish assassinating that makes Mark of the Ninja so great, there are countless titles on this services whose quality is very difficult dispute.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of those games.
The game hits you right from the get go with its gorgeously bright pixel art, which serve far more purpose than simply creating being a retro aesthetic.
The sharp, bright visuals bring the levels to life in a way that serves the gameplay perfectly, the vibrantly animated enemies movement (and dancing) to the beat in beautiful detailed fashion. The distinctively detailed enemy sprites don't just look great  - they serve to help you plan your attacks, always allowing you to quickly figure out what is going on, even when the hectic beat of the game's brilliant music threatens to eclipse your hand eye coordination.
The bosses especially are a treat, but I don't want to spoil those here. You'll just have to buy the game and discover what they are like for yourself!
Don't be at all surprise if you lose track of time playing this game. Progress is undeniably challenging but it has the "one more go" feeling down to perfection. The more you play, the more you learn the important strategies needed to beat the dozens of different enemies you encounter, the best items to help you progress, and the endless number of secrets. Then you unlock a new character, and the cycle beings all over again.
There is nothing else like this game on the market, and there may never be again. On the surface it is like many rogue-likes, challenging and requiring plenty of time, patient and skill on your behalf, but its rhythmic beat is an addiction that completely changes the way you explore, the way you fight, and the way you win. If you have no sense of rhythm, this is not the game for you.
This game deserves you attention.

I am a long time player of both fighting games, and competitive card games. I've played Fighters since the release of Street fighter 2: Championship edition, and have played games like Magic, Pokemon, and Hearthstone for a long time as well. My review will draw on these experiences.
+++:
There is no pay to win here. Once you own the game, you own it. You will never be forced to fork over more money buying expansion packs or booster sets in order to stay competitive. For a competitive card game, this is HUGE. If you were initially attracted to CCGs such as Pokemon, Hearthstone, or Magic, you know exactly what it's like and exactly how much money you can end up investing into cards that quickly become worthless. There aren't even any grind to win or unlock mechanics here - you've bought a video game, and it doesn't waste your time or demand more money to _actually_ play. Imagine that, in the year 2015.
It is a surprisingly thorough adaptation of the concept of a fighting game - you get to make all of the same exact decisions you'd make in a real match, but at a much slower space. Two concepts were lost in translation, 1 of which being controlling space, and the other being meaty attacks, which has been delegated to a special ability of a single character. Everything else is here, though - pokes, combos, blocks, dodges, throws, special moves, supers, resource management, and most importantly, "Yomi", or, reading the opponent.
You always have access to key information about the match, such as whats in your discard pile, and your opponents discard pile. You always know how many cards are in your hand and your opponents hand, and you can look at your opponents character card to understand their abilities at any time, which can clue you in to what kind of opportunities they'll want to take advantage of. It is through all of this and more that the game has such incredible depth.
---:
The interface isn't exactly amazing. It seems to be adapted from the mobile version of the game, which itself was adapted from the browser version of the game. It's functional and tells you everything you need to know, and it's certainly responsive enough, but it's not as pleasing to look at as other digital card games. The card art itself can be a little inconsistent, too - it seems that multiple artists were involved, and some were clearly better than the others. The music is kind of bland, but at least it's easily muted.
+/-:
I feel the game is being dishonest in listing itself as a $15 title with no DLC. The steam store purchase only grants you half of the characters, and unlocking the other half requires a $15 purchase made in-game. But if you can take a step back and really consider what you're getting here, even at the $30 price point, it is still a good deal. You wont ever have to drop money on expansion sets or booster packs, nor will you have to buy the Super Turbo edition of it next year or anything like that.
If you ever decide to transition to playing with the physical cards, you may be surprised to see that individual character decks cost about $10 each, which would place the price of the full game at $200, not including shipping, and this configuration would not allow mirror matches, either. This is not a price point that would allow you to own a complete set of the game and host tournaments with, but, again, take a step back here - every other CCG tournament on the planet requires you to bring your own deck, and for $10 you get a complete, playable deck. Single cards from "the other" CCGs can cost $10 or more. No matter how you slice it, money invested into this game will reward you with more gameplay options and less ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t than CCGs and annually released fighting games.
Worth mentioning:
As of this review, character unlocks are not shared cross-platform. What does this mean? Buying the game on steam does *not* give you access to characters using their webclient, or the iOS version of the game, and the same goes for the other versions - for example, if you've bought the iOS game and the expansion from the apple store, those unlocks do not carry over to the web client and steam versions - every platform is monetized separately, even in a very silly instance where the steam and web clients are nearly identical and played on the same OS, but are considered to be different platforms. Considering a single account tracks your win / loss records with each character, and stats tracked by unlocked cards are shared amongst all platforms, I am legitimately confused by the fact that unlocks are not shared. If the iOS version were priced to be competitive with other mobile games I could definitely understand this, but it's nearly a full priced game on that platform. They don't really make a point of stating this, so be aware.
As a final comparison between this and the physical version; the digital versions contain characters that have not yet been printed for the physical release. The physical game also includes rulesets for 2v1 and 2v2 combat, but they seem to be considered "for fun only" and no effort has gone into balancing characters around this ruleset, and as a result, the digital versions of the game do NOT include playable 2v1 or 2v2 modes. I suspect this is because the digital versions of the game have primarily served as a test bed for balance checks before David Sirlin had to commit to printing any one character, and the fact that everyone has been meticulously balanced over the course of several years for 1v1 play. Again, be aware of this if you were expecting the digital game to be a 100% feature complete version of the physical cards and their rulesets.
Just like any fighting game, the single player experience is lackluster. You can practice against the AI, with two selectable difficulties, and there is some sort of survival mode for you to play around with, but the meat of the game is in playing against other human opponents. The AI will teach you bad, predictable habits that real people will see right through.

Heart's Medicine - Time to Heal is an amazing game that i absolutely adore. As part of the Delicious Emily franchise, again you are brought back to the town of Snuggford where you will get to enjoy another piece of the series where most of the games are set, allowing you to fall in love with the town that little bit more!
You star as Allison Heart, a new intern at the hospital who's eager to start her first day in surgery. The grumpy surgeon doesn’t want her around, however, so she has to work her way through other areas of the hospital before landing her dream gig. While she tries to repair her career, Allison meets and befriends several other doctors, interns, and patients, all of whom play key roles in the story as it unfolds.
With minigames to play, upgrades to unlock, 90 levels and a few hidden secrets to boot, Time to Heal is great opportunity to flex those Time Management skills in a fun and enjoyable way.
Heart’s Medicine - Time to Heal hits all the right marks for casual gaming perfection. The presentation is top-notch. Everything from the visuals to the music lends itself perfectly to a high budget release. The storytelling is handled remarkably well, building suspense with each short cutscene just like a television show builds suspense with episodes. You'll laugh, you'll cry and more importantly you should BUY this game and help the developers to continue making such wonderful, well created games.

Yomi is a fantastic card game that simulates the mindset and decision making of a fighting game.
This version of the game is basically a quickly made unity game made entirely of static images from the card game itself, and with only half the characters of the full game. Music's generic. UI/Design is pretty low rent.
Everything is pretty low quality except the game play, really. It's the kind of thoughtful, belabored product that you would except from board game maker David Sirlin.
To put into perspective how woefully out of touch the pricing is for this game ($15 for half the cast, +$15 for an additional in game purchase for the rest of the cast), Shovel Knight is the same price as this game.
If the whole cast were available at $15 I would recommend this because Yomi is just a wonderful game with no real competition in terms of genre at the moment. But you're better off just saving money and buying the physical game itself: you get a lot more for your money's worth. This is, at it's heart, a card game, and nothing about this electronic rendition justifies the price point.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2D RPG sidescroller. The protagonist, Dust, wakes up to find himself without memories or knowledge of who he is, but is guided by a talking sword, Ahrah, and a flying compaion, Fidget, as they work together to save the world and find out who Dust really is.
Story
If a great story is your thing, this game isn't for you. Not that there's anything
about the story, exactly, but there's nothing good either - it's a fairly cookie-cutter, predictable plot, and the characters themselves are much the same.
Gameplay
This is generally well done. There is no real feeling of grinding for levels or items in general (maybe a little if you're after 100% completion), combat is reasonably paced and challenging for the most part (Dust Storm is OP but higher difficulties restrict this). I particularly recommend the Cirelian Trials for the real fun (although you will probably need some levels and techniques, like
, before attempting to 4-star some of them).
Audio
Soundtrack is generally great. Arguably the high point of the game. Voice acting is fairly standard, no real complaints or amazing gems to note.
Video
Artistic style is pretty nice. Definitely worth a look.
Overall
It's a good way to spend a few hours, though the replayability of the game is fairly minimal. Overall I would hesitate to recommend the game, particularly at full price, but there's certainly a lot worse you could spend your money on.

Crypt of the Necrodancer Review:
I rate this game: 8.0 / 10.0
Where to start... hmmm... Before the games full release, my friends told me this game was awesome. Looking at it from a spectators view, it didn't feel like a good game. The reason I tried it is because of the game's music. This game has awesome music, and the word awesome cannot even begin to describe how good the music is - awesome is an understatement if anything else. Well, the music better be super awesome because its main theme is a Music-Rhythm Dungeon Crawling Game. Yes, put that cloth down; stop rubbing your eyes, your glasses and eyesight are both fine. MUSIC - RHYTHM - DUNGEON - CRAWLING. Who would've thought combining those elements would make an awesome Rogue-lite game, Brace Yourself Games and Klei Entertainment did. Okay, so, I start playing the game on my friend's game on steam during the early access phase.
MUSIC AND HOW IT PLAYS
That was the starting point that sucked me into this musical addiction of dungeon crawling awesomeness. At the beginning, just like all dungeon crawling games, you don't know anything about the dungeon. You start treading about slowly, and then you realize, how come my movements aren't registering very well, are these controls buggy or broken? NO, you can only move according to the beat, you cannot move whenever you please BUT the enemies and monsters do the same, they move according to the beat. This gives the game a semi real time system and gives you little time for planning strategies. Then, when you want to attack an enemy, you just stand next to them or in range of your weapon and click the direction the enemy is at. Most of the time, you will fight and suddenly another monster comes from the top, then below, then the boss of the stage is coming for you. When that happens, you gotta dance with the enemy on the fly. Each enemy has a different "dance" pattern, and with that, you "dance" with them. This part of the game made me come back for more. When you pull it off successfully, timing the beat perfectly, dodging everything, playing with the game's advance tactics that give a single beat invulnerability, that feeling that rushes through like adrenaline - well it was like that for me.
THIS SECTION SEMI-RELEVANT ONLY
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Aside from that, just like any dungeon crawling game, itemizing is also one of the main fun points of roguelite or roguelike games. I'll write a few ITEM SPOILERS here, so if you want to find out what the items do on their own, you may wanna skip this section. Okay, At first, I loved the Broadsword which attacks 3 spaces in front of where your character is facing, not 3 spaces front, 3 spaces wide - in front of you, that box to the left and right. Unlike other weapons, this is one of the few weapons that can hit multiple targets. For the first few days of playing this game non-stop, I always looked out for the broadsword cause it was my main choice. Itemizing that with Ring of Might which gives 1 damage and combo that with a War Drum that let's you stay in one position without missing a beat and also increase your damage if you stand still. You could possibly one-shot a dragon if you use that combo with the War Drum. Then one day, I asked my friend: " Man whenever I get the Rapier, I feel like I'm bringing myself to death." Just so you know, the Rapier can only hit one target, with a range of two spaces in front of you. IF you attack a target that is two spaces away you lunge toward that target. Basically you attack and move a the same time, but why would you want to do that lunging towards a boss? If the boss doesn't die from that attack, you take a beating from the boss. Then my friend gave me the theory on how the rapier is awesome, and it piqued my interest. I practiced the rapier for another few days and apparently the rapier fit my style of combat. Then, I learnt that best combo with a rapier, Ring of Courage + Rapier. Ring of Courage gives 1 bonus damage and moves the player towards the target if the target is killed. I stumbled upon this combo, I held both items, and I was surrounded, no matter where I move, I'll get hit, and I have half a heart of HP remaining, anything would kill me, so, I YOLO-ed and dash around the battlefield killing everything in my path but eventually dying at the last 3 enemies because i messed up the beat. Along the dance of carnage, I saw myself got hit, but I didn't die, and so I realized, the Ring of Courage moves you one step forward, and gives you a one beat invulnerability. What solidified my choice of weapons to the rapier was this one time, so happen I have a damage boost ring, damage boost boots and a Glass Rapier, yes, Glass... Glass breaks your weapon if you get hit but it does 4 damage - the highest damage in the game, most mooks don't even have 3 HP. And so, with the rhythm and beats of the dancing gods i killed all of "Death Metal's" minions, I proceed to kill "Death Metal" himself, the boss with 10 HP, after a few frustrating side steps to get around his shield, i finally got a position to do a lunge attack with the Glass Rapier and I took it. To my surprise, Death Metal died. I just stood there for the next 1 minute, wondering what just happened. Scratching my head over it, thinking that there is no way possible i can hit 10 dmg in one hit, I finally gave up on figuring it out on my own and checked the wiki. Apparently the Rapier does double damage on lunge. From that moment onwards till today, I finished off most bosses with mostly a rapier.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LONG STORY SHORT, The itemizing in this game is fun and there are so many combinations to try but sadly there are only few favourites among players and people normally only stick to that because the other combinations are not as reliable. Comparing the itemizing to another Roguelite: Binding of Isaac, this game lacks in the itemization department.
ETC
The monsters and enemies in this game are very interesting to "dance" with especially in the final zone. The monsters make me want to come back to this zone with better gear just to try and fight them again. The story plot of the game is interesting but not amazing. In my opinion, it is a great story, I got mind blown at one point, and then mind blown again when I went to character select. So, once again, in my opinion, I think the story is great. Also, after getting the official full release and playing until the end of the story. I found out that you get to play as other characters to progress the story. That in turn makes the replayability of the game pretty good. Even without the extended story from other characters, I already played the entire game from zone 1 to final zone for hundreds of runs. Finally finishing the story, if im not mistaken, there might be DLC for extra levels or just Crypt of the NecroDancer 2 and I CAN'T WAIT FOR IT!!! JUST TAKE MY MONEY!!!
DOWN-SIDE
The couple of downsides of this game, is the lack of itemization options and very limited bosses. Every zone, the final floor will be a random pick from 4 bosses, and the further zones just improve their HP abit and include harder mooks in the boss chamber. I was expecting 10 different bosses in the official release. Only the Final Zone, Final Boss is fixed. The fight was amazing. To put it in words without spoilers, the game basically just told me "THIS IS THE LAST BOSS, HERE IS SOMETHING ENTIRELY NEW YOU NEED TO GET USE TO TO BEAT THE BOSS, NOW GO!!!". Now back to the negative points, the very final part of the story is ludicrous hard and I can't say any further because it would be spoilers. I consider that as a negative because it would frustrate people to a point that they would give up trying. If this game had more bosses, and more items, I believe I would give it 10/10.

Galactic Civilizations 3 is the latest in a series of space 4X games by Stardock. With this game really what you see is what you get- it really is a highly evolved space based version of civilisation. If you like Civilisation chances are you will love this. That being said there are both positive and negative aspects to this title which sets it apart from its brother. During this review I plan to outline those elements to help you make up your mind on this product. Full Disclosure, I have been a very long term fan of Stardock and their business practises- I backed the game at the $100 “all dlc included” level and in doing so you could say I have a vested interest in seeing this game succeed. That said, I still feel like I should be able to help you make up your mind.
I have been following Galciv3 since it was first announced and released into early access. One of the first things someone may ask is; how much has changed since this game entered early access? Well the game has seen an entire UI, graphical and gameplay overhaul since the initial alpha stages. Generally the patches came out once ever few months and overhauled the entire game each time. I expect this to be a similar pace to what we will see when development of DLC , Expansions and Patches begins. Stardock is very transparent with their community and often lets users see content long before release during dev streams. To get a good idea of just how much has changed, try watching one of their oldest streams before watching one of their newer ones... it is night and day.
Things are changing sure, but how is the gameplay? Well, upon starting a new game players’ have the option of customising everything similar to Civilisation. They may tweak the universe to be as hostile or peaceful as they want, crowded or sparse. Players can even design their own civilisation by choosing traits, style and AI personality. Upon starting players are given a scout ship (exploration), a colony ship (settler) and a survey ship (dedicated goodie hut finder). From here the player strives towards one of multiple goals. All the usual suspects are there in the form of Conquest, Time, Research and Diplomacy- but the game also offers alternative victory options such as influence and ascension. The maps can be any size from small 5 min blastoffs to full multi day megamatches. However if you plan on playing on the highest map size (insane) you will really need a beefy PC. Often the slightly smaller sizes of Gigantic, Immese or Excessive are much more “playable”, but they have made recent strives which have allowed me to play Insane til victory comfortably.
So just how IS performance anyway? The first thing you need to know about GalCiv3 is that it REQUIRES a 64bit OS to play- if you do not have one you really should be barking up another tree. The game seems to use a large chunk of ram and I can imagine Ram speed being a much higher requirement then in most games. Unlike Civilisation games, GalCiv3 boasts pretty impressive multi-core management. Each AI player runs on a single core/thread until all your cores are doing something. After that deal out starts again. Turn speeds will eventually become an issue, but the release version seems much better than it was even a few days ago.
The game is not flawless in its current state. There are bugs and the occasional tooltip error but Stardock says that they plan on supporting GalCiv3 for many years. Currently the plan is to release a series of DLC and Expansion packs slowly over the next few years along with free and sizable patches. How well they actually go with this is yet to be determined but they were generally pretty good with that during the past two GalCiv games. My biggest issue with the game at this time is more the perceived loss of character in the random events. The pictures for these events are not yet as diverse and interesting as they seemed in previous games and I often found myself selecting choices based on stats and ideological desires instead of picking what I would actually do. Another thing which personally irks me is the lack of “Wonders”. Generally there are only a small number of ‘one per galaxy’ buildings which are placed at late places in the tech tree. While in a game of Civilisation the question is “is it worth aiming for this wonder which everyone else could be aiming for”, in Galciv3 it is more like ‘oh, I must be the first person to get this tech. better build the wonder. No need to rush though, likely they have specialised in a different tech tree.’
In a first for the series Multiplayer is also included- though it is normally always best to play with someone you actually know as games could last a long time. Unfortunately the “Play by Email” option which was once common for games such as this is not possible. Multiplayer has not tarnished the familiar features though, nor has it taken centre stage. The signature Ship Designer feature is still very much in play, as is a scripted story based campaign. You can still watch your space battles in a pretty impressive (but hands off) way and you still have a (disappointingly simple) invasion screen. There are no Planet Busters currently (eg Terror Star) but they are planned for a later Expansion pack (much like in previous titles). Overall the gameplay is fluid and polished- playing the game feels much better than playing GalCiv2 did.
Overall I would easily recommend this game, especially if you like the promise of future DLC and Expansion packs. The game is a complete, polished and next generation 4X game which presses all the right buttons for me. Galciv3 is like the Cities Skylines to the CitiesXL or Sim City... A game which is much better optimised at doing what it needs to do, capturing the essence of what people love about the genre without killing your computer. With that in mind I say bravo Stardock- and please bring on the expansions, DLC and Steam Workshop (which will be added in version 1.1).

I started playing this game a week prior to release (Beta 6.2), mainly because I was really itching for a good 4x title.  I'm a first time reviewer, and I'm posting because Civ: Beyond Earth was a huge disappointment to me, so I'll admit I was ready for another let down.  But this has been a really fun game so far and I want to see good work rewarded!
I consider myself a strategy game veteran but not a min-maxer, so I set the difficulty at one above normal and dived in.  I got my butt kicked.  The second time I have been more successful, but I have seen the computer making a lot of smart moves.  For example, it noticed my fleet maneuvers threatening its worlds and preemptively declared war, and another AI tried a military build up while I was distracted and tried to stab me in the back.  I dumped all my production into new warships to raise my relative level of power, and it backed off.  All of this was trackable via diplomacy indicators, which was really cool.  While it is still early, it looks like the AI in this game is significantly better than I am used to in the strategy genre which is a major plus (sorry, I am not a fan of multiplayer turn based strategy).
In fact, the game seems in general “designed” for AI – the systems play to its strengths rather than being cool on paper but easily exploitable by a human player.  The diplomacy is awesome, and that is because the AI gives clear feedback on why it is reacting the way it is.  “I need to research diplomacy tech to offset the penalty from my weaker military and the fact that I am trading with their enemy” is the kind of decision making that is actually possible in this game, rather than just being attacked (or ignored) seemingly at random.
Ship design is a blast, and I am a fan of the combat system.  On the surface it appears to be a “rock-paper-scissors” type interaction between offense and defense, but this covers a higher degree of complexity beneath the surface.  For example, some weapons are fast firing and short ranged, others are smaller and more powerful but cost more to research for their level in the tech tree.  So far, it all seems “balanced” and I feel there is a lot of depth here I haven't discovered.
I am also having way more fun with the race designer than I should be.  The fact that you can design your own races (every race in the Warcraft and Master of Orion universe for me), give them custom graphics, and play against them is really cool.
My initial impressions are nothing but positive.  If you are a fan of turn based strategy (specifically, 4x), I recommend this one.  Nice job Stardock

Still in progress through the story, will update when I'm finished. I purchased the game on release but couldn't get through it then because of the bugs. Its much better now but still has flaws.
My biggest problem with this game is the performance. I've got a GTX 1060, i7 4820k and 16 GB of RAM and no matter what video settings I've got I can't get over 60 FPS in most scenarios. Being outside in New Bordeaux is a huge frame tank and I hover around 46 FPS, jumping up or down by 5-10 depending what's on screen. Walking into a building my frames will suddenly jump up to around 70-80, and if I turn the graphics down to low even into 100s, but outside its all the same.
The graphics are pretty good, but not spectacular. The textures are pretty detailed, but look muddy at a distance and the lighting is just a little. . . off. Characters, weapons and vehicles are all really well detailed and so are most items in the environment. The city is detailed and oozes late 60s atmosphere. The music is great, featuring a wide variety of period tunes ranging from Rock to doo-wop and its used to great effect in cutscenes. Still those muddy textures come back to haunt when you're outside in the streets, even though everything is detailed on close inspection, anything in the distance looks a little flat and car reflections are pretty laughable. This amounts to a disapointing phenomnea where the outside area looks pretty bad (and it has the worst performance!) and indoor or closed areas like the abandoned amusement park look pretty good.
So far as I've played the story is pretty good and character animations and voice acting is top notch. It makes for a pretty damn good presentation, with some inconsistencies, such as switching between pre-rendered custscenes and in-game. Combine that with the 60s charm and real sense of place (New Orleans) its pretty easy to get sucked into the world, especially with all its interesting districts.
The gameplay is pretty good for the most part. It feels a lot like Mafia II, but a little more slick for the modern age. Gunplay is pretty fun and I like the way death animations play out, with guys falling over and rolling on the ground groaning, or trying to crawl away. It just feels more visceral and real. The only downside is the repetitive nature of its missions. You are trying to take the city back from the Mafia and it mostly consists of completing small missions in an open world. This gives you the freedom to attack any objective the way you want but eventually it all feels the same. There's only a handful of missions types, like, Kill these guys, steal this truck, raid this base, etc and the different districts just start to feel like set dressing rather than meaningful changes of the environment. Even, the idea of disposing bodies to the gators isn't unique to the bayou, because even when dumping bodies where there are no alligators in the water, after a few seconds a scripted gator will eat the body.
As others may have said, the AI isn't so great. Their combat sense isn't particularly good, sitting in one place and shooting or charging headlong into your fire. Similarly the police situation isn't great either. In mafia II, even if you escaped the police you'd still be wanted possibly on a description of your person or your license plate and you'd have to get those changed. Not so here, you can walk past the police who were just looking for you at the scene of the crime. Similarly the traffic laws system is less well implemented than Mafia II (it might as well not even exist really) and I heard in Mafia II it was less well implemented than Mafia 1.
For me the biggest impediment to my enjoyment is the framerate. If it was just more consistent this game would feel much more polished. I would not reccomend buying at full price, wait for a sale, but its not a bad game.

Alas there are a few cons to every masterpiece, for example, very little carry over from the first Witcher game (coming from a Mass Effect background) and was quite dissapointing that there were very few references to Alvin or any of the major decisions you made (eg. What can I say about Unchained? Well its had a rocky start. I started playing this game right at launch and the base game was incredibly different. I played for about 10 hours total and then put it down since it didnt feel like the right fit for me.
But. Since then, they've patched it considerably and overhauled the gameplay to fit the classic OMD franchise. It feels like a combination of the OMD (Physics) and OMD 2 (Combat). At the point of writing this, I've clocked an additional 126 hours into the game since the overhaul patch :P
I've noticed the reviews are still split between the old and the new version and so I wanted to just show my support of the newer edition! There are still issues and bugs with the game and a need for a streamlined UI (Retry from the in-match client, maybe a little less randomness from the chests, etc) But the overall direction of this game is headed in, is awesome!
Pros:
- Classic OMD feel!
- there are (at the moment) 16ish heros to choose from
- Lots of traps and maps
- New Sabotage Gamemode
- Human enemy Faction (as well as plenty of variations- vikings, fire fiends, pirates, Ice Orcs, etc)
- New Trait system to build your playstyle
- Same old humor :P
Cons:
- Lots of RNG on obtaining traps/gear/traits/guardians
- Some connection issues on multiplayer games and matches (The devs have addressed this)
- Some maps can be pretty hard to do solo, though not impossible
- No way to retry a mission when in a match, you have to leave, go back to the client and relaunch
Back in the day, I would have given it a 5/10, but with this newer version, 7.5/10 for solo content and 8.5/10 if you bring friends.

I totally loved Mafia I & II, the car rides, the music, the atmosphere - and most of all: the love put into the game. However, Mafia III, officer stuff and all, just doesn't make it. While the overall scene-setting is great, as is the atmosphere driving around New Bordeaux, and while I totally accept the change of time and environment and love the extended cut scenes which put everything nicely into perspective, I just miss the love for the game which was so evident in the first two instalments where the developers had added lots of nice details which blended well into the gameplay - such as the car repair shops, the clothes shops, the diners, etc, all of which actually played a role in the game.
With this instalment, it seems to me that the developers were given the task of creating something 'similar to' Mafia II - but at half the cost - or in half the time. I have been playing a few hours now and still haven't found the way to customise your car, have a drink or an eat to increase your health (yeah, yeah, I can find a medicine cabinet here and there, and call in an arms dealer van, but that is way too 'clinical' for me - and totally out of game perspective), or make the police come after you if you commit a simple traffic felony.
I intended to be positive about this game because of my love for the first two instalments in the series, but sorry guys, this simply doesn't cut it. MAFIA III JUST ISN'T AS GOOD A GAME AS MAFIA II. It may be bigger in size, but the gameplay is so disappointing. The fact that I got it at a bargain price soothes the pain, surely, but while I would not go as far as to call this a 'bad' game, it still is a long way from meeting my expectations as a follow-up to a great game series. As I see it, a game in a series should be a step up from its predecessor, and this one just isn't. Quite the contrary. So while I would really like to, I simply can't recommend this game. A disappointment is what it is - and I wouldn't be surprised if it marks the end of what used to be a truly great series. RIP MAFIA.

Hope to see you soon in game people!

I've been a long time fan of the card game and initial web versions and this Steam version is good, though not without it's faults. I'd prefer if the chat window wasn't a separate page and existed within the match screen, and merging my old account to use my preferred name was a little rough, but these are minor nitpicks. A more major nitpick is that the Expansion decks are $15, but if you view it as an expandable card game (and many won't since this is on Steam) then you're getting another 10 decks for what is the normal price of 10 decks, which is not bad. The other bit of microtransactions in the game, collectable cards that track match stats, is completely optional and therefore I feel does not detract at all from the game. (There is also EX characters, but these can be unlocked through gameplay and are just for fun anyway, so I don't really count them)
Overall, there are certainly worse forms of microtransactions out there.
The core gameplay itself is fantastic, as to be expected from one of my favorite card games. It's nice to have an engine arbitrate the matches so there's no arguing over any rulings. The cards are all super high resolution, and the fight animations are entertaining for the simple little things they are. Finding matches has been extremely quick for me, and there's minimal lag in the game itself.
Highly recommended!

LiEat is an underpriced gem. It's really three small games in one, tied together by common characters and a few other details. Each game takes maybe an hour and a half at most to play, so it's certainly short. It has some RPG mechanics, but the combat is (possibly intentionally) fairly one-dimensional. Doors have functional but interesting, or more specifically large, hitboxes. Despite sounding those all sounding like bad characteristics, none of these detracted from what LiEat seemed to be doing and none of them bothered my enjoyment of it.
What LiEat brings to the table, and what caught my attention through all three parts, is a game full of charm. The mechanical and plot choices help present itself this way, making for a game that coheres with its stylistic choices. I never felt like the game was too wordy, yet I found myself repeatedly amused by item descriptions, invested in every character with a portrait I met, and sincerely trying to guess what the next piece of the story would be. The music was pleasant and atomospheric as needed. The game has a built in difficulty setting, if for some reason you want the combat to feel a little more on edge, that felt more organic than most games, where easy/normal/hard is often just thrown in settings somewhere.
All in all, if you're looking for a cute story, some well built characters, and nice music, this is a game worth playing. At a mere three bux, this game earns its price easily.

This game is short, cute, and heavy on the feels in some places. Simply put, it is a good game.
For some people, the length may bother them. It can be finished in about 2-3 hours, if you do not go achievement hunting. The pixil sprite design works well, like something made with RPG Maker or that came out on the Gameboy or NES ages ago. LiEat is divided into three parts; LiEat I, II, and III. All come with this purchase. Each story builds on the character interaction between the heroine and her caring yet curmudgeonly "papa." The other two reoccuring characters that help progress the story and develop the characters are a pair of policemen. And hidden around the game are hints to the final confrontation that occurs in part III.
Besides the short length, one other downside is that the worlds in each part are small, and you will rarely if ever need to go beyond Level 10 for each boss.
Saying any more and I fear I'll start stepping into Spoiler territory, so I'll stop here. Suffice to say, this is a short game but very good and worth the price. if I had to score, I'd give it an overall 8/10.

Let's get THE BAD out of the way first:
1) As others have mentioned, the interface could be better.  It's not very pretty, and there are a few mild annoyances with structure, but honestly you have to remember that this is - at its core - a card game.  If you'd rather not play a card game because the graphics aren't up to your standards , then you have some strange priorities.
2) This game is not customizeable.  If none of the characters appeal to you, you are out of luck.  =/  (NOTE: This is also included as a positive, below.)
So one or two minor complaints.  As for THE GOOD:
1) The creator of this game, David Sirlin, is kind of a big deal in the Fighting Game Community.  He was a pro until a nerve disability forced him to stop competing, so now he's a game designer with multiple big credits, a popular match commentator, and the admin of an educational Youtube channel about Fighting Games.  So he knows his stuff.
2) The game itself is amazing.  Sirlin set out to replicate the "conversation" that happens in high-level Fighting Game play - the headgames, the "I-know-that-you-know-that-I-know" exchanges, and the judgment calls of when to take risks and when to play conservatively - without the 1/60th of a second reflex/dexterity requirements, or the hours and hours of drilling combos into muscle memory.  He succeeded.
3) The game is simple, deep, balanced, and allows for a shocking amount of personal style.  The basic rock-paper-scissors mechanic is core to everything, but the characters manage to play SIGNIFICANTLY differently from one another because of their deck composition and character abilities.  In addition, there has been a HUGE amount of playtesting done (consistently, by hundreds of players, since at least 2010) to ensure that the characters are both true to concept as well as competitive with one another.
4) The game is not customizeable, collectable, or pay-to-win.  You buy the game, you get the same game everyone else is playing.  Period.  The only reason I win (or lose) more than anyone else playing the same matches is because of personal ability, knowledge, and experience.
In closing, I would like to say that I kickstarted this exact game's physical copy last year, for $240.  What I got here cost me another $25 (sale), and I spent it HAPPILY.  Buy it.

Anyway. Abzu is a beautiful, serene, delightful game. And sometimes tense, surprising, and even a little scary! What's not to love about a game where you can ride around on a dolphin?! And leap out of the water. I can't count the number of times I dove deeper just to swim as fast as I could to take a flying leap out of the water.
I highly recommend Abzu for anyone who isn't put off by games that aren't action-oriented. I was never bored, and found myself saying "Wow" and embarrassing amount of times, especially later in the game.
As far as gameplay, it is fairly simplistic but it's still enjoyable and the exploration aspect is interesting. There were a few times in deep water I was hesitant to really explore for those collectables and the animal spawning thingies, because let's face it--even in a game the ocean is intimidating. There were a few times, without my robot buddies, where I felt very suddenly alone. Murky waters and the absolutely massive scale of certain areas in the game really makes you feel small and scared. There is one point in the game, I am sure you will know it when it happens, that was just a moment of vague terror as I saw an area opening up before me. One of the few truly worrying moments of the game, after a somewhat disconcerting revelation. Followed by another revelation of the sort that, in retrospect, wasn't surprising but that surprised me anyway.
For the few moments you feel small, and alone, there are many more moments in which you still feel small but in sheer awe. Again, I mention the scale. There are structures and creatures in this game that are just... huge. And swimming up to them is one of the most amazing things. There are moments of the game that aren't even spoilers but that I still don't want to spoil for people because not knowing what's coming and then having it happen left me blown away quite a few times. Probably still would have had I known in advance, but still.
The controls are smooth, in my experience, and somehow surprisingly intuitive once you get a handle on them. They can still be tricky or difficult at times but I never felt like they didn't make sense or didn't respond, more that they responded in a way I sometimes forgot to expect. Although sometimes I did feel like the triple-A press didn't work as it was meant to (gradually increasing speed with each press until your fins light up) but considering this game JUST came out, a few bugs are too be expected.
Speaking of bugs, there are a few graphical glitches, though they lessened when I lowered the fish quality, and was most frequent in huge areas with many or large animals. It was more a problem before the first update. I am sure they will iron that kind of thing out.
It should be noted: story-wise, this is not a blatant plot. It's a wordless game (which doesn't necessarily preclude story) and it shows you the story more through pieces of world-building and occasional events than anything else. There will be no concrete answer. You will have to piece together the things you see. I am okay with that, I think it suits the game very well, and while I am extremely curious about the world of the game, I feel that the concrete answers of some other types of games might take away from the wonder of Abzu. (I wouldn't mind a little book with more info though ;P )
Long-story short, while not for those who prefer action and concrete plotlines, Abzu is nothing short of magical and it has immediately become one of my favorite games. I look forward to replaying it many times to bask in its beauty and swim with the creatures of the deep. (And to have epiphanies when I realize what was and was not foreshadowing)

Steam is full of many indie greats. Brilliant, inventively crafted games that spring out of nowhere, and create gameplay formulas so well refined they earn themselves a place within the halls of all the greatest classic.
Whether its the addictive simplicity of One Finger Death Punch, the relaxing, almost zen like experience of playingE uro Truck simulator, or the stylish assassinating that makes Mark of the Ninja so great, there are countless titles on this services whose quality is very difficult dispute.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of those games.
The game hits you right from the get go with its gorgeously bright pixel art, which serve far more purpose than simply creating being a retro aesthetic.
The sharp, bright visuals bring the levels to life in a way that serves the gameplay perfectly, the vibrantly animated enemies movement (and dancing) to the beat in beautiful detailed fashion. The distinctively detailed enemy sprites don't just look great  - they serve to help you plan your attacks, always allowing you to quickly figure out what is going on, even when the hectic beat of the game's brilliant music threatens to eclipse your hand eye coordination.
The bosses especially are a treat, but I don't want to spoil those here. You'll just have to buy the game and discover what they are like for yourself!
Don't be at all surprise if you lose track of time playing this game. Progress is undeniably challenging but it has the "one more go" feeling down to perfection. The more you play, the more you learn the important strategies needed to beat the dozens of different enemies you encounter, the best items to help you progress, and the endless number of secrets. Then you unlock a new character, and the cycle beings all over again.
There is nothing else like this game on the market, and there may never be again. On the surface it is like many rogue-likes, challenging and requiring plenty of time, patient and skill on your behalf, but its rhythmic beat is an addiction that completely changes the way you explore, the way you fight, and the way you win. If you have no sense of rhythm, this is not the game for you.
This game deserves you attention.
