Crypt of the Necrodancer Review:
I rate this game: 8.0 / 10.0
Where to start... hmmm... Before the games full release, my friends told me this game was awesome. Looking at it from a spectators view, it didn't feel like a good game. The reason I tried it is because of the game's music. This game has awesome music, and the word awesome cannot even begin to describe how good the music is - awesome is an understatement if anything else. Well, the music better be super awesome because its main theme is a Music-Rhythm Dungeon Crawling Game. Yes, put that cloth down; stop rubbing your eyes, your glasses and eyesight are both fine. MUSIC - RHYTHM - DUNGEON - CRAWLING. Who would've thought combining those elements would make an awesome Rogue-lite game, Brace Yourself Games and Klei Entertainment did. Okay, so, I start playing the game on my friend's game on steam during the early access phase.
MUSIC AND HOW IT PLAYS
That was the starting point that sucked me into this musical addiction of dungeon crawling awesomeness. At the beginning, just like all dungeon crawling games, you don't know anything about the dungeon. You start treading about slowly, and then you realize, how come my movements aren't registering very well, are these controls buggy or broken? NO, you can only move according to the beat, you cannot move whenever you please BUT the enemies and monsters do the same, they move according to the beat. This gives the game a semi real time system and gives you little time for planning strategies. Then, when you want to attack an enemy, you just stand next to them or in range of your weapon and click the direction the enemy is at. Most of the time, you will fight and suddenly another monster comes from the top, then below, then the boss of the stage is coming for you. When that happens, you gotta dance with the enemy on the fly. Each enemy has a different "dance" pattern, and with that, you "dance" with them. This part of the game made me come back for more. When you pull it off successfully, timing the beat perfectly, dodging everything, playing with the game's advance tactics that give a single beat invulnerability, that feeling that rushes through like adrenaline - well it was like that for me.
THIS SECTION SEMI-RELEVANT ONLY
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Aside from that, just like any dungeon crawling game, itemizing is also one of the main fun points of roguelite or roguelike games. I'll write a few ITEM SPOILERS here, so if you want to find out what the items do on their own, you may wanna skip this section. Okay, At first, I loved the Broadsword which attacks 3 spaces in front of where your character is facing, not 3 spaces front, 3 spaces wide - in front of you, that box to the left and right. Unlike other weapons, this is one of the few weapons that can hit multiple targets. For the first few days of playing this game non-stop, I always looked out for the broadsword cause it was my main choice. Itemizing that with Ring of Might which gives 1 damage and combo that with a War Drum that let's you stay in one position without missing a beat and also increase your damage if you stand still. You could possibly one-shot a dragon if you use that combo with the War Drum. Then one day, I asked my friend: " Man whenever I get the Rapier, I feel like I'm bringing myself to death." Just so you know, the Rapier can only hit one target, with a range of two spaces in front of you. IF you attack a target that is two spaces away you lunge toward that target. Basically you attack and move a the same time, but why would you want to do that lunging towards a boss? If the boss doesn't die from that attack, you take a beating from the boss. Then my friend gave me the theory on how the rapier is awesome, and it piqued my interest. I practiced the rapier for another few days and apparently the rapier fit my style of combat. Then, I learnt that best combo with a rapier, Ring of Courage + Rapier. Ring of Courage gives 1 bonus damage and moves the player towards the target if the target is killed. I stumbled upon this combo, I held both items, and I was surrounded, no matter where I move, I'll get hit, and I have half a heart of HP remaining, anything would kill me, so, I YOLO-ed and dash around the battlefield killing everything in my path but eventually dying at the last 3 enemies because i messed up the beat. Along the dance of carnage, I saw myself got hit, but I didn't die, and so I realized, the Ring of Courage moves you one step forward, and gives you a one beat invulnerability. What solidified my choice of weapons to the rapier was this one time, so happen I have a damage boost ring, damage boost boots and a Glass Rapier, yes, Glass... Glass breaks your weapon if you get hit but it does 4 damage - the highest damage in the game, most mooks don't even have 3 HP. And so, with the rhythm and beats of the dancing gods i killed all of "Death Metal's" minions, I proceed to kill "Death Metal" himself, the boss with 10 HP, after a few frustrating side steps to get around his shield, i finally got a position to do a lunge attack with the Glass Rapier and I took it. To my surprise, Death Metal died. I just stood there for the next 1 minute, wondering what just happened. Scratching my head over it, thinking that there is no way possible i can hit 10 dmg in one hit, I finally gave up on figuring it out on my own and checked the wiki. Apparently the Rapier does double damage on lunge. From that moment onwards till today, I finished off most bosses with mostly a rapier.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
LONG STORY SHORT, The itemizing in this game is fun and there are so many combinations to try but sadly there are only few favourites among players and people normally only stick to that because the other combinations are not as reliable. Comparing the itemizing to another Roguelite: Binding of Isaac, this game lacks in the itemization department.
ETC
The monsters and enemies in this game are very interesting to "dance" with especially in the final zone. The monsters make me want to come back to this zone with better gear just to try and fight them again. The story plot of the game is interesting but not amazing. In my opinion, it is a great story, I got mind blown at one point, and then mind blown again when I went to character select. So, once again, in my opinion, I think the story is great. Also, after getting the official full release and playing until the end of the story. I found out that you get to play as other characters to progress the story. That in turn makes the replayability of the game pretty good. Even without the extended story from other characters, I already played the entire game from zone 1 to final zone for hundreds of runs. Finally finishing the story, if im not mistaken, there might be DLC for extra levels or just Crypt of the NecroDancer 2 and I CAN'T WAIT FOR IT!!! JUST TAKE MY MONEY!!!
DOWN-SIDE
The couple of downsides of this game, is the lack of itemization options and very limited bosses. Every zone, the final floor will be a random pick from 4 bosses, and the further zones just improve their HP abit and include harder mooks in the boss chamber. I was expecting 10 different bosses in the official release. Only the Final Zone, Final Boss is fixed. The fight was amazing. To put it in words without spoilers, the game basically just told me "THIS IS THE LAST BOSS, HERE IS SOMETHING ENTIRELY NEW YOU NEED TO GET USE TO TO BEAT THE BOSS, NOW GO!!!". Now back to the negative points, the very final part of the story is ludicrous hard and I can't say any further because it would be spoilers. I consider that as a negative because it would frustrate people to a point that they would give up trying. If this game had more bosses, and more items, I believe I would give it 10/10.

Do you have good enough friends to waste several months in one multiplayer match with?
Then it's your lucky day, since best spreadsheet space emperor simulator finally got multiplayer! There's a chance that you will need all computer power in the world to calculate AI turns if you're playing on biggest map option several days in, but space emperors must be patient, for there's whole hexagonal galaxy to explore! Full of intelligent lumps of Christmas lights and bloodthirsty Space Squirrels, of course.
Just keep an eye over your survey ship, if it's brave captain decides to SURVEY A MOTHERFLIPPING WORMHOLE, it will take years for this ship to get back, their families will be long dead by that time and, most importantly, you will play through early game without anomaly bonuses.
Ever had a feeling that you will only play ONE MORE TURN before going to sleep? And then you realize you grew a beard and missed your daughter's funeral? That's exactly what's gonna happen if you get too sloppy! In Galactic Civilizations 2 i played until  there would be either too much fleets to control every turn without overloading my brain or until i run out of RAM and won't be able to save anymore. It may be VERY specific kind of fun for VERY special
players, but it's basically like Pringle's: you'll eat all of them even if you have whole warehouse full of these lumps of cancer.
There's traditionally not much fun in war and invasion, mainly because instead of controlling ships directly (god, i miss hijacking Antares ships in Orion 2 so much) we're getting pew-pew-laserbeams-sound-in-space-flying-bricks viewer, and so far it seems to miss really fun mathematics Endless Space had in that field (meaning a solid bunch of ship builds and fleet combinations to play around in multiplayer), but even if war mechanics aren't really top notch, AI in this game, that is probably much smarter than general public of this greenish-blue ball we live on, won't let you get bored.
One of the trademarks of Galactic Civilizations series is that AI is a DIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIICK. On high enough difficulties they will try to turn absolutely any situation to their advantage. In previous game you could've spend weeks to annihilate powerful enemy which will later surrender to even more powerful enemy, giving them all their remaining worlds just to troll you (you can, of course, abuse savescam if it made you mad enough). Or long term ally will gradually build colonies around you to protect you from common enemy, and then they will ally to crush you because you had too much ascension crystals. On top difficulties you basically have no choice than abuse known loops in game mechanics to win. It will take time to understand how the whole deal works in long multiplayer matches, game after game of course, but it seems that there's not much diversity of playstyles to exist, even with multiple victory conditions.
Overall improvements in planetary and empire management seems to be really solid, but adding connection bonuses to buildings without option to choose initial colony building seems strange. I can't also find tax slider anywhere. Well, Stardock promised to polish things and add stuff even after release, so they will probably tweak minor gameplay inconsistencies.
I personally liked shipyards in space VERY MUCH.
I still didn't fully dig enough into all mechanics and, frankly, didn't reach actual lategame there, which always turns into hell incarnate at some point, but so far, i give this game 50 000 shades of infrared out of 50 000.
I miss helicopter jokes from old science robot tho.

Its the ultra low quality attention to details that amuse me the most. I like how when most of the guns are fired, the recoil animation is the model's hands sliding up and down their forearms. Or how one of the character poses for holding the pistol is the same as holding a rifle.

Everything about this game is just perfection. Two Genres that would never have worked together, and yet it does, and beautifully at that. Every Zone has a different set of enemies, and the difficulty increases nicely with each zone. The bosses are some of the most clever and innovative bosses I have ever seen in a game. They fit so well with the game, and they still function in fun and unique ways. I mean one of the bosses is basically an entire chess set! From the makers of Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers comes a great casual puzzle game.
The game involves two... uh... gumdrops(?); one with a positive, sunny disposition and the other with a mysanthropic bent. They have to work together to escape each level by pushing a big red button.
I thought the puzzles and mechanics were all fantastic! There's enough variety that things don't get stale, while simultaneously there's enough repetition to ensure the learning curve is pretty gentle. I think of all the levels in the whole game there were maybe half a dozen that really stumped me for a while. I really do have to give a shoutout to those folks at Black Pants for the variety of different... uh... gumdrop people, for their use of clever mechanics and entertaining puzzles!
I also really liked the sound effects, particularly the voices of the two main characters! It never failed to make me smile or chuckle as I progressed through each level.
Ugh... if I have to say anthing (and I feel like I ought to for integrity sake. Weird, right?) then I guess you could critique the fact that the story is pretty non-existent. But... considering the entertainment value of the game and its genre, you *really* can't argue this case *too* hard.

I rarely touch games with Metacritic scores below the 60's, but during one Spring evening, for no particular reason, I was compelled to play Trapped Dead... and I'm glad I did.
Trapped Dead is played primarily in bird's eye view. The camera is adjustable, but the controls needed to do so will take some getting used to.
In real time strategy fashion, the player dictates the action of several characters, instructing them to move, attack, or swap inventory. Unfortunately, the controls here too can often times be unresponsive and confusing, leading to much frustration.
Despite the poor controls and optimization (you might suffer from frame drops), I found myself falling in love with Trapped Dead. Its strategic elements are unique and rewarding. Skills also come into play as you must learn to manage your characters efficiently.
This game is definitive proof to me that review scores are all too subjective. All flaws aside, I'd certainly recommend Trapped Dead.

Okay, so let's break this down in a few different ways, shall we? I'm a recent Yomi fan who's been pretty pumped about this new release on Steam. You're someone who's probably trying to figure out if they should buy this game. Let's see what we can do about this.
Yomi will likely appeal to...
Yomi is the Capcom arcade fighter of card games, literally. Well, not entirely literally--it's not actually a Capcom project, although the game's designer (David Sirlin)
work on Streetfighter HD Remix. It takes the concepts behind the world's most popular competitive fighting games and translates them into a strategic card game.
There's four different types of moves (Attack, Throw, Block, and Dodge) which form an interacting triangle that should be familiar to fighting-game veterans:
damage the opponent and blast through
, which also deal damage and wreak havoc on
(which give you more cards) and
(which let yoou counterattack), which in turn are great counters to
. It's a cycle that gets easier and easier as you play the game, and then you start introducing wrinkles like character abilties, different cards, and special moves.
There's really three parts to Yomi play, and you have to get good at all of them. They feed into one another, so the better you get at one, the better you'll get at others.
you have to be able to look at your hand of cards, and figure out what your strongest options are. If you're low on cards, Blocks become valuable. If you have a lot of high-damage cards, you'll want to look for ways to combo those cards into an attack to deal lots of damage to your opponent. Understanding how strong your cards are in a given situation is key to winning Yomi.
each character plays very differently, and you have to understand what your character's gameplan is--as well as your opponent's character. For instance, Argagarg the fish-person is playing a long game, with a special ability that deals damage to an opponent every turn. Jaina the hothead Phoenix Archer is a reckless rushdown character, with an ability that lets her return valuable attack cards to her hand after she combos them away...but she takes damage for each one.
also referred to as "yomi" by Sirlin and many players of the game, this is the skill of noticing patterns in your opponent's play and exploiting them...while realizing that they know you're doing it and are trying to outmaneuver you. This is the hardest part of the game to get a handle on, and it's a skill you'll have to hone very carefully over time, after you get used to different characters. It's also the most satisfying part of the game: when you get a read just right for the crucial final attack, it's glorious.
So, how's the implementation on Steam? Well, it's largely the same as the web client, but there's a few distinctions I noted, mainly in terms of performance. Steam Yomi is much, much smoother and faster, and it loads all the parts of the game much quicker. Having a bigger resolution is just wonderful, and it makes the cards look even better. So, relative to the web client on
, it's a massive step up.
Now, compared to other digital card games, I think Yomi winds up as a solid middle-of-the-road. It doesn't have the rockstar pizzaz and spectacle that you'd find in Blizzard's
, but the interface you do get is clean, fairly straightforward, and it feels smooth. There's a lot of little touches, like the visuals on the combat wins, which add up to a very enjoyable experience. I'd say it's comparable to what you'd find in the
app, if not a bit better, and it's clearly head-and-shoulders over something like the app for

A long time player of the
version, Yomi is a game very near and dear to my heart. Sirlin, the creator of this game, has slaved away for years to polish it to a mirror sheen.
The game is based on a simple rock-paper-scissors formula. Attacks beat Throws, Throws beat Blocks+Dodges, which beat Attacks in kind. However, the game goes beyond just throwing out options and hoping you win every time. Every character has special abilities and attacks that make some wins more important than others. One character has low combo damage, but every turn that passes slowly ticks away his opponent's life. He's quite content to sit and block all day! But that means everyone wants to throw him, so maybe he should attack in an attempt to beat those pesky throws. What to do? Every decision is tough, but success is so very rewarding!
The game features 20 characters, all very well balanced and have very unique playstyles.  The blazing fast Jaina will stop at nothing to rush you down, while the calm Argagarg will slowly and methodically grind you down. The patient Master Midori will stand against any attack, but once he can turn into a Dragon, it'll be your turn to take the beating! And of course, the community has a large number of guides for learning characters and is always willing to help. So come on and give it a try!

Some of you may recognize me and my name from my work on "Elemental: War of Magic". If you do, then you'll know that I know what I'm talking about when it comes to Stardock games.
Galactic Civilizations III is the successor to the wildly popular Galactic Civilizations II. If you are familiar with Gal Civ II then you should largely know what to expect this time around. There is a multitude of options and settings, performance tweaks and graphical settings. Everything you can think of from Gal Civ II is here and improved upon. Some of the options from the expansions of Gal Civ II are missing, but, if you know Stardock and how they do things then you know those options are coming in future expansions and DLC.
Being the first installment (base game) there are things that can be improved upon, again though if you know Stardock then you know these things are coming down the road. I wouldn't say they left things out on purpose, but more so because they know they have to have content for future expansions. Have no fear that some of those options you may notice that are missing from Gal Civ II WILL eventually be in Gal Civ III as well. If you'd like proof of this look at the base game (no expansions) of Gal Civ II, then look at Gal Civ II Ultimate Edition and everything that was added in between. This is a pattern with Stardock and they will follow the same pattern here.
The Gal Civ series has been my favorite Space 4X strategy series since Masters of Orion 1&2. The only thing lacking in Gal Civ in my opinion is directly controllable battles, though you do still have many options when it comes to battles. What roles you design for your ships and how well you design them plays a huge part in battles, and the battles are epic and beautiful. Ground battles and invasions are a bit "bare bones" at the moment, but I can promise you this will be expanded upon with further updates and expansions as well.
Moddability in Gal Civ III is Off The Charts!!! This time around basically the entire game is opened up for modding, even more so than Gal Civ II, and you don't need to be a master programmer to do it. New mods and content are being worked on as I type this and the future of Gal Civ III is as bright as the brightest star in the universe. There's nothing here not to like.
If you've ever been a fan of 4X strategy games or Space strategy games then the only thing you need to be asking yourself right now is "Why haven't I bought this yet?!?!". Don't miss out on this epic gem of a game. If you only buy 1 strategy 4X this year there's no question in what you should be doing right now. Buy it, you won't be disappointed.

I was introduced into the Galactic Civilizations franchise with number 2 quite a few years ago and I was astonished at how such a great title had slipped past my love of strategy games for so long. I had played it almost too death but then its expansions Dark Avatar and Twilight of the Arnor brought new life and experiences too an already vibrant universe and I once again plunged into the expansive galactic scene in great enjoyment.
With the announcement of the third title you can make a good guess how exited I was too re-enter this universe and couldn't wait too lose myself in it again.
I may not have too many hours currently on record but believe me that will most likely change quickly and so far I'll say the game does not disappoint. It's presentation and graphics are beautiful but as any good video games player knows, good graphics does not always define a good game. The expansive ship designer has made a gallant return and has been adjusted for easier access for new players and greater creativity for more experienced players. Of course the feature that  Gal Civ has been well praised for is it's shear capacity to let the player create the empire he wishes too with no restrictions whether it be an empire founded and risen by war,trade,culture,diplomacy and others ways.
There are a few technical bugs which are caused by either the game and/or the rig your playing on but that's too be expected and I'm sure will be addressed accordingly. However with an interesting single player story and a sandbox mode were absolutely anything can happen, strategy players with minds set on conquering the heavens in anyway they desire will not be let down with Galactic Civilizations III.

I used to play Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga all the time as a kid and I loved it. When I saw this game, I decided I would give it a try... once it went on sale. May the 4th sales finally came and I bought it. What a disappointment. The battles are not nearly as fun as the Complete Saga because they have replaced the lightsaber block with a lightsaber throw which means you are just mindlessly swinging a lightsaber instead of trying to deflect blasts. The battlefields are huge and monotonous to traverse (not to mention they have terrible camera angles.) The whole system of how you destroy blocks is extremely annoying: Only explosions work on silver. Only rapid fire units (which are rare and annoying to use) work on gold, and its not just blocks, but vehicles too. You spend most of you time trying to find a vehicle or weapon that will destroy the one target you need to capture a base. The whole "squad system" and the fact that you must coordinate multiple units to destroy one object is unnecessarily cumbersome in a game that should have simple play mechanics. My biggest gripe, however, is the fact that this game is WAY less intuitive in level design than its predecessors. I've encountered multiple scenarios in most of the missions (including the very first one) where I am completely lost and have no idea what the game wants me to do. This game is just not rewarding enough for me to even consider free play mode.
On the plus side, there are numerous jokes and visual gags in the cut scenes typical of a LEGO game.

Just finished the game with 25 hours on record. That was all the main story, a handful of side missions, and completing all the races in the game. I was originally hesitant on buying the game because of the mixed reviews on the game that I've read everywhere, but I decided to bite the bullet during the Summer Sales when it was $15.
The story in this game was absolutely enough to keep me interested the entire game, and was the sole reason I kept playing. I'd argue that this game is carried almost entirely by the story and characters. There was some repetitiveness within it during the bread and butter of the game but for the most part it was very well done.
Both of these accentuated the story very well. The voice actors did a very good job with this game and getting into character. Almost every character in the game is interesting to listen to.
The game definitely has it's pretty moments, that's for sure. But it's nothing jaw-dropping. I think the best part of the graphical side of the game is how well they did they lighting. The lighting is phenomenal in the game, as well as reflections. The UI wasn't too intrusive and was, for the most part, pretty standard. I think the part I hated the most about the UI was that I couldn't turn it off unless I had a specific mod for it.
The only reason this doesn't get a 10/10 is because I felt like there should have been more music in the game for how much you are listening to it. It felt like at some points I was just listening to the same 3 songs over and over again. The sound engineering in the game is pretty well done for the most part. Nothing in the game sounded particularly bad, and nothing sounded copy/paste from other games. Both of these accentuate the atmosphere & story very well.
The facial expressions, while not perfect, definitely added a nice touch to the main cutscenes of the game. Definitely a lot better than Mass Effect Andromeda's facial expressions originally were before they revised them. Lincoln's face in particular had some really good moments where they got the expressions spot on and it looked well done. In terms of animations, I'd argue they are adequate at best. Not horrible, but nothing innovative or revolutionary either.
The actual gameplay part of this game was extremely repetitive. Throughout what seemed like 85% of the game you are doing the same exact thing over and over and over again. There were a couple new things that popped out every now and then but for the most part it just wasn't that much fun. The only reason I ever got around to beating the game was because the game is, as I said earlier, carried by the story and characters.
I know A LOT of people have been having technical bugs and difficulties with this game on their systems. I, however, have not experienced almost any bugs during my run. I had smooth framerates throughout the entirety of the game, consistently floating at about 80fps majority of the time. The only noticeable bugs I've seen were very small and didn't really hinder my experience that much. I think the most annoying of them all were the bushes made of concrete. The amount of times I've crashed into bushes thinking they weren't concrete walls (silly me, I know) was way too much and became extremely frustrating.
Overall, the game was definitely worth picking up for $15, I would definitely recommend it for that price. I would even go as far as saying the game is worth $30. Full price for the game ($40) is a bit of a stretch though considering what you're getting. If you really wanted to, you could probably just watch the story on Youtube and save yourself the money.

When Final Fantasy VII finally came to Steam I nearly died yo.
This game is one of the greatest games of all time. I first played this game on the PlayStation (when I was only young) I played it several times and again when it was released on PSN and now finally on Steam.
Final Fantasy VII follows protagonist Cloud Strife a mercenary for hire who joins an eco-terrorist organisation AVALANCHE to stop Shinra from draining the life of the planet for use as a source of energy.
Upon its release it was an immediate critical success.
As with previous FF games it consists of three areas: A world map, field maps and a battle screen. What makes this game truly unique is the use of the turn-based battle system in which players command the characters in battles against CPU-controlled enemies. The skill system is based on Materia (magical orbs of condensed life energy) which are used for magic, summons and special abiliies.

Each level is well crafted, creating different situations every time. No two levels are the same.

Price point is a bit steep seeing as the IOS version is $1.99. I got my copy with a coupon for 80% off.

There's no pay-to-win, and no issue of players having better cards due to investing time or money; it's all an even playing field.  You can and should still invest plenty of time into the game, but it comes down to skill and mastery.  Gain -real- experience (not digital XP), learn strategies, practice and improve.  Furthermore, the community behind Yomi is very friendly and helpful.  This game displays the true meaning of good competition and sportsmanship, and is a pleasure to invest yourself into.

Hello,
I've played Yomi on and off since a fairly early beta many years ago.  Over time the game has been refined into a really engaging, deep and most importantly, fun fighting game.  Each character is really strong on it's own merit, and there are no more really bad matchups, just slight advantages/disadvantages, far better than any other fighting game I've played.
Yomi is very accessible and easy to get into, but offers a lot of depth at high level play.  There aren't really overly hard game mechanics to understand.  At its core, the game is sort of rock-paper-scissors, but evaluation gets more involving.  There are always numerous options, which change constantly.  A strong combo can leave you without much hand strength, or get blue bursted(combo escaped).  Using your best and fastest moves early can limit your combat options if you're opponent still has his.  Throwing out and hitting DeGrey's Pilebunker is one of the most #YOLO moves ever, but so satisfying to hit.  It still takes some understanding of your characters attacks and abilities, and how they match up against an opponent's attacks and abilities to do well.  Then you get to the never ending game of trying to outthink and outlevel your opponent, which is really fun.  Being a card game there is some randomness, but it's not an absurd level like Hearthstone has.  Best of 3/Best of 5 sets are fairly standard, even when just casually playing or in a ranked quick match.  Long sets are nice to establish some history and level out the variance.
Presentation wise the game is decent.  I've always found the art to be pretty stylish.  Character design is varied and well-done, thematically and gameplaywise.  Sprites on moves, especially special and super moves is great.  Rook, the Stone Golem punches hard, and doesn't dodge.  The Windmill Crusher special throw looks like it hurts and wow it does.  Setsuki, Ninja girl, is fast and evasive, but with low HP.
Other miscellaneous things:
There are a number of helpful guides for each character over on the official Fantasy Strike forums, hopefully some guides get put up here too.
Cross platform play is pretty awesome.  Hearthstone barely runs on my iPad, but Yomi runs great on it, and the touch interface works well for it.
Spectator mode and replays work well, which is a nice feature.
For new players, I recommend starting with Grave, Argagarg, or Rook, those characters are the most straightforward.  Feel free to give the rest of the cast a try and see who you like though.  Don't think that straightfoward or simple means worse though, I mained Argagarg for years when I started out and he's a still a very solid character.

This game was exactly what I was looking for when it popped up on Steam one day. I really dug it and am looking forward to what comes next in this series, or any other games from the developer for that matter. While I'm sure it won't appeal to everyone, if you're looking for a nice distraction in the form of a time management game then this comes highly recommended.

As a massive fan of both Star Wars and the LEGO game franchise of course I'm gonna love this. If you've played any of the other LEGO games you pretty much know a lot of the basics you're gonna find here. It's a great time, although I did find it infinitely more frustrating than any of the others. You can play the game in pretty much any order you want. There are three branching "chapters" if you will. One centered around Count Dooku, one centered around Asajj Ventress, and one centered around General Grievous. There's no specific order you have to play the levels in, but it almost feels like the game wants you to play them in a certain order, and I can't figure out quite what that order is. There were levels I would play and feel almost lost. There is very little explanation of what you're supposed to do, which is a surprising rarity for the series. While I like not being obnoxiously prompted toward everything and enjoy some challenge, there have already been some times I've had to check game guides to figure out how in the world to do certain things. Destroying gold structures, for instance, requires you to hit them with rapid fire or a consistent laser beam. And I only know that because I looked it up. Not once in five hours has the game told me that, which seems a detriment, especially since the game is meant for kids. However despite that it is a load of fun, and the newly added RTS levels feel very thematically appropriate, since the Clone Wars is, well, war. It works well with the story, and once you know what you're doing it's an absolute blast. Honestly my biggest problem is that it's really buggy for me for some reason, which has kept me from being able to complete certain levels. In one R2-D2 wouldn't hover no matter how hard I tried to make him, and in one Captain Rex completely disappeared after a while, right when I realized he was the only character I had who I needed anymore. But I imagine at least that last problem is something that will be fixed by restarting the level, so while it's annoying I'm assuming it's not too game-breaking.

Stardock took on a daunting task when they decided to revive their classic TBS game after almost a decade. Could they add enough to the game to make it fresh without spoiling what made GalCiv2 great? Could they deliver a game that exceed the golden memories of GC2?
Yes. And they did.
The core of the game remains much the same. Your fledgling empire starts, isolated and alone in an unknown galaxy. Move quickly, colonize new worlds, research new technologies, raise a fleet of warships and crush your enemies into powder. Or sooth them with diplomacy. Or achieve victory by ascending to a higher plane of existence.
There's a lot to this game, too much for the little blurb review Steam provides. The problems with the game stem from the weak AI and various instabilities (a particular issue in the latest builds is a brutal black screen freeze entering the battle viewer).
These issues mar what is otherwise a near perfect release. Stardock promises a constant stream of fixes and updates after release. Keep in mind that the GC2 game that people revere took an untold number of updates and several expansions to achieve.
Stardock's plans for this game are quite ambitious, with a 7+ year timeline of DLCs and expansions. They believe they've caught lightning in a bottle again, and they're right.

About Love and Hate is one of those games that you wouldn’t really go out of your way to play unless you happened to have a couple extra dollars laying around and wanted to kill time, which makes sense that it feels like that as it was originally released on mobile platforms before being recently released on steam. It is a puzzle game that focuses on you alternating between two characters and using their special abilities of pushing and pulling blocks to complete puzzles. The game is fairly slow paced and doesn’t really ever reach a level of difficulty that makes you want to slam your face on your desk and give up like a good puzzle game should. You will quickly burn through 30 levels and wonder when you’re going to get to the actual meat and potatoes of the game.

The way this game was designed feels like a game that was designed with mobile platforms in mind as the levels are something you could easily accomplish while waiting in a line or going to the bathroom, not necessarily the kind of game you would want to binge through on your home PC. As you progress through the game, it does continually introduce interesting gameplay mechanics to attempt to maintain some level of freshness to the level design, such as teleporting, blocks that make you fly, and (literally) dead bodies that act as immovable walls, however; the lack of difficulty remains prevalent throughout which hardly makes the game worth a second run through once you complete the level.
The game is charming and you can easily sink about 3 hours of gameplay into it before you’ve had your fill and decide to move on to the next game. At an asking price of 6.99 this may be a steep premium to pay for the number of hours you will invest in the game, however be sure to double check your inventory for a coupon that knocked the game down significantly lower to $1.40 which at that price you might as well pick it up and test it out.

The Lego Star Wars Games were the first set of lego games and are what made the games so popular with kids and adults alike. They are funny, family friendly and were able to tell a story simply with the character's grunts an giggles. Does Lego Star Wars 3 live up to the expectation?
The first thing you will notice is that the animations have been significantly overhauled which some may consider a good thing and some won't. The characters don't feel or look like toys anymore which I like. There's enough cartoon like momments that make the game feel like you are playing with one massive Lego set but I would have prefered they had just made the animations more realistic and left the character designs like they were in Lego Star Wars 1 and 2.
The game is quite like an RPG. The hub is no longer a small cantina, it is two massive spaceships (republic and seperatist) and a big chunk of space in between the ships. You can hop in mini lego spaceships (and some classics like Slave 1) and defeat the enemy which will convert the planet you are fighting over to your chosen faction.
The levels are what you would expect from a Lego game, simplistic puzzles that an eight year old could solve, straightforward bossfights and lots, and lots of jumping!
Lego Star Wars 3 is a good game but has taken Lego characters to the point were they look a lot more realistic, the animation overhaul is well done but there really isn't much of a challenge to be had.

If you love 4x games, you'll love Galactic Civilizations III.  I'll mention what, for me, makes this game great:
* A wicked AI.  Seriously.  I prefer to play 4x games solo.  I need a good AI to keep me challenged and interested.  On the Challenging difficulty setting, the AI expanded at about the same rate I did (sometimes a little faster), kept up with me technologically and economically, even sent warships ahead of its colony ships to clear out pirates so it could colonize worlds before I could.  It designed its warships to counter the strength of my warships (since we shared a border).  It understood the threat when I moved warships close to its border, which affected our diplomatic relations.  And so much more.
* The Ship Designer.  No other 4x game (or other game that I know of) gives you so much freedom and control in designing your own ships (if you want to; it has a basic template of ships if you don't).  From a palette of basic ship parts, combined with powerful design and even animation tools, you can create awesome looking ships that actually work and fight in the game.  Yes, weapon, defense, and other components matter in the game and can mean the difference between defeat and victory, but designing my own ships and seeing them in the game is just SO COOL.  I even created a warship that looked like a mythical dragon.
* Custom civilizations.  Powerful but simple menus allow you to create your own civilizations quickly, providing many different traits, behaviors, and strategy options.  Ten opponents not enough?  Make 20 more!  Each of them different.  You can even play sandbox games as one of your custom civilizations (which I do).
* Modding.  This game is designed with modders in mind.  Don't like something about the game?  Change it!  There is hardly any gameplay aspect of this game you cannot mess with.
* Insane map.  I like big maps and I cannot lie.  Okay, not everyone enjoys really big maps with thousands of stars.  But if you do, the insane map is for you.  (Beware that management of your empire can take awhile on a map like this.)
There's lots more and I highly recommend this game.  And, Stardock has committed to supporting this game for years to come.  As good as the game is now, it's going to get even better.

I'm writing a negative review not because the game is particularly bad - I've actually quite enjoyed the 40 hours I've put in so far - but becuase the save game method is just utter rubbish.
I'll start by saying that I'm not a save scummer, but I do usually make lots of saves in most games. So when I started Mafia 3 I was a bit dissapointed you couldn't just save the game. But after playing it, it actually seemed ok-ish, it saved regularly sure, so I figure that's ok.
However on loading the game just now, I had a power cut. Upon restarting the game again, all my saves are gone/corrupt/deleted. ALL OF THEM. There is no save from an hour before, a day ago, two days ago, a week ago, NOTHING AT ALL. My entire play history of the game is gone. Wiped clean.
Knowing that this could just happen again, at any time, and I'd be back to the beginning, I simply do not want to play the game ever again. It's for this reason I'm giving this (fairly fun) game a negative review. If I was able to save in my usual method, I would have several saves dating back over the last few weeks to call upon - and sure I'd be annoyed, but at least I would only have a bit extra to do to get back to where I was.
Shocking. Simply Shocking.

The graphics are charming and the appearance and voices of our two protagonists fit them well; Love is round and has a flower on his head with a loud friendly voice while Hate is sharp and harsh with a hissing voice that sounds like hate indeed. Puzzle games are not my main style but some are quite good and this is certainly one of best.

LiEat is very reminiscent of games like Earthbound, where there is a heavy emphasis on storytelling. It is split into three separate chapters with each one telling a self contained plot while all are connected by the overall arc of the main (and side) characters.
The game has an amazing and lovely art style and features some short animated scenes which are able to convey certain events better than its - still very clean and atmospheric - 16 bit (ish) graphics.
You combat different types of lies that will manifest and learn various new abilities as you level up. The combat system can feel a bit simplistic and easy at times but this is only a small issue, as the main focus of LiEat lies (no pun intended) elsewhere: the storytelling.
Even in its short length (took me roughly six hours to complete all three chapters with all trophies) the game made me care deeply about the characters and what would become of them by the end of each chapter. This also acts as a motivation to unlock the best of multiple endings of those chapters.  The soundtrack further strengthens your investment as it is perfectly set up to match the mood of each scene, which can vary drastically from happy-go-lucky to rather dark and sad.
Heart is what makes this game worth every penny and second of your time and this game has lots of it. It would be nice to see more games brimming with heart like this one. Even many of the missable side achievements are acknowledged by the game with a lighthearted pun or some trivia and therefore reward exploration.
My only gripe is that there is not more of LiEat at this point in time, so I am hoping for a sequel in the future.
: A game filled with heart, characters you will be invested in, intriguing stories, clever dialogue, lovely art style, lighthearted comedy and deep feels.
.

This game's had a lot of negative reviews but if you want some cheap and cheerful zombie meets axe to the head action it's not that bad.
It may be slow paced, it may feel a little bit on the dated side, and if you're looking for a story then look elsewhere, it's just a case of getting through the levels and finding ammo or the next survivor to join you, but it's a decent enough squad-based zombie fest all the same. Screenshots and reviews don't do it justice, the graphics are ok, nothing outstanding but acceptable, the gameplay is simple enough ( select a squad member then click where you want him to go and which way to face him). inventory is a basic affair but you can swap items between characters. Tactics aren't too involved, mainly choosing when to run and use stamina (which you also need for melee attacks) or stand and shoot with your limited ammo. I found the best way was to lure the zombies towards a squad member then get another character behind them with a bat or, even better, an axe and then thwack 'em. First aid is administered using the doctor with med packs but these are in limited supply, pistols, shotguns, grenades, all the usual suspects are there.
There aren't too many pickups so ammo is scarce at the start, a few more things to find (and maybe chests etc) would've been a nice addition, levels can feel a bit sparse except for the zombies and some loot locations, instead of stuff lying around, would have given it and extra degree of gameplay. All the negatives aside it's a fun enough game if you just want some relaxed undead bashing.....always a good thing in my opinion !

Wasn't sure what to expect from this. I bought it mostly because it was on sale and because I had just finished Undertale and was hoping for something that was perhaps similar to that, or to To The Moon.
It's quick to see that the combat in this game is trivial and that didn't bother me at first because I figured the emphasis would be placed on the story telling. However the story itself is not particularly interesting. The stories (there are three of them) are very obvious, have no interesting twists, and no serious amount of drama. The game is merely about talking to / interacting with people and objects in a fixed order; there is no flexibility to the story save for in the third story where you have good/neutral/bad endings based on a minor variation at the very end.
I don't really care for the relationship between the main characters, which is something the writer was obviously shooting for. Despite many "d'aww" moments of how cute they look together in some of the art, none of the relationships between characters is particularly deep.
In the end you get a game with neither interesting combat nor an interesting story. There are "puzzles" that are essentially non-puzzles, as they are obvious to the point of not being worth including in the game, and I would have liked to see something more challenging. The stories also tend to be rather rushed, and some of the explanations / motivations behind some of the stories are rather lackluster, in a "and it was all a dream" kind of cliche way (without being that particular trope).
The art and music are fine, but I would recommend either Undertale or To The Moon if you want a similar experience with a more memorable story.

When one of my friends recommended this title to me, it was something I hadn't truly expected to turn out to be so good. I mean, apart for me not really being a 2d fan, the animation for cutscenes looked like an old 1980s cartoon. Thus, firstly, I checked out the game's information online beforehand, watched the trailer, read up on details and was impressed enough in the end by its positive history to go ahead and purchase it. Secondly, duh, as soon as I started the game... I soon found that I'd been given a good recommendation and I couldn't get enough of Dust: An Elysian Tail.
Moving on, In Dust: An Elysian Tail, the game's focus features a young man/the hero whom has forgotten who he is and is helped in finding out his identity/destiny by a sagely, talking sword - Ahra - as well as a flying, female bat kind of creature - Fidget.
Truly, seeing as I was proven wrong about Dust completely, this game is worth anyone's while; even yours, dear reader. As said in other reviews before mine, this game most certainly holds true to being an action/story RPG with an easier than easy yet addictive combat system used against hardy enemies. Then there are the awesomely painted, colorful, metroid kind of styled stages with fantastic music tracks playing in the background. Along the way, you encounter funny and interestingly voiced characters. And last but not least, there's the respectable storyline... which turns out to be very deep, very bizarre, very cool and very well thought out. More so than I would've thought involved in a small Indie/Xbox arcade game.
So, my overall review and rating for Dust: An Elysian Tail? I'd have to saaaaaay... Perhaps a 9/10? Yeah, that seems about right. My only real issue with the game was with boss fights. Apart for the final confrontation, most of the bosses were a bit meh. Otherwise, yes, the rest of the 90% of the title was good and satisfying.

-Hop to the beat of a great original soundtrack, or use your own music to traverse the dungeon and wreck enemies!
-Lots of unique items and enemies with an interesting method of progression.

This is a brilliant title that stands among the greats of innovative music-driven games like Rez and Patapon. By combining the fundamentals of rogue-likes (perma-death, situational and experienced-based strategy) and Tetsuya Mizuguchi-style synesthesia (Rez, Lumines), NecroDancer provides a brand-new gaming experience that is not only engaging but endlessly addictive. As with any good rogue-like, the game includes enough unique items to discover and new enemy types to plot against to make the game last far beyong a single completion.
While the game does include a fantastic soundtrack featuring a great variety of music, one of the game's best features is the ability to customize the soundtrack with your own (MP3-format) music. Using a simple in-game menu to navigate files on your hard drive, you can replace the music for each dungeon floor, boss, and the lobby. A program within the game will automatically find the BPM of your songs, effectively modifying each section of the game to create a unique experience. I would recommend having a listen to the game's original soundtrack a few times, but the custom soundtrack option should not be overlooked.

Normally rogue-like dungeon crawlers get really old really fast, or they have the same old played out feel to them.
However, occasionally, you find the diamonds in the rough, the ones that take an innovate approach to the genre and create something worth playing and paying for. Crypt of the NecroDancer is a really neat game that requires you to progress through each dungeon to the beat of the music pumping in the background, rewarding you for staying on beat consistently. Not only is it addictive and fun, but it's also a fairly difficult game to play. 10/10 Really neat concept that translates well into gameplay.

Dust: An Elysian Tail may sound weird or seem to be just another cliché story at first, but it plays out so much more than that.
The game has characters that are actually lovable and you can see the pain in their eyes when they're sad - Not many games can do that.  Their designs are well made:  A dark past and uncertain future for Dust clouds him in shadows.  Fidget’s childish attitude and comic-relief played out so well, making her less of annoying and more of a slowly developing character.
The fighting style is simple – only using your mouse to attack – but you learn new ways of attacking as you fight and, at least by the final battle, are able to use them to the best of your ability.
The some of the other characters do tend to be cliché - The French-accented guy is snooty; the old lady is crazy; etc. - but they play it off rather well.  Even though I personally didn’t like some of the characters, I eventually felt for their downfall and saw how they move on, giving me a sense of actual humanity behind them.  Now, the voice acting isn’t perfect and for some characters can feel annoying, but it isn’t half bad:  They accent the key points, aren’t afraid to yell when it’s called for, and sound as if they themselves were in these scenarios.
The backgrounds are gorgeous, looking perfect as they are actually hand-painted.  The designs are very creative and work beautifully with the foreground.  The whole world created just moves so fluidly that feels like a nice walk through a forest or a haunting run through a graveyard.
The monsters, in most aspects, are also creative: requiring new ways of attacking, such as parrying or using the Dust Storm, instead of just a straight-up attack.  The creatures actually change depending on which climate you’re in:  Monsters underground look as if they’d evolved underground; monsters in the snow are covered up with jackets; etc.  They all attack in their own ways and give the landscape a much more challenging field to play in.
Overall, I loved playing this game.  The difficulty was fun to overcome and the characters ultimately made me really invested.

Short version:
Journey crossed with Ecco The Dolphin, what more can you want! Awesome experience.
Longer version:
Journey is my second favourite game ever (after Portal), a perfect gaming experience. It was short but I have replayed it about 5 times over the years. It is just a shame that Journey is only on PS3&4, it is a game that every gamer should play. It shows that games can be art and enjoyable and stimulating at the same time.
The trailer for Abzu drew me in, but once I found out it was by one of the art directors for Journey I had to try it. Abzu absolutely has Journey's DNA flowing through it, and the artstyle and gamplay elements are very reminiscent of Journey.
The graphics are gorgeous, much more lush than Journey.
The controls take a big of getting used to, but even when it isn't optimally executed, it is easy enough to progress through the game, it is much easier than Journey.
The "story" is more of an Eco/Gaia influence than the what I viewed as the Buddhist setting for Journey.
The game took me about 2 hours for my first play through, and I certainly missed a lot of the things to see, so I will be replaying it. People in reviews/comments are complaing about the price for the length of the game, but my main criteria is quality over quantity. Sure you could spend a similar amount for a game that will give you 100 hours of gameplay, but will you remember the experience? I bet you won't.
Actually I thought the game was too long. Journey was very perfectly honed, whereas this is padded out artificially sometimes, and I think 20-30 minutes could have been cut.
I would love to play this in VR, I hope the devs are looking at VR support.
Overall great game, though falls somewhat short of the perfection of Journey which still holds up today.

ABZI is a game much like Journey, in both art design (which is unsuprising given who was involved) and in how it feels. If you have played Journey and loved it, ABZU is an easy recommendation, however if you though it was simply okay or didn't enjoy it, ABZU is either not worth it's current price point or simply isn't worth getting.
It is a beautifull game, with stunning art design and music that perfectly compliments the moments it is present in. The controls are solid and the overall experience is amazing. However as suggested above, given it's current price point I would advice people wait for a sale. The game is amazing, but given that simply playing the game as it seems to have been intended I had reached the credits in 85 minutes, which included pausing the game to briefly making a coffee. Those suggest it is significantly longer I can only imagine where padding the time by looking at everything by swimming up close it it and staring at it, which essentially can make any game long.
Put simply, this is a must play experience for anyway who likes atmospheric games and are not bothered by minimal mechanical complexity (I can hardly say there is any present here). It just may be worth waiting for a sale unless you truly feel you have to play it now due to its very small amount of content.

Wasn't sure what to expect from this. I bought it mostly because it was on sale and because I had just finished Undertale and was hoping for something that was perhaps similar to that, or to To The Moon.
It's quick to see that the combat in this game is trivial and that didn't bother me at first because I figured the emphasis would be placed on the story telling. However the story itself is not particularly interesting. The stories (there are three of them) are very obvious, have no interesting twists, and no serious amount of drama. The game is merely about talking to / interacting with people and objects in a fixed order; there is no flexibility to the story save for in the third story where you have good/neutral/bad endings based on a minor variation at the very end.
I don't really care for the relationship between the main characters, which is something the writer was obviously shooting for. Despite many "d'aww" moments of how cute they look together in some of the art, none of the relationships between characters is particularly deep.
In the end you get a game with neither interesting combat nor an interesting story. There are "puzzles" that are essentially non-puzzles, as they are obvious to the point of not being worth including in the game, and I would have liked to see something more challenging. The stories also tend to be rather rushed, and some of the explanations / motivations behind some of the stories are rather lackluster, in a "and it was all a dream" kind of cliche way (without being that particular trope).
The art and music are fine, but I would recommend either Undertale or To The Moon if you want a similar experience with a more memorable story.

Let me start this review by saying I was lukewarm to ambivalent about getting this game at the time I got it... I just wanted something cheap with achievements and trading cards.  The description was slightly interesting, but didn't really draw me in.
THIS GAME IS NOW ONE OF MY FAVORITE STEAM GAMES!
After playing through this game completely, I have to say that it was amazingly good!
The graphics are not anything to shout about, being comparable to NES games or Greyfox or the Elements series.
HOWEVER, the STORY was in-depth and engaging, and VERY imaginative!  WELL worth the price of admission!
Also, unlike many similar RPG's on Steam, this game has smooth and responsive controls (no clunk, yay!), and no bugs that I've noticed (there are probably bugs somewhere, but none that a casual gamer will notice)!
If you want a fun, retro-ish NES-style RPG game that is cheap, has trading cards, and achievements, GET THIS GAME!
If you want a game with an imaginative, interesting story, GET THIS GAME!
If you want a game to gift to a friend that likes old-school RPGs, GET THIS GAME!
This game is middling eay to beat normally.
HOWEVER... if you want to go GOD-mode (G.reatly O.verpowered D.readnought), each of the three games has "Legendary Weapons" hidden somewhere.  The excellent guides on Steam's guide page can direct you to them.
The game is cut into 3 separate games, each with 10 achievements (some of which are pretty funny!  (Happosai achievement FTW!).  None of them are bugged, as far as I can tell, and each chapter is pretty short.  Even shorter if you keep spamming enter and skip all the text, I suppose, but you REALLY want to read the story in this, it's REALLY GOOD!
You don't carry anything over from "chapter" to "chapter", each one is started as a blank slate.  Leveling is quick and easy, with a minimum of grinding involved.
After each "chapter" is complete, you'll appear in an "after-game room" with pics and a sound test book.  Make an extra save here just for fun, and exit to go to the next chapter!
In the last chapter, there are 3 endings, each with a separate achievement... good, bad, and ug... erm, neutral!
As mentioned before, specifics are covered by several well-made guides in the community hub.

(My first impression after 75 of 80 levels.) This is a puzzle game. It is not a platformer. You can't even jump. There is no story. There is no timer. You can't die, but you can get stuck, and then you need to restart or undo your last moves. Each level fits on a single screen, no scrolling.
You guide two black dudes, love and hate, and they can pull or push other dudes around and step on them and on each other to reach the big red button. Since they can't jump and can only climb one step (unless they find one of these updraft hats and position it just right), this usually requires careful planning. You get to meet different "others" as the game goes on. Yes, it's a mobile port, which is why you don't move your dudes directly, but the pathing is fine -- all you need to do is to click on where you want them to go, and they will, if they can. If you misclick, there's undo.
The first 10  levels are the tutorial. It looks like the art changes after every 20 levels, for a total of 4 "worlds", so there are some 80 levels total. (I think there used to be 70, and they added 10 when the iPad version came out.)  The difficulty of the level varies quite a bit; they take me anywhere from 1 to 5 minutes to solve, so let's call it easy to medium diffculty.
I would love for the PC version of this game to have bigger levels, an editor, and Steam Workshop; what is has right now is a small price tag (I got an 80% off coupon for owning
), and enough of a challenge to justify it.
So the question is, how long to beat it? Well, that depends on how smart you are. As I stated up front, I have  beat 50 levels so  far, so the game should be good for 3 hours at least. Is the game inspiring me to beat it? Not really. I think the logic pathways of my brain that can solve "move boxes around" type of games have been exercised plenty before, by games as complex and inspiring as Tetrobot; and that the part of me that wants plenty of small puzzles when I'm bored is still in love with Lyne and its originality (do get Lyne on a touch device).
I like puzzle games, I got this 80% off, I certainly didn't regret getting this game, it's a solid puzzler. Recommended.

It's a bit short, and if you fight every enemy, a bit easy, but that doesn't stop it from being a great game filled with heart. This game is presented as a trilogy, with each part having it's own contained story along with a deeper running plot that winds through all three and comes to a head in the final chapter. Each part's story is fun, and comes with an enjoyable cast of supporting characters to keep you occupied as you pester everyone to play with you. Besides a fun journey with characters I came to care about (impressive, given that I completed everything in under five hours) one thing I totally fell in love with are the achievements. They are often the punchlines to jokes in the game, actions you take as the player prompt the achievement to pop up with a rebuttal or quip about the situation, it's adorable!
If you are looking to get all the bad endings, my one suggestion is to stay low level until after you get the bad endings, if you walk into the final boss fights in each chapter at a high level it may very well become impossible to lose to the boss, who will miss or deal 0 to 1 points of damage.
Totally worth checking out, and be sure to search everything and talk to everyone!

Do I build a long range colony ship and try to colonize that planet on the edge of another faction to hopefully get it before they do? Should I colonize a rmediocre  planet close to me or build a constructor to make a starbase that will allow my fleets and colony ships more range to be a better planet farther out?
Build up infrastructure while neglecting military to improve my economy, but risk being seen as "weak and vulnerable" to other factions? Build your own ships, but then what to put on them? Some defenders with low range and speed but a lot of punch? Fast ships to raid or intercept?
Should I make friends with some ais to get treaties so I won't have to go it alone? Be a warmonger or a diplomat?
What should I research first? Longer range and better engine techs for upgrading ships to explore with or weapons or manufacturing or planetary improvements? Then do I resarch Commerce or diplomacy?
It is all up to you to decide. There isn't really a wrong answer, well, until it blows up in your face :) Each game is different. Life is like a box of chocolates, you never know you decisions were right until crunch time.

What I like best about this game are the aesthetics, the hand drawn sprites, animations and backgrounds are splendid. Albeit the setting and the creatures inhabiting the world is far off from what I like, it does fit really well with the overall theme of the game.
The story is easy to follow and even easy to predict, which I think comes with the territory of making a colorful action-beat-em-up, where the inhabitants of the world are cute animals and everything revolves around a destined hero cleansing said world from evil-doers.
I was expecting more of a challenge, even on normal. You won't notice how powerful you actually are right away, but as the story progresses to the point where a game usually pit a player against more challenging enemies, I was able to slaughter everything put in front of me without lifting a finger. The reason for that is the in-game currency used and the items you loot off dead enemies. The idea is for the player to upgrade the character's equipment in a slow and steady pace (perhaps this is more noticeable on the highest difficulty), but that wasn't necessary during my playthrough.
In closing: I did have some fun playing through this game, but I won't touch it ever again. There's nothing to come back to, not even challenges (if you missed any). If you want to plow through a game of mind-numbing, chain-comboing action during the course of 7-9 hours (you do this over a weekend, not even that) then this might just be the game for you.

Each empire has a unique tech tree, the moral development choices are robust and interesting, and with "specialization" techs, your empire's progression choices feel more important and interesting, rather than just a checklist of things you need to do.
The replayability is fairly strong. Even if you don't have the strongest rig, you can enjoy the Excessive and Insane galaxy sizes. (I'm on an i7 equiv. processor with 16GB ram with an R9 290 graphics card, and Insane runs so well for me that I can tab out, play a youtube video in HD, tab back in, and still play the game.) There are some nice trait options for creating custom empires, and the resource system adds a fair amount of depth. Additionally, the devs do read player feedback and have made design changes based on that feedback before when it is compelling, well-written, and supported by the playerbase.
There is now a robust modding system, and with the first major patch there will be Steam Workshop integration, which means that in addition to a very good vanilla experience you'll also be able to Go Where No One Has Gone Before, defend the Twelve Colonies or find Earth, or even use the Force (once someone gets around to those rather inevitable mods).
I've already found a few custom playable race mods that are fairly impressive. The Kuja are one of them I highly recommend, so long as he updates the mod for release, which I suspect the author will do.
On top of all that, Stardock is offering a once only, never-to-be-repeated FREE DLC of custom ship parts for anyone who has bought the game prior to May 17. Do so, or you'll never get a shot at that DLC again.

I keep getting hint messages telling me what to do.. but still nothing happens when i try and do it. definitely not a game for those who have never played the lego games before. presume you need to be experienced with them before this is any fun
EDIT:
Perhaps I need to clarify a few things that I said above. I'm not saying that the game itself is bad, I can see it is highly regarded by others as a good game. The puzzle solving concept with a lego, star wars theme is right up my street. The problem I have with this game is that I don't feel it is a great choice if you are new to the lego game series. This is the message I wanted to get across to people. I understand that it is a sequel to existing games, however, I would have liked there to be a simple (perhaps optional) tutorial that gently walks a person through the games concepts so that I could play this game without having played any others in the lego series.
Consider my situation and then my experience with the game.
I am someone who has never played any lego game before, I do not have a spouse or sibling here with me to give me a brief overview of how to play the game.
The first thing I do is click start game. I then watch a 2 minute video that sets the scene and the game begins.
The game expects me to know
(1) what the game controls are (I think a lot of people will tend to have a brief look before they play, like I did, but I expect many will like to figure most of this stuff out as they play).
(2) Knowledge about switching players
(3) What actions each character can do
(4) Know how the use special actions with certain characters (e.g. using the force to push an object)
I feel that this is already quite a lot to have to know about, and then on top of all this, if I don't figure all of this out within a 3 minute time period, the characters get attacked by monsters and I failed that bit of the level.
I then get put back to the start menu and click play game, I have to sit through the same 2 minute video again because there didn't appear to be an obvious way to skip it.
I do this 3 or 4 times, before I google how to escape this first scene. I would say that’s a pretty poor introduction to a game... And the game goes on, without the time pressure element, but still there is little guidance for the kind of things I'm expected to do. I would say that the game hasn't given me the right opportunities to established a thought process that I need, that will allow me to explore the ideas ive already been introduced to, and using what ive learnt to complete new challenges.
Now, I believe that if the game designers target audience were new players who had never played any lego game before, this first sequence would never have passed testing! I think they would have put greater focus on a step-by-step learning process within the opening challenges of the game before the player is thrown in at the deep end. There are no tutorial level and very little in terms of introducing players to the game concepts. I therefore have to assume that the designers of the game were intending this to be a game for more experienced players.
That is all there is to it. I think that if I had known this before purchasing the game, I would definetly have bought a different game from the lego series. One that would allow a beginner to have a good time.

I can't recommend this game based on my experience with the two previous installments of Orcs Must Die. OMD 1 & 2 were fantastic games, and worth every penny. Players of all ages and experience could have fun solo or grouping with other players. Nothing felt clunky, confusing, or frustrating. Those games delivered exactly what you expected.
OMD Unchained is a completely different story. I first heard about the game at PAX 3 years ago, and was excited to have a new and improved game in the franchise with the added benefit of PvP! During the beta, instead of taking player feedback into account and making the needed changes, they scrapped the PvP mode altogether. That was a huge bummer when it was the #1 selling point for this new installment. Later it was replaced by sabotage mode, which is okay but not at all what was promised.
Pros:
- Looks great
- Runs well on my PC
- Lots of characters and traps
Cons:
- PvP was removed even though it was the whole idea of this game in the first place
- Long grind to unlock new characters (no free character rotation anymore?)
- Takes forever to get new traps and upgrades (it's also random which is frustrating)
- Rewards, upgrades, and the economy are very confusing even as a veteran player and after many overhauls during beta
- Balance between each map is waaaay off, making solo very difficult
- The menu system is extremely convoluted
After 80 hours across a couple years of beta, I'm finally throwing in the towel for good.

I'm NOT a fan of games like this, and I'm not good at them at all.
That said, this game is amazing. Despite my disinterest in and difficulty with this type of combat (twitch, combos), I have immense fun with it. I've turned the difficulty down and have a blast collecting enemies and wildly flailing about.
At that point, the other aspects of the game come into play, and this is where it really hooks me. The combat strikes are visceral, fluid, and beautiful to behold. Actors onscreen are animated with an expertise and eye for detail that I've rarely seen matched. The controls are tuned to perfection, which is important in these games.
The other systems, crafting, looting, the economy, exploration, are all exceptional. The crafting is akin to that in Dark Cloud 2; deep creation system with vibrant items, tricky recipes that are ACTUALLY USEFUL, absolutely amazing. Looting is truly addictive; like experience orbs in Minecraft, they/he got the sound and look just right. Farming for loot is lucrative without obviating the crafting or economy. A tricky balance, no doubt. You always have a reason to have money, and never have enough money. Perfect. Exploration is great because the environments are, of course, gorgeous, and the rewards for finding that hidden crany and concealed nook are tuned just right.
Not a fan of the animal characters, voices, or story, but those are personal opinions.
The animal characters are unique, detailed, and fit the world very well. The voices are spot on with the tone and diction, realistic, flowing speech, etc. The story is so far pretty good, it's created plenty of interest in me. I'm just hard to please there.

I'm one of those people who believes that video games can be art. Feel free to boo me. But, before you do, let me tell you about what Abzu is like.
Abzu is a game like Journey, but set almost entirely underwater. While it's still very linear, it leaves plenty of room to explore your surroundings, and boy do these surroundings look beautiful. It was like I was playing a painting. By the end of it, I was sure that every minute the game became even more breathtaking. However, as far as gameplay goes, it's fairly... shall I say, shallow. Occasionally there is a puzzle to solve, but most of the time you are swimming from location to location and taking in the game's sights. That being said, the game's simple controls (even though it recommends using a controller, KB+M controls work fine) make it easy for anyone to pick up and play the game. It won't be long before you can easily maneuver throughout the water. You can also grab onto fish, usually to move faster than your guy can swim.
The game is also very short. You can beat the entire game from start to finish in a single sitting. However, for a game like this, I think it's fine. It's meant to be experienced rather than played, and the game's sights, soundtrack and what happens over the course of the game will stay with you for hours after you watch the credits roll. The lasting appeal the game has is incredible.
Oh yeah, the story can be pretty abstract. It's told through simple environmental cutscenes and ancient Egyptian-like wall art. It may require you to play the game multiple times to fully understand the story. I think I might as well, considering how much I enjoyed it the first time through.
Would I recommend Abzu? Definitely. It's an experience, and I definitely won't be forgetting it any time soon. However, if it was priced a bit lower, like $10, I'd recommend it even more. $20 is too much for a game like this. Otherwise, though, I'd recommend this game.

This is the next iteration of the Galactic Civilization series. This is monster of a game that requires a 64 bit processor to play and for good reason. The largest map size would take months to complete against up to 120+ AI players plus a few of your friends. If you played other 4x games you could expect 10 minute turn times but no. The AI calculate it's turn during your turn and does so very quickly by using as many processor cores available to it. Turn times is almost instant.
The player can also create their own ship designs to fight in the battle viewer that uses a rule set to determine the final outcome. Although you don't have direct control of combat that doesn't mean combat is boring. You design a fleets to invade the enemies space and the the AI is able to adapt to your U.S.S. Pwnage and send you back to the design board.
Colony Management has a puzzel-esque feel. Each building buffs other similar buildings. So no two colonies are the exact same.
The game is beautiful. Space is filled with nebulas, black holes, asteroids and stars.

This is a must have title in my humble opinion for strategy gamers.

- Looks great
