- Lots of characters and traps
Cons:
- PvP was removed even though it was the whole idea of this game in the first place
- Long grind to unlock new characters (no free character rotation anymore?)
- Takes forever to get new traps and upgrades (it's also random which is frustrating)
- Rewards, upgrades, and the economy are very confusing even as a veteran player and after many overhauls during beta
- Balance between each map is waaaay off, making solo very difficult
- The menu system is extremely convoluted
After 80 hours across a couple years of beta, I'm finally throwing in the towel for good.

While it may not be a completely terrible game overall,
suffers from trying to split its focus between two different gameplay experiences to deliver, and never quite succeeds at either.  If you were looking for a worthy successor to
, then there's a good chance that you may be disappointed with this new installment.
The game is a somewhat bizarre mashup of the trap-placing tower defense that
is known for, a MOBA similar to
, and wave-based survival PvE. Unfortunately, none of those elements are strong enough to make the gameplay experience feel particularly satisfying. As I understand it, the game was originally designed to be a more PvP-centric MOBA with the inclusion of traps to stop enemy minions. Unless I'm mistaken, this would certainly explain the problems in the end product.
The main issue I have with
is that none of what I do to stop the enemy hordes from reaching my Rift feels very effective. In
, whether I was relying on a carefully-planned trap setup or making use of magical weapons, I always felt powerful. Traps and equipment tore through enemy numbers, making it a joy to watch Orcs get hilariously pierced, burned, shredded, squashed, and flung about. Sure, I sometimes had to step in to deal with stragglers or the occasional biggun, but it almost always felt like failure resulted from flawed planning on my part.
In
, however, traps and combat alike tend to feel rather weak. Enemies, even the disposable Orcs, feel more durable than they ought to be given what traps and heroes are capable of. Heroes get plenty of cool abilities, but they rarely seem strong enough to make a significant impact when the horde almost inevitably makes its way past my trap gauntlet and is closing in on the Rift. This is especially true when using heroes that feel like they were designed for the PvP mode that the game no longer has.
This problem is even worse when it comes to traps. Not only do the default traps feel woefully underpowered given the task at hand, the amount of traps that I can place always always feels inadequate. The game just gives the player too little coin with which to purchase traps. Time and time again, I'm out of coin long before I can even set up a decent killbox. "I'll put some barricades down here and there to funnel the horde, start with some basic wall and floor trpas--whoops, I'm out of money." Having guardians at my disposal doesn't help much; they mitigate the balance issues like a Band-Aid covers a stab wound.
The game has another major issue in the form of its launcher. All menu navigation outside of the matches takes place in a launcher, with the game itself being brought up when a match begins. While this is not a bad thing inherently, the implementation is very problematic. Graphical and control options cannot be accessed from the launcher; they can only be found by pressing Escape during a match. The problem is that doing so does not pause the game, even when playing solo. On top of that, every match begins with a countdown, at the end of which the first wave of enemies spawns automatically if all the players do not hit "Ready" in time. Did you want to fiddle with graphics options, adjust controls, or just browse key bindings? Too bad, because there's no way to do so at your leisure. Oh, and you can't change your loadout of traps and gear in-game. If you're playing a certain map for the first time and pick the wrong traps prior to the game being launched, then your only option is to quit and restart the match.
If at some point in the future, the game gets patched to fix these problems, I'll revisit it and reconsider my thought. For now, however,
just isn't very satisfying to play. I don't even have a gripe with the free-to-play business model. Make the traps and heroes hit harder than a horsefly, and let me place more traps. That's all it should take to make this game fun. Oh, and get rid of the stupid launcher; there's no tangible benefit to having it.

First things first: Mafia 3 isn't a true Mafia game. It simply feels to different, the story is way too chopped up, there are too many hasslesome distractions and it simply lacks the classic story flair of something centered around the Cosa Nostra. 2K tried something different with this entry and something different they indeed did deliver. It's not a bad game, but a bad Mafia sequel.
Disregarding that fact, Mafia 3 is a good action game with a revenge story through and through. It plays like GTA light, has great cutscenes, likeable side characters, engagingly fun yet simple combat mechanics, looks great, sports a good soundtrack and has a lot of historic cars. Which unfortunately have the worst driving physics I've seen in a long time, which in turn puts quite a dent into the game considering the fact the player is spending quite a large percentage of time getting around on the rather large map.
As for gameplay itself, stealth is just as viable as Rambo gunzerking for the first time in the Mafia series.
If you can live with it's downsides, Mafia 3 is worth a recommendation, but the mixed reviews are testimony of the fact that in fact not all people are able to overlook the inherent flaws of 2K trying to copy the Ubisoft formula by adding hundreds of unnecessary collectibles and completely senseless racing minigames which are more or less required for faction unlocks. Apart from the story, which is actually great, Mafia 3 sports a lot of bloat.
Personally, I had a lot of fun with Mafia 3, but I would have played it about 100 hours less if it hadn't been for countless collectibles and mandatory side missions I wasn't really excited about doing but did anyway for completionist's sake.

The game might have potential in the long run, but we are very far from a minimum viable product.  Give developpers a couple of month before you try it.

TL;DR: Test the game, be fair with it. It's a MOBA, it's fun. Don't mind the graphics and all that stuff. If you're reading the TL;DR you probably don't have that much time and SHOULD BE TRYING/PLAYING THE GAME!
First of all, Hunger Dungeon is a MOBA(A.K.A Multiplayer Online Battle Arena). In this game, you (normally) fight 3 opponents in an arena. You have to kill your opponents in various rounds until you reach the final round, where you have to collect energy cristals to escape the dungeon, while you try to survive hunger, buy scrolls and fight the other players. There's also team deathmatch, that's exactly the same team, but at most it's 3v3. And lastly Dragon Mode, where 4 players fight together to defeat 3 Dragons and get their scrolls.
Here's a list of pros and cons:
PROS
-Characters feel somewhat unique.
-Great character customisation for different playstiles(with scrolls and equipments).
-The hunger mechanic is ok, I guess... some people don't like it, but gives you a reason to move around instead of camping or rushing down opponents.
-It's different from other MOBAs.
-Games are from 10-20 minutes normally, which is good if you don't have that much time.
-PvE against dragons is fun and a real challenge!
CONS
-Some bugs still exist, especially in Dragon Mode.
-The balancing: it's not that good, but they're trying...
-If you don't buy the game, you can only use 4 out of the 12 characters in the game. It works on a rotation system. The part that most persons will not like is that you need to buy premium if you want all the characters. Well, now they DID add the in-game currency and, as expected, the items in the shop, like the characters, are expensive.
-Matchmaking takes a long time most of the time in Free-For-All, and all of the time in Team Deathmatch. But they now match you with bots if it takes too long, which is fine.
MIXED
-The graphics. Some people may enjoy, but some may hate. I personally like the graphics, but that's just me.
Overrall, I think this game has potential. I had a lot of fun playing it and I hope it gets more players. The Devs are fixing the problems this game has constantly. I'm still having great fun in this game, and I think most of the people that play it don't really give the game a chance. The community is decent, there are some nice and some good players. If I forgot anything please tell me in the comments, but I think I covered the most important stuff.
EDIT: This game is dead, sadly. No one plays, it's not what people were looking for.

Technically this is three games, the entire LiEat trilogy.  Each game is a relatively short and sweet rpg with a light fantasy-detective vibe.  The art is cute or disturbing as the narrative demands.  The writing is what really sells these games, though.  All of the characters are engaging and dynamic, the story of each game drags you in, answers your core questions while still leaving some backstory up to your imagination.  I don't have much background in music theory, but I found all of the songs nice to listen to and non-annoying, so there's that.  Those who enjoy stories about growing up, healing after traumatic experiences, and found families will most definitely enjoy these games.
If, however, you're super not into anime-esque graphics, or getting very little explanation for your story elements, then this is probably not the game series for you.  Also, the battles aren't particularly challenging, so if you're more into game mechanics than story this going to be another no-go for you.  Additionally, I didn't think that any of the answers to the mysteries were particularly tough to figure out way before the characters, but that might just be me.
Overall, I heartily recommend the LiEat series for those who favor story over gameplay.

Really great game. Just totally solid from every vantage point. Any review that places this game below at least a 90 in score on Metacritic is either using a 5 star system and doesn't grant half stars or doesn't appreciate the nuances of the gameplay / the difficulty of the game.
There is a large breadth of mechanics (there are tons of aspects of play like exploration, timing, resource management, risk/reward, etc) but all of which are approachable. The real startling thing is they have incredible depth and learning the nuances of each one give a decent advantage to the player (spotting loot in wall tiles, having perfect rhythm/decision making while swarmed in constant fractions of seconds, learning to love glass items, when to use a long-hit vs wide-hit weapon, etc). I love roguelikes but rarely find the types that I REALLY love, particularly those that emulate a style of gameplay similar to NetHack while not having any one aspect be broken. The amazing soundtracks on top of a game which is already very easy to appreciate on its own merits is just icing on top of the cake.
The difficulty is fine, in spite of a few claims otherwise. Dancepad mode is available for those who need slightly easier play. Altering the music can also allow for slower gameplay too. Hell, there's a character where you can avoid the beat mechanic entirely and which is very obviously there for players to train and get better, get a purer roguelike experience, or just clear the zones as quickly as possible. ANY review that bashes the game for not being easy in the main mode despite the many attempts by the devs to give easier options is just feeding into the mindset that games with hard base difficulty are bad. It's not only not fair but it's also greatly hindering games with permadeath and large death penalties from being developed. Hell, even I can't beat clear the second zone of Spelunky but I can still appreciate it.
The only criticism of this game that I found fair was that unlocking the full story requires beating all four zones with three different characters, the last of which is a hardcore player character (one missed beat or any damage and you die and have to restart the zone). With vanilla gameplay, even knowing the game VERY well it borders on being a slight bit unreasonable. Bottom line: if you're not the kind of person who complains about how hard and punishing a /ROGUELIKE/ can be and if you're willing to put in enough time to appreciate the depth of mechanics then you'll love Necrodancer.
Get the game. Love it and be a casual player if you'd like. It's perfectly made for that too. But hopefully you'll join in the more competitive scene and see how far the rabbit hole really goes. It could certainly use some action and the game can absolutely support it.

The audio and visual design in this game are spectacular.  The gameplay resembles a hack and slash, metroid style game where abilities unlock as the story progesses which allow access to new areas.  The equipment has a great feeling of progession, and money is never useless.
Complaints:
The control over movement is not as fluid as it could be.  For relying heavily on platforming (at times), the quick dash and double jump are not quite as responsive as I would have hoped.  That being said, the control scheme on an XBox 360 controller is wonderful (especially the use of vibaration feedback).
The dialog is poorly written, and some voice actors are not up to par.  This is a minor problem as I do not believe the story is driving part of the game.  However, parts of the story are done very well including some untold sections of story that the player can question.
The combat is very repeativie with no need to change combat style.  I will not spoil the tactic I used, but I can say that I always used it and never needed to change it.  That leads to boring gameplay where I just wanted to get past the enemies faster.  With no ability to change weapons (apart from a special ability of which three types exist), this is even worse.
Backtracking is necessary to find all of the collectibles which is somewhat annoying since it involves fighting past enemies multiple times.  That being said, this is optional.  It took me 11 hours to beat the game, finding all collectibles on normal difficulty.
While I took the time to write more about the negatives of the game, I feel that those are the only problems with it.  The game was entertaining.  If you have any interest in side scrolling, hack and slash style gameplay, get this game.  It is one of the best of its genre.
Very addictive. I catch myself playing obsessivly for hours at a time sometimes.

NOTE:   This is a review of the Final Release Candidate for the game, so it should apply to the released version.
Having been a long-time GC2 player, I eagerly signed up for the Founder's Edition early-access over a year ago, and have followed the development of GC3 since then closely.
Let me tell you, getting a 4X game that incorporates all the features that hard-core strategy gamers want, while remaining both relevant and competitive, is really hard. As in, EXTREMELY hard.  StarDock has done an excellent job with GC3.  That's not to say there still aren't quibbles over the direction certain features have taken, but the reality is, that if you actually want to release a game, certain decisions are going to have to be taken, and you're sure to♥♥♥♥♥♥off someone who wanted that feature and didn't get it.  But GC3 is a solid and entertaining game, if not a radically innovative one.
On to the specifics:
A big positive is a revamp of the "alignment" system from GC2, which was, frankly, pretty primitive. The new one is far more nuanced, and continues to be relevant through the entire game.
The game has changed from square-based to hex-based, and whether or not you love it or not often boils down to whether you used to be a paper boardgame player. I for one much perfer it to squares.  Movement and area of influence or effects are much smoother and visually linear.
You'll note that the game is 64-bit only. There's a reason for this: GIANT MAPS.  This is a highly-threaded, fast game engine, and high-end gaming boxes can play on a map of 1000+ planets and 50+ opponents.  Turn times are reasonable at this point, but you still want a darned powerful box if you're playing on these ginormous box.  It plays nice and smooth on a typical i5 with 8GB with modest graphics card, against 10 computer opponents on a 50+ star map, and there aren't any noticeable bugs at this point; it certainly is stable and non-crashing.   My rig is high-end (8-core Xeon & 24GB of RAM, with SSDs and a Nvidia 750), and I have absolutely no problems at all on my 200-star maps and 25 opponent games.
The planet improvement scheme is VERY much improved by adjacency bonus; it now matter as much as to HOW you place your buildings on a planet as which ones you build.  And, speaking of buildings, there's easily twice as many different ones to choose from, and three times as many "bonus" tile times.  The AI generating the tiles still needs a bit of tweaking to avoid some stupid layouts, but that's a minor quibble, and likely will be improved more via free updates.
The ship builder is more complex, and much more interesting to use. Ships now have a wider choice of weapons (including chosing between ones with different ranges, rates of fire, etc.), and larger engine selection. Unfortunately, I find it a bit clunkier than the GC2 one.
The Battleviewer is pretty much unchanged since GC2.  The promised tactical settings (i.e. "offensive", "defensive" for your fleet tactics) has yet to materialize.  Probably won't until later this year, and either an Expansion Pack or DLC.   There will be no Tactical Combat player screen. I'm very happy about that (I don't want TBTC in my 4x), but some others feel it should be there.
The Graphics are excellent for a 4X.  Personally, I think they're just right - nice, without being over the top and loading my system down with work for something that's really not gameplay-relevant.
The tech trees are custom to each race, and noticeably (if not entirely) different. A new feature is exclusive choice in some techs:  some technologies have 2 or 3 sub-techs in them, and you can only chose one.  This means you can't just load up on the entire tech tree, but have to be careful about how you pick your path through it, because certain choices simply will exclude you from possessing others.
Diplomacy and the United Planets are greatly improved over GC2 - far more meaningful interactions, and many of the "cheats" and such possible in GC2 have been either closed off, or are actively penalized.  Being diplomatic is just as important as being militarily strong.
Trading and the Economy are better overall than GC2, but require a bit too much micromanagement at this point. If anything, I hope this will be further improved by a post-release patch.  It's certainly playable now, just it gets hard when you move up to the really big maps (managing 5 dozen planets can get a bit tedious right now).
Espionage IS NOT included in the initial release. StarDock has said it will be in the first major Expansion Pack, as they want to make a considerable effort to radically improve it over GC2.  So don't expect this until 2016 sometime.
Finally, the A.I. is solid, but rather bland at this point. However, there is a saving grace:  this is a learning A.I.  StarDock has hooked it into SteamWorks, and will be datamining all user strategies to improve the A.I. performance, and will be updating the A.I. regularly when you sign into Steam.  So, as the GC3 community gets better, so will the A.I.
Overall, solid 8 out of 10 for the intial Release.
Also, note that StarDock has explicitly committed to several "substantial" DLCs per year (read: things that actually improve gameplay, not just skins or bling, but stuff like more races, new ship flavors, etc.) and at least 3 major Expansion packs over the 6-7 year lifespan. Given there track record, I fully expect that these DLCs and Expansion Packs will take the entire game in new directions, and make a very substantial impact on keeping the game relevant over time.
I fully expect that GC3 will graduate to a 9.5 star game over the next couple of years, and, given StarDock's track record of listening to its customers, much of the direction of GC3's improvement is going to be up to the community.

In this rectangular windowed Unity game, we follow Warren, a game developer, on a journey to retrieve the back up of his game from the flash drive in his computer as the original was lost due to computer error. It's a puzzle game, hosting a series of smaller puzzle games (more on that later). Going off the credits, it was made by 2-3 people.
The controls are basic; arrow keys (Warren moves on a grid, so no diagonal movement here), an interact button, and a use item button. No menu to speak of, only a quit option. With dialog boxes, you'll have to click a specific 'next' button as opposed to anywhere on the screen.
You can examine some things about the world, but few have anything to really say. The humour came off as average to me. Not ever laugh out loud, or even amusing, but at least it's not annoying. (Eg. “But your car had a license plate that said 'TOWME'!”). The game is light critique on game developer trends, hinting at it through infrequent comments like books on a shelf being blank and poking fun at absure puzzle logic when a clearer answer is right in front of you. Indeed, some of the game's own logic is a bit odd when you think about it, but I'm inclined to believe some of that is intentional.
There's some spelling errors here and there in the dialogue boxes. The font varies, denoting different characters or inner monologue. The writing is more on the ok side.
The art design is alright. The environment itself and its assets are serviceable, and are somewhat cartoony in style. Warren is in a semi-Rayman style, and because his hands are tucked into his pockets most of the time, it often looks like he doesn't have any. Also, his shoes seem to be back to front (that or the developer thought he should have tiny heels and large toes). That being said, there is some detail here – characters blink, Warren has an idle animation, and a fully animated cigarette throughout the game. The breakables in the end credits also break differently depending on where you hit them.
The sound design is alright for what this is. Warren's noises tend to be slight squeaks when moving, and speech is signified by blerts and other squeaks. The music itself is listenable, relaxing, and loops seamlessly, and I believe some of it is Kevin MacLeod's work.
The game has about five minigames beyond the basic puzzles in the overworld. They're a lot like basic flash games of different genres for the most part, actually (Balancing Act, Point and Click, Dating Sim, Puzzle, and Side-Scrolling Runner), and whilst their poor gameplay is inteded to be commentary, they're still not that pleasant to play through. The only 3D ones are the Bronie ones, and they also have the best gameplay due to having more attention put on them; they kind of make the other games feel pointless, actually, and the game would have been better had all minigames received this polish.
The Cyber Pony game is infuriating. It's a side-scrolling dodge runner. At times the direction keys will simply stop working, dooming you – and the game is long, and doesn't have any checkpoints.
Overall, it's alright. Parts of it are better than others, but don't go into this expecting Black Mesa. Is it worth downloading? That's hard to say. This feels very much like the sort of game you'd find free on a website somewhere, and I'm really not certain why the developers released it on Steam – that being said, it's better than a lot of very low-budget indies are trying to sell for money, so the fact it is free is appreciated. Consider downloading if you've got about half an hour to kill.

While it may not be a completely terrible game overall,
suffers from trying to split its focus between two different gameplay experiences to deliver, and never quite succeeds at either.  If you were looking for a worthy successor to
, then there's a good chance that you may be disappointed with this new installment.
The game is a somewhat bizarre mashup of the trap-placing tower defense that
is known for, a MOBA similar to
, and wave-based survival PvE. Unfortunately, none of those elements are strong enough to make the gameplay experience feel particularly satisfying. As I understand it, the game was originally designed to be a more PvP-centric MOBA with the inclusion of traps to stop enemy minions. Unless I'm mistaken, this would certainly explain the problems in the end product.
The main issue I have with
is that none of what I do to stop the enemy hordes from reaching my Rift feels very effective. In
, whether I was relying on a carefully-planned trap setup or making use of magical weapons, I always felt powerful. Traps and equipment tore through enemy numbers, making it a joy to watch Orcs get hilariously pierced, burned, shredded, squashed, and flung about. Sure, I sometimes had to step in to deal with stragglers or the occasional biggun, but it almost always felt like failure resulted from flawed planning on my part.
In
, however, traps and combat alike tend to feel rather weak. Enemies, even the disposable Orcs, feel more durable than they ought to be given what traps and heroes are capable of. Heroes get plenty of cool abilities, but they rarely seem strong enough to make a significant impact when the horde almost inevitably makes its way past my trap gauntlet and is closing in on the Rift. This is especially true when using heroes that feel like they were designed for the PvP mode that the game no longer has.
This problem is even worse when it comes to traps. Not only do the default traps feel woefully underpowered given the task at hand, the amount of traps that I can place always always feels inadequate. The game just gives the player too little coin with which to purchase traps. Time and time again, I'm out of coin long before I can even set up a decent killbox. "I'll put some barricades down here and there to funnel the horde, start with some basic wall and floor trpas--whoops, I'm out of money." Having guardians at my disposal doesn't help much; they mitigate the balance issues like a Band-Aid covers a stab wound.
The game has another major issue in the form of its launcher. All menu navigation outside of the matches takes place in a launcher, with the game itself being brought up when a match begins. While this is not a bad thing inherently, the implementation is very problematic. Graphical and control options cannot be accessed from the launcher; they can only be found by pressing Escape during a match. The problem is that doing so does not pause the game, even when playing solo. On top of that, every match begins with a countdown, at the end of which the first wave of enemies spawns automatically if all the players do not hit "Ready" in time. Did you want to fiddle with graphics options, adjust controls, or just browse key bindings? Too bad, because there's no way to do so at your leisure. Oh, and you can't change your loadout of traps and gear in-game. If you're playing a certain map for the first time and pick the wrong traps prior to the game being launched, then your only option is to quit and restart the match.
If at some point in the future, the game gets patched to fix these problems, I'll revisit it and reconsider my thought. For now, however,
just isn't very satisfying to play. I don't even have a gripe with the free-to-play business model. Make the traps and heroes hit harder than a horsefly, and let me place more traps. That's all it should take to make this game fun. Oh, and get rid of the stupid launcher; there's no tangible benefit to having it.

I'm one of those people who believes that video games can be art. Feel free to boo me. But, before you do, let me tell you about what Abzu is like.
Abzu is a game like Journey, but set almost entirely underwater. While it's still very linear, it leaves plenty of room to explore your surroundings, and boy do these surroundings look beautiful. It was like I was playing a painting. By the end of it, I was sure that every minute the game became even more breathtaking. However, as far as gameplay goes, it's fairly... shall I say, shallow. Occasionally there is a puzzle to solve, but most of the time you are swimming from location to location and taking in the game's sights. That being said, the game's simple controls (even though it recommends using a controller, KB+M controls work fine) make it easy for anyone to pick up and play the game. It won't be long before you can easily maneuver throughout the water. You can also grab onto fish, usually to move faster than your guy can swim.
The game is also very short. You can beat the entire game from start to finish in a single sitting. However, for a game like this, I think it's fine. It's meant to be experienced rather than played, and the game's sights, soundtrack and what happens over the course of the game will stay with you for hours after you watch the credits roll. The lasting appeal the game has is incredible.
Oh yeah, the story can be pretty abstract. It's told through simple environmental cutscenes and ancient Egyptian-like wall art. It may require you to play the game multiple times to fully understand the story. I think I might as well, considering how much I enjoyed it the first time through.
Would I recommend Abzu? Definitely. It's an experience, and I definitely won't be forgetting it any time soon. However, if it was priced a bit lower, like $10, I'd recommend it even more. $20 is too much for a game like this. Otherwise, though, I'd recommend this game.

You inherited of an old estate. You're very happy: now, you'll be finally living well. However, it seems that your mansion is haunted by a poltergeist...
Shiver: Poltergeist is a casual adventure game, with hidden objects scenes (of one type only) and puzzles. I've played The Vanishing Hitchhiker and I enjoyed that opus, so, it was natural for me to acquire Poltergeist (at a discount).
The plot is basic: a ghost, well, a poltergeist more precisely, is haunting your manor and you need to find a way to chase it down. In this case, it's reuniting with her lover. You discover the tragic love story behind and in the extra chapter, you discover what really happened when the girl died. But I was expecting something darker, so, the plot was kinda for me a disappointement.
The gameplay is the standard one in this case: grab objects, use them, clear hidden objects scenes and solve puzzles. I found the difficulty well-balanced, however, be aware that you have no map and that sometimes, it's hard to find what to do next. I had to rely on the strategy guide when I found myself very stuck. I've skipped one puzzle because I didn't understand who to solve it, even with the strategy guide. The hidden objects scenes are relatively easy apart for some actions you need to do in them as you don't always see what to do. You have also a flashlight and a camera helping you for dark areas or to take pictures to reveal clues (or just to take a picture).
The graphics were decent and the soundtrack was adapted, so, on that side, it's good.
But yeah, I'm quite mitigated with Poltergeist. It's not a bad game but I wasn't really captivated by it. I don't know what was lacking: maybe it's the fact I was expecting something more thrilling, more traps or things to happen that would be unexespected. I'm torn, because I would be recommending the game even mitigated but I didn't really enjoy this one, so, well, I'm going to say that: you love that kind of games, you can grab it and make yourself an opinion, you're not into the genre, don't even bother with it, even for trying. For me, in the end, I didn't really had fun, so, I'm going to put a thumb down.

First things first: Mafia 3 isn't a true Mafia game. It simply feels to different, the story is way too chopped up, there are too many hasslesome distractions and it simply lacks the classic story flair of something centered around the Cosa Nostra. 2K tried something different with this entry and something different they indeed did deliver. It's not a bad game, but a bad Mafia sequel.
Disregarding that fact, Mafia 3 is a good action game with a revenge story through and through. It plays like GTA light, has great cutscenes, likeable side characters, engagingly fun yet simple combat mechanics, looks great, sports a good soundtrack and has a lot of historic cars. Which unfortunately have the worst driving physics I've seen in a long time, which in turn puts quite a dent into the game considering the fact the player is spending quite a large percentage of time getting around on the rather large map.
As for gameplay itself, stealth is just as viable as Rambo gunzerking for the first time in the Mafia series.
If you can live with it's downsides, Mafia 3 is worth a recommendation, but the mixed reviews are testimony of the fact that in fact not all people are able to overlook the inherent flaws of 2K trying to copy the Ubisoft formula by adding hundreds of unnecessary collectibles and completely senseless racing minigames which are more or less required for faction unlocks. Apart from the story, which is actually great, Mafia 3 sports a lot of bloat.
Personally, I had a lot of fun with Mafia 3, but I would have played it about 100 hours less if it hadn't been for countless collectibles and mandatory side missions I wasn't really excited about doing but did anyway for completionist's sake.

This review is based on the Beta 6 series, which took place in the last couple weeks before launch. To say the game has improved by leaps and bounds in Beta 6 would be an understatement. It is now running smoothly and crash free on my system (check the recommended specs, you need a decent rig for this game).
If you are fan of GCII you will find a lot of improvements in this version. The new ideology system adds a great new strategy layer. The new tile adjacency system makes building up infrastructure on your planets much more interesting and strategic. The ship designer is more flexible, powerful, and intuitive than the last interation. The graphics have gotten a nice upgrade. The switch to 64 bit allows some truly massive maps if that is your thing (if your rig can handle it). And finally the AI is putting up a decent challenge on the higher difficulties at this point and has improved immensely over the past month.
For those new to the series, if you liked Master of Orion or other iconic games of the 4X space genere, this game is worth checking out. It's considered by many to be the best space 4X series on the market since the Master of Orion days for a reason.

This is one of the only games that I own which has nothing to do with shooting, guns, or wargaming, and I absolutely love it. The physics and gameplay are amazing. I have never seen another game that so accurately captures the challenges of offroading. How your vehicle performs in the environment is beautifully realistic, at least according to my experiences growing up in the country. For a 3 year old game, the graphics are spot on, and the scenery and equipment are eye candy to behold as you're cussing out the mud sucking you into the ground. It is also great to see such a great modding community backing up this game, filling the gaps of the limited content of the vanilla game.
The only negatives of the game, as previously mentioned, is that there is so much left to be desired. The limited objectives that there are in the game do drive the desire to succeed and provide some gratification upon completion. However, I feel that the gameplay could have been fleshed out so much more. Perhaps giving this game some RPG elements would have given the players some serious desire to succeed, playthrough, and replay. Also, more maps, and more equipment, and perhaps more to do would have truely made this game a classic.
Perhaps the developers' plan was to release a solid smaller title in order to test the market and raise funds for a larger title? One can only hope that a sequel is in the works!

Let me preface by saying that Final Fantasy VII is the last American release (by order of release date) that I have completed in the series, so far.  It is a classic, in that other video games in the role-playing genre are still compared to it today--with good reason.  I loved this game when it was released over fifteen years ago, and I still love it today.
So let's focus on the negatives, starting with the most egregious problems: whomever was placed in charge of reprogramming this game for the computer put new mouths on those characters that lacked them (i.e. Sephiroth, Jessie, etc.).  Unfortunately, they used just the one mouth position: a whorish "O."  Suddenly every character with a new mouth has taken on the appearance of a blow-up pleasure doll, an image that is only reinforced by the early 3D animation.  It is NOT a pretty sight.
For the Uninitiated: Players might be frustrated with some of the unintentional difficulties of an EARLY attempt at 3D gaming, specifically movement.  There is something of a learning curve with materia.  The graphics are dated.  Some of the mini-games are terrible (though most are thankfully avoidable).  I would also highly recommend purchasing (or at least looking up via internet) a guide, as not every quest is terribly clear.
With that said, there are mods that can fix the mouth problem.  I am also grateful that some of the more distracting translation errors have been fixed since the game's first US release.  Overall, I'd recommend this game highly to anyone who's played it and wants to relive it... and for anyone else who wants to experience a classic.
But seriously.  Get the mouth mod.  Sephiroth with that "O" face is just creepy.  Well... creepier.

I will say that this game has come a long way from when I orginally stopped playing like 3yrs before. Back then it had no single player campain and only PvP with a wierd grinding system for materials to create traps and bosses. Was the gameplay intesting? Yes it played like everyother MOBA except you created the waves and your enemies created kill boxxes that you had to push through. Was it worth grinding for? No, not really with how the grind was so unfathomably long needing almost 1,000 of 3-5 different materials that dropped randomly and only gave up to 30 per game.
However now it's gone back to it's roots and is almost like an entrily different game. No PvP anymore, but good old fashioned OMD with PvE and lots of new characters to choose from. The system is much symplier for getting new traps with simply opening chests that you earn from matches and they can give quite a bit of stuff for leveling your gear. However don't expect to play for a little bit and expect to get couple new characters, that's not happening anytime soon. New characters are at least 6K and being a low level means upgrading certain traps are much more important that a new character.
With how the game is now I can recommend this for people who want to try and get into the series without spending a dime, but try and get the previous installments if possiable.

This game is surely not for everyone, especially with an average playthrough of around 2 hours, and priced at $20. That said, I had a good time with it.
What separates this game from other short indie titles of its kind is the beautiful art and environment design, great musical score, and interactive environments, even if the rewards for exploring are fairly trivial overall.
The game is paced fairly well, too. Every time I was starting to get a little tired of a certain section, the game threw something new at me, It did a nice job with the buildup and the finale as well.
I find there's a decent amount of replay value here, since I enjoy achievements and exploring the areas. This is also one big benefit to the short playthrough time, as it makes it much easier to play multiple times without having to set aside a huge chunk of time.
2 hours for $20 is going to be a big breaking point for a lot of people, but I liked it quite a lot.

This game is a fun experience I'm sure the general audience could get in to.  Each story is told like a fairy tale and each character is okay.  There isn't much depth in this game sadly.  You mainly play this game for the story since fights can only be encountered at certain times.  The battle mechanics are okay for the few fights you're going to be fighting.  There are no shops in these games (because this game actually contains 3 stories) so you'll have to be more explorative when wandering around to find certain things like weapons, armor, or consumables.  Since this game is story driven it would be expected to have decent writing and aesthetics.  This is true.  The story as simple as it was had me hooked.  The over arcing mystery of the main female's existence interested me to no end and I believe the music and art compliments everything well.  Gameplay and most cutscenes are in a pixel style and it looks nice, but there are a few cinematic cutscenes that are in an anime style and they look nice.  Overall I would say that this game is great, but don't expect something on the scale of Final Fantasy, Fire Emblem, or just a licensed RPG title.  I recommend going into this just with the thought of having a fun and simple adventure.

As for me it'll be a while before I'm willing to take another whack at it with what will be my third vault...

I normally make stupid joke reviews, but this game deserves a serious review as to why you need this game.
LiEat is a short, indie, RPG-maker game about Efina: The lie eating dragon, and Theo: a conartist who watches over Efi. The game has three parts that come with the single, $2.99 USD purchase. Think of it as three different arcs of a story, just separated to show a jump in time.
The characters in this game are fantastic. Every character you meet is unique and memorable, even if you only meet them once, they even have their own profile to discribe them.
The music is fantastic. Even if the main battle theme "Liar" is remixed in each part, it still sounds wonderful.
This game is not difficult, nor is it meant to be, considering you can find weapons that raise your attack to 500 and your level will never exceed 20. But that's ok. Because this game is a short, fun game not intending to test your full Atlus game skills.
So why should you get this game? Because it's short, cheap, fun, and good. I don't know what else to say, just get it, you won't regret it.
With the reasons stated above, in the 2016 Steam Awards under "we didn't think of everything", you should write in "simple, but Beautiful" and nominate this game.

Paladins is a cooperative, ability-based FPS game with a wide roster of skills and champions. New content is released regularly. It can be enjoyed alongside Overwatch as they are quite different.
You select a hero out of a roster of Champions. More than half of the Champions are locked - you need Cash or Login bonuses to gather currency to unlock them.
Champions are fixed for the duration of a match. No switching is possible, so pick carefully and coordinate with teammates during the pre-match selection.
There are a few gamemodes. Notably, PointCapture+Payload Escort, as well as Payload Escort.
Even though the game is in beta, it is polished enough and does not crash very often. Everything you would expect from a game is inside, and I think it is good enough to be released.
Champions, new skins, map updates, and patches are released on a regular basis.
Players are generally very silent during a game, with little to no communication involved. It does not help that the Voicewheel is not convenient for instantaneous usage. However if you've played Source/Valve games before, it is similar.
Champions, new skins, map updates, and patches are released on a regular basis.
Please do NOT read this if you are not interested in constructive and critical comments. Since I've played both, I'll elaborate on the differences.
Paid vs Free is Apples vs Oranges. Shall not compare.
This is subjective.
Paladins has little to no toxicity. Overwatch has some toxicity.
Paladins has a smaller crowd, and they do not talk much in-game
Paladins releases skins, maps and champions incrementally. Overwatch drops big patches every few months, with multiple skins, a new game mode/event, map, or new hero.
Paladins has collectible cards that tweak skillsets. Overwatch has a level playing field since all tweaks are entirely cosmetic, where a lvl 1 player is the same as a lvl 1000 player.
In terms of complexity, Paladins offer ways to tweak skillsets via:
Paladins also places greater emphasis on things like * effect lasts .5 seconds * damage boosts by 40% etc. Basically you see quite a lot of number and time-related stuff, just like RPGs or MOBAs.
Overwatch on the other hand, favors simplicity by doing away with character modification, and effect modifiers are a hidden number.
This means that Paladins have more complexity. Although it mildly favors experienced players who have a big collection of powerful cards,

The series seems to be becoming more action/adventure oriented than an RPG meant for purists, but what this game does it does very well. The combat system has become more oriented toward player skill rather than Geralt's attributes, but this turned out to be pretty fun once I got the hang of the controls. Branching storylines encourage replayability, as in the first game. At first I had a problem with the excessive use of bloom and shader effects, though these things are implemented far better and more artistically after the first chapter, so I suggest everyone keep these settings enabled. Overall this is a very well-written and clever game and I would recommend it to fans of the first game or fans of the fantasy fiction genre in general. You won't be disappointed!

This is a fantastic blend of Roguelike meets DDR controls. With an absolutely fantastic pulse pounding soundtrack, mod support, and plenty of characters to try out and play, this one one game that will not get old any time soon.
A definite buy that is well worth every dollar of the purchase price.

Since ancient times the ruling class have kept the proletariat their slaves via religion. In doing so they have made sacrosanct service to kings, to business owners, and to other successful thieves, of varying charitable temperament. And hitherto, the best response to this condition--the response I have been recommending--has been revolution. But this month, I have discovered a new, greater answer to this terrible state of ours, and it is to play Crypt of the NecroDancer.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a “roguelike” in which you tap your keys to the beat. There are items to unlock, and dancing monsters to meet. It is a sublime experience, with an excellent soundtrack; and the game can even use your mp3s. And the boss battles! Well, there is just nothing else out there like them. All for only $15! (less when on sale!) Crypt of the NecroDancer is, I have no doubt, the next step forward for civilization. From the city states and primitive empires, we got Feudalism; from Feudalism we got Capitalism. After Capitalism, Crypt of the NecroDancer.
It’s so good.
Do you know anyone who was born into an anger-filled family? Does he or she, grown-up, feel sad? Feel broke? And lacks the confidence necessary to take on the world? Crypt of the NecroDancer is what they need.
Know a rich man or woman who made risky investments, married for money, and suddenly finds him or herself in debt exceeding 200 million dollars? Does he suffer now from insomnia? Does she now see no value in her relationships, knowing that they were all founded on money? Are the eyes in this person just, dejected? Well, ask if you can use a computer, turn up that volume, and show ‘em the answer. Crypt of the NecroDancer!
Do you know someone who went to a private school, majored in philosophy, has over a hundred grand in debt, and can’t get anything but temporary and minimum wage jobs? Tell ‘em to throw away their Epictetus, and get a copy of Crypt of the NecroDancer!
Have you been to church lately? Has your pastor asked you to donate to orphans in Africa? Did he show you pictures of the children, with sadness in their eyes, and ragged clothes, homeless? And do you realize well that the 1st world has its debts, and thus will not go nation-building? What should you do? Well, a cheap computer with speakers (such as an old laptop—see the system requirements) with Crypt of the NecroDancer would make a great gift to that starving African kid. The beats would make him popular with the cool kids, for they’d all want to play it. It’d make ‘em forget about the pain, if they have electricity.
Some of my fellow philosophers say that mass, cheap entertainments, such as computer games, exist to keep the masses slaving away for their greedy bosses. Instead of going out and living, and pursuing our own dreams, we, the people, are being kept glued to screens, living virtual life, which we pay for and aren’t willing to leave, even convincing ourselves that IT is the true life. These thinkers even claim that major news outlets deliberately depict the world as dangerous and any risky ambitions pointless; and so, my pensive comrades say, we stay in our rooms.
What my comrades haven’t seen, though, is Crypt of the NecroDancer. It is THEY who haven’t lived!
Workers of the world, unite and play Crypt of the NecroDancer!

Edit: I've been playing for 30 days now. The PVP has actually gotten worse for me. I'm still getting grouped up with brand new players despite playing the PVP everyday, which means that I lose before the game begins because it's not balanced in a way that lets new players even contribute properly. So I've changed my mind. I'm frustrated enough that I'm changing this review to a negative.
The game is free. For something that costs you zero dollars, it is plenty fun. Highly recommend you check it out yourself, rather than taking too much from reviews.
That said, the game still has a lot of flaws. PVP is incredibly unbalanced. The system has thrown me in with teammates that are brand new players, against people with expensive heroes and ridiculous traps and spells. Constantly. It's extremely frustrating. I don't even mind the grind too much for PVE, but when the grind affects my ability to be competitive in a PVP game, that sucks. PVP would benefit from a draft system, where everyone picks from a collection of things, and uses their skills in knowing what to do to win games, rather than just grinding for good traps, or paying real money for things. I don't think there's anything that can be done to make me really enjoy the PVP in it's current state, and the fact that one of the daily quests is ALWAYS winning two games of PVP, is so annoying. I want to log in everyday, do my quests and just have some fun. But being required to not only play the PVP at least twice, but WIN. TWICE. I hate it. I just want to do PVE for now. Also you can use your once-per-day quest reroll on the PVP quest, and it just gives you back the PVP quest. So I've wasted that twice because it doesn't tell me I can't reroll it, but still lets me reroll it. Just let me reroll it. It's not worth pushing people towards PVP if they're frustrated with it. It'll just encourage me to switch games.
PVP is the biggest disappointment for me, but a few other problems I had are:
- Some out of bounds areas are unclear. Sometimes you can walk past gates, other times you are slowly killed. Never know when or why that happens. Would be nice to see it on the map.
- Speaking of the map, I wish there was a better indicator of the terrain on the maps. I'd like to know where the enemies will and won't go, where I can and can't go, or if an area is even accessible at all. I don't remember which map it was, but there was a large chunk on the right that wasn't anything.
- Give us infinite time to set up in the beginning. If the maps were better, this wouldn't be such a problem, but I find myself needing to scope out the map, and sometimes there's just not enough time. I don't see why there needs to be a timer at the very start. Obviously I'm only talking about PVE.
- Pausing in PVE. I don't see why not. At least for solo.
- A store where you can just buy equipment would be nice. I don't mind grinding, but I don't see why you wouldn't have the ability to spend a chunk of skulls to just get the thing you want.
I don't really have a list of the good stuff, because the rest of it is pretty good. My friend and I have played a lot of it in the few days since we started. I'd love to stick with it and eventually get involved in the PVP, so I hope there are some good changes coming eventually.

If you are looking for a 4X game that is well crafted and allows you to play in many different ways then Galactic Civilizations III is recommended.  However, if you are looking for an innovative 4X game that redefines the genre norms, you might consider the design a bit too safe.
The race customisation options are very cool, there is decent variety in the technology tree and ideology tree.  There are lot of ways to play via the different victory types, set-up options and campaign (albeit brief the missions are fun particularly at higher difficulty).
The galaxy has a good range of events, bonuses, resources, pirates and minor civilizations particularly if you play with the Precursor Worlds DLC.
The diverse personalities of the races is very noticeable both in the diplomacy interactions and the way they actually play.  Playing against other custom factions available via the Steam workshop is quite fun.
The AI is okay but well behind Gal Civ 2.  The AI can build colonies up well but doesn't use some mechanics effectively such as Diplomacy and has extremely weak late game strategies.  The game can provide a challenge early, though.
The User Interface is intuitive and easy to use.
The game really is quite beautiful graphically for the most part (except the battle viewer, we'll get to that below).
In summary, I've enjoyed the game a lot more than I expected and had plenty of playtime.
The game is very poorly balanced and there are a large number of excessive exploits available to the player.  In particular, the diplomacy system is the most expoitable system I can recall in any 4X game ... ever.  I've posted save games on the Stardock forums to no avail e.g. Alliance Victory on Godlike Difficulty on a Huge map in just 36 turns etc, etc.
Starbases are a micromanagement nightmare.
There is a lack of innovation in the game.  Some consider this a positive, and while I agree there is a formula that shouldn't be messed with too much, I couldn't describe the game as leading the 4X genre as a result.  At least not yet.
The combat is really dull and in particularly it's graphically lame (disappointing given how stunning Sins of a Solar Empire was to look at from Stardock).
Unfortunately there are no cool end game threats (saved for expansions no doubt).  If you want World Destroyers, Stellar Converters or other cool stuff, you'll like have to look elsewhere.
Most 4X fans will enjoy the game but some are going to find the lack of innovation a turn off.
If you are on the fence about this game I would probably wait.  Stardock are committed to continuing to improve the game and do offer pretty deep sales from time to time.  That said, as a Space 4X fan, I'll likely continue to load it up again after each major update.

Let me preface by saying that Final Fantasy VII is the last American release (by order of release date) that I have completed in the series, so far.  It is a classic, in that other video games in the role-playing genre are still compared to it today--with good reason.  I loved this game when it was released over fifteen years ago, and I still love it today.
So let's focus on the negatives, starting with the most egregious problems: whomever was placed in charge of reprogramming this game for the computer put new mouths on those characters that lacked them (i.e. Sephiroth, Jessie, etc.).  Unfortunately, they used just the one mouth position: a whorish "O."  Suddenly every character with a new mouth has taken on the appearance of a blow-up pleasure doll, an image that is only reinforced by the early 3D animation.  It is NOT a pretty sight.
For the Uninitiated: Players might be frustrated with some of the unintentional difficulties of an EARLY attempt at 3D gaming, specifically movement.  There is something of a learning curve with materia.  The graphics are dated.  Some of the mini-games are terrible (though most are thankfully avoidable).  I would also highly recommend purchasing (or at least looking up via internet) a guide, as not every quest is terribly clear.
With that said, there are mods that can fix the mouth problem.  I am also grateful that some of the more distracting translation errors have been fixed since the game's first US release.  Overall, I'd recommend this game highly to anyone who's played it and wants to relive it... and for anyone else who wants to experience a classic.
But seriously.  Get the mouth mod.  Sephiroth with that "O" face is just creepy.  Well... creepier.

Let's start with the good things :
Story : ok
gunfights : basic but pretty good despite the limited number of weapons you can carry at the same time + bad ennemy AI glitches that will allow you to kill 10 guys just by waiting at the corner and whistling, waiting for them to come one at a time.
scenario : ok
music : excellent
car handling : not that bad, depends on what car you're driving
But...
The game is
repetitive. Every part of the game follows the same scenario : talk to someone, disrupt the mafia business in a defined zone (with a few killing/interrogating missions), kill local boss, assign the zone to one of your three folks. Rince and repeat. It just NEVER changes during the whole game. This will kill all the fun for most players.
Character and car customization are quite poor : only a few different dresses for Lincoln, and you can only modify cars that you won through district control, so that's a very limited number of cars you can tune.
+ You have to make your lieutenants rich (by giving them business opportunities once you've cleaned a district) in order to unlock more customization options (cars / more weapons / more health / better accuracy/reload time with a type of weapon etc), this will leave you for quite a long period of time with only the basics.
Game is poorly optimized on PC : it looks good, but you can never really remove some blurry effects and you will experience some crashes and glitches from time to time : for me, it has been a lot of game freezes, with the app remaining on top of screen without beeing able to kill the process forcing me to disconnect from my windows session and reconnect ; or just simply the game crashing and disappearing all of a sudden. Not a big deal anyway, as the game saves your progression quite often, but really annoying.

Do you recommend this game?

This is a brilliant game idea with a brilliant execution. Mix between roguelike and rhythm was never expected to be this fun. Looks simple in the surface, just four buttons and four level, but actually have a great amount of depth. Training to get better is so rewarding, especially in higher level. You will die often but never feel unfair. You will get the feeling you die because your own mistake, not because RNG. This game probably have the great balanced gameplay. Item or monster are less likely to feel OP, which is rare on rougelike genre.
As early access player, I have to say this is a good example how you do an early access game. Developer are active on forum, either on steam forum or their own official forum. Player and developer are working together, mostly on testing new feature and bug tracking. Suggestion from player are taken often. You can check update history if you want. For me, Brace Yourself Games is a trusted game developer and I won't mind jump in to their next early access project if that happening.
What surprised me is how good the final release are. First thing to notice is how big the installation size compared to beta build, it's almost four times bigger. After checking the files and trying the game for couple of hours, I realize they are adding cutscene, extra soundtrack, and some finishing touch to the game. It is indeed not relevant to beta testing but I believe it's quite important to final release. It's a good move I would say. The developer are often promised that the final zone, the zone 4, will be released in final build and kept early access player waiting for that. After finishing the zone, with some awesome boss battle, I have to say it's worth the wait. It's feel like a gift from developer to the early access player, to describe how good it is.
So the verdict is: You get this game and You never regret it.

Warning: The opening of this game is weak, but the pace and variety quickly pick up. Entertaining for a few hours. There's plenty of gear, but what the gear lacks is a choice. Every piece you find or craft is a "equip this because it has bigger numbers" choice.
Edit: My original review gave D: AET a recommended rating. After months of owning the game, I haven't had the craving to revisit it even once. The awkward characters are just painful to listen to, and the controls are outlandish. On a screen with flying enemies, you may find Dust flying around in the air for up to forty seconds, extending the period of his air time with every attack. The mechanics are almost there, and the timings aren't half bad even, but watching some of the interactions is... well it's on the verge of comedy.
Because I feel bad about being so harsh, here's what I think some players may find interesting:
-Hand drawn art
-Attacks that scale with stats
-Varied and interesting locations
-Big fat numbers popping over your head every time you click a button.
-Playing as a furry creature and humans in the game don't even question it
I'm not really into that animal-kin crowd and do my best to avoid them, but I can respect that there are people that dig it and might find an environment like that welcoming.
As for the question "Should I spend my money to buy Dust: An Elysian Tail at full retail price?", the final verdict is probably not.

I honestly wasn't sure how much I'd enjoy the game once I played it for a while. The art style kind of turned me off. I stuck through it anyway, and while it isn't a masterpiece, it was actually still quite enjoyable. I'm glad I didn't quit on this game.
The game's weakest point is the artstyle. Right now you're thinking "What? but look how smooth everything is! Those gorgeous backgrounds and that slick action!", and I whole heartedly agree with that. When you're playing the game and figthing enemies, the game looks and moves FLAWLESSLY. The backgrounds and environments are really well done and are filled with color. The game looks straight up gorgeous on these points. But when the game stops playing and tries to move the story along, it looks quite unappealing. There are moments where characters exchange dialogue and their words are displayed next to a close up of the character. My apologies to the artist when I say this, but my first thought when I encountered one of these was "What is this, Deviant Art?". That's really the best way to explain how it looks. My friend walked into the room while I was in a conversation in game, and literally the first thing she said was "Why does it look like deviant art?". I was not even aware she knew what deviant art was before she said that. For those who don't know what I mean, I'm saying that the art (character design mostly) looks very amateur. There are also animated cutscenes towards the end that also look cheap and amateurish.  I acknowledge that it's mostly due to the indie nature of this game that these flaws exist, however, it doesn't excuse them for me.
It's a shame that the art style looks so inexperienced, because the voice acting is really quite good! Honestly every character is voiced really well and all the lines are delivered the way they were intended. My least favorite voice would have to be Fidget (the flying bat girl). Her voice always comes off as someone trying to sound small and cute. It just doesn't fit well, or her lines are too corny for it to be enjoyable. Otherwise, good job on the voices all around.
The story is kind of meh. I didn't find myself particularly invested in anything. The game definitely tries to pull you in with some (really) sappy cliche'd moments sometimes like trying to make you feel bad that a character dies or something, though these moments were hardly effective. I feel like this is, again, a fault of the character design/ art style. I just couldn't connect emotionally with what I was seeing. There are moments of intrigue occassionally that'll gain your interest now and again. While the story wasn't anything too noteworthy, the end game is pretty well done. The drama comes off quite effectively towards the end. It's a shame that the cutscenese can't properly convey the same emotions the voices do.
The gameplay at first seemed fairly simple and repetetive. For the most part, it stays that way the whole game. You don't unlock more combo's only some new moves that can mix things up a bit, like a spin attack in the air or a new power for fidget. As repetetive as the combat was, I never actually felt bored playing it. On the contrary, the fighting was honestly always fun and pretty much the highlight of the game. Dust moves so smoothly and controls very well. He also looks pretty cool when you're pulling off the right moves. The levels are designed in a metriodvania fashion, though you never have to do any backtracking. Backtracking is reserved for finding secrets which there are plenty of.
All in all, a worthwhile game. Not breaking boundaries by anymeans, but what it aims to do, it does well. Try the demo and if you like the gameplay and can withstand the artstyle, you'll likely enjoy the actual game.

Quick Review: A relatively weak and uninspiring Endless Runner that gets boring as soon as the joke wears off (which is quick). At £4.79 or your regional equvilent this is an expensive game for the genre.
Longer-ish Review: "Where's My Mommy?" is an endless runner that sees you mother get ejected out of your hosts poop hole and into the great beyond. Enter our protagonist a considerably small piece of fecal matter who must go on an endless runner quest to find her.
The game has 3 main mechanics; the ability to jump over obstacles, the ability to go squishy to pass through gaps & permeable onstacles and the ability to go hard and break stuff like condoms.
While this all sounds like a silly fun laugh that is pretty much it. you amble through the levels basically trying to work out (and sometimes guess) which objects require you to go hard and which squishy. It is bizarre logic most of the time which is which and totally random others. Either way this mechanic definitely did not add to the game and I felt it would have worked much better just giving me things to jump over and dodge.
For fans of the genre there could be a fun 5 minutes here but for the price there really is better examples of the genre on the market.

If you've grown tired of crappy endless runners hitting the Steam marketplace, well, rejoice, as there's now one centered around feces.
is the tale of young Poopey in search of his mother after a terrible "earthquake" pulls the two apart. In his quest he travels through the colon in hopes of rescuing her before passing through the hole that no life has ever been seen from once it passes through, all the while avoiding a plethora of obstacles and memes along the way. But is this title worth the nearly six dollars US currency, or does its
/Newgrounds style of artwork in the trailer stand as the only aspect of the game worth noting?
For the most part the humor is subtle, but it wears thin within the first minute or two of actual game play. Playing as a mound of excrement is a running joke we're seeing quite a lot of, perhaps as an allegory for the Steam Greenlight system and approval process. This includes the recent fecal inspired platformer titled
that has your tightly packed hero collecting items and solving mini puzzles to clear a level, as well as a number of other bodily fluid inspired entries too poorly done to make it to the storefront. For
, however, you just have to jump over or through certain dangerous barriers. Some of them are cheeky, such as the skeletal remains of a hamster, bags of cocaine, condoms, as well as half of what appears to be
and, well, that's about the extent of the humor that isn't internet troll faces on gold coins or the
Aragorn meme about how "one does not simply just" to explain things such as how animal bones and diarrhea will hurt the player. There's no need for those last two to exist here unless trying to bait Jim Sterling into covering this game which, if so, it backfired as it only attracted this reviewer (so far).
The control scheme can seem a bit daunting at first but, really, it ends up just three buttons/keys. Q turns you to liquid to pass through porous or grated objects, d hardens you to destroy the others, and both a and the space bar jump. There is a double jump option but, at the time of writing this review, the second pressing of the button to trigger it doesn't always respond as well as it needs to, not to mention I've accidentally gotten it to triple jump somehow on two occasions. The instructions during the practice segments, however, show the Xbox controller scheme, and not the keyboard, so if you forget you have to play a bit of s guessing game to advance. And, really that's the height of the difficulty across the game's three modes of play.
Story mode is literally a casual runner experience, and where you'll spend most of your time trying to save your mother. It's a good way to get some practice in, though offers very little actual challenge, or anything of real interest to keep you going other than a random "Hey, look at that, how'd that get in there?" moment like the observance of a severed finger tucked away neatly. There's also Endless mode which is literally the endless runner approach to the game with the same level of difficulty, while Sadist mode throws more difficult challenges at you. Of course, those challenges are just the same gimmicky obstacles, but more of them, and all clumped tightly together.
All that said,
does look good for an endless runner style game, not to mention does have a fairly catchy soundtrack. There are some random elements like harmonized flatulence that may catch you off guard, as well as a man shouting "I need an adult!" in the background that I believe is from
, but it's hard to tell. Either way, the audio does stand as one of the more impressive aspects, but even that isn't quite enough to save the gameplay, or keep you going.
is the most basic of bare bones concepts for the style, though with a stagnant humorous set-up that doesn't last beyond the first few minutes of playing, leaving simpler titles like
, yet another cutesy endless runner with a story mode that only costs one US dollar, to be a far more viable option to waste plenty of time on because it knows what it is and isn't trying to reinvent the wheel with the same tools and strive to reach the same outcome. Instead of relying on you to care to ask "What else is up this person/animal's♥♥♥♥♥", that one focuses on being a competent game with a simple story and proper increasing difficulty curve that makes it more a score attack experience than one simply meant to shock you or play up your childish sense of humor, something I admit to have yet still found this title bland.
To put it bluntly,
is just boring. It's just a one-joke gimmick that plays off the popularity of a genre that is completely over saturated the way it is. There's little to really keep the player going except for achievements, and even then they aren't worth the time or six US dollars for such a barren experience. Even at one or two dollars, you're left with something that loses the power of its punchline almost immediately, leaving you having spent money for something that would have been better received on mobile devices or Newgrounds. Hopefully the developer does or adds more to this game in the future but, as it stands, you can only polish a turd so much before you just accept that fact that it is, indeed, a turd.

Unfortunately, none of the tech or inspired design that made Journey, Flower and flOw such profoundly memorable games emerges in Abzu. The way you explore the game is marred by arbitrary barriers with obtusely repetitive solutions, as well as on-rails segments and cutscenes that are as stressful as the free exploration is uneventful. On a more abstract level, the density and number of objects that have no function other than obscuring the view detracts from the more appealing and minimalistic foundation that does exist underneath. It's also tempting to point out that the involuntary transportation style on-rails segments could have been done while hanging on to the sea-creatures if you wished, which after all is implemented in the game, and so doing away with the sense of being subjected to pointless mini-games of "touch the school of fish for extra boost, so the segment can end sooner". That then transition into exploration areas where glimpses of interesting mechanics can be found, if you search hard and view it detached from the guided overall presentation.
Abzu, on the other hand, should be given the award for best use of the Unreal Engine to date - in spite of the limitations on the size of the sequential areas, that results in likening the experience to swimming in a series of aquariums rather than diving in the sea. But much praise to unnamed coder guy who did the aquarium growth that are pushed aside softly whenever you or larger fish swim through them. But the sporadic exceptions of aquarium growth that is dynamic in this way should probably not result in a recommendation to buy the game on it's own.

This is the game that made me a gamer. I'd played all the classic SNES titles as a kid, Super Mario World, Donkey Kong, Zelda, etc. and was a huge Mortal Kombat II nut for a while, but by the time I was in the 3rd or 4th grade, I was over videogames. They just didn't appeal to me anymore. It wasn't until the fall of 97, when I, a bright-eyed youngster just starting the 5th grade, played FFVII for the first time. I came in with no real expectations and thus, was not ready for the impact it'd have on my young, impressionable mind.
I fell in love, almost immediately. This was the game I had been waiting to play my entire life. To say I was obsessed was an understatement. All I wanted to talk about at school with my buddies was "FFVII this and FFVII that!" I drew pictures of Cloud and Barrett all over my notebooks, I spent hours pouring over all the pictures in the strategy guide and I had the time of my life. This game made me laugh (Cloud in drag lol), it made me cry (Aerith.. RIP) and I knew from that moment, that I was a gamer for life.
It's since been 16 years and no other game has been quite as important to me. Final Fantasy Tactics is perhaps my favorite game in the series and Final Fantasy X had the best battle and leveling up system, but neither can touch what VII means to me. I've played other games over the years, games that I obsessed over as well.. from Super Mario World to the Last of Us, I've had a long time to play many games.. but no other game will ever touch Final Fantasy VII. To see it still be so popular makes me happy and I really hope that one day, we have a genuine remake so that a new generation of gamers can fall in love with these characters as I did.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

In the settings you can change the battle type to "wait" which will prevent enemies from attacking while your choose your own attacks from the menu.
The game has quite a bit of extras/ end-game content such as extra boss fights, chocobo racing/breeding, ultimate weapons (some time-sensitive), extra characters, extra attacks, materia collection, etc. So you will definitely get your moneys worth in terms of content and time spent to get 100% completion. I have personally put hundreds upon hundreds of hours into this game when I owned it on Playstation.
In conclusion, although the game does show its age amongst the newer titles of a similar genre out today, It will always be one of the greatest RPGs of all time.
