Dust: An Elysian Tail is a sort of Hack n' Slash platformer game featuring cartoony anthropomorphic animals. The game starts with Dust, who is quickly met with Fidget after a magical sword flies to him. Dust is told of an ancient prophecy that doom has taken over the world and he is the legendary hero to save it. Reluctantly, Fidget joins with the promise that the sword will be returned to her after the silly venture. The heroes learn just how bad the world really is in peril.
The game features an excellent, cartoony, fantasy world that no matter where you are it is astonishing and beautiful. All the environmental and particle effects are brilliant and bring the perfect mood to the game. The voice acting is a bit like an anime cliché, being somewhat overly dramatic and has pauses when speaking for effect. The characters are all charming by their appearance and apparent personalities seen through the game's dialogue and cutscenes. The game's settings are very customisable and really does its best to make it comfortable for you. The actual controls are probably the most fantastic bit of the game otherwise. They are really simple and mouse controls are precise, with the addition of smoothing, making it even more fluid. This makes the game fantastic to play, as the controls can be mixed just about any way you want with little to no flaws (that aren't your own, of course).
This game is absolutely fantastic, especially for being made by just one person and a few voice actors.

This is a brilliant game idea with a brilliant execution. Mix between roguelike and rhythm was never expected to be this fun. Looks simple in the surface, just four buttons and four level, but actually have a great amount of depth. Training to get better is so rewarding, especially in higher level. You will die often but never feel unfair. You will get the feeling you die because your own mistake, not because RNG. This game probably have the great balanced gameplay. Item or monster are less likely to feel OP, which is rare on rougelike genre.
As early access player, I have to say this is a good example how you do an early access game. Developer are active on forum, either on steam forum or their own official forum. Player and developer are working together, mostly on testing new feature and bug tracking. Suggestion from player are taken often. You can check update history if you want. For me, Brace Yourself Games is a trusted game developer and I won't mind jump in to their next early access project if that happening.

This was a ridiculously fun game. The gameplay shines as extremely fast paced. You earn experience by chaining up huge combos, ensuring a continual stream of hacking, slashing and causing explosions to fly around the screen. One thing to note is that you may want to consider using a controller rather than a keyboard.
Sadly, the game's storyline is pretty weak and left a lot to be desired - You play as Dust, the mysterious hero who wakes up with (DUN DUN DUUNNNNN) amnesia and ends up finding himself on a quest to save the Moonblood (AKA, reptile) race from genocide at the hands of General Gaius and his legion of racist mammals, learning your destiny and true nature along the way and blah blah blah... it's pretty standard generic fare, and in my opinion, left a lot of important details unspoken that I REALLY wish would have been expanded on. It also creeped me out a bit how oddly sympathetic General Gaius was portrayed despite basically being lizard Hitler. Despite all that, the characters are pretty likable and full of personality, and the voice acting is well done.
Visuals are the other area where this game really shines aside from gameplay. Almost all of the graphics are hand drawn, with the exception of water renderings and Dust's sword (which admittedly causes an odd juxtaposition with his hand-drawn sprites). The locations, although generic (forest level, cave level, snow level, lava level etc), are all beautifully illustrated and provide gorgeous eyecandy.
If you can forgive the weak story in lieu of the strong gameplay, then I highly recomend Dust: An Elysian Tail

Brilliant, brilliant game. Like GalCiv2 - one of the best strategy games ever made - but (far) better-looking, more intuitive and all-round better designed. Have put nearly 60 hours into this baby and that's only Early Access. Stardock promise to support this game for the next 5 years at least, so God knows how much better it's going to get than it already is.
64-bit and multi-core means you can have up to *128* AI players. The largest galaxies are HUGE. It could take you weeks or months (?) to play out a game of that scale with so many opponents. The AI is smart, too, and it's only gonna get smarter.
Each game is different if you play with a random galaxy and random opponents in sandbox mode - the potential is almost limitless. This, my friends, is 4x strategy on the grandest scale it gets.
There are so many ways to win: military conquest, ascension, alliance victory, technological victory, turn times, influence/cultural victory. The replay value is massive.
The game looks and feels great. It sounds good, too. They've got the atmosphere just right.
The tech tree is massive and you can build special weapons that can only be made by mining special resources.
Design your own ships - these can really make a difference in-game and they look great. Do Star Trek, Star Wars...the possibilites are endless and you are only limited by your imagination. Many players say this feature is one of the best in the game!
Diplomacy is intelligent and that will only improve, too.
Then there is multiplayer - build empires and tear down those of your friends!
What great replay value this game has.
It's only going to get better and Stardock has a track record of supporting and constantly improving their products. The Beta currently still has a few glitches but the devs are working hard to fix them.
I think this will be one of the games of the year. My simple recommendation is BUY THIS GAME - I promise you will be glad you did!

Hits all the notes you'd want a 4X space game to hit. Additionally, I love how much flavour text is here. Most races have their own personalized description of each and every tech on the techtree, and personalized greetings specific to them and you. For example, if you're playing the Yor, the Iconians start off by expressing their profound disappointment in you, whereas the Iridium Corporation will ask if you'd ever be interested in buying some fancy oils from them. It's a very nice touch that keeps me driven to pay attention to tech and diplomacy across multiple playthroughs, knowing there's always something slightly new around the next corner.
The ship designs are pretty great, too. Galactic Civilizations continues to be the best series when it comes to customizing the look of your ships, however you don't get to control them directly in battles, and the combat isn't as tactical as Sword of the Stars or anything: You just throw your ships in there and whoever has the biggest boat with the most guns wins. There's the now-standard lasers/guns/missiles interplay to consider, but nothing really beyond that.
In all though, Galactic Civilizations 3 is probably one of the meatiest 4X space games you're likely to find out there at the moment.

A must have for anyone. Period. Especially so for those who are fans of Flowers and/or Journey for consoles. An excellent game all around with many odes and callbacks to the first two games mentioned. I have tested this on multiple setups and monitors. If you have a good rig, its really a beautiful game. More so if you have a 21:9 monitor (curved is even better) at 1440p (or even 4k) at full settings running at 60fps or higher (titan X or founders 1080).
As many have mentioned, it is absolutely gorgeous (some scenes are just jaw-dropping and amazing). And the soundtrack and overall quality leads to a very calming and almost cathartic experience. Again, as many have stated, it is a rather short game, but if you actually enjoy the experience, and dont run through it and take a lil time to explore some areas and ride some of the different sea life, 'm sure it could easily clock over 3-4 hours. Which i know for the price tag seems short, but all in all its quite worth it. Especially if you have VR because alot ofo vr games are 10-20 bucks and are basically demos and much, much shorter. Mentioning that though i will admit, if they had waited a little longer to put it on PS VR  and on PC VR it would have been so OP. By far.
All and all a great game, fantastic port job, extremely fluid and immersive, lots of fun suprises and definitely one of a kind with little comparison except for Journey. Still totally worth it but if you have a limited budget i would say maybe hold off until you can get it on sale or hopefully in a bundle before christmas. Definitely a must buy and top ten of the year, only downside was i wish it was longer, as do most, but if you played Journey you know what to expect. Some replay value, mostly in showing off the great areas and scenes that standout to your friends and family or yourself again.,.
Graphics: 9.5   (Distinct, simple at times, overly complex at times but only to the brink and never overwhelming).
Optimization: 9.5   (would never think it was a port, extremely well running with zero bugs or big framerate drops even when you have 10thousand fish in a single school at one time or tons of other on screen goodies and animations).
Sound: 10   (could soothe a thorn-pawed tiger in a second). Effects come through so perfectly. If you have a good pair of headphones its an amazing experience and goes hand in hand with the visuals all the way.
Value/Replay Value: 7.5   (lots of production but no matter what is still beatable in under 2 hours, sadly enough)
Controls: 8.5    definitely requires a controller. Works well on xbox one and steam controller. May need a settings tweak and iversion on camera for some, i did.
Overall:  9.5

FFVII was Squaresoft's most revolutionary success, and too much can be said and has been said about such. This game does offer the best story of the series, though it is esentially convoluted and full of holes. The dark theme is refreshing, but at times it feels out of context when compared to the plethora of comical hijinx and colorful characters. The materia system is fantastic in its simplicity, though it lacks any deep customization. It is more complex than bare bones leveling up, but less so than any of the following titles in the series. FFVII's difficulty is exceedingly simple, even at its gravest challenges, so ethusiast of the strategy aspect of this genre might be disappointed. The characters are all well designed yet some lack the depth of others. Its a very mid-range title in the series in many ways save for the plot. If you're somehow a fan of J-console style RPGs and have not played this title I would highly recommend it.

I was prompted to give a review, so despite avoiding looking at this game for the past few months, like an ex's profile page, i figured i might as well give my opinion, which has already long since been worn out on the forums, seeing as this game was a pretty big part of my life for the past couple years.
I wish i could give it a neutral score, seeing as it's not bad, but it's not exactly good either. The massive factor in that of course, is the removal of siege. I was never into MOBAs before i played unchained, so i was pretty indifferent to their decision to go in that direction initially. But i quickly got into it, because, dammit, it just worked. The art style, the story, the characters, it all fit into that format like a glove. It was a fun new direction to go in to keep things innovative and fresh. I mean, they actually created something entirely unique. It wasn't a traditional moba, which most of the players would have known if they stuck with it instead of running away at the sight of the word MOBA.
Survival being included ultimately killed it, and while i can't blame them for putting it in to get back the people who whined about the lack of "muh classic omd feel" (which i hear is still being searched for to this day), siege ended up being neglected development-wise, which is why it was the less popular mode (it had 2 maps dude. of course people got bored and went to survival).
It's often repeated, but if survival was always the main focus of unchained, they should have just made OMD3. I know it sucks to have to backpedal, but if a game is initially pushed as a spin off which will serve as a sort of hub for different game modes, then.. stick with that and do omd3 later.
The above blurb aside, my gripes with the game in it's current form:
It's not fun anymore.
Getting the taste of fun in siege, turned me off the tower defense format. While i still think is alright, the goal became a little less interesting, it was more of a time waster, when you wanted a change of scenery. Now the whole game revolves around it. I enjoyed it in the first two, but the format worked. Not saying it had a hugely complex story, but there was a sense of progression that felt very satisfying. The format now is very disconnected and not very engaging.
The closest thing to a campaign was the prologue and people even managed to complain about that.
It's not very single player friendly.
The first two got me used to the OMD format on my own. I never even touched co-op in 2. The satisfaction of soloing maps and being entirely in charge of your killbox became part of the experience. Some of the maps are obviously designed with multiple players in mind. Not saying people can't solo them, but they're not very fun to play on your own. The progression again touches on that, because you'll go from a tiny map to a gigantic map, unlike the first 2 where the maps changed very gradually.
The heroes now feel insignificant.
The heroes are my favourite part of this game. They're all wonderful and unique. Early in development things were more based on the overall story of order vs unchained, which made sense with siege mode and also all of the heroes being from either faction. They also had roles, either attack or defense (later pillager, but that could have been done without) and every hero felt like they had a purpose on the team, i.e Ivy as support/healer, Midnight as assassin etc.
Now they are all essentially defense and as a result feel less unique. Given the monotonous style of survival, it seems redundant to even have that many heroes as the play style won't change that drastically depending on who you are. That also kills the hype of new heroes being released, like when temper finally came back, i gave him a spin for one game and just couldn't be bothered any further.
There wasn't much reassurance from the devs about what direction the game is going in. Industry definitely won over art, in regards to them trying anything new or interesting, so you can only presume the overall plan is to polish survival, the most uninteresting mode, to please the crowd that want to play the same game over and over.
Survival in it's current state just doesn't carry this game. I would enjoy it much more if it was in contrast to another, stronger mode, or if they went for a campaign format to make progression more interesting, give single players something to do and make use of all of the characters.
Again, I wish i could give it a meh score, rather than a negative one, because i did really love this game and feel like it could be great, so i can only continue to hope robot have some fun, interesting plans for it in the future.

FF7 is a monolith of my childhood. How do you review a game with so much hype and pomp and fanatical emotion? It's easier than I thought it would be, given that I can play it again. It's just like I remember. FF7 is like putting on a warm sweater and drinking hot cider. It's a comfort-game. Let me explain.
FF7 came out when I was 11. I did not get to play it until I was 12. Everyone told me how great it was--and how it was introducing western audiences to the Japanese RPG world by storm. So when I got a used Playstation, I got the game.
I did not know it at the time, but this FF game was unlike the six that preceeded it in terms of setting and magic system. So I had no bias to base my analysis off of. All I knew was that the Materia system was great. It was easy to use and learn--and as I got better at the game, I began to think up more complex combinations of Materia and equipment. (Woo, Curse Ring and then Added Effect/Destruct in linked Armor slots) There were literally, thousands of combinations. And that's not even touching Enemy-Skill, Morph and Manipulate.
The Materia system was rock solid. You could completely customize what characters you felt would be best for certain combinations. You weren't constrained by this idea of a Character Class--at least in regards to magic. In terms of weapons, yes, perhaps that was more restricted--but I loved it. Everyone was different--it was perfect. You could create an awesome balance between tanks like Barret and speedsters like Tifa---with characters like Nanaki, Vincent and Yuffie--who were skilled physically and magically.
And of course, you can't have a game without good characters. Despite the foamy mustache that Square has gotten from milking FF7 for everything its got--don't believe what they've done to Cloud. In FF7, he was not the whiny little angst-machine that Square has turned him into. He went through big things in FF7 and he got low--but he came back. He got back up, dusted himself off and kept going. That was the entire point. But Square would have you thinking he spends all his time whining and moping around. Not true. When Advent Children came out, I was quite confused because their Cloud wasn't acting like...well, Cloud.
Aeris is your Mary Sue Last of her Race, Magic MacGuffin Carrier Female White Mage thing. I make a point to get her out of my party ASAP. This is only because I personally don't like her. I hate her snippy attitude, her selfishness and her blatant disregard of everyone around her--except for Cloud. She is the most irritating character. However---that is just my personal opinion (besides, the game did me a solid and I forgave them at, you know, That Part). As a character--Aeris moves the plot along and she IS a helluva powerful White Mage/Magic User. When I have to have her with me, I always put Cover on her and Fury---so whenever she takes a hit for someone, it ramps up her Limit Break bar and then she busts out the Holy magic.
Tifa kind of lists back and forth between annoying and cool. She's the fistfighter/monk character and between her and Aeris, I'll take Tifa. She can deal some real damage (Powersoul + Curse Ring = Constant 4x damage infliction) and she has a real connection with Cloud. Whereas with Aeris--her thing with Cloud feels very shallow---Tifa actually feels very natural with Cloud. She cares about him, deeply. And when you learn about him--he cares about her.
Barret is your angry tank/heavy gunner. I would say he's probably the least characterized (except for Cait Sith) but he's a good long range strong arm.
Nanaki, I really like too---he's very calm, collected and thoughtful. He's very reasonable, not one o pin blame like Barrett does sometimes.
Cid Highwind is my favorite--tough-talking roughneck chainsmoking pilot. He gets jipped a lot for some reason. But he's the Reluctant Leader. He can lead, he's fine with leading---but he can also follow. He's not insecure like Barrett and if he needs to step up, he does. And his crew respects him for it. He's got balls--but he's not a jerk. Cid curses and is kind of rough and tumble---but when he makes that one short speech about how their planet is wandering small and lonely in the universe, it shows a little more in there.
Yuffie is my favorite of the ladies. Okay, yes, she'll steal your stuff---but she has so much personality (and she doesn't fawn over Cloud). She's straight-forward, to the point, hilariously awful sometimes. And once you get her leveled up--she is a straight up badass. One of my favorite things to do when Cid is the leader---is put her, Vincent and Cid together to go on the Train Mission. OMG, funny. She is so hilarious. She's like a Chaotic Neutral---might save your life, might steal your car. And I love that about her. They seem to have gotten away from her character type later--which I think is a real shame. (Also, I ship Yuffie and Reno forever.)
And then, of course, the Big Bad. THE Big Bad. Sephiroth. A psychotic momma's boy, who will kil you, your dog, your dog's puppies, your kitchen table and then burn your house down. He literally does not give a crap about anyone or anything--but gaining power and reclaiming Gaia for Jenova. His brutality is brought home--and made personal. Cloud's backstory with Tifa in Nibelheim, Zack and then finally culminating with Aeris in the Forgotten City. His menace, his power--its legendary. You hear about Sephiroth at the very beginning of the game. You don't even see him until several hours later into gameplay. And even then--its in Cloud's flashback. The way Sephiroth is presented is masterful. They talked it up, told you how strong and crazy-evil he was, built and built and built on it--until you finally get to see him for yourself and for once, he's everything that you've heard.
This was what made it for me. Excellent pacing, a good blend of character types so that you can customize your party how you wanted (I'd rather not like a character, than be indifferent to the characters; FF8's characters were so bland--I hated it), an intuitive and creative magic and battle system, tons of sidequests, hours and hours of things to do. To just explore the World Map.
I feel like this was Square at its very best. When they wrote a complex but compelling story, a game where--each time I play, I find something I didn't know was there. I only recently discovered the Curse Ring in Mideel--or if you visit Johnny's parents in Sector 7 before its destroyed, his father talks about Nibelheim (I was like: WHOA!) and countless other small details that enrich the gameplay. Its what keeps me coming back over and over again. I've played this game countless times--and each time, I enjoy it.
Yeah, the graphics are old. It doesn't matter--its the story, the mechanics, the characters. Advent Children had beautiful graphics, beautiful. But its story was completely lame, the plot was ridiculously stupid--it was all just fanservice. So I dont even bother with all the other stuff that Square came out with to milk the FF7 cow.
I'd say they should just remake FF7---but I'm afraid they'd start messing around and changing things. Don't trust 'em. Haha.
This is one game--where it lived up to its hype. It exceeded my expectations. I saw FF7 when it came out on EA's website and I about had a heart attack. I bought instantly, that very night, that minute. And then about a week later, it came out on Steam. And I got another copy on Steam--just so that I'd always have it. Look passed the graphics, immerse yourself in the story and the dynamic characters. It's worth it. I would have paid $30 for a copy of this game--and they're selling it for $12. Worth every penny.

Bus Simulator 16 is a medium quality bus simulation game in which players are allowed to take the wheel of a variety of different busses and build up their own transport company. In this review, I aim to cover the good and bad aspects of this game in enough detail that you won't be left debating whether or not to actually get the game, like I was. I hope I am successful in my endeavours.
Just before I start with the review, I would say that you should, if you are planning on buying the game, get it at a discounted price. I'm not sure it's worth what they're asking for it, even if you do like the game.
Ok, so the main reason I really recommended this game was because of all of the bus simulators I have seen and/or played, this one seems to have the best balance of realism, while still being easy enough to play (unlike OMSI 2) and have...decent graphics. There's no denying the game has many shortcomings, and many have claimed it to be extremely boring as a simulator, but looking at the market, there really is not one really good bus simulator out there.
Starting off with the things I like about this game then, first is the fact it has a small story behind it. While you aren't playing a bus simulator for the story, the game starts you off by taking over someone else’s company and building it under your control to something much bigger by unlocking districts on the map and attaining more busses and drivers to operate them, thus increasing your profit. Essentially, the entire game revolves around this, and everything you do within it is to aid the growth of your business.
Actually getting to the busses, I like that the controls are easy to use, and that there are enough things you can do with the bus that make it feel like a simulation, such as kneel it, open doors, use the radio, heating, lights etc, without feeling over faced with buttons and not knowing what they're for, like in OMSI 2. However, the busses do not handle very well, making driving quite hard to get used to. The game also has performance issues, and many users notice constant lagging. For me, this is noticeable when turning the bus, but that action in itself feels clunky due to the design of the game.
Graphically, this game is nothing special. Scenery looks believable enough, but it’s nothing compared to simulators like Euro Truck Simulator 2, and others of it’s quality. The textures of the bus look very basic, and the outside of the bus looks deceptively like plastic most of the time, but as a result of the handling it is hard to stay in third person long enough to look at it because turning the bus seems to be unresponsive, and then sudden and violent, causing you to crash.
The game doesn’t allow for much adventure or free-roam, but that is probably a good thing because although you can walk around the open world, there is nothing about it that you’d really want to explore. If not for the task of taking commuters around the city, it would be immensely boring to play.
As far as challenge goes, driving the bus is the main one. It is a shame that it is not the most enjoyable task – you’d think a bus simulator would do a better job of making the driving feel smoother, but apparently not. While en route, you have to serve tickets and give the right amount of money back to passengers and get to each stop within a designated amount of time. When stopping, you also have to remember to kneel the bus, and park well, as well as indicating, in order to gain experience which helps you with the games progress. I don’t know if there is an endgame because I have not got there, but I do not think this is the kind of game that people would play for massive amounts of time. Rather, it is for those who have no aspirations to be a bus driver as a career, but are keen to give it a try just once to see what it is like. This game does a very good job of putting you off driving busses full time.
I would give it a 5/10 as the game is easy to play in terms of its controls compared to other bus simulators, but it does not run well, and consequently feels quite uncomfortable to play for long periods of time. It is also quite repetitive, with the only ‘drive’ (pun intended) really being to get a bigger business and better busses.
Thank you for taking the time to read my review. I do hope it helped 😊

The thing is: I really like rythm games but I usually get bored quickly by them because they have nothing more to offer than just doing the same songs over and over again to get a better accuracy score.
So here comes Crypt of the NecroDancer taking what I love about rythm games and combining it with another genre I've come to love over the last year: roguelike.
There are various permanent options to unlock for your rounds, be it better and differently working weapons, armor, spells or other miscellaneous equipment. You don't just buy equipment to start with though, there are randomly generated chests in each level, you unlock better items to be found in those and/or more spawned chests. Which is an awesome way to keep the procedural feeling alive and not just making the game considerably easy to blast through.
Each enemy has a certain pattern and rythm of moving and attacking, so due to the many different types of enemies there's a lot to learn and adapt to, which I love. If you don't quite have rythm in your blood, doing the constant moving to the beat and concentrating on visual patterns at the same time might get frustrating. Don't fret though! The game offers a training mode for both the basic monsters and minibosses - only ones you encountered yet, no spoilers.
The music is fantastic and the artstyle just nails the whole serious yet not serious mood of the game. I'm totally in love with Crypt of the NecroDancer! <3

While I say I don't recommend this game, I think it depends largely on the player. If you like generic roguelikes with some beat aspects... then this will be for you. If you don't like roguelikes, then you'll be like me and wonder why you thought it'd be any different than the other run of the mill 8-bit reset-all-progress-because-that's-game-design indie developments that flood Steam on a daily basis.
I spent 2 hours trying to beat zone 1 and got extremely close to defeating the bosses only to die to a bat, which reminds me of Zelda 1 and activates some PTSD flashbacks to my childhood. While that's not all bad for some people, it drives me insane because I know I'll spend hours on end making no progress. You get some heart upgrades pretty quickly from the start, but I almost wish they kept the default amount and reduced monster damage because extra hearts seem to do nothing when a raging minotaur comes out of the darkness and your only escape is a spike trap.
Maybe I just suck but like with Rogue Legacy, this game is a lot of fun but really starts to drain on you. There is Bard mode which lets you move around whenever you want rather than to the beat alone, but that feels like the cheap way out and I'd rather accept defeat. It's games like these that make me stick to RPGs - when I come back I know I won't have reset the last three levels, and I also know this will probably be the last roguelike I buy. Still, if you like them, you'll probably like it.

So you think you're dirty and footloose enough to step up and serve the Necrodancer with your breakin' moves? Perhaps, with the help of intrepid adventurer Cadence, you
. Crypt of the Necrodancer combines retro-chic aesthetics, challenging (but forgiving) rogue-like mechanics and rhythm based gameplay that combines to make a most unexpectedly amazing and fun game.
Gameplay combines simple mechanics that are easy to learn but, as with the best games, difficult to master. On the beats you can move in one of the four cardinal directions. If an enemy is in the tile you attempt to move to then you do damage to it. If they move to the same tile as you at the same time or you move in a manner that brings you into a tile beside an enemy without killing it then you take damage. The basic weapon is a one-tile dagger but there are many different weapons that change your attack pattern. From a longsword that lets you attack two tiles away to a whip that lets you attack diagonally. Different materials for each weapon changes the damage amount, adds special attack powers and can even heal you.
Defeating an enemy nets you gold and increases your gold mulitplier that increases the amount you pick up while timing your movements and attacks to the rhythm of the song keeps that multiplier going. Attempting to move off of the beat causes you to lose your hard danced multiplier. Gold allows you to pay to activate shrines or buy one of three randomly selected items from a shopkeeper on each level (
the shopkeeper can be killed, with some difficulty, to get the items for free).
Each level also includes a diamond in one of the rooms and an additional diamond hidden in a wall that allows you to buy upgrades in the hub world. Permanent upgrades that increase your maximum health or increase your minimum gold multiplier are available as are unlocks for new weapons and items. There's a Boss training area that lets you use diamonds to unlock a boss to practice against and even a character that will sell you one of a few items to take with you on your next dive into the dungeon can be rescued.
A rhythm game is worthless if it doesn't feature good music and the chiptune music on offering is simply amazing. Catchy tunes and easily trackable beats makes keeping rhythm with the game easy (with practice) and fun. I also fully recommend buying the soundtrack as it includes two alternate versions of the music including a metal version by FamilyJules7X and a more dance oriented chiptune version by A_Rival. You can use those songs in the game or even add your own to dance your foes into the ground.
Wholeheartedly recommended. Don't save the dance for a sale! Take the lead, turn it up and beat the Necrodancer into the street.

This is a dissapointment when compared to Orcs Must Die 1 and 2.
Bad Decisions:
- Timer on purely PvE modes that counts down even when nobody is ready. On a first time playing a new map, my friends and I take a long time to look through the map and strategize. But even when none of us have readied up, the timer will still tick down. This makes no sense in PvE modes.
- Grindy F2P Model. This is fine if it was on cosmetics and heroes only, but OMD!U forced traps behind paywalls/loot chests. This is an incredibly bad decision as players cannot choose from a variety of traps anymore, and are forced through the luck of getting them through loot chests.
- Trap Upgrade System. Traps are now upgraded through, yep, more loot chests/paywalls. This is literally pay to win.
- Game focus on MOBA rather than being a Tower Defense. If you look all the new heroes, a lot of them aren't focused on traps at all. Most of them focus on combat, and in no way helps with the tower defense, PvE aspects.
- Game Lobby detached from actual game. The game lobby is a window separate from the game. When you finish a map, you are booted off the game. This makes it so that restarting a map is impossible without turning off the game and restarting it from the game lobby. Who thought this was a good idea? If I want to 5-star a map, and I let one runner slip into the rift, now I have to exit the game, go into the game lobby, and reload it, taking almost 2 minutes. None of the previous iterations of this game had this problem.
- Barricades being nerfed. This was the final straw for me. On certain maps that have multiple enemy spawns, it is impossible to block off the main path, forcing enemies to an off-path, even though there is clearly a way for them to. Idiotically, the pathfinding is not strong enough, or is purposely made to not detect these paths, and blocking the path becomes impossible. So much for letting people strategize. Barricades are already extremely expensive, and can be destroyed by enemies. Rather than blocking the best part of your game, i.e. letting player strategize, you designers opted to take the lazy way out. It would've been easy to make barricades not the best options, such as having bombers that blows up barricades. This design choice tells me that the designers were definitely NOT, in ANY way, looking to create a good, PvE experience that would hold a candle to the previous iterations.
TL:DR
-Bad game design choices that stunts strategy for MOBA heroes design.
-Poorly made game lobby system
-Grindy F2P Model
-Worse than Orcs Must Die 2.

Note: I have 100% Abzu and ran through it two and a half times.
Abzu is an underwater adventure game; it's primary purpose is to present the player with interesting vistas and situations. From the art director of the critically acclaimed Journey, it tells a familiar story with half the heart.
I enjoyed Journey immensly, it was layered and complex, and interpretation was far more varied and open to speculation. Abzu is surprisingly less so, whether you prefer this is up to you (for me it's a bit of a negative). I can still think of Journey and wonder about some aspects, this game less so.
It struggles in the gameplay department as well, there is far less to explore and see than Journey and locomotion is nowhere near as fun. You swim in all directions by aiming and holding right trigger (on 360 controller) and can perform a speed boost by tapping the A button in a particular rhythm. This becomes pretty mindless and honestly tiring holding RT down for so long.
Though these sound like pretty big negatives, one of the main draws of this kind of game is the graphics and imagery; in this regard the game is rather successful. Few games have adequately demonstrated ocean life in a vibrant and interesting way, Abzu succeeds in this where others have failed. There are plenty of interesting and beautiful moments to be had within.
A major disappointment for many people is the price tag, this is an issue I've never had as it's quality over quantity for me. If it is for you though, I cannot recommend it; the game clocks about 2 hours for your first run through and then maybe another 2 in order to 100% the game (Which I have done). The payoff for 100% really adds little as well so I'd only recommend if you enjoyed it enough to discover a little bit more.
I'll conclude by saying this, it's no Journey but it's still a fantastic game. If you haven't played Journey and don't care about quantity over quality for games, I definitely recommend Abzu. If however you really want something new and exciting in video games having already played Journey, there is relatively little new to see here. It's enjoyable enough but I think for a majority of people this game will not blow them away.
Abzu is a solid 7/10 for me.

I'm going to start off with the good points as there are a lot. The music is amazing. You get bits of Fantasia, Alice in Wonderland, and other disney movies. It's really well done, fits well, and it adds to the mystique and wonder of the game. The visuals are amazing as well. There were several parts where my jaw hit the floor with just how breathtaking some scenes were. When there were a plethora of colours, you could just swim around and just stare in amazement at how pretty everything is.
Now for the bad. The game is short. Like, unapologetically short. Even going back and forth to other and even stopping at parts to ooo and ahh at, I still finished in under 2 hours. Certain parts of the game were very meh, as they were dead in colour or lacked the enormous detail that most of the game had. And that also effects the replayability. Most of the ooo and aaah parts, you saw it once that was it. Cool, that was amazing. That was breathtaking. It's not going to be breathtaking again, as I've already seen it.  Plus after the 2nd time of going through the "Shrine" parts, I didn't want to see it again. And I did. For 2 more times. And the couple of times where you walked? Geez, move faster huh? You can go super fast in water, but move at a snail's pace on land? There's no reason for that. The game is also one hell of a resource hog. Used about 50% of my cpu, that's not a good thing. I played it just fine, but I did have to turn the visuals just to stream it. I don't even have to do that to stream The Witcher 3 at max settings.
So to encapsulate this, the game is really beautiful to look at and the music is amazing. But, the game is way too short for 16 bucks, you're most likely not going to be replaying this, and there were a lot of parts that broke the pacing.

That was the time when I wanted to put down the gam, becasue it got quite boring. The minute differences in the missions are what kept me going. It picks up in variety again, about 3/4 of the way through the story.
The graphics are bland and blurry, I ended up using a mod/enhancer, that makes the colors pop and removes the blurry edges and adds a bit of lens flare.
Combat gets repetitive, you get a choice between full on stealth (which is very satisfying) or guns blazing (the decent amount of guns kept this option so interesting). Aiming feels very floaty at first but it gets better. The driving physics were alright, although somethimes it felt like I was in a boat. I was really happy with the races, which were different, very fun and very rewarding.
The biggest problem were definetly the bugs that shouldn't be there this late into the games "life cycle". Small pesky things were what made it less enjoyable. The game runs version 1.08 so that explains that. Its too bad that the 30fps lock on release destroyed this game, it deserves more than its given credit for.
If you are patient and like the open world genre and all that comes with it, then this game is for you.
TL;DR

Overall, an enjoyable open-world game. The combat mechanics are solid (if a bit basic) and make it almost too enjoyable to walk around shooting gangsters in the back of the head and knifing pushers in the neck. The driving mechanics are enjoyable--it's pretty easy to start powersliding around town with wreckless abandon. And the world created for the game is absolutely gorgeous.
But I think the best part of this game, and what kept me involved, was the story, the voice acting, oddly enough. Yeah, sometimes the writing gets a little heavy-handed. The downside? The gameplay was repetitive as hell. Interrogate some dudes, drive somewhere, talk to some dudes, drive somewhere, kill a bunch of dudes, drive somewhere, talk to some dudes. Now, I’ll be the first to admit that the Witcher series flew completely under my radar for the longest time. The first time I was really introduced to it was when I saw the trailer for Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings on TV on some random day. I thought it looked pretty cool so I bought it on console, since I didn’t have the pleasure of having a PC powerful enough to run it at the time. The game did capture me in the beginning, which is also used as the tutorial for all things combat in the game, but as I got to the first town, Flotsam, there were a lot of moments where I got lost due to not really knowing much about the Witcher world because I never played the first. So I stopped playing it.
It wasn’t until a few years later that I got to build the gaming PC I am using now and own both of the Witcher games in their Enhanced Edition versions. One of my friends definitely recommended that I started with the first because it had a save import system that carried over the various decisions I made in the first. There is a ton of differences between these games.
Witcher 1 nearly turned me off with its combat system. I’m not a fan of it. It’s not to the point where it made the game completely unplayable but the frustration that I got from dying so many times because I got hit by an enemy that I was in no way close to really didn’t help me. And no, I didn’t have Bleeding or Poisoned or any other sort of effect. But I steeled through the combat to experience the story, which is definitely the strong point of the game. The lore of the Witcher world is dark and you get to see just how dark the further you go into the game. Since I mostly focused on finishing the game, doing a few side quests here and there in order to keep a moderate income of orens, I beat the game at about 30 hours. Immediately, I went straight into the sequel.
Not only had the game improved thanks to the engine that CD Projekt Red was using, but they also overhauled the combat and many other things. And I welcomed most of them, only a couple things I thought was bothersome but I’ll talk about that in a bit. The combat is much more direct. Instead of clicking at just the right time in order to pull off a combo, the combat is now reliant on your own skill as a player.
You have two main weapons that you use against humans and monsters, one Steel sword and one Silver sword respectively. That right there already adds an element of strategy because you will have to change between swords at some points in the game, since a Silver sword won’t do as much damage as Steel to humans and vice versa with monsters. You’re given fast and strong attacks and the ability to block and counter your opponents. The counters you’re only able to do if you time it correctly. And you have to be careful with this combat system because the enemies can be brutal at higher difficulties.
In fact, I’ll have to note that the tutorial isn’t that great and doesn’t really explain combat very well so that is a negative that I experienced. I ended up dying a couple times on the VERY BEGINNING of the game because I wasn’t used to the combat. Eventually, I got the hang of it and was able to handle most enemies I encountered.
Anyway, you’re also given a few spells that, as a Witcher, you’re able to utilize at any time. All of them have an effect that you use to either do direct damage, like the fire spell Igni, or gain control of an enemy temporarily with the Axii spell. There are a few others that allow you to summon a barrier to protect you from a certain amount of damage or set magical traps that stop your opponent from moving and allow you to barrage them with your swords. Not only that, but you are also given sub-weapons like bombs or throwing knives that have their own status effects and allow even more strategy for the player to use. The new combat system was definitely welcome in my opinion.
Another thing they changed was the character models and made them much more lifelike. Like with Triss, she now looks just as she was described in the first game as one of the most beautiful women in all of Temeria. Dandelion, a famous bard and a lover of many women, and Zoltan, a hilarious dwarf that is loyal to a fault to those he deems his friend, look much more detailed and had a few changes here and there to befit their characters. And, of course, the main character, the Witcher known as Geralt of Rivia, has a much more intimidating appearance thanks to the piercing yellow eyes with slit pupils that told anyone what he was.
The world of Witcher 2 is beautiful, with so many detailed environments and cities that are filled with places for you to explore. I spent many hours simply going around the forest around Flotsam, fighting various monsters along the way, and tried to see everything it had to offer. There aren’t many games that really immerse me so much that cause me to do that so I have to give props to the level designers for a job well done. The people around you also have such natural conversations with each other; some of them talking about you when they think you’re out of earshot when you’re really not and are either wondering what you eat or calling you a mutant that is a menace to society.
Thanks to my rig, I was able to experience all of this at the maximum quality possible so I was constantly seeing many wondrous sights in the Witcher world.
The story and side quests were always interesting to see turn out. I was always on the edge with anticipation to see the various twists happen in them. With both of these, you’re given decisions that you must choose between that will most likely go on through to Witcher 3 and there also different ways to complete a few of the side quests. There are plenty of suspenseful decisions in the main story so you won’t have to fret about that. I was never bored in doing as many side quests as I could because the ones that didn’t involve hunting monsters had an interesting story behind them. Like finding out what happened in an insane asylum that became haunted after someone died viciously during a time of war. Or even collecting quite a hefty amount of harpy feathers for a guy that says it’s for his “client” but he ends up using them to make himself a bird costume. Quests vary from humorous to going back to the dark thematic type that really suits the world.
I could go on with the positives but I don’t want to make this stupendously long. So, I’ll go on to some of the problems I have with some things. Like with the inventory. I was constantly unequipping things by accident and that happened right before a boss fight, ending up with me fighting without boots. Another thing was that I couldn’t take potions whenever I wanted, only when I was meditating. There aren’t really chances in a fight to sit down and allow yourself to take a potion so that you can keep yourself alive.
I would mention the combat can be a problem but the developers themselves have even gone as far as to make a mod that rebalances the combat and refines it for players. Which is a pretty cool thing to do on their part to acknowledge that and help everyone out with it.
Other than those things, I really don’t have many more problems that I encountered. Really. There are so many more positives in the game that overwhelm the negatives. I was able to simply get past the inventory and potion taking problem rather easily when I was distracted with side quests and wonderful environments to explore.
My final verdict for Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is 9/ 10. It’s a great game that has a rich, dark lore and is worth every penny you lose when you buy it.

TL;DR Below.
Like many other people say: You need to be a fan of Edmund in order to fully enjoy this collection. I myself had no idea who he was until I played this collection and his story is truly fascinating. I really do recommend people to go and hear his story because I'm sure many people can relate to him on different levels. Despite that, the majority of games were not my cup of tea but that doesn't necessarily mean they're horrible.
I absolutely love Super Meat Boy and was amazed to find the original in the collection. Aether was also another interesting game I thoroughly enjoyed. Every other part of the collection was "meh" and I found it to be quite boring if not too frustrating to fully enjoy.
Another problem I had was the frames. All games of the collection require little graphical demand to run and I have a top of the line CPU and GPU but still found games running at a frame rate as low as 10. This obstacle makes some games almost impossible to play as they require some complex platforming. The reasoning I believe is because they're made in flash and are in fact flash games. These are the infancy stages of what he's created and since they are flash games, you can easily find and play them elsewhere with better performance than on this, with no cost. That being said, you are in technicality paying for behind the scenes.
Regardless of the problems I had, The Basement Collection is an interesting one at that and is one I can only recommend if you're quite fond of Edmund McMillen. The games as a game in my opinion are quite mediocre but that is because they are "flash games", but if you can connect to Edmund as well as his games then I think you would truly enjoy them. Being able to relate to Edmund can really make his games pieces of art.
The collection as a whole unfortunately I cannot recommend because of it's performance issues, gameplay mediocrity, and price tag. Even though I said I recommend it to people who are fans of Edmund, and his story is fascinating, this review is geared towards the game/collection itself, not Edmund.
TL;DR: You will only really enjoy the game/collection regardless of the poor performance fully if you meet very specific criteria. (Personal conflicts, Fan of Edmund McMillen, etc.) Buy at own discretion.

The Basement Collection is a pretty nice variety of games made by the talented Edmund McMillen. It collections contains a bunch of games, which can be either found online or playable in this game only.
Let's start with Meat Boy. If you played Super Meat Boy before, you should know the story. Your girlfriend Bandage Girl has been kidnapped by the evil Dr. Fetus. The plot is nearly the same, and was the original plot that later appeared in Super Meat Boy.
In Spewer, you play as a little creature that tries to escape the scientist's lab by spewing puke, activate traps and avoid the traps. One of my definite favorites, and requires some thinking.
Time ♥♥♥♥ (that's getting an sequel soon) is another puzzle game that features Steven, a person who has no idea in what situation he has trapped himself in and tries to find himself the way out. A very strange puzzle game.
Coil features a story similar to well, how a person gets made. It's been a while since i finished that one. It's pretty short, but still a fun one-time experience.
In Triachnid you play as a three-legged spider called Triachnid that wants to explore and find his lost larva. I always had trouble controlling this one, but you will get the hang of it.
Aether has this kid that rides his octopus-like creature and sticks onto planets and discover the 5 different moons. The game also features some hard to find easter eggs that require both exploring and playing with coordinates.
And finally, Grey Matter. This plays similar to a arcade game and you have to make triangular shapes as much as you can while avoiding all kinds of stuff. Quite difficult.
Each of the games feature special unlockables and other stuff when completing certain chapters or the whole game. These may vary and could be things like prototypes, videos, art and more. There's also 2 special games that can be unlocked by completing multiple games.
And that's the Basement Collection. Should you get it? I think you should. If you like Edmund's work or you just like to play a bunch of games in one with special unlockables, you will most likely have fun and have some rage-inducing moments. The $4 is definitely worth the price.
I just would like to say that the game runs most games in Flash, and tend to make them laggier. The menu will not have this problem.
Do yourself a favor.  Stop what you are doing right now and play this game.

Unless you have a deep and abiding love for certain kinds of Anime, this isn't the game for you.
It follows many of those story tropes so hard it hurts, leaving very little original or interesting takes on characters.
So, you may ask, if you aren't playing this game for the story, how might one find it?
This one finds it terrible. The controlls are painfully sluggish, lagging behind input considerably. If the game didn't rely upon counter-moves, this might be forgiven but due to the fact that you're supposed to easily build up combo chains and defend against attacks for extra points throughout, this creates an extra antagositc difficulty in trying to do so. Additional moves such as sliding and I guess double jumps (standard fare everywhere else these days) are opened up only when the story demands it, causing you to have to go back through completed areas several times order to find things you were forced to miss earlier. The platforming is probably the worst aspect. The game's graphics are only remotely related to where you can land. Spikes will hit you far from where they're drawn. Jumping is a best-guess situation where you'll find yourself hoping that you can clear a pit/spikes/enemies because those borders are simply not forgiving nor closely tied to what you see on your screen. Nor is how far or high you can jump a constant.
All in all, a rather frustrating play experience combined with a boring, trite story. I cannot help but implore others to skip this game.

Galactic Civilizations III is a great turn based strategy game. The civs of the galaxy have fun personalities and play differently from one another.  There is enough lore to draw me in but still enough room to make my own stories up about the civs I play. With the ability to create my own custom civs (and even design my own ships) and play as or against them the galaxy can really start to feel alive. Throw in the minor civs and set the map size to a larger setting and the galaxy is bursting with opportunities to expand, trade, make friends, and kill foes.
The tech tree is nicely executed. Each civ has their own unique techs scattered around the tree to make each civ more unique, but not so much that it feels like I have to completely relearn each civs tech tree when I play them.
Warfare is also well done. I can choose to focus on 1 of 3 weapon types and 1 of 3 defense types (or spread out and tech up a few tiers in each).  I can take these weapons and apply them to ships how I see fit. This gives me the ability to construct a hard hitting and slow megaship and construct tiny fast fighters to protect that megaship. Once 2 opposing fleets engage I can just view the results of the engagement or watch it play out in a nicely done battle viewer. I have no control in the viewer, but I think it is pretty satisfying to watch my fleet work how I intended (or watch horribly as my fragile gunboat charges in because I set it to the wrong behavior).
The UI and Empire management has its quirks but works. It is not too hard to find information when I need it, but sometimes I need to go through a few menus before I find it. However there are a lot of options for management. Example: There is a global chart that allows me to choose how all my planets divide their work force. Plus I can set how much production is going to military vs social projects. On a finer level, these same charts and values can be set on a per planet basis. As with most large strategy games, a few hours in and I started to get used to the quirks.
Diplomacy feels good. I have not really played around with it that much, so I can't comment on the depth of it. For the most part however the AI tends to make reasonable requests, trades, and agreements.
The AI is worthy. It has improved greatly over the past months but still has a few kinks. Most of the time, they seem to make sound decisions when it comes to empire management and warfare. However, some of their actions are questionable. Example: The AI will often send a colony ship into the heart of my cultural influence to establish a colony. Within a few turns that colony has flipped to my empire. With the multiple difficulty levels the AI meets my needs for a challenge.

The game has five "stages": DEFCON 5 to 1. During DEFCON 5-4, you can place down your units (airbases, silos, radars) and your fleets. When it hits DEFCON 3, you can engage other fleets for naval supremacy. When it finally reaches DEFCON 1, ready your silos, submarines and bombers because it's time for nuclear war. For each million deaths, you gain two points. For each million civilians you lose, you lose one point. Terrifying, I know.
The graphics are nothing special, but it adds a certain aesthetic to the game. You really feel like you're someone deep inside a bunker giving out orders.

En Este Review dare mi Opinion de Hotline Miami con sus Pros y Contras
--------LORE--------
Controlamos a Jacket, un Hombre Normal el Cual tiene su departamento, Un Día Comienza a tener Llamadas estrañas las cuales lo mandan a Hacer Algunos Recados, los Cuales son Matar Mafiosos Rusos y Maleantes, Para empezar nos Dan una Simple mascara para ir a Completar nuestros Recados, Segun la historia, Si no se Cumplen las ordenes podrán pasar cosas malas en tu entorno. Así que Obligatoriamente Nos Tendremos en Nuestro DELOREAN a Nuestras misiones.
En uno de sus Trabajos, Jacket encuentra a una Chica la cual estaba Secuestrada, el Protagonista la lleva a su departamento y empiezan a convivir (Mientras hace todos esos Brutales Recados). Durante el Juego, iras encontrando mascaras que te daran habilidades.
--------PROS--------
-. A Pesar de ser Un Juego totalmente hecho con Pixeles, Le da su toque de los 80', Lo Cual te hace sentir verdaderamente bien con el juego.
-. La Dificultad va Variendo cada nivel que avanzas del juego
-. Al las mascaras tener habilidades, Esto te da muchos estilos de Juego los Cuales Probar.
-. a Pesar de que el juego no tenga Mucho Dialogo o "Cinematicas" te deja Bastante clara el desarrollo del Personaje y su Historia.
-. Es un Juego bastante Desquitante en el cual puedes descargar todo lo que tienes matando Mafiosos.
-. Los Combos te dan el Objetivo de pasar Los niveles cada vez Mejor para llegar a sacar una A, una A+ o una S.
-. Un Muy Buen soundtrack, la Musica es uno de los Factores mas importantes del juego, Le da su "Toque".
----CONTRAS----
-. La IA Es un Poco rara a veces y te acaba Matando de maneras un poco extrañas.
-. Algunas Mascaras son Totalmente inservibles y Algunas a veces demasiado Rotas.
-. Muchas veces Alguien Nuevo en el juego no sabe que tiene que hacer en algunas Misiones espicificas.
-. No se Puede saltar Directamente las escenas del Departamento de Jacket despues de pasar de un capitulo a otro.
-. El juego a veces Crashea sin saber por qué, perdiendo todo tu progreso si hacias un SpeedRun o colectabas las Letras Secretas.
------RECOMENDACIONES-------
-. No Juegues con Ningun Tipo de mando, solo se te hara mas dificil jugar, el Teclado es lo mejor para jugar este juego.
-. No Te tires a lo Loco contra los mafiosos.
-. No desactives la Música, es lo Suficientemente buena Como para disfrutarla mientras Lo Juegas.
-. Intenta Comprender la Historia del Personaje.
-. Prueba Todas las armas y Mascaras que puedas para variar el juego y hacerlo mas divertido.
-------Conclusion---------
Hotline miami es un Buen juego para pasar el rato y desquitarte, te asegurara mucha diversion las horas que dura, Lo encuentro en muchos casos mejor que el Hotline Miami 2, No Dudes en Comrarlo si lo ves en oferta.

Now, without further ado, let's get down to brass tacks. TBoI is a randomly-generated "rougue-like" heavily inspired by games such as The Legend of Zelda, which happens to be one my all time favorite franchises. The items you acquire on each new and different run alter both your playstyle and your appearance, forcing you to adapt to new strategies and find new ways to overcome your foes. All of these elements combine to create one of the most complete packages I've ever seen in a game. Tack on a DLC that doubles the content and a remake on the horizen, and you've got the best game $5.00 (or $1.24) can buy.

Note: I have 100% Abzu and ran through it two and a half times.
Abzu is an underwater adventure game; it's primary purpose is to present the player with interesting vistas and situations. From the art director of the critically acclaimed Journey, it tells a familiar story with half the heart.
I enjoyed Journey immensly, it was layered and complex, and interpretation was far more varied and open to speculation. Abzu is surprisingly less so, whether you prefer this is up to you (for me it's a bit of a negative). I can still think of Journey and wonder about some aspects, this game less so.
It struggles in the gameplay department as well, there is far less to explore and see than Journey and locomotion is nowhere near as fun. You swim in all directions by aiming and holding right trigger (on 360 controller) and can perform a speed boost by tapping the A button in a particular rhythm. This becomes pretty mindless and honestly tiring holding RT down for so long.
Though these sound like pretty big negatives, one of the main draws of this kind of game is the graphics and imagery; in this regard the game is rather successful. Few games have adequately demonstrated ocean life in a vibrant and interesting way, Abzu succeeds in this where others have failed. There are plenty of interesting and beautiful moments to be had within.
A major disappointment for many people is the price tag, this is an issue I've never had as it's quality over quantity for me. If it is for you though, I cannot recommend it; the game clocks about 2 hours for your first run through and then maybe another 2 in order to 100% the game (Which I have done). The payoff for 100% really adds little as well so I'd only recommend if you enjoyed it enough to discover a little bit more.
I'll conclude by saying this, it's no Journey but it's still a fantastic game. If you haven't played Journey and don't care about quantity over quality for games, I definitely recommend Abzu. If however you really want something new and exciting in video games having already played Journey, there is relatively little new to see here. It's enjoyable enough but I think for a majority of people this game will not blow them away.
Abzu is a solid 7/10 for me.

I'm going to start off with the good points as there are a lot. The music is amazing. You get bits of Fantasia, Alice in Wonderland, and other disney movies. It's really well done, fits well, and it adds to the mystique and wonder of the game. The visuals are amazing as well. There were several parts where my jaw hit the floor with just how breathtaking some scenes were. When there were a plethora of colours, you could just swim around and just stare in amazement at how pretty everything is.
Now for the bad. The game is short. Like, unapologetically short. Even going back and forth to other and even stopping at parts to ooo and ahh at, I still finished in under 2 hours. Certain parts of the game were very meh, as they were dead in colour or lacked the enormous detail that most of the game had. And that also effects the replayability. Most of the ooo and aaah parts, you saw it once that was it. Cool, that was amazing. That was breathtaking. It's not going to be breathtaking again, as I've already seen it.  Plus after the 2nd time of going through the "Shrine" parts, I didn't want to see it again. And I did. For 2 more times. And the couple of times where you walked? Geez, move faster huh? You can go super fast in water, but move at a snail's pace on land? There's no reason for that. The game is also one hell of a resource hog. Used about 50% of my cpu, that's not a good thing. I played it just fine, but I did have to turn the visuals just to stream it. I don't even have to do that to stream The Witcher 3 at max settings.
So to encapsulate this, the game is really beautiful to look at and the music is amazing. But, the game is way too short for 16 bucks, you're most likely not going to be replaying this, and there were a lot of parts that broke the pacing.
I loved Flower and Journey, but I'm barely liking this game after being done with it. And that's a disappointment for me.

Okay so i just finished the game and heres my review.
COMBAT: Its okay, the controls are pretty basic, there's no big mechanics to it and it really never changes. Different weapons dont feel that different and the selection is rather limited. Personally i always ran with a shotgun and a silenced pistol i unlocked late game. Only fun part is the hand to hand but there are no mele weapons. The way enemy dificulty scales seems to be just based around how much damage they do, single shots from handguns start dowing a quarter of your health bar.
AI: Pretty clucking terrible if i do say so. Anytime i would be driving down the street (oh and we'll get to that monstrosity in a moment) and would veer slightly, and i mean slightly, towards the sidewalk the pedestrians would dive out of the way, normaly towards the care resulting in their heads on my wheels. Enemy AI feels like AI, it feels like a robot and thats never a fun feeling, they act very mindlessly and much of the time when fighting you'll get rushed by 4 or 5 guys all clupped up and its frustrating when u try to use the sometimes unresponsive cover system. Cop AI is probably the most annoying while also being the worst. I can drive 100+ miles down the road right by a cop, sideswiping a car and running into a lightpole and they have no interest in pulling me over. The only way to agro the police is to hit them, shoot them, or let them see you with a weapon. Their form of takedown is centered around rushing you down or ramming into you until theres cars all on you which feels awful when you play. So the AI is bad.
GRAPHICS: admitidly good but you cant appreciate them unless you have a really beefy graphics card, i have a fairly nice one and i had to run everything on low and i would still drop frames while playing.
DRIVING: This is a category because its the thing you do the most.  You drive. So. Much. The cars handle pretty poorly which is very hard to deal with when the city streets are small and crowded, theirs a mechanic of slow mo which allows you to have extreme handling while time moves much slower and this is the only way to compensate for this problem. (btw the game didnt originally have this feature but was added in later when they realized it was such an issue).
MISSIONS: If you play the first hour of the game thats how the rest of the 30 hour campaign goes. (much of which is driving remember) This is probably the biggest issue. You do the same missions with different looks with the same animations basically the whole game.
SIDE MISSIONS: Same thing as main missions, In all of them your either killing someone, stealing something, or destroying something, sometimes taking two of those and mixing it together. Its bad, boring, and not fun.
STORY: I've seen a lot of people say the story is really good buttttttttt i dont see it. Its a basic revenge plot but instead of going after the guy that actually did it you go after literally everyone else that has connections to him first.
SOUND/MUSIC: The music is great. Like really good.
DLC: its OKAY. Its too bad this mission style of different things and missions wasnt applied the whole game but for 15 dollars i dont suggest buying it, it should've been standard not extra.
Overall score: 4/10

Now, I’ll be the first to admit that the Witcher series flew completely under my radar for the longest time. The first time I was really introduced to it was when I saw the trailer for Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings on TV on some random day. I thought it looked pretty cool so I bought it on console, since I didn’t have the pleasure of having a PC powerful enough to run it at the time. The game did capture me in the beginning, which is also used as the tutorial for all things combat in the game, but as I got to the first town, Flotsam, there were a lot of moments where I got lost due to not really knowing much about the Witcher world because I never played the first. So I stopped playing it.
It wasn’t until a few years later that I got to build the gaming PC I am using now and own both of the Witcher games in their Enhanced Edition versions. One of my friends definitely recommended that I started with the first because it had a save import system that carried over the various decisions I made in the first. There is a ton of differences between these games.
Witcher 1 nearly turned me off with its combat system. I’m not a fan of it. It’s not to the point where it made the game completely unplayable but the frustration that I got from dying so many times because I got hit by an enemy that I was in no way close to really didn’t help me. And no, I didn’t have Bleeding or Poisoned or any other sort of effect. But I steeled through the combat to experience the story, which is definitely the strong point of the game. The lore of the Witcher world is dark and you get to see just how dark the further you go into the game. Since I mostly focused on finishing the game, doing a few side quests here and there in order to keep a moderate income of orens, I beat the game at about 30 hours. Immediately, I went straight into the sequel.
Not only had the game improved thanks to the engine that CD Projekt Red was using, but they also overhauled the combat and many other things. And I welcomed most of them, only a couple things I thought was bothersome but I’ll talk about that in a bit. The combat is much more direct. Instead of clicking at just the right time in order to pull off a combo, the combat is now reliant on your own skill as a player.
You have two main weapons that you use against humans and monsters, one Steel sword and one Silver sword respectively. That right there already adds an element of strategy because you will have to change between swords at some points in the game, since a Silver sword won’t do as much damage as Steel to humans and vice versa with monsters. You’re given fast and strong attacks and the ability to block and counter your opponents. The counters you’re only able to do if you time it correctly. And you have to be careful with this combat system because the enemies can be brutal at higher difficulties.
In fact, I’ll have to note that the tutorial isn’t that great and doesn’t really explain combat very well so that is a negative that I experienced. I ended up dying a couple times on the VERY BEGINNING of the game because I wasn’t used to the combat. Eventually, I got the hang of it and was able to handle most enemies I encountered.
Anyway, you’re also given a few spells that, as a Witcher, you’re able to utilize at any time. All of them have an effect that you use to either do direct damage, like the fire spell Igni, or gain control of an enemy temporarily with the Axii spell. There are a few others that allow you to summon a barrier to protect you from a certain amount of damage or set magical traps that stop your opponent from moving and allow you to barrage them with your swords. Not only that, but you are also given sub-weapons like bombs or throwing knives that have their own status effects and allow even more strategy for the player to use. The new combat system was definitely welcome in my opinion.
Another thing they changed was the character models and made them much more lifelike. Like with Triss, she now looks just as she was described in the first game as one of the most beautiful women in all of Temeria. Dandelion, a famous bard and a lover of many women, and Zoltan, a hilarious dwarf that is loyal to a fault to those he deems his friend, look much more detailed and had a few changes here and there to befit their characters. And, of course, the main character, the Witcher known as Geralt of Rivia, has a much more intimidating appearance thanks to the piercing yellow eyes with slit pupils that told anyone what he was.
The world of Witcher 2 is beautiful, with so many detailed environments and cities that are filled with places for you to explore. I spent many hours simply going around the forest around Flotsam, fighting various monsters along the way, and tried to see everything it had to offer. There aren’t many games that really immerse me so much that cause me to do that so I have to give props to the level designers for a job well done. The people around you also have such natural conversations with each other; some of them talking about you when they think you’re out of earshot when you’re really not and are either wondering what you eat or calling you a mutant that is a menace to society.
Thanks to my rig, I was able to experience all of this at the maximum quality possible so I was constantly seeing many wondrous sights in the Witcher world.
The story and side quests were always interesting to see turn out. I was always on the edge with anticipation to see the various twists happen in them. With both of these, you’re given decisions that you must choose between that will most likely go on through to Witcher 3 and there also different ways to complete a few of the side quests. There are plenty of suspenseful decisions in the main story so you won’t have to fret about that. I was never bored in doing as many side quests as I could because the ones that didn’t involve hunting monsters had an interesting story behind them. Like finding out what happened in an insane asylum that became haunted after someone died viciously during a time of war. Or even collecting quite a hefty amount of harpy feathers for a guy that says it’s for his “client” but he ends up using them to make himself a bird costume. Quests vary from humorous to going back to the dark thematic type that really suits the world.
I could go on with the positives but I don’t want to make this stupendously long. So, I’ll go on to some of the problems I have with some things. Like with the inventory. I was constantly unequipping things by accident and that happened right before a boss fight, ending up with me fighting without boots. Another thing was that I couldn’t take potions whenever I wanted, only when I was meditating. There aren’t really chances in a fight to sit down and allow yourself to take a potion so that you can keep yourself alive.
I would mention the combat can be a problem but the developers themselves have even gone as far as to make a mod that rebalances the combat and refines it for players. Which is a pretty cool thing to do on their part to acknowledge that and help everyone out with it.
Other than those things, I really don’t have many more problems that I encountered. Really. There are so many more positives in the game that overwhelm the negatives. I was able to simply get past the inventory and potion taking problem rather easily when I was distracted with side quests and wonderful environments to explore.
My final verdict for Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is 9/ 10. It’s a great game that has a rich, dark lore and is worth every penny you lose when you buy it.
