And now for the truth:
You should totally bag this game, it is extremely satisfying and a nice place to spend some time.
The physics are a triumph.  All the trucks control the way you'd want and expect them to, they all have a sense of weight to them and feel cumbersome in a good way. The winch works beautifully and once you get it figured out its a joy to haul a huge truck up a 1:1 gradient or to smash an inconveniently placed tree that otherwise wouldn't bend without a heavy truck using the winch and power to all its many wheels. There is one very nice touch when the truck is in water and you can hear bubbles coming out of it. Points to the dev who had that idea.
But the star of the show is the mud. It acts like real mud and interacts with your tires and their level of grip, its fluid dynamics or something like that and your (oft deep) tracks stay where you left them. No other game in the history of whatever does it like this.
The only thing I've ever seen that is anything like Spintires is an old French movie called The Wages of Fear (Le Salaire du Peur - 1953) Don't check it out because you won't like it but you can take it from me, the senses of suspense and precariousness do not exist anywhere else. Did you ever play Jenga? Did you like it? If yes then buy the game.
I got it for €15 on sale and  due to the lack of content that's what its worth but if you have even a fleeting interest in getting into one of the most innovative driving games of all time then this belongs in your library and you'll keep coming back to it.
A wonderfully competent trucking-over-very-difficult-terrain-with-heavy-loads simulator, in some cases moving a few hundred metres is a tall order but fantastically satisfying once you get the hang of it. Nothing is gained from completing the objectives unless you count a short piece of gilette ad worthy shlock-guitar music. Hm, better than nothing and its reasonably nice I suppose.
Optimization is excellent, system requirements are low and it'll run on an old rig no problem.
The object of the game is to move logs about. Around 2-4 truckloads of logs from one side of the map to the other. Sound boring? Well its not because that seemingly easy task could very easily take three hours to complete and involve several trucks by the time you get the ones doing the hauling all fuelled up and repaired. And that's before you get any of them stuck and have to winch them out with something bigger.
Installing new trucks is a breeze and can be done in-game. Installing maps however requires you to copy files to the right directory and merge folders and all that mess. I wouldn't go too mad on the trucks at the start, the default experience is very good but after you've been through a few hours get yourself the M1070 HET, it rules and all the attachments work with it (unlike some of the botched nonsensemobiles you'll eventually run into.)
Multiplayer works fine and if a hosting player has a truck installed it'll automatically install on your game. Just watch out who you're playing with as this is how I got about 100 stupid and useless trucks installed. To remove the silly ones as I did, go to spintires>community>workshop>your files and find your subscribed items. Now I have 14 good ones.
Controls are imperfect but reasonable. I use an xbox 360 controller which works great and for the driving part there are no interruptions but due to the insane camera I sometimes need to take my hands off it and use the mouse to load attachments to the trucks. Many reviews say you get used to the camera and they're right but that's not an excuse for a very very VERY odd design decision. I got a mod for it that made it more normal but then I needed to validate which overwrote the mod and I thought screw it, I got logs to move.
In conclusion Spintires is far from perfect, quite far and it requires some work and forgiveness on the part of the player but it is really really good. If there is ever a sequel, and I sincerely hope there is I'll snap it up like it was Mass Effect 2.
Congratulations on getting to the end of my review, now go buy Spintires, lock your diffs and enjoy.

LiEat is a series containing three short rpgs, featuring Leo, a traveling conman, and his companion and somewhat adopted daughter Efina. At the start of each chapter the two have arrived in a new location after assuming new identities, and are almost immediately thrown into some chaos as a local legend comes to life. By making use of Efi’s ability to materialize and consume lies, the two unravel the tales of the people and places they come across. In each chapter we’re also given a better understanding of Leo’s character and what Efi means to him.
In this world there are humans (who often do not look human by our standards) and dragons. Dragons are born from the wishes of humans, and their powers are shaped by the nature of the human’s wish. While I felt like I was presented with just a slice or two from an entire pizza, I did find the tidbits about the world juicy to nibble on. The character designs are inventive, and the colors used set different tones for each of the three games.
The soundtrack makes use of tinkling music boxes, bells, harpsichords, accordions, piano and more to create somewhat classical-inspired tunes. It’s not an in-your-face soundtrack but some of the tunes are quite catchy and most are great for the scenes they’re used in.
While there may be some confusion about where to go and who to talk to in order to trigger the next event, the areas are small so being lost for any significant period of time is impossible. Each game lasts maybe an hour to an hour and a half, most likely less for anyone who has played the free version before (which are still out there, by the way, the Steam version is here just to support the dev with a few bucks). About the only thing I didn’t like about LiEat is that there isn’t more of it. Okay, okay, if I have to force out something negative, it’s that the battles offer no strategy or challenge at all. They’re more a means to an end, and the game would likely be just as good if they were replaced with something else or removed entirely.
When all is said and done, I’m left impressed by the colorful world and some of the especially nice touches that you typically wouldn't expect from little indie rpgs like this. Despite the short length, I felt attached to the characters. Hopefully there will be more entries into the LiEat world.

Galactic Civilizations III, is the obvious 3rd installment of the series. I never played GalCiv 1, however I logged hundreds of hours in GalCiv2, especially with the mods it accumulated throughout the years. GalCiv3 is very close to being released in May 2015 so I feel it’s at a point it deserves a proper review. I’ve been playing this early access since day 1 and really haven’t started to enjoy it until recently.  Although it was extremely fun to be a part of the development with StarDock within the Twitch Live streams, and the forums, this game really wasn’t fun to play throughout its development cycle until recently.
Galciv3 feels a lot like a GalCiv 2.5 HD version, besides going 64bit (which I praise) it really doesn’t try to do anything new or innovative like its predecessor did for a 4X game. I feel StarDock is really trying to just play it safe with the (if it isn’t broken don’t fix it) approach. There’s still several things that bug me, and these are just the major Issues I have with the game:
First off the ship designer is something we’d expect since GalCiv2 had a simple and yet enjoyable designer. However this one is a lot more complicated. I usually start trying to design a familiar ship model from Star Wars or Star Trek and it always ends up being something completely different due to the complexity and limitations of working with 3d models. I really wanted to try to build an X-wing or a star destroyer but get frustrated. That said some might not see this as an issue and makes ships look unique. However after spending about 30mins trying to build a ship that meets my requirements and only having a couple turns in the game, I end up just using the stock ships and play the game never returning to the builder.
The other thing that disappoints me is the planet view. This really has not changed from GalCiv2, it’s almost a direct clone of its predecessor, besides an animated spinning planet on the edge of the screen which looks nice, but serves no purpose and doesn’t change based on events. The Planet view is flat and the building aspect is just a 2d tile of buildings (think SimCity 1). I voiced my concern on the forums and in the live dev streams about this dated look and really hoped it was just a stand in until it was polished, but it hasn’t really changed since it’s alpha stage. I was really looking forward to a modern equivalent with an Isometric 3d point of view where you can spin the map and see many animations and vehicles and people moving and be dynamic based on the happiness/war/events of the galaxy and you culture, sadly this never evolved from GalCiv2. Also when you click on a planet to research an upgrade which doesn’t require a building it moves the selected tile to the next one leaving it blank, making this experience feel broken and confusing.
The last negative issue I have encountered is the ship technology upgrade management. Once you build a stock or custom ship and add new technology which you unlocked from researching it and send it out into space, you’ll have a difficult time upgrading it with newer tech especially in mid and end game when you have dozens of ships all over the map. There’s no real easy way to see which ships have the latest technology that you recently unlocked, and it could get very tedious with having a MK 2, 8, 14, 23, 32 version of the same ship with each having just one tech module updated.
I will close with the positives. You can tell the game was designed with passion and love which most games lack these days, the amount of detail from the graphics, cut scenes, gameplay, and features makes this game stand out from the typical cash grabber games like EA produces.  This aspect weighs very heavy on my review more so than any of the negatives I mentioned above.  I’ve yet to really feel full immersion in this game like I did in GalCiv2 but I’m hoping it’s because the game isn’t completed yet.
Should you buy this game? If you played previous GalCiv’s yes I’d recommend it. If you never played either but understand what a 4X strategy game is I recommend it as well. This is a turn based game which somewhat mimics a board game, it’s not real time so some users might be disappointed. You can’t control ships in the battle viewer or the invade screens because it’s simply not that type of game, which is fine.
+polished UI, entire game is made with passion
+64bit utilizes your PC’s maximum potential giving you very large maps and fleets
+Graphics and lighting look great and very modern
+Balance and AI is good not great

-Planet view hasn’t been changed since GalCiv2

Having freshly finished the Witcher Enhanced edition and being thrilled by its mechanics and features I was very eager to start playing the Witcher 2.
I can't really describe what a huge disappointment it was. Although at the beggining the nice graphics (and the main characters love interest nicer body :P) and the immersive environment (making you really feel the way you would probably feel in a military camp or a dungeon) I was disappointed once actual combat and gameplay started. Actually the graphics and the environment might be the only positive factors in this game.
The EPIC combat system from the Witcher is gone, replaced by some standard and comparably  mediocre one in which you just chain right clicks after left clicks, while aiming a bit randomly, seeing that there is no crosshair or sth to help you aim and there is no more group fighting style. Where the Witcher was a bit to easy to play even on the highest difficulty, the WItcher 2 is too difficult, complicated and comparably frustrating to play even in normal mode. For some reason the makers even totally changed the mechanics and key bindnings, so that there is no common link between Witcher and Witcher 2 playing styles. Now, instead of wrecking enemies with your mutant strength and agility, you just jump around trying not to get hit and hitting the enemies from behind, not even being able to defeat a shieldbearer head on, although in the ridiculous killing animations you are flinging bodies around as if you were Hercules. A bunch of cool sounding extra combat moves have been added, like manual parrying and arrow deflection, ripostes, and knife throwing, non of which are really usefull, seeing that you have no effective way of handling groups of enemies in order to enable you to have time to specifically time your moves to deflect and riposte. And of course the extreme realism of planintg traps IN FRONT of the enemy, who then just takes the bait and steps into a (not even conceiled!) apparatus is beyond me!
Now you have to meditate to even drink potions (like telling you to drink while you sleep so that you don't get thirsty during the rest of the day), making potions useless in combat and various situations, except if you "somehow" already know what you are going to encounter. A weight limit has been added, as well as the possibility to pick up whatever items you want, culminating in a typical Skyrim situation of "HOLY F*CK HOW AM I GOING TO HAUL ALL THIS TO A MERCHANT?!?!". You can get overencumbered by the end of the introduction with no merchant available anywhere durign the introduction and part of the next chapter.
The story process, decision making options and their impact are even more obscure and iritating than the ones in Witcher 1. Having, as said, finished the Witcher while helping the elves and dwarves and getting the King to grant them equal rights, I imported my save to Witcher 2 and got my armor and weapons (now ofc nerfed down so you actually have to get diferent equipment during the game, that is logical). Now I find myself being the lackey and bodyguard of a King who promptly followed up on ostracizing and fighting the elves and dwarves, assuming daring commando missions to slay groups of other humans just because he sais so (Witchers are supposed to be monster slayers -_-)  and having a negative attitude and killing elves without getting a chance to do otherwise at the beggining.
The achievements are also a joke, being granting for difficult tasks like drinking a potion and finishing quests you have to finish anyway!
The only reason I OBJECTIVELY give this game 5/10 ('cause subjectively it would have been even less!) is that it still holds up with some not too bad RPG's that are around on the market. I seriously hope that they will add good old vanilla Witcher stuff in Witcher 3, else I won't even bother buying it.

This is the most impressive rogue-like I have ever played.  CoND beautifully integrates tile based combat with music.  Each turn lasts for a beat of the current level's song, leading to fun, fast paced action.  Even during early access it felt like a complete game, and the full release is a masterpiece.
The controls are easy and straighforward, requiring only the arrow keys to play.  The graphics are simple but well made.
The music is great.  The soundtrack was composed by Danny B, and each song is edited masterfully into the game.  CoND lets you use your own music for the levels, but I have never done it because I love the core soundtrack so much.  Despite hearing the songs hundreds of times, I never get tired of them.
The various weapons and equipment provide a wide variety of play styles and item interactions.  The enemies are well designed, each with varying movement and attack mechanics.  The boss fights are unique and wonderful experiences.  Each one is musically themed, and the varying musical styles reinforces the awesomeness of the game's music.
There is a very large amount of content and replayability.  Between items, enemies, and floor layouts, there is a lot of variation between runs.  There are high score and fastest time leaderboards which are very competitive, and people frequently race the game live.  CoND can be very difficult at first because you have to learn each weapon's mechanics and each enemy's attack patterns, but there are many tutorial and training mechanisms built into the game.  Practicing is well worth the time, and mastering the game is very rewarding.
I recommend this game to anyone.  It is an absolute must play if you like rogue-likes or music based games.

I'll start by saying that this game is seriously under-rated, when you leave out the price tag. Me, I paid the full price because I was excited. I know there's a few people on here that had purchased the game and were disappointed. There's a few points I want to hit on:
1. The Price
There's two sides to this coin. It really comes down to whether or nor you'd want to spend the money on the game. If you're a fan of the franchise, then yes you should buy it (especially if you're a die hard like me). If you don't want to spend that money, then don't. Who cares about the price - it's your money, dude.
2. The Engine
This is where I get kinda irritated about some of the existing reviews. Honestly, man, it's a 2D top-down tactical game. How good can the engine actually get? Yes, Gateway to Caen was graphically better, but they're using the exact same engine as Panthers in the Fog. They added 32-bit into the engine because it allowed for better graphical animations and transluscency. It's really not that big of a deal, guys. It's Close Combat, and anybody that's been playing the series for a long time will tell you the graphics have pretty much always been the same. I re-iterate: IT'S NOT THAT BIG OF A DEAL. Close Combat has always looked like this. The upgraded engine has slightly better AI and better stability, as well. As far as I'm concerned, this is not a game-breaking issue. Hell, when I play it I don't even think about that. Close Combat was never about the engine - it was about the gameplay.
3. Less Content
Let's take a look back into the majority of the series. Each game, with the exception being the re-releases like the Longest Day, have all been unique in their setting. In this case, it's the German counter-attack known as Operation Luttich. Me, I dont gripe about the content when it comes to Close Combat. Historically, those are combat elements that took place in the battle. That's the way it is, so you really don't have a position to complain about it. Personally, I wouldn't place that among the ranks for a review. Yes, it has less diverse unit selections, and yes, it has slightly fewer maps. Unless you're expecting them to cover ther entire war's range of the unit types and the majority of the Bocage, this isn't an issue.
So, that's the rant of this review. Now to core of it:
It's the classic simple interface I've come to know and love about Close Combat. It's 2D bird's eye view, and I think that's awesome. There's alot of depth they've put into this particular perspective, and all it would take is a time or two through the tutorial and you're ready to rock. Also, there is a level of depth in tactical decisions in this game that I think a good majority of the existing reviews have overlooked, from elevation all the way to effective ranges of period weapons and the fact that a mortar team has to zero in on a series of coordinates rather than the round magically landing where it needs to be. If you make a mistake in a battle, you pay for it. That's strategy, and unless you learn tactics you're going to get your♥♥♥♥♥kicked. 'Nuff said. The graphics and gameplay is simple enough to master pretty quickly, yet with enough depth to become a good simulation, simulating morale, cover, etc.
My conclusion is that if you're a big fan of strategic, tactical gameplay and you're a history buff about world war 2, this is definately a game you should consider.

ABZU is less of a game and more of an interactive art piece. Those who can appreciate that will have an absolute blast with this title. You're taken through incredibly simple objectives to progress through an implied storyline as deep as the ocean itself, but the simplicity of the progression is really not the point here, as the levels and different underwater biomes are meant to be explored in a long, curious intermediate between moving through the story.
Movement is so fluid and satisfying on your character as well as the sea life around you, which are all expertly modeled into real and recognizable sea animal species, calling ABZU a virtual aquarium is the least credit it deserves.
Finally, the soundtrack. One of my favorite aspects of the game, the music is so elegantly done in a dynamic orchestral ambience that moves with the events around you, and truly brings the game's beauty forward even further.
All in all, ABZU is a gorgeous work of art that anyone can enjoy and appreciate. Honestly, if I ever feel stressed or depressed, I'll come straight to ABZU to calm the waters.

I love Steam, but in this case I hate the simple review system that limits the final review score to recommend yes or no and the aggregate that determines the final rating.
The original Close Combat was a game changer.
No longer were "realistic" wargames limited to turnbased hex gameplay with complex computations, but basic visuals. Not only did Close Combat look good, but it was real time and easy to play.
With an emphasis on men and their morale you experienced the thrill of getting your men through the fight in one piece.
In short you really cared and were excited about what happened on the battlefield.
That was back in the mid nineties.
Close Combat Panthers in the Fog (2012) does a reasonable job in extending the original experience, but doing so with the original engine, even when it is tweaked to include 32bit hires graphics and an improved strategic layer, does limit its appeal to gamers that can look beyond the age and structural limitations it has inherited.
Here's when I'd like something more than a simple yes or no recommendation.
This game can easily be recommended to war gamers who enjoy the Close Combat-series.
But I would never recommend this to someone who's into more dynamic game play and up to date visual experience.
Of course the developers are equally aware of the situation, so work continues on Close Combat Bloody First with its new 3d Unity based engine. This will finally allow the basic Close Combat game to progress beyond the limitations of a 20 year old game engine.
I'd describe Close Combat as a light company level war game. Fun for a quick round, but without becoming too casual or a RTS click fest.
The good thing about Close Combat in general is that it is easy to play, but with enough depth and a good sense of history to draw in the more advanced war gamer.
The continued (niche) success of the Close Combat series is probably caused by a lack of alternatives: RT, WW2, top down, easy to manage and historical.
Close Combat still stands alone in its particular niche.
To sum it up.
Plus:
- It is Close Combat
- Easy to get into
- WW2
Minus:
- It is still the old (albeit improved) Close Combat engine
- AI pathfinding can (still) be terrible - btw not unique to CC
- price
The old engine combined with the high price are imho the most limiting factors in recommending this game to anyone but fans of the series.
As an old fan though I am enjoying my "relapse" into the series and I will certainly buy Bloody First and any spin off for some time to come!

1. GAMEPLAY
Quite enjoyable gameplay (6/10) - especially at the beginning, when you need to discover the game potential. I like to manage my base, relocate dwellers, train them or send on quests, read about their abilities and item descriptions, looking at the room gear animations, planning further rooms and their usage, cloth my people in manner that indicates my strategy (e.g. everyone are suited as soldiers or warriors, the most experienced units got Officers Uniforms) or that complies with room specification/outfit.
CONS: Game start to be monotonous very quickly, because of lack of rooms and its customization. Gameplay is based on real (I mean: REAL REAL TIME) time events, so you need to spend a lot of time waiting for finishing training, traveling to the quest destination or completing current task. If you don't want to cheat (e.g. by looking for Fallout Shelter Editor or manipulate on preferences of your local system time), and you don't like the idea of micropayments suited in the game, you must be prepared to play regularly for a couple of minutes once a day for weeks, to gain measurable results of your progress, and not to waste your life on observing how the clock pointer is ticking. :)
CONS: Base rushes: from outside or inside can be painful, especially when you have unexperienced dwellers or when you are attacked by radscorpions! :) But they variance are countable, and the level of opponents are not challenging after a couple of days you have played and after boosting your dwellers on training rooms.
CONS: armors and outfits do nothing (or this is not visible) except changing dwellers looks. When you boost a dwellers ability to 10 (maximum), wearing an outfit that increases that ability to 15 or 17 does nothing. Moreover, suits do not protect you from enemy damages, radiation or environment dangers (e.g. during a fire).
2. GRAPHIC
Warm and sympathetically graphics (6/10), which reminds me of Pip-Boy icons from Fallout 1 / Fallout 2. But it is not very... time-consuming, precise and well made. I mean: it's ok, but for Casual Games quality flash technology standards. :)
3. MUSIC
Music is almost unnoticeable, not impressing and average (4/10).
4. OTHER
Very smart move with implementing lunchboxes, pet boxes and starter boxes, from where you get randomized items. This is, probably, the most enjoyable element of the gameplay: clicking on cards and waiting for what will be dropped from the box this time. But this is not recompensating the game monotonous - just a little pros for the game retention. ;)

As someone who was a big fan of Mafia 2, I was naturally interested in checking out Mafia 3 but after hearing about the technical issues, a lock frame rate at launched, and criticism to the core gameplay I decided to hold off from checking it out at launch. One year later, I pick it up from the summer sale and after finishing the game, I can say that while it's not as bad as some reviews make it out to be, the criticisms are legitmate and certain issues with the game still persist to this day.
The Good:
*The voice acting and capture work is some of the best i've seen in a video game and taking that extra step really helps the player get invested.
*There's great attention to detail given to recreating the 1960's with licensed songs from Jefferson Airplane, Cream, and Creedence Clearwater Revival  just to name a few.
*It's story, while a revenge tale, was able to keep me fairly interested with not only it's main portagonist but addressing unanswered questions from Mafia 2 for fans.
*Variety of weapons at your disposal is nice.
The Bad:
*The gameplay (like with most titles) is what is going to determine if you stick it out with Mafia 3. The problem is that there is barely any variety. The goal is to conquer multiple disctricts and in order to achieve this, you have to speak to a specifc person in each district. Once that is done, sub missions will appear in each district that either involve killing a certain target, destroying property, or interrogations. Once you have completed enough of these, you are then give the task of killing the boss of that district and then assign it to one of three people who are helping you conquering the city. It's rinse and repeat and the monotony sets in real quick.
*Enemies feel like bullet sponges at times. I would pump 5-6 bullets into an enemy with a pistol and they still wouldn't go down so I just focused on getting headshots
*Fast Travel (as far as I know) is still absent
*had to restart the game a few times due to it freezing or characters who you needed in order to progress the mission would be stuck behind doors
*While the city is visually impressive, It's doesn't give the player an activies outside of ones found in the main story or side quests. It's a missed opportunity
if you are coming to Mafia 3 looking for a "Grade A" experience in terms of gameplay, it's not here. In fact, most open world games do a much better job handling this crucial aspect. It delivers on its story and creating compelling characters but unlike my experience Mafia 2, It's hard to dismiss the other issues that surround this game. This may be due to the fact that the game is doubled in length when compared to Mafia 2. Normally this would be a good thing but not when your game suffers from repetative mission design.  I'll say it's worth owning if:

Well, the game is definitely fun. I've played it enough to know a bit about it. I definitely enjoy the adorable art style of the game and how it was made. It's very well thought out when it comes to the story. For the most part it's about a con man and his dragon girl, Efina. Efina is abnormal compared to the other dragons in the world, as she has a different diet that revolves around, 'lies', lies are physical beings created when a character in the game lies. It's your job to determine which is a lie, and which is the truth.
Pros:
-Really fun
-Adorable
-Great story, it's super fun to play
-Characters act human like
-Entering homes with the space bar instead of just walking in - This feels more natural to me than just walking into some place as if the door automatically opens for you.. I like it more.
-Features a minor use of the mouse. Not many games do this, I kind of like it.
Cons:
-Issues figuring out some controls, for newer players (like myself)
-Fighting is a tad bit too easy in the beginning.. - Gets a BIT harder, by introducing something like an eight on two battle..
-Some issues arise with the music, making it sound kind of.. Troublesome, and problematic to want and listen to. The looping situation isn't all that good, and definitely could've been better.
-Clunky use of the Fn keys, it's all scattered around.
-Problems with the FPS change.. Not really made for it
-Sometimes when holding a button for a full second will cause you to instantly skip text you may have wanted to read..
-Kind of throws you into the game.. Without instructions
-English translation is still having some issues, but so far it's getting there, example is at the top.. It doesn't translate well... Or at all in this matter.
-Really short if you rush
Question:
- Why isn't there a WSAD implementation into the game? Alongside the Up, down, left, right arrows? Kind of like Undertale has? It's possible to do..
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Now upon further investigation there's a few things not notted that I kind of wish were in the game fully as an, 'option' setting. See, the thing about the options is that they aren't fully labled. They utilize the Fn comands, such as F1, F2, etc. Now, not all are used but I will list the ones that are used. To help newer players figure out how to change around some things. Also not included inside of the game in any way is instructions on how the game plays
Keys that don't do anything:
- F1
- F2
- F3
- F6
- F7
- F9
- F11
Keys that have use:
F4 - You start with the default screen which can be too small to some users. Or too big. Press it once at the default size, and it'll grow larger. Press it again, it'll become small. Once more and you're back at the default screen size.
F5 - The game itself runs at 60 Frames Per Sec. By default this is the source frames you're going to get to determine how fast the game plays. By pressing it once, the game will lower the FPS to 30 Frames Per Sec. Pressing again will lower it to 15 FPS. If you press it again, the game will bring it back up to 60 FPS, and it'll be the default speed.
F8 - If you don't use the default FPS setting made by Steam to determine how many frames you're on. The game has a built in FPS counter that's VERY accurate. It works the same as the default FPS setting in Steam, and is just as accurate.
F10 - If you HATE the default screen sizes and would rather play it in full screen, the game can be played in full screen by pressing F10. The resolution isn't bad, but it looks a bit better and makes it easier to see when using it.. Not sure why this key wasn't binded to the same one as F4. But, it still helps if you want it, just press F10 to go out of full screen.
F12 - By default Steam utilizes a screenshot mechanic that allows you to capture games, this is useful if you wanna screenshot it.
ESC/X/Backspace - The escape key, X key and the Backspace button are all used to open your menu, this will allow you to swap items and view other things in your inventory.
Space Bar - Allows you to go through text, press it and it'll go to the next screen.
UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT arrow keys - All used for movement. Different from the WSAD movement, this game uses that.
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

3D will never hold the same place in my heart as 2D, and this might be the most beautiful 2D game I've ever played.  The environments and character animations are absolutely gorgeous, completely immersive.  And beyond that the gameplay is just plain fun!  I'm a complete sucker for the "Metroid-Vania" style of side-scrolling combat with light RPG elements, and "Dust" nails everything that makes that particular school of design so enjoyable for the obsessive-compulsive "must find everything" backtrackers like me.
That having been said, it's not perfect.  The bosses, as have been noted by many others, are a bit lackluster (none quite so much as the final boss); the anime cutscenes can't live up to the beauty of the in-game animations; and, much as I hate to say it, the main story arc didn't quite live up to its full potential.  It's the last one which will probably get the most people up in arms at me, as the story has been near-universally praised from what I can tell.  And don't get me wrong, I'm not saying it's *bad.*  The characterization is fantastic, and all of the little moments with Dust and Fidget in particular are both amusing and, occasionally, touching.  It's just that these little moments, I think, work better than the big ones.
All in all, the highest praise I can give to "Dust" is that it left me wanting more.  I would LOVE to see a sequel.  If this is what Dean Dodrill can accomplish virtually single-handed, I can only imagine what he would produce with a dedicated team.  I absolutely loved this game and know that it is one which I will be revisiting over and over again.  Well done.

For a game still in beta, Galactic Civilizations III is already a solid 4X game. But it still has bugs, and the campaign is also not available yet, so if you want to play a complete game, wait until the release. But if you are dying for a science fiction strategy game and can live with the bugs, then go get it. And it will continue getting better, even after the release.
You can design your own ships, and not only regarding its weapons and components: you can completely change their look, add blocks and parts to create your own aesthetics and etc. You can make your own unique custom civilizations, give them special traits, characteristics and ships. The visuals are awesome. The game will be fully modable, that is, modders will be able to create incredible things. The battles look epic, but beware that you can't play them, as they are meant to be looked at and see the efficiency of your ships against the enemies rather than to be played. The AI will be getting better and better as the release approaches. There are several events with choices for the player to make, but so far, there are no "massive" events that change gameplay or add new factions, which I would like a lot to be added. Also, the devs are awesome and listen to their fans.

. But even if you aren't interested in the story, you can always play a normal game outside of the yet to come campaign and create your own backstory.
One of the things I feel that is lacking in the game though is a deeper soul. It need politics, bigger events (like I mentioned above) and more things to illustrate the universe and your civilization. But the devs do have plans to include LOTS of interesting things in the expansions to come... so I have hope for these features.
*After game launch edit*
Well, apart from the obvious improvements and polishing, the only relevant thing I've got to talk about is the campaign. I just finished it today and have to say that it is short. But I didn't do all of the optional objectives - I rushed in several parts, and didn't play the campaign with the same depth and care I would have done in a normal game. That's because I was more interested in finishing it than enjoying it. So the campaign can be a lot longer and more interesting if you play it correctly.
My opinion about the game is still good. Honestly, I don't think that the campaign is meant to be the main game mode. It is comparable to the scenarios from Civ V. They are only a secondary game experience. The core of the game is, instead, to play the classical mode - just choose your opponents and map type and win one of the victory conditions. The same applies for GalCiv III.
I really can't understand the massive negative reviews the game is getting. I haven't got bugs so far - although I might be lucky regarding bugs - and if you followed the dev streams like I did, you can rather easily understand the little flaws of the game, which the devs said they would be fixing until after the game launch. In fact, they clearly said that they will continue to add new features to the game even after launch through free patches. And if you think the game still need some deeper and more immersive mechanics (which I agree with), such as a more in depth diplomacy, United Planets system and population characteristics, then don't worry, because Stardock has said that they plan to add all of these things in future expansions and DLC, so that they can develop these features with more refinement and polish.

Really great RPG. Complex plot with refreshingly realistic characters. The bad guys all have real motivations rather than your typical "I want to end the woooooorld and also bwahahahaha!" kind of stuff you find before a standard last boss battle.
There's a bit of a steep learning curve with the fighting mechanics. Most RPGs will leak a skill at a time, adding a spell every few levels as you become comfortable. The Witcher 2 gives you all the abilities right from the get go. This means you may gravitate toward one or two abilities and ignore the rest, but I'd suggest taking some time dying repeatedly in the early stages just to get comfortable with using all the skills.
About your equipment: You can upgrade your swords, armor, and even character stats with permanent item enhancements. Because the enhancements are irreversible, you might hold off upgrading in hopes of finding juicier upgrades. Don't do this. Because I was so worried about ruining a good sword with a bad enhancement, I ended up playing through the entire game without using a single enhancement. Don't be like me, don't hoard your upgrades. Smoke 'em while you got 'em.

This is one of the best RPGs I've ever played and the first game that actually makes me want to go back and spend another 30 hours to see how some of the other choices will play out. The witcher games have a larger overarching story across them (and that will continue with the upcoming 3rd title) but they do a good job of making each individual game feel complete even though it leaves some things with a cliffhanger. You can play this game without having played the first and won't feel like you are missing too much.
The story:
Let me start here. The story is griping and kept me coming back to the game. There is a main plot surounding a mysterious assasin who is killing kings and causing a lot of trouble for our hero. The story is filled with political intrigue and has some twists and turns that keep you guessing. There are a number of concurent stories happening as well, most of the other main characters have their own agendas and teaming up with them will drag you in and out of their stories too. The game does a good job of juggling the different stories and moves you in and out of them without being confusing or losing sight of the main storyline. The choices you make will affect how other character's stories play out and change the path you take on your own main story.
The choices:
The choices in this game are great, they feel much deeper than RPGs with complex morality systems that have very clear 'good' and 'evil' responses to questions. Many of the choices you make are really 50/50 and you feel like you could make either. Some decisions have heavy consequences that really make you want to play the game again and choose some different options. There are so many more decision points that don't carry these heavy consequences but even the small choices feel important. This is due to the characters and writing...
The writing:
The dialouge is really good. All the characters you meet have unique personalities and this comes through in the dialouge. Even some of the lowly shop keepers are memorable. The writing really makes you love the characters...
The characters:
There is an interesting and unique cast of characters. Although the world and lore of the game is quite large the game focuses on a few main players and it isn't long before you learn most of them and who they are. There is a glossary in the game that keeps bios on a ton of the other smaller characters that get mentioned so even though you are focusing on a small cast the world still feels huge and very much alive.
The gameplay:
I would be lying if I said the gameplay is what makes me love the game. The fighting mechanics aren't perfect. They feel a little clunky and fights can be pretty hard in the early parts of the game. Once you get used to the fighting and get some good weapons and level up the signs though you really start to enjoy it. All in all, it's a decent system that can be both fun and challenging, it's just a little rough around the edges.
Graphics:
Graphics are great and the world is beautiful. The world is well realized and feels alive. Dingy areas feel dingy, dark areas feel dangerous, and lush areas look beautiful.
Menus:
This was the biggest annoyance for me. The menus are clunky and confusing to navigate at times. You get used to them and they certainly work, but there is a lot of room for improvement. Fortunatley you don't spend as much time in the menus as you do in some other RPGs so it is easy to look past.
Over all this is one of the most memorable games I have played and would recommend it to everyone.  I can't wait for the 3rd game.

I like the tower defense/action games like these (Dungeon Defenders 1 and 2, Sanctum) This right now is on the top of my list.  This game knows what it is and does a good job at it.   Traps are to help you kill the enemies but they will not do it all for you.  Also you level up your equipment in very straight forward way.   There is no hunting for the right item with the stats you want.  Just get enough cards for a trap and then you can upgrade it.   When they get big enough you can slot in various bonuses if you have them.  Until you max out an item (long time to do) you will not get useless items from a chest.
Each map can be cleared to 5 stars (1 to complete, 2 for completing with a minimum life left, 1 for no life lost, and one completeing it fast).
Grinding levels your account and makes your heroes a bit more powerful but if you don't clear new stars on new levels or clear daily quests you wont get new items.   You can of course pay to get chests and new heroes if you want to level faster but you don't really need to.
As a free to play this is REALLY good.   I do recomend the DLC options of the Character pack (I think with that pack that is what I would have paid for the game) and maybe the starter pack (It's a great deal though if you have the character pack you may not need this)
The PvP option is even really well done and works almost the same as the solo and group play.   As I said this game knows what it is and does it well.   I like other games like this as well but some of them have a problem of not knowing what they want to do and it makes it hard to really get behind it.

Final Fantasy VII returns to Steam with a port directly from the good' ol' late 90's PC version! New features include a non-functioning Cloud saving feature. (Seriously Square, what's with you and not having good connectivity for your services?) You can opt out to local saving so there's no worries that you'll lose your save file on the interwebs, The "Character Booster" is rendered useless as well, since it requires an internet connection to use.
Other than those few negative points, and yes I mean few, this is still a perfect game. The world feels massive and open as did when I first played this game when I was around twelve years old. The Achievements give you something to work towards.

Zero disc swapping.
Controller support.

ABZU is less of a game and more of an interactive art piece. Those who can appreciate that will have an absolute blast with this title. You're taken through incredibly simple objectives to progress through an implied storyline as deep as the ocean itself, but the simplicity of the progression is really not the point here, as the levels and different underwater biomes are meant to be explored in a long, curious intermediate between moving through the story.
Movement is so fluid and satisfying on your character as well as the sea life around you, which are all expertly modeled into real and recognizable sea animal species, calling ABZU a virtual aquarium is the least credit it deserves.
Finally, the soundtrack. One of my favorite aspects of the game, the music is so elegantly done in a dynamic orchestral ambience that moves with the events around you, and truly brings the game's beauty forward even further.
All in all, ABZU is a gorgeous work of art that anyone can enjoy and appreciate. Honestly, if I ever feel stressed or depressed, I'll come straight to ABZU to calm the waters.

Close Combat has always been my favorite wargame series. I cut my teeth on the game with Close Combat 5: Invasion Normandy, went back and bought all of the previous ones, and even bought a few of the later entries into the series. For a while the series fell off of my radar, but I recently noticed this game on Steam and decided to purchase it.
I can safely say that Close Combat is still amazing. Panthers in the Fog feels like the better installments of the game, yet is upgraded, with more realistic reinforcement pools and better graphics. The game is still very detailed, with each soldier's mental state, health and supplies tracked, but never in a way that requires micromanagement of any kind. One of the things I always loved about Close Combat, thanks to these features, is how an unintentional narrative can unfold around squads of men under your command. The ability to rename squads allows you to give them nicknames based on this unintentional narrative.
The maps are not 3D, which may turn some newer gamers off, but really, they're beautifully painted maps with a ton of detail (remember that holding the right mouse button allows you to see the elevation and type of cover under the moused-over area, which is important for keeping squads alive).
The game is much slower-paced than more recent WWII wargames. I just did a battle that lasted a good 45 minutes because the AI and I were trying to outmaneuver one-another's tanks without really firing any shots. But that is part of the appeal of this game and other Close Combat games: the level of tactical depth is hard to find these days. Strategy will make or break your victory chances.
There are some things I wish they would move into 2015 though: why are tanks still silent? We should be hearing them echoing across the battlefield. And where are my weather effects? Still, these are all such minor details compared to the things that make Panthers In The Fog and other Close Combat games so good. This game is a worthy entry into the franchise.

This is the most impressive rogue-like I have ever played.  CoND beautifully integrates tile based combat with music.  Each turn lasts for a beat of the current level's song, leading to fun, fast paced action.  Even during early access it felt like a complete game, and the full release is a masterpiece.
The controls are easy and straighforward, requiring only the arrow keys to play.  The graphics are simple but well made.
The music is great.  The soundtrack was composed by Danny B, and each song is edited masterfully into the game.  CoND lets you use your own music for the levels, but I have never done it because I love the core soundtrack so much.  Despite hearing the songs hundreds of times, I never get tired of them.
The various weapons and equipment provide a wide variety of play styles and item interactions.  The enemies are well designed, each with varying movement and attack mechanics.  The boss fights are unique and wonderful experiences.  Each one is musically themed, and the varying musical styles reinforces the awesomeness of the game's music.
There is a very large amount of content and replayability.  Between items, enemies, and floor layouts, there is a lot of variation between runs.  There are high score and fastest time leaderboards which are very competitive, and people frequently race the game live.  CoND can be very difficult at first because you have to learn each weapon's mechanics and each enemy's attack patterns, but there are many tutorial and training mechanisms built into the game.  Practicing is well worth the time, and mastering the game is very rewarding.
I recommend this game to anyone.  It is an absolute must play if you like rogue-likes or music based games.

You may expect a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game (as I did), but you are wrong - this is one of the best co-op shooters for a unreasonably low price.
Futuristic soilders fighting dinosaurs is a weird combo, but it turns out great. Well-balanced classes, weapons and enemies is the most important part of a shooter, and this game has it. It's a little bit confusing at the beggining, but when you get used to it it's a easy to play.

Orion: Prelude (previously known as "Orion: Dino Horde" and before that "Orion: Dino Beatdown") exemplifies poor design with just about every detail, from the graphics to the gameplay. Visual effects (Motion blur, lens flares, water droplets) are overused to an extreme, actually making it very difficult to see what you're doing in some cases. It's as if the developers saw an effect they liked and put it in because it looked kind of cool, without any thought to how it meshed with the rest of the experience. This pattern holds true for the rest of the game: features are either half-baked (class system is totally useless) or just poorly done (sound design and animations are just awful).
Perhaps the only thing worse than this game is its the community: they really put the "cult" into "cult classic". Look at any review online and the comments section will be littered with comments ranging from claims that "the game is much better now and deserves a re-review" to outright accusing the reviewer of slandering the developers. It holds a "mostly positive" ranking on steam simply because fans bombard the review board with meaningless positive recommendations (probably so they can appear in one of the games trailers).
The idea had potential, but there really isn't anything redeeming about what Trek Industries made with it. The only selling point is that it's so cheap, but I'd actually recommend not buying the game just on the principle of not supporting such a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ product.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a colorful 2D action side-scroller designed by Dean Dodrill under the moniker Humble Hearts. The player controls the titular main character Dust who cannot remember who he is or where he comes from. Dust almost immediately finds the talking sword Ahrah who obviously knows everything about Dust but isn’t ready to divulge any information just yet. The sword’s guardian, a flying weasel thing named Fidget, reluctantly joins Dust on his quest to recover his identity and save the world in the process. The story actually doesn’t turn out to be as cliched as it sounds. However, the storytelling is horrible which is made worse by the fact that there’s a lot of story exposition. The writing is mostly infantile, the voice acting atrociously annoying and the characters dull and uninteresting. It’s the sort of thing you would find in a really bad anime or Japanese RPG.
On the gameplay side, things are better. The combat system is sound, if rather simplistic. As Dust, you will be using the sword exclusively, but you can also use Fidget’s ability of releasing ranged projectiles such as balls of fire or lightning. And by whirling your sword, you can actually direct these projectiles onto enemies. Dust has a decent number of combat moves at his disposal most of which are visually impressive. However, it’s not enough to really bring much depth to the combat system. Coupled with the fact that the vast majority of enemies are less interested in attacking you than jumping all over the place and you have a game in which it is perfectly viable to just button mash your way through each and every enemy encounter. You will press buttons and amazing things will happen, that’s pretty much the gist of the combat system.
The level design is really simple as well. Most of the time you will be going left or right in a straight line with some occasional platforming here and there. There’s a healthy amount of exploration here with lots of treasures and secrets to be found, but it is hampered by the fact that everything is sort of jumbled together. There are no actual dungeons and thanks to the worthless map and flawed teleport system, backtracking is more cumbersome than it needed to be. The game also features really, really simple role-playing elements such as leveling and crafting. Each downed enemy drops certain materials which you can then use to craft better equipment such as armor.
The production values are hit or miss. The locations are lovely although rather predictable (forest, snow, volcano), but the character and enemy designs are poor. Also, some of the effects can be rather disorientating. For example, the snow blizzard or the rainstorm are sometimes so severe that it’s hard to see what’s going on. Also, during the arduous trek to the final boss, there are loads of friendlies and enemies around and they all overlap making it virtually impossible to distinguish them. Sometimes I couldn’t even make out where was the main character, never mind where he is facing resulting in some annoying backstabs. The soundtrack is mostly really good during gameplay, but it often takes a fast detour into awful piano-led trash during some truly cringe-worthy melodramatic cutscenes again obviously inspired by really bad Japanese RPG’s.
Dust: An Elysian Tail manages to provide some semblance of enjoyment thanks to its flashy action and rewarding exploration, but it is deeply hampered by simplistic design, shallow combat and absolutely terrible storytelling.

I have never played a MOBA game before this one, and really felt like this was the game where I could see myself getting my start with them.
After this intial 4 hours or so I've played, I can safely state that this game is truly fun as heck, and actually mildly addictive.
I only have one complaint about it so far, and that is the fact the game has TWO windows. Once you start a match, it puts the match into a completely separate window, while the inital window lies open as it's apparently strictly for menus & lobbies, just not the literal game (the matches).
This is truly frusterating for those of us, like myself, who hadn't priorly known this, and attempt to livestream and/or record it. Even in knowning now, it makes this a pretty dang complicated endevour. I legitamately cannot figure out why exactly the devs felt that the actual gameplay (matches) needed it's own window, separate from the other. Even if it does have a good reason, I really wish they would kindly keep the entire game within the first inital window instead of multiples.
Otherwise, I have no other complaints/cons about it so far, and look forward to playing it so much more. It's a game I'll happily recommend to just about anybody, especially considering it's completely free, unless you know, you really want that headstart set of DLCs.
Side thought:
From the mixed reviews, I do assume one of the main reasons is likely because other players of the game that are into and very familiar with MOBA games find this one somewhat deviating from the norm a bit, and thus dislike it. This is just my guess on it. If this is true, I'd say that deviating from the norm is overall a good thing, specifically if you take some notes of what the community behind the game wants, while balancing it with your own (developers) wishes.
Deviation leads to innovation and new things that might not have been experienced in games before, so, if you have a problem with deviation from the norm, remember that without this, most of the things us gamers love so much likely would not have existed. No deviation means no innovation.

I purchased Mafia III Deluxe Ed. during this year's Steam Summer Sale. To be honest, I was quite skeptical regarding the deluge of negative comments and issues this game garnered since its release. Still decided to go for it as I always have the option of returning the game.
After playing around 10 hours, I can conclude that the optimization glitches which plagued the game at release are removed to about 90%. The game runs buttery smooth, even on my mid range old pc and looks absolutely stunning in the new one (both are powered by AMD GPUs).
The voice acting, cut scene animations are visually engaging and gripping, although the main game missions tend to be repetitive, but anything else cannot be expected since it follows the story of a man who is bend on revenge and destruction of the Italian mob and it does involve a lot of killing.
Without disrespecting others' opinions, it feels awesome to play as Lincon Clay - a bulky, oversized beast of a man, who desereves to be the protagonist in one game atleast.
True that this game does not match up to the classique Mafia II but it is not that bad either and definitely not a game to ignore. It can be tried once if it is on sale. I mean, come on, Arkham Knight was also a debacle but we all ended up playing it anyways.
Optimizations are done well after the recent updates and framerates are much improved (framerate cap also removed). Other than repititive missions, less customizations for your character, there's nothing really bad in Mafia III at this moment and it does deserve a look.
And dont expect to get a GTA 5 experience.

The Binding of Isaac is a unique, refreshing, infinitely replayable and fun game.
The combat is pretty standard, WASD to walk and arrow keys to shoot. The thing that makes the game shine is that it is all about managing and making the most of the items and pick-ups that the game gives you. You always have to make choices about how to use your items and how to act. Sometimes there is a clear right answer but sometimes you're faced with a tough dilemma. Bombs, coins, keys and items are all have an important role and in every run you are under pressure to improve your damage and capability of survival.
Since the items you get are randomized, there is a lot of luck involved but it's not all about luck. Knowledge of what each item does and how to use them efficiently can make the key difference. That's also why the game grows on you as you play it longer and there is always more to discover.
I strongly recommend also getting the Wrath of the Lamb DLC together with TBoI as it adds a ton of content to the game and it's worth the price,

This game is cute.
The game is split into 3 seperate games in the same world. It's an rpg about a mysterious con man and his little dragon girl, Efina, who has the ability to eat people's lies. They live in a world inhabited by "dragons" and they go from town to town solving problems acting as detectives( since Efina is basically a lie detector), all the while the man sells info for cash. Humans and dragons have a rough relationship with eachother. Dragons are sometimes seen as slaves, however they are allowed to be in positions of power and allowed to live among humans.
The "dragons" in this game aren't dragons in the traditional sense. They are still born from eggs and each can breath fire, but they are human in appearance and each is born from wishes. They each have a special ability based off of the nature of the wish.
The characters in this game are likable enough. The con man, who gets several diferent names throughout, is your typical rogue with a heart of gold who still wants to help people but usually at a price. He tells lies, but with good intentions. Efina is a cute, naive, dragon-girl who sees the con man as her father. Her power is to eat lies as mentioned above. She wants to help her father stop lying one day.
The side characters are mostly just there for world building and to help Efina understand her powers. There's the police force captain, Captain Neill, who is also a dragon and he is just your generic captain who is stern and helps people. The vice captain, Brett (also a dragon), is a little more angsty and hates humans. Each game has its own set of characters for that game's story obviously.
The art style is consistant and cute. It's pixel art with a chibi look to it and It's styalized in a sort of fancy gothic way. Everything has a dark outline and it's just nice to look at. The two main character get diferent outfits for each story and they fit pretty well with where they are. The music is pleasant and fits with the setting. However, it's not very memorable by itself. There is also a problem with the music and the cutscenes. When a custscene plays the music will often just stay the same or keep playing even as the cutscene is happening. So something might be happening in the cutscene but the music doesn't help portray it very well.
There is also something to be said about the rpg elements. You get the basic stuff (switching items, leveling, looting, etc.), and you fight enemies. But the enemies aren't random encounters, they often just appear as you progress the plot. There are enemies that you can fight over and over however to level up. But there really isn't much need to, as you just get the levels you need during the story anyway. You get rewarded with money from winning battles. But as far as I can tell, there is nothing to use the money on so it's ultimately pointless.
The game isn't very difficult and is more just about the story. There are multiple endings to each game depending on what you do. To get each ending you just have to do one or two things diferently. There is a detective element as mentioned above, where you have to figure out wether lies are actually lies or if they are the truth, but there really isn't a punishment for guessing wrong so you can just guess until you get the right answer. You can also just find items by looking around that can make you completely overpowered to futher drop the difficulty.
The game is also very short. Each story can be beat in just under two hours at most. You could probably get a little bit more time out of it to get all the endings and achievments, but you just need to use an old save to do that unless you want to play through it again.
Honestly though it's an alright game for the price. Short and sweet, not to difficult, and just plain cute. It does have flaws just mechanically but nothing that gets in the way. If you have a few hours to spend I'd say give it a try.

I have never played a MOBA game before this one, and really felt like this was the game where I could see myself getting my start with them.
After this intial 4 hours or so I've played, I can safely state that this game is truly fun as heck, and actually mildly addictive.
I only have one complaint about it so far, and that is the fact the game has TWO windows. Once you start a match, it puts the match into a completely separate window, while the inital window lies open as it's apparently strictly for menus & lobbies, just not the literal game (the matches).
This is truly frusterating for those of us, like myself, who hadn't priorly known this, and attempt to livestream and/or record it. Even in knowning now, it makes this a pretty dang complicated endevour. I legitamately cannot figure out why exactly the devs felt that the actual gameplay (matches) needed it's own window, separate from the other. Even if it does have a good reason, I really wish they would kindly keep the entire game within the first inital window instead of multiples.
Otherwise, I have no other complaints/cons about it so far, and look forward to playing it so much more. It's a game I'll happily recommend to just about anybody, especially considering it's completely free, unless you know, you really want that headstart set of DLCs.
Side thought:
From the mixed reviews, I do assume one of the main reasons is likely because other players of the game that are into and very familiar with MOBA games find this one somewhat deviating from the norm a bit, and thus dislike it. This is just my guess on it. If this is true, I'd say that deviating from the norm is overall a good thing, specifically if you take some notes of what the community behind the game wants, while balancing it with your own (developers) wishes.
Deviation leads to innovation and new things that might not have been experienced in games before, so, if you have a problem with deviation from the norm, remember that without this, most of the things us gamers love so much likely would not have existed. No deviation means no innovation.

Now, I'm on the fence about that, personally,  but the fact that the game feels way more like classic Orcs Must Die! than it use to is still a massive improvement. What makes this game the best of the three is it comes with an impressively diverse and now decently balanced roster of characters, decently flushed out solo and 3 player online multiplayer (with really low queue times for pve), a proper Endless Mode, and most imprortantly the potential for continued growth overall as a game if it gets enough love. And at this current moment in time, I'd say it deserves it. Plus it lavishes you with rewards for the dumbest things, really. Three day log in? Have 100 Premium Currency (Coins)! Beat this lvl 1 map with THIS character for the first time? Have a chest. Get three stars? Have another. 5 stars? Make that three. There's no real reason to pay at all, and if you save up you can even get everything in the game you could buy with money for free anyway.
Current flaws: The PvP from the beta is gone entirely, and Sabotage could use a little work. This new mode often comes down to wave 1 kobold spams from EVERYONE, as well as stun and speed spells (as these are all standard IE unlimited use spell cards). The result is wave one, hundreds of kobolds zoom through everything like the crack-fueled rat-hedgehog mutant hybrids they are straight into your rift. Oh, and while you get sunned for like five solid seconds. Expect this VERY often, and there's little that counters it. At least, at my little entry level currently, but that's still something to watch out for.
That is, if you ever get in a Sabotage match to begin with.

Unit customisation - In GC3 you make military decisions from your technology choices through to the artistic choices you make for your units. Do you want Lasers, Rail guns, Missles??? Armor Plating? Star bases - Probably one of my favourite aspects of GC3 were the use of star bases. Having extra things to throw resources at when a planet has filled its current building possibilities was great, and I think is missing from other 4X games.
There are though many finishing touches to be made to GC3. But with the community around it the mod's that will come should make this game the 4X in space game every one has been waiting for.

Just to make clear:
It's fun if you don't take it too seriously.
I played this game and achieved top 50 on the global leaderboard for a few days, before losing a few games and losing the will to play it seriously. You will meet the same strategies again and again no matter what you do, and you get punished for trying anything different. The game becomes frustrating and annoying after meeting the same strategy over and over, without any apparent weakness. The only times you win over it, is because your opponent messes up. The game is unbalanced, and therefore becomes boring fast.
A few things I hate:
Monkey Engineer, Cobra, Ice Tower, Spike Factory and Sniper Monkey being out of meta.
They are only decent if you have a specific strategy where you've played them so much that you gain a strategic upperhand over your opponent, else they're just worse than the other towers.
Round 13 rush counters.
Yes you heard me, I hate the counters for round 13 rushing. I have nothing against building up a defence with 5 Monkey Apprentices with Lightning, or something like that. But paying 4k for a Tack Shooter upgrade to just eliminate all the bloons, or 4k for a Monkey Ace with a boost to eliminate all the bloons, or 5k for a Boomerang Thrower 2-4, and then selling it again to only lose a few hundred cash, while the rusher lost at least a few k. (Also Submarines, hate them) And if they then rush again, you can do the same again.
Dart Monkey + Banana Farm
The most used strategy in all of Bloons. I hate these two towers so much. It's barely a choice if u want to use Banana Farm, and if you use Banana Farm it's barely a choice if you want Dart Monkey, else you'll have to do Buccaneer, Ninja or Apprentice. There's just not much room for variety, if any room at all. And the Dart Monkeys can be upgraded 2-4 to pop MOABs, hell even ZOMGs. And if you upgrade them 4-0 you'll be able to crush ceramics + rushes (also round 13 if you have 2-3 of them or a few 2-3 Dart Monkeys), and then you still got another tower, and in almost any gamemode a random tower too. You only need those two towers to succeed. Dart Monkey has early game, is cheap, has anti-rush, anti-MOAB, anti-Ceramic, anti-Camo, I mean the tower is just so god damn efficient! And then you just have Banana Farm as the most efficient way to make cash in the game, and can also be sold whenever you're sure you'll win with a rush, or if you miscalculate so you're about to die to a rush (if you're fast enough). Most of them use Bomb Tower as third tower as it's efficient to clear groups of bloons, which is the one thing Dart Monkeys aren't the best at. Most others use Monkey Ace, Tack Shooter or Boomerang Monkey to stop Round 13 rushers, and then sell them again to focus on more Banana Farms. If you don't rush them by Round 13, their cheap efficient Dart Monkeys (and Bomb Towers, if they use them) will easily beat you economically and their 2-4 and 2-3 Dart Monkeys combined will rek the ZOMG's you send, else you can play the waiting game and try and win in a game longer than 20 minutes, but that's just down-right f**king boring.
Do it all towers
Some annoying towers include; Dart Monkey and Submarines (also annoying: Ninjas and Apprentices)
They just outvalue every other tower if you have Banana Farm (which everyone has) then you basically need a "do it all tower" and something good against MOAB's, BFB's and ZOMG's. This makes Dart Monkey and Submarines in particular extremely good. They work against everything, Submarines can counter rushes, can beat ZOMG's and can beat normal waves (obviously), their only weakness is what? They need a few upgrades before they have much influence, but seriously a single tower that can beat basically everything!? And then you still have room for another specific tower and a random (given you use Banana Farm).

TL:DR - I can't recommend this game enough. At the time of this review, it's about the price of going out for a bite to eat and a movie (or less). Buy this instead, you won't regret it, and you can revisit it again anytime you want.
The game has no user interface or spoken words but instead uses abstract environmental storytelling. The controls are fluid and give a great sense of freedom in your movement. There is some light puzzle solving and an item collection challenge, as well as quite a few steam achievements. On my machine (i7, GTX 980) the game ran buttery smooth.
Abzu for me is an emotional journey of childlike wonder. It made an impact on me that is going to last a while, and I'm glad that I can go back to experience it all over again. I went into it expecting a simple game where I would swim with fish and whales and maybe learn a thing or two about the oceanic ecosystem. What I got was so much more than that, and I experienced a story that was told in a way that I hadn't experienced in many years. Fair warning, much of it is easy to miss if you don't take the time to look around and absorb what your seeing. This game is short, but so very sweet. In today's games, it's too easy to blast through them as we move to complete objectives. I had to unlearn that while playing this game, and take my time to enjoy and appreciate the experience.
I'll also say (hopefully without spoiling anything) that this game isn't exactly rooted in our current existence as we know it. Time is a thing, and if this game was an educational tool, it would reveal just as much history as it would what our ocean is like today. Speaking of educational tool, I wouldn't have any problem letting my kids play this. My son watched me play this game and said "Woooooooow" more than a few times. And in closing, that is what I appreciate the most about this game. It reminded me what it was like to be a kid again, to look at the world through a different set of eyes that was curious and wondered in absolute amazement about both what exists and has existed in our world. I hope you, the reader will take the time to experience this, and will enjoy it just as much as I did.

Finally the Full Release is here for NecroDancer! I got it in Early Acces a few months ago and could see the evolution of this game into the great game that we have now. But what is Crypt of the NecroDancer exactly?
Well, it calls itself a Roguelike  Rhythm game - and what that means is, that as opposed to your usual Roguelike game, you will have to follow the beat of the music (the Standard soundtrack is produced by Danny B., and trust me, it's possibly his most awesome work). There are also 2 greatly done remixes of the Soundtrack that you can select, in addition to that you can also choose your own custom music.
The main difficulty comes from learning the patterns of the enemies, weapons, what items and shrines do and how to manage all of this while keeping the rhythmn. Now that might sound overwhelming at first but the game has a beat system that is fairly lenient, which means that you can be half a beat off without losing your multiplayer and screwing up. Which is good since the monsters will make you sweat bullets later on. Patterns in the beginning are fairly easy though, so don't worry about getting stuck from the beginning.
The Lobby system of NecroDancer allows you to train against monsters, bosses and practice with different weapons, so that you can find out why that red bat utterly destroyed you last time. Aside from that you can earn Diamonds when you play the separate zones to unlock items to find in the same mode. The All zones mode has everything unlocked item wise from the beginning, but it is advisable that you learn the ropes by starting with just Zone 1. Generally it is a good idea to practice with Zones separately if you have problems with them. Once you are familiar, you will probably stick with going trough all Zones, similar to how Spelunky works, to build up good equipment over the run.
Every run is different, as the layouts get randomly generated. There is a fair variety of items, from weapons to rings, weapons, spells, potions that give you an extra life to boots that make you light as a feather (advised for escaping from fire and ice!). Generally speaking, and that is the second comparison to Spelunky, you should be able to get through even with your base equipment, since Crypt of the NecroDancer is mostly skill and Rhythm based. However, getting a Bow, Spear, Long Sword or other weapons will give you more range and/or different attack patterns which you can use to get an advantage over your fellow Golems, Goblins, Slimes, Bats and many, many more monsters. The variety of enemies is huge and you will learn to love and hate most of them.
Each Zone is separated in three level Levels with a mini boss at the end (you will love Red Dragons) and one Boss Level. For the first three Zones, you will face a random Boss, the fourth has a special one. The boss fights have unique songs and all very well done, reaching from playing a well paced Chess game to keeping the beat against a Death Metal Skeleton Master.
The is also a roster of different characters with varying difficulty to them. Your standard character is Cadence and she is pretty straight forward, while other characters have some unique movement patterns or restrictions attached to them. If you feel like playing a classic roguelike game, you can choose the Bard. With him, you don't have to follow the beat. You make a move and then the monsters move afterwards. He is best used for learning patterns but be warned: it`s possible that you will struggle a bit with normal characters when you switch back to them. Another noteworthy character is Adria, if you screw up with the beat than you will face the fate of instant Death. Best used to either challenge yourself or to practice performing well under the positive stress of the beat ^^
The game also offers a Daily Challenge, a seeded run that is the same for all players. You can also play in local co-op (the mode is a bit easier) with your buddies. And if you feel like it, you can also use a Dance Pad for it.
All in all, I can recommend this game completely. It has been my go-to example of well done Early Access games and now that it is released, it's as of now my game of the year 2015. What is left to be said is me wishing you fun with it and thanking the awesome developers for listening to community feedback and polishing their game up to this gem that we have now.
Since I reviewed this game, it also got some free, well done soundtracks added. Good to see such great long term support for a game.
