RECOMMENDED ON SALE ONLY, $30 IS FAR TOO PRICEY FOR THE CURRENT LACK OF UPDATES/CONTENT.
That being said, this is a fantasticly fun, and relaxing game.  Its fun to drive through the Russian wilderness in large offroad vehicles and drive though the worst of road conditions.  I have put 16 hours into the game and still not attempted to complete an objective.  I thus far have simply explored the maps a bit, tried out different vehicles, and learned how to get my vehicles unstuck from different situations.
Biggest complaint other than lack of content is as others have said, the camera system is ATROCIOUS. Part of the game is just fighting the camera, they need a cockpit view, and also a way to set the camera and leave it, instead of it flying around willy nilly.
That is ALL there is to it, besides having a multiplayer component.  There are not even any snowy maps in the vanilla game, which is ludicrous considering its an offroading game taking place in Russia.
Frankly this is one of those examples where a 2 year old game with little (but excellent!) content is being sold for $30.  Change the base price to $15 or even $20 and then hit it up with a sale, that seems much more appropriate IMO.
They have added workshop support, but I'd rather have a few more good maps added by the devs first before allowing the modding community to have at it.

This game is cute.
The game is split into 3 seperate games in the same world. It's an rpg about a mysterious con man and his little dragon girl, Efina, who has the ability to eat people's lies. They live in a world inhabited by "dragons" and they go from town to town solving problems acting as detectives( since Efina is basically a lie detector), all the while the man sells info for cash. Humans and dragons have a rough relationship with eachother. Dragons are sometimes seen as slaves, however they are allowed to be in positions of power and allowed to live among humans.
The "dragons" in this game aren't dragons in the traditional sense. They are still born from eggs and each can breath fire, but they are human in appearance and each is born from wishes. They each have a special ability based off of the nature of the wish.
The characters in this game are likable enough. The con man, who gets several diferent names throughout, is your typical rogue with a heart of gold who still wants to help people but usually at a price. He tells lies, but with good intentions. Efina is a cute, naive, dragon-girl who sees the con man as her father. Her power is to eat lies as mentioned above. She wants to help her father stop lying one day.
The side characters are mostly just there for world building and to help Efina understand her powers. There's the police force captain, Captain Neill, who is also a dragon and he is just your generic captain who is stern and helps people. The vice captain, Brett (also a dragon), is a little more angsty and hates humans. Each game has its own set of characters for that game's story obviously.
The art style is consistant and cute. It's pixel art with a chibi look to it and It's styalized in a sort of fancy gothic way. Everything has a dark outline and it's just nice to look at. The two main character get diferent outfits for each story and they fit pretty well with where they are. The music is pleasant and fits with the setting. However, it's not very memorable by itself. There is also a problem with the music and the cutscenes. When a custscene plays the music will often just stay the same or keep playing even as the cutscene is happening. So something might be happening in the cutscene but the music doesn't help portray it very well.
There is also something to be said about the rpg elements. You get the basic stuff (switching items, leveling, looting, etc.), and you fight enemies. But the enemies aren't random encounters, they often just appear as you progress the plot. There are enemies that you can fight over and over however to level up. But there really isn't much need to, as you just get the levels you need during the story anyway. You get rewarded with money from winning battles. But as far as I can tell, there is nothing to use the money on so it's ultimately pointless.
The game isn't very difficult and is more just about the story. There are multiple endings to each game depending on what you do. To get each ending you just have to do one or two things diferently. There is a detective element as mentioned above, where you have to figure out wether lies are actually lies or if they are the truth, but there really isn't a punishment for guessing wrong so you can just guess until you get the right answer. You can also just find items by looking around that can make you completely overpowered to futher drop the difficulty.
The game is also very short. Each story can be beat in just under two hours at most. You could probably get a little bit more time out of it to get all the endings and achievments, but you just need to use an old save to do that unless you want to play through it again.
Honestly though it's an alright game for the price. Short and sweet, not to difficult, and just plain cute. It does have flaws just mechanically but nothing that gets in the way. If you have a few hours to spend I'd say give it a try.

P.S. IMO devs should really think twice about using social commentary in order to specifically sell games to particular audiences. It may work for movies but not for games.
ADDENDUM:
Best thing about this game is the driving. Old school arcade style driving on automatic without manual.  The most fun and challenge in this game is to beat the records on the various tracks. Not only that you have a 60s good vibes soundtrack and customisable "muscle cars". However, selection is limited. As for the gunplay, it is pretty good and satisifying - its a pity the AI is unintelligent.
As mentioned, if you do not do stealth, you miss out on a bit of further exposition and some background dialogue (including some cutscenes). Occasionally re-doing the same scenario will have different dialogue. It seems to me that the devs have toyed with the idea of doing a RPG-style branching storyline (apart from the ending) but not invested into it throughly.
Which leads to the open world. "New Bordeaux" is quite small (despite quite good looking in places) and not very interactive. A comparison can be made to the Watchdogs series where you can play various mini-games etc. but in this game there is no multi-player. If you are going to sell a game at AAA prices, the expectation is that the game will be chock full of content - hence at $60 I agree that its a 3.5/10 whereas at  $15 its a solid 7/10 IMO.

If you were thinking to get a simplified OMSI game, sadly it is not the case.
The game is underwhelming on almost any single aspect. I did play Euro Truck sim for quite a while, so I was expecting a similar experience, but it is not the case. The game is neither a simulation, nor an arcade; try to do everything and end up achieving poorly.
The graphics are disappointing; it looks like someone took standard assets from the Unity store and made a city out of it. The shaders for the building, the road, people, cars and trees all look different; as if someone did not even spend time trying to use the same shaders and give a consistent look. Animations of cars are quite bad, with them sliding on the road, like an early 2000 3d game. People are basically stiff and lack any sort of natural feeling. Nobody was expecting AAA graphics but at least some efforts should be put to give the game a decent look.
Sounds are OK; some standard sound here and there, nothing really good or bad. The engine noise is muffled a bit; can't say if it is realistic since I rarely even take the bus.
Interface is decent; simple to the point, although it is hard at times to click the right icon, since some are really big, while other are quite small. Bus customization is simple and straightforward.
Driving model: it is quite horrible to be honest. As mentioned before, coming from ETS2, I was expecting something similar, due the fact that both the truck and the bus has comparable mass, although having a torsion point where the trailer goes, give a different feel to the truck. Although turning around the city is quite disappointing, since the bus feels like "on rail"; there is no inertia, the streets are designed pretty bad; if you look at where cars stop at roadlights, you either hit them or hit something on the sidewalk (and hitting a pedestrian send your bus in the sky, before a message tell you that you did hit a pedestrian so your session is terminated). There is really a lot to do on this aspect; and if you call your game "bus simulator", someone would expect that you did nail the driving model for the bus; while it is not true.
Traffic feels unnatural, even more than ETS2; at least cars stop when you use indicators to let you go. Cars models are really bad; there are maybe a couple of models that are decent; the rest is not that great.
Lights are also disappointing; the whole map feels flat; someone did forget to turn on GI in the engine I guess. Also they look like a point, which is not really realistic (again, take out the "simulator" part from the name if this is what you deliver).
I did play a bit trying to enjoy it, but seriously this is a disappointment in every single way. May be pleasant for a game now and then, but honestly, the driving model is so atrocious that it is impossible to play it for long sessions.
Steer away, unless the game does not improve considerably.

I liked Witcher 1 more. Mostly because the music and environment was much more immersive. To the latter, I felt more like a WITCHER in the first game, whereas the second, I was Geralt, the character who has friends and enemies and dark mysteries and schemes to unravel. I didn't care about that in the first one. I liked being a guy, who is told to go out into a varied wilderness (swamp, snow, field, island, forest) areas, kill lots of monsters (that are also varied) and get money. That was immersive to me. The fact that a vampire would come out in the middle of night and ♥♥♥♥ with the townsfolk while I'm looking for a quest, and I'd go "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥," and jump in and ♥♥♥♥ him in the♥♥♥♥♥ was a good feeling for me. Entering a catacomb and fighting tons of ghoulies, or trudging through swamps to find a certain ingredient, blowing all my money on recipes to live off the land and fight anything and everything within an inch of my life...go to beautiful Island locals, and fight wolves under the full moon.
You don't do anything like that in Witcher 2. Witcher 2 is more story focus, and less "witcher focused." And I think that hurts the game for me a lot. The reason I loved Witcher 1 was because it was part Monster Hunter, and part Morrowind in the amount of freedom it gave on the areas. The areas in this game (sometimes) give the illusion that you are free to traverse different places and landscapes, but it's all foresty-sameness, and actually small (at least in feeling) compared to the first.
I'm assuming most of the money was blown on story, etc. Which is okay, because it's a really interesting story, with some interesting elements. I absolutely LOVED some of the enemies in this game, just aesthetic wise. For example, my favorite enemy was the Draug in the mist. He's an incredibly designed enemy, and just pure originality in regards to games. I think that's why some people reflect that Dark Souls and the Witcher games have a somewhat close aesthetic.
Is it worth playing if you played 1? Sure. Is it better combat? Sure. Story? Not quest based story, absolutely not. For example, The Heat of the Day quest in 1 has and always will be my favorite quest in that game
, along with Ripples
.
Witcher 2 Main story? Sure. I give it props for giving the option to walk away from "the final fight," but other than what I said above, it didn't impress me the way the first did. The first one was much more subtle, using the quests and the NPC's in them to tell really fascinating and interesting stories. Almost like a fairy tale.
But definately a good and recommended game.

I'm giving OMDU a positive rating because there's nothing between a yes and a no in steam reviews.
The basic PVE co-op experience is solid. However, I'm extremely concerned with how annoying and difficult the grind for new gear could be.
Positive thoughts:
+ Game looks nice and is well animated!
+ Gameplay requires a fun and engaging level of teamwork to pull off a five star rating
+ If you want you can get all of the characters in a relatively inexpensive package
+ Traps chunking swaths of enemies is as satisfying as you remember
Things that look like serious problems:
- Upgrading your traps is done by getting more of the same trap. They can be bought from the store (with skulls, the free currency) on a timed rotation or awarded through chests earned by completing various challenges. If you really want to upgrade a specific trap you'll have to grind for skulls or pay for more chests. It's a fundamentally unsatisfying way to gate player progression.
- The game doesn't seem to be balanced at all for solo play. It's possible, but OMDU is very clear in its intentions as a co-op experience.
- Time to kill is an issue. Two of the free characters (War mage and sorceress from OMD2) do a ridiculously low amount of damage. You can shoot the war mage's crossbow at a standard orc in light armor for a good three to five seconds before they die. That really adds up when you've got a full group of bumbling orcs and sprinting kobolds gunning for your rift. The weirdest part is the tutorial video for the war mage shows him doing almost three times as much damage as he actually does. All that said, if you play a character other than Blackpaw get used to watching enemies stream past you since there's nothing you can do when your skills are on cooldown.
- You need skulls for almost everything. Which means grinding for almost everything.
-Matchmaking doesn't care about what missions you've already completed. You're repeatedly put into matches which will get you no reward. Also, most people you'll play with are dumb.
The biggest issue:
I feel like playing OMDU right now, but I won't, because I know I'd be in for a frustrating experience trying to play alone as a new player. I'll wait until some other time when a friend is online and down to play.
So the game's fun, but don't even attempt to play it alone.

If you dont feel like reading all this picky-but-positive writing, just know that this game, in a word, is awesome. A must-play.
This game did a fantastic job on keeping me deeply immersed through the whole thing. Though I did not see the narritive show much through gameplay mechanics, it was still delivered strongly enough through dialouge. I got to know the characters well, credit to the writers and fully-casted voice acting crew. The art, soundtrack, characters, and story's conflict and reolution were great to experience.
I found the combat mechanics to be very solid; I got frusturated a few times, but was able to retry lost battles with a different approach, which made things still engaging.
There are a good number of sidequests to do throughout, and my engagement with the game made me feel compelled to do all of them. I never felt tangled up even though I held at least four at a time; most of them get comlpeted smoothly as you go.
The only thing I found negative, which broke the immersion once or twice, is a few voice-acting recording mistakes. Plus, I think Dust's voice sounds like that of a teenager who is trying too hard to sound epic and emotional. This still adds to Dust's character though.
Lastly, (light spoiler) this is one of just a few games so far that have nearly made me cry at the end. I was so engaged.

Finally the Full Release is here for NecroDancer! I got it in Early Acces a few months ago and could see the evolution of this game into the great game that we have now. But what is Crypt of the NecroDancer exactly?
Well, it calls itself a Roguelike  Rhythm game - and what that means is, that as opposed to your usual Roguelike game, you will have to follow the beat of the music (the Standard soundtrack is produced by Danny B., and trust me, it's possibly his most awesome work). There are also 2 greatly done remixes of the Soundtrack that you can select, in addition to that you can also choose your own custom music.
The main difficulty comes from learning the patterns of the enemies, weapons, what items and shrines do and how to manage all of this while keeping the rhythmn. Now that might sound overwhelming at first but the game has a beat system that is fairly lenient, which means that you can be half a beat off without losing your multiplayer and screwing up. Which is good since the monsters will make you sweat bullets later on. Patterns in the beginning are fairly easy though, so don't worry about getting stuck from the beginning.
The Lobby system of NecroDancer allows you to train against monsters, bosses and practice with different weapons, so that you can find out why that red bat utterly destroyed you last time. Aside from that you can earn Diamonds when you play the separate zones to unlock items to find in the same mode. The All zones mode has everything unlocked item wise from the beginning, but it is advisable that you learn the ropes by starting with just Zone 1. Generally it is a good idea to practice with Zones separately if you have problems with them. Once you are familiar, you will probably stick with going trough all Zones, similar to how Spelunky works, to build up good equipment over the run.
Every run is different, as the layouts get randomly generated. There is a fair variety of items, from weapons to rings, weapons, spells, potions that give you an extra life to boots that make you light as a feather (advised for escaping from fire and ice!). Generally speaking, and that is the second comparison to Spelunky, you should be able to get through even with your base equipment, since Crypt of the NecroDancer is mostly skill and Rhythm based. However, getting a Bow, Spear, Long Sword or other weapons will give you more range and/or different attack patterns which you can use to get an advantage over your fellow Golems, Goblins, Slimes, Bats and many, many more monsters. The variety of enemies is huge and you will learn to love and hate most of them.
Each Zone is separated in three level Levels with a mini boss at the end (you will love Red Dragons) and one Boss Level. For the first three Zones, you will face a random Boss, the fourth has a special one. The boss fights have unique songs and all very well done, reaching from playing a well paced Chess game to keeping the beat against a Death Metal Skeleton Master.
The is also a roster of different characters with varying difficulty to them. Your standard character is Cadence and she is pretty straight forward, while other characters have some unique movement patterns or restrictions attached to them. If you feel like playing a classic roguelike game, you can choose the Bard. With him, you don't have to follow the beat. You make a move and then the monsters move afterwards. He is best used for learning patterns but be warned: it`s possible that you will struggle a bit with normal characters when you switch back to them. Another noteworthy character is Adria, if you screw up with the beat than you will face the fate of instant Death. Best used to either challenge yourself or to practice performing well under the positive stress of the beat ^^
The game also offers a Daily Challenge, a seeded run that is the same for all players. You can also play in local co-op (the mode is a bit easier) with your buddies. And if you feel like it, you can also use a Dance Pad for it.
All in all, I can recommend this game completely. It has been my go-to example of well done Early Access games and now that it is released, it's as of now my game of the year 2015. What is left to be said is me wishing you fun with it and thanking the awesome developers for listening to community feedback and polishing their game up to this gem that we have now.
Since I reviewed this game, it also got some free, well done soundtracks added. Good to see such great long term support for a game.

I'm in two minds about this game. It has massive potential and wastes almost all of it, but none the less, it is "acceptable" - I wouldn't rate it higher than that.
The biggest problem is the limited map. If, rather than adding just DLC buses, they had optimised and expanded the routes that you can drive on, then it would have a lot more fans, a lot more mod support (Workshop is utterly wasted on this right now) and the developers would have more income to expand on it further. Unfortunately, right now, it doesn't matter how many DLC buses you buy, you're still driving the same roads in the same "efficient" order... or turning around and driving them the opposite way, for the same effect.
It's still enjoyable if you like driving buses, but it could be so much more - and so much better optimised at times!
Edited to add: I'm half tempted to change this review to "negative", given that they're now including all of the DLC buses with the game at the same price people paid before, but if you already own the original release, you still have to pay full price for each individual add-on. Let me get something out of the way, yes, this game is fun, and I like it. But this game needs major changes for me to consider recommending it to others, to characters mainly.
Torvald: No damage, no movement speed, only there to soak up damage, (technically he has 16000 health, if he has his shield break, recharges, breaks his shield again then gets killed). Getting hit while recharging should interrupt it.
Skye: No skill required for a high DPS. Both of her basic abillities make her go invisible (I don't mean cloaked like in halo or something where it is harder to see them, I mean straight invisible).
Maeve: Again, no skill for high DPS. First off, she is one of the thinnest and shortest characters, has high movement speed and a double jump. It is rediculously hard to land hits against her, especially with Lex and Androxus.
Victor: High DPS, no real skill. Doesn't really feel original (it feels like the devs just decided to copy from COD when making him).
Tyra: Feels and plays very similar to Victor, with minor changes.
Kinnessa: Another incarnation of a sniper character, executed poorly with no real skill required
Sha Lin: Same complaints as Kinnessa
I say this because the skill required for a character should directly correlate with their DPS potential (noob characters should be easy to use but shouldn't be too strong, characters for skilled individuals should have a high DPS potential, but be hard to use).
The servers leave plenty to be desired, some matches I get 3-4 huge lag spikes.
Also, one final complaint, the matchmaking in this game is terrible, you often are getting wrecked or wrecking, not often do you get close matches.

Ultimately, even with all these issues, the game is fantastic, the combat, strategy, upgrading and crafting all felt great (I was skeptical about the potion mechanic but actually quite enjoyed the strategy and planning it added).

First things first, I am still playing the game, so this is a review in progress.
First impressions:
1. Gorgeous Visuals - The characters and the environments all come to life in stunning fashion, it's gritty and realistic true to the "era."
2. Audio - The sound is good, I won't say amazing. There are a few times where in a dialogue between myself and 2+ others I can only hear the guy in front, the others speak but I have to use the subtitles because the game doesn't realize they are as close as they actually are.
3. Story - Just started here, never played the first, but so far it's very enjoyable.
4. UI - Bad, bad, bad. I'm sorry, but I don't see the point in going throuigh 3 seperate menus just to drink a potion. I believe this UI probably worked amazing on console versions, but it is utter sh*t on the PC....which leads me right into controls!
5. Controls - Ok, I was going to just slam them but instead I will explain why I can't get used to them. Firstly, your camera is locked to 4 ft from your character's body, this causes some "fun" viewing angles near walls. On top of this camera that seems to hate you, to be effective you need to Focus on a target for combat, which would be no big deal if you could actually point and select which person you want to focus on. So far, if I try to take on more than 1 person at a time I am frantically trying to dodge, parry, riposte numerous targets at once, but it only let's me do this to the 1 I have focused...which leads me to die quite often. Then, if you want to cast a "Sign" you have to hit the number keys, which takes your hand off either parry, or the attack with the mouse. This is another thing that feels more like it was optimized for a console.
There's more, I will update it as I progress. So far I give it a 5/10 just for the wonky controls and UI.

Perhaps the most terrifying game on Steam. FNAF move over because this is a horrorifying game like no other.
Command your airforce and navy to launch aircraft and defeat your opponents whilst you prepare to fire the ultimate weapon or more accurately, fire enough nukes to blot out the sun for the enemy.
As you watch your nukes hit their targets, a cold tingle goes through your spine for the genocide you have commited and the irradiated wasteland you have made the world.
The true horror of the game comes with the utter dehumanisation of humanity's demise. Your death count is just numbers on a screen or as Stalin said "the death of one person is a tragedy; the death of millions is a statistic". As the victory countdown begins, you start to realise the future of the world is a silent radioactive dump. The music fades into a slow moan as humanity all but extinguishes itself to extinction, along with everything else that crawls.
You must remain the rest of your life thinking of the death you have caused and the utter pointlessness of life.
That is more horrifying than any horror game; the end of everything.

A very enjoyable addition to the series, my favorite so far! I will say that at present, games with medium maps or larger get buggy midway through and tend to crash, best off playing smaller games. However, one thing that needs to be tweaked is culture... When you consider all the tech you have to develop to invade your neighbors, it makes little sense to go through all that work when you can just build three or four cultural centers clustered together and be quite confident that you'll be culture flipping planets left and right once the game hits the midway point! Honestly, I spend half the game giving leaders back their planets in small map games, whereas the game tends to crash in larger ones.
- That one criticism aside, it is wonderful how far you can lose yourself in the tech tree, and finding the home planets of your competitors and setting up starbases to increase your range for profitable trade routes can be an adventure in and of itself! - Definitely recommend, but it is a work in progress still!

Developing video games is tough, even from the outside that seems obvious. It's not impossible, but it's one hell of a challenge, one that takes patience, time and talent to name just a few of the requirements to make it in the industry. So designer Dean Dodrill's accomplishments with Dust: An Elysian Tail is one to be applauded. Having developed the vast majority of this charming action adventure game himself, it's clear throughout that this is Dean's baby, resulting in a game that's beautiful, fun and one of the most captivating 2D side-scrollers I've played in years.
Dust: An Elysian Tail tells the story of Dust, a being with little knowledge of his past or his own identity. He's Awaken from slumber by a talking floating sword called Ahrah and the swords protectorate Fidget, a flying bat slash cat creature thing. This strange partnership must band together to help Dust figure out both his past and future in the lands of Falana, which have been beaten down by the terrors and horrors of war. For a story, it's one that nicely contrasts against much of the games visual design and isn't afraid to touch on some mature story points from the death and killing of innocents to the terrible physical and mental impact of war on those that survive it. I found myself surprised by the direction taken by the story till the very end and it's an area of the game that held strong throughout resulting in a story that benefits in developing the world as much as it keeps the tale chugging along.
Now upon it's release Dust received some criticism for its art style, which to some degree I can understand. It's most certainly not an ugly game by any regard, the wonderful 2D landscapes are gorgeous with an impressive level of attention given to almost every level of the game, but some might find themselves turned off by the furry like characters that popular the lands of Falana. Personally I was charmed with it's interesting cast of characters all voiced to an high degree resulting in a world that's more interesting than you'd think it had any right to be. Dust's small but useful sidekick Fidget in particular is an high point thanks to some great dialogue and cute voice work by Kimlinh Tran. It all results in an high level of polish that you can't help but admire considering the time and effort put in by the mainly one man development team.
An action packed side-scroller, Dust is primarily inspired by the likes of Castlevania and Metroid with it's walled off sections that make traversal and map navigation part of the challenge. Anyone who's spent time with the genre will feel right at home here thanks to the fact that navigation is a breeze and finding all those treasures and secrets as always been part of the real fun with these sorts of games. An Elysian Tail is no different and while you'll be traveling a large variety of regions, you'll find himself traveling back to lands you've already visited in search of treasures that were once inaccessible to you. On his journey Dust will have access to new and varied powers that can be used to discover and access these treasures and even be used in combat. The powers range from the ability to slide under walls to secondary jumps to be able to double jump and reach higher points in the landscape. What's great about all these powers is that there just as effective in combat as they are when platforming.
Falana is a land filled with a nice variety of baddies to swing your magical sword at and thankfully combat remains fun for the most part, even if I did find myself button mashing most of the time. Enemies will reappear if you exit and reenter an area so it's possible to grind your skills and levels if you wish. One note I'd add is that on normal, Dust can be a little to easy and whilst there are a few challenges here and there, it's not exactly a difficult game so you might want to consider playing are a harder difficulty level if that's your thing. Leveling up and enhancing skills is a fun addition, as is the ability to craft and equip new items to wear, although some might find crafting items becomes a nuisance once you near the end. All that said, every gameplay mechanic at work plays well together resulting in an highly polished experience and one I had fun with until the very end.
So Dust: An Elysian Tail is an impressive achievement by Dean Dodrill and his team of various contributors in the two years of development. It's an impressive achievement because you wouldn't guess that the majority of it's development was worked on by only one man. Rich in content, visually beautiful and sounding great, not to mention a story that's more memorable than you've come to expect from the genre, it all results in a game I'd highly recommend you play for yourself, even if you're turned off by the character designs. Dust: An Elysian Tail is one of the most charming games I've played in quite a while.

text:
Sorrow so deep its' bottomless.
It is with
that I come to you with the sad news that this gloomy first person exploration game of the so-called spooky horror kind, containing bandage-crafting elements, vision-inducing pills, and batteries for your flashlight, is as short--if not shorter!--than the epic Ravenholm chapter in HL2.  And that chapter came with a gravity gun, this game doesn't.
Dark are the visuals, strobingly noticeable are the items you can pick up, slow is the run speed, and the enemies--when you get all f-cked up on pills; and you do get all f-cked up on those pills--appear as big raging campfire flames, with that bright white in the center and eerie green around the edges.  They patrol hallways in timed fashion like programmed automatons, or they just hang around rooms, chillin in the same spot as campfires should.  If you get near them, they scream a heavy knockback effect at you, pushing you while busting wooden crates along the way (which actually helps clear a way to safety for you!).  Before you know it, you wake up.  And it's game over.  And you realize you got five out of six achievements, because the sixth one required you to find all eight memory pieces, which you didn't do.  So, you replay the game, and instead of it taking 30 minutes to beat, it takes less than 15 minutes to do so while finding all eight memory pieces.
I enjoy first-person exploration games with atmosphere and story.  Sadly, with a bottomless kind of sorrow, this one is just too short, and void of story.  I liked it.  I liked the elements at play.  I liked the visuals.  I liked the simple achievements and simple puzzles.  I liked the cheesy flaming enemies.  I liked getting all f-cked up on pills to see them.  I liked strategizing my flashlight consumption, not that I really needed to.  I liked exploring painfully drab rooms for a bunch of stuff to make bandages.  Truly, it was all okay.  But, why oh why, does it have to be soooo short.  1-2 hours worth of story, puzzles, and situations could have made this go a long way.  15-30 minutes doesn't cut it.
Final recommendation is:  it's worth checking out if you're into the FPX genre, or easy 100%... but it's storyless, and too short to have a price tag on it.  Buy it when its free.

is a game that has a similar feel to the game
, both in graphics and in atmosphere.  You play as an unknown main character trying to save his friend who one day vanished as he mysteriously had an urge to vanish into his own family's bunker.  It's your job to rescue your friend Andre.
People say this is a walking simulator and I'll agree.  It's mostly about walking around in the dark and wisely choosing when to use your flashlight, bandages, and pills (which are used to see the "monsters" attacking you).  As other users have said, this game isn't too scary, but the atmosphere does give a creepy vibe.  In case you're wondering about these monsters if you're a coward like me, they're simply pillars of green fire that walk around and emit an echo-like "scream" (an echo shockwave is more accurate) to heavilly damage you and everything around them...these attacks are the only real scare in the game.  My biggest problem with these "monsters" is that you cannot easily see which way they're facing, meaning you have very little idea on how to avoid them.
If you know me, you know I'm really not a horror guy...in fact, I had to read reviews and ask someone to play it first to give me the scoop of if I'd be able to handle it.  Aside from the enemy attacks and the lack of eyesight from going down some bad paths first, there's not really much to be truly terrified of, which means this is good if you're as light-hearted as I am.
Do I recommend it?  This game is only about 30 minutes long in my experience and the horror is light, but the issue with the "monsters" is confusing and the ending makes no sense (thus only frustrating the player as a reward).  If you're looking for a fast and easy 100% while needing something somewhat light on the horror side, then this would be your best bet.  But if you're looking for a fun game to enjoy, then this is not your game.  Good for maybe a few playthroughs, but after that, it'll gather dust in your Steam library.

It's a fun game but there's this weird thing with Gsync going on...
There's a graphical option that allows to set the fps to 30, 60 and unlimited. Here's the thing, setting this option to unlimited will uncap the fps, if you're running fraps or msi afterburner you'll see the fps going above 60. But if you own a Gsync monitor with a built-in refresh rate counter, you'll notice the refresh rate beign stuck at 60Hz.
So let's say msi afterburner could be showing 120 fps, but the built-in monitor's counter is only showing 60Hz.
The solution, run the game in windowed mode, set gsync to be active for windowed mode in the Nvidia Control Panel, and that's it, problem solved, and working as intended.
Wanted to write that little heads up for all of you guys, I've never seen such an issue with any other game. Enjoy!

Those of you who are looking for a shorter pros/cons list, scroll to the bottom.
Lieat is an RPG with three chapters to it, all about a con artist and a lie-eating dragon who met him after hatching and is now following him around. During these chapters they'll come across challenges that ends up with having to to do some detective work, which results in going into battle to eat the lies in people's alibis. Along the way they'll be some recurring characters you'll learn more about and about the world around you. I'll try to keep this short and as spoiler-free as possible.
The story, having three chapters, is actually a lot shorter than most RPGs. Each chapter has about the length of one short story, and yet is still capable of keeping you wanting to know what comes next in the further chapters. All while the story goes on, the game manages to inform you about the world and characters without falling into the pit of having too many exposition dumps. I mean, sure, they do have some, but doesn't all games at least have a few?
The characters are another big part of the game, giving the recurring characters life and background quickly, and still giving you immersion. Most of the characters are quite endearing, and has some quirky trait to make them stand out. I would agree that the game does have some holes in certain supporting characters, but these characters usually last only as long as the chapter.
The battles and mechanics are very barebone, with nothing special about them. In fact, most of the battles are just ways to move the story(thanks to all the enemies being physical manifestations of lies, and beating means said lie-eating dragon eats them). This doesn't mean the combat is bad, however. It's just very average and short-lived. Although the lack of grinding or needing a good strategy can be a bonus if you are more interested into the story rather than combat.
The soundtrack is actually pretty good to listen to as well, espcially if you enjoy the sort of piano-and-bell sort of music. Add the fact that the most recent update to this game has let you listen to them through steam's music player makes the sounds track another bonus to this game.
Here I'll be listing some bonus points, in case you care. The endings are mostly there to set yourself up to see the next chapter, but saying anything more would risk spooling the game. There's also bad endings, but luckily, you won't automatically run into them so long as you don't do something stupid like run into a back alley in the middle of the night. I also enjoyed the achievements, especially the ones that shame you for taking items that don't do anything out of people's houses just for the sake of taking them. And yes, there are trading cards.
Add this all together at a price of about 3 dollars, and you've got a good game.
Pros
-Good story
-Endearing characters
-Good soundtrack
-Trading cards
-Cheap price
-Funny achievements
Cons
-Bland combat system
-Relatively short story, won't last as long as more expensive RPGs
I'd recommend it to anyone who likes RPGs with good stories, and have a few bucks to spare for it.

As a long time fan of the Galactic Civilizations series, initially I was concerned this game would be merely a graphical update on the (fantastic) mechanics present in GalCiv II.
However, GalCiv 3 has taken the core of what has made the series great thus far, as well as the best of both the old and new Sid Meiyers Civ games to craft something BEYOND fantastic.
Naturally, in beta, it still has polish passes and a few more features to implement, but the potential is there, evident and clear to see that this game will honestly be the greatest modern offering in the genre.
Beautiful, strategic and deep, it offers up every feature (and then some) you could hoep to see in a turn based strategy game.
I can only look forward to what Stardock have planned for future expansions too, as GalCiv 2's expansion made it arguably the best game in the genre to date, I'm excited to see where the future of GalCiv 3 takes it.
But until then, I'm ready to play Space Emperor, with GC3 as my interface.

TLDR: Being the generals at NORAD waging nuclear war is fun. Try the demo!
I really enjoy this game. Playing diplomacy online is some of the most multiplayer fun I have ever had! You get to talk to other players and try to form alliences! very tactical and fun. It can be hard to find a game but usually in the late afternoon and evenings (US) there are enough people on for a game to be going.
Just like In real life, getting a first strike on the opponent's silos is vital to ensuring they don't nuke the heck out of you. You also have to watch out for the rest of the nuclear triad: Nuclear bombers can be lanuched from airbases and aircraft cariers to launch short range nukes. Submarines can surface and can quickly kill millions if you have no forces in the area to respond.
This game is more Real Time Tactics than a true Real Time Strategy. There is no building of units. What you have at the start of the game is what you must win with. I personally love this feature as it removes a lot of annoying managment that games like starcraft have. That doesn't mean the game is simple, far from it. Microing your navy is really fun and needs considerable skill. Bombers can fire very effective antiship missiles from long range but are vulnerable to fighters. Fighters have a limited range and are easily shot down by battleships. Carriers launch fighters and bombers and can fire depth charges at subs but can't directly defend themselves from battleships. Submarines can fire torpedoes at ships while safely submerged, but this reveals their location.
I don't play this game a ton but I really enjoy it when I do and I think it is worth the money. How many other games allow you to wage nuclear war across the entire world? The game isn't for everyone so try the free demo!
Other people say the game doesn't work in high resolution so maybe try the demo if that is you. My computer is 1920x1080 and it works great. Also pressing escape twice will quit the game without warning!

I was sitting there, watching the screen as the timer ticked to zero. My heart has pounding, my mind was racing with thoughts. Each tick is the sound of an approaching thunder storm, with each getting louder. Then the machine finally broughts it's arm to it's position. Then, everything stood still for moment. Everyone was in a fixed trance. Intricately study the screen of the world as if it as a Picasso Pianting. Then the call came in. It was time. We sent the orders. The suddenly yellow dot began to appear on the screen. Soon more and more where showing up, As if someone just released a moth farm in here. When we saw it, no moved from their spot. Some were shakely, some tried to quietly clam themself. We were trained as professional, but even after many years of training none of us were prepared for it. Inside we were all just childern. By the time the first proctile struck a major city, heaven and hell had all been burned away. We knew what we did, for this we are forever condemmed to walk in this burnt world. As the world is slowly being cleasned of humanity, all of use were left to our own thoughts as we patiently waited for "Game Over" text.
That was my experience with the game. As you can see, game lates you simulate the feeling of a being a NORAD commander, in war that will end humanity. The gameplay is pretty simple, cause as much damage to you opposition's country without you taking too much. To deliver this destruction to your enemies you have missile lauchers, subs, carriers, fighters, battleships, and bombers. Though they are limted in numbers, making it often for you to be conservative with your forces.  The graphics is very simplistic looiking like it came from a 1960 computer, but is very fitting for the Cold War theme. Generally the game moves at a snail pace, but that is all for creating this sense of realism. You can speed up though, but I prefer not to for it ruins the atmoshpere for me. The soundtrack is hauntingly beutiful doing an incredible job of setting up a beautiful, but sad atmosphere. The downsides of this game for me, is that some of the match can become very time consuming, and finding a good match online is can take a very long time.
Overall, this game to me is like art. If you let the game slowly meld with you and you get involved the world, it can give you an experience you have never felt before. Plus this game lets you nuke Zurich as Canada.

I don't think I can possibly recommend this game enough. It has excellent fast-paced gameplay, a short, straightforward yet deep and moving storyline, and most of all it has beautiful graphics with an excellent soundtrack. +Exellent fast-past gameplay, even if it's a bit hack-and-slash
+Allows you to develop your own custom build (to a certain extent)

Cons:

-Take massive damage late-game, even if you pool all your stat gems into defence
-You may find some characters annoying

Dev Guy is an interesting game, albeit, an easier kind of puzzle game to solve with minigames here and there that have a kind of charm, reminiscent of the old flash games many of us played when they were so popular. I recognized much of the music used in the game as well that felt as aged as the minigame looked which gave a pleasing feel to it. The art style is cute, and even though it isn't the best, it's a free game; how could I complain? It also has a reasonable difficulty for people not familiar with all of the different genres, and I caught on quickly to the things I didn't know. It was very clearly expressed, and although there were some typos here and there (I couldn't help but detect a comma splice early in the game, sorry, just took an English test,) but it was nothing to bicker about either.
The only problem is...I never actually completed the game. I got pretty far into it, and just when I thought the conclusion was in my hands, I had to play CyberPony. Oh dear. This is where the difficulty spiked and I couldn't bear it. It's a simple enough game, but at the same time, I couldn't help but exit the game feeling dissatisfied with myself and it. Some walls were practically impossible to clear without at least clipping it which felt frustrating and out of my control. Not only that, but the controls as well. Towards the end is where I always got the game over, not only because it was difficult to perfect moving at such a speed with a cramming area, but also because the controls seem to break there, and looking into it, I'm not the only one with this same issue. The keys won't respond enough, causing the player to lose their mindset quickly and to ultimately fail from something out of their own reach. It's almost inexcusable, as I noticed no issues with controlling until that one point. It could just be a thing intended to screw us up on purpose, but that gains no credit from me, and it almost feels like a dirty trick if that's even what you meant to do. Don't even get me started on the repetitive music and gameplay here either, I don't want to waste any more of your time writing about it. I'll just leave it at I had to mute the game during that.
That one minigame, however, was your only setback as far as I'm concerned. It was a nice little adventure to set off on, and I'm sure the rest of it was just as great, if there was even that much more left after CyberPony. Perhaps one day I'll return to it and see if I can complete it next time. I have to admit, I don't have a lot of patience when it comes to retrying one game over and over, so that may just be a bum quality on me, but nonetheless, it's a pretty solid work. It was enjoyable, and the fact that I got enough kicks out of it for free is certainly enough for me to recommend it alone. Things could definitely be improved, but games always have heres and theres to fix.

Pros:
- Unique Concept!
- Challenging enough
- Well-executed
- New Experience Everytime
- Plenty of Characters, Zones, Items and Enemies to keep the game constantly interesting
Cons:
- Music can be repetitive (However you can use custom music)
- It can be extremely frustrating sometimes
- Unlocking new characters can sometimes be hard
Gameplay:
The experience of playing Crypt of the Necrodancer is never the same everytime. Crypt of the Necrodancer is a game where the dungeon constantly changes, and each time is different from the last. Because of this randomization, this gives the game an extremely high replayability factor! It also varies the difficult of the game and you'll notice that you find new things every time. The gameplay is challenging and enjoyable, and although I think it is quite hard, it is a game that you grow better at with each play. Because of the random maps and items and mobs, this challenge works, and doesn't allow you to get too frustrated. I admit to being stuck on Zone 2, but the game gives you multiple shop owners to help you get better at the game. To get more characters and shopkeepers, you have to free them in the zones as far as I know, and although I think this is an excellent way to unlock them, I found myself attempting some of them over and over. It's a small price to pay, and hey! You might be better than me at it, so I say it's not a huge issue.
Visuals:
Can I just say? I adore the graphics. The pixel style is perfect for the type of game it is! It opens up with lovely pixel art, and the character and shopkeeper pixels are small and simplistic, but sweet! I think they certainly pulled out all the stops with the visuals of this game. The visuals are clear and very obvious in what they're telling, such as the direction of mobs too. The actual dungeon visuals before completion were admittedly bland and repetitive, however upon completion, I have no qualms with the new visuals for the dungeon and think they're much nicer and I think they certainly set the tone of the game incredibly well!
Sounds:
I love the music and sounds of this game. They're memorable and perfect. With the musics in the zones, you can hear the beat clearly and that helps the gameplay immensely. The music is sweet and definitely sets the tone of the game even further. It helps you know when bigger mobs are approaching too. It's all extremely unique and I can't say anything against. The only downfall I found is if you play, let's say Zone 1 over and over, you will find yourself hearing the music constantly. I think that it's hardly a huge issue though, because if I'm honest, the music is so good, it hardly matters.
Story:
What story you get right off the bat is given in the opening of the game. You're introduced to why you're down there, and it's explained as to why you can only move on the beat. I find this to be incredibly smart in fact, and I enjoy it immensely. I don't know much about the actual story itself, but it certainly seems interesting. Although there is a story to the game, the main focus is gameplay, but what story there is provides a good foundation.
My Opinion:
I think it's quite clear that I enjoy this game! I have played it for a while, and although I don't have many hours actually on record, I still enjoy it! I think it's an incredible game, and the effort in this game is astounding! I think this is a game a lot of people will enjoy though not all will like it, but I still think it's fun! Just give it a go I think.

One of a Kind. A Must for Any Gamer Who Likes A Challenge.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a rhythm roguelike unlike anything else produced to date.  It takes a turn based battle system and turns it on its head by having the turns fall on the beat of the game's killer soundtrack.  Yours and your enemies' moves fall on beat as you navigate randomly generated dungeons in search of paths deeper and deeper into the crypt.
What makes it great?  For starters, the soundtrack.  In a rhythm based game, a great soundtrack it crucial to success.  Crypt of the Necrodancer hits it out of the park.  Danny Baranowsky, composer of the soundtracks of the hit indy games Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Isaac, created what it easily his best work to date for this game.  The driving beats keep you immersed in the game for hours and hours.
While it COULD only take you less than an hour to complete the four levels in this game, the Necrodancer will not likely allow this so easily.  The game is quite difficult, requiring many attempts to learn the patterns of the enemies and what items will best serve you as you travel deeper into the crypt.  But don't let this scare you.  The game is easy to pick up and play and you will find yourself unable to put it down as you get better and better at slaying the countless undead jamming out in your way.  With three challenging floors and interesting bossfights in each of the four zones, you will feel accomplished and rewarded with every victory.  You will have earned it.
With well over 100 hours on record since early access, I can say that you will find plenty to do in this game.  With 10 unique playable characters and tons of item unlocks, there is no end to the replayability.  Leaderboard and daily quests will keep you logging in frequently to test your skills.  Have a dance pad?  The game fully supports it.  Yes, the controls are simple enough to allow you to easily control the game with a pad.  It is the definition of easy to pick up, hard to master.  Wish you could Necrodance to your favorite tune?  Load it up.  The game supports custom tracks using MP3s.  Want to create your own level layouts?  There is a level editor. There is very little the developers did not include in this game.   It is chock full of everything you could ask for.
Whether you are a roguelike veteran or someone new to the genre, Crypt of the Necrodancer is a game worth picking up.  It is a refreshing new experience in a video game world that has grown a little stale of new ideas of late.
While you are at it, pick up the soundtrack.  It is that good.

LiEat:
~~~~
I guess everybody in their lifetime has managed to tell a couple of lies (or embellish the truth) here and there. Well, imagine you come across “Leo,” a caretaker, and “Efina,” a demon who is a lie detector, nourishing herself by eating lies. You would probably be in a rather awkward position, wouldn’t you say?
LiEat is a rich story /JRPG game where you play “Efina” and her caretaker in three very well written short stories (LiEat I, II and III). Leo is essentially a con artist who is selling information from one town to the next and keeps changing his name and appearance all the time. Efina was born from a dragon egg; she has the appearance a four year-old child but she is only two months old. She call Leo (Hal, Theo, Albert and god knows what) “Papa” (father) due to the fact that he has raised her since she hatched.
In each location they visit, they will be faced with strange events, will investigate them and aim to find all the culprits. You will interact with interesting characters in each of the stories and even have the ability to read their bio’s at the end of each episode. I like that, as it really reinforces the thoughts behind all the characters in their journey.
There is a combat phase, which is not the big aspect of this game; it is easy and provides you with a little bit of respite between the reading stages.
The Pixel graphics lent the game a nostalgic feel, reminding me of playing on my colour Gameboy. Some people may find the low resolution a bit of an issue but all I can say is, do not worry about it. Great price point, only $2.99 for practically three games. No voice over in this game, however the soundtrack is good.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Three short and rich stories
-	Interesting characters
-	Nice Pixel graphics
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Combat phase could have been better
LiEat series are well written and enjoyable to play (mostly reading).  Whether you already like this genre or have not yet been introduced to it, I recommend this series.

Dust: An Elysian Tail. Oh wow. Tail. I just realized that part after finishing it. Not clever right there, especially when you have an entire cast of anthropomorphic characters. I spent 12+ hours on the game, second highest difficulty, most spent on boss attempts.
Gameplay is similar to Castelvania, gathering powers and techniques to help build up your character while bashing enemies. I started out the game with a decent list of melee techniques for the sword. However you don't get any more than what's given at the tutorial. Combat becomes overly hectic, once you get a certain projectile power you'll find yourself using nothing but that for the rest of the game. The reason for spamming that projectile skill? The challenge for most of the game comes from hyper-agressive enemies that will flood the screen, at certain points (especially when there's particle effects flying everywhere) you will lose track of your character and enemies attacking in the crowd.
The RPG systems can make these fights drag on for quite some time, especially when you've done the same encounter three times in a row because you can't leave the screen without clearing enemies from it. Save points will do autosaving, but they don't heal you beyond 1/4th of your health. Something I could concede on, but that means the majority of your healing will come from food and ressurection gems.
The art direction is fairly solid in many aspects. Character design is not one of them. The characters don't look entirely appealing or even alive, there are definate animation shortcuts used in scenes where dialog is involved. Don't even get me started on animated cutscenes. They're not well done. However, the environment and background artwork looks nice and doesn't intrude on the game-play for the most part. There's also several instances of having to thumb through the pause menu to skip cutscenes I've seen a dozen times.
The story feels like an afterthought. It follows Dust, a guy without memory of who he is, somehow gets a mysterious talking sword, and Fidget, a flying rodent of sorts. The three of you wander around the land trying to figure out who Dust is. This ultimately culminates to the point where he is to stop a warlord from exterminating a race of lizard people called Moonbloods.  This and most of the answers given to you are almost hand-waved off as the devs clearly showed they ran out of time. If the character is supposed to be at odds with himself internally, why wasn't this shown through game-play at any point? These questions and many more the story barely makes an attempt to answer.
I can't honestly recommend this game. It's like a poor man's Symphony of the Night, with almost half the content gutted from it.

There are some games where you think to yourself "I could have thought of that" and other games where you think "Wow, why didn't I think of that?".  Crypt of the NecroDancer is none of those.  I don't think anyone would have thought to put a rogue-like rpg into a rhythm based game.  But it works, oh does it work so wonderfully well.
The first level you will be trying your damndest to get a rhythm going but once you spend enough time you will be slashing up enemies while setting up others for a nicely timed fireball blast from afar.  And all the while it feels so satisfying when you progress.
The controls are near flawless as well.  As you die multiple times, over and over and over, you never feel the need to blame the game for being cheap or unresponsive control but instead you know its your fault.  I always felt this was a sign of a great designed game, such as in Rogue Legacy or Super Meat boy.
Don't even wait for this game to go on sale, buy it and, hell, buy it for a friend.  It's that good.

Everyone (including me) is judging this as an unofficial follow up to Journey, so let's tackle that.
It's very pretty, and Austin Wintory's score is amazing as always.  Several scenes caused me to stop and admire the art direction, use of color and light, and bustle of fish all around me.
I finished in about 2 hours, finding roughly half the hidden shells and meditation points.  I recommend the game whole heartedly, but for those looking for Journey 2, consider the following.
Moving the diver around is fluid, but often I wished it were faster.  You can tap a button three times in a rhythm (tap-pause-tap-pause-tap) to get a brief boost, but I missed the soaring, zooming feel of Journey's traveler.
Austin Wintory's score is again amazing, but I wasn't as moved as I was with Journey's, possibly because the vague "story" didn't add emotional resonance to the score.  The music told me I was supposed to feel melancholy or excited, but the game didn't tell me why.  Journey told an incredibly sad tale through environmental context, cave drawings and music.  This game tries to do the same, but just didn't hit me the same way (emotionally) at all.
If this sounds negative, it isn't. I'm comparing it to one of my favorite games of all time, and perhaps the makers of this game set the bar a little too high by making so many obvious allusions and homages to Journey to begin with.  Still,  I don't regret buying it in the slightest.  It's a beautiful game with a terrific score, and I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys these type of explorative, meditative and artistic experiences.

I usually write an in-depth review on the games I play, but I'll write a quick "first-impression". The game is on sale at bundlestars and I figured why not.
1) Graphics - their not terrible, but they could be better. The mirrors are no where near the quality of Euro Truck - they do provide extra info when driving (visually), but lack in representing it properly. I have NOT EXPERIENCED LAG ISSUES THUS FAR WITH FRAMERATES (which is good too). The mirrors are a big part of the experience (for me anyway). The right mirror needs a little more emphasis or maybe just fix it to the top right of the screen? Add an option for it? (Bang up job with the options in the game - turning cashier on and off is amazing).
2)Details - from cashier, to options, to heat, to bus tilting, to ramps, to people running late, to getting on and off your bus to fix doors etc... There here definitely. You can customize your bus and put adds on them for extra revenue. Annoyances (such as cashier-ing) can be turned off. It's only annoying as you cannot select individual buttons with the controller and must use the mouse. The dialogue is very cool and promotes positive citizens. Very nice to hear productive dialogue rather than dramatic. The turn signal even turns off after taking a turn. This is cool!
3)Driving - No where near Euro Truck standards as it feels blocky. Driving is okay for the most part and the controls can be customized to your liking (which is a huge benefit). Lots of room for improvement here. Angles feel sharp and awkward at times, space margins don't feel right in First Person.
4)Environment - It is pretty cool to drive a big vehicle in a busy city with pedestrians and cars. The crashes aren't the most details or greatest, but the game does note your driving habits (i.e speeding tickets or running red lights). Watching the emergency vehicles pop up makes me want an emergency driving simulator. I would love to be put in some tight situations... i.e certain stops have certain turns which make them challenging (but fun)!
5) AI - The AI getting in and out of the bus is not smooth. There are a lot of waiting/pausing/collisions. Likewise with the traffic, cars will randomly stop in intersections or when you are around them. There isn't much a variable concerning how cars drive either than "stock" or very regular. Would be nice with some curveballs thrown in.
6) UI is quite friendly and easy to use. Bus routes cannot be set up manually as they are already fixed on the map. The player can see how much each route makes after a shift, but cannot see it from the main menu.
I sank two hours into it instantly. I like the options given and the premise of the game, but I feel a lot more can be done to make this game better. Some will like it for what it is as there is not much competition regarding bus sims. Others will really hate the driving physics.
I'll recommend it - with caution though! Do your homework as I think it's only worth a purchase on a major sale!

I have never played any of the previous editions of this game; however, I have been playing this game which is still in beta since August 2014.
I have been extremely impressed with how well the developers have improved the game play and added new features and options. They provide weekly Dev Streams where the lead designer demonstrates the capabilities of the game, explains their development intentions, and answers questions from the audience. Copies of the Dev Streams are available for viewing on YouTube.
So far, I have submitted over 24 bug reports and Stardock support has been very quick to respond to each of them. Most of the issues I raised have already been resolved via game updates or hotfixes.
The game is 64-bit and therefore will demand more than 2 GB of RAM to operate. How much memory is used depends primarily on how big the map is. On my PC, a small map starts using about 1.7 GB, a huge map starts with about 3.1 GB, while the insane map starts running at about 4.1 GB. Please note that this is about 50% less than what the game was using three months ago with smaller maps and the developers have not finished optimizing it.
I find the game exciting to play, especially in the beginning phase. However, it becomes tedious when my empire approaches 100 planets with only a third of the map explored. Towards the middle of the game it is downright boring due to the number of repetitive tasks (e.g., starbase improvements) and a passive AI. The developers are working to address these issues but they still have a long way to go.
The game has multi-player capability but this option is broken in my opinion. I suspect this may be due to how the background calculations are transmitted between players since most of the game freezes and crashes occur during the handoff to another player. I look forward to Stardock resolving this issue.
If you want to participate in developing what may be the premiere space 4X game of the decade then I recommend you join in the fun, and frustrations. If you dislike things breaking for no apparent reason or desire a fully implemented game then I suggest you place this game on your wishlist.

First of all it is critical to understand that the game is still in beta testing and therefore has some glitches.  That said it has been pretty stable for me.   (Four year old dell xps 8100 with 16gb and a 750 Ti video card).   At present the plan seems to be to a go for a final release in May.    There will be frequent patches before then and perhaps a beta 6 release (beta 5, with enormous additions, was released yesterday (Mar26).      If you don't like encountering bugs and reporting them to help the game, then wait for the release.   Of critical importance remaining is tuning the AI to be smarter and more aggressive, imo.
That said, with yesterday's release the game is really starting to take shape.   I played and enjoyed Galciv2 (for which, coincidentally, a community update is being finished at the same time).    But GC3, even a couple of releases ago, just looks so much better, and the game will optionally be so much bigger (largest size is "insane" and it is just that, largest number of factions...100!) with many more custom races allowed, more minor races and a much improved ship designer (which is a game in itself that one can get lost in).     Colonizing of planets is more tactical with the new adjacency bonuses and on planet resources.     The battle viewer will remain a strategic choice rather than a tactical  (one can organize one's fleet with different numbers and classes of ships, of which support ships are critical) but it also looks much  better than GC2.    You can change camera viewing angle during the battle.   Watch a 30 vs 30 ship battle, enough said (check
to see live stream game examples).   Then there are various galactic items like nebulae which restrict defence and accuracy as well as numerous strategic resouces to mine in addition to relics that give civilization wide benefits.  The ideology table gives some sharply different choices depending on whether you feel good, bad, or neutral.   Diplomacy is rapidly improving but has some way to go (as I said)  and will I think be a key to success in a big game.
Well, I could to on and on.  I am a long term 4x player (started with civ 1 in the day) and my advice is that this game will give a 4x challenge that feels, looks, and plays much different from, say, Civ 5, but with the same next turn tension and the same scramble for multiple objectives that makes a 4x game enjoyable.
Update May 13 (day before 1.0 release)
I am updating this review because the official release is roughly 24 hours away, and because the numerous patches and updates since my original reviiew have changed the situation.  First, my comments about "glitches", at least for my system and experience, are, as I predicted they would be, largely history.  In fact, the improvement in the performance of the game is beyond what my expectations were.   For example, as of the original view my CPU was running in the low 70 C range, (which is not a problem, mind) but since Beta 6 it has been running in the mid-60s C, a surprising improvement.   As a second example, a typical issue I was having was freezing in the mid to late game.  I have not seen this whasoever for several weeks.   As two more examples, key issues were occassional battle viewer and invasion hang ups. These appear to also to now be completely solid.    Perhaps the biggest change, though, is the enormous increase in content, of which  I might mention the inclusion of custom classes, meaning that I can now create my own races with an enormouse range of choices for abilities and characteristics, or borrow other peoples' creations (which I have done), to  include in my games.  I can, and have, played against the Angry Joe Army.   I have about 30 available right now, all tested and working.
I should add that this is important if one want to play on the "excessive" or "insane" size galaxies, so that there are sufficient factions to fill in the univierse.  Yes you can play with dozens of AI opponents and the game works.
In other words, as we count down to official release, my take is that things have progressed better that I predicted or expected.   I think that is important to mention.   And looking forward there is a schedule of a steady stream of patches, updates, expansions planned for GalCiv 3 over the ensuing months and years.
I wish I could give 2 thumbs up.
================ After Crusade ==============
Thought I would add a few comments post 2.5  (first big patch after crusade).
Big points:
1.  Performance even on Ludicrous size maps) is much improved and continues to get better without warning, that is, the devs are always working on it.  Late game ludicrous, there are still slow downs at time.  There is a lot going on, LoL.
2.  With Crusade  a ton of busy work is by the board.  Pretty much all of the constructor spam stuff is gone, for example.   Hence, lot more time thinking, less clicking.   I should add that there are additional tools to help even more, but of course they have to be learned.   I played a ludicrous game, 40 hours (what you often get out of  a single game that is half-way decent!), and did not crash throughout while finding lots of ways to organize and simplify stuff.
3.  I haven't even gotten into creating a custom race...there are so many available created by others.
4. I have barely scraced the surface of what could be done with the citizens.  I know with espionage - for one - you can really hurt another player.  The big thing wth citizens is that one is forced to make tough choices, not just which to choose, but how to deploy them, whether to promote them, etc.
5. I like that the research is becoming more "tiered".  For example, going from one size ship to another burns a lot of research and means it will take time to build the damn things.   Again, you have to choose.
Summary, it's worth another look.  Not the same game it was two years ago.

For someone who started on Tough mode, having to live off Wall Chicken stung at first, but as I got further and further along and started to get regen equipment, I found it to be an extremely enjoyable difficulty level. Heck, even at the max level the final area was still able to beat me down yet not be unsurmountable, so well done on that. The Voice Acting and music are both some of the best I've heard of in a video game, they fit the atmosphere at all turns and really helped me feel like I was actually there, in Dust's shoes. All in all, this game is a MUST have in ANY gaming library- I would recommend getting it even if it were twice the $15 price tag, easily. You will have a lot of fun with it, from start to the bitter end.

INCOMING ARTSY FARTSY REVIEW!
ABZÛ is a game I didn't really know about until a couple of months ago. But Austin Wintory tweeted about it and I follow him so I figured it must be good, if only for the music. Wintory composed the soundtrack for Journey, which is still my favourite game of all time. And that's good, because ABZÛ is very similar to Journey. It maintains the design choices of Journey: minimal user-interface, minimalist storytelling and a focus on music and visuals (specifically architecture) to tell a narrative. At the same time, however, ABZÛ managed to carve out its own identity with a heartwarming story with a strong moral, a beautiful aesthetic and immersive (pun) gameplay.Read more...
ABZÛ's gameplay is relatively simple: you move around underwater and can activate certain items and ride certain fish. It's incredibly simple, but in a way that gives it a purity that makes the protagonist an extension of the player. This simplicity allows for ABZÛ to tell its story while still engaging the player with simple -- very simple -- puzzles to maintain their interest. It's akin to a "walking simulator" in that sense, though ABZÛ, like Journey, has the barest minimum of obstacles and challenge so that it's more of a game than the games lumped into that genre. Also, again like Journey, there are parts where the ABZÛ's gameplay serves to create meaning and further the game's story. Things like how the main character can interact with fish becomes relevant later on, and how you interact with some objects and characters serves to create a connection between the main character with this lost civilisation and the ocean life. Also, at times, again like Journey, ABZÛ decides to really give you some fun by letting you swim through strong currents with large schools of fish. The visual feedback combined with the sound makes it such a beautiful experience, you'll probably miss some of the collectables (which are also in the more slow-moving areas).
Where ABZÛ shines is in how it builds its world and story. You're dropped into the game without any context, just like Journey, and so you simply make for whatever seems most interesting, in this case underwater tunnels. However, throughout he game, recurring motifs -- like the main character ahving a triangle on their back, and the old civilisation's gateways being shaped like triangles -- make it clear that you are somehow connected to a destroyed underwater civilisation that somehow managed to harness a sort of magical water energy (as in water beneath water) connected to ocean life. And at the same time, the recurring threat of deadly sharks makes it clear that they were somehow involved with this civilisation in one way or the other. As the main character tries to seemingly restore this lost city, more and more of the full story is revealed and you can piece more of it together. This more complicated manner of delivering story allows for some real surprises, as you find that your interpretation of events are played with wonderfully. Plot twists aren't explained to you at all; the wall-paintings, events, shifting colours and music is enough to convey meaning. And all of this intrigue manages to tell a story with a simple moral, but one that feels earned through how complex its delivery was. That's all I can give without spoiling, but suffice to say, the way ABZÛ plays with your expectations is wonderful, and I wish more games did this.
Visually, ABZÛ goes for the simplistic, high-contrast style that's gotten popular recently in games like The Witness. But where it works is that it's not relying on a sheer variety of colour and just upping the contrast on everything. ABZÛ has a coherent art style: the fish are beautiful but not overdone. The main character is beautiful in their simplicity and animation. The architecture of this lost civilisation has a great unified look to it, and the clashing aesthetic of that architecture with the main character and their drones creates a good contrast that serves to actually tell the story! Thigns aren't perfect; I played the game on Ultra and maintained 60 fps, but I had some framerate drops in extremely large schools of fish. "There are also some clipping issues every now and then that takes away from some of the immersion.
Wintory's score is, as expected, beautiful. ABZÛ's music is how much meaning is made of its visuals, so falling short would mean the entire endeavour falling apart. But ABZÛ's soundtrack is full of beautiful orchestral and classical music that will guide you on your journey. The music ramps up and sweeps you away when the aforementioned current does the same. It's looming and disturbing when a shark intimates you. Wintory's music is beautiful and gives much of ABZÛ's scenes more meaning. It's not as good as Journey, but it's still an amazing sounding game.
ABZÛ, more than anything, is a game about simplicity and the depth that comes from that. The mechanics are simple. The story (at least my interpretation of it) is simple. The art style is relatively simple. But it has depth in how it uses this simplicity to create depth. The fact that ABZÛ doesn't hold your hand and encourages you to interpret what you're seeing, hearing and doing is what gives it depth. ABZÛ, like Journey before it, is what you make of it. And to me, it's a game which uses its simple gameplay, gorgeous aesthetic and beautiful soundtrack in tandem to tell a wonderful story that plays with your expectations and has real meaning.
