The Basement Collection is a collection of different indie flash games, created mostly by the creators of Super Meat Boy / The Binding of Isaac.
Most of what the games have to offer is their gameplay and art style, but some of these games have a really unique story. Meat Boy and Spewer barely even have one for example, whereas Coil is really story driven, even if its story is not really clear, and it requieres your own interpretation of the game. Time ♥♥♥♥ and Aether's stories are present and interesting, but really aren't the core of the games. Finaly, if you unlock AVGM, I'd say that its the game that has the most meaning in the list, this game is litteraly a parody of other games and is only worth playing if you understand what the games is making fun of (or if you want the achievements !)
Trust me, there's going to be at least one game that you'll enjoy playing in there. Most of the games are hard to beat completely, like, really hard. Even if you reach the "end" of the game, there's going to be advanced levels or achievements that will take a while to beat and obtain.
I guess you already know how Meat Boy works, since it's basically the original version of Super Meat Boy (one of the best and most challenging platformer I know of). Spewer is an amazing platformer as well, but requieres a bit more tactics than Meat Boy. Aether is like... the smallest sandbox game I've played, it's fun to play and really is different from all these really hard games. I didn't play Triachnid much but it's gameplay is quite unique, even if I found it a bit boring after a while. Grey-Matter is like one of these old Starship arcade games, it's hard to describe. It was fun but I'm a noob at it :( Time ♥♥♥♥ was my favorite one to play and has an awesome idea behind it. It requieres a lot of attention and reactivity, especially in the harder levels. I'd say that it's half puzzle, half platformer, it reminded me of Fez in a way. The only problem with it was the saving system, make sure you click "exit" on the right, under the person who speaks to you (no spoiler) so that the game saves your progress, and try to quit the game with the in game option (top left).
Knowing it's a flash game... the performance was pretty bad for what the games had to offer, but it was totally playable. I did have to lower my screen resolution to play Spewer and Aether properly, as the games were quite laggy (kinda like the first Binding of Isaac was, for me). The game can't be rendered by my GPU (because it's flash I guess ?!) and uses integrated intel graphics :( Probably won't be an issue if you have a desktop PC with more a more recent CPU.
As always with Ed, i'm not dissapointed. It's not as full of weird wonderful things as The binding of Isaac, but pretty much each game has it's own look and feel. Triachnid and Aether were especially enjoyable to play simply because of their art style. Time ♥♥♥♥ wasn't especially nice visualy, (I know that the pixelated look was what was desired) but the game clearly isn't about it's graphics. Finally, the music. Wow. Danny Baranowsky is by far my favorite video game soundtrack composer. If after playing Time ♥♥♥♥, Meat Boy and AVGM, you don't have the melodies stuck in your head you must be deaf.

LiEat is just lovely from beginning to end.
Though it's labeled as RPG, it plays more like a visual novel, laying heavy focus on the story and containing only rudimentary elements of traditional JRPG. It's not hard to find the few hidden items and it's harder to lose the battles than to win them. That being said, the game is still quite enjoyable since it's really relaxing but still gives you the feeling you actually have to do something to progess instead of just clicking and sometimes making a choice like most visual novels.
The story is divided into three arcs each considered their own game, making it a trilogy. While it certainly doesn't deliver the most depth, the lovely characters manage to pull you into their world and make you want to unweave the mysteries and see the solving. There are multiple endings to each arc based on your decisions and the key parts of the story are beautifully illustrated/animated.
Another part about the game that really stuck out to me was the music. Every arc has it's own set of 10 themes and most of them became stuck in my head at first listen. Not only is the soundtrack diverse and catchy, it's also always perfectly fitting the current mood, enhancing the atmosphere in every situation.
Each arc of the LiEat trilogy takes about 1-2 hours depending on how fast you read and how meticulous you search for hidden stuff. While I do wish there was a little more focus on the RPG elements, I enjoyed the game a lot and can only recommend it. 3€ is 1€ per arc, which I think is more than fair.

While the mysteries are nothing mind-bogglingly ingenious, and it can be unclear at times where you need to go, they're generally well put together and suit the overarching theme of the game very well.
The characters are truly charming, especially the two main characters, who (amusingly) kind of serve as foils to each other. Learning more about them through their interactions with each other and the other characters is highly engaging, and I found myself surprisingly invested in their fates by the time the game's ending rolled around, which might I mention actually varies depending on your actions, and has the potential to CRUSH YOUR SOUL like it did mine.

When I saw Markiplier and co play OMDU Siege mode during open beta, I was beyond thrilled to find that there was a game that brilliantly merged a moba game with the traditional OMD style.
I played over the span of a couple of months and then took a hiatus from gaming to focus on school.
When I came back today, I was deeply saddened to find out that not only had all the data for accounts been reset, but Siege had been stripped from the game because "it was unpopular and least played".
Yet every match I had played had been full of diverse people who loved the mode. I easily played over 200 matches, and besides party members, I was never matched with the same people multiple times. On top of that, they refuse to even compile the data to prove to us that it was the "least popular gamemode", which once again, I find interesting. Queueing up for siege would have you a match within 1 minute. Queuing up for survival would take at least 2.5 minutes, if not more, the key here being that it took more people to get a match of siege going vs survival (I think survival only had 3 or 5 people, while Siege took 10 people in a match).
So please, let's see some data supporting your "least popular gamemode" argument. I'm sorry, but I cannot come back to play a game where the devs stripped the favorite gamemode of many people I know and played with and have since also quit playing the game due to this change.
Right now, it feels like classic OMD with a reskin and a few new characters. It honestly feels that way as someone who has experienced the whole franchise.
Siege brought something new to the game, and that's what attracted people to OMD:U. It was something different from the old games.
If Siege was going to be removed, I'm honestly very surprised there appeared to be limited outcry, which makes me wonder if it was a surprise move when they did the resets, which it appears to have been, and knowing the devs not being very open about patch changes until they were made, it wouldn't surprise me if such a thing was done.
It can only lead me to believe that the devs only claim to listen to community feedback, but never actually read the reviews, read the reports, read the opinions and suggestions us community members gave.
It was an honor to participate in the open beta. I wish the game luck, but I cannot play this anymore.

Edit (5/24/15): It's out now, it's shipping. It's like I thought, they did fix whatever memory leaks it had, and all the production level code is rock solid. Ok, I think I've played enough to write about the game.
I come from playing a LOT of Civ 5, so this will be from a Civ 5 perspective. So, planets are more or less cities. There are a lot less places you can settle on the map. Deciding where to settle is more or less not that interesting. See planet, settle on it. You'll need to hunt for planets, most of them are dead.
Starbases are what you use to "mine" strategic resources with. Given strategic resources you can then build special improvements and ships. You can mine strategic resources by building starbases in someone else's territory! They might declare war on you though.
So all of colonization consists of balancing between building colonizers and construction ships.
I guess the big thing that's different is the actual planets/cities themselves - you can build improvements that cluster to synergize with each other to boost manufacturing, research, happiness, etc.
The tech trees are just bizarre from a Civ 5 PoV. They resemble more of the tech web from Civ BE than anything else. Even the tech web is less bizarre than these though. And there are these strange limits on how far down a tech tree you can go too. These "Ages" throttle the depth. What governs when you flip over into a new Age? Dunno. There's no Civilopedia to explain anything to you. In fact, Stardock, if there's ONE thing you could do to improve your game, it's this. Civilopedia - look into writing one. I'm sure you have a tech writer at least on contract, get them to write a Civilopedia. I know, call it something else but do it.
The whole set of combat units you can build is also bizarre too. In CIv 5 you have melee, ranged, naval and air units, and once you know the basics of all four of those, they do come in slightly different flavors of those four, but how they play more or less remains the same. They've split combat units up into both ship type and weapon type, and the resulting table of different ship types is daunting to say the least. And again, there's no Civilopedia to tell me what the difference is, and what would make you want to build one over the other.
So is it worth picking up, if you like playing Civ 5? Yeah. Sort of. What word exists between "yeah" and "meh"? Be prepared to do a lot of out of game research on the combat mechanics. In fact, I'd say read whatever strategy guides exist on the internet before buying this game. If the strategy guides pique your interest, then go for it.
And like always, you might want to catch it on sale when you do, unless you're a fan of the series. I bought mine for $25 on sale and I think that's a good price.

quick disclaimer; this is all my personal opinion and experience. i haven't played paladins competitively yet but im working on it. my opinions on the game might change when i do.
as someone who has put over 2,000 hours in TF2, and is over level 100 on Overwatch; and have played both games competitively i reckon i have some grounds on which to stand when comparing Paladins to them.
in short, no, they are not at all the same. it seems like the entire internet likes to jump on a giant bandwagon of hate when a new fresh FPS is released, and it almost always calls games "rip offs" or "copy's" of other games. from experience, i can say that paladins is a game more balanced around the skill of an individual, but still requires good teamwork and cooperation to win games. you can technically still "carry" as certain characters, but even if your individual skill is amazing, you won't win unless you work with the team. in TF2, an individual could carry their team to victory in a non-competitive scenario. one sniper who hits all of their important shots could carry the team hard enough to win the game. in paladins, you could have 50 kills and 2 deaths but still lose the game because the team simply didn't work together. in overwatch, if you don't play by the meta; you're almost always guaranteed to lose. overwatch also relies heavily on teamwork, to the point where even players who have never touched the game before could still win games by simply working together. there are no "carries" in overwatch, and the game is simply reliant on teamwork and having a good handle on characters that work for the meta.
if you enjoy working as a team, overwatch's competitive scene is definitely the way to go. if you enjoy simply carrying your team, TF2 is your way. a perfect blend between them, in my opinion - would be paladins. it's wicked fun, it's free, and you can meet some wicked people. the game is also blessed with having a community and developer group that care and constantly update the game, which is something that TF2 didn't have, which is the main reason why i left it.

This game, with the right group of friends, provides an amazing return on enjoyment for the cost. It brings back memories of playing Halo 2 co-op on XBox with it's graphics and gameplay, but also the enjoyment and replayability of L4D2. I can play the same maps over and over with friends and always have a different game.
One day I'll get trampled by a Triceratops, but kill it with one hit point left with my pistol, ala Saving Private Ryan. The next day I'll take to the skies in a helicopter and save my medic-playing friend from the hoard of raptors she had missed while fixing the generator. The day after that, I'll track a nasty pteranodon carefully with my sniper rifle and line up an expert shot, only to be picked up by a completely different one, dropped in the middle of the fight, and quickly eaten by a Spinosaurus.
The game's difficulty is easy to control. If you're looking to relax, pop it on Easy and add some ambient dinos in a Conquest map, and spend two whole campaigns blasting T-Rex's with a tank. Or if you want a challange, throw it on Expert and dive into a King of the Hill map with equally skilled opponents. The maps are wide, beautiful, and varied, and there's plenty of details to catch every time you play. There's something to be said about mowing down rapters in the middle of an arctic wasteland only to have your visor freeze up with ice. There's something to be said about wondering where the hell you're taking damage from in a huge rain storm until you finally clue in and punch that nasty ankle-biter to death.
The game is glitchy at times. Some days it wouldn't let me join or host multiplayer maps, and that issue resolved itself without me figuring out why. Changing game settings while the game is active will crash it entirely. However, I've yet to have a single issue once I've actually gotten into a game and just kept playing. I would heavily recommend this game to any group of friends who are looking for a way to casually stay up until 4 in the morning, accidentally. That fun. That well made.

Even though I am not much into furries, this is now one of my favourite games. And explaining why seems to be the most difficult thing I've ever written.
Let's start simple, the music is pretty damn gorgeous! There are only a few games that fit flwalessly to the game and are really enjoyable to listen independetly as well. None of the tracks gets annoying over time and they support the game flow from start to finish.
The story is well-written, and even though I normally prefer darker and more brutal atmosphere in my games, having a fairy taler occasionally can feel refreshing. And this one really does! The two main characters are really fun to take through the solid yet somewhat simplistic main story, their interactions with each other never fail to characterize them both and their bond. Some of the supporting characters are not so strong, though, but it didn't really bother me.
But the real meat here is the fighting system and especially the controls. I've never played a game with as tight control set as Dust. If you die, it's your own fault for making a balant mistake. You really feel like you are in control at any time. The system itself is really simple, yet it never got boring in my first playthrough. Every fight was thoroughly satisfying and the platforming, while I usually hate it, felt natural and fun to play.
The only bad thing I can say is the difficulty level, which is too easy for me. And the fact that after completing this game, other games feel dull and colourless... =D

I'm so excited to finally be able to review this game post-launch!
I pre-ordered Crypt of the NecroDancer back in 2013 when they started allowing people to do so, and I've been playing the alpha since it became available in April of 2014.
It's a rhythm-based roguelike with some small measure of cross-play achievements (you unlock things as you progress in the game for future playthroughs in other modes), and while all items start identified (i.e., you always know what a scroll or weapon is, unlike a 'true' roguelike), their placements and whether or not they even show up is randomized.
The dungeon randomization is great, and you can specify specific seeds if you want to share levels with other players or work on one specific layout, but where the game really shines -- and its purpose, really -- is the music.
You can only move, attack, use items, cast spells, and anything else *on the beat*. Monsters also move on the beat, and they move in routinely predictable patterns so that over time you learn how to anticipate them and counter them, and in fact some monsters require you to learn these patterns and match the beat in order to even damage them. The skill cap is pretty high, the amount of replayability is immense (there are 9 playable characters and a 10th 'challenge' character, all of whom greatly alter the gameplay in different and interesting ways), and there's even a 'beatless' character that allows you to play the game like a traditional roguelike (monsters move when you do, and you're not forced to stick to the rhythm). And if you want a real challenge, you can even play on a dancepad...
As someone who has been playing roguelikes ever since actually growing up playing Rogue, and who used to religiously follow rec.games.roguelike, I am so delighted to see an injection of 'newness' into the genre like NecroDancer. It's sorely needed, and while I doubt we'll ever see it emulated, I hope it inspires another developer to merge *their* love of two genres into something as incredibly engaging, challenging, and outright *fun* as this.

Abzû is an interesting little fish, made by a team led by Matt Nava, art director on the games Journey and Flower. The game has VERY beautiful visuals and music (by brilliant composer Austin Wintory) and is kinda meditative (for the most part, it gets a little jarring in places).
There's not that much "gaming" in it per se, just a few very simple door-opening puzzles and some collectibles, but the experience is very much worth the approximately two hours it takes to complete. Some will call this another "walking simulator" (I call it a swimming simulator myself), and that's okay. The term has some negative connotations, but we ARE talking about a linear progression from point to point, so why not? Nothing wrong with that when it's as gorgeous as this.
I think I'll probably come back to some of the early levels, just to swim around in the sunlit sea and look at the fishies. Really peaceful.
NOTE: The store page says a controller is "highly recommended". That should be "MANDATORY". If you try to play this with mouse and keyboard, you will come away severely disappointed.

Bus Simulator 16 does exactly what it says in the title (that's always a good start)!  You start out with a simple route and basic vehicle, and you drive the route to collect fares, keep to a timetable, avoid accidents and (hopefully) make a profit.  When you have enough money, you can hire new drivers, buy new vehicles and drive new routes too.  This is a true simulator (not necessarily a 'fun' game) so will likely feel a bit dry for anyone looking for heaps of excitement!
Whether you enjoy this simulator or not will come down to how well you treat the simulation.  If you ignore kerbs, corners and road positioning, you can hare from stop to stop and then it's done - boring.  However, if you play it as a trainee driver and use your mirrors to make perfect corners without clipping kerbs or hitting anything, (ie a bit of real-life stuff), then you will get much more challenge and simulation experience out of the game.  A wheel is recommended for the driving, and there is a full set of cockpit controls that you can click on in 3D view (a little like Train Simulator) or you can use button shortcuts instead.
I've driven several buses and coaches and I have to say the handling of the buses in-game isn't bad at all.  Some things are simulated perfectly, like mirrors and cornering (and reversing into your garage if you're feeling particularly cocky)!  This is as real as it gets and Bus Simulator 16 nails it perfectly.  Wheels on a bus or coach are a few feet behind the driver, so you must drive out into the junction straight before you can begin the steer.  Unlike a car, steering is not a single arm-wrench of the wheel and skid around that corner (pity)!  It's a nouanced set of movements (steer the front, straighten, steer again for rear wheels) that is difficult at first, but it's very true to life.  This is what the game does exceptionally well.  In reality, overall steering tends to be a little lighter and easier than is represented by the game, with only slight steer giving quite a turn, but the game wanted more steering than I would usually expect.  That could be that I don't have my in-game wheel settings balanced correctly though.
Talking of wheels, many are supported but do check the forums as some people are having a few problems.  The newer Logitech 920 isn't currently working properly (the devs are looking at it).  As for older wheels like the Logitech G25 and 27, they do work after some fiddling.  It entails downloading Logitech's newest driver which no longer supports the G25/27 (nice one Logitech in forcing obsolescence in £200+ game controllers) and taking from the new drivers a DLL file and adding it to the game (all explained in the game forums), then reinstalling an older G25/27 supporting driver.  A nuisance, but doable.
The graphics are a bit basic for today's PCs, though they're not necessarily so important as the game mechanics are in a simulation title.  There is ONLY right-hand driving, which sucks for anyone in a left-hand drive country because this game actually makes quite a neat training aid.  The overall vehicle handling and steering response (particularly on straight roads) tends to be a little too heavy (steering of these vehicles is typically very light).  Oh, and there is no driver customisation which is a minor point, but being able to customise features, skin-tone and gender could have been a neat addition.  That's nit-picking though.
If you're looking for a pure simulator title, then this is a good place to start.  It offers everything you need in setting up and driving basic bus routes and is actually good enough as a training aid for driving any long, non-articulated vehicle in managing corners well (all mirrors are recreated perfectly).  However, if you're looking for more of a 'game' experience, it might be a title you won't enjoy so much.

Of the various Totem games in this series (Ironclads collection), I found this one the most playable.  I believe this was the first one they issued.
The interface allows the ships to be separated into individual squadrons. While historically inaccurate, it renders the game much  more playable, plus helps illustrate just why ships of this era used the line tactics. Later games of this series only allow grouping the ships, and once a ship is heavily damaged, it (uncontrollably) breaks off. Whilst very realistic, also very frustrating (Hey! I’m gonna go get sunk by running past the main battle group).
The projected path feature is really nice, and allows you fair control of the course.  The various armaments display when a shot is available, albeit for a split second sometimes. Pausing the ship motion is controlled by clicking icons on the display panel, and judicious use of saved games.
The data displayed and ship information is very detailed, and appears fairly accurate. The same applies to the ship names.  The models are very well done, and looks like a lot of work and research went into them. I can’t believe other reviews complaining about lack of animated crew jumping about!  Really?
Overall, I believe this is a fun game and enjoyed it.  This was a great work of programming and modelling. Other reviews need to cut Totem some slack – I don’t see any Americans making anything like this. It very much reminds me of the Yaquinto boardgame Ironclads, with some similar elements of gameplay.
Recommendations for the Totem staff:  apply this control interface to the later games in the series. It was very well done here. Also, muting the soundtrack would be nice. отличная работа!

quick disclaimer; this is all my personal opinion and experience. i haven't played paladins competitively yet but im working on it. my opinions on the game might change when i do.
as someone who has put over 2,000 hours in TF2, and is over level 100 on Overwatch; and have played both games competitively i reckon i have some grounds on which to stand when comparing Paladins to them.
in short, no, they are not at all the same. it seems like the entire internet likes to jump on a giant bandwagon of hate when a new fresh FPS is released, and it almost always calls games "rip offs" or "copy's" of other games. from experience, i can say that paladins is a game more balanced around the skill of an individual, but still requires good teamwork and cooperation to win games. you can technically still "carry" as certain characters, but even if your individual skill is amazing, you won't win unless you work with the team. in TF2, an individual could carry their team to victory in a non-competitive scenario. one sniper who hits all of their important shots could carry the team hard enough to win the game. in paladins, you could have 50 kills and 2 deaths but still lose the game because the team simply didn't work together. in overwatch, if you don't play by the meta; you're almost always guaranteed to lose. overwatch also relies heavily on teamwork, to the point where even players who have never touched the game before could still win games by simply working together. there are no "carries" in overwatch, and the game is simply reliant on teamwork and having a good handle on characters that work for the meta.
if you enjoy working as a team, overwatch's competitive scene is definitely the way to go. if you enjoy simply carrying your team, TF2 is your way. a perfect blend between them, in my opinion - would be paladins. it's wicked fun, it's free, and you can meet some wicked people. the game is also blessed with having a community and developer group that care and constantly update the game, which is something that TF2 didn't have, which is the main reason why i left it.

Well, Well, Well.
Sad state of affairs Robort entertainment, made two great games prior to this one, and I would have prefered a OMD3, with a soild single player storyline to follow, and then the improved multiplayer as a secondary thing here. The fact that it is a PTW game, as the grind required to unlock anything with skulls along is boring, dont let me game time fool you on here, i played on a different account on its standalone launcher.
The gameplay is still there, but the fun is sapped away with all cool stuff locked away behind a paywall. PvP should never have been introduced into this series, it was fine the way it was  as a PvE fun trap filled dream of gibs and chaos. This game is just not fun, you cant play it solo, and you have to play with friends otherwise you just get destroyed.
Forcing people like me who dont have any mates to play with, to not enjoy the game. The game itself is fun and gameplay is there, the level designs are great, but the PTW and the move from Single player tower defence gameplay to a be it, an orginal pvp system keeping the core of OMD alive, is a good idea.
But i did not want this for my next OMD game, I wanted OMD3. This game is not that. its a free to play cash in on the license, if there was an option to unlock everything like a retail price, included traps and all the consumables and then u just farm skulls to use them, then that would be better all around.
You go from a 14.99 game at release, upto 24.99 with dlc in OMD2 and 6.99 or 9.99 for OMD1, which i paid and played to death and own all those games. Then you get to here, yes they have a deal to unlock all characters for 17 quid, but you still have to buy real coins  to get anything else, which can cost over a 100 quid.
Just to touch on the grind itself, when you win you unlock chests, (from the daily, or daily login bonus) - these are pure RNG, and they will bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥a few times, you get parts for traps 99% of the time will be common drops, i never saw one rare or epic drop in my opening of boxes. This is really annoying, and if you have cash to burn, you can buy tons of chests and try the more luxary boxes giving the edge to the PTW player and completely ignoring the P2W player, i supported the developers and I played in open beta as well when they were trying to MOBA the game to a new audience, im glad they stayed with the original format. But without more grinding options or a better way for a player to earn more skulls other than getting stomped in Sabotage and earning around 200 - 400 skulls a game, you will just straight up get annoyed that those that pay in this game, have a massive advantage. I get that its a F2P game and they have to make the money somewhere.
I would prefer a standalone version of all the maps from 1 and 2 and all the dlc and the new ones from OMDU as well in the OMD2 engine with co-op and leaderboards, if they did that, even if i had to pay 19.99 for it, i would because that to me is what i want, fresh maps and to be able to play single player. Not forced multiplayer and hope to find someone who is OP and has tons of traps so you can actually earn some skulls, either get carried or get destroyed in frustation is not a fun way to play.
In short the game is great, but without friends its impossible, the grind is way to long i am still going to play the game, but its just so frustrating that the devs would do this in place of OMD3. I hope that there will be an OMD3 one day, and this is just a way for robot to make a few quid to support new OMD games, if that is all it is, then im cool with it. But if OMD stays as a F2P franchise, i will be very upset and said that Robot have taken this route.
Despite all that thou, i am still going to recommend this game, as i am a diehard fan of the series, and there isnt many games out there with this level of production and fun. Despite its really long skull grind, and P2W system, there is a fantasic game underneath all that, i just want some friends to be able to enjoy the game, so if you want to play this with me, then please add me.
P.S. Dev team keep up the good work , i hope there are going to be QOL improvements to the game in the future and a fairer system for the F2P player like me, who has played both previous games, and loved them to death.
Cheers.

When it comes to the illustrious Final Fantasy series, this one is certianly brought up constantly. While I don't think it's the best the series has to offer (play FFVI if you like batshit crazy villains) it still has a solid story and great gameplay. The materia system in this game offers tons of ways to customize your characters, effectively turning EVERYONE into battle mages if you play like me, and the music is top-notch.
More notes on gameplay: if you're not a fan of grinding, then this may not be for you. Certainly if you're lucky/play your cards right with certain materia, then you don't need to grind (BIG HINT: invest in your enemy skill materia; there are a few spells where, if you get them as early as possible, a good chunk of boss battles in the beginning will be absurdly easy). If you want Aeris to have all of her limit breaks as soon as possible, then you need to gind, BEFORE ENTERING THE TEMPLE OF THE ANCIENTS. Also, grinding and good gear is pretty much the only way to grow your materia, and boy do you need good materia for certain battles.
Graphics: Yes, they aren't particulary good in regards to what we have now, but let us remember this was the mid 90s and cutting edge at the time. I think the story and music more than make up for Cloud and his polygnal freedom fighters. Also, there's a mod to update the graphics if you're interested.
If you're only going to play one FF game, don't play this one, pay VI for the SNES. However, if you are curious as to what all the fuss is about, then give it a go, especially since it's dirt cheap right now thanks to the winter sale. AND FOR GOD'S SAKE PLEASE COMPLETE AERIS BEFORE THE TEMPLE OF THE ANCIENTS.

Although I wasn't really exposed to the metroidvania style of games when I was a kid  ( Sega does what Nintendon't),  I have always been a fan of horror and monsters so I picked this up.    After playing and dying a few times, then dying a few more times, I finally beat the game, unlocked a few characters, and called it a day.   A week or two pass and I decide to pick up the game again.  I start exploring the rooms and  I am instantly walled by some little mini-boss (one of the seven deadly sins) and die.  I start again and get through the dungeon with little trouble, so I head to the boss room.  I'm immediately confronted by some  little freak, riding and horse, who  decides tramples me to death.  It turns out that the difficulty had jumped on me while, at the same time, my skills had degraded during my break.  I reset the data to reset the difficulty but then realized too late  that I would have to unlock my characters again, so I uninstalled the game in a bout of ragequit.

My point in all this is that this game is not for a casual player.  The Binding of Isaac (BOI) will make you cry,  knash your teeth, and pull your hair out until you get a good feel for the game.  Even then, the game appropriately makes itself more difficult to keep a dedicated play coming back for more.

More recently,  I have been buying more roguelike games and decided to give this game another try.  This time though  I have been playing more frequently, so my skills have been improving at a steady rate.  Needless to say,  I am hooked again.
Aside from a bug that doesn't register achievements to Steam (there is a short term fix),  it is an excellent game with an insane amount of replayability, variety, and an art style that will keep you coming back for more.

This game is nowhere near finished at this point. If you want an idea of how development is going and what the game is going to really look like, you can pay for that now. But you won't be paying for a game. Keep that in mind. Think of it as a tech demo. It's a beta, people. It isn't complete, nor will it be for some time yet. They're working on it though, and I have faith in them giving me my money's worth when the final product is ready to play.
My original intention with buying this was to see the shipbuilder, but that is very clearly incomplete and missing a crucial feature from GalCiv2 which allowed you to manipulate the camera angle in 3D space in order to see different attachment points.
Oh right, those. The little red arrows.
Yeah don't try to use the shipbuilder unless you want to give yourself a brain aneurism.
The little red arrows have no textures, and no outlines. They are pure red, and you cannot rotate the camera, so you'll very quickly be seeing a red blobby mass that will be impossible to work with. Don't bother.
I can't entirely recommend that the reader buy this, because it's unfinished. I can however, tell you that if you like the 4X genre, you should click 'follow' on the store page and throw this on your wishlist while you're at it. You probably don't want this game now, but you will, eventually. I can promise you that.

First of all, this game is still in beta so purchase at your own risk.
tl;dr: Great game for those who love complex strategy and/or creativity and don't mind a few technical issues. However still lacking features and still prone to crashes and bugs.
The game is fun and nostalgic for those who played older GalCivs but it's still far from being complete. The game itself is quite complex, mostly ranging from managing your economy and research whilst also building up your armada to defend your civilization. Other than that, you can build your own ships tailored to the situation and your own creativity, you can build anything from the smallest scouts to intimidatingly huge battleships. You can also build specialized ships like fragile but deadly snipers or even a craft specialized with sensors to see the enemy coming from sectors away. You can even win in your own way, conquering through military (let's be honest, the most fun and easy method), cultural or technological might. These elements combined with future content seems rather promising for a strategy game, especially as the developpers seem keen to both add content to the game and fix current issues.
However, let us remember that it's a beta and is therefore prone to many, many issues, amongst the most pressing:
-Many, many bugs, rarely play over 30mins without any technical problems (especially true late game)
-You lose your save data (or, to be precise, the ability to use them as they are no longer compatible) every few patches
-Many features have yet to be implemented
-The AI can be somewhat... crude and annoying
Despite this, I will still recommend this game as it is still fun and keeps me in the "one more turn" mentality for hours on end.

quick disclaimer; this is all my personal opinion and experience. i haven't played paladins competitively yet but im working on it. my opinions on the game might change when i do.
as someone who has put over 2,000 hours in TF2, and is over level 100 on Overwatch; and have played both games competitively i reckon i have some grounds on which to stand when comparing Paladins to them.
in short, no, they are not at all the same. it seems like the entire internet likes to jump on a giant bandwagon of hate when a new fresh FPS is released, and it almost always calls games "rip offs" or "copy's" of other games. from experience, i can say that paladins is a game more balanced around the skill of an individual, but still requires good teamwork and cooperation to win games. you can technically still "carry" as certain characters, but even if your individual skill is amazing, you won't win unless you work with the team. in TF2, an individual could carry their team to victory in a non-competitive scenario. one sniper who hits all of their important shots could carry the team hard enough to win the game. in paladins, you could have 50 kills and 2 deaths but still lose the game because the team simply didn't work together. in overwatch, if you don't play by the meta; you're almost always guaranteed to lose. overwatch also relies heavily on teamwork, to the point where even players who have never touched the game before could still win games by simply working together. there are no "carries" in overwatch, and the game is simply reliant on teamwork and having a good handle on characters that work for the meta.
if you enjoy working as a team, overwatch's competitive scene is definitely the way to go. if you enjoy simply carrying your team, TF2 is your way. a perfect blend between them, in my opinion - would be paladins. it's wicked fun, it's free, and you can meet some wicked people. the game is also blessed with having a community and developer group that care and constantly update the game, which is something that TF2 didn't have, which is the main reason why i left it.

At the time, I was skeptical of what could be achieved to improve the gameplay in the amount of time remaining before the final release of the game.  To my surprise, Stardock has done a very good job of putting an appropriate level of polish into the game over the past couple of months.  Many of the glaring issues - such as a faulty and exploitable AI now appear to be patched up.  In particular, I encountered situations where I could purchase the entire military of a race who was far ahead of me in military and tech power, and immediately turn a losing game around where I should not have been able to.  This appears to have been fixed (I tested out this specific situation) and the AI in general seems quite a bit more intelligent in diplomacy.
I can't speak for every facet of the game - I haven't played multiplayer, the campaign is still not yet released, etc, however what I have experienced thus far is very good - a complete turnaround from the state of the game two months ago and a true successor to the greatness of the previous games.   As a result, I am changing my recommendation on this game to a resounding 'Yes!'.

This game, oh this game. You are in for quite the treat if you enjoy action-RPG like games. The action is super fluid and once you get some abilities rocking, and the controls are mastered, you can be chaining people for days, swooshing around the screen, crushing your enemies into dust (heh). The story is hit or miss with some people, but I enjoied it very much, it sucked me in and kept me hooked until the end, almost making me tear up. Not only the the combat and story good, but the world itself is nice, it's beautiful to look at and has plenty to explore, since this game takes the metroidvania path of letting you explore and find goodies scattered across the land waiting for you to pluck them out. Along while doing this, you have a wonderful soundtrack, playing fitting tunes for all the areas as you run about looking for things to kill, finding goodies, or doing sidequests to help you level Dust further. The game has a crafting system which lets you make better items, once you gathered all the materials, and you can find better recipies lying about the world, which, if found and made, are well worth the hassle. Due to this however, can make the game a little grindy, thus making combat a little stale for some. For an indie game however, this game is wonderful, and if you enjoy action-RPGs then I have no idea why this game is not in your collection already.

Okay, I should start by saying that I'm a little bias when it comes to this game. I liked as a kid and so there's a great deal of nostalgia at play here for me. That being said, lets dive in.
Final Fantasy VII (Steam Edition) is more or less a slightly enhanced port of the PS one game of 1997, or the PC game of 1998 if you prefer. The game itself is fun and engaging and a little edgy for its time. You follow the character Cloud Strife on his various adventures with the eco-terrorist(?) group AVALANCHE. Along the way you will encounter various tropes from Sci-fi, other Final Fantasy games and popular Japanese sub-culture movements of the times as well as a few issues that are still concerns of the modern day.
If you are looking for an RPG that is Skyrim related or a hack-n-slash type game, I would strongly urge you to go no where near this thing.
That being said, if you actually are familiar, or already like, the traditional JRPG turn base format (Final Fantasy, Persona, Mario RPG) then this is a pretty solid game that will give you a wide variety of stuff to do and give you a story is pretty interesting to follow, even if it does get away from itself a lot...a lot.

First off, let me start by saying that this is probably one of the best games on Steam right now in terms of the creativity and awesomeness that went into this game. I first saw this being played by the great SpeirsTheAmazingHD on the ever wonderful YouTube and after becoming 100% engorged in the video, I decided to hop on over to the beautiful and sexy program called Steam to buy the game.
I figure I will write this review like many others have in the past and most likely will do in the future by doing a Pros and Cons section. So, without further carrying on and procrastination (not really), here we go...
PROS
- Seriously amazing graphics for the price of the game and it doesn't take $1,000 worth of PC to run it (although something better than a GT XXX card is recommended believe me...)
- Strong and solid Workshop community; I have never seen so many mods to download. However, I wish some more maps were able to uploaded (not sure if that's possible?)
- The physics are very well engineered, probably some of the best I've seen in a game. The way the vehicles react to terrain and how the terrain reacts to the vehicles is impressive (and I have played BeamNG.drive)
- Customization is another wonderful aspect boasted by the game and is very unique and fitting to what the game was made for. If you're like me, I love watching certain vehicles pulling certain trailers on varying types of terrain and simulating real life scenarios
- Overall, this game is bada$$!
CONS
- The only gripe I have with this game is the Campaign/Missions gameplay. I cannot for the life of me figure it out and I have already ruled stupidity trust me. There is just something about it I can't get, but fortunately, it doesn't stop me from both trying and playing the game.
- I have no other cons to add :)
All in all, I give this game an 11/10 rating simply because it is incredibly entertaining for me and the only time I ever stop playing is when I have to work or sleep. And if you're reading still thinking that you might buy it, go watch videos on the gameplay on YouTube, you will not regret it.

For being creative in the Roguelike genre by adding Rhythm game elements (Dancepad-style controls and gameplay), it's awesome that this game did something out of the ordinary and did it WELL.
New to the game? Don't worry, there's a lot of stuff in the game for beginners, from tutorials to training rooms, to get to up to par with the better players. Wanna challenge yourself? Go right ahead! There's daily challenges, seeded runs, speedrunning, and you can remove items you've unlocked from the dungeon. Like modding games? It's got that too. Just throw some pixel art together and make yourself a new character or two, make a dungeon with the level editor, or edit some of the game's XML data for lulz.
If you've come for a fun time, the soundtrack, got a recommendation, or to introduce yourself to Roguelikes, you won't be disappointed. Just keep in mind, this game doesn't throw punches. The enemies are tough and there are a lot of them. They do however follow patterns, so try to learn them.

I cannot understand the many negative comments on this game. Im not sure what people expect from a relatively cheap, non-AAA game. Im playing on the 'test' performance version and it runs well and have not had any crashes thusfar and I get the feeling many of the earlier gripes have been attended to.
PROs:
+ It looks decent enough.
+ The performance patch has made the game a lot better.
+ Very good G27 steering wheel support, ready to play when I plugged it in.  Not even Project Cars or Assetto did that, and it took me an afternoon to set up my wheel on OMSI 2!
+ Very accesible and super intuitive user interface
+ Ability to run your own company, hire and fire drivers, create  lines: these add to the fun and  playability.
+ Has an easy to use, uncomplicated cashier system with English speaking Passengers
+ Driving is not as realistic as OMSI 2 but, it definitely is not  completely arcade. Realism is at the very worst, passable.
+ Its surprisingly stable and bug free.
CONS :
- Single map limits the game somewhat, making it easy to burn out on the gameplay quicker than Id like.
- No force feedback for engine vibration or terrain, makes the driving experience feel 'floaty'.
-Workshop items are a little sparse.
I think if the developers continue to work on the realism and physics of the gameplay and continue to implement suggesstions made by the community, as they have been doing, this game will hands down beat the competition.
If you are looking for a starter Bus SImulator - this is the better choice. If you want an excellent, hightly realistic driving experience, but dont mind wrestling with a horribly quirky user interface,  dealing with lots of German and have the patience to figure out a hard to access, complicated routing system, get OMSI.
Dont hate me, but I have been playing this as my bus simulator of choice. It may not be as realistic as it gets, but its great fun.

Right now Steam cites me at about 30 hours. In reality I've probably plunked down double that while not connected to Steam. There are a lot of reviews that read like kids looking for a quick giggle, which is understandable. But this game strikes a heavy chord for anyone who is old enough to remember the Cold War.
This game is, in a word, sobering. It is incredibly simplistic, the controls are very basic, and the gameplay doesn't change much. I kind of doubt the production team was attempting to build as complete a simulator as they did because if I were sitting in NORAD and lighting off Peacekeepers and scrambling Stratofortresses, I would imagine it would feel a bit like this. The ambience of the game is probably the most unnerving part of immersion. Hearing people sobbing and coughing while you're watching nuclear warheads pass each other over the polar cap does something to you.
The real upshot to the game was multiplayer, especially with randos. Unfortunately the multiplayer landscape for the game tends to be unpopulated due to the age of the game and more addictive (and casual fun) games like LoL.
I would suggest buying this game if you are looking for something that you can play with a friend or two and aren't looking to break the bank. The AI is good to teach you the basics, but very predictable. Be sure everyone understands how to speed up the game, too, and you can do 45-60 minute matches.

Paladins is a great team shooter beside for a few flaws that don't awfully diminish the fun of the game.
Pros:
-There are plenty of opportunities to use skill to get kills and to not die.
-All the gamemodes feel unique, and fun situations are created in the game design.
-Stealth is actually properly implemented in a character.
-Even when you die, the game only keeps you out of the action for as long as it has to.
-Every character feels different and requires different tactics and skills (i.e. Androxus is about being able to aim properly, Lex is about hunting specific targets, Pip is about assessing the situation and predicting enemies, Evie is about whipping all over the place and being tough to hit while hitting opponents).
-The communications system is pretty good, even though there are voice coms.
Cons:
-Games often feel pretty one-sided. I'm not saying that it isn't fun to farm stats on other players, but matches
-I don't recklessly abandon matches, but in the few cases that something actually happens, a bot replaces you - which is worse than nobody at all.
-I personally don't care because it does not conflict with the way I play, but people have problems with the loot system. I've never ran out of my currency, and I've been pretty creative with builds and other things.
-It may just be that the game is in Beta, but I see similar things in Smite. A few bugs pop up every now and then, and some actually negatively affect the gameplay. At least they're not as bad as those that make the game literally unplayable in Smite.
-Some particular characters are a little boring, but every role has a few fun choices.
For anyone complaining that it's similar to Overwatch, I suggest you play it when you become somewhat tired of Overwatch. The gamefeel of Paladins is completely separate from Overwatch in three major ways. The first is that teams are made up of five players, rather than six. This means that an individual player's skill can heavily influence the match, for good or for bad. Secondly, every character feels somewhat tankier and can regenerate health when out of combat for some time, which changes the overall feel of engagements. Some may think that this takes the focus off of reactions and skills, but it creates a much more emotionally charged environment. It also makes 5v5 team deathmatch all the more exciting. Thirdly, the pacing is somewhat more gameplay-oriented. Maybe it's just because I'm far better at this game than I an at Overwatch (or all the players are bad) and die less, but I feel that the game wants players to meet each other around the objective. The maps are somewhat less nuanced and are shaped for engagement. The game also allows players to rush into the action after death on a horse.

Just so you know. I've played all of the previous Galactic Civ series and all of the Master Orions before that. This is the succcessor to those and it shows.  While the game is still in beta, it certainly playable and new things are being finished/adjusted and added regularly. Going to 64 bit only has really allowed them to make immense glaxay settings available, so much so that you can't get all of the possible galaxy on a 1920x1080 monitor at once. :)
Many things are similar or familar but with tweaks. Most obvious first change is that the game map is now hexagon based. The tech trees are per race, and there are big differences per race. As another reviewer noted, it's easier to build your colonies with automated updates, but as they now give bonuses for similar neighbooring improvements so careful  planning can be game changing.
You have significant off planets things to mine or harvest- asension crystals, artifacts, resources and asteriods (although asteroid mining isn't implemented as of Beta 4). Grabbing these can also make a large difference in the game, depending on your play style.

War. Deceit. Terrorism. Murder. Sex. Treason. Prostitution. Violence. Loyalty. Espionage. Racism. If somebody tells you that Witcher 2 is for mature audiences, this isn’t because it’s exceptionally bloody or gory for a title of its genre – it’s because of the world and stories that it presents.
It’s true: the graphics are mostly really good, even stunning in places. Battle is tactical and you have to learn how to use both your weaponry and your magic abilities in order to succeed. Music and sound are pretty good - the nice use of different dialects is a good reason that you should consider playing it in English even if that’s not your native language. The flaws that actually bothered me were few - like the fact that Geralt (your character) puts up the same facial expression for 80% of his dialogue.
Yet it’s the storytelling and the way you shape WHAT story unfolds that I enjoyed most.
Geralt has a real talent to end up as the “right guy in the wrong place”. And even though he progresses through the quests for pretty personal reasons, he constantly finds himself forced to make decisions that have a much larger impact than his personal fate.  Who will you trust? Who will you help? By the time you finish the first chapter you will have made decisions that will not only control the way you experience the rest of the story, but also will shape the lifes of many of the characters you met and – in the end – maybe even the rise and the fall of the nations that you cross. As usual in the Witcher games, you will find that not all of your decisions have the effect that you hoped, and often you only can try to choose the lesser evil.
When I finished the game I felt the urge to play the Witcher 3  (which isn’t released at the time of this writing). Not because of the (hopefully) good gameplay and graphics that I expect – but because I wonder where Geralt's personal story and the big events that happen around him will finally lead.
So do yourself a favor, get past the crappy tutorial and average prologue and then – starting with the first chapter - play one of the finest RPGs that are out there.

A simple yet incredibly entertaining top-down 2D game. Who'd have thought a game with pixel graphics where the entire premise consists of nothing but clearing out rooms of bad guys could be so satisfying?! What makes Hotline Miami awesome is not only the great soundtrack, but also that it rewards both good tactics and good reactions. You have to be very fast and deliberate about every movement, every kill, every shot, every throw and punch. An insta-death game which means you have to restart the level initially sounds frustrating, but the fact that there are no load times and the weapons available and enemy patterns are slightly different on each restart, as well as the amazing soundtrack, make this a joy to play and extremely rewarding when you can combo waves of enemies.
There are plenty of satisfying skill-based games out there, but I've yet to come across one which makes me feel like a total badass every time in the same way that Hotline Miami does.

I seriously can not understand where the hate this game is getting comes from. It does exactly what it says on the "box", and does it very well. While not a perfect game by any means, this is a great effort from a smaller company, that fills a niche I've personally desired for over 10 years.
When I was a young lass, back in my high school days, I used to take the public bus to commute to school and back, and also to travel from place to place on my weekends. I spent hundreds of IRL hours on various models of IRL busses, and I always wanted to try driving one. This game finally allowed me to live my fantasy. I honestly never thought a company would ever bother to make a bus driving game, but Bus Simulator 16 actually goes above and beyond that, and includes management and a bit of strategy as well.
In Bus Simulator 16, you'll assume the role of a man who has just started a bus company, and won a minor contract with the local city of Sunny Springs, and a few cheap models of busses to chose from. You'll start alone, with a limited amount of startup cash, with a small area available to you. Over time you'll prove to the city you can handle bigger contracts, which will give you access to more districts of the city, and more modern/expensive models of busses.
Gameplay consists of 2 parts: driving your routes, and managing your company. Your company can be single player (offline) or co-op multiplayer (online), but if you choose to bring your company online it can not be undone.
Managing your company consists of buying/maintaining busses, hiring/firing NPC (or other online players if you go multiplayer) drivers, and planning routes. You can paint your fleet various colors, and add advertisements to generate extra income.
Driving is the heart of the game and you will need to drive each new route yourself first before you can assign that route to an NPC driver. You will be able to choose various models of busses to drive, including bendy (two car) busses. The in game tutorial is quick, easy to understand, and teaches you everything you need to know about driving. You will need to make all the stops on the route, while obaying traffic laws, keeping your schedule on time, charging passengers the correct fare, and making change, and accomidating any unexpected situation that may pop up.
Driving the bus feels natural, and the controls are easy to pick up. The AI is dumb, and pedestrians will occasionaly step out in front of your rig, or change lanes into your path, but for the most part you can predict their behavior.  Weather, traffic jams, and various events (bouncing drunk passengers, unjamming stuck doors, extending the ramp for wheelchair bound passengers, etc.) will add variety to your routes.
The dev is German, so the city/roads/laws are very european; As an American, this took some getting used to. In America, bus drivers expect you to have exact change for your fare, and carry no change. I don't know how they do things in Germany, but in this game you are expected to do math and count out correct change for everyone. This is the one part of the game that really sucks, but you'll soon memorize the appropriate amounts for each bill/fare and life will go on.
The graphics are pretty bare bones, and honestly, what can you expect from a small dev making a game that will appeal to a niche group of players? I'm just happy this game got made at all. You will encounter some bugs here and there, but nothing that breaks the game or prevents you from running it smoothly (at least in my experience).
Overall I would say if you're one of the people who is intrigued by the prospect of managing/driving for your own bus company, you should buy this game. It does what it sets out to do, and it works without crashing. What more can you ask for?

Just so you know. I've played all of the previous Galactic Civ series and all of the Master Orions before that. This is the succcessor to those and it shows.  While the game is still in beta, it certainly playable and new things are being finished/adjusted and added regularly. Going to 64 bit only has really allowed them to make immense glaxay settings available, so much so that you can't get all of the possible galaxy on a 1920x1080 monitor at once. :)
Many things are similar or familar but with tweaks. Most obvious first change is that the game map is now hexagon based. The tech trees are per race, and there are big differences per race. As another reviewer noted, it's easier to build your colonies with automated updates, but as they now give bonuses for similar neighbooring improvements so careful  planning can be game changing.
You have significant off planets things to mine or harvest- asension crystals, artifacts, resources and asteriods (although asteroid mining isn't implemented as of Beta 4). Grabbing these can also make a large difference in the game, depending on your play style.
6 or 7 different ways to triumph, including a turn limit/overall score mode, make this version potentially superior to the previous ones replayibility and variety.
The beta isn't polished or complete, but is worth having. Oh, did I mention multiplayer? Haven't tried it yet, but should be interesting to see how they keep it moving.
Buy this. The nice thing is that Stardock has a great history of continuing development (not just bug fixes) way past the point more rational developers would start making the next version. You can tell that this a labor of love.

I honestly don’t know should I recommend this game or not.
First of all, it’s buggy to the core. I had no stability issues, yet freezes haunt the game (for me decreasing he drawing distance from 300 to 250 meters helped, but c’mon). The routing is glitchy, the game tends to suddenly and unlogically change your route, and I was already being fined for unscheduled stopping and skipping the same stop at the same time.
Then, the visuals — they’ll remind you of 2005, and not of the best of the time. Basically, it looks and feels almost like SCS's early Bus Driver.
On the other hand, somehow it works. Random event are here, you have to fix things on the go and deal with a troublemaker from time to time, traffic isn’t rediculous like in OMSI 2, and the buses have at least all the everyday life related controls, and you should actually use them. That makes the game much more interesting and challenging then you can expect.
The version of the game is 0.0.8~ at the moment of wrinting this review (12/26 2016), so I guess the game can be considered the early access. The developers seem to listen to the community and at least try to make it better.
The only worthy competitor at the time is the already mentioned OMSI 2, and BS16 is much more accessible, visually appealing, and with much more sensible price tag. On the other hand, OMSI is the much deeper simulation experience. So if you always wanted to get in the bus driver’s seat, get the BS16 on sale — it’s a good starting poing.

Hotline Miami is a top-down shooter by Dennaton Games, where the player controls a mystery man of few words known only as Jacket as anonymous phone calls send him to perform hits on different places belonging to some sort of mafia.
Graphically the game is... Well it's primarily gorey pixel art from a top-down perspective with the added layer of trippy flashing colors, blinking lights, shakey camera, moving text... yeah, in general, the game gives a rather strong impression in that regard, and definitely isn't intended for those with epilepsy.
Sound design, you mostly get basic sound effects like gunshots, melee hits etc. The interesting part is the music, which is a hit-or-miss for me. Some of the electronic renditions are headbang-worthy (my favorites are Perturbator, Inner Animal, Knock and Turf Main), but some others just make me wish it would stop. Generally the more, well, trippy scenes have the less bearable music, which kinda fits I guess.
The gameplay is pretty much what you'd expect: get in and make sure everything dies. Every kill is bloody and, well, satisfying, if you have a tendency for being a psychopath. The game in general is a lot more technical than you'd think - while your enemies aren't very bright and will charge or shoot you the moment they see you and generally die to a single weapon hit or shot, the same applies to you, meaning cover and careful movement are your friends. There is a pretty large selection of weapons, melee and ranged alike, with each one behaving a little differently. You can charge in guns blazing and survive, but only if you're good enough to do it. The game also heavily encourages it with its combo system for kills, but that's only if you care about getting high scores (and unlocking some extra stuff). If you die, you can restart the entire floor instantly by pressing a single button, and you also get infinite lives, so it's fair in that regard. The game itself tends to be rather well balanced and not amazingly difficult, but fairly challenging at times, except for a few specific floors that can be a bit of a difficulty spike.
The story does not appear to be very clear at the start, with maybe some extra newspaper scraps you can find around the main character's house each day giving some background as to what the hit was about clearly. The normal ending also does not explain much either.
Overall, this is a pretty good, if a little bit... sensory-overloading experience. The gameplay is fun but gets a little bit repetitive if you play for longer than an hour at a time, and the conclusion is actually a little deeper than you'd think. This definitely isn't a game for those who are sensitive to flashing lights or pixelated gore, but otherwise it's worth giving a try.

One of the greatest classics from Squaresoft, before they became lousy Square-Enix that release half baked games that make little sense in why they were made.
FF7 is the first FF in full 3D, it's release marked an expansion towards asian jRPG type games, which made tremondous impact on games later released. The rest of the world had to admit defeat and adjust to the new demand type, a 3D accelerated video games market started from this game, which in my personal opinion is the best RPG of 1997, hell I'd go even further. To me it's the best RPG PC game of teh decade.
The pro's:
- The PC version of the game was slightly altered from it's PlayStation version. The greatest change was made towards the fast and furious PC players taste, the difficulty of the battles was greately increased.
-This game, although having a nearly fully linear story telling, also has some really well designed side stories (not side quests) which also blend into the mainstream of the story quite well. The additional characters (Yuffie and Vincent) are not essential to complete the game, however getting tem gives us new encounters, a set of additional bosses to fight with and an array of conversations that ARE influenced by their being in the party. Some characters trigger different responses during a conversation with one of the main stream story NPC. This makes a huge change in understanding some bits of the story of the game. Additionally not having Yuffie or Vincent automatically blocks our access to some equipment and Materia, and teh story is in some places a bit awkward.
-Flexible battle difficulty. The game, like most Final Fantasy games, has a very interesting battle setting system. if you keep it on WAIT or Recommended, you will likely not have any problems. WAIT is a setting when on every character turn or enemy turn, battle time stops. If you are a careful type of player and want to slowly enjoy the game, this setting is for you, slow and steady. However your game time will not stop and your hours playing will just grow like mushrooms :)
the Recommended setting is less forgiving, because as the game progresses the battle time changes, if you encounter a whole new enemy it usually lets you wait to make a decision, but on the next turn, battle time will likely not stop, depending on how you defeated the previous enemy. Recommended does stop for a while on boss fights.
-the last setting is for players that know what they want to do, and combined with fast battle pace time makes up for a very difficult game time, which is highly enjoyable.
-3D Battles Area. Everything in the battle area is rendered in 3D and is fully animated, the re-mastered version (here on steam) has a fairly re-hashed and refreshed 3D rendering graphics set to use the full capacity of our new kind of hardware (in 1997 it was not so much powerful as today, so it's a big help, if you have the original try playing one of the minigames on a new todays rig and count how long it took to clear teh highway without losing :D )
-Minigames: The game offers several minigames that the player HAS to do in order to get through the story, there are actually 3 minigames that the player HAVE to clear. The Highway, The Snowboard and teh Submarine. these minigames are actually really fun, but there are several other minigames available in the Gold Saucer. the Gold Saucer is actually a very good place to get some rare items as well as main characters final Limit Break, and some decent Support Materia.
It's also the only place where you can battle one of the Bosses again.
-So Much to do! literally a lot of stuff to do and not enough time to make it happen, we gotta save the world, for the Xth time :)
-Actual romance! Yes my friends, this game has an actual romance plot, and it's not funny, it's actually very interesting how things develop. And if you get things do some weird stuff, you might even end up on a rare date with ... a beardy marshmellow black bear with a gun as it's hand :D
-Music: Nobuo Uematsu. If you guys ever get your hands on the Original Sound Tracks for Final Fantasy VII you will FEEL the music from teh real genius at work. That man made music for all FF games and majority of Squaresoft's games back in the day until 2004. Now he makes wonderful music for (occasionally) Square-Enix and for Sakaguchi's Mistwalker studios.
(Hironobu Sakaguchi is the original creator of the Final Fantasy series who also left Square-Enix in 2004)
Final Fantasy VII is a game that a fan of jRPGs should play as a must. In my top 3 Final Fantasy Games, it is second best from all the FF games out there. And all because of the teamthat was still making great games for gamers, and not so much for the money.

Okay first off this game is beautiful.  I'm running a laptop with a GTX970m and didn't see any framerate drops or problems with everything set on ultra.  The sound on this game is wonderful.  The movement and controls are perfect (even though it says a controller is recommended I used mouse and keyboard and didn't have any problems.)
Now, some negatives.  This game is short, and I mean really really short.  I logged 3.4 hours and that was with the game paused to make supper, eat supper, and troubleshoot a windows install issue on another computer.  I still finished the game within this time, so that would make the entire running time about 2 hours.  To be fair I didn't find all the collectibles.  I still have a couple of spawn pools I didn't find, 8 meditation points, and who knows how many secret shells (since I didn't even know they existed until after the game).
The plot in this game is vague to say the least.  I think I have some idea of what is happening but I'm not entirely sure.  This is both good and bad.  Don't expect everything to be laid out for you in any form.  No voiceover, no flashbacks, no notes to read.  You will find some scattered hieroglyphics and the rest is just based on what you observe.
I have never played Journey so I don't know how similar this is, but I'm glad to have paid my 15 toward this game, especially if it might help get Journey on PC so I can try it.  This and Firewatch, while being two totally different experiences tonally, are very similar in some ways and if you like one, you may like the other.  I know it seems strange comparing a voiceless game to one that is all about conversation, but the sense of awe and the stunning vistas you see give me reason to compare the two.
If you don't feel it's worth it to spend 15 on two hours of gameplay then don't.  But, if you want something beautiful and relaxing, if you like exploring and seeing an entirely new world, then this game is for you.

One of the best top-down shooters I've ever played and an amazing timewaster. If you love roguelikes or dungeon crawlers and are a fan of randomization then get this game.
Pros
-Randomization: Every run is different as the items you find will be different, leading to many unique runs
-Extreme amounts of content: With unlockable items and extra levels there's enough content to last you 100+ hours easily
-Skill-based gameplay: While the items and room layouts add a degree of randomization, the game is still heavily skill-based and you'll have to master it in terms of knowledge and technique to get to the true ending
Cons
-No saving of active runs: Some longer runs can take up to an hour and if you have to turn the game of for some reason, you'll have to start a new run
All in all, it's a great experience and well worth the price.

I have had my eye on this game for some time, and was unable to resist the 50% discount available over the weekend. After about 15 hours of gameplay I now cannot shake the feeling that I was totally sucked in. Galactic Civilization 3 is little more then a graphically upgrade to its predecessor, the only *revolutionary* new features, the Idealogical Traits and the Era-based restrictions on technology are currently so woefully imbalanced as to be game breaking. If these are fixed, and all the old, disabled features are added in, GalCiv3 might be worth a 10% premium over GC2. (You might value gameplay over graphics more than me,and I can assure you, I’m getting mightily cheesed off at Steam for throwing a dozen Indy games and their 8-bit graphics at me everyday, in which case it might be worth an extra 20-30%). Currently, with GC3, GC2 is the by far the more complete and satisfying game, and its cheaper to boot.
Some notable flaws:
-Entering the AGE OF WARFARE (one would assume the mid-game) despite not having encountered another race or researching a single military tech.
-Not being able to colonize some planets because the technology required cannot be researched until the AGE OF ASCENCION (the Endgame?)
-Every colony comes with an ethical dilemna. Establish half a dozen colonies and pick the Malevolent choice and you’ll be able to unlock a third tier Malevolent trait which makes your entire empire immune to to cultural warfare. Cultural warfare has traditionally been overpowered but this is a no solution. A planetary upgrade that grants immunity, unlocked at the fifth tier, with idealolical points generally being harder to aqcuire would be workable, making the effort better balance cultural warfare and resistance would be prefered. Blanket immunity, so easily accessed is ultimately the reason I have decided to stop playing this game, the reason to post my first game review, and the reason I will not be recommending this game

LiEat is a relatively short JRPG which includes three different chapters, both approximately around 1 hour long (if you're not speeding through the text and really tryin to look into every nook or cranny). If you're a fan of such games as Ib, The Witch's House, Alice Mare then LiEat is probably a game meant for you. Although it isn't quite horror oriented other than for mild body horror, it is a very story-driven game, which focuses on two main characters, a con artist named who goes by many names and a dragon girl named Efina.
There are 30 Steam achievements for this game, most of which can be found on your first playthrough if you're looking everywhere and talking to each character. Such dedication is rewarded with not only more information about our main characters and their history, but also different items, some of which make our heroes nigh impossible to defeat. As it might be evident of my high play time I sought out all achievements and replayed each chapter at least 30 times due to just wanting to explore on my own and uncover secrets without helpful guidances. However, getting the last few achievements proved to be quite difficult, so if you get stuck, be sure to look up vgperson's site, who translated this game, along with many other.
The graphics are adorable and the pixel portraits are very nicely done, so those who enjoy 2D pixelated graphics will definitely enjoy the game. The soundtrack is nice as well, it never seemed to get on my nerves or annoy me after listening to the music for hours upon hours. LiEat knows how to create atmosphere, whether it is to make things silly or horrifyingly dreadful, something which can definitely be experienced throughout the chapters, especially in the last one.
If we want to go by Funhaus Spoole's view on the worth of games, which is 1 Dollar 1 Hour, aka if you pay one dollar that equals one hour of gameplay, then buying LiEat gives you more than enough content over 3 hours. As you can see I've gotten good 7 hours from this game just trying to complete it and get all of the achievements.
Honestly, the game is just three dollars and if you really enjoy story-driven 2D games, LiEat is definitely for you.

Don't let the "Loli" Steam banner fool you.
This isn't a JRPG that panders to the Loli-crowd. Instead, I'll hazard to say that LiEat (I, II, and III) doesn't pander at all. Instead, the developer focused on bringing us a solid and well written story. The story itself isn't anything amazing, and often, the mysteries solve themselves in the first act. However, what really kept it interesting were the characters. The characters are endearing, mysterious, and funny.
The game includes 3 Chapters. Each has multiple endings. The first two chapters each took me about 1.5 hours, and the last one stumped me for a bit when I couldn't get the Good Ending.
The BGM are great and sets the mood as well.
I highly recommend this to anyone looking to play a short game with memorable characters. Just don't expect this game to last you any more than 5 hours tops.
EDIT: Also, any achievement that includes Ranma 1/2 is gold in my book: Happosai~!
