I always look forward to trying out a new Flump Studios shooter -- look forward to, and dead. I dread having my fragile mind blasted into tiny mewling fragments while trying to come to grips with the batshit crazy mechanics I come to expect from these games.
Flump Studios' games always demand your brain be running on more than one core. You're gonna need those extra threads to handle all the bizarre, out of context, new and fresh tasks they relentlessly pummel you with.
Hyper Bounce Blast is guilty of all of the above -- and it's freakin RAD. My favorite thing about this developer is his ability to subvert the shooter genre. Sure, this is kind of a 'vertical shooter'... but it's also a twin stick shooter, a platformer (with walljumping... WALLJUMPING) and a puzzler.
Throw all of that in a blender with a super slick presentation and an awesome soundtrack, and you wind up with this... infuriatingly gorgeous video game that has (probably) "for adrenaline junkies only" plastered all over it.
I salute Flump Studios for bringing me one step closer to a straight jacket being mandatory and therefore eliminating wardrobe decisions... AND giving me an alternative to caffeine.  <3 <3

Foremost, it's a game about an assassin -- literally a shadow -- but you only get high marks if you ... don't kill anyone. Then, you spend
80% of your time guessing which parts of the screen you can teleport onto, but don't be one pixel wrong, or you'll teleport onto the side of a wall and slide down into the guard's lap or something. Seriously, you're not hearing me about the rage-inducing cursor mangement this game requires. Finally, and this was the final straw that noped me out: the camera is over your shoulder, except when it's not - if you find yourself in a bush, well, you
the camera are in the bush, so congratulations, just
when it's safe to walk out of the bush. Both of my woes collide in that you have to coordinate the triangle of you, your camera, and the spot pointed to by your cursor in order to see enemies, mark them, be able to set up a teleportation target, everything.
Pros
- Interesting mechanic
- Relatively nice graphics
- Pseudo Japanese lesson
Cons
- Gives you a sword, punishes you for using it
- Camera is a disaster
- Cursor requires pixel perfection or too bad for you
- All landscape is basically the same, so good luck finding any hidden things

- The whole game is one big judgmental anxiety trip

I really enjoyed this game as a youth, and then as I got older I grew apart from turn based RPGs. I was really suprised to find that I not only still enjoyed this game, but absolutely loved it years later. What stands the test of time is the characters and world that the game so carefully builds as you play. You want the good guys to win and you want the bad guys to lose. Every character you gain feels like they have a good reason to be there. I often found I wanted to bring more characters along than my party would allow.
That materia system is great and ties into the world's background really well. Its very simple and versatile, and leaves you carefully considering what kind of equipment you would like to equip to plan for the proper amount of slots.
While I say that I enjoy the translation this game, it is not without its issues. There are a few times where plot points are not explained entirely well, and it can be hard to keep track of exactly "who" is talking. This is perhaps why the game has a reputation for being "deep" or "artistic" in its writing, because it leaves much to the players interpretation.
In the end, I would reccomend this game to anyone who likes turn based RPGs or JRPGS. To anyone who once enjoyed this and thought it would not hold up, I would reccomend you give it another go, because I ended falling in love with it all over again.

The developers even said that they tried giving the player more freedom of control, but it made the game too easy. You *need* this game. Seriously.
EDIT
Now that the final release is out I'm updating my review. Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of those games you really just have to play to understand the hype, and yes this is one of those rare cases where the hype is 100% justified. The game just hits every note perfectly (haha). The gameplay is increadible. Even though the look is familiar, the mechanics are like nothing else out there (which is quite a feat in todays gaming age) but still seems to satisfy on some primal level. It's kind of like speed chess if it were fun. Each enemy moves in a unique pattern and each item effects the behavor of your character. Every move could either result in success or death, but you only have a split second to decide what to do. It really puts you on the edge of your seat especially when playing "all zones" mode. Then there's the music. It's amazing. In fact it's so amazing I bought the soundtrack version and uploaded the songs to listen to on my iPod. Of course thats the kind of music we've all come to expect from Danny Baranowsky of Binding of Isaac fame. The great thing about the music is that it makes you dance. Not in the game, but in real life. I can't play this game without dancing around with a big grin on my face like a complete idiot. My fiance thinks its hilarious, whom by the way, can't stand video games yet still found this game to be entertaining. On top of all that the execution is really what brings it all together. The way the shopkeeper sings to the music, how the music in the fire/ice stage transitions from metal to classical music seamlessly, the quirky sprite animations, and the light up disco tiles, it really brings a smile to your face. Its games like these that remind me why I game in the first place. I'm really quite pleased that amidst all the Call of Duty garbage you can still find little gems like this one.

Hyper Bounce Blast was developed by Flump Studios and published by KISS ltd. It is described as a Shoot Em' Up combined with the classic platformer style which is kind of unique for this style of gameplay. It also seems to be a sort of bullet hell game but without the free flying and sort of wall jumping along.
This game seems to be a rather different kind of Shoot Em' Up/Bullet hell game with some platforming elements combined into the game, which make it much harder than your average Bullet Hell / Shoot Em' Up. The main mechanic is being able to wall jump from the left and right wall, which means there is also gravity involved in the game. This really separates it from other similar games of this genre, and makes a different sort of gameplay style from other games like this. I rather liked the platforming elements that are implemented into the game, it gives it that more difficult sort of feel when you are trying to avoid the bullets but are trapped in the corner.
Although it seems to be that bit more different from the other sort of games of this genre, it does have a big flaw that I personally don't like. Some of the bosses in the game have a rapid amount of bullets that are being shot at you, and compared to the size of your character makes it so difficult to avoid the bullets. Especially if you wall jump and try to swerve your way through the bullets you are almost certain to get hit. I really don't like this, even though this game is really fun, but just a bit too difficult that takes some of that fun out of the game.
With the game being practically the same over and over again, you would expect there to be several different types of game modes. Some of which are locked and can be unlocked by progressing far enough into other game modes. You have the Arcade Classic, start with 2 lives and try to fight through all the waves, you get a checkpoint before and after each boss battle. Arcade Arrange is the same as Arcade Classic except you have no extra lives but you get a checkpoint after each level. Time rush, see how far you can get with in a fully powered up ship when the game speeds up each wave. Lastly there is Tournament Mode, see how far you can get in a fully powered up ship with each wave increased speed.
There is a nice range of different game modes to keep you entertained for longer than you normally would. There are also 2 locked gamemodes which I don't know what they are as I haven't progressed enough to unlock them. I for one don't personally like the locked gamemodes for the game, forces you to get far into the game to unlock other modes which you may or may not like. There is online leaderboards, if you are the more competitive sort of players and want to try to beat other people at their score, I for one am not very competitive so it doesn't compel me to play more and try to beat other peoples score.
+ Has some platforming elements, makes it unique from other games of the similar genre
+ Lots of Game Modes
+ Online Leaderboards
+ Full Controller Support
+ Steam Trading Cards & Achievements
- Lots of bullet, makes the game too hard and takes some fun from the game
- 2 Locked gamemodes, unsure why they are locked
Hyper Bounce Blast is a unique Shoot Em' Up / Bullet Hell game that has some platforming elements to it, the game itself is fairly difficult a bit too difficult that it takes the fun out of it at times. There is plenty of game modes to play through, although two of them are locked. There is a competitive leaderboard, full controller support, steam trading cards and Achievements. Would recommend to those of you who love Bullet Hell games.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is easily one of the best games I've ever played. In terms of the actual game design, it's easily earned a place among indie legends like Cave Story, Iji, and Super Meat Boy, but with art direction, fun factor, and sheer consistent quality that stand out among
games. The voice acting is
believable, with the exception of the titular hero at rare times, the gameplay is exciting and well-balanced, the controls are tight and make Dust enjoyable to play as, and the artistic vision is both fresh and amazingly nice to look at. The only real downside to this wonderful experience is the main character's storyline, which appears to follow in the age-old tradition of making one's OC as angsty and super-special as possible. However, despite that fact the game takes that story and makes it both well-executed and emotional, so it's not that much of a problem unless you're a serious literary critic. And even if you are? I still think this gem is worth it for the gameplay alone.
Quick Pro: Some of the best Metroidvania gameplay in existence.
Quick Con: Dust (character)'s story ends up reading very similar to a typical OC's.

While I enjoy rhythm games, dungeon crawlers, and rogue-likes, combining those didn't seem like something that would translate well to fun.  Surprisingly though, I might have put as much time into this unfinished game as I probably have any other in the past 12 months.  While it's missing a few things, all the content that is present is very polished and works extremely well.  The Danny B soundtrack is unsurprisingly fantastic and worth paying extra to add to your music player.  Like Spelunky or Binding of Isaac, you can be dealt a rough hand or have a run-through go sour very early on.  What's somewhat unique to Necrodancer is that it's almost never felt unfair as success relies more on taking deliberate, thought out actions with the execution itself being very straightforward.  I've never felt quite as underpowered as I have in those games, and I've rarely felt ridiculously overpowered.  There are already a lot of great different ways to play and it's a very easy one to keep coming back to.  Well worth the money.

Note: The Tomorrow War ended up being a 'middle of the road' game for me. It had a lot of potential, but one has to review based on what was, rather than what could have been. I was tossing up if I'd call it a very low positive review or a very high negative review. Given I think the 'average' gamer would struggle with it, I had to go the latter option.
---
The internal visuals of people interacting look on par with Half Life 1, so late 90's, despite the game being released in 2009. External visuals I didn't mind though. There's something nice about watching the fighters flying in formation. An advantage of lower level graphics, however, was that it allowed for a large number of objects to be on screen at a time. This is especially obvious when flying in asteroid fields.
The missions you perform in the game are short, often with long auto-pilot sequences with nothing going on. These long flight sequences might be 'realistic', but come across as boring filler to bulk out the game. At times it wasn't clear what you were required to do either, leading to periods of guesswork/trial and error.
While the missions were often short and dull, the dogfights were fun. Long range missiles (requiring lock-on) and short ranged machine guns/lasers. Once your missiles are depleted, you'd often spend most of your time flying in tight circles, trying to get your target back in your sights. The AI could have been better during these fights. Additionally, some variety to the way the AI would fight, especially between different races, would have added to the enjoyment.
The game is based on a Russian book series and has assumingly been translated after game release. The dialogue comes off very dry and flat and shows an obvious sign of being directly translated. This means at times, the dialogue isn't making much sense. Voice acting is terrible and at times sounds like computer generated voices. Additionally, while the game has subtitles, they aren't strict to the dialogue and are often played well ahead of the audio.
This is in part due to translation issues. The story would often jump all over the place and often quite quickly. For the first half of the game, you'll do a mission or two with one faction, and then you'll be swept off to another, not allowing for any development to occur. The second half of the game was where the 'primary' story takes place, but it too suffered from the story jumping and came across as poorly written (though possibly a translation issue too). I think there was a good story in there somewhere, but I think the developers needed to focus more time on developing and delivering upon it.
While a lot of the piloting mechanics are pretty common for this kind of game, a number of them are hidden away. A good read over the key configurations prior to getting started is certainly recommended (Especially engaging/disengaging planetary engines!). A brief tutorial at the start of the game and/or tooltips could certainly have helped.
The game had a number of bugs and was very rough around the edges. One repeatedly annoying bug was the game's difficulty with collision detection. A number of times you would be required to land on a surface, only to fall through that surface and ultimately die. Another issue (poor design rather than a bug) is that the mission screen would pop up when your mission changed/updated. The problem with this is that you're unable to control your ship until you close it, but the game doesn't pause, resulting in my ship crashing a number of times. A lesser issues were dialogue being played twice, skipped or played in the wrong order.
A few little lack of polish items that I'd lastly like to raise: There seems to be a personal inventory system in place that doesn't seem to serve any purpose. It seems like a feature that was discontinued but never removed; At one point you're offered the option to buy information for some side missions that you never really get the opportunity to do anything with; There's a currency system in the game, where for maybe 1/4 of the game, you're required to purchase your own weaponry / ammo with money you're earning on the missions (never enough, mind you). Now this might simply be because during that period, you're a mercenary whereas the rest of the game you're a military pilot, but the concept of the currency persist through the rest of the game.
The Tomorrow War certain had potential, but I feel it was never probably finished. If you're patient and like space shooters, you might enjoy this game, otherwise it might be best to look for another title.

This game is a very creative take on a shmup with platforming elements. Shoot the reds, bounce on the blues. Kill all of the few green enemies in each wave to reach a very fun bonus round. Gameplay is simple and easy to start, but difficult to master with so much going on! I was immediately reminded of Geometry Wars not only by the visual style but also by the mess of things happening all at once. Fortunately, in this game you are completely invulnerable to enemy attacks as long as you stay airborne by bouncing off the blue enemies. As an added bonus, when bouncing, you actually absorb enemy fire to power up your screen-obliterating special attack! Despite the invulnerability, it can still be quite challenging as blue enemies aren't always spaced out evenly. If you aren't keeping the reds and their projectiles thinned out, hitting the ground can spell the instant loss of a life. Boss battles limit your bouncing and provide a bit more of a bullet hell experience, but are not too challenging and very fair once you learn their patterns.
All in all, Hyper Bounce Blast is a lot of fun and can be very addicting. I definitely recommend it!

Hyper Bounce Blast is a sort of follow up to Horizon Shift, as in it's an another game that puts an another new twist on the classic arcade shooter genre. Now Horizon Shift was a cool game however I felt confused by it's mechanics at times (probably my own fault because i'm not that used to crazy mechanics) however this game is a completely different story.
HBB's main mechanic is as expected, bouncing! You bounce off blue platforms and enemies and while you are in the air bouncing, you cannot be killed and the higher you bounce, the more points you will get when shooting enemies.
So it becomes an interesting game of multitasking because you have to maintain your bouncing while also dealing with enemies and obstacles that appear in later waves and frankly? It never gets TOO HARD, it's always fair, so when I mess up it is my fault because I wasn't paying attention because everything in this game is telegraphed very well in advance.
Also the bosses definitely not dissapoint and make full use of the mechanics, so expect hectic platforming shooting action on those!
Overall, I highly recommend this game for everyone, even those who do not play these games. PS. Try to get 5 stars so you can witness the amazing tribute to a classic ;)

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a RPG-Metroidvania where you take control of "Dust", a misterious creature who seems to have lost his memories. Without an aparent reason he will be followed by a flying "batcat" and a talkative mystic sword, who will help Dust and guide him in order to know his purpose in this world, as also as to get his memories back. The game also provides a background of war and its consequences.
Graphics: 8.5/10 - This game is absolutely gorgeus. Every visual thing is extremely polished and colourful, as well as an awesome handprint. This game proves that sometimes you just don't need a 3D graphics, triple A game to say "wow, nice graphics".
Soundtrack: 8/10 - The soundtrack is also amazing, yet it comes to be quite secundary because of the pace of action the game is exposed to. All tracks goes into an epic/orchestra path and they're all as beautiful as the game looks like. Nevertheless, and as I said, this game is so fluid and fast that the own game's FX sounds overrides the soundtrack, making it hard to appreciate how good it is.
Controls: 8.5/10 - As a non-casual player of Metroidvania games, I was pretty satisfied with Dust controls. Movement is fluid and once you learn its mechanics you won't have a problem here. Every mistake I experienced in this game was my own fault and not the game's one. Combos are really cool and they are set to let the players make their own strategies with all different movements.
Duration: 7.5/10 - Dust: An Elysian Tail will provide you more than 5-7h of storyline (unless you rush it), and about another 5-7h if you go for the extras, such as new skills, completing sidequests. finding treasure chests, etc. As many Metroidvania games, this game has some RPG features, like character level progression, which can lengthen your experience and gameplay even more (it is always nice to farm your level!). Moreover, the storyline is surprisingly interesting, and might keep you playing without pause until the end. And yes, the whole story is pretty good. Definately not a disappoint.
Difficulty: 6.5/10 - This game, compared to my idea of the average difficulty of its similars, is basically "not too hard, but not too easy either". Four difficulties can be chosen from the start and can be changed during your gameplay, and that means that on higher difficulties less HP recovery items will be spread, stronger (yet not faster) enemies, tougher bosses and HP damage, etc. Overall Dust: An Elysian Tail can be played by everyone and shouldn't disappoint either new players or the veteran ones.
OVERALL: 8.5/10 - I was kinda hyped when I finally purchased this game and my expectations were dangerously high. However, Dust: An Elysian Tail answered to them VERY well. This game is another demonstration that a small company can make huge things into the gaming industry. I'm really happy I decided to try out this game, it was worthy and I feel this can like you all too because I found it really hard not to enjoy it.

To save your time I am going to start with a TL;DR in a form of a pros/cons list:
Pros:
+ Endless replayablity
+ Easy to master controls
+ Unique design
+ Huge item pool
+ Nice soundtrack
+ There is a DLC available which makes the game even more awesome, adding more items, enemies, game mods etc.
Cons:
- Quite sluggish sometimes due to the Flash limitations
- Might be insanely hard if you get unlucky with the items drop
- Could use a built-in manual for the items (I am using
Wikia page as a reference)
- VERY addictive.
- Sometimes achievements doesn't work out of the box (I am using
)
You navigate your character through a series of randomly generated dungeons, each divided into "floors". Each "floor" is essencialy a number of "rooms", most of which contain various monsters. In order to progress to the next "floor", you need to defeat a boss.
The character can carry a set of items, some of which are passive, some are activated and some are single-use power-ups.
There are also unlockable characters each with unique gameplay style.
The story develops as you complete the game numerous times and is pretty much wowen of the Bible references and allusions
This game is great in terms of value-for-money ratio. Almost endless replayability turns achievements like "Complete the whole game 9 times" from a nightmarish grind into a funfest. Well maybe not a funfest, cosidering the fact that sometimes the almighty random makes it really hard to finish your run - you progression is highly item-dependent and all item drops are entirely random.
The game features a good soundtrack (which may get a bit old after a few dozens of playthroughs), outstanding and recognizable character design and over a hundred collectible items - some of which interact with each other creating either a deadly combo that will annihilate your enemies or a rather wonky skillset that will hinder your further progression in the current run.
Controls and battle system are intuitive - you will get the ropes few moments into the game. The only thing you might find yourself lost at is the huge pool of items - especially considering the fact that not all of them are provided with a full description.
So to sum up - this game is a great bang for a buck. I was not sure if I should buy it at first, but I have no regrets now that I bought it. Recommended!

You *need* this game. Seriously.
EDIT
Now that the final release is out I'm updating my review. Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of those games you really just have to play to understand the hype, and yes this is one of those rare cases where the hype is 100% justified. The game just hits every note perfectly (haha). The gameplay is increadible. Even though the look is familiar, the mechanics are like nothing else out there (which is quite a feat in todays gaming age) but still seems to satisfy on some primal level. It's kind of like speed chess if it were fun. Each enemy moves in a unique pattern and each item effects the behavor of your character. Every move could either result in success or death, but you only have a split second to decide what to do. It really puts you on the edge of your seat especially when playing "all zones" mode. Then there's the music. It's amazing. In fact it's so amazing I bought the soundtrack version and uploaded the songs to listen to on my iPod. Of course thats the kind of music we've all come to expect from Danny Baranowsky of Binding of Isaac fame. The great thing about the music is that it makes you dance. Not in the game, but in real life. I can't play this game without dancing around with a big grin on my face like a complete idiot. My fiance thinks its hilarious, whom by the way, can't stand video games yet still found this game to be entertaining. On top of all that the execution is really what brings it all together. The way the shopkeeper sings to the music, how the music in the fire/ice stage transitions from metal to classical music seamlessly, the quirky sprite animations, and the light up disco tiles, it really brings a smile to your face. Its games like these that remind me why I game in the first place. I'm really quite pleased that amidst all the Call of Duty garbage you can still find little gems like this one.
I really can't recomend this game enough! :D

For starters, It is NOT Overwatch. Period.
Anyway, I started quite skeptical when begining to play the game due to everyone saying it's just a clone. Then, I got past training, which, was fairly descriptive, and the best part: FAST. Everyone hates a 20 minutes tutorial on how to play a first person shooter. They really did great at addressing that problem. Secondly, you dont have to pay for a single thing in game with real money. Of course, you CAN buy things with real money, but only after you have unlocked them by actually playing the game. They also have implemented a VERY balanced play-style. If you choose a damage class, yes, you have a much lower amount of health. BUT, you deal much more damage and move much more quickly. If you pick a front line, yes you are slow and they can hit you much faster, but you have LARGE amounts of health from the start that they do not have, making it quite fair. Furthermore, there is so much more content than many of the other free to play games.
All in all, its just a great game overall, small download size, plenty on content, different game modes, customized game modes, and much much more. Before you go out and pay fourty dollars for Overwatch, give this a go. I bet you forget why you borrowed money from your dying grandmother in the first place.

While The Binding of Issac is not an easy game, it is a very fun one. With randomly generated levels, multiple characters and secrets to unlock, and many enemy and boss types it won't get boring immediately. But the real kicker is that after you beat a playthrough you will unlock extra floors to traverse and more randomly generated items to collect on your next playthrough, and the trend will continue on through your next playthrough, and the one after that, and the one after that one, and the one after the other one. And so on and so on. Couple that with a great soundtrack, a fantastic art style, and a cheap price and you have a winner of a game. It's a wonderful game to add to any Steam collection of any stripe... so yeah... go get it.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a RPG-Metroidvania where you take control of "Dust", a misterious creature who seems to have lost his memories. Without an aparent reason he will be followed by a flying "batcat" and a talkative mystic sword, who will help Dust and guide him in order to know his purpose in this world, as also as to get his memories back. The game also provides a background of war and its consequences.
Graphics: 8.5/10 - This game is absolutely gorgeus. Every visual thing is extremely polished and colourful, as well as an awesome handprint. This game proves that sometimes you just don't need a 3D graphics, triple A game to say "wow, nice graphics".
Soundtrack: 8/10 - The soundtrack is also amazing, yet it comes to be quite secundary because of the pace of action the game is exposed to. All tracks goes into an epic/orchestra path and they're all as beautiful as the game looks like. Nevertheless, and as I said, this game is so fluid and fast that the own game's FX sounds overrides the soundtrack, making it hard to appreciate how good it is.
Controls: 8.5/10 - As a non-casual player of Metroidvania games, I was pretty satisfied with Dust controls. Movement is fluid and once you learn its mechanics you won't have a problem here. Every mistake I experienced in this game was my own fault and not the game's one. Combos are really cool and they are set to let the players make their own strategies with all different movements.
Duration: 7.5/10 - Dust: An Elysian Tail will provide you more than 5-7h of storyline (unless you rush it), and about another 5-7h if you go for the extras, such as new skills, completing sidequests. finding treasure chests, etc. As many Metroidvania games, this game has some RPG features, like character level progression, which can lengthen your experience and gameplay even more (it is always nice to farm your level!). Moreover, the storyline is surprisingly interesting, and might keep you playing without pause until the end. And yes, the whole story is pretty good. Definately not a disappoint.
Difficulty: 6.5/10 - This game, compared to my idea of the average difficulty of its similars, is basically "not too hard, but not too easy either". Four difficulties can be chosen from the start and can be changed during your gameplay, and that means that on higher difficulties less HP recovery items will be spread, stronger (yet not faster) enemies, tougher bosses and HP damage, etc. Overall Dust: An Elysian Tail can be played by everyone and shouldn't disappoint either new players or the veteran ones.
OVERALL: 8.5/10 - I was kinda hyped when I finally purchased this game and my expectations were dangerously high. However, Dust: An Elysian Tail answered to them VERY well. This game is another demonstration that a small company can make huge things into the gaming industry. I'm really happy I decided to try out this game, it was worthy and I feel this can like you all too because I found it really hard not to enjoy it.

I enjoyed The Witcher 2, and I think you would too.
On the bright side, the story is rich and interesting, although a bit confusing a times because of the vast amount of details provided by the characters and the number of players involved. If you want to move beyond killing foes, you will need to dig into the extensive documentation (and supplement it with details online).

On the not-so-bright side, the fight system is just average. The character development system is, unfortunately, vaguely explained. You will have to go online to fully understand it, and you should do so since it is a critical part of your success in the game.
In summary, I am about to start my second game-through. The developers have done a good job bringing to life the comics and books' atmosphere, but a bit more structure for the non-initiated would have been appreciated.

Spent a good bit playing this game, loved every second of it. In it's current beta state it's still a bit buggy (however I left it running overnight for 8 hours and then returned to play, so it doesn't get worse over time, just how beta-stage games are), never crashed on me. If you were a fan of Gal Civ II, then this is definitively a continuation of that game and the few new mechanics introduced already make a positive difference.
I particularly enjoy the feature of choosing sponsors for shipyards, which makes them much more effective facilities that do not require extensive infrastructure or research. The graphics aren't dramatically different (which I actually like), they're just cleaner and clearer. The core gameplay mechanics haven't been altered either, which I like as well (the method through which starbases are upgraded remained the same, planets still have the grid), they really retained a lot of Gal Civ II, making the game very easy to pick up after not having played in years. Needless to say they didn't try fixing anything that wasn't broken to begin with, like many other companies do with the sequels of their most successful games.

Moderately fun side scrolling hack and slash plat forming RPG game. Played on the second hardest difficulty with a usb playstation controller and it took about 10 hours to beat it just doing the main quest line. About 2 hours of that was just grinding because I didn’t bother with the crafting system so my gear wasn’t that good. The enemies are not that difficult until you get to the last area. The greatest challenge came from the platforming as jumps were often very difficult to make. Your regular jump often does not reach high enough so you have to attack in mid air to get that extra height boost, but this makes sticking your landing in the right spot more difficult. You also often just randomly fall through platforms when you land on them which can be frustrating. I also had to restart the game on several occasions because I would just randomly fall through and get stuck inside of walls. The good thing is there are a lot of save points so even if you get stuck you don't have to restart that far back. The story line/dialog is kind of cringey, but I just skipped most of it. The environment looks pretty nice, but sometimes it is hard to tell what you can jump on or what hurts you as the background and foreground kind of blend in with the main area at times. I wouldn’t recommend buying this game at full price, but since it was included in the humble bundle 11 you can probably get it for cheap.

Firstly, I initially had a frame rate issue with this game that only a community-made patch could solve. Without said patch, the game was completely unplayable even on lowest settings. As it is, I had to play through the entire game on both lowest settings and easy (though I meet the RECOMMENDED, not MINIMUM, specs), because the community patch "fix" still didn't result in the frame-precision necessary for some of the specific maneuvers the game demanded.
Secondly, the combat is annoyingly awkward. When just fighting one opponent it's okay, but even with investment into group-fighting skills actually taking on a group can be a complete mess. Part of this has to do with how the combat is still somewhat tied to dice-rolls despite the emphasis on real-time and precision maneuvers. The worst maneuvering is demanded by the boss fights, each of which was utter hell (only partly due to the above-mentioned technical issue I had). Admittedly, I also find that I prefer either the freedom of combat of a game like Dark Souls, or the complete removal of the illusion of said freedom as is common in many D&D and turn-based fantasy games. You may find you like the combat, assuming your PC can keep up.
Finally, the story, the foundation of the entire experience, is one that I find to be flawed. Witcher 2 merely sets up a sequel, and while I hate this I could accept this if the game managed to tell its own story. Witcher 2 starts off strong, and impressed me a great deal with its initially mature handling of both characters and sex. The sexuality is constant, but a general emphasis towards feminine beauty without much space for male beauty beyond violence quickly reduced the story to "rescue the princess" for a good portion.
The finale tries to salvage the experience, but 20 hrs really isn't enough time. The male characters are largely unlikable idiots outside two or three of the main characters, and almost all the women are shallow and, in the case of the sorceresses, annoyingly fragile. Fans of the Grand Theft Auto school of character design will likely think everyone is "deep." However, revealing a self-confident sorceress to be a lesbian and throwing it in the player's face in the most over-blown way possible is NOT character development; it's a businessman begging you to get a boner.

"Reward in rushing" is the message that is routinely reinforced as you play. "Rushing" a room is a core game mechanic and something of a miniature gamble that you engage in to make progress. You rush to get resources. Rush rush rush. Rushing brings rewards. That is what the game tells you. Rush, reward. Rush, reward. You must rush to get rewards.
That is what makes Fallout Shelter's Pay-or-Delay scheme so lucrative. The game conditions you to rush then frustrates you with delays. The way to move forward is to pay for Nuka-cola speed-ups.
Remember, please, that according to fallout lore Vaults were social experiments done on stupid people. For this game remove "Vault Tech" and replace it with "Bethesda". This is a game that plays you.

I recommend this game, but on a scale from 1-10 it's a solid 7.  The game being repetitve is not a matter of opinion - it's a fact.  70-75% of the game is taking down rackets and while it might be fun the first or 2nd time you do it, after that though, it's not.  Hangar 13 took the criticsm of not having enough to do in Mafia 2 and filled it with grindy objectives.  Kill this guy, interrogate this guy, destroy these boxes over and over and over.
That's not to say that there's nothing good about this game though.  The music is top notch, the story is interesting, and the theme is extremely well done.  I also have to say this game is EXTREMELY buggy.  In my 31 hours of playing this game I had to reload from the most recent checkpoint five times because I experienced game breaking bugs that wouldn't allow me to continue.  These kind of bugs shouldn't be in the game even at launch and especially not 8 months after it originally came out.
Overall, wait to pick this game up cheap on a Steam sale.  I paid 26 bucks CAD and I felt I got my money's worth.  If I paid $80 CAD I would have been livid.  It's a good game, but the weakest in the Mafia franchise.  I feel disappointed more than anything because this game could have been something special if 2K gave Hangar 13 more time, but they wanted to get it out the door for Holiday 2016 sales.

Firstly, I initially had a frame rate issue with this game that only a community-made patch could solve. Without said patch, the game was completely unplayable even on lowest settings. As it is, I had to play through the entire game on both lowest settings and easy (though I meet the RECOMMENDED, not MINIMUM, specs), because the community patch "fix" still didn't result in the frame-precision necessary for some of the specific maneuvers the game demanded.
Secondly, the combat is annoyingly awkward. When just fighting one opponent it's okay, but even with investment into group-fighting skills actually taking on a group can be a complete mess. Part of this has to do with how the combat is still somewhat tied to dice-rolls despite the emphasis on real-time and precision maneuvers. The worst maneuvering is demanded by the boss fights, each of which was utter hell (only partly due to the above-mentioned technical issue I had). Admittedly, I also find that I prefer either the freedom of combat of a game like Dark Souls, or the complete removal of the illusion of said freedom as is common in many D&D and turn-based fantasy games. You may find you like the combat, assuming your PC can keep up.
Finally, the story, the foundation of the entire experience, is one that I find to be flawed. Witcher 2 merely sets up a sequel, and while I hate this I could accept this if the game managed to tell its own story. Witcher 2 starts off strong, and impressed me a great deal with its initially mature handling of both characters and sex. The sexuality is constant, but a general emphasis towards feminine beauty without much space for male beauty beyond violence quickly reduced the story to "rescue the princess" for a good portion.
The finale tries to salvage the experience, but 20 hrs really isn't enough time. The male characters are largely unlikable idiots outside two or three of the main characters, and almost all the women are shallow and, in the case of the sorceresses, annoyingly fragile. Fans of the Grand Theft Auto school of character design will likely think everyone is "deep." However, revealing a self-confident sorceress to be a lesbian and throwing it in the player's face in the most over-blown way possible is NOT character development; it's a businessman begging you to get a boner.

If I had played this game only once, I would have given it a thumbs up. I was feeling like my choices mattered, and I really liked their diversity (one particular scene had no less than 14 options). However, one does not simply play a game like this only once. One plays it again to see how different the story would have been if one acted differently. And that's when the whole positive idea I had of this game fell to crumbles.
In my first playthrough I was very careful and paranoid. I didn't use my time-freezing powers for personal gain or anything evil, and tried to stay under the radar as much as possible. On the second one, I went the completely opposite route: I used my powers to pester people, robbed people and organizations multiple times, and generally tried the dumbest options I could, just to see how different the game would turn out. I made over $200k in money on this playthrough, compared to less than $1k on the first, but that didn't seem to change anything. The game still treated me as if I was poor.
All the major events still transpired in largely the same way, and I got the exact same ending!
As an example, even if I was a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥to my friends and refused to comply with the instructions of key characters, I still found myself going through the same situations with them. Even by stating multiple times that I didn't think my roomates were my friends at all and that I thought they were annoying, towards the end of the story the game was still treating them as my friends and saying the main character cared about them. It makes no sense! This is only one example among many.
The things that changed didn't really matter in the end, and I got a couple more achievements. That was it.
Other reviewers recommended other games by the same company saying choices matter a lot more in those, and I truly hope they are right. Because this one is only worth it for one playthrough. Don't even bother redoing it.

I have to admit, at first, I really didn't like this. Even right through to the end I found the characters and their art and voices to have an extremely amateur flavour. The entire thing seemed like a bog standard furry Flash on Newgrounds. Your companion especially is pretty much godawful throughout, with the occasional humourous quip. However, I persevered, and with a second launch of the game I started to overlook that initial shortcoming and start to get into what is in fact, a very good game. The settings and backgrounds were gorgeous and varied (why couldn't the artist that did that do the characters?) and I also liked the majority of the monster designs. The levels had a satisfyingly open feel with a nice sense of scale and immersion; I especially liked the zombie meadow level. The combat, levelling and crafting systems work well (although my completionist nature did seem to make my character rather overpowered towards the end of the game, making the final boss fight extremely easy), and the game has a decent amount of varied and interesting equipment to kit out your character with. While primarily an action game, I found many of the hidden treasures and their puzzles quite satisfying, and especially liked the secret 'Friends' and their bonuses. The hidden Trials were also quite a lot of fun to master, giving a little bit of extra to the game. I also found the story good with an interesting setup, although suffering from the standard aribtrary development stifling (AKA "You'll find out later because no reason other than it'll make the story longer").Overall a good an unique contender in the Metroidvania genre, worth picking up if you're into that sort of game and don't mind the characters and amateurish aspects.

One can assume that this game is simply a diving simulator however this is far from it. Abzu is a game of both visual and audiable discovery. The music sets the mood and the visuals complements it. The game draws heavily from Journey, a game on the playstation. Many of the same mechanics flow over such as your character interacting with the world with a chime. The game lacks the random drop in multiplayer and instead replaces that with a few mini subs that accompany you as you make your way through the world.
If you ever wanted to play Journey but never had a PS3/PS4 then ABZU will give you the underwater experience of its desert counter part. If you have played Journey you will feel at home with that familiar feeling bar an unknown companion to join you as you discover the world around you.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is the game where you think you're good at beating down monsters to the beat... then you unlock hardcore mode. You think of this as impossible as Zone 3 is one giant zerg rush of skeleton horses and elemental enemies. Nonetheless you try it anyway and manage to get some decent gear. Then a red dragon comes along and says "♥♥♥♥ you!" and you get one shot by a fireball because you can't do the sacred red dragon dance at that moment. (That's my life, i cri evertim ;;)
But seriously, this game is amazing in many aspects. It's hard to find a game where a particular character dies from picking up GOLD, of all things! Since the levels are randomly generated there is no true pattern to the game and permanent death is indeed a thing. So that guy that dies from picking up gold? He's no exception, better watch your step! Oh yeah, and the only way you can move/attack/dig/open chests is by hitting the arrow key in the direction that you want to go on the beat of the song that's playing. There's a nice little tutorial in-game for that, though.
However, there is one thing that bugs me about Crypt of the Necrodancer. That is, the diamonds that are used to purchase items to be put into the item pool for non-hardcore runs. It would make more sense to have everything unlocked already, like hardcore does, but you are forced to buy it using diamonds you find during non-hardcore runs. It's a bit more harmful than helpful and everything should just be unlocked for you to use when it's found.
Despite that, this game is well worth your time. I've got 60+ hours and counting clocked into Crypt of the Necrodancer and it's not like I'll be stopping anytime soon. If you like challenging games, get this game. If you like rogue-likes, get this game. If you like rhythm based games, get this game. The point is, just buy the freaking game! What're you waiting for? Scroll back up and click that "Add to cart" button!

I usually tend not to enjoy F2P games. Either the content is lacking or the microtransactions cripple it. Surprisingly, this game has a large amount of content and you can play without putting a single dollar on it.
It's a colorful and light game which won't let you go. It's very addictive. There's always something to do - something to click on, something to manage. You get potential access to everything the game offers, so there are no unlockables that require you to spend real money on it. If you are patient, all the rare items  ( Mr. Handy, pets, etc. ) will eventually start coming. Investing money only lets you get those things faster... But I'd recommend not to spend too much money on it, otherwise the fun you'll have collecting stuff will fade away much quicker. Then again, I think this game deserves a few bucks just for how it was designed.
Although we have bright visuals, the game retains the Fallout atmosphere. You'll hear sounds you're used to and encounter creatures or characters you know.
Managing your shelter isn't that hard but it still requires some thoughts. You can almost run out of stuff at first because you have to learn how things work, but as soon as you have enough electricity, food and water-producing rooms, you'll get the hang of it. Doesn't take much time.
The addictive part comes when your shelter begins to get bigger and you have more inhabitants to take care of. You assign jobs, breed them together, level them up and (later) can modify their appearance. At some point, you'll be able to venture in the wastelands much like you do in the regular Fallout series and they'll collect rare items, caps and encounter mini quests. A few hours of gameplay later you'll unlock real missions which involve travelling long distances which lead you to buildings where you usually fight enemies and collect items as well.
There are a handful of events which happen in your shelter, but I wish there would've been a little more. At some point, it's just the missions that are truly fun and interesting. Lots of stuff becomes routine and you realize the game has its limits when it comes down to replay value.
If there's one thing truly missing from the game, it's multiplayer. Man, this game would've been a blast with multiplayer. Invading or defending other shelters, trading items or characters, going on missions together, all this and more could've been done. What a wasted opportunity. I would've gladly paid for this.

Aragami is a stealth game in which you play as an... well... Aragami, a vengeful phantom destined to disappear at sunrise. Brought into this world by a captured summoner as a last-ditch effort to free herself, you are her tool to achieve freedom - and maybe take out a few of the invading force's soldiers on the way.
True, the story is not the best out there, but there are some twists and turns that make it enjoyable. Cutscenes are also presented compitently with some nicely choreographed fights. You'll probably see the final twists coming, but overall it's not a bad story overall.
Now, the gameplay is where Aragami really shines: As a shadow creature, Aragami's stealth gameplay is all about using shadows. You can teleport between them pretty effortlessly and even conjure up some short-term shadow-spots. As long as you stay in shadows, your ressource for using these abilities will also regenerate pretty quickly.
Both of these abilities can be used in very imaginative ways. Teleport behind a guard as he comes to investigate? Sure, you can do that. Climbing up a cliff by coating the edge in shadow? Nothing's stopping you. It's a very pleasant way to get around in a stealth game.
You also get some other secondary abilities which are your usual stealth-game fare: Marking guards, temporary invisibility, placing decoys, or, if you choose to go lethally, destroying enemies from afar or disposing of their bodies
Speaking of lethal options, the game doesn't penalize you for killing enemies aside from subtracting points from your score. You won't miss out on an ending or anything like that, so feel free to let loose.
All in all, Aragami is highly recommended if you love Stealth games. It gives you some excellent movement options and is pretty lenient when it comes to detection. Even the bossfights are pretty enjoyable, and even put some of the bigger stealth game bosses to shame.
The only bad things I can really say about this game is that sometimes the indie roots of this title shine through. Limited voice acting, stiff animation and sometimes wonky terrain collision (sliding off a roof, for instance) are the things that come to mind.

In his hometown of New Bordeaux there are businesses that proudly display “no colored allowed” signs in their windows. There are whole neighborhoods that Lincoln Clay cannot be in without getting the side-eye from white citizens while walking by. The police will always watch him, call him “boy” and will open fire on Clay if he commits any crimes in their vicinity. To everyone else, he is defined by the color of his skin; a man barely qualified to supply menial labor for his supposed betters. Despite all this, Lincoln Clay will shortly own everything in New Bordeaux because he is the star of Mafia III and whatever social commentary the game has will be lost in an open-world grind.

While it's not as good as OMD 1 or 2, it's a pretty solid F2P edition of the OMD series. With free to play games, people are quick to shout PAY2WIN, but I don't think that's the case here. I haven't bought anything (sorry, Robot Games!) and I've enjoyed it and haven't had too much trouble advancing through the stages. The best 3 heroes are the 3 default ones you start with. Compared to OMD1 and 2, heroes feel weaker and enemies seem stronger, so that can be frustrating. This effect is heavily amplified if you play with other people, because your damage is super nerfed and scaled down if you play with multiple people. First time players may struggle a lot. Good strategy will prevail! It's normal for it to take you a few tries to beat one map.
Even though it's geared toward Multiplayer, I've just played it single player (I played the desktop version a lot before moving to the steam-based version). Trying to play with random folks sounds like it would be frustrating to coordinate your defense build ideas, but it would probably be fun to play with friends you talk with over mic.
CON: There's no "restart" button/command yet, so if you misplace a trap or two and a bunch of enemies get by, you have to exit the game and then relaunch it for a do-over, which is annoying. edit: they added a restart button!
Another CON is that all heroes feel slow and there is no "Run" command/action. In a game where you have to frantically hurry from one point to another, being slow can be brutal, especially with some of the maps being really big. I hope they add some way to run/dash. Instead they put in a couple of "Speed pads" on some maps, which are few and far between and only speed you up for a short time. Not too helpful. Some maps are like Mazes and are confusing to get aorund as well, and the mini-map can only help so much.
The Trap Limit is also kind of annoying. Maybe it's there for performance reasons, but I feel like I should be able to buy as many traps as I can afford.
All in all, it's fun and free! I've gotten 200+ hours out of it just playing solo!

I'm a big fan of OMD! 1+2, truly great games. OMD! Unchained shares some of the similar concepts, and although it's improving, I still cannot recommend it yet. I am still going to play it, hoping that one day it will get to the same point of its predecessors. Here is a list of pros and cons:
Pros:
- Good graphics
- Great gameplay mechanics
- Wide variety of heroes
- Wide variety of traps and trap mods
- 3-player online co-op
Huge cons:
- Maps, despite being quite big, don't allow or at least do not encourage strategy. This is the biggest difference between OMD! 1+2 and OMD! Unchained. The fun part of the previous games was the strategy and thought that went into each map, trying to funnel the orcs into your killboxes. In OMD! Unchained this is almost impossible to do, 90% of the time it's better to simply spam arrow walls and spikes everywhere, with no real strategy behind it, which brings me to the second huge con:
- Most traps are useless in most maps. Pretty much all you need is spikes and arrow walls, with the occasional barricade and swinging mace (or pounder).
Minor cons (these are minor things that will most likely be fixed before the final release, so I don't really consider them as negative right now, just annoyances):
- Can't simply restart a map. You need to exit the map, your party members have to do the same, and then you have to re-form the party. Pretty annoying when you're trying to 5-star a hard map.
- Chest system: I get why this is in place, Robot Entertainment needs a way to make money, and this is probably a good way. It still makes leveling up a grind-fest, since there is no way to pick which traps you want upgraded, but you're completely relying on RNG, hoping that the chests will drop the traps you're looking to upgrade.
As I said, I still cannot recommend this game. The 2 huge cons overshadow all the many improvements done over OMD! 1+2, giving the game a different feel, way less satisfactory. I am still hoping that this will be fixed, making OMD! Unchained the rightful successor to the previous masterpieces.

I am updating my review since my original was when the game was in early access.
To summarize: The game is playable and alright.
That being said, it isn't innovative and doesn't offer much in terms of grand strategy.
The visuals are beautiful in GC3 and there is much detail given to each sprite, model and bloom of light.  The faction/ship creator gives the player customization options, albeit limited unless venturing into the modder sphere.  The ship designer is definitely the most 'fun' aspect and can entertain more than the actual game. The learning curve isn't difficult and the AI is quite predictable with a mediocre diplomacy mechanic.  Combat is still regulated to a cinematic experience, with a basic/simple system of offense/defense, nothing special but it looks nice.  Trade and economics is pretty standard fare akin to the Civ series.  Faction interaction and dialogue is pretty boring with scripts being generic and used across the board (meaning interactions don't feel special).  The game does become sluggish, with not much to do but press turn.  There isn't much to interact with on the main map...you send a constructor to build a station here and there, move ships from point A and B.
There are plenty of other pros and cons to the game. Most can be seen just by viewing the official forums for Stardock.  Overall, in my opinion, the game is standard fare, looks pretty and offers nothing new to the evolving grand strategy genre. It will possibly keep the player entertained for short bursts, but isn't a must-play considering competitors that have enhanced mechanics.
I would recommend buying this game if it were on discount and if you are just looking for something to do outside of your normal go-to library. It gets an "Eh" rating of apathy from me.

This is hands down one of the best examples of why Early Access should be a thing. Amongst the piles of early access games that are slow to update, have uncommunicative developers, and don't strives for self-improvement, Crypt of the NecroDancer continues to add more content and build upon itself.

A clever blend of rhythm game and rogue-like, Crypt of the Necrodancer is a fun challenge that urges your every move to be carefully thought out and chosen...in the length of a beat. The music is incredibly catchy, the bosses and characters are charming, the design is delightfully elegant, and the different playstyles made available always keep things fresh. And there's still more characters, zones, and content to come!
I've yet to try out the importing of custom music, nor have I used the custom level editor to its fullest potential. But I honestly can't say I'm missing out; I'm still addicted to the game's levels as they are!
Do yourself a favor. Buy it. Support the developers. And bide your time until you can confront the NecroDancer in a lethal tango.

Did you like Journey? This is Journey underwater. Thumbs up for that if you're into that. Thumbs down if not. Also, the length versus the price tag is an issue. But I honestly didn't want it to be any longer it was, so it's not really a question of "value for money" as the experience is about as long as it should be. However, it's a question of "are you willing to pay for 2 hour game?". Make up your own mind. My score is somewhere between thumbs up and thumbs down, so I'll round up this time.
So, I finished the game in just under 2 hours. I didn't do everything there is to do. But I didn't rush like a crazy person, you could, I imagine, stretch it to two or three times the length; if you are looking at every nook and cranny. But I didn't, and the reason was that I can't turn the music off or make it more quiet versus the sound effects.
I didn't enjoy the music in the game about 60% of the time, but that's not because the music is bad.
I am just one of those persons who when plays a game, first thing I do is that I turn off the music. Unless it's ambient. This score is very active and very orchestral and those are two things that make me anxious. Yes, orchestral music makes me uncomfortable. So, don't take it as a bad sign.
That said, there is an upscaling option in the graphics which is really cool, but not much else, few basic options to help you out if you can't run it, but otherwise it's pretty bare.
The game is basically Journey (except it's on PC too) but underwater, there's not much to do. Some basic puzzles and very nice art direction, and then it's done. The game does defy expectations at least twice, but it's not exactly breaking new ground.
Now, whether it's worth the price tag, for 2-4 hours of fun? In the case of INSIDE, I'd say yes (it's min 2+ hours), but in this case... I am not sure. If the music was more calm and ambient oriented, I'd say it is a meditative game for relaxation. As it is now, it's actually not all that calm.
Honestly, it's what it is: Journey underwater. If you like that, go for it. In that spirit, I am giving this thumbs up.

Thanks to this game I find I'll be unthinkingly humming the tunes and twitching my fingers along to the beat.
So, I never really played many rhythm games before, aside from some Guitar Hero at a friends house. I picked this up because I read a couple of the reviews and thought to myself "Huh, why not?" (That, and I was suckered in by the name.) A couple hours later and I find myself VERY glad I picked it up.
Each monster has it's own movement and attack pattern, so the fun of it is figuring out exactly how they are gonna move and how you are gonna kill them. Fairly easy early on when the patterns are simple, and most monsters dont' have special abilities. However, as time goes by, the monsters grow in strength and numbers, and inevitably you'll find yourself panicking as you are surrounded on 3 sides by skeletons, goblins, and a dragon and you are desperately trying to put some distance between you to figure out which attack order won't leave you in a bloody and broken heap on the cave floor.
To add to the fun, there are tons of items and equipment that will either randomly spawn in chests that can be found either out in the open or hidden in walls, or randomly chosen to be available for purchase from a friendly merchant. These, combined with the various different layouts that are created each time you go down, makes it so that each time is a different experience.
That said, until you get sufficiently skilled you can pretty much live or die depending upon your luck with item and monster and mini-boss spawns. You might get something relativly easy, like a minotaur. Or you might get stuck with something that can one shot you like a red dragon. If you are REALLY unlucky, you'll get the worst enemy known to crypt-explorer-kind. Bats. Bats are horrible. Real life bats are great. CotN bats are something spawned from hell itself.
So, if you are on the fence about spending some money on this early-access game, I'd reccommend you suck it up and give this a shot. I'm pretty sure you won't be dissapointed. Unless you hate fun.

'Deponia: The Complete Journey' is a point-and-click adventure game compilation that consists of the first three games of the series: 'Deponia', 'Chaos on Deponia', and 'Goodbye Deponia'. Together, they tell the story of Rufus' quest to leave garbage-filled surface of Deponia for the idyllic floating town of Elysium.
'D:TCJ' is the best way to experience the grand scope and epic nature of Rufus' journey. The pacing of each of the three games is somewhat uneven, with overly long middle sections that seem to go nowhere. Thankfully, it is in these middle sections that we find the more interesting puzzles and fun mini games, which help you stay motivated. All three games, when played back to back in 'D:TCJ', present a clearer story and character arcs.
One of the most captivating aspects of 'D:TCJ' is the beautifully drawn characters and locales. The appealing art design, and the detail with which the characters and locations are realized, give the recent Remastered releases of LucasArts games a run for their money. The trash-covered planet of Deponia is an imaginative and visually stunning one, which was surprising to me at first given that it is covered with garbage. However, Deponia is a lot more lively and vibrant than one would imagine.
The English voice acting in 'D:TCJ' is also spot-on, adding personality to the interesting characters. Rufus is particularly unique among adventure game heroes. Whereas main characters of popular adventure games can be heroic, quirky, clumsy, or perhaps have their share of foibles, Rufus is just not (very) likeable and not even an anti-hero at all, for he is egotistic, narcissistic, and self-centred. And yet, he is captivating as a playable character, in part due to the great voice acting by Kerry Shales. Even when reasons for Rufus' faults are revealed and explained, it feels abrupt and a bit like damage control. You will definitely find divisive opinions on whether or not Rufus is a good main character in an adventure game.
You may also find divisive opinions on the jokes in 'D:TCJ'. Some find them funny, some not. Personally, I find the game amusing -- not very funny, but entertaining enough. This could be due to the funny bits being lost in translation from the original German (and the game is very self-aware of it), or it could be simply due to what people find funny. However, I did find some scenarios, jokes and characters depiction off-putting, sexist, and culturally insensitive. Whether or not you can overlook these flaws is up to you.
However, I can definitively say that the puzzles in this game are fun. Some are challenging, some require some form of moon logic, and some tickle your brain just enough. Despite the length of the game (I easily clocked in over 24 hours of gaming time in total despite what my stats say because I played parts of the game offline), there is a good variety of puzzles to keep gameplay fresh. The art and the puzzles are definitely highlights of 'D:TCJ', and I very much enjoyed the game in spite of the flaws I previously mentioned.
'D:TCJ' is a great adventure game. It embodies both strength and weakness of great adventure games that came before. Questionable quality of jokes and content aside, it definitely deserves the accolades that it received. It is a must-play for anyone who enjoys point-and-click adventure games.
P.S.: For achievement seekers like I, you will find some achievements for 'D:TCJ' very difficult to get, let alone figure out what they are about. mishalunchbox wrote fantastic walkthroughs and
that you should definitely consult if you are interested in getting all achievements.

A lot of people who dislike the game seem to have issues with the humor or the protagonist. I, on the other hand, didn't really have an issue with either of those. I played through the first game, which was a slog, and part of the way into the second before losing all motivation to continue and giving up on it. The only "pro" I can think of, looking back, is the animation is great.
Roughly halfway through the first game the game I was already having issues listening to / reading all the dialogue, because it just wasn't engaging or funny and droned on and on. I'm not a stranger to story driven games or point and click adventure, but this was a bit of a red flag. My biggest beef with the game, and ultimately the reason I gave up on it, is the horrendously unintuitive puzzles. Puzzles that actually make any semblance of sense are exceptions to the rule. It most often falls back on point and click formulas of the 90s, where you try to combine everything with everything else until something works, then try to combine that with everything else, then try everything on everything until that something works... It's horrid.  The second game seemed only marginally better, with slightly more intuitive puzzles, but it quickly devolved into the same formula. You got occasional hints from dialogue, but few and far between.
The story is not engaging enough for me to recommend wasting all the time necessary to go through the motions of combining everything with everything until something works, then using that on everything until, again, something works. Nor was it engaging enough for me to recommend a walkthrough, seeing as I found myself bored halfway through the first game. Not being engaged by the story could be a "me problem", it just wasn't my jam; but the "puzzles" (and the resulting formulaic sequence thereafter) are, by and large, hamfisted, convoluted garbage.

This game sits between games like ETS 2 and Omsi 2. Like ETS 2 the world is open and explorable, and there is a managment part where you run your company. Unlike Omsi 2 the game actually looks good and runs well, though the details of each bus are nowhere near as involved.
It /is/ a simulator, you have to start the bus, use indicators, open doors, all by either clicking on items on the screen, using the keyboard or mapping them to controller buttons. While its somewhat arcadey there is a learning curve but its enjoyable discovering how the bus works and how you need to use it in the world. The developers seem to be listening and working hard to update most of the complaints they've recieved. For example the orientation of the gps map or auto turn off of indicators when you straighten out the steering wheel. The game play is smooth, I haven't quantified the framerates but it doesn't stutter or go slowly unlike Omsi 2 which is notorious for doing that even on massive high end systems.
The sound quality is high, though somewhat generic. The only complaint I have is how harsh some of the penalties are. Hit a pedestrian? Game stops and you have to start the scenario over, even if it happens as your pulling into your garage. Accidents are very costly, as are speeding fines. All well and good for sim realism I guess but annoying. Finally, the game is fairly easy to use with my G27 steering set up, though I did have to futz a little with the settings to get things nice. Again, more like ETS 2 in that and a hell of a lot better than Omsi 2.
Overall I give it four and a half out of five stars.

Edit 11/3/2016:  Last update was mid-summer 2016.  The dev responds vaguely to forum questions but any early access title with tons of posts asking if the game is dead or abandonded is probably a suggestion that things aren't going very well.  A lot of promises are still being made, NPCs, multiple islands, but the game still feels so much like one of the hundreds of mobile apps out there and not like a true PC game.
So.  Beware.  I buy all these sandboxy games because I figure one or two in the pile might rise above mediocrity.  To no surprise, it seems this game has stunted somewhere, as the last update brought what would normally be considered regular changes to a growing project's fundamentals- and it seemed as if the developer wanted people to fawn over it- when all you see now are comments about how that so-called "update" broke the game for like, 75% of players.
Having "Free updates" as a Key Feature in a game that is in Early Access is a HUGE red flag, if you're into "waiting to buy" like a normal person without the same hatred for your own sanity like all of us early access torture junkies.
I could be wrong and it could just be a financial hurdle they're attempting to jump.  A bit of a shout-out would be nice, instead of a near-mute changelog and very little in the way of mapping out how this game is supposed to progress into a full release.  I don't imagine this one exiting early access without a band-aid and a wipe of it's forums.  Who knows, it could see it's potential someday, because it does have the basics ready to go.
One thing that bothers me is the fact that I've asked around and nobody seems to know whether or not this game is related to a game (not naming it here) on the Play Store that has a similar title and almost identical assets.  The Android thumbnail used to be the icon used by this game in the Steam browser.  The game on Play has a slightly different premise, but most telling of all, is that it's release date is close to Forsaken Isle's, and it has, since December 2015, had a "50% Sale" banner slapped on it.  I might be stretching here, as I've been known for simply being out of my gourd sometimes, but I think there has to be at least a slight case of fair use abuse going on.
Anyway.  At the price it is now, you'll probably spend more time with it than I did, you might even love the heck out of it.  To me, $8 is well under my expectation threshold for Steam these days.  There is a game here, it can be played and replayed thanks to a fairly well-designed map generator.  Just don't go expecting it to win any awards for leaving Early Access in style.

I think the phrase "practice makes perfect" very much sums this game up. Every time you die you're expected to start over and play the game again and again, and while that may sound redundant, Hotline Miami makes you want to be good.
With most games that involve a protagonist running around murdering people, it's okay to slip up and get shot once in a while; but here it's not. You're expected to plan out every detail of your murder spree, and when something goes wrong, either learn to adapt or try again. You *want* to be good at this game and every level you're challenged to be creative, patient, or erratic with your playing style.
And the replay value is immense; I've beaten this game several times because I want to play each level again and make every adjustment for perfect runs or maximum combos. This last time I played I actually wanted to understand its very nuanced and dark story; a very surreal experience.
You need Hotline Miami in your repertoire of games, it's an innovative take on shooters that keep you wanting more.

Unfortunately, after giving it a fair bit of time, I must say it not only doesn't live up to it's predecessors, but is seriously lacking even with all the DLCs purchased, and therefore I have changed my rating. I'm not sure where to start, so I will list pros/cons instead:
Pros:
1. Nice graphics, good attempt at the designer idea
2. Some good ideas everywhere
3. Better UI than GC1/2
4. Hours of gameplay without a crash in sight (except for the designer)
Cons:
1. Complete lack of shortcuts, there are only few, you can count on one hand
2. Ship designer is 20% complete - lacks many features which are there but still don't work since the alpha. Crashes like hell if you happen to use workshop designs.
3. Loads of bugs around the custom factions - naming conventions, definitions, sometimes game will not load it anymore.
4. Every game I had so far (roughly 15 with different custom made factions) started with all out war against me in the first 150 turns.
5. The game always puts you at a 10:1 disadvantage, either via lack of resources, long distance between planets, very low class planets, or simply by making everybody declare war on you on first sight.
6. Ship movement/route finding is illogical and unreasonable. No way to queue moves either.
7. Starbases are weak and useless if at war. Basically two medium class ships can obliterate them anytime, even when at full strength with all possible military upgrades, the 200 hit points is often less than ships flying around - where's the logic in that. They should be 20000 hit points, so that they are scary when they should be.
8. The explore feature is brutally dumb wasting time coming back to explored space ALL the time. This is also connected to the bad AI pathing.
9. There are simply not enough tiles on planets to manage them correctly. Many tiles are ridiculously  and illogically spread over the map. Examples: Planet wide 50% bonus to research, and tiles are unconnected, or taken by added bonuses for tourism or approval instead. Terraforming and soil enhancements should allow me to choose any tile, not just some - that's why it's called TERRAFORMING!
10. I should be able to chose where to put the colony, but the game does it for you instead, often leaving you with unconnected colony tile, which sometimes can't be connected even with enhancements.
11. UI issues: like inability to make informed choice by checking the values before answering - there should be a way to postpone decision in the same turn, make necessary checks and get back to the dialog to answer - no the game forces you to choose NOW - which leaves you with mistakes or makes you reload last save and hope for the same to happen.
Another UI problem is lack of required details, like: Why is the morale only 65% on my colony. It only shows you what adds up to it but not what takes away. If it started at 100% I would expect to see the reason, why it went down.
12. No way to move colonists from one planet to another as I could do in the GC2. It's the best or sometimes the only way to speed up the colonisation.
13. The mechanics of shield/armor/point defense are incorrect. Armor should always protect the hull, point defense only takes care of missiles, and shield protects from all until depleted. This is not how it works here however, as you will find the three systems work separately to each other.
14. The battles are simply put - dumb, and there's no logic in most of them. If I have a starbase with 2 ships defending it, I would think that the 3 together would have a good chance of standing up to the enemy, but: GC3 engine sends all the ships to die, and then leaves the starbase to itself.
15. I the recent play I decided not to research a translator, and it turns out that at turn 120 I was at war with four factions all 10-20x stronger than me for whatever reason, and none of them had the chance to contact me first before declaring the war. Then they didn't attack any of my assets for about 100 turns, so I'm not sure what was the point of declaring war at all.
