WARNING: If you have a fear of the ocean and how vast it may be, you may get anxiety from this game.
Abzu is a new game by the developpers of Journey and Flower and somehow in my opinion it's even better than those two.
PROS:
-Simulates the ocean and its wildlife very well
-Promotes exploration
-Beautiful graphics that always gave me a sense of awe
-Beautiful environements
-Very fluid controls especially considering the game is in water
-Riding other sea creatures is very fun and inspiring
-The scenes involving strong water currents are fantastic
-A scene involving whales is probably the best thing i've ever seen in gaming
-Amazing soundtrack
-Ending is great
-Only 20$!!!
CONS:
-Depending on your computer, you may get some minor frame rate drops
-The puzzles can be a bit repetitive
-Towards the middle of the game, we are introduced to mines and although they seem threatening and can electrify you, they don't actually kill you and you don't get any consequences for hitting them which is disappointing
PROS/CONS depending on who you are:
-Gamepad controls are much better than keyboard controls
-Puzzles are almost too simple
-Some collectibles are very well-hidden and can be very hard to find
-Game can be beat in just over 1 hour if you aren't looking or exploring a lot
-Story is up to interpretation
-Feels very similar to journey but underwater
Overall, I recommend this game as a must-buy and one that everybody should experience especially if you loved Flower or Journey 9/10

Crypt of the Necrodancer is the game where you think you're good at beating down monsters to the beat... then you unlock hardcore mode. You think of this as impossible as Zone 3 is one giant zerg rush of skeleton horses and elemental enemies. Nonetheless you try it anyway and manage to get some decent gear. Then a red dragon comes along and says "♥♥♥♥ you!" and you get one shot by a fireball because you can't do the sacred red dragon dance at that moment. (That's my life, i cri evertim ;;)
But seriously, this game is amazing in many aspects. It's hard to find a game where a particular character dies from picking up GOLD, of all things! Since the levels are randomly generated there is no true pattern to the game and permanent death is indeed a thing. So that guy that dies from picking up gold? He's no exception, better watch your step! Oh yeah, and the only way you can move/attack/dig/open chests is by hitting the arrow key in the direction that you want to go on the beat of the song that's playing. There's a nice little tutorial in-game for that, though.
However, there is one thing that bugs me about Crypt of the Necrodancer. That is, the diamonds that are used to purchase items to be put into the item pool for non-hardcore runs. It would make more sense to have everything unlocked already, like hardcore does, but you are forced to buy it using diamonds you find during non-hardcore runs. It's a bit more harmful than helpful and everything should just be unlocked for you to use when it's found.
Despite that, this game is well worth your time. I've got 60+ hours and counting clocked into Crypt of the Necrodancer and it's not like I'll be stopping anytime soon. If you like challenging games, get this game. If you like rogue-likes, get this game. If you like rhythm based games, get this game. The point is, just buy the freaking game! What're you waiting for? Scroll back up and click that "Add to cart" button!

That's a hard one... and I'm on the fence.
Game have potential - I'll give it that. But it's trying so hard to be thing it can not be, while ignoring what it should be (and what fans demand it to be).
First of positives:
+Graphics - game looks goregious. The stylisation like in OMD! 1&2 is outstanding!
+Game runs smooth, really smooth.
+Gameplay - in pure "runing, slashing 'n trashing" sense - game is pure gold.
+Variety of heroes to play with
And the negatives:
-It can be any other game - there's no feeling of OMD! in it. Lost somewhere on the road.
-Developers are running circles around base idea, with no concept of what to do next. The changes are fundamental and are reversing what game is doing for months over and over again.
-One (or two actually) of those resets evaporated all the heroes I crafted ingame, so be prepared to lose all the progres somewhere down the road if the developers choose to switch the gears again.
-Community is small and partially toxic... which is problematic, because You can't block people and will be playing with the same vermin over and over again - only because they are only active players around.
-Evolution of game seems extremly slow. Everytime I think creators reached the point of going foreward with game, after concept-change ofc, they pull the plug again and start over, reintroducing things that were working for months now.
-Ah! I almost forgot - You will stick to basic traps for... welll - for the game. Spikes and wall arrows are the best, witch undermine core concept of a game.
-If anything is better than basics, You will have to farm Your brains out to lvl it up to usefull state.
-There is cash shop from early beta stage. I don't have anything against cash shops in general, but to milk your testers? Seriously? They are not even costumers - they are litteraly testing the game for developers for free. They are doing someones job (and hell of a good one) for free! They spend their time to do it and have nothing to show it every time devs pull the plug.
-aaaaand the cash shop leads to something that looks awefully familiar to P2W system. Not yet - not quite there, but You can smell it.
That all lead to poor quality of expirience for me... add it to this wound grain of salt, that is server migration, that players have to do manually on their end and I'm uninstalling the game alltogether. Why bother?

"Being careful is for people who can't handle surprises."
Any classical point-and-click adventure at its core is a relatively linear set puzzles that tells you a story when you solve it. The premise of this story is simple: a young man Rufus wants to leave his home world Deponia. That is understandable, because Deponia is a junkyard of planetary proportions. There is, however, one twist to the classical hero's journey. Apparently, our 'hero' is a s--tstain on humanity! Surprising? Maybe. But let's have a little thought experiment. Say, you've encountered one of the three playable characters of the LucasArts classic "Day of the Tentacle" in person. What would you say about them? Right, they are utter maniacs! Dangerous, unpredictable, with tendency to pilfer every object that isn't screwed tight to the surface it rests upon. And if it is screwed tight, they will just come back with a screwdriver. Then they will recombine the stolen commodities in bizarre ways and you better run when they put their mccguyvering to use.
Our protagonist Rufus is the logical conclusion to this line of thinking. Rufus doesn't pretend to be a good guy. Everything in the world will serve his goal to leave his garbage-riddled home Deponia and reach almost mythical Elysium. Rufus will leave nothing but chaos and destruction behind, and you, the player, will guide him through the challenges. But perhaps exactly because Rufus is so unabashedly self-absorbed, in the crucial moment when he does something indisputably selfless, you will be truly touched. So be reckless, blast your way through the junkyard that is Deponia, enjoy the story loaded with witty, sarcastic, and sometimes even dark humour, and in the end Rufus may pleasantly surprise you.

Ahhhh FF7, the cornerstone of my rpg exposure from days past. It's good to see this particular title make it to Steam (honestly I was starting to think I was the only kid that had it for his PC back in the day). I remember growing up playing on my old win 95 pc, juggling between 7 disks contorting my fingers to use the numpad controles. But I'm not here to bore you with my nostalgic bantering lets go over the good the bad and the ugly.
The good:
This is a pretty basic jrpg thats real easy to pick up and understand. If you never played an rpg before this would be a good well-rounded game to break into. As far as game-play mechanics go, it's got a very gentle learning curve where if you take a moment or two to read some material explained on some of the games finer points and tool around with some of the settings (like ATB if you're new or want a purely turn-based combat style) IMHO, if not personal opinion, the magic and skill materia system is just more easily managable than previous/alternative character-class styles or the ill-recieved drawing/job-skill system of other games in the franchise.
The bad:
Looking at the story and analyzing it a little bit closer since growing up I've started to notices the flaws I didn't notice before. True it tickles my nostalgic core to no end playing this game and the characters and story is going to be something that sticks with me forever but looking closer and taking an outside perspective it's impossible to overlook some of the major story flaws. Plot points will be brought up that lead nowhere (or if you're a Square-enix executive, you'll just write whole new games around these points to cash-in on the fanbase). Yet one of the things that killed me playing this game again was the blatant continuity errors. Characters will mention or prod the player in a direction that they really wouldn't know about in the first place. Compared to other RPGs it's these flaws that I think may have made this and other similar games too watered down to appeal to a larger base audience like say the kind that don't like investigating, talking to every npc, or just simply spending the time to make an attempt at trial-and-error. Now, this doesn't break the game mind you. It's just try not to expect wracking your brain too much with this casual game.
The ugly:
Keyboard controls.... nuff said. Pick yourself up a xbox controller or logitech if you're cheap but do yourself the favor.

Controls: 4/10
Nostalgia-boner: 9999/10

I played through the original witcher twice. I enjoyed the original deeply because of the amazing story, alchemy, and monster killing. When I heard that there was a sequel to this awesome game I decided to pick it up sometime when I found it on a steam sale.
I regret purchasing this game and it is one of the very few games that I have bought and never finish. There are many reasons why I believe this is a bad game. I put in about 10 hours into the game but just couldn't handle all of its issues.
1) story - the original witcher had Geralt being a character with a strong personality set into a world that had a clear theme it wanted to address. However, in the sequel, I find that the story is lacking in many areas. Why would Geralt be the king's bodyguard? why would he involve himself in a war when he spent a great deal of the last game staying out of it? This games seems to have devolved into just chasing around this assassin instead of exploring rich theme and interesting characters
2) combat - the original witcher had a combat system that many people complained about. I too had a few issues with it but overall it did a decent job. For the sequel, the combat was completely redone. The combat is focused around a first person fighting scheme based around light/heavy attacks, signs, blocking, and evasion rolls. This system might have worked but it is generally sloppy. transitioning from parrying to attacking is choppy at best. Evasion rolls and parrying often are choppy resulting in a late parry or bad roll. I also found that this system works decently in solo battles but is terrible with groups of enemies. The game allows for traps/bombs/signs/throwing signs but their use is also choppy so they are generally less effective than one could imagine. It is also near impossible to tell if enemies are going to use a heavy, light or special attacks (some bosses also have possible insta kill attacks). This can be incredibly fustrating during boss fights or fighting enemies with special effects (such as bleeding or poison).
3) alchemy/potions - for starters, the menu for potions is absolute garbage. The alchemy list can be long and it can take awhile to find the potion you are looking for. Most also have significant side effects and they no longer have those awesome secondary effects that could be made in the original. Potions also can only be used during 'meditation' (out of combat). So if you are like me and exploring the environment and get ambushed, you either need to fight on (which can be tricky if they hit you from behind and take most of your health) or run away so you can drink a potion.
4) minigames - the original witcher has several minigames that I found fun and useful to gain extra cash. However, the sequel made the dice game absolutely terrible. it is impossible to make much money since they limited the max bet for Geralt and only the CPU can raise the pot. The game itself is also terrible. The dice themselves are hard to read, there is a quick and poor tutorial (if you even find the tutorial person, I didn't), and you have to physically roll the dice (which can easily fall off the board). The arm wrestling minigame they put in was pretty decent. They turned the fistfighting into a quick time event which I thought was pretty good.
5) crafting - there exists a crafting ability in this game. This ability is useful since traps, weapon, and armour crafting can be useful. However, the menus for crafting are ugly and can take awhile to decipher. There are also ALOT of design plans for crafts; this can then be a pain to find useful plans since each merchant can have a different set. You must also craft from talking with certain NPCs, I understand that I would need to do this weapon/armour crafting but do I really need to talk to some elf so I can make simple traps and bombs? I can make complicated potions in the middle of a forest but I can't make a simple snare trap myself? There is also a cost to crafting EACH ITEM which does a good job to nickle and dime your moneys.
6) stealth - it's just plain terrible. No way of telling LOS of guards or when they can see/hear you. The mechanic that 'stuns' guards that you sneak upon is sloppy and often does not work out well.

The game is a 2D hack 'n' slash with RPG elements. I would say it reminds me a lot of Muramasa: The Demon Blade (Wii). Muramasa overall is better, but it is a full retail game anyway. For an indie game, Dust does a superb job.
It's awesome. You are given a fairly extensive combo list right at the beginning, and you learn more moves and maneuvers along the way.
Gorgeous sprites, backrounds and effects.
You can collect, buy and sell materials to craft weapons, armor and accessories. Every time you level up, you choose how to distribute points to your attributes, prioritizing the ones that you care more about.
The game is challenging, but not frustrating. If you play it in the tough difficulty, get ready to buy and use A LOT of health items, or else you are going to have a bad time. And you have a one-button shortcut to use health items, so the action does not slow down.

I have mixed feelings about this novel. While the concept was interesting, I felt it was poorly executed. You find your character in a number of contrived situations and you get the choice of how, or whether or not, to use your power to stop time. In my first playthrough I chose the options that best represented what I believed I would do, and while I found that the options were (usually) sufficient for that, between chapters I was given a narrative about how my character had been fighting crime and helping people with his power, which was completely contrary to how I had been behaving, as for the most part I'd been conservative with my powers, and those few times I had used it, it was for the gain of myself or my direct friends, not random people on the street.
Aside from that, I feel that many of the things that happened were quite unrealistic. For instance, stopping time, doing something, moving back to the position you were in and then starting it again - There is simply no way that you'd be able to get your body back in the exact same position it was in, and to other people, it would appear as if you suddenly jerked in an unusual or perhaps even impossible way, and this wouldn't be ignorable. Yet somehow nobody seems to notice.
If you can look past the issues I've mentioned then I suppose I recommend this novel, but if it sounds like things like this would get on your nerves, then I don't. Personally, they got on my nerves.

I think the phrase "practice makes perfect" very much sums this game up. Every time you die you're expected to start over and play the game again and again, and while that may sound redundant, Hotline Miami makes you want to be good.
With most games that involve a protagonist running around murdering people, it's okay to slip up and get shot once in a while; but here it's not. You're expected to plan out every detail of your murder spree, and when something goes wrong, either learn to adapt or try again. You *want* to be good at this game and every level you're challenged to be creative, patient, or erratic with your playing style.
And the replay value is immense; I've beaten this game several times because I want to play each level again and make every adjustment for perfect runs or maximum combos. This last time I played I actually wanted to understand its very nuanced and dark story; a very surreal experience.
You need Hotline Miami in your repertoire of games, it's an innovative take on shooters that keep you wanting more.

A deceptively intuitive, dark, and horrifying game of nuclear apocalypse. You play as a general in an underground bunker, and make the decision to launch the missiles to (hopefully) kill more of them than they kill of you.
PROS:
+Deceptively easy to learn, difficult to master.
+Absolutely minimal graphics requirements. You could likely get this to run on Windows 95.
+Yet the above-minimal requirements work for the aesthetic, which calls back to the maps in NORAD from WarGames.
+Game can be played both at a high speed (completing in as little as 30 minutes) or in real-time (stretching to as long as eight hours).
+Game has a notable focus on the Nuclear Triad, with the ability to launch missiles from Bombers, Submarines, and Missile Silos.
+Game has an amazing atmosphere. Even in victory, you take one look at the total civilian deaths and feel empty inside.
+Highly strategic game with an emphasis on placement of your bases (including radar, airbases, and missile silos). Poor placement leads to an easy defeat.
CONS
-Not for everyone. Some people can't handle the long, slow gameplay many games stretch out to, while others simply don't like strategy games (perhaps even on this scale).
DEFCON holds a dear place in my heart, and is best played with all of the lights off, in a room where the only light comes from the monitor fortelling the end of civilization as we know it.

When about half of the UI buttons are greyed-out and read "COMING SOON" and your game is
(the Diplomacy in its' entirety)... Yeah, I'm sorry Stardock, but you don't get to call your game a "beta" yet. Late-alpha at most. Certainly nowhere near beta.
When the chance of getting the game running off the bat is something of a 50-50 due to a graphical bug that can render all UI text invisible,
.
Now, I only recently got into the Gal Civs 3 "beta" but from what I've gathered on the game's forum, that little issue has been around since the last apha build. So there's that to look forward to if you just got the game.
The issue's "easily averted" by telling the game to not use your dedicated graphics card. And once you're past that, well then- Welcome to Gal Civs 3: COMING SOON. Ok, I won't rip on an Early Access game for not having all its' features present. But really?
"Beta" implies you're "feature-complete". I.e- you've implemented all of the major mechanics and features you intend for your game and are balancing and tweaking them for best effect, along with dusting for the odd bug.
The current state of the Gal Civs 3 "Beta 1" is missing all sorts of features. From tactical combat to the above-mentioned Diplomacy mechanic. Instead, once you meet another faction you're immediately considered "at war forever", which makes playing against more than one opponent tricky at best since they will all kinda gang-up on you. Even if they them selves are technically at war with eachother, the AI will much prefer targeting your ships and colonies over other factions'.
Targeting ships and other stellar... targets (wow, such vocabulary) in itself is kind of underwhelming since fleets in themselves aren't really a thing yet either. Meaning most of the combat will involve single ships. Winners are auto-determined by a stat-check and apparently nobody bothered telling captains that retreat is an option.
The game also seems to have a hard time letting go of its' pre-made ship designs. It generates a "new version" of the stock designs every time you unlock a new technology (even if it had nothing to do with spaceships). What's either sadder or funnier about it (also irritating) is that they're not even slightly different than the previous version it gave you. Unless you've unlocked a new module, that Corvette M1459 will be the same as the Corvette M1458. It just adds the next number up after the name of the design. No, game... I know you spent many a sleepless night over those blueprints but why would I use designs that are inferior to the ones I come up with. That and mine are inspired by Star Trek... Yours look good and all, but again... Star. Trek. (I mean the designer literally has all the parts you need to make your own TOS Enterprise or TNG Warbird.)
Speaking of the ship designer. Who's the genious that made the background pitch black and then gave the parts' no lighting effects when viewed from below? I already wear glasses. You're not helping, game... The camera controls are also glitchy at times and somewhat frustrating, but that can be deat with. The designer also fails to tell you what direction is forward. Or to give you a unified indication of which direction you're augmenting a part (dimensions
relative in space). So if you ever wanted to see how the USS Enterprise moves in reverse... You can do that...
Other than that, I don't have any major complaints. Some part models are missing thumbnails and the player-made ships don't have thumbnails as well, but at this time, that's a non-issue.
The designer is really impressive, quirks aside. Other "reviewers" compare it to the Spore one, since I'm guessing the one from Gal Civs 2 is before their time. But to compare it to its' past iterration would be like comparing a crossbow and a rifle.
Although not
graphically advanced, the fidelity of the game's textures is impressive. I can see why they're going for the whole "64-bit development only". And both the devs and I do mean it-
, the warning at the top of the Steam page is there for a reason. Even the smallest maps available are quite big and the game renders
at all times. Ship icons on the map are the fully-rendered model of the ship in question, rendered to its' fullest. There can be a dozen black holes on the map, all animated and spinning at all times, as well as stars with planets and moons; and although planets don't spin around their suns (yet?), the moons do. There's also nebulae, dust clouds and asteroid fields, as well as randomly generated wormholes that can be used as shortcuts around the map (if you don't mind not knowing where you'll end up). And everything's always on. For all factions. The game doesn't drop a single model off memory.
Which means that A) It runs like a truck. Alt-Tabbing is guresome, albeit not impossible, even when running it in a window. Loading times are also a pain. With optimisation it's probably gonna get better. But then again B) The actual in-game response is really nice. Once everything's been loaded at least once, the only long waits you're gonna have are if you're loading between multiple saves. You'll still get the odd stutter but that's usually when the game autosaves and takes only a second.
The technology and ideology trees are vast. Really, really vast. If you thought the "tech-web" from the upcoming Civ: Beyond Earth was staggering... This might just one-up it. While not an "interconnecting web with randomised technologies" and still sticking to the tried-and-true linear tree, each faction gets its' own, separate, technologies with different benefits, increasing the variety available to the player. The whole "age of expansion, war and ascention" thing means that at certain times, different techs will cost more or less turns, depending on what tree they're from. Since the ages actually progress as you research technologies under them, it also means that you can't actually research every single technology (as far as I can assume, haven't gotten to the end yet; will change as I do).
The ideology system is equally interesting, albeit as of yet not fully-featured. As you colonise worlds you'll get events with a Pragmatic, Benevolent or Merciless resolution. Each adding to a pool of points you can spend towards some form of passive benefit. That's pretty much all there's to it right now but I'm intrigued at how they advance this feature.
And that sums it up, for now. The AI is from what I can tell limited to "expand as much as possible and produce as many ships as possible" which usually means they have control of about half the map by the time you encounter them and from then-on you get regularly assaulted by the stock "bomber" ships of the faction of your choosing, only later, and then still rarely, being "graced" by a larger vessel's incursion. Imagine someone releasing a swarm of mosquitoes that only comes in small waves and you have a bug-zapper and infinite supply of repellant. Not really a challenge unless on higher difficulties but I'm expecting that to change once they add Diplomacy and fully-feature the tactical combat.
Other than that, I have nothing else to say about the Galactic Civilisations 3 "Beta".
Due to Steam insisting on the "yay-or-nay" system, I'm going to "thumb up" this just because I have faith in the franchise.
However. I will insist on what I said in the begining. A "beta" is "feature-complete" and Gal Civs 3 is anything but that. Do not buy into it at its' current version ("Beta 1"/Ver 0.40) unless you're absolutely OK with not having a fully-featured game. As a long-stanging Kerbal Space Program fan, I can deal with that. But you need to answer that question for yourself. Think before you buy.
Addendum: I would strongly recommend the opt-in patch.

Having just finished the game, my thoughts and feelings about this game are very fresh and may not be as well-rounded as someone who has played this game many times through. These are my first impressions.
Short version of the review: This is a WONDERFUL game. If you don't mind paying the $15.99 price (which I recommend doing before the 20% opeining-week sale goes off), you will seriously not be disappointed.
Now on to some more detailed information.
Abzu is "abzu-lutley" (ha) goregous. From the art style to the graphics- from the fluidity of motion to the terrifying fascination of the world, this game gets full marks from me. I've been noticing a trend for very stylized, polygonal type games and I'll be the first to admit that I am not complaining. Abzu fits into this category with ease as you get immersed into a beautiful and vibrant underwater world. The sea life is incredibly detailed with lighting and the natural flow of the water current really aloowing you to forget that you're playing a game. Most larger sea creatures you are able to ride but with different styles of riding. Medium-sized fish like your groupers and manta rays you have full control over while more predatory oriented ones like sharks and aggressive fish you are pretty much just holding on while they hunt. There are some MASSIVE creatures that you can also ride, but good luck trying to get them to go where you want them to. One of the most satisfying feelings in this game is to grab onto an animal like a dolphin, boost as fast you can towards the surface, and tear through the surface to float in the air like you are on display in an aquarium. All of these things lead to a beautiful game experience like no other that I have played.
Another thing that lends itself to the immersion of the game is the controls. There are actually very little buttons that are used (mainly swimming, interact, flip, and ride) but the way that you move in the water is unreal. Well, I say unreal, but it actually is the most "real" feeling swimming that I have found in a game. The fluidity of your character's movement is astonishing and really gives you the feel that you are underwater. You can do underwater loops, flips, breach through the surface yourself, and generally do all the things that you wish that you yourself can do in the water. That paired with the amazing implentation of the sea creatures' movements, you really feel as if you are the character swimming through this surreal ocean.
The story of this game, if you want to call it that, is very ambigious. There are clues as you progress through the sea, finding bits of information through hieroglyphics that give you somewhat of an idea of your place in this world. Having only played the game once and not really focusing too terribly much on the story and enjoying the experience, I was able to get a rough understanding of what the backstory is and what the goal is. The overall theme of the game is actually a bit darker than I had anticipated but left me feeling content and accomplished at the end.
There are so many facets to this seemingly simply exploration game. Some parts left me with warm, fuzzy feelings inside, while other more intense parts made me somewhat intimidated. The ocean being as vast as it is can be terrifying and Abzu is no exception. This for me is much less of a game and much more of an experience. A lot of me wishes that I had more TO experience... I didn't take my time on my first playthrough but I didn't rush through it either. I explored each area with a fair amount of scrutiny, looking for any rare fish or collectibles that I could find. My firist playthrough took about an hour and a half. I can justify the short length of this game because I got more enjoyment out of this for $16 than most movies that I have seen in the theaters for a similar price. I am excited to get back on the game for another run and see if there is anything that I missed! Unless Giant Squid adds some more content, I don't really see too much replay value in Abzu.
"Cut to the chase, Clay!"
Ok fine.
To reiterate what I said at the beginning, I VERY HIGHLY recommend this game. It is an experience that I am thrilled I got to enjoy and I'm definitely going to tell my gaming friends about this. It is something that you should pick up and experience yourself because words don't do it a ton of justice. Good job, Giant Squid. You are definitely on my radar for future games.

This game in its entiriety is simply beautiful. You'll enjoy this game, especially if you like a mixture of RPG, side-scrolling, action/adventure, and hack-and-slash games.
And it's a good thing that almost anyone of all ages can get themselves imersed into this amazing game. First of all, this game very much reminds me of The Legend of Zelda, but instead you're an animorphic animal that fights against mythical creatures in a mysterious land with the super-powerful Blade of Arrah.
The story is very complex and mysterious too, as Dust (the main protagonist) is trying to remember his memories in order to discover who he truly is. He also has to deal with helping the people that inhabit the land in order to restore order and balance.
And man oh man the hand-drawn animations and scenery are incredible! It gets better as you get closer to finishing the game's story, because towards the end of the game you will see a few, but very well done, fully animated cutscenes. Also, you gotta love the soundtrack. It also ensures that a beautiful looking game can sound beautiful too.
The combat is fairly simple too. You have a button for slashing, and a button for shooting projectiles. The button combinations for sick combos are limited, but easy to master. At the very least, its almost as simple as picking up and playing Super Smash Bros. against your friends. And if you want to find every single treasure that is in the game, then you'll need to do some back-tracking.
The characters are lovable for the most part as well. There was some great talent put into all of the characters to give them enough personality to make them even bearable to communicate with throughout the game.
I almost thought that Dust's friend Fidget would be super annoying, but it turns out that she was a likable and hilarious character. The main antagonist, General Gaius, is also been made to become a menacing and a formidable foe as you learn more about him.

I played through the original witcher twice. I enjoyed the original deeply because of the amazing story, alchemy, and monster killing. When I heard that there was a sequel to this awesome game I decided to pick it up sometime when I found it on a steam sale.
I regret purchasing this game and it is one of the very few games that I have bought and never finish. There are many reasons why I believe this is a bad game. I put in about 10 hours into the game but just couldn't handle all of its issues.
1) story - the original witcher had Geralt being a character with a strong personality set into a world that had a clear theme it wanted to address. However, in the sequel, I find that the story is lacking in many areas. Why would Geralt be the king's bodyguard? why would he involve himself in a war when he spent a great deal of the last game staying out of it? This games seems to have devolved into just chasing around this assassin instead of exploring rich theme and interesting characters
2) combat - the original witcher had a combat system that many people complained about. I too had a few issues with it but overall it did a decent job. For the sequel, the combat was completely redone. The combat is focused around a first person fighting scheme based around light/heavy attacks, signs, blocking, and evasion rolls. This system might have worked but it is generally sloppy. transitioning from parrying to attacking is choppy at best. Evasion rolls and parrying often are choppy resulting in a late parry or bad roll. I also found that this system works decently in solo battles but is terrible with groups of enemies. The game allows for traps/bombs/signs/throwing signs but their use is also choppy so they are generally less effective than one could imagine. It is also near impossible to tell if enemies are going to use a heavy, light or special attacks (some bosses also have possible insta kill attacks). This can be incredibly fustrating during boss fights or fighting enemies with special effects (such as bleeding or poison).
3) alchemy/potions - for starters, the menu for potions is absolute garbage. The alchemy list can be long and it can take awhile to find the potion you are looking for. Most also have significant side effects and they no longer have those awesome secondary effects that could be made in the original. Potions also can only be used during 'meditation' (out of combat). So if you are like me and exploring the environment and get ambushed, you either need to fight on (which can be tricky if they hit you from behind and take most of your health) or run away so you can drink a potion.
4) minigames - the original witcher has several minigames that I found fun and useful to gain extra cash. However, the sequel made the dice game absolutely terrible. it is impossible to make much money since they limited the max bet for Geralt and only the CPU can raise the pot. The game itself is also terrible. The dice themselves are hard to read, there is a quick and poor tutorial (if you even find the tutorial person, I didn't), and you have to physically roll the dice (which can easily fall off the board). The arm wrestling minigame they put in was pretty decent. They turned the fistfighting into a quick time event which I thought was pretty good.
5) crafting - there exists a crafting ability in this game. This ability is useful since traps, weapon, and armour crafting can be useful. However, the menus for crafting are ugly and can take awhile to decipher. There are also ALOT of design plans for crafts; this can then be a pain to find useful plans since each merchant can have a different set. You must also craft from talking with certain NPCs, I understand that I would need to do this weapon/armour crafting but do I really need to talk to some elf so I can make simple traps and bombs? I can make complicated potions in the middle of a forest but I can't make a simple snare trap myself? There is also a cost to crafting EACH ITEM which does a good job to nickle and dime your moneys.
6) stealth - it's just plain terrible. No way of telling LOS of guards or when they can see/hear you. The mechanic that 'stuns' guards that you sneak upon is sloppy and often does not work out well.

This can make your character run around in circles while you (the player) panic and reach to your phone ready to call 991... er... That didn't happen, really. It probably won't happen to you either.
For this early access game, I say yes, it's worth the price. At the very least, it'll show Smoodlez I enjoyed it. You'll have to decide for yourself if you do.

This title, "A Wise Use of Time", however, I cannot bring myself to even FINISHING it.
The pacing... is slow. Oh my god is it slow. I appreciate the fact that it's trying to build itself up, but it managed to break my will to read another chapter.
But really that's not the real problem I had with this game. I do not enjoy the fact that the choice of this game is mainly divided into 2 factor. "Good" or "Evil" - like the "Paragon" or "Renegade" system in Mass Effect. I personally hate this, because it over simplifies our emotion and desire. Previously in the "Choice of Robots", you had to choose what purpose you will give to your robot. Will it represent beauty and grace, or will it spread fear and overwhelming power? Or, will it act like a living human being, and become your friend? It was up to you. The world evolved around you, which is the sole purpose of a "text adventure" game.
Here, it's not like that. Yes, it has many branching paths, but the main dilemma is "Will you, or will you not overuse your power to bend time for your own benifit? Consequences may happen." And this alone may be an interesting book or a conversation - but not a game, which is about the "game play". And it feels like the choices that this game presents are not intriguing enough for me to choose this game over a well written book.

While Final Fantasy VII is a great (if very dated) game at its core, this has every symptom of a poor console port.  It's just a repack of the original port from over a decade ago.  Some things that show it's an effortless port:
-Characters faces are bugged.  All eyes are open, even if they're sleeping. All mouths are gaping, which looks ridiculous after a time.
-Controller mapping is awful (XBOX 360 controller).  The D-pad can't be mapped, which makes battle menus a pain.  You'll often accidentally slide to the side and choose Defend when trying to scroll down the menu.  R2/L2 can't be mapped.  The OK button decides to go "turbo mode" frequently and skip dialog.
-No 16:9 mode (I don't count 4:3 awfully stretched to 16:9)
-Lots of odd crashes.  If you tab out of fullscreen, it will crash.  If your controller idles off while tabbed out in windowed mode, the game will crash.  For a non-autosaving game with 90s-style spread out save points, this is infuriating.
-If it can't sync your cloud saves, you can't save the game unless you exit and turn off cloud saving (losing your progress in the offing).
If you played this in the 90s, and you want to give it a nostalgic run, go for it.  But know that you're going to have to accept a lot of lousy-port-isms.  If you didn't play this in the 90s, the dated graphics, old gameplay mechanics and PC quirks will make you regret the purchase. I wish I could give it a 6.5 instead of a "Not recommended" because it is still fun, and it's great to go back and play.

Having just finished the game, my thoughts and feelings about this game are very fresh and may not be as well-rounded as someone who has played this game many times through. These are my first impressions.
Short version of the review: This is a WONDERFUL game. If you don't mind paying the $15.99 price (which I recommend doing before the 20% opeining-week sale goes off), you will seriously not be disappointed.
Now on to some more detailed information.
Abzu is "abzu-lutley" (ha) goregous. From the art style to the graphics- from the fluidity of motion to the terrifying fascination of the world, this game gets full marks from me. I've been noticing a trend for very stylized, polygonal type games and I'll be the first to admit that I am not complaining. Abzu fits into this category with ease as you get immersed into a beautiful and vibrant underwater world. The sea life is incredibly detailed with lighting and the natural flow of the water current really aloowing you to forget that you're playing a game. Most larger sea creatures you are able to ride but with different styles of riding. Medium-sized fish like your groupers and manta rays you have full control over while more predatory oriented ones like sharks and aggressive fish you are pretty much just holding on while they hunt. There are some MASSIVE creatures that you can also ride, but good luck trying to get them to go where you want them to. One of the most satisfying feelings in this game is to grab onto an animal like a dolphin, boost as fast you can towards the surface, and tear through the surface to float in the air like you are on display in an aquarium. All of these things lead to a beautiful game experience like no other that I have played.
Another thing that lends itself to the immersion of the game is the controls. There are actually very little buttons that are used (mainly swimming, interact, flip, and ride) but the way that you move in the water is unreal. Well, I say unreal, but it actually is the most "real" feeling swimming that I have found in a game. The fluidity of your character's movement is astonishing and really gives you the feel that you are underwater. You can do underwater loops, flips, breach through the surface yourself, and generally do all the things that you wish that you yourself can do in the water. That paired with the amazing implentation of the sea creatures' movements, you really feel as if you are the character swimming through this surreal ocean.
The story of this game, if you want to call it that, is very ambigious. There are clues as you progress through the sea, finding bits of information through hieroglyphics that give you somewhat of an idea of your place in this world. Having only played the game once and not really focusing too terribly much on the story and enjoying the experience, I was able to get a rough understanding of what the backstory is and what the goal is. The overall theme of the game is actually a bit darker than I had anticipated but left me feeling content and accomplished at the end.
There are so many facets to this seemingly simply exploration game. Some parts left me with warm, fuzzy feelings inside, while other more intense parts made me somewhat intimidated. The ocean being as vast as it is can be terrifying and Abzu is no exception. This for me is much less of a game and much more of an experience. A lot of me wishes that I had more TO experience... I didn't take my time on my first playthrough but I didn't rush through it either. I explored each area with a fair amount of scrutiny, looking for any rare fish or collectibles that I could find. My firist playthrough took about an hour and a half. I can justify the short length of this game because I got more enjoyment out of this for $16 than most movies that I have seen in the theaters for a similar price. I am excited to get back on the game for another run and see if there is anything that I missed! Unless Giant Squid adds some more content, I don't really see too much replay value in Abzu.
"Cut to the chase, Clay!"
Ok fine.
To reiterate what I said at the beginning, I VERY HIGHLY recommend this game. It is an experience that I am thrilled I got to enjoy and I'm definitely going to tell my gaming friends about this. It is something that you should pick up and experience yourself because words don't do it a ton of justice. Good job, Giant Squid. You are definitely on my radar for future games.

In Abzû, you can explore various underwater biomes, from green kelps, to dark purple reefs. Freedom and fluidity of movement, simple yet beautiful graphics, combined with a peaceful, graciously composed melody, sooth you into Abzû's world. Made me cry of happiness at the first water stream, as you collect groups of fish to swim with you, while weaving through the ocean's canyons.
Review:
> The story is very straight forward, easy to grasp and to follow. No need to focus to try and understand what is going on.
> The puzzles, if they can be called that, are very cheap, and can be repetitive after the 3rd one.
> You can collect seashells across all of the biomes, and release packs of fish trapped in water wells. You can also unlock meditation statues, to which you can return from the main menu and observe the fish you have discovered.
> I completed the game in 2/1 hours. Didn't collect everything, but also didn't rush through the levels.
> Replayability is locked to going back to specific levels from the main menu, and/or restarting the game.
If you're looking for a one day chill game, this is the one for you. Beautifully constructed levels, music is spot on, explore as much as you want, simple and fun story. If only it had more stuff to do.
PS: Best credits screen ever. ;)

Firstly, all respect to the developers.
This is a game that started out bad. Like, really bad. One of those bad games you remember, yeah, you know the ones.
It's only that this time around the developers said "Hey, we made the game, let's like, fix it and stuff." Then they did. Then they added billions of loads worth of content. So much so they renamed the game about 2 (or 3) times based on how much they updated.
There are tons of maps, modes, weapons, and just variety in general that should make this game a jurassic cluster♥♥♥♥ of nonsensical fun. Why "should" ? Because beyond all of what they have added, all of what they have continued to put into the game, I canno't for the life of me enjoy it.

Every single weapon is simply not enjoyable to use and makes the game feel boring and bleak.
Everything feels like a pop gun with the volume put to 2. I swear to god that sometimes the guns make literally no noise at all. They designed these huge awesome looking assortments of weapons, but they all feel so static and weak it's a joke, and aside from that there is very little feeling of actual impact when shooting anything.
This is seriously a big problem that hinders the entire game unenjoyable, or at least for me. I mean come on, this is supposed to be a giant battle for survival against huge, glorious dinosaurs, but there is nothing-- NOTHING about doing anything in this game that's at all fun to do.
This should be so easy to fix, and I hope to christ they make an update to the game that completly reworks weapon animations, sounds, and effects, because as of now it's loads more satisfying to fling rubber bands at a picture of Jeff Goldblum.
Also the occasional heavy lag and frame drops don't exactly help out.
Is the game worth a doller? Well to you and some others it might be, but there is nothing here that can bring me back unless they just update the guns to make them feel like actual, powerful guns.

"It's global thermonuclear war, and nobody wins. But maybe, just maybe, you can lose the least"
Sums up the whole game in two sentences. The AI is one hell of a challenge. The sounds of children playing and people chatting in the background give it a sinister and forebording side. Graphics aren't very 2006, but this is a Cold War game, based on a Cold War 80s film. The graphics aren't meant to be great, and it helps give an authentic feel to the game. Also, at €10, it's not exactly breaking the bank.
Like no other game out there, this game really brings home the horror and loss that war inevitably causes, and all without any blood/gore effects. It's just the cold, distant '2.1 MILLION DEAD' reports that calmly appear after each hit that show you the impersonal and overwhelming destruction that MAD would have visited on the world. Just like in the film, you'll keep replaying, convincing yourself that you can win, that next time you'll be faster, smarter, better and outdo the enemy. But, just like the film, the only real winning move is not to play.
For best results, use a projector and stand with hands clasped at your back watching the bombs rain down.

Release update:
After almost 2 months of playing the stuff, I don't think I can say much more than somebody like MoldyToast. However, here's my 50 cents:
-Trap disparity is indeed real, and so is Korean RNG. Of the two equal Master-RL Epic traps, I have one T7(+4 spare), the other can't reach T5.
Furthermore, there is Trap Part disparity. I've posted about the subject to, I believe, zero response. The trick is that you can get the same Trap Part infinitely, even if it's almost as pointless as it gets.... OR, and here's the kicker - if there are FOUR traps total that feature this part, you can be sure as hell to get 6+ parts. Because why not, lol. While 30-40% of all parts remain helpfully "unobtained".
-Community is very toxic for this kind of game. Whatever you do - steer clear of DIscus. It exists mostly for veterans to circlej3rk. Don't expect any discussions there, there is NO OMDU community. Some of this applies to the forums.
Oh and... If you know what is the "Barrens chat" - you'll know better than to use the ingame Global chat. You have been warned.
-Gotta handle it to their customer support, they reply very often, although, personally, I think this is the last line of communication one would have to take.
-The F2P system is quite solid, though it is a very hit or miss situation. If you invest into a few weeks of the Pass, you can get much better one-time rewards for the first completion of each star. If you don't... You won't get as much benefit later as you could have.
So, why do I still recommend the game? Because it is fun. And it's not robbing you, like some companies do. Does it have gated content? Yes. Poor community? Yes. Good devs? Yes. Some P2W? Now more than before, thanks Sabotage(sarcasm).
But it's still generally up to you. If you can moderately grind some content, and you are contEnt with not finishing the game, but only progressing up and through Rift Lord(without 5*) - this is a great game to play with some friends, on voice comms, tweaking your crappy T2-5 traps, having fun, listening to great music and lively heroes.
I recommend it, because it is an OMD game. And, no matter how MMOF2P it became, the soul is still there. It's not hopeless. And if you don't have friends - the game scales well in Solo. However, you might want to learn about traps, how to upgrade them and build killboxes - before you choose to solo 3-4 gate maps.
P.S.: Oh and, of course, Sabotage... What can I say...
"It's a mess". This is probably the most apt description, on a many levels.
What is the target audience for Sabotage, based on multiple factors? Ultimately end-game community. The guys, who can do RL 5* with their eyes closed. Who have beaten every endless. Got all hero reward chests. Can oneshot weeklies for 5* on any character. Instead of any kind of improvement to PvE content(like random maps, random enemies, new events, multiplayer rewards, endless rewards) - the devs threw .... THIS.
Just so that these people could pwn each other. Golfclap. And, of course, with the absurdity of the daily quest, the matchmaking, the per time spent reward - comes RANKING.
This here is the point - competitive. You either play this mode competitive, or you play Survival, because you aren't getting anything actually relevant in Sabotage(no chests(besides the daily), no traps).
But... this is a game of grind. Acc\difficulty\trap progression. And, as of the time of writing, it all affects you in Sabotage. So... after being matched as an 80 with people ~10-15, I don't want to think about it any further. They have weeklies with preset traps and fixed level 1, until they do it for Sabotage, kthxbye.  One of the reasons Siege was removed - was because queueing up for it, healthily, was impossible. Premades were babypunching everything. Don't see why this wouldn't happen again.
Also, the whole process of Sabotage - is very protracted. This PvE "twist" comes with delayed waves, persistent "consumable" picks, and, if\until you play TO WIN, and so have some cool consumables, some luck and a good team - pretty much everything you choose is quite pointless. Most likely you will survive all the waves, and how will it settle afterwards? No, no draw, no appreciation. It's PvP, mutha...  You get Sudden Death, a clusterduck of overleveled mobs rushing for your Rift, and... here's the fun part - if your team doesn't have BiS heroes with lots of CC, you are done ducked right there. No matter if both of you scored 25\25 rift points on last wave. This stupid dice will decide the game.
If that is fun to you - I'm glad I could help. If not... well, you can always wait until they polish their "release kicker" into something stable.

There are many things I could say about this game, some good, some bad, but since my final verdict is that I do not recommend this game, I will only list my concerns.
-
Meaning that anyone who was purchasing those loot boxes in the hopes of getting highly desired items was getting robbed of their money because they had 0% chance of getting them.
- The "Chaos Trial" game mode was fantastic when it was introduced. Then they broke it. The random modifiers added to each stage of the mode are fun, it is the hp scaling that is ridiculous. The developers have stated in the forums that not reaching the final stage of the Chaos Trials should not feel like a loss i.e. it is not designed to be beaten, even if your traps are maxed. If that is the case, why the 12 round limit? Of course people will feel like they lost if they don't make it to the last round offered as a possibility. If a 12 round limit is not designed to be beaten at the 12th round, it is poorly designed.
- The "Sabotage" competitive mode has a ranking system which people were abusing by dropping from games if they felt they might not win it, to preserve their rank. This made the people who worked hard to rank up feel like their effort was pointless. When it was mentioned in the forum, the devs simply said they were aware of it, and it was not fixed for another 1.5 months. More recently, devs basically flat-out stated that they are not "catering to competitive players". If they are going to have this attitude, why is there a ranking system? Why are there winners and losers? FFS.
- After spending 1300+ hours in-game and getting all the available loot boxes, I still had some low-tier traps, including one tier 2 trap. I was able to level it up a few more tiers within a few months after "Chaos Trials" and the "Premium Shoppe" were introduced, but that is a bit ridiculous.
- Maps keep getting changed in ways that reduce the enjoyment level.
- Mob behaviour keeps being changed so that mobs behave in illogical ways. This game is a hybrid that is moving quickly away from being a logical thinking game and towards being a FPS-style chaotic mess of randomness.
Immediately after leaving a negative review 8 months ago, listing some of these concerns I shared here today, I started receiving msgs in-game from people saying "kill yourself" and other rude things. I was exclusively a solo player at the time, so I can't help but feel like that was backlash due to the negative review. I deleted that review when the game was officially launched and hoped for the best, but since many of my concerns are not being fixed and are instead getting worse, I feel compelled to warn others of what they are getting into.

In Abzû, you can explore various underwater biomes, from green kelps, to dark purple reefs. Review:
> The story is very straight forward, easy to grasp and to follow. No need to focus to try and understand what is going on.
> The puzzles, if they can be called that, are very cheap, and can be repetitive after the 3rd one.
> You can collect seashells across all of the biomes, and release packs of fish trapped in water wells. You can also unlock meditation statues, to which you can return from the main menu and observe the fish you have discovered.
> I completed the game in 2/1 hours. Didn't collect everything, but also didn't rush through the levels.
> Replayability is locked to going back to specific levels from the main menu, and/or restarting the game.
If you're looking for a one day chill game, this is the one for you. Beautifully constructed levels, music is spot on, explore as much as you want, simple and fun story. If only it had more stuff to do.

Adventure games tell a story which, when told, has no reason to be told again - you know what happens. So they have only one, big shot, and they've got to make it count. Deponia's bullet into my heart is here to stay.
A game that made me scratch my head for ingenious solutions, laugh it off over puns, jokes and references, and hold it in shock over the successive twists.
I loved the varied minigames, unique environments and detailed comments on every possible combination. The author's commentary made me feel at-home, and the meta-references excited my inner gamer. I wish I knew german so I wouldn't miss out on some puns, so if you speak german, definitely play it on that language! The only thing I felt missing from the game were choices - I know it would take tons more work on possible outcomes (and practically a different game genre), but for me it would add tremendously to the dynamic of the story.
Injected with heavy doses of satire and never allowing you to take it seriously, the game paves an unlikely way to your brain, where it exposes different sides, personas and behaviors of society - but it abstains from any judgement, and allows for a cooled-off, conscious overview.
Its blatant anti-hero pierces his way into your heart, turning from the most loathed egomaniac to the most improbable genious (an inspector Clouseau of sorts) and unexpectably lovable companion - to the point that his misses, sacrifices and heartbreak hurt your very feelings. His story of chasing a discouraged dream hooked me from the beginning and
.
The game is, as defined in the beginning of each of the three chapters, "junk, junk... and more junk". Its very honesty, self-consciousness and questionability makes it a definite masterpiece!

I would happily call this game a 9/10.
The voice acting is greatly improved over some of the zany terribleness in the first one.
The combat, while not absolutely perfect, is streamlined from the previous entry, and fits the game and its environment very well.  You are forced to utilize your potions and upgrades if you want to be successful, and some of the extraneous things are removed from the last one.
As with the Witcher 1, the game's story is mature and steeped in the politics of the world's nations.  For some, that might be a little heavy, bit in the day and age of Game of Thrones, I think most people will be able to enjoy it for its intrigue and depth.  It speaks volumes that I didn't skip through any of the story, even though I knew on several occasions that an NPC was about to talk for at least 15 minutes.
The graphics and sound in this game are both great, no real drawbacks to be found there.
The only thing that I would have liked to see improved on is the fact that the levels, while large, are disconnected from each other, which makes the game feel a little more linear than I would like.  This is something they've addressed by creating a fully open world for Witcher 3.
I would strongly recommend playing through this now, in preparation for Witcher 3 when it hits.

I have been a fan of Edmund Mcmillen ever since he was back on Newgrounds, so the second I saw a compilation of all of those games redone come on sale, I was quite excited to jump back into the fray of the physics-platformers the man is known for, especially the original Meat Boy, which is fairly nostalgic to me.
Now, briefly, let me sum up the games: they're fine.
They're still well designed, sometimes brilliant little games that achieve so much with so little. I enjoy Spewer's, Time ♥♥♥♥'s, Aether's new smoother, crispier selves. Meat Boy was thrown under the bus.
Meat Boy is a very good game with consistent controls. These controls, while a tad floaty, are suited to the game's design. Meat Boy jumps just within the right height and width the character needs to see to the end of the level, turning this struggle into an elegant foray of taps and clicks. Every time you press the space bar, you feel in control of the hang time and brevity of the leap. It's simple and comfortable for a game with vertically designed levels in mind.
Super Meat Boy's levels are, for the most part, horizontal, and designed for a controller.
So, whoever decided to throw out the original controls in turn for these new ones is an idiot.
Meat Boy, as a game where it's levels are designed with the controls in mind, does NOT work with new controls.
Simple.
Now the game plays like an awkward, floppy piece of meat, where instead of dancing across levels, now feels as entertaining as swinging a stick around in a figure 8. Also, the stick is falling apart, constantly. As SOON as you let go of the space button, Meat Boy plummets to the ground as fast as he left. There is no arch like there was in the original, just because more people played Super Meat Boy and that's what they're used to.
And hey, on a controller, I'M used to that too! But guess what? No controller support!
AND, you can't change the controls back to the original!
MAN. I LIKE THIS REDESIGN.

Following sometime after the events of the first game, The Witcher 2 (W2) is a continuation of a dark, gritty tale rife with political intrigue, shifting alliances and conspiracy, hard choices, and even redemption and love.  The story feels suitably epic and the dialogue quality tends to be fairly good, although there are still some awkward bits at a mechanical level--for example, questionable word use from a linguistic perspective and the flashback segues arekind of stilted, although at the same time the dynamic journal entries are often a treat to read through.
Combat mechanics are changed from W1, and although a bit awkard to get used to at first, I ultimately found them to be more satisfying and tactical.  There are only two combat styles, essentially "light" and "heavy," plus active blocking, parrying/counters, Sign usage, bombs, and thrown daggers.  Combat felt much more intimate and interactive in general, rather than just a series of glorified quicktime events, which was a definite improvement over W1.  But despite this, there were still a few frustrating, gimmicky, or annoying QTE's spread throughout, like with the Kayran boss fight in Chapter 1, which could have either been reworked or even eliminated to the betterment of the overall game.
Some of the sidequests and related puzzles are good, deepening immersion and further enhancing the player's understanding of the game world; however, some of the less inspired kill quests, fetch-tasks, or obnoxious rune puzzles merely distract and muddy the experience.  More astute players than myself would probably be less frustrated with them, but I found myself skipping non story-related sidequests some of the time, just because the sheer effort required to complete them totally broke the game's flow for me.
Skills (aka talents) in W2 are also an improvement, although they are doled out far too sparsely, so I would suggest modding the game to give yourself at least two talent points per level, if not three, rather than the paltry single point that the game defaults to.  Doing so will allow you to become a true wrecking ball by game's end, although you'll likely want to turn up the difficulty at least a bit.  Relatedly, assuming you start the game on normal or above, the first chapter will be very punishing and unforgiving, but the difficulty curve really starts to flip midway through the second act, meaning that a lot of the combat challenge is gone by the time you're ramping up for the end game--short of difficulty increases or related modding, of course.
More generally, W2 is like its predecessor in that the game is full of many different shades of grey--sure, some characters and actions are demonstrably better or worse than others, but there is very little of the decidely binary, black/white morality-type stuff that is by far and away the norm in CRPG's these days.  The game presents thorny sociopolitical issues and racial dynamics, and it regularly forces the player to chose what is, at best, the lesser of two evils in the service of the greater good (assuming that's what you're going for, of course).  Even though the games decision points can sometimes feel a bit forced, it's still a rare treat to play through a gritty, epic fantasy tale that addresses racism, terrorism, imperialism, and a whole host of other adult subject matter in a believable and engaging way.
Highly recommended.

The storytelling is excellent. It is presented in chapters narrated by a bard, which makes it feel like you are truly experiencing a real story. The voice-acting is quality but the facial animation is quite mediocre. The lore is rich and obtained in standard fantasy fare: books and townsfolk. The art design is excellent: monsters, NPCs, and the world itself all feel cohesive. The audio augments the atmosphere as you trudge through sewers, hike through forests, and explore ancient ruins. This game presents moral choices, in shades of black, to the player which affect the world and your companions. It should be noted that the sidequests in this game range from mundane fetch quests to some of the best I've seen in a RPG. A drunken troll and haunted ruins of a hospital are just two that spring to mind (they are also excellent examples of the ambiguous morality of the world). The UI needs a bit of work: It is cumbersome and the save files cannot be deleted in the menu of the game. Many items are seemingly useless (not even fetching a nice profit from merchants), some of the mechanics are poorly explained (mutagens), and the signs (equivalent to magic in other games) are inconsistent in usefulness (Quen, for example, is overpowered, while you will rarely use some of the others). However, this is a quality low-fantasy game that tells a tale of political intrigue and anyone interested in investing ~30 hours should definitely play it. Oh, and nudity.

Mafia III is one of these titles that begin off a rough patch, literally.
Serious bugs that have been fixed ovee time, particularly in game mechanics, the 30 FPS frame lock, among others.
Despite its' achievements as a spiritual successor to Mafia II, an excellent game in its' own accord, Mafia III is a let-down.
Let me tell you why:
(a). Graphics: For the kind of resources that Mafia III demands, graphically, its' not worth the system requirements. Terrible textures, even on Ultra, and a serious resource hog even on current-generation rigs.
(b). Repetitive, mundane tasks: Find this guy, kill this and that. No, seriously, even with the new DLCs, it falls short of what an 'open-world' game ought to deliver.
(c). Character development: The story telling is amazing, and some characters shine off really well. However, it feels as if the villains are severely underutilized. The "Vaas Issue" in Far Cry 3 play back all over again. The variery of choices and consequences do add some replay value somewhat.
All in all, a great game with great potential let down by serious missteps such as late DLCs and initial show stopping glitches that are still being addressed.
What would have saved this game and brought it at least to parity with Mafia II would've been a timely release of its' DLCs and a break from its' rigid, nearly linear story progression and mundane progress.
Another gem: Is this worth the $50 asking price? Not even close.  If you must get this game, do so on a sale.

Where to begin w/ this game.... Spoilers may be in this review, they will have the black spoiler covering however should they appear and should you choose not to read them.
I really wanted to like it, really I did. The idea of playing a black man in this time line (not long after MLK's assassination IIRC)  could've offered some solid tension. The game also mildly solved a question myself and others had w/ Mafia 2 in that there are side missions to make the city more than just an open world to joy-ride around in before you start the next mission.
The problem is that for all the attempted good they tried to add, Hangar 13 still fell short.
You play as Lincoln clay, an African American veteran of the Vietnam War. The very fact that this gets glossed over felt like a pretty huge mistake. Mafia 2's opening scenes (wherein you play as an infantryman in WW2 during the invasion of Sicily) gave a sort've baseline, we know WHY Vito (Mafia 2's Protagonist) was intrigued in the Mafia because of witnessing Italian and/or Sicilian soldiers lay down their arms at the behest of a Sicilian crime lord whom they respected and/or feared.
We don't really get an image or idea of WHY Lincoln is the way he is because aside from a brief mentioning of a 'rough childhood', we know next to nothing about the character.
Theres also the fact that while Hangar 13 put up a warning at the start that the game uses racial slurs and tries to apologize for the racism...theres really not much overt racism going on in this game. There are a few instances of people using &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; which while offensive is hardly the most racist thing we've ever seen in gaming. There are a few instances of buildings not wanting you there because they're segregated for Whites only...but thats just part of the era. I felt the warning was a smart move as it made it clear they don't condone this and generally preventing easily offended schmucks from getting up in arms but if you're going to use the warning, I would've rather seen them go all in and truly highlight just how tense the situation was.
Next we have the side characters....and while each had their own little details I found annoying, I found myself sympathetic to only several characters in the entire setting. 4 to be exact, all of them side characters, your allies to be exact. One of which is a character whom returns from the previous game in the series (Mafia 2). The rest of the characters could've fallen off the face of the earth and I wouldn't feel the slightest emotion over it.
So..The gameplay...Combats actually not bad, the problem is that I never really felt a need to buy any weapons beyond the M1 carbine and a silenced pistol (For when I need to be sneaky). The rest were all useless, most of the items you get from allies are in fact useless Molotovs and courier (for dirty money) aside.
They've added in some degree of vehicle and clothing customization which is nice but was a band-aid on a rather festering wound of the game's release which tanked. While I mentioned the fact that there are side missions for you to complete now, on the whole, they are incredibly repetitious....in fact this entire GAME is repetitious. Your missions generally comprise 3 things:
Drive from Point A to Point B
Drive to Point A, Kill target B
Blow something up.
There ARE a few moments in the game where interesting moments come up but for the most part its just more of the same and the ending is terribly anti-climactic

I have always been a big fan of Jim Datillo since his release of "Zombie Exodus".( Which I reccomend anyone to pick up if you have available funds) What draws me to Jim is his style of writing and choices that he presesnts his reader, however I feel "A Wise Use of Time" sadly fell a bit shorter than I would have expected or liked. I am not going to say that I didn't enjoy it becasue I clearly did, it just didn't feel like it had that big of an impact on me compared to some of his other work. The characters in all of his stories are phenominal and the situations he places you in always feel real, and this can be said for this game. But in my opinion of where this game falls short is consequence. I didn't ever feel like I was doing something wrong or that a choice I made could alter the story heavily in any way a.k.a there wasn't a breaking point for me. Another issue would have to be the fact that although the characters were very well made, I didn't feel a real connection to them compared to some other reads. It also didn't have me yearning for more after it was over or during it to be honest. It was a slow ride that I went through and like a decent book I only picked up whenever I saw fit.
My review however may be slightly biased becasue I am comparing this work to "Zombie Exodus" which is a completely different setting. There really is nothing wrong with this peice especially if you are into the "Choice Adventures" so I would reccomend it, but I personally just felt slightly disappointed in it. I just don't know how to share my thoughts on this piece of work correctly, so instead I will leave it at a rating. 7.75/10
P.S. He has a current sequel to Zombie Exodus in the works right now. This makes me as giddy as a school girl, also

Minecraft, Terraria, Stonehearth... All are great Survivor/Collector/Adventurer/Builder games.
Forsaken Isle puts a fresh spin on these greats with an early access, but solid concept with the appeals of some of my personal favorite types of games. After my first few deaths from starvation, wraiths, and other carnivorous monsters, I began to get the hang of this little game. before long, I was mining ores for weapons and armor, farming too much food to eat, and catching the all too cute piggies for my pig pin. I've been chopping through forests, fighting tribal tiki people deep in marshy jungles, and fought hordes of zombie pirates and goo balls in the cavernous depths below my growing homestead. before I knew it, 6 hours of my life were gone, and I had only bought it 7 hours ago.
there's plenty going on in this game for an early access, and I'm hoping there will be a consistent updating... Forsaken Isle could go places on the right track.
As for what attracted and hooked me in to this? Well...
-Terraria-esque, pixel-art graphics paired with an overview, fixed angle camera, gives the feel of good old' Dungeon Crawlers.
-painfully simple controls make the learning curve a breeze, and easy to get in to.
-Collect, craft, and survive a rugged land full of monsters, mysteries, and many things to explore.
-An interesting crafting system encourages you to discover new items through trial and error.
-A simple and clean farming system; no watering, no fancy irrigation layouts, just a tilled plot of land and an interesting selection of fruits and veggies.
-Thwack, smack, and slash monsters with an array of weapons from swords to boomerangs, to blowpipes and throwing knives.
-wide variety of crafting stations start you from humble wood and stone tools to the fancy living style of jewelry and pizza.
--The biggest of my qualms that I have with the game is the rapid pace that your hunger bar drops, leaving you scurrying around for food, or dying of starvation (it will happen... more frequent than you'd think.).
--Armor, you get a head, torso, and 3 accessory slots for the likes of rings, boots, etc.
I'd like to see boot/leggings get their own slot, and maybe some sort of shielding... but perhaps it's best in its simplicity.
--my other issue, it a small one... the sounds... there's a squawking bird that could come down an octave or two, but that's why they made mute buttons.
Altogether, Forsaken Isle, with its retro pixel art graphics, easy to learn aspects like farming and fighting, will quickly have you losing hours off your day. And if you're a fan of the likes of Minecraft and Terraria, this needs to be in your Library.

I'll preface this review by saying I love the "choice of games" series and CYOA novels in general. As a standalone CYOA game, I believe that it performs admirably especially when accompanied by a suitable youtube mix (I recommend most epic music ever by HDSounDI). While as a whole, the text was uniformly above average, there were certain sections where I thought that the choices presented and the outcome that results were disjointed or even directly contrary to what I chose. These moments only occured twice, yet it was the first time I've ever encountered an event like that in any of the choice of games series.
When comparing this title to previous choice of games I couldn't help but to feel a little disappointed. While the obnoxious use of weird pronouns evident in the previous title "Versus: The lost ones" was not present, the choices presented seemed less meaningful. Directly prior to playing this I played "Choice of the Deathless" and when I finished that, I felt a deep sense of contentment; a belief that the choices I made in the novel shaped how the story unfolded. Sadly, I did not experience anything similar to that when I finished this interactive novel. In fact, I had barely any sense of closure from finishing this, which makes a certain degree of sense due to it being the beginning of a new series but was still quite disappointing.
Due to my profound love of this genre, I would still recommend this game, yet if you are just getting into the choice of series, I would advise you to play choice of robots or choice of deathless first as they are much stronger novels. Following that I would play the greek hero story, then Versus and the heroes rise trilogy. Once you finish those and are still aching for more, there are a variety of text adventures on their website which can be bought easily using google wallet. Basically, what I'm saying is play their other games first, and if you need more then come back and buy this.
TLDR: Yes, but only if you are a veteran to the Choice of games series. Otherwise go buy choice of deathless or choice of robots. They are much better uses of your money and time.
