Forsaken Isle is a sandbox crafting game where you start with nothing and advance by crafting more powerful tools and weapons (wood to stone to copper, etc) while exploring the region and fighting monsters.  Although it is Early Access, it is very stable and fun, but could use a bit more polish.  I'm still having a lot of fun crafting items and designing my home base, however.
PROS
+ Simple, effective controls make gathering items and fighting monsters a breeze
+ Large overworld with multiple biomes and underground cave systems to explore
+ Building house/farm/base is easy and fun
+ Progressive crafting and hunger systems encourage exploration
+ Charming graphics
CONS
- Experimenting to find recipes is fun and rewarding at first, but quickly grows very frustrating
- No tutorial, quests, or instructions makes the initial hour of the game seem a bit daunting
- Dragging items from inventory to storage or crafting window sucks (needs a "Shift-Click to move" setting BADLY)
- No storyline or quests makes it seem a little lifeless
- Minimal sound effects and virtually no music

NOTE: THE SCREENSHOTS ON THE STORE PAGE ARE NOT AN ACCURATE DEPICTION OF THE GAME, AS OF V. 0.9.4, WHICH I HAVE BEEN PLAYING ON. (Currently V. 0.9.6, still recommending.)
It's like a top-down Terraria, which is fantastic. This means there isn't platforming, but rather strafing (M+KB), but apart from that much of the gameplay is similar. I will add here that the sprite work is WAY better than Terraria's and though you get less customization overall (1 helm slot, 1 armor slot, 3 accessory slots), I expect this to change as the game develops.
The farming in this game is absolutely fantastic and mesmerizing, easy to pick up and satisfying to do (also super quick, though I expect this to be tweaked later; currently it's way too easy to just farm up a few hundred loaves of bread and solve your hunger forever).
This is a criminally overlooked game, probably because in-game there's no guidance whatsoever (might change but I hope it doesn't; discovery is great in it as it is currently).
Pros:
- Simple and easy controls, mechanics
- Visually beautiful - I expect there to be more variety as the game develops as well
- Familiar gameplay progression (build X to build Y, which lets you build Z, etc.)
- Farming is satisfying and rewarding (best foods through farming AFAIK)
- Exploration is satisfying and rewarding (required to get forging materials, early on you get some good stuff through just walking around)
- You can raise your own pigs/sheep/chicken, something that is often overlooked in many games like this. Unlike Minecraft where you had to gimmick rooms to spawn cows/sheep/whatever before, ranching is built into the game here.
- Auto-detect nearby crafting stations so you're not always switching back and forth for a single item. Bunch up your related crafting stations.
- A lot to do in-game despite early access
Cons (NOTE: The game is EA when I write this review, I expect most of these to be solved on launch because they are quite significant IMO)
- No multiplayer yet. I would be very sad if the game finished without multiplayer, this seems like a REALLY fun MP game.
- Hunger rate needs reworking IMO, currently it drops a bit too fast so you're forced to spend a lot of time foraging until you build a farm, after which your hunger issues go from "urgent" to "non-existant" really fast
- (Saves lag my PC for unknown reasons) < Fixed in 0.9.5
- No way to make multiple items at once (shiftclick, ctrlclick, hold click, etc.); really annoying when you have 1000 logs and need to turn half of those into sticks.
- (No way to split stacks of items, gotta move them wholesale.) < Fixed in 0.9.5
- Item organization button would be extremely useful tbh, it's annoying to manually have to move items every time you craft something.
- Monster variety could probably be expanded a bit.
- Updates are slow. AFAIK the team is super small so don't expect this to fully release any time soon. The game is definitely playable but not finished.
Also under cons, but more bug-related:
- Items never disappear from the map (they just blink forever)
- You can activate doors and refill troughs from across the screen, not sure why this happens
Overall, for an EA game it's surprisingly well polished and I'm really looking forward to release. Honest 9/10 if you don't count the mildly annoying bugs that come with the game not being finished.

I could not bring myself not to do a review on pretty much one of my favorite games.
This game is one of the best platformers I have ever seem. Or Brawler.. or RPG.. or all of them. It is really mixed on what it is.
Now, the fact that, in my opinion, that you are buying a $15 (Or Regional Equivalent) that took 4 years, and only by ONE person.
. (His name is Dean Dodrill, praise him fo what he created)
It's backstory in sales that it was an XBLA Title, during the Summer of Sales (Or whatever the hell it was called) and it was ported to PC. Which, most say the PC port is the best because of how much its graphics are better and run smoother. Christ, I even am playing this on a laptop with max settings and it runs just the same with the lower graphics!
Pros (Settings):
Full on great graphics. Everything is hand-drawn, and the fact that there is just SO much great graphical abilities, it just oozes creativity.
Great Controls. The game has easy-to-learn controls. LMB is to attack, RMB is for Dust Storm, MMB is for Fidget's Projectile attack. Don't have a mouse or have one of the worst mouses out there that scurries away before you plug it in? The game also binds a couple of keys on the keyboard when you need them! It also comes with Gamepad Support.
Cons (Settings):
No "low" resolution. It means that if your framerate sucks (Which I doubt it would), it can only be put to normal, and then you have to turn down resolution all together.
Now, the gameplay is great. It has one of the tightest responses there is. Breathing on your "D" key would make him move mabybe 1/1000 of a millimeter (Not really) And it just has a great system for combat. It is simple, and easy to play.
Pros (Gameplay):
Easy to learn combat system. It even gives you a move list in the "How to play" option.
Responsive Controls. Can't explain that further.
No ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Quests. Sure, there are fetch quests, which almost every RPG has, but it does it with a twist, either meaning you have to get a certain ability or you have to defeat a certain enemy and hope they drop. Or, if you are like me, you cataloug every material you have.
Catalouging System. This system is simple. Sell a material that vendors don't have Catalouged, come back later, more of that come in. There are 42 items to cataloug in all, ranging from rare drops from strong enemies, to extermely common, *cough* Maggots *cough*, and easy-to-find ones.
Pretty much a 3 basic attack system. 3 basic attacks. Swordplay, Fidget's Projectiles, and both combined using Dust Storm.
Cons (Gameplay):
A buggy "No Escape" system. What happens is that if a group of enemies are nearby, you can't move on to the next area until you kill them. Which is good, but the fact that you can just do a perfectly-timed Dash and go through it.
Lack of weapons. Your only weapons are Ahrah and Fidget's Attacks, no bows or shotguns, or special little bombs. This is 45% good, 55% bad, as for the fact that enemies can kill you in the air or with cheap high-damage attacks with no block ability.
The Story is a great narritive. It truly is. It's not a yiff and anthro fanfic like most ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ would expect, but instead it is a great story of loss, death, and redemption. I rarely see how even the character is actually something else than he thinks.
Pros (Story):
A highly believeable story. This story is actually like as if you knocked your head on something, went into a coma, had terrible amnesia, remembered your bad deeds (or at least what you think you did), and redeem yourself for what you did.
The furry/anthro undertone can be removed and nearly nothing would be changed but the mood.
Things are usually explained. As I mean this, either what happens is explained through dialouge, notes, or the unfolding story. I.e. There is a large enemy known as a "Trolk", and they ae explained that they can only be killed by stunning them, mainly because how thick their skin and sheilds are.
Cons (Story):
Independent Voices. This is only reflecting the bad of it, which is the microphone and recording quality. They are actually different, some are obviously extremely far from their microphone, while others are actually talking in the right sense.
No real "Choices". The only choices you really get are that, in a side quest, you choose to add poison ivy to an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥'s clothes. (Either way is an achievement). Sure, there is only a "Good" ending, but that means what would be the bad?
Overall Score:
9.5/10

I got the Deponia trilogy as part of a sale and wanted to try it out since I've been itching to play a point and click adventure game after so long. The first game immediately impressed me with its art direction, voice acting, and humor. Some of the puzzle solutions were a bit harder for me to solve since I had difficulty finding which items could be interacted with or picked up. I think readability is an issue that's present in all three games as there is a dedicated button to show you all of the interaction points in a given scene, which, in my opinion, shouldn't exist in a game where what you click on is supposed to be relatively easy to find?
I had high hopes for the main character having some sort of arc but as I went on playing, I grew tired of him and his egotistical and rather insulting personality. It's fine to have an unlikeable character as a protagonist but when they experience no growth whatsoever, even after being reprimanded and unbelievably forgiven by some who were deeply wronged by him, it starts to feel a little irreverent. Most times he doesn't even suffer consequences for his actions which made less and less sense the more the story went on.
There's also some characters, most of them women and minorities, which are handled poorly throughout the games. I rolled my eyes at some of the tropes used like an Asian character being given a "mystical" background and funny accent to a trans woman in the process of transitioning being a source of humor but some of the later game's humor are worse.
Anyway, if you really want to play this trilogy i liked the first and second games but I definitely wished I skipped the third game. It's not worth it.

The Deponia series is a classic point-and-click adventure where you control Rufus, a young man living on the planet of Deponia, and trying to get to the idylic floating city of Elysium.
As far as point-and-clicks go, Deponia is pretty-much what you'd expect. You talk to characters to learn about the story and figure out what you need to do to progress, as well as pick-up, combine, and use items to solve problems. The series also features mini-games, though if that isn't your thing or you just get frustrated with them, there is the Skip option which auto-solves them for you so you can continue.
Design-wise the game looks great, with its animated style. The characters are quirky and interesting, and the voice-acting is good as well. It's a funny game that had me laughing out loud more than once. There were a few occasions where the solutions for puzzles were a bit out of left-field, but they are, for the most part, fairly solid. The only actual gameplay issue I had was the fact that, for some reason, it didn't always like to let me select items in my inventory. For whatever reason, I would sometimes need to click an item multiple times to select it. Thankfully, that was only an issue for the earlier parts of the series.
Here's the basic premise of the story:
Deponia is a planet whose inhabitants generated so much garbage over time that the world is literally covered in it. Things are so bad for Deponia that finding clean water is like striking oil or discovering a gold mine. At some point in Deponia's history, the upper-crust elite built Elysium for themselves, an idylic city floating way above the trash-heaps, and conected to Deponia only by a single tether, which is guarded and patrolled by their military servants known as the Organon. Rufus, a citizen of Deponia, has long dreamed of escaping their garbage-heap of a planet and living in the lap of luxury in Elysium. Unfortunately for him, and everyone around him, Rufus, while remarkably clever in his own crazy way, is too lazy and conceited to bother with such things like considering the potential consequences of his actions or myriad ways in which his inane schemes could go wrong. As a result, he's known as a walking disaster, and is a social pariah. (Not that his ego would let him consider that he's anything but the greatest person on Deponia.) Things, however, take a different turn when Rufus comes across an Elysian woman named Goal, and realizes that helping her return to Elysium may be his own ticket in. Thus begins his adventure.
One of the more interesting things about Deponia is Rufus himself. Unlike most "heroes" he is only tolerated at best, and with good reason. He's careless, egotistical, and his main motivation is "how will this help ME?" This fact is often lampshaded by his friends as they groan in exasperation and wonder what spectacular way he'll screw things up this time. However, as terrible as Rufus can be, it also helps to highlight his good points. He may be an egotistical, self-serving jerkass, but that doesn't mean he doesn't care. In fact, there are several points where his zany schemes may actually have worked out if he hadn't sabotaged them himself to save his friends. (Of course, they wouldn't have been in danger if not for him, but still...) Rufus is a flawed character, a BADLY flawed character, but one can't help but root for him in the end.
The rest of the other characters, both major and minor, play pretty well off the ego-centric Rufus, and the overall story and progression of the games is interesting, exciting, and amusing. If you're looking for a wacky point-and-click adventure that's laugh-out-loud funny, intriguing, and more than a little insane, I'd highly recommend Deponia.

If you're not playing on hard difficulty, it doesn't really matter, and most strategies are taken on rambo style. Body modidications increase health, increase firing rates, jump heights and more. I've seen the deathmatch in the game, but the lack of players leaves it hard to fight for any top player space.
It's not really good, but not really bad either. I like it, but not that much. There are lots of qualities that come up and can be taken advantage of to make your game even more fun, but there's nothing entirely worth mentioning. For the price, you should get it for sure. Great RPG with a complex, branching storyline, fleshed-out lore, mature themes and featuring a cast of flawed thus interesting characters. You can talk to almost every NPC, open practically every door.
Combat offers a variety of strategies, between the different signs, potions and oils, so if you feel like mixing it up to keep things interesting as you play, you can.
I do have a couple of points to criticize.
First off: the tutorial. So poorly executed it almost puts you off the game (prompts badly explained, providing way to much information too fast or not clearly, etc.)
I also feel the level design, particularly in chapter 3, is too labyrinthine. Not to say I need straight lines, but you spend an awful amount of time trying to figure out how to get from one area to the next, because of walls not on the map. More frustrating than challenging to me. And that ties in with my main criticism: the map/quest trackers. In a game so densely populated and interactive, I could really have used better quest trackers on the map. I approve of not displaying the location of a quest giver before you've even talked to the guy, but once the quest has been handed out, or if you've already met the NPC, a map marker would save you having to run around the map clicking on pratically everyone to find the person you're looking for. I ended up using quite a bit of pen and paper to keep track of NPCs, puzzles and the like because the map and to a certain extent, the journal were insufficient.

Underneath the crusty PC port is the game I love, shining like a jewel. But, with cloudsaving that, more often that not, doesn't work, an immensely rocky entry because of an account requirement for a single-player  game that should not have been a concern even months after launch on Steam, and multiple progress stealing crashes, FF7 for PC is not a game I can recommend, even as a diehard fan. It is just too much hassle, both in and out of the game.
Update: Not really as upset with the game, but I still don't recommend the game, even to my friends. People who love Final Fantasy will play this regardless, just as I have. I don't encounter nearly as many crashes as I used to because I play it on a stronger computer, but have still encountered some. Cloudsaving is still a consistent problem, however. Though it works more than it doesn't, the times it doesn't are frustrating and can go on for as long as an entire day. The irony in this is that the player requires an account or linking of Facebook info, in part, because of this feature. To force a player to go to such lengths just to play a game that never required this in the first place for a feature that works so infrequently is not a good justification. This is not even mentioning that Steam has these functions covered, should the effort be put in. In text, it seems like a poor port.

First off, I'd like to say that Paladins is not an Overwatch clone. They were in development at the same time, but OW was released one month earlier than the Paladins closed beta.
With that being said;
Paladins is a very, very fun game. All of the champions are pretty well balanced (for the most part) and the game runs very smoothly with easy controls. The tutorial isn't super deep in but it's still very helpful in comparison to if you were to just be thrown into the game.
While some may complain that you're up against bots until level 5, I think it's great. You need experience before being in a match with experienced and amazing players, experience that the game provides. It's not like leveling up is hard either. I'm almost level 30.
I do have a few complaints which aren't really that affecting of the game, but should be worked on:
- Not being able to leave a match unless your party member isn't in it
- Being thrown back into a match even after you've closed the game unless you restarted Steam
- Getting hardly any gold from a match unless you buy the boost and/or have the party boost
- The amount of coins it takes to buy a single part of an outfit for a character is almost as much as it costs to buy a new champion
- Skye not having a movement ability
Other than that, the game is wonderful. I definitely suggest getting this game. It's not a pay to win like many other games are and I hope it stays that way.

I am a game developer with a decade of experience. This is absolutely among my favorite interactive experiences of all time.
I started Miner Ultra Adventures skeptical. You may see the run animation and assume, ignorantly, that it's the result of a novice animator. Not so. You'll notice our Miner is not in a mine. Why, you may ask, would this miner, this hero, be out in the dangerous wild lands? Context clues imply the all too common spine related mining accident. The characters back story is immediately developed.
Who is this unnamed vigilante though? He’s unable to mine, that much is certain. We know he was willing to do literally back breaking work. This isn't a man of half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥passion. So after retiring from the depths, why would anyone assume his life would fall into complacency? No, there must be more.
After meticulous speculation, I saw it. The back issue, that so many would use as a crutch, a weakness, has been harnessed into power. Atop our bold hero's head, rests a weapon of legend. A simple hat, with a bond to our hero and in turn the player. I say “a bond” deliberately. This is not some megar boomerang, its connection to the miner stretches to a metaphysical level, more on that later. Consider its power, this hat could not be comprised of fickle straw. Upon contact with its target it causes a blazing combustion. Consider the weight of such a device. Consider the balance necessary to bon it. Our hero embraces their stiff back as a method of balance.
Now to the aforementioned metaphysical cap connection. The hero does not throw the hat, despite common censies. No, their hand never makes contact with this weapon. An out stretched arm simply wills the cap into combat. Perhaps there is a sentients communicating with the miner, I don't want to speculate on such things, let's focus on facts.
The enemies in this savage world are relentless. The Miners very house is built as a tower, to shield them from the infestation. The infestation of ignorant judgement. What, you may say, these are simply monsters. Don't be foolish, like all of the visuals in this master piece, there is depth beyond first impressions. These creators are giant eyes supported by hopping legs. Obviously this is a prophetic commentary on ignorant reviews only scratching the surface before scoffing. Perhaps further, a commentary on our culture's perspective of the disabled. They eyes creep closer, in masses, stealing the very heart(s) of our hero. Only with the bond of unwavering friendship, between a humble man and his companion headwear, can such things be dismembered.
And so our hero traverses a vast and unpredictable world. One could consider this a homage to Mario, but it went on to inspire mario itself. Mario Odyssey is a clear clone. A magical throwable hat, miner ultra adventures has been there and done that. The student becomes the teacher.
Please, I beg you. Do not do yourself the disservice of passing by this hidden gem.

Very original concept, very nice visual style, silly humor, wacky characters, point and click adventure with some design twists. Deponia is must play for anyone who likes classic puzzle adventures.
Main character Rufus is very chatty and chaotic, and if you dont like him from start its alright. But his lazy, self-centered, and stupid personality will probably grow on you, and you will be curious what next catastrophe he will bring on others and himself. And he definitely has a bit of a good heart, that allows you to like him, or at least pity him. But you will probably pity everyone around him, so there will be nothing left for Rufus.
Puzzles tend to be hard from beggining and easier later, maybe depending on how you get used to games logic, but almost always they make some sense. So you need to use walkthrough very rarely. Of course you need to think hard and use your imagination and association capabilities to maximum, and you will be stuck sometimes, but I think its worth of feeling your own success.
Story is pretty straightforward in its core, but with a lot of complications and sidetracks along the way. So brace yourself for a short (50 hours), but very eventful ride, that will feel like a weeks in the end. I would like to be more specific, sadly I fear of spoiling something even in general sense, so I will restrain myself from that. It is a well-thoughtout, humorous story, with good ideas, and some surprises, easy to remember characters and funny interactions between them. I noticed some people didnt like the ending, but I believe it was decent, and the sequel "Deponia Doomsday" addressed it very well.
I definitely can recommend this game.
Oh, and I want to give a shout out to artists on this project, because game looks visually amazing, with a lot of details, consistent theme and functional composition. It was pleasure to look at all the work they have done.

Early Life
Osama bin Laden was born Osama bin Mohammed bin Awad bin Laden on March 10, 1957, in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, to construction billionaire Mohammed Awad bin Laden and Mohammed's 10th wife, Syrian-born Alia Ghanem. Osama was the seventh of 50 children born to Muhammad bin Laden, but the only child from his father's marriage to Alia Ghanem.
Osama's father started his professional life in the 1930s in relative poverty, working as a porter in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. During his time as a young laborer, Mohammed impressed the royal family with his work on their palaces, which he built at a much lower cost than any of his competitors could, and with a much greater attention to detail. By the 1960s, he had managed to land several large government contracts to build extensions on the Mecca, Medina and Al-Aqsa mosques. He became a highly influential figure in Jeddah; when the city fell on hard financial times, Mohammed used his wealth to pay all civil servants' wages for the entire kingdom for a six-month period. As a result, Mohammed bin Laden became well respected in his community.
As a father, he was very strict, insisting that all his children live under one roof and observe a rigid religious and moral code. He dealt with his children, especially his sons, as if they were adults, and demanded they become confident and self-sufficient at an early age.
Osama, however, barely came to know his father before his parents divorced. After his family split, Osama's mother took him to live with her new husband, Muhammad al-Attas. The couple had four children together, and Osama spent most of his childhood living with his step-siblings, and attending Al Thagher Model School—at the time the most prestigious high school in Jedda. His biological father would go on to marry two more times, until his death in a charter plane crash in September 1967.
At the age of 14, Osama was recognized as an outstanding, if somewhat shy, student at Al Thagher. As a result, he received a personal invitation to join a small Islamic study group with the promise of earning extra credit. Osama, along with the sons of several prominent Jedda families, were told the group would memorize the entire Koran, a prestigious accomplishment, by the time they graduated from the institution. But the group soon lost its original focus, and during this time Osama received the beginnings of an education in some of the principles of violent jihad.
The teacher who educated the children, influenced in part by a sect of Islam called The Brotherhood, began instructing his pupils in the importance of instituting a pure, Islamic law around the Arab world. Using parables with often-violent endings, their teacher explained that the most loyal observers of Islam would institute the holy word—even if it meant supporting death and destruction. By the second year of their studies, Osama and his friends had openly adopted the attitude and styles of teen Islamic activists. They preached the importance of instituting a pure Islamic law at Al Thagher; grew untrimmed beards; and wore shorter pants and wrinkled shirts in imitation of the Prophet's dress.
Osama was pushed to grow up rather quickly during his time at Al Thagher. At the age of 18 he married his first cousin, 14-year-old Najwa Ghanem, who had been promised to him. Osama graduated from Al Thager in 1976, the same year his first child, a son named Abdullah, was born. He then headed to King Abdul Aziz University in Jeddah, where some say he received a degree in public administration in 1981. Others claim he received a degree in civil engineering, in an effort to join the family business.
From Hero to Exile
But Osama would have little chance to use his degree. When the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan in 1979, Osama joined the Afghan resistance, believing it was his duty as a Muslim to fight the occupation. He relocated to Peshawar, Afghanistan, and using aid from the United States under the CIA program Operation Cyclone, he began training a mujahideen, a group of Islamic jihadists. After the Soviets withdrew from the country in 1989, Osama returned to Saudi Arabia as a hero, and the United States referred to him and his soldiers as "Freedom Fighters."
Yet Osama was quickly disappointed with what he believed was a corrupt Saudi government, and his frustration with the U.S. occupation of Saudi Arabia during the Persian Gulf War led to a growing rift between Osama and his country's leaders. Bin Laden spoke publicly against the Saudi government's reliance on American troops, believing their presence profaned sacred soil. After several attempts to silence Osama, the Saudis banished the former hero. He lived in exile in Sudan beginning in 1992.
Formation of al Qaeda
By 1993, Osama had formed a secret network known as al Qaeda (Arabic for "the Base"), comprised of militant Muslims he had met while serving in Afghanistan. Soldiers were recruited for their ability to listen, their good manners, obedience, and their pledge to follow their superiors. Their goal was to take up the jihadist cause around the world, righting perceived wrongs under the accordance of pure, Islamic law. Under Osama's leadership, the group funded and began organizing global attacks worldwide. By 1994, after continued advocacy of extremist jihad, the Saudi government forced Osama to relinquish his Saudi citizenship, and confiscated his passport. His family also disowned him, cutting off his $7 million yearly stipend.
Undeterred, Osama began executing his violent plans, with the goal of drawing the United States into war. His hope was that Muslims, unified by the battle, would create a single, true Islamic state. In 1996, to forward his goal, al Qaeda detonated truck bombs against U.S. occupied forces in Saudi Arabia. The next year, they claimed responsibility for killing tourists in Egypt, and in 1998 they bombed the U.S. embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Tanzania, killing nearly 300 people in the process.
Osama's actions abroad did not go unnoticed by the Sudanese government, and he was exiled from their country in 1996. Not able to return to Saudi Arabia, Osama took refuge in Afghanistan, where he received protection from the country's ruling Taliban militia. While under the protection of the Taliban, Osama issued a series of fatwas, religious statements, which declared a holy war against the United States. Among the accusations reared at the offending country were the pillaging of natural resources in the Muslim world, and assisting the enemies of Islam.
9/11 and Final Days
By 2001, Osama had attempted, and often successfully executed attacks on several countries using the help of Al Qaeda trained terrorists and his seemingly bottomless financial resources. On September 11, 2001, Osama would deliver his most devastating blow to the United States. A small group of Osama's Al Qaeda jihadists hijacked four commercial passenger aircraft in the United States, two of which collided into the World Trade Center towers. Another aircraft crashed into The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. A fourth plane was successfully retaken, and crashed in Pennsylvania. The intended target of the final aircraft was believed to be the United States Capitol. In all, the attack killed nearly 3,000 civilians.

DEFCON is a very interesting game. You take control of a nation's strategic nuclear arsenal, along with their air bases and fleets. The goal is simple: eliminate your enemies at all costs by destroying their defenses and ultimately their cities, while minimizing the civilian losses on your side.
The game begins at DEFCON 4, where you begin to deploy your defenses and units, however no fighting occurs. It slowly counts down through the stages, reaching DEFCON 3, then 2, and finally DEFCON 1, where nuclear weapons are authorized and imminent mass destruction is assured. The game's progression through limited engagements, heightened stakes, and finally unrestricted warfare at the nuclear level perfectly simulates the breakdown of communications and international order that would pre-empt a nuclear war.
You will find yourself paranoid at every movement of the enemy: is their fleet simply moving to defend their coast, or repositioning in order to get within range of your radar? Should you send your submarine fleet in order to prepare to launch nukes on the enemy's towns, or keep it in reserve in order to find hostile navies attempting to attack your homeland? This is especially prevalent in the alliance mode, where an alliance with every player in it is created at the game's start. Slowly, players will suspect one another, causing a breakup of the alliance into smaller factions until everyone believes that their neighbor is trying to nuke their favorite casino.
Games can last from thirty minutes to two hours, depending on players' skill and the game mode, with the fastest games being concluded in 15 minutes or less. I recommend picking this game up with a few friends whenever you can find it on sale. Just be prepared for a few ragequits.

The stealth mechanics are interesting and punishing when you're actually spotted (especially on harder difficulties.) There's no fighting your way out of a situation as a last resort; your only actualy choice is restarting or reacting quickly enough to teleport back into the shadows.
The vibes/graphics/soundtrack are all really solid, and create an immersive experience. (one which is pretty tempting to sink into)
Overall, great game. Would totally recommend getting it.

When I was a Kid I grew up with Games like Battlecruiser,
3000AD, Ultima VIII, that all had certain trends But occasionally, a game comes along and
says "screw That trend!" And in the case of Final Fantasy VII
the end result justifies the means without question. Final
Fantasy VII is, without a doubt, the Greatest game of my
Childhood.
To begin with, Final Fantasy VII is longer than every console
RPG than any other game in that era. It took me a few months to complete the game
the majority of which was spent getting my *Bleep* kicked While getting lost it
is possible for the game to be completed in less time, rushing
to complete it is definitely not recommended.
At least three hours are spent uncovering the main character's
past, with an additional hour each for several other
characters. One of the game's "secret" characters has his own
hour of backstory, complete with his own town that is not even
necessary to visit during the game's normal progression.
What is necessary during the game's normal progression is the
capacity for awe, The game begins in an
enormous industrial complex housed in a futuristic city, and
remains there for the first seven or eight hours of play. Just
when it appears that the entire game will take place in the
city, the venue changes to a fully 3D, fully rotatable engine,
and players will find that the city is a mere dot on the
enormous world map.
When not travelling in the world, players will navigate through
static, hand-drawn locales. And in another huge leap forward
for RPG's are the many ways to travel Players can walk in,
around, on top of, and through submarines, glaciers, amusement
parks, reactors, farms, and dozens of other places. Since the
backgrounds are static, the developers were able to put all
their attention into animating the iconic representation of the
party leader, which is represented in super-deformed polygons,
making it look like crap but who the hell cares
It is unknown who came up with the idea for the polygonal
battles first, Sony or Squenix, but Squenix has been in the
business longer, and it shows in Final Fantasy VII's combat
engine. While only three members can be in the party at one
time, the effects more than make up for the game's only
shortcoming. The graphics are as "realistic" as possible at
least to that extent, considering the genre, with each
character having a distinct look. And since each character uses
a different style of weapon, the animation is different for
each character. But it doesn't stop there - each character also
has several other attack animations, based on their equipment.
The special attacks and spells, however, are the game's
strongest points. All nine characters have "limit breaks",
which can only be used after the character takes a certain
amount of damage. When the limit is reached, the character
attacks and does extra damage to the target. Each character has
at least four, with one having nine.
The spells are the most graphically impressive part of the game
(the game's CG sequences run a close second). There are 70 in
all, 16 of which are FF3-style summons which may be why the
demand for the game has been so huge.
The game's plot is deep and typical of Squenix's prior efforts
quite epic. Squenix takes great pride in its storytelling
abilities and uses a number of flashback sequences, and loads
of rendered sequences and prerendered FMV-Graphics engine to
add greatly to the mood and emotion of the story.
Adult themes and even some uncensored language are in the game
was censored the teen rating for the game is well deserved due
to such mature sexual and violent themes.
All in all, it is impossible to not at the very least not hear
the name "Final Fantasy VII" and automaticly know what it is
about.

The Binding of Isaac manages to mesh a very interesting set of genres and themes like no other video game. There is the obvious roguelike comparison to make, with the random generation and perma-death. But you can also comapare it to RPGs, top down Shooters, Puzzles and Gambling. The systems interact in such a way that you will always be making interesting decisions. Should I use this bomb to detroy this rock and get an item, or should I save it for a boss, maybe I should use it to destroy a slot machine instead?
Early playthroughs will seem greatly based on luck but as you get familar with how the game works you understand it's based on skill and making the correct decisions. It is entirely possible to complete the entire game without ever using an item or upgrade. For this reason and many others The Binding of Isaac is a brilliant game for those who don't have much time, and for those who are prepared to sink hundreds of hours into it. It is as big or as small as you make it yourself.
It may take a while to get into, but that initial time commitment is well worth what you will get out of it in the long run.

The songs that introduce each act is gloriously catchy.
Difficulty-wise, I only occasionally had to resort to a walkthrough (but that's been true of literally every point-and-click game I've ever played!), but on the whole, the puzzles made sense, and even the walkthrough-bits was either that one thng I'd just missed somewhere or made perfect sense in hindsight. (I think there was only one puzzle in the entire trilogy I would have said was a little bit obscure, but even that is debatable.) There's a lot of variety, with little minigames and a few gimmicks that keep it all very interesting and the world and characters are charming.
I feel I should comment on the ending, as it is a contentious point I saw in the other reviews; I didn't have a problem with it myself and felt it was fitting. I can't - shouldn't - say more than that, but we're not talking ME3-levels or anything here, in my opinion.
Overall then, I can definitely recommend this game.

A genuine masterpiece, I can't bring myself to stop playing it at this point. I've had plenty of laughs but also frustration with this game.
Let's start with the pros:
Innovative level design, think Mario 64 (I haven't played it since I don't support nintendo as a company) but aimed at modern audiences, so it's a bit more casual I suppose but still very accessible and fun.
Great combat, it actually is very punishing since sometimes the enemies are unpredictable and learn from your usual patterns, kinda like Shadow of Mordor but more advanced, I'm pretty sure the developers had hard time over designing the combat which I suppose took years to develop. Apparently the game got additional funding from the Brasil government (I think that's the country of origin, whatever it was the government of the country the devs are based in that helped them) which sped up the process by a huge amount.
It's fortunate that happened since we wouldn't have other games have their combat and puzzle design inspired by this. MUA (not to be confused with Marvel Ultimate Alliance) has been a breakthrough title in many aspects since its release but many games unfortunately claim they have invented new mechanics which actually come from MUA.
So, I'll just round it up with a list of features
Pros -
Impressive combat
Great puzzle design (I'd consider myself a puzzle game afficionado and this still blew me away in the first hour)
Amazing replayability, although to note here that I still haven't finished it but I've watched a lot of speedruns
Cheap price, it's pretty insane how cheap it is but in Brazil this money gets you same stuff as in the developed world would with a full 60 dollar release so the difference feels stark only to us.
Continuous dev support, you can send them suggestions and they still release DLC which is amazing!
Cons -
60FPS lock, but the graphics make up for it.
Thank you for reading guys, hope you see my other reviews in the future!

For an indie game I was immediately struck by how detailed and customizable the main options menu was. Usually when you see indie devs using the Unity engine, you maybe have a launcher using the default precepts named "Fast" and "Beautiful" and the like, but here the devs went the extra mile and made sure your average PC gamer could tweak, rebind and customize most of what you'd expect to fit your preferences.
Performance was a bit low, but acceptable on my laptop.
Story is serviceable, nothing to write home about. Artstyle is great, sleek and beautiful, controls and stealth mechanics serve as a good foundation, nothing too complicated, some nice upgrades to spice up your playstyle. The shadow mechanics are a nice twist that work in the context and as the gameplay mechanic.
Aragami also made me think about the puzzling rarity of Stealth Coop out in the market.
Aragami in coop is insanely fun, an intuitive puzzle game, with cooperation not seen in most genres, the plotting it allows, being the decoy or planning traps and movements, makes stealth games the most fertile ground for great coop experiences in my opinion.
Yet there's maybe only something like two other games which have attempted it.
Splinter Cell Chaos Theory, potentially the one most similar to the experience Aragami provides, can't speak more on that as it's hard to play these days without servers (Tungle or Evolve might work though).
And Splinter Cell Blacklist, though I think it falls into many modern AAA trappings.
(Maybe Sniper Elite games by Rebellion allow a fun dynamic coop stealth experience?)
Why are publishers and developers of traditional studios so blind to how potentially lucrative and popular these sorts of gameplay experiences that Aragami provides can be?
They seem to assume that stealth games belong in the singleplayer sphere exclusively, and we have many great ones like that, but if they assume coop would be too boring, as stealth requires a lot of downtime and sheer observation, then they have never thought of how talkative and plotting two friends can be over a microphone.
Which results in lot of fun banter, scheming, and by definition cooperation.
Seriously, everyone, take a look at Aragami and get on with copying what works.

A beautiful tale of love and war, of diplomacy and intrigue, of common people and royalty. The Witcher 2, though set in a fantasy world, feels so very real, as if it escaped from a medieval chronicle or saga. That is the power of the plot that drives it and the highlight of the game. Presented in a very cinematic way, it is absolutely brutal and doesn't shy away from showing things that are considered a complete no-go in this industry. Yes that includes nudity and sex. This gloves-off approach helps build a suitable atmosphere for the story and enhances the experience further. Add to that the numerous choices you have to make that greatly affect how the story plays out and its no wonder this game has the positive reputation it has.
But looking past the story and the atmosphere, the praise subsides. The game is sadly not polished enough. The controls are clunky and sometimes downright annoying. Giving the impression that not enough time was spent on them. The inventory is full of oversights as well, with items ranked in a very arbitrary fashion and never flagged properly. For instance I was stuck with 2 copies of the same book that I couldn't get rid of because it was a quest item... 2 chapters ago. Then there is the difficulty rating system, which I can only describe as broken. I started playing on normal and the game was totally unforgiving, forcing me to reload again and again. So I tried easy, only to be disappointed by the complete lack of challenge.
All things considered though, and despite the numerous flaws, I can only recommend this game. It is a gem, a very unpolished and flawed gem sure, but a gem nonetheless.

An absolutely beautiful game with fluid animations and solid brawler mechanics.
While there is very little in the way of weapon variety, you're still provided with a range of options for taking out enemies from your basic brawler combos to parrying and aerial throws, all of which are animated gorgeously. Despite being limited to one weapon, you do earn additional magic powers and movement skills, such as double jumps and wall clinging, as the game goes on, which help open up new areas to explore places you couldn't before.
The majority of the skills you learn in the tutorial will be your bread and butter through a majority of the game. Thankfully, enemies later in the game do test everything you've learnt, so relying on a single tactic won't do you many favours, with some being only vulnerable to parries and others to magic attacks.
Combined, the combat looks and feels great and doesn't outstay it's welcome for the 9 to 12 hours it takes to beat the game.
The game also borrows a lot from RPGs with a level up system, side quests and a crafting mechanic, allowing you to build upgrades from blueprints dropped by enemies and found in chests. The upgrades usually add an additive or multiplicative effect to stats, item drops or health regeneration, which doesn't occur naturally otherwise.
The entire game is fully voiced, which is an impressive feat for an indie title of this size. There are points where the dialogue feels forced, which can be chalked down to a problem with the script at points, but the main cast do a pretty spectacular job with their characters and help compliment the animation work nicely.
If you have any experience with videogames in the past at all, I'd highly recommend playing the game on the Tough difficulty setting, as the Normal difficulty is far too forgiving. The Tough difficulty gives you a good reason to buy and use consumables without piling things on enough to make you ever feel overwhelmed.
Mentioning the game is programmed and animated by one person is a moot point, but one that's bound to be brought up if you read up on the game on other sites or reviews. The game easily oozes enough quality and polish that, outside some late game cutscenes, you'd never realise or believe one man did all that work over four years.
I highly recommned this game so much, that I even spent time writing out a review of this length. Hopefully, it's filled with enough information to make you consider trying it out. :)

Ed Mcmillen is, arguably, a video game auteur (though, no one would really contest that). If he isn't an auteur yet, he certainly is a recognizable personality and a welcome individual to the world of video games.
The Basement Collection is a bundle of Mcmillen's flash work prior to his big hits ("Super How the Hell Did I Miscalculate That?" and "The Binding of Why The Hell Can't I Stop Playing?"). So, the big question is, do the games hold up?
Well like any art or artist, it takes time to develop skill and hone one's-oh wait, nevermind these games are gold. Honestly, you would think that at some point Mcmillen and his team screwed up and made an awful game somewhere and had to bury it like a dirty secret.
None of these games are some crayon drawing that a parent puts on the fridge to make themselves or their children feel better. The games included in this compilation are all fascinating and top notch, and all of them feel very different from one another. These games all share the familar Team Meat aesthetic and challenge. Out of the games here there should definitely be at least one that will warrant a purchase from you. Maybe it will be the somber story of the adventure game Aether? Or maybe the frantic Grey Matter? Maybe Time ♥♥♥♥, the perplexing puzzle platformer with a dark twist? If you can't find one game here to enjoy, there honestly might be nothing that pleases you.

: Smoodlez
: Smoodlez
: A key for this game was provided by the developer for the purpose of writing an informative review. No other compensation was given.
==========
"Ahoy matey! Me ship crashed on this island, leavin' me alone on this godforsaken island. It's up t' me t' find a way t' survive! This be a survival craftin' game, much like Minecraft, Terraria, and other games in t' genre. I have t' collect resources t' make what I need t' get by. Fightin' monsters, buildin' shelter, makin' food...all be skills that I will need t' survive on this mesterious island."
==========
Forsaken Isle literally dumps you onto a large island with next to nothing. There is no story, except for what is found on the store page. You play as a pirate whose ship crashed on this island. You don't start with anything. You'll have to forage for supplies and gather resources to build and craft tools to build and survive. The first night is very important, as you should be able to build some walls around yourself with a campfire to light your area, to ward off monsters.
There is a somewhat robust character creator (robust for this type of game with it's graphics), allowing different heads, hair, and other features. There is also a random option.
As you discover new materials and resources, new recipes are made available to you. But it's your job to discover them and put them to use! This is one of the fun aspects of any survival game: figuring out what does what, what makes what, and what's useless. You can also find/craft weapons and armor, which grant you different effects, such as increased defense or movement speed.
==========
Forsaken Isle is entirely pixel based. Everything looks really crisp and detailed for being sprite-based. While this isn't a heavy 3D modelled game like something from a AAA title, it works. The retro pixel style they've used here is very appealing, and suprisingly pleasant.
Equipping different tools, weapons, and armor all change how your character looks. Put on a Wolf Helm, you'll see a wolf head on your character. Holding a sword? You'll see the wooden sword being brandished.
==========
This is the game's lowest point: There is absolutely NO music in the game whatsoever. MOst everythign has a sound effect though: sword slashes, digging, animals, picking up items...but no music. Not even ambient sound effects like crickets or whatnot. Being an Early Access title, it is safe to assume that the music is just not ready to be implemented yet, and I'm sure it will be in the future. For now, this is a great game to play with your own playlist blasting in the background!
==========
In the dozen hours I played I ran into no issues with the game. No FPS drops, no lag, no stuttering. It's a very minimal game, no one should have any issues running Forsaken Isle. Heck, even a toaster could run it!
==========
A worthy entry into the survival genre that's not an obvious copy of another title, it's almost too good to be true! With some great systems and gameplay already set in place, Forsaken Isle should shape up nicely in the coming months as it runs through Early Access. If you don't want to drop the $8 on it now, just keep an eye out for the next few updates. Even if you do buy it now and are disappointed, $8 isn't as much as some of the AAA titles that have bombed recently and there's a chance it'll shape up into something you'd enjoy later.

Rhythm-based Rogue-Like Dungeon Crawler. Yes. Please.
Everything you do is to the beat of the music, you move to the beat, attack to the beat and die to the beat. And the enemies do too. Every enemies has an attack pattern so if you can feel the beat, you can avoid taking damage, but it's not always that easy when you have a limited amount to time to react (IE. the beat) The music is the first thing you'll notice, composed by the indie game music GOD Danny B. who did the soundtracks for Binding of Isaac and Super Meat Boy (He's done many other games as well, but those two are the other two that I've played and can personally vouch for the music) so you know that the music in Necrodancer is top-notch...which is good considering that's the prime game mechanic.
You'll groove your way through 4 zones, beating monsters, collecting gold, buying items and beating bosses until you reach the final boss which is sometimes different if you play the different characters. All the different characters are truly different and all play very differently and some even have limitations as to what items they can get. All the different characters ensure that you never get bored with the game and always provide a new challenge if you're feeling up for it. Played too much Cadance lately? Switch it up with Melody. Don't like how Melody plays? Try out Eli. Feeling strong with Eli? Now try Dorian. There are 10 different characters to play, including one final, truly insane challenge character that literally nobody has beaten yet so there is always something new to aim for with this game. And even if you can't play some of the harder characters like Aria, Bolt or Monk, you can always lay beatdowns to the beat with all the other characters.

When I was a Kid I grew up with Games like Battlecruiser,
3000AD, Ultima VIII, that all had certain trends But occasionally, a game comes along and
says "screw That trend!" And in the case of Final Fantasy VII
the end result justifies the means without question. Final
Fantasy VII is, without a doubt, the Greatest game of my
Childhood.
To begin with, Final Fantasy VII is longer than every console
RPG than any other game in that era. It took me a few months to complete the game
the majority of which was spent getting my *Bleep* kicked While getting lost it
is possible for the game to be completed in less time, rushing
to complete it is definitely not recommended.
At least three hours are spent uncovering the main character's
past, with an additional hour each for several other
characters. One of the game's "secret" characters has his own
hour of backstory, complete with his own town that is not even
necessary to visit during the game's normal progression.
What is necessary during the game's normal progression is the
capacity for awe, The game begins in an
enormous industrial complex housed in a futuristic city, and
remains there for the first seven or eight hours of play. Just
when it appears that the entire game will take place in the
city, the venue changes to a fully 3D, fully rotatable engine,
and players will find that the city is a mere dot on the
enormous world map.
When not travelling in the world, players will navigate through
static, hand-drawn locales. And in another huge leap forward
for RPG's are the many ways to travel Players can walk in,
around, on top of, and through submarines, glaciers, amusement
parks, reactors, farms, and dozens of other places. Since the
backgrounds are static, the developers were able to put all
their attention into animating the iconic representation of the
party leader, which is represented in super-deformed polygons,
making it look like crap but who the hell cares
It is unknown who came up with the idea for the polygonal
battles first, Sony or Squenix, but Squenix has been in the
business longer, and it shows in Final Fantasy VII's combat
engine. While only three members can be in the party at one
time, the effects more than make up for the game's only
shortcoming. The graphics are as "realistic" as possible at
least to that extent, considering the genre, with each
character having a distinct look. And since each character uses
a different style of weapon, the animation is different for
each character. But it doesn't stop there - each character also
has several other attack animations, based on their equipment.
The special attacks and spells, however, are the game's
strongest points. All nine characters have "limit breaks",
which can only be used after the character takes a certain
amount of damage. When the limit is reached, the character
attacks and does extra damage to the target. Each character has
at least four, with one having nine.
The spells are the most graphically impressive part of the game
(the game's CG sequences run a close second). There are 70 in
all, 16 of which are FF3-style summons which may be why the
demand for the game has been so huge.
The game's plot is deep and typical of Squenix's prior efforts
quite epic. Squenix takes great pride in its storytelling
abilities and uses a number of flashback sequences, and loads
of rendered sequences and prerendered FMV-Graphics engine to
add greatly to the mood and emotion of the story.
Adult themes and even some uncensored language are in the game
was censored the teen rating for the game is well deserved due
to such mature sexual and violent themes.
All in all, it is impossible to not at the very least not hear
the name "Final Fantasy VII" and automaticly know what it is
about.

Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of those games where you didn't know you needed it until someone finally made it.
When this game was first recommended to me, I found the concept intriguing. A rhythm-based roguelike game? It was unlike anything I'd encountered, even in the myriad of Flash rhythm games I played as a tweenager. I decided to buy it on a whim, and boy am I glad I did.
Every element of the game I've encountered so far is practically perfect as-is, even in Beta. From a gameplay perspective, the rhythm and roguelike elements blend together near-seamlessly, with the movement patterns of the player and their enemies syncing with the music; this also adds an element of strategy, as the player learns each enemy's movement patterns and figures out the best way to traverse the different areas. The weapons, items and spells the player picks up can change their play style, whether in a minor or major way, and the option to unlock extra pickups with diamonds (which are found in the levels – no micropayments here!) quickly makes each runthrough of a zone unique. All of these elements are handled with skill and finesse, and ensure a balanced and fair gameplay system; if you die, you know it's your own fault.
The controls are simple and easy to learn, with almost every command mapped to the arrow keys (for example, a bomb can be placed by pressing the left and down arrows simultaneously) and the commands to perform specific actions always visible on-screen. The game is rather forgiving, even for those with little rhythm skills, which makes it easier for new players to learn how to approach enemies or use a new item. None of the commands feel awkward to activate, and the game is incredibly smooth, with little to no lag.
The art design of the game is well crafted; the player character models stand out against the vastly differing backgrounds of the zones, and the enemies are almost instantly identifiable by their silhouettes and color schemes, allowing the player to easily assess a new floor or room. The visual designs of the weapons, items and chests are also well thought out, with the easily distinguishable designs and color schemes of a weapon telling the player what it does and what enchantments it has instantly.
Being a rhythm game, the soundtrack is excellent. Each song is unique to its zone, and all of them are easy to keep in time with. They also set a steadily increasing difficulty curve by increasing in speed, carry the mood of the different areas and give auditory hints (like the location of the singing shopkeeper, or what an enemy hidden in shadow is).
All in all, this is one of the most unique and addicting games I've played to date, and is just too fun to pass up.

I want to preface this by saying I absolutely love the OMD series. I've recommended the first two games to pretty much everyone I know and then some. So when I have to say I don't recommend this, it saddens me quite a bit.
This game feels like, as a friend of mine put it, a chinese knock off of OMD. The game feels far more shallow and bland than the original two games, and as far as polish goes, it feels like the project of someone who never made a game before in their life.
Visually and musically, it looks and sounds great. But when it comes down to the actual gameplay, its like they stripped everything fun or strategic from the game. Now you need to upgrade your traps by collecting hundreds of copies of them to increase their stats minutely. Weapon variety has gone completely out the window, instead replaced by several different characters. Weapons which used to offer different gameplay now are just activatable passive buffs to damage now from what I can tell. Also it seems like headshots are gone? Attacks feel generally weaker, and for some reason theres both a cooldown and mana cost associated to secondary abilities. Which wouldn't be bad, but it seems like the abilities themselves have such a long cooldown that for some characters you couldn't hope to drain your mana enough to ever get down to even half.
I will say that the game isn't terrible. Its playable for certain, but it feels incredibly bland and lifeless compared to the other entries. If you absolutely must play a game like this, there are better options. Smite if you want a more PVP focused game, even Dungeon Defenders 2 is a slightly better PVE experience, though not by much.
Also, for a game thats been in development for what? A few years now, the game feels incredibly unpolished. I'm not sure why it needs to launch a small..browser? Window for basically handling management of traps and buying stuff, then need to launch a full screen game whenever you actually enter a match and visa versa. Kind of weirdly jaring being pulled to fullscreen and back out again every time you finish  or start a stage.

finally finished this game after a long time -- i think i started it years ago, but the save file stayed around every few months i might play it a bit more, do a dungeon, then neglect it. but finally after a few years i finished it. i didn't finish all the quests, or find all the hidden locations, but i beat the main quest and saw the credits, so i figure i'd write a review.
i've been a jrpg fan since dragon quest 1 and final fantasy 1 on the NES, so keep that context in mind -- if you aren't, you obviously might not like the game. but i felt it was pretty good as rpgmaker games go; quite long, lots of exploration, tons of secrets.
on the negative side, the story wasn't that interesting -- at least, not until late game, then it got somewhat more intriguing, but it was never a story that kept me on the edge of my seat, and i never really cared about the characters or plot or setting. but it did have some interesting npcs, the occasional bit of clever dialogue, or an interesting puzzle or dungeon here and there.
also, the main character in particular was annoying, he was constantly insulting abusing the second main character for no good reason, often when she hadn't said anything he just felt the need to throw in a random (pun, his name is "random") insult her way. his entire personality can be summed up by 'randomly insults his allies, and brags incessantly' or even 'donald trump: the jrpg protagonist'. on a scale of likeability of heroes of protagonists, with tidus from final fantasy being a 1/10 and, say, fei fong wong from xenogears or being a 10/10, random is like a -10/10, he's that bad, and it often detracts from the game to have a main character who you hate to play as.
the other characters are not as bad, but they are often forgettable, and their personalities are often 'jokey sidekick iguana', 'copy of rena from star ocean 2', 'guy with a moustache and big muscles', and other stereotypes and stereotype variations.
also, as a game developer myself, there's a lot to learn from this game in terms of clever quests, interesting dungeon design, and hidden secrets everywhere. it's well-crafted in terms of exploration gameplay, generally. the only thing i can complain about there is no easy way to teleport to where you've been to in the past until the end of the game, which is an issue even dragon warrior 3 solved 30 years ago with its wing of the wyvern mechanic.
the combat is a mixed bag. it's fun, and generally balanced, but there is a lack of description of what each stat does, or what each status ailment does. maybe it's in the manual? but i didn't read the manual, if it has one, and the game itself has no in-game explanation of its mechanics, so often i had to guess. but that isn't uncommon in older jrpgs, so i don't really hold it against it.
overall... if you are looking for a relatively long jrpg with lots of stuff to do, and if, like me, you have already played through all major jrpgs that often appear on 'top 100 jrpg' lists, and are tired of replaying them, you might want to try something new, and there's a wealth of 'new' in rpgmaker-land.

A shooter platformer and a damn fine one at that!
Duck game is one of those games where you could say the Devs thought about everything.
If you grab some friends you can dive into the main game of fast paced deathmatches on a variety of maps with both gimmicks and balanced designs in mind. If you somehow get bored of those, you are covered by a very intuitive level editor as well as the steam workshop where you can get content ranging from maps to weapons, hats and stuff like that.
Locally and over the internet, it supports a wide number of controllers and it's really simple to set up games and customize to your liking in many ways.
Alone? Not a problem really, single player challenges and the level editor can keep you busy. The single player portion of the game can teach you a ton about the mechanics and also make you practice some skills that will be useful for multiplayer, you can even unlock cosmetics and mutators too.
Gameplay wise the game really shines on both it's vanilla map design and weapons, you are sometimes forced to be creative and even stylish with the way you use them and will always keep learning new mechanics and intricacies that can add some really satisfying depth to the combat.
In terms of movement  nothing is ever wasted in this game. Ducks are nimble and control superbly. You can hold the jump button after a jump to flutter (Which also makes you aim diagonally and then up in just a few frames, keep that in mind :>) Ragdolling makes you gain some more momentum for those high jumps you thought impossible, you can slide while running to break windows as well as dodge bullets.
Pretty much every movement option in this game has at least a couple of uses that may not be apparent at first glance.
With a few exceptions, the weapons of Duck game will kill you in one shot and since the game is a platformer. Every player can see each other and when fights are not mayhem and explosions at break-neck speeds, they can turn into tense mind games and some amazing plays. Or comical accidents that will be rewarding anyway.
When you think of aesthetics Duck Game is impeccable with it's Genesis inspired soundtrack and clean pixel art which looks nice and is easy to understand even with the game's frantic pace, If i needed to describe the songs and atmosphere in a more subjctive way. I would say they feel like summers when you were young. They are some catchy tunes with a care-free attitude as well as adrenaline pumping songs that will accompany any situations with ease and really fit the personality and charm the game has.
Overall I think this game can be an amazing experience for anyone and even more so in groups, games don't take too long and never really get frustrating or boring, it can be addicting and is such a joy to pick up. It's just one of those timeless games that you will probably remember some years later and have fun the same way you did when you started.
I highly recommend this game and wish you all good luck and good hunting!

Ah yes, Orion: Prelude, or as it will always be known to me, Orion: Dino Horde! This game has been quite criticized through the years (and in all honestly quite rightly so). they game if filled with bugs and lots of tedious grinding achievements. Still, despite all that I can't help but to love it. In fact it is the only game which I haven't uninstalled after reaching 100%.
So, there's no story to follow in this game and it's a pretty straightforward king of game. You're dropped as one of three classes (assault, recon and support) into a base where you're supposed to defend a generator against incoming waves of attacking dinos that don't enjoy your presence there. If all teammates dies or the generator is destroyed (a timer starts when it reaches 0% health and if it isn't repaired before time runs out it's destroyed) you all loose. If you survive all waves (10 for normal games and 30 for conquest games) then you win. Pretty simple. To your help you can buy a quite big assortment of weapons and perks and each class comes with a specific perk of their own (assault can jetpack, recon can cloak and support can heal).
This game has a lot of various pvps but there are only a couple which I really enjoy such as king of the hill and team elimination. The place where this game really shines is in regular Survival mode when you play together with a good, tight and cooperative team. This is where this game is at it's best! I don't think I've made as many friends in any game as I've made in this one.
So, in conclusion, if you want a good cooperative game and don't mind a few bugs here and there and can either ignore, or work through all the grinding achievements then yes, you will enjoy this game!

I personally enjoyed the way the game handled the full cutscenes. The jumps in time were handled well and I really liked watching them. They told the story from a Discovery Channel esque "real crime" drama taking place in 2010. It was unique and I liked the idea
Now we get to the negative parts of Mafia III. The graphics are generally poor and un-optimized. I tend to ignore graphics so long as they're not horribly bad. These are not great. You can tell this is a poorly done console port. This could potentially be excused if the gameplay was good
However, the gameplay, after the first act is extremely dull and repetitious. The first act is done well. It hops around in time, like in the cutscenes and is scripted well. It's generally fun. Afterward, though, it is a repetitious wreck
The AI is awful. Don't get me wrong, it's not the worst I've ever seen. The collectables are a tad-bit silly and really really pointless
There's no particular "advancement" in the game. As far as I can tell, you are given all the clothing at the beginning of the game and in addition, you have a large variety of weapons, that are pretty much all available at the beginning of the game, and are all pretty dull
In conclusion, the game is not really worth it unless you enjoy doing the same thing over and over to really good music. If you want to play a good Mafia game, play its sequel or if you find a copy, play the original, which is ten times better than this and that was made over fifteen years ago!

As a long time fan of the Mafia games, I already knew what i was getting into. Load times are horribly long, taking you right out of any action you were just in. Story wise, the game is true to its own lore, often dropping in names from the first two Mafia games. Old characters make cameos as either supporting characters or just a one time reference.
Major plus for this game is its the first open world Mafia game. In previous installments you had to do a mission in order for anything to happen in game. Meaning, that in this one you can go entire in-game days before doing any missions. Cars are few in variety with most of them having rusty versions.
Major downfall, and possibly what might very well end the Mafia franchise are the bugs that never seem to be patched. Bugs that make playing the game impossible. For almost all interactions with the major characters, the cutscene never seems to trigger the first time around. Infuriating since when it tries to trigger, your HUD is removed.
Another major issue is the map suddenly zooming in and out at random. Roads disappearing from the map, and the map acting like your still indoors. A problem for trying to navigate anywhere or trying to find a collectable.
Unlike other Mafia games, you can have only two weapons at a time; leaving shoot offs as boring instead of exciting. If your on your first playthrough, you'll find the game loves explaining things you already figured out. In game pop ups are a menace as they pop up during action or driving, taking you right out of the game.
No matter how powerful your computer is, you will never be able to run this game properly due to bugs 2K chooses to ignore daily.
If you are a patient fan of Mafia or love era-centric games, then youshould pick it up....when its at least 50% off.
If you're expecting a fast pace GTA clone, then skip this game.

A ragtag collection of Ed McMillen's old flash games. If you liked playing all sorts of games on Newgrounds back in the day, like Ed McMillen's work, and want to see what his old games were like, I guess this might be for you. In all honestly, it was pretty hit and miss with me.
Coil was pretty abstract and didn't really give you instructions on what to do, which was the draw I suppose. Honestly wasn't too engaging.
Triachnid was pretty slow, and the physics can get really bothersome at times. Interesting atmosphere and way of telling it's story.
Meat Boy was pretty fun when it was on Newgrounds, and controlled pretty well at the time. But now after Super Meat Boy came out, it really doesn't hold up. The controls are really primitive and half the difficulty of the game is just fighting the controls. Several of these levels would be nowhere near as difficult if you put them into Super Meat Boy. Not really a fan of this one unfortunately. Super Meat Boy is just much better.
Time ♥♥♥♥ pretty much plays out like those old flash puzzle games. Kind of interesting and neat, and it did get a new set of levels in The Basement Collection. Unfortunately, those play out more like a ROM hack of this game instead of just being more levels fo play through. Those aren't really fun.
Spewer is my favorite from this collection of games. It's a puzzle platformer where your character has basically a barfing jetpack mechanic to help him get to certain places. The levels are pretty fun, and the main gimmick has plenty of ways to work out. Unfortunately, it can get a bit finnicky at times.
Aether is kind of a puzzle adventure game that's kind of interesting once you play through it. Unfortunately, finding the space landmarks for the achievements just isn't fun. Kind of interesting, but not much to it.
Grey Matter is a interesting game that I didn't find too engaging. It's a shooter type game, except you have to run into the enemies, and avoid the bullets. It was kind of fun, but I didn't have any real interest in the end.
A.V.G.M. is an unlockable game, that's a satire on cow clicker type games. The joke ran too far, and the joke itself wasn't that great.
Overall, a really mediocre collection. Get it if you're interested in Ed McMillen's old games, but there's really not much reason to get it otherwise.

Duck game is one of those games where you could say the Devs thought about everything.
If you grab some friends you can dive into the main game of fast paced deathmatches on a variety of maps with both gimmicks and balanced designs in mind. If you somehow get bored of those, you are covered by a very intuitive level editor as well as the steam workshop where you can get content ranging from maps to weapons, hats and stuff like that.
Locally and over the internet, it supports a wide number of controllers and it's really simple to set up games and customize to your liking in many ways.
Alone? Not a problem really, single player challenges and the level editor can keep you busy. The single player portion of the game can teach you a ton about the mechanics and also make you practice some skills that will be useful for multiplayer, you can even unlock cosmetics and mutators too.
Gameplay wise the game really shines on both it's vanilla map design and weapons, you are sometimes forced to be creative and even stylish with the way you use them and will always keep learning new mechanics and intricacies that can add some really satisfying depth to the combat.
In terms of movement  nothing is ever wasted in this game. Ducks are nimble and control superbly. You can hold the jump button after a jump to flutter (Which also makes you aim diagonally and then up in just a few frames, keep that in mind :>) Ragdolling makes you gain some more momentum for those high jumps you thought impossible, you can slide while running to break windows as well as dodge bullets.
Pretty much every movement option in this game has at least a couple of uses that may not be apparent at first glance.
With a few exceptions, the weapons of Duck game will kill you in one shot and since the game is a platformer. Every player can see each other and when fights are not mayhem and explosions at break-neck speeds, they can turn into tense mind games and some amazing plays. Or comical accidents that will be rewarding anyway.
When you think of aesthetics Duck Game is impeccable with it's Genesis inspired soundtrack and clean pixel art which looks nice and is easy to understand even with the game's frantic pace, If i needed to describe the songs and atmosphere in a more subjctive way. I would say they feel like summers when you were young. They are some catchy tunes with a care-free attitude as well as adrenaline pumping songs that will accompany any situations with ease and really fit the personality and charm the game has.
Overall I think this game can be an amazing experience for anyone and even more so in groups, games don't take too long and never really get frustrating or boring, it can be addicting and is such a joy to pick up. It's just one of those timeless games that you will probably remember some years later and have fun the same way you did when you started.
I highly recommend this game and wish you all good luck and good hunting!

Give it a try and I hope ya'll enjoy it!
