IT'S AN OMSI 2 FOR NOOBS (and that's a good thing)
I was always interested in the various bus simulators, but always found the learning curve to be too steep. Games like OMSI 2 while great, are too insanely detailed for their own good, putting off someone like myself from really giving it a chance.
ETS2/ATS on the otherhand proved to me that you can make a accessible simulator while keeping it just deep enough to please the hardcore. I simply wanted a bus simulator that followed the ETS2 mold and Bus Simulator 2016 is a great first step at that.
PROS:
- Easy to pick up and play. It comes with a nice tutorial for first timers.
- The city feels alive and lived in. There are a variety of passengers (including drunk and wheel chair bound patrons).

Defcon first thing I have to say in my review. I love the game is motto, everybody dies. Also upon launching the game and gazing upon the menu. I noticed that apparently the official URL for the games website is titled. Defcon Everybody
, which I personally found to be absolutely hilarious. Also I love the plot of the game which is apparently it is 1983 and you are a General, Hidden away in an underground fallout shelter. While are you are leading your chosen alliance into total Nuclear armageddon. Simply just the setting and the plot of Defcon reminds me of the novel, On the beaches. In that novel pretty much the same thing happens at the end, everybody dies, no survivors. I love the art style of the game, which reminds me of a radar screen thing. I also love how the game plays this very eerie music, that simply reminds me that this is the end of the world. And I am a guy who appreciates excellently written and performed game soundtracks.
But so far I've only played against the AI, but I still found the matches to be extremely entertaining. Even though a lot of people would say otherwise. Because I simply love strategy games. Defcon is simply right up my alley. It is just simply mesmerising to me seeing my nukes giving hell to the Russians, especially Moscow. And also see Beijing getting flattened at the same time as well. But when the match is over, and the population display is entirely red. Indicating that everyone has been practically annihilated in those areas. And the matches final score is tallied. For some reason it feels so dam rewarding to have practically murdered so many millions of people. And my real first match I played as what is practically the EU. (before the UK left) in a solo match against the USSR AI. I murdered as my final score 45.6 million Russians. Even more people than Hitler and Stalin combined could have ever hoped for. But they are all Communists, so who gives a dam?! Also I may have killed Putin as well loI. love how when you start a match you have a brief moment of calm, before the storm when everyone is on Defcon 5. For you to decide your strategy. Placing down your missle launches/air defences, fleets, bases, and finally your radar stations. Also the game does have modding support which is really neat. But so far the only mod I've seen is a mod that changes the map to an real world map.
But however I do have a couple of issues with Defcon. I don't like how in a full match it is practically just a big free for all. No allies or alliances, but I supposed you got give some slack. After all, it is the end of the world. So why the ♥♥♥♥ not as we give the UN, The only thing a supposed to be stopping a total nuclear war from happening. The middle finger, as we go into the point of no return, otherwise known as Defcon one, everyone will die. Also the normal asking price for the Defcon is 11.99 NZD. Is a bit too much in my opinion considering that Defcon doesn't have a lot of content or replay ability. I think 5 NZD is away more reasonable asking price. However I bought my copy on sale, 85% off - 1.79 NZD. Which I think in my opinion is way more reasonable, and you should deathly wait for a sale to buy Defcon. But for mods there are no steam workshop support, which is quite unfortunate.
But above all as my final conclusion. I can happily conclude that Defcon is deathly a game worth buying and recommending, for anybody who loves strategy games. Especially if you are like me, and loves post apocalyptic books and so on. If I was to give an score rating of 10. It would be 6 out of 10.

I grew up as a young child in the '80s playing the first Final Fantasy on the NES with my father. I was too young to read, so he had to read the dialogue to me as we played. As I grew and learned to read myself, I spent hour upon hour with the sequels, Final Fantasy II (IV in Japan), and III (VI in Japan), both for the SNES. I have a strong memory involving the time I walked several miles to my friend's house after school because he had a new PlayStation, and a copy of Final Fantasy VII, a game that I was hugely excited to experience given my history with the series. I had spent the past few months reading about the game in various video game publications and was hyped out of my mind to try it.
It was autumn, 1997, and I was 12 years old at the time. 20 years ago. I've replayed the game a dozen times since then, and mostly recently delved back into the Steam port to examine how the game has aged and how well the port runs.
The very first thing that I noticed about the game was the chasm between how well the audio design and soundtrack have aged versus how poorly the graphics have. It becomes clearly apparent that sprites have aged far better than polygonal characters when comparing this game to an older, sprite-based games in the series such as Final Fantasy VI. Sprites carried a certain charm to them, and remain tolerable despite their lack of beauty. Polygons, for lack of a better description, just look strange and ugly. Their blockiness represents a human character far more poorly than even a sprite can. To compare it to Hollywood, sprites are like Disney cartoon of the '70s, while polygons are like the bad special effects of the '80s. The audio, however, has aged gracefully. Nobuo Uematsu's score has always been perfect for the game, and I remembered how fond I was of it the first time around immediately upon starting the game again.
The characters are generally well-realized, if not helped by some shoddy translation. Cloud is such a deep and human character that it's worth playing through the game just to witness his growth. By the end of the game you come to realize how deeply flawed a person he is, and having such a flawed hero leading the game was something that was quite groundbreaking for JRPGs at the time. Sephiroth's villainy hasn't shown age, either. He's still one of the best gaming villains in history, a title well earned through his enigmatic actions and intriguing backstory. Some of the characters lean more heavily towards comic relief, like Cait Sith, but are still given the depth they deserve in a game as large as this one. Each character's backstory is engaging. I will always fondly remember being shocked at how much depth was given to Red XIII, a character you meet in a lab early in the game who seems at first to be nothing more than a cool-looking, speaking attack feline. Cosmo Canyon looks amazing, the background music is fantastic, and the story it tells about Red XIII will hook your emotions immediately.
It's obvious what to expect from the gameplay. This game is purely old school JRPG. It doesn't bother me, as it's a type of game that I once had a huge affinity for. I can jump back into the more slowly-paced, active turn-based battle systems any time and still enjoy it. To others, it may be a bit more tedious. This is especially true regarding random battles. The tedium of random battles may be intolerable for others that are more used to the real-time fare of old CRPGs or more recent Western RPGs. It's difficult for me to be objective enough to say. I don't mind random battles even now, but I never have.
One thing I will tout is the materia system. I've always loved it. It's my favorite form of character development in any Final Fantasy game, and it holds up. Growing your materia through the management of your weapons is so much fun, and the high-level materia such as Slash-All and Double Cut really make you feel all-powerful toward the end portion of the game. They're scaled very well.
The main complaint from my latest replay is an issue that never seemed to bother me before. The control of Cloud through the various pre-rendered areas is absolutely atrocious. Pressing up on the directional pad will sometimes cause him to go left or right, and pressing right or left on the pad will sometimes cause him to go down. There's no clear indication of when this will happen -- It's unique to each area. This becomes particularly annoying in areas where random battles occur. Very often I'd find myself doubling back due to this, and fighting far more random battles than I actually had to.
I wouldn't be able to conclude this without mentioning the cutscenes and minigames. The idea of rewarding players with a CGI cutscene during certain parts of the game was a fresh, new concept at the time of the game's release. Seeing the devs at Square flaunt their graphical prowess was mind-blowing, and the cutscenes were unlike anything in video games at the time. They truly were rewarding, and I remember being so impressed as a 12-year old first playing this game that I recorded them on a VHS tape for later playback. The minigames were also groundbreaking, but have aged poorly. Bad control plagues many of them, specifically the motorcycle and snowboarding games. But the inclusion of these changed the genre for years; the lack of minigames in a post-Final Fantasy VII JRPG would be a strange omission for a later title.
Final Fantasy VII has got its problems. In some cases, it's aged beautifully and become the historically powerful title that gamers expected it to be upon its release. Final Fantasy VII brought RPGs as a genre into the mainstream. The graphics and control, however, will be nearly unbearable to any gamer going back in time to play this game for the first time.
I do have some complaints specifically regarding this Steam port. Every resolution that isn't 640x480 windowed looks terrible. They've upped the resolution on the characters and NPCs, but the pre-rendered backgrounds are the same so they look awful in any other resolution. And don't even think about going to 16:9. All it does is stretch the picture to fit the screen.
There's also a persistent black bar along the bottom of the screen that is only ever filled in when accessing the menu. Imagine you're watching a film in letterbox, except that there's only one black bar on the bottom of the screen and no matching bar on the top. Just awful.
On top of the graphical issues, Square's ridiculous DRM is present. You must log into Square Enix when you first start the game. People already hate Uplay. Why would Square do this? It's an idiotic move.
People have also mentioned the music quality being subpar compared to the PS1 version, but it honestly didn't affect my experience at all. I definitely noticed the music being a bit different, it didn't seem any worse than the original game.
Despite the wear of aging and the shoddy port, I still believe this game is a must-play for anyone who liked the original or any gamer looking for a history lesson. There is still enough depth in the characters, immersion in the environments despite their age due to a phenomenal soundtrack and great art design, and player investment in the story. Like an old painting, Final Fantasy VII continues to be historically relevant and is worth seeing and experiencing if only to recognize the influence it had on present day gaming. Os desenvolvedores desse jogo demonstraram que houve muito carinho na produção desse game.
A história do jogo é contada à medida que o jogo se desenrola, e o jogador fica envolvido na trama de executar instruções estranhas recebidas pelo telefone.
Hotline Miami em si é muito fácil de ser jogado e não necessita de uma supermáquina para funcionar. Com os gráficos pixelados, traz um pouco da sensação de estar jogando um jogo retrô de fliperama. Fica claro que o objetivo do game é o de ser rápido e que não gaste muito o tempo do jogador. A visão do jogo é superior ao personagem e como cursor de mira podem ser usados o mouse ou controle. Confesso que jogar no controle requere um pouco de hábito, mas como jogo muito no teclado acabei optando por essa opção. A dificuldade apresentada pelo game é clara, cada level apresenta um diferencial e dentro de cada level pode apresentar anexos (1 level com 3 andares por exemplo). No jogo é normal e fácil de você morrer, portanto uma mensagem de "aperte R para recomeçar" é recorrente. Durante o jogo é possível desbloquear outras máscaras para usar nos massacres e cada uma delas possui uma habilidade especial. O legal desse jogo é que ele permite que você realize combinações de especiais de máscaras com a sua gameplay, fazendo com que seja possível a execução de movimentos loucos e de matança muito rápida.
O jogo apresenta um editor de "level" e pode ser compartilhado via Workshop da Steam. A trilha sonora do game é fantástica, muito agitada e combina muito com a época.
Além disso, conta com 35 achievements que realmente testam a habilidade de quem joga (no geral, alguns são muito difíceis de conquistar!
Espero ter ajudado um pouco à aqueles que ainda não conhecem o jogo. Experimente!

It's as if Robot took all the good things about the previous two installments (quick and fluid movement in both map navagation and control input, streamlined UI, fast load times, charming art direction, carefuly crafted map design, and a SINGLE PLAYER/CO-OP EXPERIENCE) and just chucked it all as a desperate ploy to get in on that sweet sweet MOBA money. The franchise was already a blend between shooter and tower defence, this experement pushed things one step too far by flirting with MOBA style vs mode which has permiated into the single player side of the game. Sadly it offers nothing in the way of what fans of the series want, which is often as simple as more of 1 & 2, but with greater map variety and a longer list of scenarios and levels, or at least a map editor and maybe mod support.
Granted this is beta, so much of it's core design feels like a step backwards.
Edit: I'll clarify, while the game is *now* single and co-op, the core mechanics have been designed on a MOBA foundation:

Those core mechanics have bled through production to the extent that everything looks and feels 'cheapened' for the sake of pvp. Perhaps this has more to do with the engine than the early MOBA direction, I can't say, though other aspects reflect that carry over. Systems for loot, leveling, currency and even difficulty levels are all based around a protracted grind and the fact that you can just outright buy gold and skulls as a microtransaction indicates that while Robot may have backpeddaled away from Unchained The MOBA, they certainly didn't fully re-commit to a proper single or co-op focused experience.
To that end, Robot can now justifiably reap the rewards of a moba while not having to worry so much about hero and item balance. This in turn allows them the ability to lock away disproportionately powerful heros and items behind paywalls and turn a blind eye towards power creep.
What worries me most about all this is that if Robot is commited to turning the franchise into a long term microtransaction engine then we can forget about a proper follow up to the fantastic first two games.

Orcs Must Die! Unchained follows suit of its two previous installments with a wide array of changes.
You play as a hero and you've gotta to kill alot of orcs (mobs) before they reach your rift with only 25 points. You can place traps on walls, the floor, and the ceiling and you can use your heroes' abilities and mainline fighting style to dispose of your enemies.
However, it's just simply not fun, and playing the game feels more like a chore.
"Oh I've got to remember to relog everyday to get the dailies and then play two maps and finish my profile dailies." And why? To get a chest or skulls (the in-game currency). These chests open up to randomly give you your traps that you can use inside maps or they can give you traits to equip, or other things that help you fight off the horde of mobs headed for your rift.
You are able to buy new heroes with their own array of abilities and style with currency earned through playing maps (skulls) or with real world money currency (gold). In the lower difficulties you earn from 100 skulls to about 500 and heroes costs' go 6000 skulls and up.
I came back to this game after they removed their PvP mode (or modes idk) and refocused on what made the original games so fun and it just doesn't feel half as fun. Without getting guranteed traps much like the older games as you progressed through the story, you randomly get traps (through chests) and then you have to upgrade them and then can equip them with parts (in which you can randomly find these super rare parts also through chests).
Upgrading the traps increase only one aspect of the trap: the damage, or rate of fire, or slowing perecentage, or HP. Upgrading traps costs skulls.
There's an in-game store in which has a section where you can buy with skulls randomly picked out traps with a select quantity of it (for example you can one day it might have 'Spike Trap X 100' for 1500 skulls [which is very little at higher levels at a costly price] and another day they might have the same deal but only for 500 skulls- I'm not sure how it works exactly). But the reason for the 'in-game deals' store section is so you can buy (if you have enough skulls) traps you don't own because you can't seem to acquire them from chests.
Having alot of new heroes is cool and all but I liked the old way the original OMD and OMD2 did where no matter who you were, your main weapon changed but your choices of weaponary remained with you. Traps were always cool and didn't have to "Level 5" or above before you faced the final difficulty and you didn't have to refarm old maps to acquire a currency.
But then again, this game is free to play so I suppose all of these changes from previous installments were necessities of the game. "I like the game"-ish but it's too riddled with F2P mechanics to be enjoyed as the originals were.

Speaking to the point, this game is good! You get to be a real badass mother-♥♥♥♥er in this game. Dont get the tonnes of negetive reviews push You away! The negetive reviews are mainly due to this games' predecessors(expaination below). They set a very high expectation level for this game, and this game does not meet it.. That is the only major reason for tonnes of negetive reviews.
More explaination and detailed review below, read if You have time...
Ok, now the tonnes of negetive reviews are because of this game format, which is totally different from the prior installments of this series. Mafia 1 and 2 were more like story driven and things happen in a flow. You get to do lot of things and there is a variety in the missions offered by the game, which puts mafia series in its own level in open world games.
However, Mafia 3, developed by a different dev team, has repetative gameplay. Yes, this game does have a story and its good as well, but this game does not offer connectivity or flow in the story, like the previous installments did.. And thats the main reason for all the negetive reviews.
This game is more like, fight for a teritory at a time (totally 9) from one of the enemy boses and hand it over to one of Your underbosses. Why You fight for this territory and how You get underbosses etc is part of the story and I do not want to reveal it. Each underboss give their own perks to You for handing over a territory to them. The decision is up to You and the way You handle the territories will be a deciding factor on how the side story unfolds, but the main story remains the same. The underboss perks include weapon/ammunition upgrade, car steal upgrades, insider edge etc, depends on the type of boss You hand over the territory to.
Yes, there are bugs still lurking in this game and You might need to restart/load a previous saved game sometimes to workaround it, but thats not a major issue.
To summarize, The graphics is good, story is amazing, game is good but not as good as its predecessors. Overall, I'd recomend this game and its DLCs. A must have game, if You have not played its prior installments(i.e. Mafia 1 and 2). A good game to play otherwise.

A throwback to adventure gaming, highlighting both the high and low points of the genre, but saves face with the charm of its utterly charmless hero.
Pros: Well voice acted and witty writing throughout. Surprisingly engaging story and characters. Most of the logic puzzles are intuitive and fairly challenging. Art style of the game is unique and whimsicle, squeezing a substancial amount of creative juice from the trash planet motif.
Cons: Most of the designated puzzles (switch puzzles, slider puzzles and whatnot) distract from the flow of the game rather than enhance it and the game would be stronger without them. Some technical issues (Once I was forced to download and install a save game file in order to progress due to a crash glitch). Characters will break character at times to keep the narrative going or in an attempt to shock the player with a plot twist (Goal in particular tends to suffer from this trend a lot). Game's treatment of women in general might cause consternation and seems less ironic and more unintended (Your first clue being that the female costar is named Goal).
Would recommend to: Monkey Island fans specifically or fans of LucasArts or Sierra adventure games in general, who don't mind having to google up a working save file. Anyone looking for a genuinely charming tale of a misanthropic dreamer and his unfortunate coterie (who, again, can find that save file).

- Almost MASTERPIECE
Finally I completed my second Witcher 2 playthrough. So now I feel like I am competent enough to review this game. Now the main marketing focus was the non-linear story, and that is what I would like to concentrate on. I feel like non-linearity in games is like choices in the matrix... as long as you have the illusion of choice, it is good... Now, do I feel, that the non-linearity in the W2 lived up to it's hype? No.
Do I believe, that this is the most Non-linear Game ever made (with nice graphics at least...)? Yes.
The devs have been bragging about the 16 endings, now... does this really qualify as 16 endings? Let's go with a Mass Effect comparison: you have like 12 companions, each one can be (dis-)loyal at the end, each one can be disloyal and each one can die. Now ask your selfs: How many possible ending-scenarios would that be: more than 400 plus destroying collector base or not and you can double that number. So the final outcome of the Witchers Non-linearity is not THAT amazing and it comes down to who lived, who died. JUST as in Mass Effect 2, or is there more to it?
Well there is more to it, because the game is not about the (over-hyped) endings. It is about the various ways your journey will go, to get you to the one ending with 16 variations. And that is the ground by which the Witcher 2 dethrones EVERYTHING that has come before it!
BioWare games go like this:
Go to location 1. Fight. Choose A or B.
Go to location 2. Fight. Choose C or D.
FINALE which is impacted by decisions from locations 1, 2. The End -with trillions different WRITTEN endings in DA:O -with 2 different animated endings in ME1 -with one ending in ME2
Now, I am not saying this is bad. I love me a good BioWare game, loved all of them besides one... you know which. But: Enter the Witcher 2.
You get to choose one of (OMG!) 2 different paths to get to the 1 ending (with 16 variations). Now that still does not sound very non-linear. Just two? Well, for one thing, THAT is already twice as much as any other BioWare game. Those paths are not just side missions, they completely change the location, the characters, the quests, the tone, it is COMPLETELY different. Playing it the second time around I felt like "touched for the very first time". OK, but let us get to the question no one asked. Are both paths equal... most comments I read, said the elven story is better and although both were engaging and fun I have to agree... if you choose to go with the Elves it seems there is simply much more to it. I recommend to play both paths, because they are both great. BUT the Elven story is definitely stronger in it's narrative!
So in the end... is this the holy grail of non-linear RPG? No
But it IS the closest thing anyone has come close to.
Now the other thing: Save game import... Is it done great? Does it justify playing the earlier game just to get different starting scenarios?
Well ask youself: DO YOU LIKE THE EARLIER GAME? If no... than you might miss out most in the Mass Effect franchise. If we are talking about Dragon Age the import is really under-utilized here. The Witcher is somewhere between those 2, closer to the DA. The save game import is not really a very sophisticated function and it really needs to grow.
I am sorry I am comapring this so much to BW, but BW is my favorit company, so I know their games. In both ME and DA the sex seemed more explicit in the first ones, then in their sequels. The Witcher goes the other way... is it better because of it?
I have heard praises as wall as critiques, here is my take on this:
The sex cards were a stupid concept... but well executed. The soft-porn scenes are a better concept... but they are not that well executed. The voices, the sounds, the whole audio in them seems badly done. The editing is not exactly top. But I support sex in games. Best sex scene ? ME1 then Heavy Rain then The Witcher2!
OK, so lets cut to the basics, and lets get to the end of this. The Witcher 2 has lots of bugs, which annoy, but do not destroy the it!
The Witcher 2 has 2 big patches which make the above statement just 40% true!
The Witcher 2 gets free DLC with every patch!
The Witcher 2 has great combat,
The Witcher 2 has one hell of a great story, which seems to really find it's ending in the next Witcher... or the one after that...
The Witcher 2 is simply one great game and I accomplished not to
mention up to now the beautiful locations and all around graphics...
Is this the official dethronement of Bioware? No.
Is this the official dethronement of Dragon Age? No. Dragon Age committed
suicide in my opinion...
This is just another top notch RPG... and we do not get many of them! So
buy it... play it! And than buy all Dragon Ages... and than go buy Mass
Effects... And Deus Ex... and Elder Scrolls... and Fallouts... (although I never liked the last two... ahh well.. here comes Skyrim, will give it a chance) RPG needs to live! It needs you to buy it! In all its forms!
Just for the record... Across three playthroughs I spend around 150 hours ingame!

I was interested in Edmund McMillen since I saw him in a documentary about game designers. I knew about Super Meat Boy, so I wanted to learn more about his style with this collection. So far I've only played Time ♥♥♥♥ so I'll talk about that:
This game is the best mindf*ck I've experienced in a looong while. It exemplifies the struggle of self and identity, reality, life and death. What I love most about it is the main antagonist, who seems to be you from the future: now trapped in this alternate dimension of maze-like rooms you find yourself in (which feels an awful lot like purgatory). As you go room to room and solve puzzles, this other self constantly puts you down and spouts all sorts of disturbing nonsense, while simulatenously cheering you on and pleading for help. Imagine something like an existentialist GLaDos, only crazier and more negative. If you can imagine that.
The game itself raises a multitude of philosophical questions and really makes you think deeply beyond the creative puzzles. The puzzles themselves can be maddening; the fact you have a limitless amount of lives and continues only adds to the sense of hopelessness, but you feel so fascinated and driven to keep going and solve each one, just to see what happens next...
Good game for the price.

Even with just a few hours put into the game so far (3 as of writing this review) I have added this ga to my favorites list and am absolutely in love with it!
The gameplay works great, moving and interacting with the environment is intuitive enough that learning the controls isn't frustrating (because there is no in-game tutorial to teach you how to move or use things). WIth just a little experimentation I was able to understand how to play the game.
The art style is very fun, and overall very well done. The way the game plays with pixel art effects is fantastic and makes the whole style tie together. Unlike some pixel art games that look like the developer was attempting to be lazy with the graphics, Forsaken Isle looks well polished and refined.
The lack of a tutorial is both a pro and a con in my book, depending on how you look at it. Pro: it gives the game a lot more feeling. You really have to learn everything to survive. Con: before you can play, you have to learn the basic controls on how to move and interact with stuff. I would assume that our character knew how to walk and pick up rocks before he became Forsaken on this Isle.
Another thing is the lack of a full-featured save system. You can save your game, but only one game. I haven't really found this to be an issue because I love just taking a few minutes to go into my Isle and do some farming or build another room for my house and having this long-running story where I'm focused on just one character. But on the other hand, I am currently working on an introductory steam guide for the game and would love to have the ability to quickly choose between loading different save files so I could have a main save file for playing and a different one for taking pictures or exploring for the guide.
I realize this game is still in Early Access so any negatives stated above could very well be fixed by the time the game is finished. Some other early access problems that exist right now is the lack of usage for crafting tables or resources. Some crafting tables have very few things you need them for (so far the only recipe for the cooking table is pizza, unless there's one I haven't discovered) and some resources have very few uses. I expect problems like these to sort themselves out though as the game progresses.
All in all this is a fun game! It is definitely poised to become one of my favorites!

Stuck In Mud Simulator. You drive a large vehicle on the muddiest of roads, and it gets stuck in the mud. I suppose there are two kinds of people in this world: those who enjoy getting stuck in the mud, and those who think it's an aggravating waste of time. Some say "oh, it's more fun in co-op!" Yyyyeah, so I only played this game in co-op, and I did so with a girl who loves driving games. Once you get out of the mud enough, you drive around trying to complete objectives that neither my friend nor I were able to complete a single one of. We just drove around, either getting stuck in mud, or sinking in a river and having to restart repeatedly because the vehicle got stuck underwater.
Comparing the full-sale price point to the actual gameplay, I would say that based on pure dollar-to-enjoyment value, this is one of the worst video games I have played in my life. I see little point in discussing this game's content because by now it's probably common knowledge. So what's the deal with this release?
Well it's on PC, Steam, has cloud saving, a booster thing that makes the game easier, and achievements that made me play this game much more than I otherwise would have (I'm crazy, ok?). It also has a piece of DRM that i've heard is a real nuisance for some, but I didn't have too much trouble with it. You have to make an account, but once I linked it with my Steam account I never had to worry about it again. The real problem is the instability of their server, which takes down cloud saves during busy hours (during the sale it did, but not after that was done with). It does save locally though, and it updates your cloud save once that gets going again, so it's not really a big deal. Nevertheless, I felt the need to mention all this.
Aside from that, this is FF7 as it was on the PS1 ~15 years ago (I still have a [friend's] copy :o). Everything. The story, gameplay, optional content, and even some glitches (W-Item) carry over to this version.
That's really all I need to say, I think. Chances are you already know if you like this game or not. And if you never played it... well, you can if you want to. I had a decent time, but people tend to love or hate this game. Less because of what it is and more because of what it did: became a "standard" for JRPG's that has more or less remained the same ever since, for better or worse.
Ok, i'll stop now. Buy if it interests you. You get what you expect: an aged PS1 classic that plays competently on the PC and has a few nice little additions.

Necrodancer is a rhythm, turn-based, roguelike. It can be played with just directional keys, so dancepad friendly.  You move your character  to the beats of Danny Baranowsky (Super Meat Boy, Binding of Isaac) as you make your way through 3 (4 upon release) zones, each containing 3 levels and a boss fight.
There are currently 7 playable characters offering various challenges with a variety of weapons and items to utilize. Floors are randomly generated and you can race for better times or complete to get the highest score. The game is challenging, but fair so when you die, it was probably your fault. The game provides a training feature so you can practice against any enemy and hone your strategies. Other features include a daily challenge, seeded runs, and creating your own levels. You can even customize the music that plays as well as mod in game sprites.

For an RPG Maker game, it is quite solid and as professionally put-together as any classic title from some of the major companies of the SNES era.  The story is only slightly lacking, but the characters are varied and interesting, the combat is engaging and challenging, so that even in normal mode, you can't just make it through by continually selecting the attack command.  And even outside of combat, you must strategize what to equip for different areas and especially certain boss encounters, as weapons and armor that are higher costing and have better stats on the surface are not always the best options.  My only complaint, and it's not much of one, is that I feel as though the game goes into the final stretch too soon after I've gathered together my last few party members, and once you cross the threshold, there's no going back until you defeat the final boss.  This means either you'll have to grind for a few levels and to buy the best equipment for the last two or three members, or you simply avoid using them.  However, the game doesn't end with the final boss.  You get an ending, certainly, but you can keep playing, and there are higher challenges and more secrets to uncover afterward.  I personally don't like the trend of modern RPGs of making the final boss not the most difficult battle in the game.  On the other hand, it does increase replayability.  Another thing that increases replayability is that you can download three custom save games from the creators themselves, one of which adds a hardcore 'Nightmare' difficulty level, but allows you to start with the Goddess Yveen (formerly unplayable, but a large part of the story) as your party member.  Another gives you access to all playable characters in the game (except the goddess) at the beginning, all at experience level 1.  And the third save state starts you off at the beginning as normal, except for the main character being at level 55.  If you love retro JRPGs, then you will love this game.

I haven't liked this game very much. It has a very entertaining story, badass characters, and hilarious dialogue, but it lacks the most important thing about a game... GAMEPLAY. It's the same problem with Bioshock Infinite for me. The gameplay is awful compared to how amazing the story and the world is. Witcher 2 truly does have a wonderful world. But the combat is so boring. Geralt likes to telegraph the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of his own attacks, spending two seconds just winding into an attack, and taking another two seconds to get out of it. This makes any fights that aren't one on one nearly impossible, turning them into ridiculous chases where I might take a stab at one enemy before getting hit, losing most of my health, and running in circles again. And then in one on one fights, you stagger lock your enemy to death. The combat is just boring. Plain and simple. Not to mention the awkward sex scenes that this game has to cater to the lonely "PC mustard race" weirdos that did nothing but make me feel uncomfortable.
Also the UI is ♥♥♥♥ing atrocious and too complicated for a video game. There's a fine line behind spending time to learn a game and wasting time to figure out problems that could have been fixed easily.
I think you'd need to heavily consider this game before buying it. It is not for anyone with even the slightest amount of "casual" in them.
It's a damn shame, because the one cutscene of King Foltest's assassination was enough to push me through a couple hours of dying over and over. It's so ♥♥♥♥ing badass at times, but it's hidden under boring and clunky combat.
>>>>EDIT<<<<<<<<<<
So I gave the game another shot, and I have changed my view completely. The game is about patience. It is difficult. It punishes rushing through things. Combat is a lot better than I made it out to be. Enemies do have generally a lot more health than you do, or they deal more damage than you do, but it is actually pretty fun. The combat and such are above satisfactory to me, but what really wins is the story, the dialogue, the environment, the world itself. The enemies are diverse, there's A LOT of stuff to do, but sidequests aren't just shoved into your face. It's actually a wonderful game, but my original statement of witcher not being for anyone with "casual" in them holds true; this game requires dedication, and what you get out of it is definitely worth it.
ALSO, THIS GAME QUITE POSSIBLY HAS SOME OF THE BEST DECISION MAKING AND DRAMATIC EVENTS EVER. As I stated in the comments section of this review, few games have made me smile stupidly like the witcher in how giddy I felt over certain actions/events/dialogue options. Cutscenes are also top notch. I'm SO glad I gave it another chance.

You, understandably, start backpedaling while firing rapidly in the little creatures direction. It moves forwards towards you, and now the fun starts. In real life, you would have little trouble dealing with this tiny thing, kicking it away once it got close and then filling it with lead. In this game, however, it will phase through your body and start biting you from the inside. This is quite annoying, since shooting it is now made considerably harder. Add in the fact you have to land about 25 shots on it while it has to land 2, and you can tell where this goes.

As promised, here is my review of the bus simulator  16. I played for nearly 8h and streamed it the whole time.
While this is true the game is not optimized at all and this could make it impossible to play for some people, this game is far from the 45-50% rating it received on release. I'm glad it's back to 60% as I'm writing this review and I believe it could deserve to be a little higher like 70-75% because the game itself isn't bad. The devs just have a very hard time to optimize it and they are working on it very hard. I cross my fingers they release a fix quickly. But don't be fooled by those bad reviews. Almost none of those rate the game for what it is, they are just bad reviews of angry players not able to launch the game and not patient enough to give the devs a chance to release a fix.
This game is not OMSI 2! If you seek for an incrediblely detailed bus simulator, don't buy. This game is more arcadish. If I had to compare it to other games, I would say it's like if OMSI 2 and Cities in Motion had a baby together. You have the management part of Cities in Motion (you create bus routes, assign drivers and busses to them, make sure they are giving positive income, etc). And with that you have the driving part of OMSI 2 (you drive buses, interact with passengers, deal with traffic, etc). You can interact with buttons in cockpit view. I was surprised there was so much to interact with in fact. So while it's not OMSI 2, it's still not a lazy game where you only accelerate/decelerate/left/right and nothing else. The driving is not the most realistic one but still very fun and it works very well with G27. Just a bit hard to set it up on first time but pretty fine after some gaming time.
The multiplayer is a nice add considering lot of driving games never have one. Sadly, it's not a real multi. As you cannot see your drivers (AI) on the road, well you cannot see other players aswell in multi. I'm really on the fence about 3 Stars of Destiny. For all the interesting gameplay mechanics it has and the general enjoyment of other games from RPG developer Aldorlea Games, there are enough problems to warrant a skip for anyone looking to try out yet another fantasy-based RPG.
We all know the problems with RPGMaker. That software has allowed anyone with a will and a few hours to spare the ability to pop out a carbon-copy clone and put it on Steam, to the detriment of the genre as a whole. While I generally enjoy (and even love) Aldorlea's output, 3 Stars definitely ranks as one of the lowest in terms of enjoyment-to-grinding and the storyline.
It's not actually mentioned anywhere on the store page, but the game is a prequel to the Laxius Power/Laxius Force series, which were the first games released by Aldorlea back in the early 2000s. Those games had the same three characters, but were generally a lot more mature in their storytelling (for instance, characters swear, have sex, get married and lose their loved ones), even if they're incredibly dated because of the early RPGMaker graphics/blocky character models.
3 Stars takes place years before the series, and has a god named Ozur kill a witch so he can find 3 prophecized leaders because of "reasons". At the same time, protagonist Random Pendragon sets out from his home on an adventure and meets Sarah (an elf) and Luciana (a enchantress), who learn about Ozur's plot and work to stop him before he can do any more damage to the world.
Those relationships and camaraderie found in the Laxius games doesn't translate to this prequel. Random and Sarah spend the majority of the game pointlessly bickering and sniping at each other, while Luciana just sticks around seemingly to keep things from escalating further. There isn't a whole lot of variety to the characters you meet, and the plot itself feels less like a coherent story and more a series of random setpieces on the way to the final showdown.
The biggest problem I faced is twofold. For one thing, Aldorlea's RPGs have a lot of items and useful gear that are easily missed due to being hidden in secret rooms (see the Millennium series for a greater example of this), and if you don't have the requisite guide, you're pretty much out of luck. Secondly, there is no in-game map to track where you are or where you're going, and considering there are points where you have to backtrack long distances to complete a quest (and the level design is linear), it can become extremely frustrating to figure out where you're supposed to go. That latter point nearly put me off the game for good.
However, I never actually finished the game. I got to a point just before the final battle where I was stuck in an area with few to no supplies, facing enemies who had a major difficulty spike and were wrecking my party easily. Faced with this problem, I quit the game and never went back.
That's not to say it's all bad, though. The battles are generally engaging and varied (despite an overreliance on enemies dropping status conditions on the party), there are a lot of interesting gameplay mechanics like the bond with your other party members strengthening depending on how long they stay in the active group, and there are some amusing setpieces during the late game.
In retrospect, however, I don't see a lot of people really getting invested in this one as much as some of Aldorlea's other games (and this is coming from someone who put 27 hours into this game).
3 Stars of Destiny exists more as unrealized potential than an enjoyable prequel. You'd be better off trying the Millennium series for this kind of RPG action.

If you liked Orcs Must Die 1 & 2 - give this game a chance. Why not? It's free!
A lot of the negative reviews here are, I think, from the first iteration of the game. Since December 2016 there has been a huge update and (for me) this is a significant step in the right direction. They have completely removed the PvP (which never felt right and put me off the game early on) and are now focussing on the 'classic' Orcs Must Die experience - battlegrounds. The PvP set back this game's development but we now basically have an Orcs Must Die 3 with the following changes:
i) Free to Play model, which to Robot's credit is not intrusive, although it does lead to some grind.
ii) Up to 3 players in a team, a natural progression on the 2 player co-op from OMD2.
iii) Tonnes more characters, each of which plays in a unique and interesting way.
iv) Many more levels of difficulty, allowing a significantly more hardcore experience in War Mage, Master and Rift Lord difficulties.
v) Hangover 'balancing' compromises from PvP such as no headshots, slower-than-necessary heroes and server-side infrastructure (meaning no pausing during games and a 'trap cap' of maximum traps per team).
I don't leave many reviews but I've been really enjoying this game so far, and I know how important steam reviews are to developers (and prospective players). There are still issues with the game, but based on the recent changes I feel optimistic. If you gave this a pass before, now might be a good time to dive back in and give Orcs Must Die Unchained a go.

The Binding of Isaac. Top down shooter roguelike dungeon crawler shoot em up, wakka wakka other stuff. If you're into games with lots of RNG and a bit of skill as well as a healthy dose of morbidity then you'll probably want to pick this up.
This game has some pretty solid controls, stylized artwork and great gameplay, but it's a flash game and as a result doesn't run super dooper well even if you have a beast machine.
The basic plot is that you're a child and your momma is tryina keel ya. You jump in the basement...which the entrance is apparently in your room...and you go around killing the abominations that your mom apparently keeps stored down there. I can't really say much else as far as that goes because it would spoil the game...kind of...although that's pretty much it.
Along the way you pick up random♥♥♥♥♥♥lying around and ♥♥♥♥ yourself up with it. Literally. At one point you'll probably get the coat hanger and jam it through your skull. I think the whole self mutilation thing is the most interesting aspect of the game because it's not overly done and it's an interesting way to 'upgrade' your character. It's visually fun to upgrade so to say.
There's also a plethora of unlockables including different characters and mushrooms and alternate endings. This game has over 10 endings...shame they all suck. As far as that goes, most of the endings are generic 'unlock' endings and then some weird music. The ones that aren't unlock endings are 'left to speculation' which in my opinion is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ way to be a lazy writer.
The controls are simply. AWSD to move and Cursor keys(or mouse) to shoot. Shift drops a bomb and space uses items. Real simple and well implemented. No problems here.
Each time you start a playthrough the rooms are randomly organized, but will always be square. The games not 'fully randomized' but follows the generic 'procedurally generated' system with pre built rooms that are randomly arranged with random monsters. Even the monster placement is static, but that's so the game isn't an♥♥♥♥♥to you and have a monster spawn on top of you I guess.
Another great aspect is the soundtrack. It fits very well into the game with a series of 'darker' themed tracks. The best track is ultimately the final few bosses of course, but the rest really set the mood.
There are quite a few uppies for this game and not a whole lot of downies.
Uppies:
Solid controls.
Interesting graphics and graphical concepts(upgrading yourself by mutilating yourself).
Great soundtrack.
RNG is well put together.
Fairly well balanced game.
Memorable enemies and upgrades/items.
Good AI (not great, just good).
Downies:
Overarching plot is lazy and overal just lame.
Level design is bland even for a game that's supposed to be dark and dreary. (Just because it's supposed to be horror doesn't mean you can't have a ♥♥♥♥ING FOREST. SPLATTERHOUSE HAD A FOREST LEVEL AND IT HAD WATER.)
Unique bosses are mostly just reskins.
And that's it! This game was worth about 15 bucks to me, but you'll likely get it around 2.50 if you buy it on sale. I feel it's definitely worth the 5 bucks. As far as the expansion, it's more DLC oriented as it's 'more of the same', but it's cheap and also worth it IMO.

The story is enjoyable for the journey though I'd say some characters and behaviors are a little out of place. And the ending feels a bit incomplete.
As with the puzzles they are a bit on the difficult side exactly because of the humor that makes you try all sort of absurd things instead of trying what logically makes sense. And a couple of puzzles are just... too absurd or too out of the box.
For a puzzle game it is actually long. Particularly this version, if you don't run in a hurry and don't read any walkthrough it will be with you for a while. And you will soon discover that the game's producer loves minigames.
It is not a perfect game but it is recommended very much if you want to be entertained by this kind of game for a long time (relative to its kind).

Natural Selection 2 is a unique game that allows people to be a commander (someone who oversees the game like in an RTS, makes building decisions etc.) or a regular foot soldier/alien. From this perspective, the game is very unique and this dynamic creates moments that you simply cannot experience at any other game.
I read some of the below reviews and there is a mention of toxic community. I haven't really experienced that. There are a number of Rookie-only servers where people who haven't played the game that much can get together and play in a balanced way. I've yet to see them empty even in middle of night. So don't worry about finding people to play.
Commander role is very important and a bad commander can and will make you lose the game. I sometimes see people getting annoyed with commanders but it was always civil. If you are very annoyed, you can start a vote to kick people and eject commanders. It requires high participation so you won't be kicked accidentally or some loseer cannnot eject you just because you didn't drop some ammo to the other side of the map etc.
I highly recommend NS2 for people who are bored with current FPS games and want to experience something that's a layer deeper.

Aragami is a really good stealth game.
The game revolves around the concept of shadow and light. While your character is in the shadows, you collect energy you need to use your powers. In the light instead, you lose said energy and are an easy mark for your enemies. So more than ever in a stealth game you are forced to move within the shadows. The cape of the character show the amount of energy you have.
Also on the character's cloak you can find the amount of charges for your skills and your currently equipped skill (which you can change on the fly if you want to). There is quite a range of skills you can choose from. To unlock those skills you need to collect scrolls that are hidden within the levels. You start with a basic 'blink'-skill, which you can use to quickly hop from shadow to shadow or behind enemies to take them out. Other skills enable you to throw kunais, create shadow for you to jump to (with blink), creating decoys, placing traps, hiding corpses and some more. Within the levels there are shrines, which fill up your skill charges once. That way your use of skills is limited and you are encouraged to make good use of them.
The game has a two-step suspicion system. If you've been seen just for a moment the enemies get suspicious (question mark above their heads). If you remain seen, a bars quickly fills up with red and if it's full, the enemy that saw you will alert the others and they will search the place for you. If you've been in range when that happens there's a good chance, the guy that detected you will straight up kill you (one-shot/hit). So you have a good chance to escape, but you're better off not to be detected in the first place.
The levels ramp up in difficulty and size and you will encounter some bosses on your way.
You can choose between 3 difficulties and you unlock skins for your character if you complete levels in a certain way (kill everyone, kill no-one, remain unseen). Things like how often you've been seen and how successful you've been in the level are considered for your final rating after a mission. Getting the best rating, collecting all scrolls and stuff encourage you to play the levels once again (maybe also on a higher difficulty).
+ good range of skills to unlock and use
+ limited use of skills encourages clever management
+ no hud/game elements like skill and energy charges and mission destinations integrated very well into the game
+ replay value because of rating, difficulty and collectibles
+ nice art
+ it's stealth man
+/- boss fights
+/- story is okayish, but not the best about the game anyway
Recommended for fans of stealth games

A smooth and very interesting platfomer/beat-'em-up game. If you're turned off by anthropomorphic characters, then this may be steer clear of, but you will be missing out on a very good story and very likable characters. Voice acting runds the gammit, somtimes good, sometimes passable, sometimes other, though rarely ever poor. Smooth gameplay, though it can cause lower-end PCs to slow down due to the detailed spritework and backgrounds. However, it rarely makes fights seem unfair, as the game runs smoothly enough, it rarely lags. Music and artistic quality is fantastic, even for a 2D sidescrolling beat-'em-up. It has some RPG elements, though they're not very important, since you only gain skillpoints to power up attack, health, defense and your little partner, Fidget. Difficulty could be a little higher, enemies rarely feel like a threat, as do bosses. But the game is so well done that that is a minor complaint. The controlls are tight and responsive, and this is probably one of the best indie console to PC ports I've ever seen. Also, I should note that it's made by ONE man, Dead Dodrill, who deserves every cent he gets. Over all, this game is fantastic, it does most everything it sets out to do with flying colors, I'd highly recommend it if you long for the nostalgic days of early video game mascots and Don Bluth type animation. Dust: An Elysian Tail is a definite favorite of mine.

It's pretty hard to find words for this game..
I am playing on normal with normal enemy counter.
For the first hours I was running from one point to another .. and back again.  And what for? To have a 1 minute talk with a party member where we decide to go back to the place we just came from. You don't have much money to buy stuff and if you want to heal yourself at a bunny safepoint (which can be pretty useful), it costs you half your money. Every. Damn. Time. Just why? Good point is: there is much stuff lying on the floor waiting to get picked up.

A really fun game that has been gutted...
I, like many others, am very skeptical about Robot's decision to remove Siege Mode. I have barely played the game since they have as it was the only mode I really had fun playing. The sad reality is that OMD!U is a game that benefited from departing a bit from the original games. It built up a fanbase of MOBA fans and then removed the MOBA elements... It's no suprise as to why the servers are dead.
OMD!U may have been one of the few games that were enhanced by its bravery to dabble into different genres for a new title, and the devs decided not to continue doing so, returning to the game to its roots. My question is: Why bother making a new game the whole idea is to just make it the same as the last? Isn't that what we all hate about Call of Duty and Assassin's Creed? This was a game that was taking some risks and for some silly reason decided not to continue doing so.
At first the excuse was that Siege Mode was the least popular mode (even though this is a lie, ask any player). Siege Mode had the fastest queue times, meanwhile you'd wait upwards of 5-10 minutes for any of the other modes, all of which had less players per match. Now that they've been caught red handed, unwilling to show us the real numbers, the excuse has turned to: "Oh well Siege Mode just doesn't fit the original vision."
Whether or not its the dev's corporate masters, they are sabotaging their own game. If this "huge update" happens to be any good, maybe I'll change this review but as it stands. Nope. Don't bother unless you want a more limited version of the previous games. If the original OMD! gameplay is what you want, you're better off playing the others in the series.

By far my favorite Early Access title thus far. Crypt of the Necrodancer (CotN) should be given a ton of credit for pitching a title that perfectly melds rouge-lites and rhythm-based gameplay.The main mechanic revolves around moving and attacking to the beat of the music and failing to even miss one beat results in a multiplier reset, which altogether works very well. CotN also deserves points in the style department; enemies dance, the floor lights up when the multiplier is up, and the shopkeeper sings along during the high points of the songs. Even though the game retains many rogue-like tropes, it truly separates itself from others with the way it was designed. Music is absolutely stellar (composer of the original Super Meat Boy). Controls are intuitive (you only need the four-directional arrows!).
Like in Rogue Legacy, you can unlock equipment after each subsequent run if you have enough crystals (which you can find after each level). The lobby serves as a way to access this content. Here you can also find individual monster training rooms and various other modes like Hardcore or Daily Challenges.
For the price, it's definitely worthy of the admission. If you're either a fan of rhythm or rogue-like games, this is without a doubt a must-have.

Release Re-Review:
So OMDU has now officially "released", therefore it must work really well now and function like a game that is out of beta, right? Wrong. There are good things about the game, don't get me wrong but there are a LOT of glaring elephants in the room that make the game unenjoyable longterm and kill any replayability.
Pros:
-The game looks pretty
-Characters are colourful and exciting
-The maps all feel quite different, although many are repeated across difficulties
Cons:
-You get 3 characters for free, the rest are behind a relatively large paywall, or a long playtime wall. There is no "hero bundle" to get them all, you gotta do it 1 by 1 and it sucks
-Chests seem to roll garbage 9 times out of 10, while they are planning a "gib store" for dupes of *cough* Steam Vents *cough* and Push/Spring Traps the issue still stands that until you hit tier 7 you get a lot of garbage
-All cosmetics are payed, and really expensive. You get no "mastery" skins or anything to reward longterm play
-A completely F2P player looking to play start to finish through maps will get completely rolled late game unless you hit straight aces in chest rolls, which is near impossible
-All "gear" and "guardian" chest rolls seem to have about a 0.001% chance to drop
-Trap part drops are skewed so heavily you'll never see a lot of the important parts
-The GRIND, getting to t7 on 1 trap takes an unreasonable amount of time, let alone a full set of traps
-The new PvP mode is again just throwing dice and hoping for double 6s. If you get poor card drops and the enemy has 1000 hours in the game with 100 copies of every card, gg you lose
-On that note PvP has seemingly no matchmaking putting brand new players against veterans
-PvE matchmaking is also non-existant and you cannot even pick a specific map to play, you just get to repeat that map you 5 starred first try solo
-Finally, there are only 2 server locations, NA and EU. For all people in OCE, SEA and so forth, you get 350ms of pure rubber banding fun with abilities failing to cast, phasing minions running through walls and unhittable kobold runners
The game is just not worth the time, you're better off buying OMD2 if you want to smash orcs and play tower defense, or just go find a better f2p game

Gobal Thermonuclear War.  Mutually Assured Destruction.  In the final war, nobody will win, and everybody dies, but in DEFCON perhaps you can lose the least.
Taking inspiration from the 1983 film Wargames, you take control of a global superpower on the verge of the nuclear apocalypse.  Deploy your silos, radars, and submarines, defend your territory while blowing the other guys away forever.
The game takes about 15 minutes if played on the fastest speed or up to 6 hours to complete if left on the slowest setting.  You can jump back and forth between them as you see fit, allowing you to give orders in very slow time without being overwhelmed, then speed up time to see the results of your actions.
Boiled down to its core, this is a game of chicken.  Should you strike first, hoping to cripple your opponents chance for retaliation?  Or should you wait, attempt to outlast their attacks, and deliver your own killing blow when they’ve been depleted?  Do you send your naval forces aggressively towards the enemy coastline or keep them close to home in order to defend?  It takes them a long time to travel the whole ocean, so your decision will be a lasting one.
The music is somber and funereal, as it should be in a game about dealing instant fiery death to untold millions of people.  The graphics capture that cold, heartless, military wargame style perfectly.
There is no campaign to work through, no storyline to finish.  There’s just the single scenario of global destruction to play again and again, though depending on the numerous modifiable game settings and which continent you play, they will always turn out different.  You can make it so losing your own citizens is weighed more heavily than killing others, or vice versa.  You can make alliances unbreakable, or change the number of units each team will have.  There is endless replayability here.
It’s a good thing that this scenario is no longer in the forefront of our minds like it was in the 60′s, 70′s, 80′s, and even 90′s.  We no longer fear this afternoon of destruction, where the entire world is wiped out due to a domino effect of retaliation.  Yet it is still very much possible in today’s world.  Nuclear arms are still held by numerous countries the world over.
DEFCON is an interesting little strategy game with some really good decision-making opportunities.  This would be a perfect game for a LAN party full of deal-making and backstabbing, but playing it alone is a rather somber experience.

The aim is to navigate throughout each level so that you squish the specified plants. "One more go".
This is what I thought about 25 times when trying Square's Route for the first time.
It's a game which seems "easy and harmless" when you first play it, with its cute graphics and simple control system, and the first few stages are extremely simple (some of them can be completed in a matter of seconds).
Then the game throws you more colours, more environments, more dangers... and I was hooked.
Square's Route is genuinely challenging: you not only need to think ahead to make sure you land on the target with the desired side of your cube and reach the end of each stage within a certain number of moves/rolls, but you also have to deal with less-than-friendly fauna and lots more dangers.
The secret of the title is that it gets everything right for a puzzle game: a simple control system, an excellently thought-out learning curve (basically, the first 10 levels are a fun tutorial which teaches you how to play and gives you the chance to learn the importance of "landing" on the right side of the cube), a very solid gameplay mechanic and A LOT of levels, which become a real challenge for your brain (but not before level 14) and a bait for your ego, "because I can get 3 stars in that damned level!"
Graphics are very clear and crisp, with a "solid" look, and are extremely functional, with no visual element constituting an obstacle to your view of the playing area. The soundtrack is nice, but it gets repetitive after a few minutes.
Square's Route is an excellent puzzle game. Recommended to anyone who likes to plan their next move ahead and is not scared by hard challenges.
You will spend with this game a lot more time than you'd originally planned to, and it's going to be fun times.

A smooth and very interesting platfomer/beat-'em-up game. If you're turned off by anthropomorphic characters, then this may be steer clear of, but you will be missing out on a very good story and very likable characters. Voice acting runds the gammit, somtimes good, sometimes passable, sometimes other, though rarely ever poor. Smooth gameplay, though it can cause lower-end PCs to slow down due to the detailed spritework and backgrounds. However, it rarely makes fights seem unfair, as the game runs smoothly enough, it rarely lags. Music and artistic quality is fantastic, even for a 2D sidescrolling beat-'em-up. It has some RPG elements, though they're not very important, since you only gain skillpoints to power up attack, health, defense and your little partner, Fidget. Difficulty could be a little higher, enemies rarely feel like a threat, as do bosses. But the game is so well done that that is a minor complaint. The controlls are tight and responsive, and this is probably one of the best indie console to PC ports I've ever seen. Also, I should note that it's made by ONE man, Dead Dodrill, who deserves every cent he gets. Over all, this game is fantastic, it does most everything it sets out to do with flying colors, I'd highly recommend it if you long for the nostalgic days of early video game mascots and Don Bluth type animation. I can't say enough about Hotline Miami. I must admit that I am a retro game lover, and I am one of the people who will never grow tired of the indie flood of 8 and 16 bit games. Hotline Miami looks retro, but that is where that ends. I lived through the 8 bit and 16 bit era and we never got anything like this. The controls are so smooth that even if you are not familiar with the format, if you play any games, you will have a blast with this one. There is the forgiving nature of infinite continues, and if you are just playing it through, not set on getting an A+ for every scene, you can work out a strategy for every level. There are some levels that just picking the right mask is all of the strategy you need, but there are a million ways to beat each and every level.
I can't get over the soundtrack. It almost hypnotizes you into rhis land of senseless repetitive violence, and it makes the game that much more enjoyable. I was a huge fan of Nicholas Winding Refn's movie Drive,  and though the violence is turned up a million othces, I can definitely see the movie's influence on the game in the Jacket scenes. It also has the draw of being something you can just pick up and play whenever you are having a bad day just to blow off some steam by crushing some bad guy skulls in and watching them spray around the room.
Is it worth $9.99? Absolutely. Luckily, with it being an older game you can wait and find it on sale as well. But the beauty of it being an older game made with retro graphics, it is essentially ageless. You go into the game knowing that the pixel graphics are on purpose, and I cannot foresee the ease of control ever being improved upon. I will always be down to reccomend this game to anyone (except maybe easily impressionable youths). If you don't have it, get it. If you have it but never sat down and invested time in it to get the hang of it, play it. Play it until you reach the end. Then come back here and give this awesome game the credit it deserves for being the most amazing game ever made by such a small group of people.

Release Re-Review:
So OMDU has now officially "released", therefore it must work really well now and function like a game that is out of beta, right? Wrong. There are good things about the game, don't get me wrong but there are a LOT of glaring elephants in the room that make the game unenjoyable longterm and kill any replayability.
Pros:
-The game looks pretty
-Characters are colourful and exciting
-The maps all feel quite different, although many are repeated across difficulties
Cons:
-You get 3 characters for free, the rest are behind a relatively large paywall, or a long playtime wall. There is no "hero bundle" to get them all, you gotta do it 1 by 1 and it sucks
-Chests seem to roll garbage 9 times out of 10, while they are planning a "gib store" for dupes of *cough* Steam Vents *cough* and Push/Spring Traps the issue still stands that until you hit tier 7 you get a lot of garbage
-All cosmetics are payed, and really expensive. You get no "mastery" skins or anything to reward longterm play
-A completely F2P player looking to play start to finish through maps will get completely rolled late game unless you hit straight aces in chest rolls, which is near impossible
-All "gear" and "guardian" chest rolls seem to have about a 0.001% chance to drop
-Trap part drops are skewed so heavily you'll never see a lot of the important parts
-The GRIND, getting to t7 on 1 trap takes an unreasonable amount of time, let alone a full set of traps
-The new PvP mode is again just throwing dice and hoping for double 6s. If you get poor card drops and the enemy has 1000 hours in the game with 100 copies of every card, gg you lose
-On that note PvP has seemingly no matchmaking putting brand new players against veterans
-PvE matchmaking is also non-existant and you cannot even pick a specific map to play, you just get to repeat that map you 5 starred first try solo
-Finally, there are only 2 server locations, NA and EU. For all people in OCE, SEA and so forth, you get 350ms of pure rubber banding fun with abilities failing to cast, phasing minions running through walls and unhittable kobold runners
The game is just not worth the time, you're better off buying OMD2 if you want to smash orcs and play tower defense, or just go find a better f2p game

By far my favorite Early Access title thus far. Crypt of the Necrodancer (CotN) should be given a ton of credit for pitching a title that perfectly melds rouge-lites and rhythm-based gameplay.The main mechanic revolves around moving and attacking to the beat of the music and failing to even miss one beat results in a multiplier reset, which altogether works very well. CotN also deserves points in the style department; enemies dance, the floor lights up when the multiplier is up, and the shopkeeper sings along during the high points of the songs. Even though the game retains many rogue-like tropes, it truly separates itself from others with the way it was designed. Music is absolutely stellar (composer of the original Super Meat Boy). Controls are intuitive (you only need the four-directional arrows!).
Like in Rogue Legacy, you can unlock equipment after each subsequent run if you have enough crystals (which you can find after each level). The lobby serves as a way to access this content. Here you can also find individual monster training rooms and various other modes like Hardcore or Daily Challenges.
For the price, it's definitely worthy of the admission. If you're either a fan of rhythm or rogue-like games, this is without a doubt a must-have.

I'm not a fan of horror, I also get nauseous easy and panic easily. Binding of Isaac since it's debut was a game I mentally boxed as something other people with stronger mental fortitude play. It's creepy and disturbing, with a disarming art style and hearing the story second hand (And knowing the roots of Abraham and Isaac) did intrigue me but also made me uneasy. The Winter steam sale gave little more incentive for at least buying it, but I wouldn't recommending waiting for another sale, this game is immensely fun.
There's a few games that walk, and talk like a horror like Gregory Horror Show and their ilk, which did put me off initially easily became a cult-classic, and this outclasses 'bubblegum goth' genre for quirky horror games. The game has little in way of a tutorial, and even less explanation of what every item does, but part of it's charm is exploration in a dark basement of the unknown and working things out for better or worse. Each run and level is randomly generated to keep you on your toes, there's various items that will help deal with the hideous enemies of Isaac's long-begotten and far less loved (or Lovely) siblings, of which they are legion and twisted in their variations.
The game also while simple to grasp, does involve a deal of strategy later on; particularly when you find you can make a deal with the Devil for items that could turn the tide of your misfortune. Other more common rooms make such promises, that you'll need to crawl through a spiked door way to get to. Some items affect your primary weapon, which is a gag in itself, that you fight through the waves with your own tears. Give the game a simple test run, and you'll understand why this has unlimited ammo. The items also affect Isaac visually, and accumulating into making him just as horrifying as the abyss around him, and to be helpful: Even if you look like a Demon's Spermatozoa decked in black membrane with long, sharp gnashy teeth touching enemies will still kill you. I still have no idea why I thought I could eat them, .. but apparently this form gives me flight to get over ledges.
Still Enjoy.

As a dungeon defenders player, this game is right up my ally and I love it. I am having a blast playing it.
There is a good sense of progression with the trap system. I see a ton of people complaining that the chests are a cash grab, but I have to disagree completely. First of all, the ammount of skulls that you receive in the game are plentiful. You get tons of skulls to buy both heros and trap upgrades. The reviews are saying that the game is suffering due to the chest system, but the game can be played 100% FREE at no detriment as long as you just play the game. Second of all, these types of games are about grinding and it seems that people just want everything up front without working for it. I think that is where most of the negativity lies in the reviews - people don't want to work in a game that is focused around progression.
I have yet to unlock all the heroes (less than 20 hours on record, at least 5 of which were sitting in the menu), but the ones that I have played seemed fun and fairly well designed. That being said, there is definitely room for improvement in future champion designs. I’d like to see characters fit more specific roles than they do now. I want certain characters to thrive on maps that fit what they are good at. For example, a high mobility champ to be better on larger maps. At the moment, all characters feel like they can fit any role with slight gameplay tweaks. This is both a good and a bad thing, but I’d like to see more of a balance in versatility versus specific strength.
I think the biggest detriment to the game is the lack of levels. The game is in beta, so there is plenty of time for new content to be added, but in the current state I can see the levels getting stale after many runs. (As of 20 hours play time, I have in no way gotten bored of the current stages. I am still finding the optimal builds and unlocking new difficulties.)
The combo system is a great way to make it fun to replay the maps and try to get that best score that you can; it's like an old arcade game in that aspect, which I love. This system additionally adds strategy and min-maxing to every stage in the game with every character. I think this game would benefit GREATLY from a leaderboard system where players can compete with each other for the highest scores on each map.
I would highly recommend OMDU if you like action tower defense games, progression based games, or strategy games. The game is solid and very satisfying to play. The issues it does have are not major and can be fixed with content updates. 8/10.
