I have played through the game and beaten it twice and enjoyed every moment of it.  I'd definitely recommend to anyone looking for something fun and simple to play, while still having enough of a challenge to be interesting.  I found the characters charming and the interactions to be amusing and while the story wasn't amazing, it wasn't boring either.
Pros:
+Nice selection of party members with different skillsets to appeal to any sort of playstyle.
+Really lovely artwork in the battles
+Character interactions are amusing and charming and you definitely can see some growth in the main characters as the quest progresses
+Multiple difficulty modes with choices on encounter rates to please everyone.  Also the Rush selection can be great to quickly get through easier battles.  Enough challenge to make battles fun but not so much that one feels a need to grind.
+Lots of optional sidequests and hidden things to find.
+Love the friendship dynamic and how having certain people together in a party for a length of time can grant bonuses in battles and give you preemptive attacks.
Cons:
-A bit on the short side, story is about 20 hours of play
-A couple of broken achievements (though dev has been responsive via email about it)  Edit: As of 4/24/2015 the game no longer has broken achievements.

Overall, I'd recommend this game to anyone who loves old school styled RPGs and enjoys the RPG Maker style of graphics.  Personally, I adore the style of RPG Maker's graphics and do not consider that a fault.  The game tells a nice simple story of some fun characters and I had a blast playing it and look forward to playing some more of the dev's other games.

Overview:
The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings is a fantasy RPG set in a medieval landscape.  The player controls Geralt of Rivia as he trys to uncover the truth behind the events that take place in the beginning of the game.  An expansive story awaits and is effected by the player's actions.  The choices you make really will effect the outcome of events.
Pros:
A great and detailed story.  The story is definitely the best aspect of this game.  There are a lot of important characters throughout the game who will shape events as they unfold.
Content.  There is a lot of content here.  Each area has a few side quests in addition to the main story quests.  Even if you just stick to the main quests, the story will take you around 30 hours.  Crafting is also available and can take a considerable amount of time.  If you want a break from the main game, an arena area is available with leaderboards.
Cons:
Crafting.  Don't bother trying to craft that really awesome armor set the vendor is selling.  For one, you will probably never get the money to even buy all the recipes.  If you do manage that, it can be quite time consuming to gather all the leather.  Each armor set comes with a sword recipe for your regular and silver sword.  The swords are the worst part of this crafted set.  They are really awesome for the current area, but require you to have the complete set equiped to use.  Each time you move to a new area in the game, the previous armor set recipes become unavailable.  So, if you spent time just crafting the swords and move to the next area, all that time and resources are now gone.  Crafting armor pieces can be pointless as better or equivalent items can be found by simply thoroughly exploring the area or gambling with random NPCs.  Other than potions and enhancements, crafting is just a waste of time.
Combat.  Although Geralt has access to a few spells in addition to swords, the combat is rather simple.  You can easily play the entire game just slashing as fast as you can and dodging away.  You can parry your opponent by waiting for them to attack, but this locks your character in place and is not advisable when taking on multiple opponents.  Since basically every fight has you facing multiple opponents, parrying can leave you open.
Story Presentation.  The story is pretty good, but sometimes it is not presented very well.  The player mainly controls Geralt but at times will very briefly control a side character.  This can happen at random times and can be better handled by just showing a cut scene.
Tech Issues.  The audio in the game is all over the place.  Sometimes character dialog will be very loud and other times a wisper.  I also did not care for the narrator's voice when transitioning to new areas.  When I had a lot of saves the game would continually crash when trying to load.
Level Design.  The world consist of mainly tight corridors with very little open space.  It would have been nice to have more room to roam around.
Conclusion:
The Witcher 2 presents a great story in a not so great way.  The levels feel claustrophobic, the combat can be very simple, and the crafting can be pointless.  If you put that aside, this is still a pretty good game.  There is a deep story here that can be guided by the player.  If you haven't played a serious RPG in awhile and are looking for something decent, play this.

Final Fantasy VII. Is there anybody who doesn't know it yet? PC users may find it worthy for the updated music, but those who played it on Playstation 1 are not missing much here. That said, if you have never played Final Fantasy VII, you should at least consider buying it here. All gamers should play this game at least once and cement an opinion about it from their experiences.
Get this if you are a hardcore fan who wants to play Final Fantasy VII on the PCs of today, or a newcomer who wants to experience it for the first time. Make sure you grab it on a sale.

A classic game, but the PC port/update is...less than exemplary. There's the cloud saving system, for instance, but it uses your Square Enix account, not Steam's built-in Steam Cloud, and has gone down for significant periods a few times already. There's also the character booster, which is kind of a neat extra, though it depends on the cloud saving system. There are also achievements. Aside from these small value adds though, nothing seems to have been changed since the original PC port, including the inferior MIDI soundtrack from the PC version. The game can be modded to fix that and other things, but there's a catch; doing so will prevent you from using cloud saves (the system rejects any save made in a format it doesn't expect), character booster (which depends on the cloud saves), or achievements. So if you intend to mod the game to make it look better or to bring back the original soundtrack or whatever, you lose everything that Square Enix added and may as well look up the original PC port.
The game is good (of course, it's FFVII), but it sucks that Square Enix made such little effort on this new version and made it impossible to update yourself without losing the only things they did add. Another problem is that it doesn't allow you to map the D-pad on your controller to movement keys. It supports the analog stick, but it's almost unusable. I had to download Xpadder and map the D-pad to arrow keys for the controller to be a functional control scheme.
tl;dr: good game, bad port

Final Fantasy 7 – the first Playstation RPG I got my hands on back in the good old days. And even today I remember this one as a shiny gem, the best of the Final Fantasy series. But thats just my opinion soaked with a lot of nostalgia whenever I play it.
So, whats this game about?
You are Cloud Strife, an EX-"Soldier",who used to work for Shinra, the world biggest corporation. Shinra's only interest is to suck as much "Mako"-energy out of the planet as possible and use it to increase their power. So you end up with a group called "Avalanche" to oppose them. Cloud does not seem to care much about this at first - his reason to "join" Avalanche is referable to Tifa Lockhart, a childhood friend - but as you progress in the game, you will end up on a big journey facing a threat much bigger than Shinra.
The graphics are a little bit outdated, even the once beautiful backgrounds did not age to well, but the story and the amazing soundtrack do more than compensate for the graphics. You can also download some textures for the characters if you like to, which will make them look pretty impressive (Check the community-hub).
Final Fantasy 7 can be played with a keyboard but I find it much more comfortable to play with a controller. The 360-pad works fine but I recommend a keybinder like JoytoKey (freeware) so you can use all of your buttons and bind everything to your needs.
Steam is actually selling it for 12.99€ and let me ensure you; totally worth it!
It's extremely easy to put 100h+ into the game. First there is the main story, I think it took me about 60h back then. But there is much more to do(and discover) in between or at the end of the game including sidequests, hidden materias(magic) and items,breeding chocobos, some kind of RTS-battlefield and the Gold saucer; a huge theme park with attractions, minigames and an arena to test your skills.
My final verdict:
If you are into RPG's Final Fantasy 7 is a must have. For everyone else, if you judge a game just by it's graphics you might get disappointed otherwise give it a try (battles can be fought in ATB or turn-based).
The only downside is,that you have to register at Square-Enix to play the game. It sure get's a little bit annoying nowadays to create an account for every single publisher to play their games but atleast it is not a huge program, just create an account, check the mail and you are ready to go. Took 5 minutes for me.

PvE is the only direction the series should go in. The PvP was unique, but it was broken as all hell, especially since there was no benefit to playing against other people rather than the bots. The meta game of PvP made the game stale and boring. Multiple types of currency was frustrating and confusing for new players. The PvP was unbalanced and frustrating while PvE didn't feel like it had the right amount of attention. The game had to be adjusted for PvP, but that meant that many of the heroes were useless in PvE.
By removing the PvP, the game is actually fun again instead of the grind it used to be. The PvE was the focus of the series in the first place and now it's been beefed up and adjusted for multiple styles of play rather than the standard tower defense. There is still room for improvement, but leaving PvP out is a major step in gettng this game out of beta.

Short review because this is still beta and I don't want to crap on it a bunch.
- Game feels more like the OMD genre now.
- The optimization seems pretty good so far minus a few hiccups.
- Plenty of Orcs to kill.
- They completely scrapped PvP and most MOBA aspects, trying to bring it back from the trainwreck it was.  Seige mode is history.
- Extremely fun with a party.
- Weekly Challenge mode is great, and it lets you try out heroes you may not own yet.
- Lots of UI bugs.  I won't go into detail, but a few examples would be chats not autoscrolling if you click out of them to do something else, having to click buttons more than once to get it to register, etc.
- Everything UI wise feels bulky right now.  I play on a high resolution and I still feel like there is so much clutter and that a lot of the UI aspects could be smaller and rearranged better.  Especially on the client before game.  Opening up a chat window or your friends list takes up so much space.
- Game options are slim, very slim.  You just have a couple basics to switch around.
- Upgrading your traps is based on RNG using a chest system that will require either a daily quest grind or spending money in the cash shop after all dropped chests are received throughout the levels.  I have no idea why this is set up like this.  There's a 75% chance that I'll get upgrade/part components for a trap I barely, if ever, use.  Would like an option to be able to upgrade traps at my leisure, even if they were to make it a little more expensive in skulls to do so.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
I've missed this game and I'm glad that they've changed direction from their original idea.  I have hope that they will continue to switch things around and make the game even better.

Contains tiny spoilers:
An RPG-Maker game that visually looks the business for those seeking a JRPG-Experience for Indie-RPG money, but sadly lacks any great depth when it comes to the story.
While I say this is a 'Negative' review, ultimately this depends on what kind of gamer you are. If the appeal of levelling a character, while walking around some fairly lush and well-thought-out landscapes appeals to you - or indeed the simple mechanics of character levelling - then you'll probably rather enjoy this title.
If, like me however, you prefer a game that hinges on good storytelling and drama, then you'd best look elsewhere - for the plot is about as thin as a pair of aged underpants.
In a nutshell, this game is about an Orc who tries to suck powerful energy from three teenagers (no, really) - but in order to do so must lure them to an alternative dimension where he can directly interact with them. THEN THE PLOT DISAPPEARS FOR 3/4 OF THE GAME while you guide the protagonist through a series of pointless trials in order to go to a well-to-do school in a town called Rillia. A school, that even when you do manage to find it - you only attend a single 'lesson' (Go and obtain some mushrooms a-la any MMORPG you care to mention) - then you get kicked out. THEN SUDDENLY THE PLOT REOCCURS.
It's a shame, as it's at that point where the plot picks up again that the game actually starts to shine - some real JRPG elements creep in, and it feels a lot more solid - and is by far the best portion of the game, though I am not sure how many will stick around to find out.
A game which shows great potential, but falls down on plot - or lack thereof.

Final Fantasy VII. Is there anybody who doesn't know it yet? Unless you have been living under a rock for more than 16 years, you have at least heard of this, one of the most famous games of all time, loved by many and hated by others, with almost no one remaining indifferent. But what matters is, is this port worth the time? It's basically the same as the game that was released on Playstation 1 and PC years ago. The only thing that is new to this re-release is achievements, which in my opinion are a stupid thing to put in any game whatsoever; the character booster feature, which basically makes battles easier and allows you to buy lots of items and equipment without worrying about grinding for gils; And the music, which uses the Playstation 1 tracks rather than the old and low-quality PC tracks. PC users may find it worthy for the updated music, but those who played it on Playstation 1 are not missing much here. That said, if you have never played Final Fantasy VII, you should at least consider buying it here. All gamers should play this game at least once and cement an opinion about it from their experiences.
Get this if you are a hardcore fan who wants to play Final Fantasy VII on the PCs of today, or a newcomer who wants to experience it for the first time. Make sure you grab it on a sale.

A classic game, but the PC port/update is...less than exemplary. There's the cloud saving system, for instance, but it uses your Square Enix account, not Steam's built-in Steam Cloud, and has gone down for significant periods a few times already. There's also the character booster, which is kind of a neat extra, though it depends on the cloud saving system. There are also achievements. Aside from these small value adds though, nothing seems to have been changed since the original PC port, including the inferior MIDI soundtrack from the PC version. The game can be modded to fix that and other things, but there's a catch; doing so will prevent you from using cloud saves (the system rejects any save made in a format it doesn't expect), character booster (which depends on the cloud saves), or achievements. So if you intend to mod the game to make it look better or to bring back the original soundtrack or whatever, you lose everything that Square Enix added and may as well look up the original PC port.
The game is good (of course, it's FFVII), but it sucks that Square Enix made such little effort on this new version and made it impossible to update yourself without losing the only things they did add. Another problem is that it doesn't allow you to map the D-pad on your controller to movement keys. It supports the analog stick, but it's almost unusable. I had to download Xpadder and map the D-pad to arrow keys for the controller to be a functional control scheme.
tl;dr: good game, bad port

The only reason I write this review is that hopefully some change might be done.
When I first saw this game coming to steam I was happily suprised, as I am a long timer in this game, playing the mobile version for a very long time and reaching the tops of global leaderboards.The problem I have with this game is not defenetly the quality of the game, or the system the use for microtransactions, which I actually feel is pretty fair.
The base problem I have is that the game is stupidly easy once you figure one single tactic. The tactic in question is the Dart/Ninja monkey + anti lead (usually sniper monkey or ninja stun grenades) + banana farm tower combo, with the round 13 regen rainbow rush. For the people that aren't deeply aware of this strategy, let me enlighten you how a normal game could look like:
*Placing down dart/ninja monkey
*Placing down banana farm
*Upgrading towers.
*Round 12 sell all your farms and use both powerups.
*Round 13 just spam the send for regen 3 rainbow ballons and win.
This is litterally all you have to do to have success in this game. Once you do it you WILL find success. Currently my winrate is about 85 percent and all my losses is to other people with the same strategy but they are just slightly faster spamming the Rainbow ballons. This is REALLY bad for the game long term, and is the reason why I abandonned it on mobile despite being among top players in the world.
Please now, take care of your game. Use your tools at disposal to nerf this strategy and the game might actually turn out pretty fun and tacticly interessting. This problem isnt new at all, but please do something now.
*note: I know they did a slight price nerf to the dart monkey, but it isnt a big deal at all as you have more than enough money from the banana farm to kill your opponent round 13. Simply not a good nerf enough.

Final Fantasy 7 – the first Playstation RPG I got my hands on back in the good old days. And even today I remember this one as a shiny gem, the best of the Final Fantasy series. But thats just my opinion soaked with a lot of nostalgia whenever I play it.
So, whats this game about?
You are Cloud Strife, an EX-"Soldier",who used to work for Shinra, the world biggest corporation. Shinra's only interest is to suck as much "Mako"-energy out of the planet as possible and use it to increase their power. So you end up with a group called "Avalanche" to oppose them. Cloud does not seem to care much about this at first - his reason to "join" Avalanche is referable to Tifa Lockhart, a childhood friend - but as you progress in the game, you will end up on a big journey facing a threat much bigger than Shinra.
The graphics are a little bit outdated, even the once beautiful backgrounds did not age to well, but the story and the amazing soundtrack do more than compensate for the graphics. You can also download some textures for the characters if you like to, which will make them look pretty impressive (Check the community-hub).
Final Fantasy 7 can be played with a keyboard but I find it much more comfortable to play with a controller. The 360-pad works fine but I recommend a keybinder like JoytoKey (freeware) so you can use all of your buttons and bind everything to your needs.
Steam is actually selling it for 12.99€ and let me ensure you; totally worth it!
It's extremely easy to put 100h+ into the game. First there is the main story, I think it took me about 60h back then. But there is much more to do(and discover) in between or at the end of the game including sidequests, hidden materias(magic) and items,breeding chocobos, some kind of RTS-battlefield and the Gold saucer; a huge theme park with attractions, minigames and an arena to test your skills.
My final verdict:
If you are into RPG's Final Fantasy 7 is a must have. For everyone else, if you judge a game just by it's graphics you might get disappointed otherwise give it a try (battles can be fought in ATB or turn-based).
The only downside is,that you have to register at Square-Enix to play the game. It sure get's a little bit annoying nowadays to create an account for every single publisher to play their games but atleast it is not a huge program, just create an account, check the mail and you are ready to go. Took 5 minutes for me.

Short review because this is still beta and I don't want to crap on it a bunch.
- Game feels more like the OMD genre now.

- Lots of UI bugs.  I won't go into detail, but a few examples would be chats not autoscrolling if you click out of them to do something else, having to click buttons more than once to get it to register, etc.

Especially on the client before game.  Opening up a chat window or your friends list takes up so much space.
- Game options are slim, very slim.  You just have a couple basics to switch around.

I have no idea why this is set up like this.  There's a 75% chance that I'll get upgrade/part components for a trap I barely, if ever, use.  Would like an option to be able to upgrade traps at my leisure, even if they were to make it a little more expensive in skulls to do so.

Aragami is a game of contradictions, and perhaps appropriately so in that it follows a strong theme of light versus darkness.
Initially, it feels very impressive. The art style is refreshing and consistent, and the soft Japanese music certainly adds to the feel of the game. When you start learning the moves and are set loose to assassinate guards, it feels very satisfying - that feeling of satisfaction of pulling off a well-planned kill does keep you playing until the end. On top of this, the shadow mechanics really feel meaningful - when you stick to the shadows, you are all-powerful. You can teleport from shadow to shadow, and kill effectively. When you stray into the light, you very quickly feel hamstrung by how conspicuous you are to your foes, and the non-regeneration of your energy. This contrast is by far the best part of this game.
Style aside, the experience is hampered by several problems that, while individually wouldn't be too bad, in combination make the game feel a little rushed and disjointed, and in the later stages leaves you with a cynical outlook on it.
Part of the joy is that you are a highly-skilled assassin. You carefully select your kills, and the order in which to complete them so that the alarm isn't raised. Often, this means hopping up to treetop level to take out pesky archers who make life on the ground very difficult. You would think a skilled assassin like this would be able to inconspiciously deal with these archers, but alas no. Once the archer is dead, his body is left to slump to the floor, governed by ragdoll physics. Being that archers tend to stand close to the edge of their platform, half of the time you assassinate them the body straddles over the edge of the platform, eventually falling off. Any guards underneath at any point henceforth will see the body and raise the alarm. Not such a slick killer after all - you find yourself shouting at the screen for him to just grab the guy before he falls!
It is absolutely infuriating when you get 80% of the way through a level with perfect stealth, only for it to be thrown away by these clumsy but necessary incidents. However, it does get worse. On several levels, there are patches of grass and foliage. The first thing that you notice about these is that their "sway in the breeze" animation is set way too fast, so rather than swaying it vibrates like a guitar string. More importantly, in the game these patches of grass and foliage render as exactly the same colour as shadows. Given that it is so satisfying to pull off perfectly executed sequences of kills, you try your best to strike quickly and fluidly - especially in the later levels, where there are more enemies. However, on countless occasions, when darting between points, I found myself right-clicking on a bushy bit of grass or foliage, Aragami didn't teleport, and in that lost moment he is discovered by a guard and summarily blasted with a fatal light slash. Having to start levels over and over again makes you feel far less inclined to challenge yourself and complete the game with style, as it gets to feel like you are fighting against these annoying issues rather than against the guards.
Lastly, the skill tree feels like a total afterthought. There are no points in the game that strictly require any of the skills, and for the most part they just make the game easier. For instance, one ability lets you "disappear" bodies, removing a key aspect of planning in levels. Another permanently marks all enemies in the vicinity so that you don't have to scout around. Another, even more powerful ability allows you to silently assassinate an enemy, disappear the body, and regain an ability point all in one go - this particular ability to refuel points and ultimately use these powers infinitely makes clearing a level extremely trivial. As a result, I ended up ignoring the skill tree apart from the "show objective location" ability, simply in order to give myself a bit of a challenge.
All of these things combined, by the time the somewhat flimsy story is over, you are almost glad for it. In most levels, once you've been killed 5 times halfway through or further, thanks to the above glitches, you end up realising that detection by guards doesn't really matter, and you don't get punished for it. If you so wish, you can quite easily dart from shadow to shadow and get to the end of most levels without even touching anyone. If anything, it's even better when someone sees you, as the alert draws all nearby enemies to the place you were spotted - with all the guards occupied in one spot, you can just sprint through the empty level until the next time you're spotted, then start blinking through the shadows again.
If you're an absolute stealth fiend, give it a go. But overall, as an experience, it does feel rather thin, rushed, and disconnected. There's no real incentive, other than personal drive, to play it as a smooth assassin rather than a headless chicken - and that personal drive is constantly worn away by niggling issues with the game.

The story is suprisingly good. It starts off fairly regular, but begins to twist and change as the game proceeds, making for an interesting experience.
I have few complaints, but I do have some. Aragami encounters a few glitches, especially in the multiplayer. Only once did I encounter anything that could be considered gamebreaking, and it just stopped me from completing a single level. I did however encounter several annoying minor glitches. Really my only other real complaint is that the ending boss fight is underwhelming and kinda boring.
Overall Aragami is very well made for the indie company that made it. It's unique, interesting, and takes a fresh approach to the stealth genre. I can definitly say that Aragami is my favorites coop stealth game, and for that I would reccomend it for any stealth fans.

The plot is ok, the acting is solid.
The Witcher 2 is the only game I've played that does morality correctly. You don't have a meter on the side to measure "Paragon" or "Renegade" options. And it doesn't unlock new abilities for being a good guy or bad guy.
In the Witcher 2 you feel the choices that you make. Sometimes being a jerk will help you and sometimes doing the right thing is its just reward.
Here's an example: (NOT A REAL QUEST)
You're approached by a guy who wants you to find a sword that was stolen from him. An heirloom that he'll reward you for handsomely. During the course of your investigation into the matter you discover the man is actually a drug deal who targets children. Your choices are turn him in to the proper authorities and forget about any reward, or get him the sword and get paid.
That's a poor example, but it's very similar to many of the choices you'll have to make. Often times I'll lament a decision I'd made hours ago and the developers are really good at allowing you feel the weight of these choices. Sometimes you'll side with a degenerate just to fill your pouch with a few more coins. The life of a Witcher.
I really like the difficulty of the game, but the combat is a bit klunky.
In a game where you're attacked from all sides you'd expect him to be a bit spry being a mutant and all.
But there is a distinct lag or delay in the starting frames of his moves and attacks. It's noticed the most in his dodge and thrown weapons.
It feels like he throws a dagger about .5 seconds after you input the command when I was hoping he'd be more like batman with a baterang.
It can be buggy as well. There were times during my game that he would get interrupted in mid throw by an attack, I would roll away only to have Geralt attempt the throw again after the roll was complete. I've had him throw knives, bombs, and counter-attack the enemy all without my say so. As if his character had an auto pilot feature.
Not that this happens ALL the time, but I would bet money you'll run into it at least once during a play through.
So like I said it's an ok game, but not worth full price. 50% off or more and definitely pick it up.

Get this game, now. I've sunk far to many hours into this game to say otherwise. This game is perfect in tone, setting, and scale. At this point the game is a bit aged, but the point still stands. All my experiences with this game have put me on a scale of thinking that no other game has come close to.
First off, it's a wonderful strategy game. From a gameplay perspective, it's simple, but it gets the point across. You get your Subs, Airbases, Carriers, and Silos. Your main offense, then you get Silos, Battleships, and Fighters for defence. You may notice Silos twice. They can be set into 2 modes. Offence, and defence. Offensive launches ICBM's at enemy cities and bases, while Defence protects from the same agaisnt you. The simple horror of changing into the wrong mode when a fleet of subs surfaces off say- The Eastern US Seaboard.. It's sumply unparralelled.
Now, the setting, the tone. Spotlessly refined, and beautiful. The soundtrack, ambiance. It all fits in perfectly. The low music, gentle rumbles of detonations over Europe, and a low sobbing from a control operator. It all meshes together with a Siren declaring a launch by the Russians, and the gentle whirring of machines. It makes you feel like the 'general in the bunker' persay, or on the go.. It makes you feel like the commander toting around his launch codes, ready to fire on a  moments notice.
The setting does what few other games do. Make you feel.. guilty. You feel guilty as you switch a Silo into launch mode, deliberatly sacrificing Atlanta to make a strike on Asia. Those 2.3 million people didnt NEED to die, and they could have been saved by simple planning on your part. The swarm of missiles and white clouds of nuclear fire strike you deep, as hundreds of millions perish in an instant.. You could have spared them, or saved them. I've killed countless soldiers, civillians, and cops in all sorts of video games. But nothing strikes quite like a simple white dot, and a message reading: LONDON HIT: 12.6  MILLION DEAD
So, my review. A solid 8.5/10. It has its flaws, it's a little heavy on price (pick it up on sale, and it's a buck or two. WORTH IT) But it's a game that's gonna.. stick with me. It's great fun, and good to play with friends, as well. Just make sure it's one's you can physically hit, when they break off the alliance mid-game.

Secret rooms, one-chance quests and equip, bonus areas and challenges that can hardly be done without these secret weapons and well-trained characters (I'm talking about the hardest difficulty here, nothing else does the game justice.) and so on. Rush through it, and you get a decent game. But take your time, and it's awesome.
P.s. Unlike most similar games, you can't save everywhere in 3SoD - this makes it feel more "old school". And I absolutely loved the music and some of the areas. Especially Outer world made me chill.

Aragami is a well polished stealth game with striking visuals and smooth controls. The various shadow powers are quite fun to use and allow you to complete the missions any way you want. Upon completing a stage you can earn 2 of 3 possible medals depending on whether you killed the guards or were detected. Aragami also features online co-op and workshop content allowing you to play and create custom levels for added replayability. The game does suffer from some performance issues mainly due to being made with the Unity engine.Another minor complaint is that you can't really hear enemies walking around even when very close, this can lead to some unwelcome surprises. There is however an ability that marks all nearby enemies so you can see them through walls but it wouldn't be as necessary if the sound design was a little better. Overall a solid stealth adventure with a slightly cliched story, I would suggest waiting for a sale however since the game is fairly short. If you like sneaking around Aragami is worth a playthrough, but maybe not at full price.

One negative thing though, it's typically very easy, even on Tough difficulty. You will one-shot the standard monsters after only a couple of hours. The difficulty does spike at random sometimes though, which is a bit weird. Expect to die a few times and think "wait, what?!" I'm about 6 hours into the game ATM, and have 40%'ed it.
- The story of the game is nothing special. Dude called Dust wakes up, remembers nothing of his past, talking sword and flying creature wants him to go on an adventure, so he does. He finds villages destroyed by the monsters, and searches for whoever is behind it all while trying to figure out who he is himself. The standard RPG stuff.
- There's not much to say about the soundtrack, other than the fact that it is great. It nicely compliments the hectic battles and what not.
- And then there are the graphics. I love how areas look, the environments of Dust are beautiful! But the characters? I don't know. One word: furries. Well, anthropomorphic animals, but you know what I mean. I am not bothered by this, but you may be. You'll know right away. I think it'll be difficult to play this game if you totally hate furries. So whatever, I like the game, play it if you want, don't play it if you don't want to! Whatevs, it's fine!

I am really enjoying 3 Stars of Destiny. If you dont like RPGMaker Games then this isn't for you. Personally I find the full maneuverablity with the mouse, story and graphics more appealing compared to older JRPG titles which can be cumbersome with their controls (except for Kemco on IOS). It does take about a good 3 hours to get into the meat of the story and battles and I personally found it rewarding onwards from the Mt Zulle Trials onwards.
The fact that you can choose what mode (Casual to Hard) and the Encounter Rate means that you can level up and play according to your style and preferences (I prefer Casual and a Normal Encounter Rate).
The characters are younger and this is relected in the storyline which I found has an innocence and humorous/playful tone. The game is massive in scope and it is the patient gamer who is rewarded. There are many secret rooms and items scattered about. Rush at your peril. Some of these are really great items, weapons, armour, stat boosts, money and quest items which can make a big difference to the game. Explore every nook and cranny.
If you are sometimes impatient like me there are many tips and walkthroughs available on the Aldorlea website. An easy way to switch between the game and a webpage is Alt + Tab.
I still have a long way to go but am loving playing this again and highly recommend if you are after a fun, entertaining and great value RPG.

Hotline Miami is top down shooter with color palette of GTA: Vice Cities and all the gore to go along with it. Hotline Miami uses a 32-bit graphical style to show its wide palette range and buckets of gore that hearkens back to the 80's movies it is critiquing. If there is an argument for mechanics as metaphors, Hotline Miami has them. 
At the end of every level you get a score and a letter ranking. Kill a guy with your bear hands get hardly any points and a low letter ranking. Now kill that same guys with a shotgun and when his buddy nearby comes to check on the noise. You through the gun and curb stop him, get massive amounts of points and a high ranking. This incentives the player not only to kill quick, but also more brutely Making so with every run you care less and less about the guys you are gunning down and more and more about the score at the end. There are also tow types of collectibles one called masks, which you can get to give your character different bonuses such as running faster, attacking quicker ectc, and let you customize the way you want to play the game. These can either unlocked by getting a high score in a level or finding them in the level. The other collectibles are letters that will find through each letter that you need a certain mask "to see", Which will unlock a secret ending that in my opinion is the real ending and really helps to bring everything together. As for the story. 
You play a man named Jacket who gets visits from strangers who give you little pieces of info, but always leave you with more questions than answers. Is this a dream? Am I being drugged? Is this the Matrix? The game never gives you any clear answers until you find the secret ending, and even than it makes you really reflect on what you just and why you did it. It reminds me of the conversation Liquid and Solid Snake have at the end of MGS 1. This game will make you question things without shoving it into your face and that's a good thing. 
Overall I would highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the late 80's movies, GTA, or games that make you question your beliefs after you have play them

The Witcher 2 is the only game I've played that does morality correctly. You don't have a meter on the side to measure "Paragon" or "Renegade" options. And it doesn't unlock new abilities for being a good guy or bad guy.
In the Witcher 2 you feel the choices that you make. Sometimes being a jerk will help you and sometimes doing the right thing is its just reward.
Here's an example: (NOT A REAL QUEST)
You're approached by a guy who wants you to find a sword that was stolen from him. An heirloom that he'll reward you for handsomely. During the course of your investigation into the matter you discover the man is actually a drug deal who targets children. Your choices are turn him in to the proper authorities and forget about any reward, or get him the sword and get paid.
That's a poor example, but it's very similar to many of the choices you'll have to make. Often times I'll lament a decision I'd made hours ago and the developers are really good at allowing you feel the weight of these choices. Sometimes you'll side with a degenerate just to fill your pouch with a few more coins. The life of a Witcher.
I really like the difficulty of the game, but the combat is a bit klunky.
In a game where you're attacked from all sides you'd expect him to be a bit spry being a mutant and all.
But there is a distinct lag or delay in the starting frames of his moves and attacks. It's noticed the most in his dodge and thrown weapons.
It feels like he throws a dagger about .5 seconds after you input the command when I was hoping he'd be more like batman with a baterang.
It can be buggy as well. There were times during my game that he would get interrupted in mid throw by an attack, I would roll away only to have Geralt attempt the throw again after the roll was complete. I've had him throw knives, bombs, and counter-attack the enemy all without my say so. As if his character had an auto pilot feature.
Not that this happens ALL the time, but I would bet money you'll run into it at least once during a play through.
So like I said it's an ok game, but not worth full price. 50% off or more and definitely pick it up.

With incredible intensity and a twisted story, Hotline Miami is a true gaming expirience unlike any other. At first it may seem as it's just a top down shooter, but when you start the game itself, it's much more than that.
The gameplay is what really gets you hooked. It's unforgivingly hard difficulty (which can't be changed) is extruciatingly soul crushing, yet extremely rewarding when you succeed. It's moments of hopeless may result in the greatest accidental play of your life. With one bullet left and an enemy with plenty, I can't stress enough how amazing it feels for the enemy to miss you, and for you to blow his head off.
It's fast paced and really about planning, pacing, and strategy. Death happens a lot, so after dying over and over, you get more ideas on how to approach certain scenarios. It's what keeps you playing.
The variety of different masks and different abilities is also a reason to replay certain levels. One may start with a knife, or kill with it's fists. Another may see longer distances by aiming, and one might even keep dogs away from you. It's refreshing to this variety with different ways to play.
The music is fantastic. It fits every level and intermissions so perfectly. It's heart-pumpingly intense beats when murdering through corriders may transition to a calm and wonderful track during the epilogue of that level. The music is a perfect compliment to the already astounding gameplay.
The story is also pretty engaging to. It's really the backdrop of everything else, but it's interesting and engaging . I'm not going to discuss it, as it may spoil it.
Now, the issues with some unfair scenarios (Unseen enemies killing you, shooting in an opened elevator shaft causing an enemy to walk through the wall and kill you), and some load up issues, it's not perfect.
But it comes damn close and it's easily worth every penny. Go get it. Have a blast.

I originally played the first game a couple of years ago. I liked it enough to buy the entire collection, and I'm really glad I did.
The setting is Deponia, a planet filled with the trash of a once-thriving civilization. A space station called Elysium is a paradise of sorts where the high-class folk live, isolated from the rest. The protagonist is Rufus, a mechanical whiz from Deponia who dreams of going to Elysium. The plot starts when Rufus' latest attempt at escaping actually causes a girl from Elysium to fall into Deponia. From there begins a wacky journey filled with twists and turns.
This is a point&click, as is usual with Daedalic. They tend to have a traditional approach to genre, inspired by classics such as Monkey Island or Day of the Tentacle. Much like those two examples, Deponia is pretty cartoony in nature, though the writers also take comedic cues from stuff like Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
The art style is colourful, and the animations are pretty well done. They're fairly basic in the first game, but they improve immensely in the sequels.
The gameplay is usual fare: take random stuff from the ground, steal random stuff from people's houses, combine items randomly until you find something, all with the goal of tricking someone, or getting items into the hands of people who want them. They also include Layton-style minigames peppered throughout the plot, which are a nice change of pace. They range from genuinely challenging to "easy-but-funny".
They play with the formula from time to time (especially in the later games), but that's the main gist of it. Puzzles follow cartoony logic, main character makes a joke when describing items, etc.
The catch in the middle of all this is that Rufus is a massive jerk. Essentially, he actually is written like someone who tricks and steals stuff from other people for selfish goals. And this is not a case of "Jerk with a Heart of Gold", he really doesn't give two figs. He's barely better than the villains. Much of humour comes from this, the sheer audacity of some of the things Rufus pulls (and says). The beginning "merely" has him cause mayhem in his home town by destroying some buildings, but as the plot progressed, they kept finding new lines for him to cross, ranging from animal cruelty to invasive surgery to...worse.
It's black humour, essentially, and it doesn't pull any punches. Most of it works (in fact, I found myself laughing out loud a few times), but when it doesn't, it can leave a really bad taste in your mouth.
There're also some neat extras here. For starters, The Complete Journey provides something I absolutely love: Developer's Commentary. This one gets especially silly, as the director may provide genuine insight into the writing/animation/design process on one screen, and then on the next one just pick up his guitar and play a full-length song instead.
The achievements are pretty cool, I've dedicated some time to getting them all. They're usually some joke hidden in the game (for example, if you use the sunglasses on a pile of garbage, you get a bizarre Terminator reference), but there are a few that require you to scour the backgrounds for well-hidden collectibles.
Another cool thing (for me, at least) is that the game was originally made in the German language, meaning I can put the audio in German and text in English. This was pretty important in helping me improve my German while here in Frankfurt.
Unfortunately, it means that some jokes and puns may not have translated as well. Usually stuff related to how certain words and accents sound (there are a bunch of jokes involving a character's accent that may not sound as funny in English, for example). That said, I think the English voice actors sound fine, from what little I heard of them.
A big flaw in the series is the abundance of bugs (once again, this is usual for Daedalic). It's easy to see from the community at large that every game had a few annoying bugs that impeded progress, screwed up the layout, or something along those lines. Most of them were cleaned up in The Complete Journey, but some remain (I myself found a handful of minor ones, and one where I had to close the game and reload).
Overall, I found the Deponia trilogy to be a great series, and an example of the Point&Click genre done right. No disrespect to Telltale games, or stuff like Life is Strange, but my favourite brand of P&C is the one that presents a big town to explore and lots of items at your disposal, and then demands some out-of-the-box reasoning to beat.
Overall, I rate it 5 out of 5 stars. Highly recommended, for fans and newcomers to the genre alike.

Before I get into any details, let me lead with the most important thing. This game is fun. It isn't perfect, and there are things I would like to see improved, but I find myself enjoying the game. Beyond that, everything else pales in comparison.
A lot of the negative reviews I've seen on here are criticizing two things, the random loot drops and the power progression. Both are quite polarizing, and despite what many people think, there are actually advantages to both of them.
First, the random loot drop. While it can be frustrating, I like how this has forced me to learn how to use traps that I never would have considered before. As someone that has played both previous games in the franchise, I had grown accustomed to a specific set of traps that I always used. The random drops took some of those traps off the table at the start. This forced me to expand my knowledge of what I had at my disposal, and I've had a better time playing as a result.
Second, the power progression/leveling. Basically, leveling up makes you stronger and this makes early levels eventually become trivial and late levels impossible at first. As a longtime MMO player, this system seems perfectly natural to me and has a delightful benefit of allowing people to control their own difficulty curve. For experts returning to the game, they can constantly be pushing the boundries of what they can beat. If someone wants a more relaxed time, they can spend more time doing maps in the lower end of their range and more gradually approach end game. As a side effect of this, people have commented that it is hard to bring friends in because as a high level playing they can crush the early game. True, but not insurmountable. I had that experience with a friend, so I just self limited my power. I only spent half my coin and didn't use any moves that could wipe out large swaths of enemies. This allowed both of us to participate without it being like playing with a demigod.
Most importantly, I'd like to reiterate my first point, the game is fun. It's free, so give it a shot and see if you like it. Try new things with your traps. And enjoy making those orc giblets fly.
Also, my play time is low because I don't generally boot up Steam to play this. I play it far more than I should.

- Dust is a 2D metroidvania style RPG with very, very satisfying gameplay. Running around and destroying monsters feels incredibly responsive, and it's so damn fun. One negative thing though, it's typically very easy, even on Tough difficulty. You will one-shot the standard monsters after only a couple of hours. The difficulty does spike at random sometimes though, which is a bit weird. Expect to die a few times and think "wait, what?!" I'm about 6 hours into the game ATM, and have 40%'ed it.
- The story of the game is nothing special. Dude called Dust wakes up, remembers nothing of his past, talking sword and flying creature wants him to go on an adventure, so he does. He finds villages destroyed by the monsters, and searches for whoever is behind it all while trying to figure out who he is himself. The standard RPG stuff.
- There's not much to say about the soundtrack, other than the fact that it is great. It nicely compliments the hectic battles and what not.
- And then there are the graphics. I love how areas look, the environments of Dust are beautiful! But the characters? I don't know. One word: furries. Well, anthropomorphic animals, but you know what I mean. I am not bothered by this, but you may be. You'll know right away. I think it'll be difficult to play this game if you totally hate furries. So whatever, I like the game, play it if you want, don't play it if you don't want to! Whatevs, it's fine!

Okay... That was an... experience, I guess. I'm usually more eloquent in my narrative but I can't even begin to describe this bottomless pit of fool's errands named
. It is an adventure game with the illusion of an aim that sends you out into a blatantly foolish settlement with a Herculean list of item catching... Oh, darn! Let me take this from a somewhat proper beginning, okay?
We take the role of a journalist appointed to take an interview from the mayor of the city of Tundel, concerning the discovery of a UFO site. We take on a train journey and arrive at the said town, but reaching the mayor will be a task that shall take the totality of our gameplay. Congratulations! Tundel is a settlement with the ordinary habitant with an average IQ of room temperature. You'll keep encountering eccentric individuals with ridiculous problems and absurd enough situations that you'd constantly feel the need to check if you're involuntarily attending the enactment of a Guillermo Mordillo cartoon. Nope, I wouldn't want that for my worst enemy.
Yup,
is an adventure game with HOG and puzzle elements, yet it's mostly a casual game. You'll be given the whole city of Tundel with more than 50 locations and even more so NPCs to get errands from. Your main goal is to eventually collect enough money through your tasks and buy a plane ticket (!) to reach mayor's island! Through my playthrough, I've been able to discover 114 tasks and complete them all, yet there were still some items in my inventory that I had no idea to their purpose. Obviously, I've been missing even more things to do. It is not only possible, but likely to complete the game without completing all errands and the function of the open world map interaction is a bit frustrating. So I highly recommend
trying to complete all errands! It is maddening! Eventually, they'll all serve to be futile anyhow... that ending... but no spoilers!
Graphics are annoying plastic animations and character models are intentionally appalling rather than funny. Oh, and get ready to stumble upon &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; at every corner. Nope, it's not a remark.♥♥♥♥♥♥really happens in Tundel.
There are some actual HOG sequences and some puzzles with investigation properties - yet nothing rewarding enough to actually make you keep playing this game. I've been playing games for 20+ years, hunched over playing half-life 1 or descent on AOL dial-up.  To put it succinctly, this is the only game I've played that does RTS/FPS very well.  And it is the only true team game in the best sense of the word.  Almost all AAA FPS I've played have 'team-work' loosely associated - most of the time you just rambo and try to max your K/D or hope your random teammates hold a point with you.  There isn't a real or dynamic 'objective.'
This game is different.
The FPS portion of it has the intensity, communication, team-work and goal-oriented experience like a Raid in Destiny.  The RTS portion of it has the experience of any other RTS like Starcraft
The combination of both is potent; with two teams trying to get an edge on the other.  Objectives are dynamic and change on the fly as one team accomplishes something the other has to communicate and adapt.  Maps are large enough so that areas are individually significant but small enough to maintain that intimacy and individual importance.
On top of that, the asymmetric sides are extremely well done - with aliens being agile, fast, deadly but fragile.  Marines with traditional guns, jet-packs, mechs.
100% recommend
While I love this game, to be upfront, the problem with it is the learning curve for new players.
Like in Destiny, there are certain objectives that are more important than others that are not immediately clear to the new players.  Like in Starcraft, there are build orders and map locations that generally are more effective than others
And like the above games, you can't expect to beat a raid or win an online bnet battle your first time in.  You will probably lose, until you listen and learn and figure out how to be more effective
The community can be hard on people who just jump in the command chair and start playing their own game without any experience and without asking any questions.  This is a team game after all; and the commander is the most important
The community is good with people who up-front let people know that they are new, but are willing to listen and and learn.  A mic is also helpful

Bus Simulator 16 was developed by still alive studios and published by Astragon. The game released on the 2nd March 2016 for a price of £18.99.
In Bus Simulator 16, you are in charge of a bus company and must also drive around the bus collecting and dropping off people on various routes. During my hour of playing this game I had many ups and downs but the eventual ending was me stuck outside my bus and also stuck outside the depot with no way back.
Positives:
+ Good attempt at an entry level bus simulator – The game was designed to be a really good bus simulator but unfortunately falls quite short of that bar. The game feels more entry level but a good attempt at it.
+  Steam Workshop – With steam workshop there will be mods to improve the game and adding own designs and busses.
+ Tutorial – The tutorial is pretty good and I’m glad I did it. The amount of options and choices to the game is overbearing at times but I feel after an hour more confident  to try and drive a bus around.
+ Multiplayer – This is a great add to the game, you can play online and manage routes together too, the only problem for me is that I lack friends with the game 
+ Cops/Police – When I was idle at the station trying to figure out buttons and such a Police car went flying past me with the lights on. I found this so cool – however it may just be normal for most people.
Negatives:
- Floaty handling – The handling is not too good on this game and most the time I end up crashing and bashing when taking corners because the handling is too light.
- Overwhelmed – There are just so many options, buttons, choices in which you must do and then to add to the top of all that the doors get jammed and the customers expect you to give them change from money which you can’t really make out.
- Voice acting – If you can make it through the game without laughing at the terrible voice acting I commend you. I laughed quite often due to this fact.
- Long loading times – It may just be my PC but I experienced agonising load times and very bad FPS.
- Price – I feel the price should be halfed for the product because although you get a lot of content the quality is subpar.
Unfortunately I felt this game had a lot of potential but the execution was pretty bad. I was hoping to finally get an Omni 2 experience on Steam but unfortunately this falls well below expectations and to me feels more of an entry product. I could only recommend this game to people with low expectations or standards (huehue). I played this game only for an hour but  I was left out in Sunny Springs in the rain, trapped from my bus and depot. Although I slate the game I enjoyed it for what it was but can’t possibly recommend the game at the current price point. I’m just glad the game never crashed on me because that would’ve been the icing on the cake.
Score: Wait for a sale

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10

This is now the definitive version of the game now that they added PSX music. The translation and graphics are superior to the PSX version and it's most likely going to be cheaper than actually purchasing a physical copy.
As for the game itself, the flaws are all still there and have become as glaring as ever with its age. The story still is as nonsensical as ever, the super deformed characters still look ugly, and the materia system actually destroys the traditional RPG formula for balance and makes each character essentially blank canvases outside of their base stats and limit breaks. That can be fun at first glance but it becomes very bland when every character essentially operates the same way and the end game becomes so single-minded. It's also a turn based/random encounter affair so if those kind of games get on your nerves you should avoid this at all costs. Lastly, the characters are your standard JRPG affair (although at the time, these archetypes in video games weren't common in North America) and most don't really evolve past their initial character development, especially outside of the party.
The good?
-The materia system is fun, flexible, and broken. I can't say I agree with it on a balancing or variety level but on the surface it's fun and gratifying.
-The story ends up being paced pretty well throughout the entire journey which doesn't happen very often with JRPGs.
-Random encounters are paced very well for a JRPG and I didn't find myself ripping my hair out until the final dungeon (two battles every screen with a mastered Enemy Away? Nah).
-There are many side-quests that feel naturally implemented into the world and I enjoyed most of them aside from Chocobo breeding which was nothing but tedious.
-The pre-rendered backgrounds are also usually pleasing to the eye (then again, they're a stark contrast to the awful character models that populate them).
-The music and sound effects are great and overall the presentation has a charm to it that most JRPGs don't.
My personal outlook on the game may have soured a bit over time but the core of the game holds up fairly well to this day despite some obvious flaws. I rate it overall a very strong 7. A worthwhile experience that I think gamers insterested in the history of the medium should attempt to tackle, especially those who are familiar with Japanese RPGs.

You probably know that this game wasn't really what it was expected when it launched, having problems and all that. And even after many patches it still doesn't feel very optimised, especially in the big part of the city where there's tone of frame dropping. But from my perspective it was ok, even though the gameplay was very repetitive.
Firstly, I really liked the story, well put together along with the characters and I got to say that the cutscenes kinda made all the game, it felt like you were watching a movie, pretty much an amazing experience also with very good dialogue.
The second thing that I really liked were the capos missions which were diverse, fun, and different.
The third thing are the cars, which in my opinion were very good, even though you didn't had that many options (especially with the vehicle delivery service), but they felt pretty nice and the tuning was also somewhat decent.
Pros:
+ good story and characters
+ amazing cutscenes and very good dialogues
+ amazing soundtrack
+ good graphics (but also I turned off the motion blur and the depth of field, felt way blurry)
+ big open world with districts that are well different from each other
+ good boss (capos) missions
+ the cars felt quite good (even though there aren't many of them in my opinion)
Cons:
- very repetitive gameplay
- doesn't fell very optimised, even after all this time
After all this I can say that this game could've been something great with a little more work on it, a successor worth it's money, but in my case I pretty much enjoyed it as I don't really look for spots to blame a game for in general, so i'd give it a 6/10 for the other things that made this game playable and quite enjoyable.

is a quirky little game that offers no innovation to gameplay but still boasts a very strong and unique identity. It breaks away from many of the traditional stylings of the point-and-click adventure genre and offers a nice experience that will appeal to those who want to stay within the genre without having to settle for another clone of a clone of a clone of a hand-holding, linear game.
The aesthetics and presentation of the game neither add value to the game nor do they take any away. It doesn’t have the prettiest graphics, the trendiest soundtrack, or the most refined atmosphere. But it does have a cute and functional, Saturday-morning-cartoon inspired presentation that will appeal to anyone’s inner child (or to anyone fortunate enough to still be a regular child).
The gameplay boils down to a classic point-and-click, inventory-based, puzzle-oriented experience. And, as is always the case with the genre, it is very relaxing and casual. You are mostly free to solve the puzzles at your own leisure and should never feel any pressure to succeed. Most of the gameplay consists of gathering the correct inventory items and giving them to the correct NPC, however some of the puzzles are more like mini-games and there are also a number of hidden-object-pictures as well.
But what mostly allots this game its charmingly unique identity is the relatively large and very open world. Instead of being ushered from one plot point to the next as you solve puzzles and complete tasks, you are free to explore the entire city at your own pace and complete tasks in any order you choose (save for those which are locked behind other solutions). The main goal is to acquire a certain amount of money which unlocks the ending area and allows you to “beat” the game. That money is obtained by completing the various tasks available.
Through this openness inherent in the gameworld, the quirkiness of
really comes to life. As you wander around and meet the various NPCs, collect many inventory items, and slowly build up currency, you will be exposed to all sorts of simple playfulness and silliness. You will quickly come to find that it certainly is a city of fools.
There are some noticeable flaws to the game as well, but nothing egregious in any way. For one, there are so many tasks to keep track of.  There is a journal which will point you in the right direction for each task, but it doesn’t remind you of the location of the task-giver. And so you may occasionally find yourself struggling to remember where to find the NPC who wanted to buy the <Insert Item> you just obtained. Relatedly, there is a map which will help you out, but no fast-travel option. Not too big of a deal, because exploring the city is part of the fun; however towards the end of the game when you’re just trying to finish up, it becomes more noticeable that a fast-travel would be appreciated.
In summary,
is an enjoyable and quaint little game. It won’t appeal to everyone, but fans of the point-and-click genre will very likely appreciate the novelty of the game design and won’t even have to leave their comfort zone. And if you are generally on the fence regarding the genre, this may be one you will want to consider, due to its unique identity compared to the majority of similar games.

This was a really entertaining game.  It's a sort of point-and-click "adventure" combined with minigames, but if you're someone that normally plays H.O. style games, it has a very different feel to it.
The plot is very simple: you're a journalist and you want to interview the mayor, but you find he's on his private island when you arrive to the town.  The rest of the game is essentially questing around to help the townspeople in order to 1) get authorization to travel to the island and 2) make enough money to buy the plane ticket.
Although the plot isn't that detailed, the gameplay and puzzles were a lot of fun, and much more intuitive than some games (while I like having to think about things, I don't like having to twist my brain into a pretzel to make the logic work).  As a good, casual game, it really pays off.
As another benefit, you don't actually have to complete all 122 tasks that are available to do.  While some reward items that will help you progress, most of the time it's a monetary reward that gets you closer to your plane ticket.  As a result, as soon as you have enough for the ticket, you can dispense with all of the other quests (if you want to) and proceed to the end.  This adds some replayability if you chose to bulldoze through the first time and want to go back and see the rest of the game later.
I won't say that it's perfect; I found the navigation perplexing especially at first, but the waypoint system on the map helped a great deal if I knew where I wanted to go and just needed directions.  The ending felt a little lacking as well.  However, I was entertained enough by the game as a whole that I would still heartily recommend it even with those minor issues.
Pick it up on sale if you're unsure, but I felt that the full price was reasonable.

If Rube Goldberg had been a game designer he would have easily fit in with the developers of Absolutist Ltd.  (How to build a better mousetrap, anyone?)  This game is a convoluted, hodge podge of absurdly "normal" (yet quite obsessed) characters who for various reasons all want something from somewhere else before the gamer can obtain the one thing they really need.  At least the characters pay well, in most cases.  Take notes my friends, you will need them, and SAVE YOUR GAME.  This game does not automatically save when the gamer quits.
Story: Your newspaper editor has sent you to Tundel to interview the mayor about a possible UFO cover-up.  Seems a simple enough assignment until you get to Trundel.  You discover the mayor is on his private island.  Finding the airport is simple enough and getting to the island seems easy until you learn the "plane" ticket costs $1264.  Now you just have to earn the money to get there.  This begins the convoluted "adventure" of finding items located somewhere in Tundel.
Gameplay:  Defintely point and click with unusual puzzles and odd Hidden Object scenes in an open, do as you please, world.  Nothing usual or standard fare in this game in any of those genres.  Earning enough money for the plane ticket is the whole point of the game, but there is so much more that can be done.  Depending on the gamer's play style or interest about 80% of this game is NOT in the direct storyline.  Money is earned through running errands (mostly through running errands, all over town (warning: take good notes)), gambling, a shooting gallery (using a rubber band slingshot through your fingers), opening lockers (I found/guessed 7 combinations), putting together an orchestra, the pot plant and collecting bottles and empty cigarette packs.  The gamer does not have to do all of those things if they do not want to, except the running errands to earn cash.  There is also one maze (no money) which random clicking will more or less get you through, though there is an actual path but no map.
In each scene there are arrows to indicate possible direction of travel which include up and down.  In the apartment buildings there are generally two floors.  NOTE: There are two places where there are no arrows to indicate the gamer can go there, one is the construction site (This area is indicated by pink arrows but one can still get in.) and the other is the hospital.  Both areas are on the map but getting inside requires a bit of lateral and intuitive thinking.  AUTHOR SUGGESTION:  Everyone who plays this game should ride the "subway" at least once.  It made me laugh but then again my humor runs toward the irreverent and absurd.  In some scenes, especially in the apartments, there are side rooms where puzzles, hidden object scenes, and point and click items can be found.  Do not forget this is a point and click game so look around and into things, so one does not miss, at times, vital items needed.  Look carefully around any inside area and outside in the town areas as well.  One hint here: Look for a blue car (not necessary for direct storyline play).
Another hint:  Make sure you know where the water sources are.  (No spoilers)
The map of Tundel is easy follow and has a flag which can be placed anywhere as a destination.  When leaving the map two white arrows appear to indicate the direction the gamer needs to go to reach their flagged destination.  Makes traveling around town so much easier since in first person view one can easily get "lost".  The map also gives street names and house numbers so when taking notes (which I highly recommend) one can keep track of where one has been, who has what, and where one needs to return to.
Achievements:  There are only six and easy to get (depending on play style).  Three are achieved through gameplay and the other three require buying all the stock out of the shops (which requires lots of money.)  Most of the items in the shops are not required or needed for direct gameplay.
One final note: Again:  SAVE YOUR GAME.  This game does not automatically save your game when you quit.  So save your game before leaving or hours of work and playtime may be lost.

CONS:

Can get a big laggy as you progress in levels. It depends on your device.
~
DO I RECOMMEND?:

Edit: Gameforge is gone.
New update has been released and a lot of things has changed.
The PvP has been removed, I personally enjoyed it but as many people pointed out OMD is a tower defense game and they should keep it like that instead of trying to create another MOBA.
PvE has been changed as well. Now you get stars for clearing levels within time limit and with all the rift points. The stars award you (one time) with skulls (main currency) and chests. You can also get chests from daily quests, clearing a level as a new character and 1 a week (at least in EU) for daily log-ins.
Crafting materials have been removed but now it's probably worse than before when it comes to unlocking traps. First of all most traps are locked until you reach a certain level, only after reaching that level you can get them, BUT you must get lucky and open them from a chest. You don't get to pick which traps you get, you are at the mercy of RNG. So after ~50 hours of gameplay and getting most chests awarded for getting stars my friend and I have only 2 "Epic" traps each and there is still 8 more to unlock if I remember correctly.
When it comes to upgrading traps you have to get them again from chests to collect enough parts to upgrade them so that's more RNG dependant progression.
Right now my friend and I have cleared almost every map and there is nothing to do really. There are daily quests, weekly challenges and endless mode (where you also get chests once) and that's it. There is an incentive to repeat beaten maps as other characters to get 1 chest but at least for me it's not motivating enough to play as a character I don't like to get a chest and get upgrades to healing well that I'll never use.
Overall the game is fun until you beat every level, then the only thing you can do is repeat older levels as all different characters. The biggest problem is the RNG.

Fun inventory puzzle point & click "adventure" game
The
of this game shows over 50 houses, and each one has one, sometimes two quest givers. They're all fairly weird people with strange requests: some of these involve going into the next room and fetching some stuff (the hidden object part), but most require you to fetch something from somewhere else in the city. If you've seen the item at the pharmacy or at the store, it's easy; but if you don't, well, you'll be sure to run across it later. If you do, and realize "this is what the guy from earlier wanted", that's usually followed by the realization that you have no clue where you found him. Well, you'll be sure to run across him (or her) again later...
So, yeah, it says "hidden objects", but that's not the main thing you're doing: you'll be running all over town doing these quests (there are 122). There's a journal that helps you keep track of all of the tasks, and the map, and on it there's a pin you can use to mark a place of interest - maybe I should've used it. Or maybe I shouldn't have chosen the hardest difficulty (who needs hints). Oh well. In fact, you can switch the difficulty back to "casual" at any time, and then you can use the button that adds hints to your journal. There is a main plot/goal, but it hardly matters. (That's why I put "adventure" in quotes above.)
There's one slight annoyance: the locations are static, i.e. the player clicks on a arrow and moves to the next position, and each position only has a single camera angle, which means that half the game you're going backwards: you'll need to have a good memory and sense of orientation or use your map a lot. Also, some of the translations are slightly off: a wrench might be called a key (but still look like a wrench, so that's ok). I didn't have any real problems with either, and at the end, I was zipping around the town like a pro.
The graphics may not look like much (it runs at 1024x768 windowed and 1366x768 fullscreen with black sidebars), but the game has various kinds of subtle and not so subtle humor that appeal to me, and that extends to the impeccable sound effects. (Please realize that one of the first tasks is helping someone in the train station toilet with their diarrhea - and they didn't just do the trains perfectly). You just have to release your inner child a bit to enjoy this game - don't be serious! Also, I'm a sucker for open world games, and I've never seen one made like this.
