Aragami is a stealth-based game developed by Lince Works. The player takes control of the titular Aragami, a vengeful spirit summoned by young girl Yamiko to avange her family and people from the tyrannical Army of Light controlling the whole country with an iron fist.
Aragami is a pure, challenging, stick-to-the-shadows kind of stealth-based videogame: as your playable character takes only a single hit before being killed off, you must be careful to navigate the various levels while evading all the enemies and conceal yourself in the shadows in order not to be seen. Shadows play a huge part in Aragami, since the protagonist's abilities are all related to shadows (like teleporting from one shadow to another or create a shadowy duplicate to hold your enemies' attention) and you can recharge their uses by hiding in the dark. On this front, Aragami manages to be a rather good stealth-based game: walking around your foes to reach your current objective at times require a lot of thinking and carefully manuvering, and the opposition you face will become trickier and trickier to bypass the more you progress through your mission.
The Story Mode of the game is made of 13 chapters where you must for the most part lead Aragami from the beginning of the area to the next one, with at times some items recovery assignments. This mode also features two interesting boss fights and collectables in the form of scrolls you must collect in order to gather skill points and acquire new abilities or improve the ones you already got. The plot of the game in itself is admittedly simple enough, but it's very interesting and ends with a nice plot twist and a final act that really makes it shine. At the end of each chapter you'll recive a score based on your performance and may unlock certain medals (because you actually didn't kill anyone in the level, for instance).
Aragami also features a Mission Mode where you can play your map of choice with the desired complexity and difficulty. There's also a SteamS workshop where people can create their own, highly customized missions for the other players to download and complete. The game also features a Multiplayer Mode, but, at the very least at the time of this writing, finding an open match to jump into is nearly impossible, so I couldn't possible vouche for it.
Despite being an indie title, Aragami is an incredibly solid stealth-based game with a fair amount of longevity if you really want to milk it for all its worth, by for istance keep playing custom missions or improve your scores and medals gains in the various chapters of the Story Mode

A Stealth action game that feels like Dishonored if Dishonored was set in Feudal Japan and Corvo was a vengeful spirit Ninja. Clearly the devs took a lot of inspiration from Dishonored for gameplay, and some from Mark of the Ninja for visual style, and perhaps even a bit from zelda with some puzzle aspects as well as a blue (often) spherical follower giving advice on the current situation. The game does however see some flaws in those games and learns from it. For example in Dishonored once a single corpse is found everyone is on extremely high-alert and the game becomes more of a rambo shooter than a stealth rpg, whereas in Aragami if you really want to go undetected you can choose to just die as there are plenty of checkpoints. Aragami also doesn't seem to condemn the player for choosing a lethal playthrough. Skill-upgrades are optional, though very handy as they help with hiding bodies, finding more skill upgrade scrolls, stealth and revealing enemies, though none are really required to pass the game (but they do significantly affect your succes rate). Didn't finish the game yet, but so far I can say I would recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Dishonored. Never played Mark of the Ninja but if you're into that you'll probably appreciate this too.

I didn't enjoy this expansion, but I am not declaring it to be an objectively bad game by any means. Fans of Dawn of War who want tons of army choices for single player and/or a variety of armies for multiplayer and who don't mind a near non-existence of story will likely be happy as pigs in mud playing this expansion, because unlike in Dawn of War, where you get one army, or Winter Assault, where you can choose between two sides (which are different armies) and get to flip flop between two armies on either side, Dark Crusade gives you access to seven different armies. Holy crap, that's awesome!
In Dark Crusade, you can play as Space Marines, Imperial Guard, Orks, Necrons, Tau, Eldar, and Chaos Space Marines. That's so impressive. When I loaded up and saw that, my jaw dropped. Then I started the game up and my jaw sunk even lower. I must've looked like a snake trying to eat an ostrich egg in that moment, because the game displayed a large territorial map with all seven armies on it, and its own little gameplay elements such as reinforcing positions and relocating to take over other regions.
I can envision this being a Mecca of delight for someone who wants to play bunches of 40K armies and spend many, many hours doing battle for control of the planet. That is unfortunately also where my own dissatisfaction comes in. I enjoy a succinct story for an army without drawn out missions. The original Dawn of War really appealed to me for that reason, as it had a story which went from start to finish, and when you completed a mission, it was complete. In Dark Crusade, however, when you conquer a territory, you may have to play that same territory (map) several times to defend it from follow-up attacks from the six armies you're fighting.
Repeating the same maps, even though you get to keep your previously standing structures, didn't really appeal to me at all, and felt like a stretching of the material available. There is plenty of content in this game to have just playing it once be a delight, but when I need to play each one multiple times without any real gain, it gets old fast for me. There is an auto-resolve option, but the game explicitly informs you that you have a much greater chance of losing your territory if you go automatic instead of manual.
Aside from having to repeat the same maps over and over again, the lack of a persistent narrative discouraged me from continuing as well. With Dawn of War, I was rewarded with little intro and outro cutscenes, and sometimes even mid-mission cutscenes. Here, you get an intro for each army, and that's all you're going to get until an ending, which I didn't stick with long enough to watch. That's all well and good for a game that lasts a very short handful of hours, if I'm having fun with the gameplay, but I need some story stimulation with a game that is going to take me a significantly longer span of time to complete.
These are just my issues with the game, however. Like I said, it's not objectively bad. The variety of armies and the war map likely make this game a 10/10 for people who aren't phased by the things that were negatives for me. If you feel similarly to me when it comes to fighting on the same map repeatedly and a lack of story development in a long-ish campaign, then avoid it, but if not, this game might be right up your alley.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Short Version: It's a must buy to play locally with friends and must have, and you want to push the developer to make it bigger and better.
Warning: At the moment of this review there is no "online multyplayer", or local AI to play against. It's for you and your friend to play on the couch at home as games "used to be", so that your screams of joy and suffering can be heard while someone is on a destruction rampage.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Long Version:
Looking in to the Steam games for Local coop, you don't find much of appealing games for a nice evening and party with your friends, the choices are quite limited to few choices: Magicka, Towerfall, Gang beasts... but the rest doesn't look solid enough for a buy or lasting fun. Lance a Lot was a nice surprise, it looked good, the gameplay seemed nice and so I decided to give it a go.
Results? The game is very fun, and it was a surprise that is one of the game overlooked by Steamers because it is a nice hidden gem. Reading more about the developers, you quickly realise that this was a short experiment that it became much more popular that the developer expected. It's a pity because they deserve someone to sponsorship them and give them more funds, the game has much potential and it could be refined even more with many interesting features, because I sincerely want this game to grow.
Flying on a rocket on the sound of hectic classical music (great choice by the way, I was screaming the song while trying to impale my friends), and than discovering that you don't need to just impale your friends to win, but you can even punch them, or push them out of bounds, or make explode with the holy granade or barrels it add a small layer of tactic into the game.
Other positive things about the game is the choice of 4 modes (without counting the tournament option) on the skirmish play: Last Man standing (doesn't matter the kills just survive at the end!!!), Capture the Flag (get hold of the flag and run away like a master chiken that wish to fly before someone else kills you), King of the hill (or better Pinball of the hill, you hit a target and try to keep off people from to touch that target) and Kill mode (the most kills wins, but don't die by suicide or you'll lose point. Damn thorns map, I hate you!!!).
Than you have as well customization of parameters that make the game more interesting, like full throttle acceleration (so you cannot stay still anymore), length of your Lance (tiny lance fights are ridicoulus and hilarous) etc...
Some maps have interesting surrounding effect, thorns if you hit them twice they can kill you, the floating air if you stay too long you die, the damn trees that you get often stuck into and try to get free from it, the teleports that teleport you when you least expect when you try to avoid an enemy lance, the holy granade, the explosive barrels and the rotating stick of doom! (I wish that this one was moving a tiny bit faster).
This game show at his best with 4 people playing on the gamepads. We laughed, we cried, we promised doom and destruction on each other. So yes, it's a game to show off at your gaming party nights and it is assured fun.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Suggestions for the developers:
- I wish like some other guy told on the forum, to have a random button for this kind of settings or have a play mode on which every round the setting just change automatically, because choosing them it's good but most of the time when you are into the zone of fun, you just don't want to think and I want ready solutions.
- I want more maps, at least 4 more. One in particular that I imagine it is a simple single file line on which we need to charge each other for 1vs1, and maybe you can do it like a cross so in 2vs2 we can meet crashing each other in the center.
- The map with thorns with the mode who kill the most, was stressing and fun at the same time... maybe that map need a bit more space because of the thorns, it was the longest game and I believe quick and fun it's the best deal of the experience.
- You need to explain a bit the dynamic of the punch that it's not clear at all how to achieve it into the game (we had different trial until we figure it out).
- I agree with everyone saying multiplayer over AI, if you can do it, do it. And I understand the difficulty of lobby for the game, the latency etc... maybe wait for a bit more success or look for investors to fund it. Don't give it away, if this was your training ground game, think of it as training and get better as team.
- Give me one more game mode, I loved the capture the flag, because I was defensless and I had to run the whole time. Maybe something like Rocket League on which you have a bouncy spike ball that you need to try to score (or maybe kill someone else with) good for a 2vs2 game or 1vs1 game. We have always game everyone againts everyone, but not modes on which we can team together vs another team. And I believe that could be even fun to have a specific game mode that is 3vs1 like the capture the flag (like you have the fast rocket and longest lance, but your enemies have short lance and slow rockets but you need to avoid them and kill them all).
- If you ever introduce AI, think about co-op mode. 4 knights vs hordes of monster to defend the entrance of the castle. Friendly fire obviously is on, so while try to save the princess you can kill your friends anyway at the last 10th wave :D

Fallout Shelter is just another experiment made by Bethesda where more genres are tested on Fallout franchise. Instead of FPS open world sacavange hunt (Fallout 3, Fallout New Vegas and later Fallout 4), Bethesda tested mobile device platform and made a scavange hunt simulation. The game is very simple and limited: basically you're doing vault managment, signing tasks to dwellers, sending dwellers on missions, building rooms, etc. Controls are somewhat clumsy, it's bit awkward to pick and move dwellers. Combat is very simple, visuals look nice, there is large variety of weapons and armor, but those are the only good points.
The game suffers from constant critical situations, there are fires in the vault and creatures (such as raiders, ghouls, radscorpions, deathclaws...) attack all the time and there isn't much time to build rooms, send dwellers on missions or assign them to a room. I remember having at least four waves of attack before I got a chance to send my dwellers to explore the wasteland. The game becomes nothing but a nuisance that you start looking around where will radscorpions crawl out next or where fire will start.
The concept of vault managment sounds interesting, but project execution is poorly made. Players get only a feeling that they just click at stuff and don't get any feeling they accomplished something because the moment they finish something, a fire starts or deathclaws attack, which just keeps them busy. The game would look interesting if there were more difficult missions (with more slots for dwellers) such as attack on a supermutant camp, to get more Fallout experience, not doing silly missions which barely have any relation to the franchise at all.
In the end, the game was made for smartphones, so it's basically just a way to kill boredom. it's allright to play the game from time to time, but playing more often will start to become annoying since the game doesn't have anything to offer but constant fires and deathclaws attacks.
For all that it's probably a bit too easy on anything but the highest difficulty, I really enjoyed Dust: AET. It has a great art style, soundtrack and just generally really fun combat.

A fast and furious game where you and your friends or a bunch of strangers play ducks who try to murder each other with some weird weapons, ranging from swords and hammers to guns and laser rifles.
The controls are tight, the maps are fun, and the game is just plain funny (there's a quacking button), but the real meat is the weapons themselves.
They all have different properties, different ammo counts and firing rates and basically, you need to learn how to identify and use each one.
I mean, picking up a one-shot gun won't do you much good if you spray and pray, and if you pick up the game which for some reason the ducks hold the wrong way (barrel facing you), you'd better throw it before you accidently fire.
There are also plenty of single player challenges that are hard enough to make you master and actually get better at the game with, and they're certainly fun enough, but at the end of the day they serve as training for the real thing.

Alrighty... to start things off, I don't know how it took me two months to even consider writing a review on this masterpiece.
I'll try to make this a brief review. Knowing that this is an indie game, before I saw the trailer, I was pretty concerned in terms of how good Dust: An Elysian Tail would be. After seeing the trailer and buying the game right after, I had a lot of expectations for this game - and, on that note, this game exceeded all of those expectations. Honestly, I don't even know where the hell to start.
Dust is a pretty short game, but it's able to fit everything a good game's supposed to have in it. That is, the story, characters... the works. The levels look more and more gorgeous as the game progresses, and the voice acting is [almost] top-notch. And the music. Oh my ♥♥♥♥ing gawd, the music. The soundtrack for this game is so beautiful that I really don't know how the hell to explain it. Really the only problem I have with this game are the bosses. They're way too easy.
If you don't mind playing a game in which every single character is a furry, you're in for a real damn good time... In other words, you'd better buy this. If you hate/have a lot of things against furries, on the other hand, you might not want to buy this game.
Like I said - the game's pretty short, but it's worth EVERY SINGLE EFFIN' PENNY. I recommend this game like a madman.

OK, let's make something perfectly clear. I've spent at least 17 hours in Witcher and although I've recommended it in my Steam review, I don't think too fondly of that game. Although a friend of mine (Witcher fanatic and a gaming journalist), a guy that says Skyrim can suck his balls, recommended Witcher 2 to me on more than a few occasions and although he pointed out the game is different than the first one, somehow I've managed not to get it until this last summer sale. And I didn't buy it this summer, either - this friend bought it for me as an act of protest because I've neglected an awesome game.
Did I say awesome? Yes, I DID. Witcher 2 is AWESOME. It goes straight into a Chamber of greatness which includes titles such as Doom II, Duke Nukem 3D, Quake II and Morrowind.
Witcher 2 brings an awesome and oh-so-needed upgrade to every single system of Witcher universe. The story gets really suspenful and interesting now, so great it leaves the first one in the dust. It makes it funny. Combat? ♥♥♥♥ing finally. No more mini-games click-on-time attacking that made me so nervous. This is a proper sword-wielding and cast-spelling game. Fighting numerous opponents is a joy now. You can dash and stab almost in perfect harmony; fights in Witcher 2 are soul-soothing experiences. Quest finding and resolving is easier and more logical, menus are no longer a cluttered mess, girls are more naked and dwarves curse and drink like late GG Allin.
Witcher 2 is a great, great game that shall be rewarded with a CLASSIC title as the time goes bye. Its living and breathing world will suck you in and you will choose a side. And you'll ENJOY IT.
Once again, DO NOT SPEND YOUR MONEY AND TIME ON WITCHER. Get Witcher 2 and don't let the first game keep you away from this masterpiece.

Finicky abilities, lazy cover mechanic, bizarre AI, and a nonsensical point system. I'm only on Chapter 3 and I've already fallen through the map three times. But, hey, the game does look really cool.
Let me start off by saying: Anyone who approached this game after being told something along the lines of "It's the spiritual successor to Tenchu." – DO NOT BELIEVE THEM. This game is nowhere near as solid as Tenchu. It's barely even a shell of what it does set out to be. So, to try and place Aragami in same league as Tenchu is just setting it up to be an bigger disappointment than it already is.
Finicky Abilities
Using Shadow Step has often been a chore. Most of the time, it works well. But, at moments when I need to be very precise in my timing and location, I find that I have to wrestle with my positioning before the game will give me a solid indicator on the teleport. It's the same with Aerial Kills. If I'm standing above the enemy, I've often had to step away from the ledge and come back to it repeatedly before the Aerial Kill would prompt.
I'd like to talk more about Shadow Step. It's the game's main mechanic and the main means of mobility. With that being taken into consideration, I will never understand why using it would ever cause me to teleport underneath the map where I'd fall to my death. This feature should have the most solid functionality in the game, yet it's only about as functional as North Korea's missile program. You have generally tell it where to go, but the odds of blowing yourself up are much higher than anyone would want to admit out loud.
Lazy Cover Mechanics
Call me crazy, but there were times when I've approach the corner of cover and Aragami actually pressed himself against it in a fairly seamless fashion. My research makes it appear as though this is a real feature in the game, yet I cannot seem to ever get the character to do this on queue. There are plenty of squared and flat objects within the game which I would expect this feature to apply itself, yet there does not seem to be any consistency to how or where it takes effect.
Likewise, with shadows likely being the main cover element, There doesn't seem to be any difference in enemy detection rate/distance whether you're crouching in shadow directly in front of them or whether you're crouching in shadow off a bit to their sides. In a stealth game of this era, I'd really expect the enemy's peripheral vision to be weaker than at the direct center of their vision cones.
Bizarre AI
That said, perhaps it's more to do with the enemy's ability to just walk like a normal human. It seems to be very difficult for the NPCs to round a basic corner without having to adjust their direction left & right several times as though they were drunk. Maybe they are. Maybe it's a part of the lore that all the guards are drunk and I just haven't discovered it yet. I'd probably be guzzling down rice wine too if my commander tasked 60 of us to stand around in a cemetery for no apparent reason.
But that still doesn't quite explain why in the name of Merlin's saggy left♥♥♥♥♥would distracting an enemy with a sound at the bottom of a set a stairs send them detouring around the entire map and using an altogether different set of stairs before finally finding their way to the sound? This pathfinding is something I'd expect from a – Well, actually, there are plenty of recent triple-A games out there with even worse AI so nevermind. I would still think the developers of this game wouldn't want to lumped into the same category as Ubisoft when it comes to time spent polishing a game.
Nonsensical Point System
Which brings me to the point system. Does it even need to exist? How much time was spent determining how point distribution should work? Why is there a category for "Enemies undisturbed" and a category for "Enemies distracted" when the points awarded for both is a solid 100? Surely leaving enemies undisturbed should yield more points than distracting them? Logically, why should distracting them yield any points at all?
Even more strangely, you're deducted points for being "spotted." However in this game, being spotted only means the enemy *thinks* they saw you. It's different from instigated their combative/alert stage. In being "spotted," the AI's behavior is exactly the same as being distracted. They'll investigate, and if they find nothing, they'll return to their normal patrols immediately. It seems to me that allowing the enemy to "spot" you should be a valid tactic to lure a single enemy over to your position. Yet, even if you stealth kill them during their investigation, you're still deducted 50 points at the end of the chapter for every enemy you made curious in this way.
There's also a category which awards points for playing through the mission without ever restart from a checkpoint. This would be fine if using Shadow Step wasn't akin to playing Russian roulette with 2 bullets in the chamber.
The One Good Thing
As for what I've enjoyed about the game... It's aesthetically pleasing. Oddly, I can't always tell the difference between shadow and average light, but I do still appreciate the use of shadows in this game. The way Aragami's character skins interact with the shadows is easily this game's best-executed idea. I just wish the rest of the ideas executed could have been improved through updates before I started playing this wretched excuse for a stealth game.

To my personal taste, I do prefer ARENA type shooters but decided to try this one out. Whether it is 5 years after the release, the gameplay doesn't appeal much to me but might be something you would enjoy.
Natural Selection is not a brainless shooter. It requires strategy and heavy teamwork. That's how it is based upon and you are required to play that way.
Alas for NS2, there seems to be some requirement to play on specific servers... the ones who's got the most players online. So there you go, jump hopping server to server trying to find one that won't kick you out.
The visuals are still decent now in 2017. There is a good tutorial that explains the basics of the game and that is very welcomed to newcomers.
Conclusion: I'd say for newcomers, this game is really unfriendly right now. We are late to the party and most servers just kick you straight out OR you are the primary prey for the opposing team (if you can join that server that is!). Again, this is not my main kind of competitive FPS so that affect my recommendation against it but if you are willing and VERY patient... and maybe find tons of friends, you may get some good fun out of this!

I have over 500 hours in SpinTires and over 300 hours in the SpinTires editor creating custom maps for the game. After reading a lot of the negative reviews I realize why some people think this game is not worth the money. It is true the developers have been very slow on releasing any updates but the modders have taken this game and turned it into the best offroading game out there.
Custom Vehicles: Currently the game now has workshop support for all modded vehicles. All you have to do now is subscribe and at map selection you can pick whatever vehicle you want to drive. Modders like Sid, Brute, Vengeful Maniac and many others have created highly detailed and realistic offroading rigs to drive.
Custom Maps:  There are tons of free maps made by modders on spintires.nl. The maps are usually around a 50mb to 100mb download. They come in a zip file. You open up the zip and there are two level folders inside. All you do is drop those in your Spintires/Levels folder and start the game up. You will have to disable achievements to play with custom maps and trucks.
The other mod that makes this game amazing is Spintiresplus. Its a simple download and install from Spintires.nl.  You simply drop the files into your main Spintires folder and its done. It has a config file that you can edit with notepad to change little things in the  game like a battery winch so you can flip your vehicle back over if you get stuck without any friends around.
If you can handle that little bit of mod installation then this is hands down the best offroading game out there with new maps and vehicles being released on almost a daily basis.

Ten Million is a nice little match 3 puzzlegame in which the end goal is to score ten million points.
Your run ends when you run out of time, with your character slowly moving towards the left of the screen as time goes on with the left edge being the end of you. Taking damage through enemies pushes you even further quickly, getting kills among other things pushes you to the right again.
You play by dragging a line or column around and then having at least 3 of the same tile in a line. There is only a few tiles that dont change either and each has its own use, swords and staffs do physical and magical attacks, keys unlock doors and chests etc. Above the field you can see what you are currently faced with and therefor know if you for example need to match key tiles.
During each run you gain ressources that all serve the purpose to make you stronger and go further, be it by having your attack tiles do more damage or by increasing your defense or increasing critical hit chance etc. While this means you grind for ressources run for run it doesnt really feel like a grind upgrading is more like something on the side to do next to playing the game.
Another distraction is the little side quests that you get, many are luck based or happen sooner or later anyway, like matching 5 of the same tile in a single strike multiple times in one run, others require you to use specific items (that you randomly acquire during runs and since you can only carry 3/4  use quickly again anyway)
While you will gain ressources no matter how you play the game does reward you for playing well, for example if you manage to be so far ahead of time that you end up on the right edge of the screen and can keep that up for a bit it gives you a nice amount of bonus experience or gold and big chain reactions or 5 tiles in a row etc also benefit you.
In the end getting to the 10000000 scorepoint isnt that complicated, especially if you have every single upgrade and think carefully what potions to use, however the steam achievements crank it up a notch requiring you to achieve that same score with a much lower point multiplier, setting an endgoal even people who are good at these games will have to work for to reach.
You can probably beat the game in less than 4 hours though i would say it isnt really made to rush through in one sitting, rather to unwind with a little puzzlegame for a bit every evening, or something like that. And while the pricepoint is higher than many similar games I would say it is almost worth it and totally worth it when on sale for even less.

Mafia III is a beautiful game with plenty of action. It does have it's flaws though. I liked it more than most others, and I'm glad I bought it. At the moment I haven't played the other games in the Mafia series, so I can't compare it to anything.
If there's something there's plenty of, then it's action. Mafia III just is a very exciting game most of the time, mainly because of the two following pros:
Name says it. The word 'Mafia' reeks of great story and exciting gameplay. Very in-depth story, makes you want to keep playing.
The characters of this game are just amazingly deep. All of them have a unique story behind them. Mafia 'veterans' might notice the main protagonist from Mafia II, Vito Scarletta, along with other characters.
Without spoiling too much, I can say that you'll have to choose which mob boss get's control of the various disctrics you conquor. That is quite important, seeing how you don't exactly want a mad mob leader after you, right?
Noticed how multiple pros have started with 'Great'? That's just 'cause the game is great. Especially the graphics. I were impressed when I saw Fallout 4 and GTA 5 on Ultra quality, but this beats it. Especially the cinematic trailers and cutscenes.
The main protagonist is a young male called Lincoln Clay. His dark skin gives him some problems, seeing we're in 1968. Lincoln's just come home from the war in Vietnam, and that sure does help him in his 'endeavors'.
While the Open-World feature doesn't improve Mafia III that much, it's still a good and favorable feature. And I also just generally like Open-World (I can barely even
of playing a non-Open-World game for more than 50 hours).
While the character customization isn't very impressive, the custom cars sure are a sight to behold. As you play the Racing minigame you'll unlock more awesome decals, engines and tires.
I always think "Oh, this is great, that's going in the review" whenever I'm playing a game, but when it comes to writing the review, I always forget most of it, which is a shame. But there are many more pros, I guarantee you that!
I've sadly experienced some very annoying sight blocking texture glitches, but luckily they were easy to fix (I still haven't discovered a way to completely remove them yet, though). Links to screenshots will be featured here soon.
While I like the way the missions are structured, it does get a bit tedious in the long run. But as a huge fan of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (basically just a fetch-and-return game), I can cope with it. And trying out all the different ways to play makes it easier.
You've surely heard this before. In the beginning the game ran perfectly with 58-60 Frames Per Second. But as I played the game for more hours (about 7-9) I began to experience some quite serious FPS drops. I thought that the 40-45 FPS drops were annoying, but now I'm lucky to have more than 35 FPS. I've had to learn how to live with the lag that occurs even with a good rig like mine.
Hopefully I won't have to encounter any more cons, and hopefully the FPS drops won't get worse.
Mafia III is an overall amazing game that I would definitely recommend. But if you can get it on sale it would be nice, 50€ is a big number. I got it on sale for ~16€, and I'm at times glad I didn't pay the full price. But 50€ is a pretty reasonable price for a next-gen game like Mafia III. Get it if you like great stories and multiple choices. The great graphics don't make it any worse.

BIOS offers an interesting and addicting concept for a game that suffers from poor optimization which single-handedly ruins the gaming experience. Unfortunately, as noted in many other reviews, this game cannot hold a stable framerate, even on high-end hardware on the lowest graphical settings. For a "racing" FPS, this is unacceptable, as dipping framerates and inconsistent frame-times can lead to botched runs and impossible maps. As expected, there are going to be many obstacles to overcome throughout BIOS. Unfortunately, these obstacles are the very cause of the game's issues, as the (highly) destructible environments and constant explosions kill the framerate.
Were the developers to fix these issues, BIOS would be worthy of its $14.99 asking price. Until then, I do not reccomend purchasing this game.
Just below the game's technical issues lies a great and unique experience. Movement and combat feel quite nice, although the weapons you are afforded in the game all handle the same. The game's pace, as one would expect from a game of this concept, is fast. Your input must be calculated and practiced if you want to get anywhere on the leaderboards. The game's visuals are polished and consistent - it looks nice while not being the most technically inclined game on the market. The audio is average, meaning that it is nothing more and nothing less than what one would expect from a modern game. The soundtrack is low-key when contrasted with the rest of the game -- probably a good thing for this kind of gaming experience.

16GB 1600MHz DDR3 RAM
WD Blue 7200RPM HDD - WD10EZEX
ASUS Xonar U7 (External)

There's no doubt that this game is a classic, whether you like or not. But if it's actually held up all these years, that's a little more subjective.
Expect blocky character models and low resolution (but still quite good looking, IMO) static backgrounds, and all the spelling and grammar errors from the original PC release are still here. However, the music has been replaced, the original MIDI soundtrack is now the same music used in the Playstation release, and the game overall has been optimized to run on new systems. The actual game mechanics and combat system are solid, and the story is also still good.
If you've never played the game, don't come in expecting something that can stack up to a game released today in terms of graphical quality. If you can look past its age there's still a great game and plenty of time to be wasted in it, though. If you're looking for a nostalgia kick then it's definitely worth the price as well.
The only detractor from what's overall a good game is the extra layer of DRM, requiring a Square Enix account, but considering it can be activated with your Steam account and ignored once you set it up the first time, it's hardly a hassle.

This game has something for everyone:
Looking for a good RTS? Play as the commander, giving orders to everyone on your team, making a base, expanding to new locations on the map to launch attacks and gather resources, and researching new weapons or abilities to give your players an edge over the competition.
Looking for a good shooter? Be a Marine.
Looking to help your teammates or be a siege player for attacking hives wih a grenade launcher? Maybe you want to grab a flamethrower and open a hole through the aliens defences. Or maybe you want to grab an LMG and provide covering fire for a group of allies? As a Marine you can customize your loadout to do any of these things and more!
Or maybe you want to be center of attention all the time. Hop into an exosuit and destroy the enemy!
Looking to be crafty and have to outflank and outplay the competition? Aliens for you.
Looking to destroy the enemy expansions, and escape from the area before reinforcements arrive, or harass single enemies? Play as the crafty Skulk.
Looking to wreak havoc with strong melee attacks? Play as a heavy Onos.
Looking to be a supportive player that hangs back and defends? Hop on in as a supporting, building Gorge.
Want to be an assassin, killing any small groups of Marines? Play as a ninja fast Fade.
Want to fly around, doing recon and attacking from afar, and harassing enemies at high speed? Soar into action as a Lerk.
Looking for a good tactical game that gives you many options to follow? Play Natural Selection 2!

Natural Selection may be one of the grandparents of Asymmetrical gameplay, but the fidelity of these maps holds up to many games being released today.However, the depth of the game play may be offputting to some people and enticing to others.
People good at FPS will be successful on the side of the Space Marines, people with squad oriented friends will be even more successful. Safety in numbers.
The aliens are bit more complex in that the base alien is melee oriented, with several evolutions to branch into, ranging from bat like creatures that shoot at people, to giant rhino like beasts that trash everything.
What I haven't mentioned yet is the RTS style gameplay of the commander role. The commander issues orders to the real people of the marines and the aliens to take and protect resources in order to buy upgrades and build fortifications. A half decent commander is hard to find, but its worth noting that a bot commander gives you HP or ammo immediately no questions asked, so there's almost room for every player to just know enough to push the supply lines along by building stuff, and then getting out so the AI can give field aid faster than a human. A high quality human command will probably always be best though, so if you find a cool commander, consider befriending them, because they would probably appreciate a coopartive foot soldier.
No matter what roll you choose, there is quite a lot to know and understand about the mechanics of the game, so if the playable tutorial provided aren't your thing, I'll bet there's some "What you should know before starting Nat S 2" videos on YT.
I'll admit I played this more on my friends acct/rig because the graphics were better, but the servers are still impressively active considering how long this game has been out, and I think that attests the most to how fun Natural Selection 2 is, wish I had more homies who played it.

TL;DR - Fallout Shelter is fun for what it is - a quick diversion while you drop the kids off at the pool, or when things are slow at work, etc.
I played the game on my phone for a couple weeks and maxed out my dwellers and rooms, and so forth.
Opinions and things of note from my playthrough:
It's a pseudo-strategy upgrade'em up, vault-building farmville-like game that is also reminiscent of Sim Tower.
The comic art-style is well executed with cutesy and fun animations and effects which the dwellers exhibit while carrying out their lives.
Bonerkill Alert: Grabbing and dragging dwellers is awkward and inaccurate, even on PC, especially when zoomed out -> grabbing them accurately requires zooming in, but moving them to where they need to go often requires zooming out again.
DOUBLE BONERKILL ALERT: The emphasis on microtransactions in Fallout Shelter are disappointing, although not unexpected considering the original platform and target audience.
Entitled gamer conclusion: It's unfortunate that Bethesda used their time and effort, and this great IP to make a weak mark on it's legacy. I think I speak for many fans when I say we would have been happier to pay outright for a more serious entry for mobile platforms, perhaps something along the lines of Fallout/II/Tactics.

As far as I know, there's only one word that can aptly sum up Dust: An Enlysian Tail - and that's "phenomenal". There's a reason that a small, somewhat niche game can sell over a million copies and it's simply because it's that good.
Let's start at the beginning, and that means story. If a little convoluted at times - which can to an extent serve as a point in the writer's favour - the story is mostly simple, without being patronizing or slow. Players are given tiem to go at their own pace, but always met with a warm welcome when they do decide to push ever onward. Obviously avoiding spoilers, I'll tell anyone that this game has a story to rival almost any AAA game out there.
The next point I want to make is the combat, because I can't go very long without talking about Dust's combat, because it's better than any other scroller/fighter I've ever played, and that's quite a few. The problem with fighters like this is often response times or getting locked into an animation, making for slow or frustrating combat when you can't react to things as they happen. Dust eliminates that, as the combat is smoothe and I can personally say I never felt like my reactions were being hindered. Another good point is the simplicity (yet again, far from patronizing) of the combat. Again I'll say that personally I've never seen combat done quite as well as Dust, so I'll give you the best example. In most fighting games, I'm reduced to button-mashing. Boo me all you want, it gets results. In Dust however, I knew my combos and I knew the 4-5 buttons I needed to pull off the exact string of moves I would need in whatever situation I was handed. This stems from simplistic controls and memorable keybindings.
One point I don't particularly enjoy talking about is graphics, since I tend to see a reliance on graphics as superficial, but I'll talk about them here. Of course, it's more art than graphics; all hand-drawn by a single animator, Dust is stunningly beautiful. Not only is it brilliantly drawn, the art matches the tone of the game perfectly; light, bouncy and adventurous. There were times I just had to stop and admire it, and very few games will do that to me. Literally stunning.
I think that's all I had to say about Dust so tl;dr, Dust is amazing and I highly recommend you find yourself a copy.
